units.la: SI unquam, certe, hoc, non minus erudito, quam summorum ingeniorum feracissimo seculo, non ab uno, sed quam pluribus, laboratum fuit de perficiendis disciplinis, hisque non paucis, sed omnibus; viris egregijs de compacto quasi agentibus, & quibusdam circa has, aliis circa alias utiliffimam operam navantibus, quæ tamen opera longe felicius procederet, fi iis, qui ex professo hoc agunt, luberet agnoscere, quousque illi, qui nos præcesserunt, pervenerint, atque quid ab iisdem, ut perficiatur, fit derelictum. Sed, dum quisque fere sibi nimium quam plaudit, & palmam, in medio pofi tam solus vult obtinere; non solum antiqui sapientiæ autiftites, quibus, tanquam merito maximo coronatis, tot per secula omnes eruditionis fapientiæque candidati aflurrexerunt, velut infidi duƈtores spernuntur, verum etiam nemo vel parem, vel æmulum pati potest, atque ante omnia solicitus est, qua ratione submovere queat eos, qui idem egerunt, nec non opprimere viros, qui cum laude videbantur hoc ipsum volvisse saxum. Ob hanc causam, librariorum officinæ, non solum libellis eristicis, à sola ambitione dictatis, sunt instructissimæ; verum etiam Academiæ disputationibus inutilibus & Christianæ religionis professoribus indignissimis inquietantur, dum quisque lingua & stylo non solum pro novis suis placitis digladiatur, verum etiam eos, qui præcesserunt, de gradu præcipitare omni conatu molitur. accedit, quod quisque (quasi sub antiquorum Sophistarum sidere natus esset) quam longum sectatorum discipulorumque agmen ducere conetur, atque æstimari ab improvida juventute, quæ haut aliter atque pisciculi, quos fallaci hamo imposita esca perdit, capiuntur ab iis, qui institores sunt novorum dogmatum
units.tr: If ever this has been true, certainly it is true of this age, no less learned than it is fertile in the greatest minds: the work of perfecting the disciplines has been undertaken not by one man but by many, and not by a few disciplines but by all of them. Distinguished men have acted as if by agreement, and some have devoted their most useful labour to these subjects, others to those. Yet this work would proceed far more happily if those who make it their profession were willing to acknowledge how far those who went before us have got, and what has been left for them to finish. But while nearly everyone applauds himself too much and wants to win the palm alone, placed in the middle, not only are the ancient leaders of wisdom, to whom all candidates for learning and wisdom have risen for so many ages as to men crowned with the greatest merit, scorned as unfaithful guides, but no one can bear an equal or a rival. Above all, each is anxious to find a way to remove those who have done the same work, and to crush men who seemed to have rolled this very stone with credit. For this reason the booksellers' workshops are stocked not only with contentious pamphlets dictated by ambition alone, but academies are troubled by useless disputations and by professors of the Christian religion who are most unworthy. Each man fights with tongue and pen not only for his own new opinions, but by every effort strives to hurl from their rank those who went before him. Add to this that each man, as if born under the star of the ancient Sophists, tries to lead as long a train of followers and disciples as he can, and to be esteemed by heedless youth. Such youth are caught no differently than little fish that a bait placed on a deceptive hook destroys, by those who are the hawkers of new dogmas.

units.la: cum, quæ non possunt non palato juniorum summopere allubescere, quod omnes homines rerum novarum quam avidissimi sint. Ne vero citra judicium videatur inventus ad hos illosve doctores divertisse, illi, quos non tam eruditior quam major chorus delectat, sollicite dant operam, ut videantur instructi esse tali Methodo, ex cujus præscripto non solum feliciter compendioseque studia queant institui, verum ipsæ quoque disciplinæ reddi perfectiores. Non inficias eundum, inter hos, multos occurrere viros egregios, quos fatendum est, in ordinanda, sive universali, sive particulari Methodo, plurima cum ratione monuisse, quæ si observarentur, & labor compendiosior redderetur, nec periculum foret à variis erroribus, quos veritatis insignibus velatos, vix ipsi scenes exuere possunt, quod à teneris eos imbiberint, diuque in sinu suo quam arctissi
units.tr: ...with things that cannot fail to be most pleasing to the palates of the young, since all men are eager for novelties. Lest it be thought that the author has turned to these or those teachers without judgment, let me say that those whom a larger crowd delights, rather than a more learned one, take great pains to appear equipped with such a Method. Its rules, they claim, allow studies to be pursued not only happily and more briefly, but also allow the disciplines themselves to be made more perfect. I do not deny that among these there are many outstanding men, who, it must be admitted, have offered much sound advice on arranging a method, whether universal or particular. If this advice were observed, labour would be lighter and there would be no danger from the various errors which, veiled in the marks of truth, they can hardly strip off, because they drank them in from their tender years and have long held them in their bosom as closely as...

units.la: arctissime foverint: sed, dum adversa fronte inter se concurrunt, & unusquisque ex asse suæ Methodo, licet aliorum quoque observationibus substructæ, omnem laudem & gloriam vindicare contendit, ultra Methodum vix proceditur, disciplinæque non solum sperato destituuntur ornamento, sed ipsi quoque discipuli in vestibulo solo detinentur. Laudare possem ultra viginti viros celeberrimos, qui intra seculum varia evulgarunt scripta aut de Methodo, aut de perficiendis disciplinis, aut de augmento earundem, qui tamen parum aut nihil in una quoque disciplina, pro illius perfectione, præstiterunt. At, quid juvat perpetuo de via quærere, eamque nunquam ingredi? Medicina, Astronomia, & Geographia, multo hac ætate, quam olim sunt perfectiores, non quod alia tradantur Methodo, sed quod locupletatæ sint observatione plurimarum rerum, quas
units.tr: They have cherished them most closely in their bosom for a long time: but, as they clash with their faces set against one another, and each one strives to claim all praise and glory for his own method, though it is built upon the observations of others too, scarcely any progress is made beyond method, and the disciplines are not only deprived of the hoped-for adornment, but the students themselves are kept standing in the vestibule alone. I could praise more than twenty very famous men who, within the last century, have published various writings either on method, or on perfecting the disciplines, or on their enlargement, and yet who have contributed little or nothing to the perfection of any single discipline. But what good does it do to keep seeking the way and never to enter it? Medicine, astronomy and geography, in this age, are far more perfect than they once were, not because they are taught by a different method, but because they have been enriched by the observation of very many things, which

units.tr: TO THE READER

units.la: quas antiqui aut ignorarunt, aut minus prob e exploratas habuerunt. Si cogitaremus, quid in quaque disciplina adhuc cognoscendum restet, &c, ad illud explicandum omnes ingenii nostri nervos intenderemus, brevi aliam faciem multæ disciplinæ præ se ferrent, exactæ licet ad lineas Methodi vulgaris. Quum vero mihi sæpe incidisset hæc cogitatio, conandum aliquid esse pro perficienda Philosophia potissimum, quam per plures annos doceo; visum fuit initium facere à generalissimis, atque antea astruere certitudinem scientiæ, eorumque præsidiorum per quæ comparatur, quam certæ alicui disciplinæ manum admovere. Eoque, congressus sum cum Scepticis, & quam fieri potuit accuratissime eorum ineptias non minus excutere institui, quam disciplinarum singularum existimationem asserere. Quo cum successu, rogo, citra amorem & odium, expendere digneris ris, quisquis in hoc opusculum incideris. Ob chartæ difficultatem, per quam prœla multa quiescunt, coactus sum in duas partes id distribuere, utque priorem solum hoc tempore exhibeo, ita posterior Theologiæ non minus, quam Jurisprudentiæ, & Medicinæ, nec non Practicæ Philosophiæ, comparandæ cum Theologia & Jurisprudentia, certitudinem contra quoscunque astruet: &, quoniam hoc seculo longe maxima seges est Semi-Scepticorum, [licet haut difficitendum sit, quosdam per calumniam iisdem accenseri] in eorum qua molimina, qua axiomata libro sexto ubertim inquiram. Accipies vero, Lector, hanc posteriorem partem propediem, modo typographi diligentia non hebescat, circa ea, quæ paucarum solûm hebdomadarum impendium efflagitant. Interea vale, atque conatibus meis fave. Groningæ Non. Septemb.
units.tr: Which the ancients either did not know, or held to be less thoroughly tested. If we were to consider what remains to be known in each discipline, and devoted all the strength of our minds to working it out, many disciplines would soon present a different face, even though they are still shaped by the lines of the common method. Since this thought had often occurred to me, I resolved that something should be attempted for the advancement of philosophy above all, which I have taught for many years. It seemed best to begin with the most general matters and first to establish the certainty of knowledge and the safeguards by which it is acquired, rather than to apply my hand to some particular discipline. For this reason I have engaged the Sceptics, and I have resolved to examine their absurdities as carefully as possible, no less than to vindicate the standing of the individual disciplines. With what success, I ask, please weigh it without love or hatred, whoever you are that come upon this little work. Because of the difficulty of paper, by which many presses lie idle, I was compelled to divide the work into two parts. I am presenting only the first at this time. The second will establish, against all comers, the certainty of Theology no less than of Jurisprudence, Medicine and Practical Philosophy, and their comparison with Theology and Jurisprudence. And since in this age the largest crop by far is that of the Semi-Sceptics, [although it must be admitted that some are counted among them through slander], I shall examine at length, in the sixth book, their devices and axioms. Reader, you will receive this second part shortly, provided the printer's diligence does not flag, since it requires only a few weeks' expense. In the meantime, farewell, and favour my efforts. Groningen, Nones of September.

units.la: ESt Deus in medio librati pondere cœli, Solis & annorum dirigit inde vias.
units.tr: There is God in the middle of the poised weight of heaven; from there he directs the courses of the sun and the years.

units.la: Est Deus in pelago, fluviisque tumentibus, hincqj Qualibet immensum personat unda Deum.
units.tr: There is God in the sea and the swelling rivers; hence every wave resounds with the boundless God.

units.la: Est Deus in terra, campisque virentibus, inde Auctorem celebrat qualibet herba Deum.
units.tr: There is God in the earth and the green fields; hence every herb proclaims God its Author.

units.la: Est Deus in nobis, quicquid mens alta revolvit, Vnius arbitrio statque caditque Dei.
units.tr: There is God in us: whatever the lofty mind turns over, it stands or falls by the will of the one God.

units.la: Numen adest, ubicunque latet, quocunq; moveris, Omnia (ne dubites) omnia plena Deo.
units.tr: The divinity is present wherever it lies hidden, whichever way you turn: all things (do not doubt it) are full of God.

units.la: Quod genus ergo hominum, quæve hanc tam barbara pestem

units.la: Ora tulit, summum quæ negat esse Deum?

units.tr: And in denying it, he says he does not hear, he denies and does not see; he thinks there is neither sea nor ground.

units.tr: And he cries that the swift fires of the stars are mere dreams, the dreams that the deceitful gate of ivory sends forth in vain.

units.la: PAg. 11. l. 9. post verba, quod nesciret: adde subsequentia: Hoc in Socrate agnovisse videtur ipse Aristoteles, quando apud Eusebium lib. 11. de Prep. Evang. perhi-bet eum natura factum fuisse non solum ad cavillandum, sed omnia in dubium vocanda. Ut non mirum sit, teste Platone in Gorgia, inter accusationis illius capita, hoc quoque occurrisse, quod juventutem corrumperet, docendo eam dubitare de omnibus. quid quod in Symposio Platotonis, Philosophiam suam vocat difceptationem somnio non absimilem.
units.tr: Page 11, line 9: after the words quod nesciret, add the following: Aristotle himself seems to have recognised this in Socrates, when he reports in Eusebius, book 11 of the Preparation for the Gospel, that Socrates was made by nature not only for mockery but for calling everything into doubt. So it is no wonder that, according to Plato in the Gorgias, among the heads of that accusation there also occurred this charge, that he corrupted the young by teaching them to doubt everything. Indeed, in Plato's Symposium he calls his own philosophy a discussion not unlike a dream.

units.la: Pag. 15. l. 9. post termini, addantur ea, quæ sequuntur: Notandum siquidem, Socratis ævo, Sophistas regnasse, atque circa res naturales quam plurimum suam venditasse scientiam, somniantes se jam pervenisse ad interiora earum penetralia, cum circa umbras & cortices solum occuparentur: quos, ut Socrates & Plato contunderent, ea, quæ notata jam est, ratione illos aggredi instituerunt. Patet potissimum ex Hippia Majore, qui non nisi lusus esse videtur in Sophistas, ad eorum fastum retundendum institutus. Quod & innuit ipse Plato in Charmide sic loquens: Quæ nullo modo quis nescit, non potest cognoscere se ignorare, quæ insciitia supra fatuam Sophistarum ostentationem, quæ arguebatur a Socrate, posita est.
units.tr: Page 15, line 9: after termini, add what follows: It must be noted that in the age of Socrates the Sophists held sway, and boasted greatly of their knowledge of natural things, dreaming that they had already reached the innermost sanctuaries of those things, when in fact they were occupied only with shadows and bark. Socrates and Plato set out to crush them, and they undertook to attack them in the manner just noted. This is evident chiefly from the Greater Hippias, which seems to be nothing but a jest against the Sophists, designed to humble their arrogance. Plato himself hints at this in the Charmides*, speaking thus: "One who does not know a thing in any way cannot know that he does not know it," and this ignorance is set against the empty show of the Sophists, which Socrates refuted.

units.la: quentia subnestantur: Interim Ciceronem, tanquam sibi in Academicis speculationibus non constantem, misere Lactantius exagitavit, lib. 3. Divin. Instit. cap. 14. sic in eundem insurgendo: Studuisti nempe Philosophiæ, & quidem sic, ut nullus unquam diligentius: quippe qui omnes cognoveris disciplinas, sicut ipse gloriari soles, eamque ipsam Latinis literis illustraveris, imitatoremque te Platonis ostenderis. Cedo igitur quid didiceris, aut in qua secta veritatem deprehenderis? In Academia scil. quam sequutus es? quam probasti? At hæc nihil docet, nisi ut scias te nihil scire. Tui ergo te libri arguunt, quam nihil à Philosophia disci possit ad vitam. Hæc tua verba sunt: ( liber, in quo fuerunt hæc scripta, nunc intercidit. ) Mihi autem non modo ad sapientiam cæci videmur, sed ad ea ipsa, quæ aliqua ex parte cerni videantur, hebetes
units.tr: ...are underpinned. Meanwhile Lactantius mercilessly attacked Cicero, as one who was inconsistent with himself in his Academic speculations, in book 3, chapter 14 of the Divine Institutes, rising up against him thus: "You studied philosophy, and indeed so thoroughly that no one ever did so more diligently. For you have, as you yourself like to boast, come to know all the disciplines, and you have illuminated that very philosophy with Latin writings, and you have shown yourself an imitator of Plato. Tell me then what you have learned, or in which sect you have grasped the truth? In the Academy, I suppose, which you followed? Which you approved? But this teaches nothing except that you know that you know nothing. Your own books therefore prove how nothing can be learned from philosophy for life. These are your words: (the book in which these were written has now perished.) But to me we seem not only blind to wisdom, but dull even regarding those things which seem to be seen to some extent."

units.la: ADDENDA.
units.tr: ADDENDA.

units.la: betes & obtusi. Si ergo Philofophia est magistra vitę, cur tibi ipse cæcus ꝰ hebes & obtusus videbare, quem oportuit illa docentem & sentire & sapere, & in clarissima luce versari? At quam confessus fueris Philosophiæ veritatem, docent ad filium [respicit libros de Officiis] composita præcepta: quibus monec, Philosophiæ quidem præcepta noscenda, vivendum autem esse civiliter. Quid tam repugnans dici potest; si noscenda sunt præcepta Philosophię, ideo utique noscenda sunt, ut recte sapienterque vivamus. Vel, si civiliter vivendum est, non est igitur Philosophia sapientia: siquidem melius est civiliter quam philosophice vivere. Nam si sapientia est, quæ dicitur Philosophia: stulte prosecto vivit, qui non secundum Philosophiam vivit. Tuo itaque judicio Philosophia stultitiæ inanitatisq; damnata est. Idem in Consolatio-ne
units.tr: betes and obtuse. If therefore Philosophy is the teacher of life, why did you yourself seem to be blind, dull and obtuse, when you ought, by her teaching, to have been perceiving and wise, and living in the clearest light? But how far you have confessed the truth of Philosophy, the precepts composed for your son [he refers to the books On Duties] teach: in which you advise that the precepts of Philosophy indeed are to be known, but that one must live civilly. What can be said that is more contradictory? If the precepts of Philosophy are to be known, they are surely to be known so that we may live rightly and wisely. Or, if one must live civilly, then Philosophy is not wisdom, since it is better to live civilly than philosophically. For if that is wisdom which is called Philosophy, then surely he lives foolishly who does not live according to Philosophy. By your own judgment, therefore, Philosophy stands condemned as folly and emptiness. The same in the Consolation...

units.la: ADDENDA.
units.tr: ADDENDA.

units.la: ne, id est in opere non ioculari, hanc de Philosophia sententiam tulisti: Sed nescio quis nos tenet error ac miserabilis veri ignoratio. Ubi est ergo Philosophiae magisterium? aut quid te docuit illa vitae parens, sic verum miserabiliter ignoras? Hactenus Lactantius.
units.tr: ...in a work not meant as a joke, you have delivered this opinion about philosophy. But I know not what error holds us, and what wretched ignorance of the truth. Where then is the teaching of philosophy? Or what has that mother of life taught you, that you so wretchedly ignore the truth? Thus far Lactantius.

units.la: Pag. 71. lin. ult. post definire, sequentia suppleantur: Majori forte jure Scepticis accensueris Abrahamum de Balmis, Rabbinum, & Grammaticum non incelebrem, de quo sic Sebastianus Munsterus in Praesatione praefixa Grammaticae Eliae: Abraham de Balmis [scripsit Grammaticam, cui titulus Mikne Abraham, sive peculium Abrahami] nihil aliud agere mihi visus est, quam veterum doctrinam perpetuo convellere atque impugnare, magis in infectando occupatus quam in docendo. At in dubium tantum vocare priscorum praeceptiones, cum interim nihil certi statuas, non docere est, sed ridere.
units.tr: Page 71, last line, after definire, the following should be added: Abraham de Balmis, a rabbi and no undistinguished grammarian, may with rather greater justice be counted among the Sceptics. Sebastian Münster says of him as follows in the preface prefixed to Elias's Grammar: Abraham de Balmis [wrote a grammar entitled Mikne Abraham, or Abraham's Treasure] seemed to me to do nothing else than constantly overthrow and attack the doctrine of the ancients, being more occupied in infecting than in teaching. But to call into doubt the precepts of the ancients, while meanwhile establishing nothing certain, is not teaching but mocking.

units.tr: ADDENDA.

units.la: PAg. 76. l. 14. post instituerunt, hęc addantur : In Scepticos quoque aliquid videtur molitus fuisse Caspar Barlæus, si fidem habemus τῶ πἀνυ Dn. Vossio lib 1. de arte Grammat. cap. 3. sed quod hactenus lucem non aspexit. Exarmare quoque eosdem laboravit Thomas Campanella lib. 1. Metaph. sed, uti omnes censent, nimis generaliter, atque suo more confuse.
units.tr: Page 76, line 14: after instituerunt, these words should be added: Caspar Barlaeus also seems to have attempted something against the Sceptics, if we may trust the most learned Dr. Vossius, book 1 of De arte grammatica, chapter 3; but it has not yet come to light. Thomas Campanella also laboured to disarm the same men, in book 1 of the Metaphysics; but, as all agree, he did so too generally and in his usual confused manner.

units.la: LIBER PRIMUS CONTRA SCEPTICOS. CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: BOOK ONE AGAINST THE SCEPTICS. CHAPTER ONE.

units.la: ANtiquissimi Philosophi (quos Academici & Sceptici pro se laudare solent) dubitarunt, an ulla rerum cognitio daretur. Heraclitus Ephesius, Gorgias Leontinus, Anaxagoras, Democritus, Empedocles, Parmenides, Xenophanes, Protagoras, Zeno Eleates, ac Nausiphanes consortes Scepticismi fuerunt, aut saltem ad eum accedere visi sunt.
units.tr: The most ancient philosophers, whom the Academics and Sceptics are accustomed to claim for their side, doubted whether any knowledge of things was possible. Heraclitus of Ephesus, Gorgias of Leontini, Anaxagoras, Democritus, Empedocles, Parmenides, Xenophanes, Protagoras, Zeno of Elea, and Nausiphanes were companions of Scepticism, or at least seemed to approach it.

units.la: ERRORES, qui absurditatibus proprijs everti creduntur, ut plurimum praesidium in antiquitate inveniunt, quam dum velut scutum aliquod objiciunt, non solum perennant, sed praeter plebejas animas, haut paucos ex ijs quoque, qui supra vulgum sapere videntur, corripiunt ac transversos agunt.
units.tr: Errors which are believed to be overthrown by their own absurdities mostly find their protection in antiquity. While they hold it up like a shield, they not only persist but also seize, and lead astray, not a few of those who seem to be wiser than the common crowd, as well as plebeian minds.

units.la: Quæ vetustas si aut palliando aut excusando errori servire debeat, Scepticismus ejus patrocinio se defendere poterit: non nuper enim aliqui Philosophi dubitare ac disputare cœperunt, an aliqua rerum cognitio detur, sensibusque credendum sit; sed qui inter eos antiquissimi censentur, quam maxime circa hanc rem animo fluctuarunt, quod majus præsidium in authoritate, quam ratione invenire viderentur: Quos non solum, Academiæ novæ conditores velut terribile quod Medusæ caput ostentare solent, sed illi quoque qui post Pyrrhonem Sceptici dicti fuerunt. Ignorare nos non sinit Cicero, cujus hæc in Lucullo verba occurrunt: Primum mihi videmini (novæ scil: Academiæ sectatores) cum veteres Physicos nominatis, facere idem quod seditiosi cives solent, cum aliquos ex antiquis claros viros proferunt, quos dicant fuisse populares, ut eorum ipsi similes esse videantur. Repetunt jam P. Valerium, qui exactis regibus primo anno consul fuit: commemorant reliquos, qui leges populares de provocationibus tulerint, cum consules essent: tum ad hos notiorcs, C. Flaminium, qui legem agrariam aliquot annis ante secundum Punicum bellum trib: pleb: tulerit invito senatu, & postea bis consul factus sit: L. Cassium, Q. Pompejum. Illi quidem etiam P. Africanum referre in eundem numerum solent. Duos sapientissimos & clarissimos fratres P. Crassum & P. Scævolam, ajunt Ti: Graccho authores legum fuisse, alterum quidem, ut videmus demus, palam, alterum ut suspicamur, obscurius. Addunt etiam C. Marium, & de hoc quidem nihil mentiuntur. Horum nominibus tot virorum atque tantorum expositis, eorum institutum sequi dicunt. Similiter vos cum perturbare, ut illi Remp. sic vos Philosophiam bene jam constitutam velitis, Empedoclem, Anaxagoram, Democritum, Parmenidem, Xenophanem, Platonem etiam & Socratem profertis. Idem speciatim de Arcesila testatur Lactantius lib. iii. Divin. Instit. cap. iv. Arcesilas, inquit, Academiae conditor reprehensiones omnium inter se collegit, confessionemque ignorantiae clarorum virorum: armavitque se adversus omnes. Arcesilae similis Pyrrho, [ex Laërtio & Sexto liquet] omnium prope antiquorum Philosophorum, imo poëtarum, authoritatem sollicitabat. Omissis autem poëtis, & inter illos Homero, quem non solum Laërtius lib. 9. in Pyrrhone sed etiam Sextus Empiricus primum Scepseos parentem constituit, itemque septem Graeciae sapientibus, quos in eodem luto haesisse secundum quosdam perhibuit idem Laërtius, accedimus ad illos, qui Philosophia jam aliquo usque provecta, idem sensisse videntur. In antecessum vero observandum, quosdam cum ratione ad Scepticos referri, alios vero quasi per calumniam. Inter illos occurrit primo Heraclitus Ephesius, cui secundum Senecam Epist: xii. cognomen Scotinon fecit rationis obscuritas; is vero non solum de anima sen-
units.tr: If that antiquity ought to serve error either by covering it or by excusing it, Scepticism could defend itself under its patronage. For it is not recent philosophers who have begun to doubt and dispute whether any knowledge of things is given and whether the senses are to be trusted. Rather, those who are counted the most ancient among them wavered most of all on this matter, since they seemed to find a greater defence in authority than in reason. The founders of the New Academy, as well as those who were called Sceptics after Pyrrho, not only display these men, as if they were the head of Medusa, but ... Cicero does not let us be ignorant of this. His words in the Lucullus occur here: "First, it seems to me that you (the followers of the New Academy, I mean), when you name the ancient natural philosophers, do what seditious citizens usually do when they bring forward some famous men of old whom they say were popular leaders, so that they themselves may seem to be like them. They now recall P. Valerius, who was consul in the first year after the kings were expelled. They mention the others who, while consuls, passed popular laws concerning appeals. Then, to the better-known ones, C. Flaminius, who, some years before the Second Punic War, proposed the agrarian law as tribune of the plebs against the will of the senate, and was afterwards made consul twice; L. Cassius; Q. Pompeius. Indeed, they are accustomed to count P. Africanus in the same number. They say that the two very wise and very famous brothers, P. Crassus and P. Scaevola, were the authors of the laws with Tiberius Gracchus, one of them openly, as we see, the other more obscurely, as we suspect. They add also C. Marius, and about him they certainly tell no lies. Having set forth the names of so many and such great men, they say they follow their practice. In the same way, you, who want to disturb philosophy, now well established, as they wanted to disturb the state, bring forward Empedocles, Anaxagoras, Democritus, Parmenides, Xenophanes, and even Plato and Socrates. Lactantius bears witness to the same thing about Arcesilaus in particular, in book 3 of the Divine Institutes, chapter 4: "Arcesilaus, the founder of the Academy, gathered together the objections of all men against one another, and the confession of ignorance of famous men, and armed himself against all." Like Arcesilaus, Pyrrho (as is clear from Laertius and Sextus) assailed the authority of almost all the ancient philosophers, and indeed of the poets. But I set aside the poets, and among them Homer, whom Sextus Empiricus, as well as Laertius in book 9, on Pyrrho, makes the first parent of Scepsis; and likewise the Seven Sages of Greece, who, according to some, as the same Laertius reports, stuck in the same mud. We come instead to those who, when philosophy had already advanced to some degree, seem to have held the same view. It must be observed beforehand that some are rightly referred to the Sceptics, while others are so referred by way of slander. Among the former, first appears Heraclitus of Ephesus, to whom, according to Seneca, Epist. 12, the obscurity of his reasoning gave the surname [σκοτεινόν] "the Obscure"; and he held not only concerning the soul,

units.la: [Note: the scanned line "ratio nis obscuritas" appears as "rationis obscuritas" in the text.] sit, nunquam eam reperiri posse, quantalibet quis via spatia conficiat; verum etiam opinionem sacrum morbum vocavit, & visionem mentiri dixit: ut post Diogenem Laërtium lib. ix. testatur Hesychius libel.de viris illustrib. Hinc apud Sextum Empiricum lib. adverf. Mathemat. exclamat: Mali sunt testes oculi hominibus, & aures barbaras habentium animas. Quod Sextus dein ita explicat: Est barbararum animarum credere sensibus rationis expertibus. Quoniam autem obscurum dicendi genus amabat, [quo respiciens Empiricus l. d. eleganter dicit, quis ex superciliosis grammaticis Heraclitum intelligere potest?] & obscurius ea docere videretur, quæ clare & sine involucris à Pyrrhonis discipulis proponebantur, hinc quidam apud eundem Sextum lib. i. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. xxix. Scepticam Philosophiam, viam esse dicebant ad Heracliti dogmata. Quanquam autem hoc ferio in Onesidemo eo loco Sextus castigat, quod Heraclitus multa dogmatice dixerit: existimo tamen infra censuram esse, quoniam in illis, in quibus dogmaticus fuit, adeo obscurus est, ut difficile sit dicere, dogmatice an Sceptice progrediatur. Nec Sextum juvare potest, quod Heraclitus communem & divinam quam rationem, velut normam omnis scientiæ, jactaverit: eam enim ad declinandam invidiam & arcana occultanda excogitatam fuisse, alio loco in hoc opere probamus. Heraclitum excipit Gorgias Leontinus
units.tr: that it could never be found, however far a man might travel along its paths; but also he called opinion a sacred disease and said that sight lies. So Hesychius reports after Diogenes Laertius, book 9, in his On Illustrious Men. Hence in Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians, he exclaims: "Eyes are bad witnesses for men, and ears for those who have barbarian souls." Sextus then explains this thus: "It is the mark of barbarian souls to trust the senses, which lack reason." But since he loved an obscure style of speaking, [with which in mind Empiricus, in the passage cited, neatly says, "who among the haughty grammarians can understand Heraclitus?"] and since he seemed to teach more obscurely the things which were set forth clearly and without wrappings by the disciples of Pyrrho, therefore some, in the same Sextus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism, book 1, chapter 29, said that the Sceptical philosophy was a road to the doctrines of Heraclitus. Although Sextus, in that place, seriously rebukes Onesidemus for this, because Heraclitus spoke many things dogmatically, I think it is beneath censure, since in those matters in which he was dogmatic he is so obscure that it is hard to say whether he proceeds dogmatically or sceptically. Nor can it help Sextus that Heraclitus boasted of a common and divine reason, as the norm of all knowledge; for we prove elsewhere in this work that this was devised to ward off envy and to hide his secrets. After Heraclitus comes Gorgias of Leontini,

units.la: Sophistarum nobilissimus & antiquissimus: qui quanquam aureus in Pithys templo erectus est, ut de eo testatur Philostratus, viam tamen ad Scepticismum strávit. Ignorare nos non finit Sextus lib. advers. Mathemat. Gorgias, inquit, Leontinus fuit ipse quoque ex ordine eorum, qui sustulerunt id quod judicat. Nam in libro qui inscribitur, de eo quod non est, aut de natura, tria ordine constituit capita. Unum quidem & primum quod nihil sit: secundum autem, quod etsi sit, ab homine non possit comprehendi: tertium, quod etsi possit comprehendi, enuntiari tamen & explicari non possit proxime. Scepticismo favérunt quoque Anaxagoras, Democritus, & Empedocles: docet hoc Cicero non solum in verbis ex Lucullo modo allatis, sed etiam lib. 1. Acad. Quaest. ubi ita loquitur: Arcesilas sibi omne certamen instituit, non pertinacia, aut studio vincendi, ut mihi quidem videtur, sed earum rerum obscuritate, quae ad confessionem ignorationis adduxerant Socratem, & veluti amantes Socratem, Democritum, Anaxagoram, Empedoclem, omnes pene veteres: qui nihil cognosci, nihil percipi, nihil sciri posse dixerunt, angustos sensus, imbecilles animos, brevia curricula vitae, & ut Democritus, in profundo veritatem esse demersam, opinionibus & institutis omnia teneri, nihil veritati relinqui: denique omnia tenebris circumfusa esse dixerunt. Quod ad Democritum, de ejus Philosophia sic Sextus lib.
units.tr: The most noble and most ancient of the Sophists, though a golden statue of him was set up in the temple at Pythos, as Philostratus testifies, nevertheless paved the way to Scepticism. Sextus, in his book against the Mathematicians, does not let us ignore this: Gorgias of Leontini, he says, was himself also of the group of those who abolished what judges. For in the book entitled On What Is Not, or On Nature, he set out three heads in order. The first and foremost is that nothing exists; the second, that even if something exists, it cannot be comprehended by man; the third, that even if it can be comprehended, it cannot be expressed and explained to another. Anaxagoras, Democritus and Empedocles also favoured Scepticism. Cicero teaches this not only in the words just quoted from Lucullus, but also in the first book of the Academica, where he speaks thus: Arcesilas set himself every contest, not from obstinacy or a zeal for winning, as it seems to me, but from the obscurity of those things which had led Socrates to confess ignorance; and, as it were, lovers of Socrates, almost all the ancients, Democritus, Anaxagoras, Empedocles: who said that nothing can be known, nothing perceived, nothing understood; that our senses are narrow, our minds feeble, our span of life brief; and that, as Democritus said, truth is sunk in the depths, while all things are held by opinions and customs, and nothing is left to truth; in short, they said that everything is wrapped in darkness. As for Democritus, Sextus speaks thus of his philosophy:

units.la: 1. Pyrrh. Hypot. cap. xxx. Democriti quoque Philosophia communionem habere cum scepsi fertur. Quo loco bene notari debet illud dicitur: ut enim ipse Sextus eo loco fateri cogitur, Philosophia ejus à Scepticorum opinionibus distincta fuit. Observarat hoc ante Cicero in Lucullo: Nec Arcesilæ calumnia conferenda est cum Democriti verecundia. Dubito an sola verecundia suspicionem hanc circa Democritum concitarit. Ipse enim in lib.qui Canones dicitur, apud Eusebium ita loquitur: Tenebricosa quidem hæc omnia, visio, auditio, gustatio, tactio: nec præter rationem jam olim puteus illius proverbio locum fecit. Quantum ad Empedoclem, idem Sextus in opere adversus Mathematices de eo docet, quod docuerit, in sensibus non esse veri judicium. De eodem idem ex parte censetPhilosophus lib. III. de anima cap. III. text. 150. ubi accenset illum ijsPhilosophis, qui idem docebant esse sentire & intelligere; quod existimarent judicis partes nullo modo sensibus, sed uni rationi ex asse deferendas esse. Frustra vero est Picus Mirandulanus, quando lib. II: cap. XI. & lib. VI. cap. VIV. de vanit. doctr. gentium, Empedoclis patrocinium contra Peripateticæ Philosophiæ dictatorem suscipit. Ipse enim Lucullus apud Ciceronem, cum antiquos PhilosophosScepticis eripere studeret, fluctuat circa Empedoclem: Isti Physici raro admodum, cum hærent aliquo loco, exclamant quasi mente incitati, Empedocles quidem ut interdum
units.tr: In the first book of the Outlines of Pyrrhonism, chapter 30: The philosophy of Democritus too is said to have a fellowship with scepticism. At this point the word is said ought to be carefully noted: as Sextus himself is forced to admit in that place, his philosophy was distinct from the opinions of the Sceptics. Cicero had already observed this in the Lucullus: Nor is the calumny of Arcesilas to be compared with the modesty of Democritus. I doubt whether modesty alone aroused this suspicion concerning Democritus. For in the book called the Canons, he speaks thus, as reported by Eusebius: All these things are dark: sight, hearing, taste, touch. And not without reason did that well of his give rise long ago to a proverb. As for Empedocles, Sextus in his work against the Mathematicians teaches of him that he taught that there is no judgement of truth in the senses. Concerning the same man, the Philosopher in the third book of On the Soul, chapter 3, text 150, in part gives his opinion: there he counts him among those philosophers who taught that to perceive and to understand are the same, because they thought the office of judging must be entrusted entirely to reason alone and in no way to the senses. But Pico della Mirandola labours in vain when, in the second book, chapter 11, and the sixth book, chapter 15 of On the Vanity of the Teaching of the Gentiles, he takes up the patronage of Empedocles against the dictator of the Peripatetic philosophy. For Lucullus himself in Cicero, while eager to snatch the ancient philosophers away from the Sceptics, wavers over Empedocles: These natural philosophers, when they stick at some point, very rarely cry out as if moved in mind, as Empedocles sometimes seems to me to rave, when he says that all things are hidden, that we perceive nothing, see nothing, and can discover nothing of what sort anything is at all.

units.la: interdum terdum mihi furere videatur: abstrusa esse omnia, nihil nos sentire, nihil cernere, nihil omnino quale sit posse reperire. Quoniam vero jam olim maxime circa Heraclitum, & Empedoclem disputatum fuit, an ad Scepticismum accederent; Tertullianus lib. 3. de Anima cap. 17. circumspecte admodum loquitur, quando dicit; Horum [scilicet sensuum] fidem Academici durius damnant, secundum quosdam & Heraclitus, & Diocles, & Empedocles. An in hanc classem referri quoque debeat Samius senex, sive magnus Phythagoras, non sine ratione quis ambigat. Si Heraclidi Pontico apud Laërt. in Præf. fidem quis adhibere velit, docuerit quasi, nullum hominem esse sapientem; sed quis inde tamen colligat eum paria cum Empedocle fecisse? Ut enim modestia ei suasit pro sapientis nomine Philosophi titulum amplecti; ita de alijs idem exististimavit, quod de semet ipso ingenue fatebatur. Succedit dein Parmenides, quem non solum inter antecessores Scepticorum recenset Eusebius lib. xiv. de Præpar. Evang. cap. vii. Sed etiam Diogenes: ut lib. ix. enim innuit, docuit, sensus minus ad judicandum idoneos esse. Imo, si fides adhibenda Theodoreto lib. ii. de Curat. Græc. Affect. nihili faciendum esse sensuum judicium perhibuit. Ex antiquissimis Philosophis superest Xenophanes, cujus ut Scepsis fautoris meminit non solum Cicero supra ex Lucullo ad partes vocatus, verum etiam Eusebius; ubi Colophonium hunc Xenophanem ijs accenset, qui sensuum judicium in dubium vocabant. Priusquam pergimus in enumerandis vetustis Scepticismi conditoribus, de his, quorum jam facta mentio est [Heraclitum & Gorgiam si excipias] observandum existimo, quod Cicero in Lucullo annotat: Majorem partem mihi quidem omnes isti videntur nimis etiam quaedam affirmare, plusque profiteri se scire, quam sciant. Quod si illi tum in novis rebus quasi modo nascentes hesitaverunt, nihilne tot saeculis, summis ingeniis, maximis studiis explicatum putamus? Quibus verbis Lucullus [is enim ibi contra Academicos disputat] significare vult, eos subinde in luto haerentes instar Academicorum loqui, caeterum alibi fateri plura se scire, quam ignorare; ut per omnia firmpse lege cum Academicis, aut Scepticis censendi non sint. Aliud existimandum de Protagora, Naufiphane, & Zenone Eleate, de quibus ita Seneca Epist. LXXXVIII. Protagoras, ait, de omni re in utramque partem disputari posse, ex aequo & de hac ipsa, an omnis res in utramque partem disputabilis sit. Naufiphanes ait, ex his quae videntur esse, nihil magis esse, quam non esse. Zenon Eleates omnia negotia de negotio dejecit, & ait nihil esse. Quod ad Protagoram, is Sophia, sive sapientia vulgo, teste Diogene, vocabatur, aut ut apud Suidam occurrit, lógos, vel lógos emmisfhos; de eoque præter Senecam, Plato in Theæteto testatur, quod statuerit, nihil omnino esse : addit�que Laërtius lib. ix. illum quendam librum exorsum suisse ab his verbis: De Dijs statuere nequeo, neque an sint, nec ne. Sunt enim plurima quæ id scire prohibeant, quippe & summa rei incertitudo, & brevis hominis vita. Præ cæteris vero distincte sententiam ejus recenset Ammonius in Prædicam. Relationis, ubi testatur, eum statuisse, nihil certam habere naturam, & nihil esse simpliciter verum aut falsum; sed tantum esse verum id, quod videtur tale, & pro diversitate opinionum diverso modo res esse veras, vel falsas: quoniam autem opiniones hominum variæ sunt & incertæ, ideo scientias quoque esse varias ac incertas, ac proinde nullam esse certam rerum scientiam & veritatem. Zeno quia popularis ac discipulus Parmenidis, aut, ut loquitur Laërtius audivit Parmenidem, vel, ut Empiricus, notus eidem fuit, Præceptoris dogmata non tantum imbibit, verum etiam sic propagavit, ut meruerit non solum in hoc catalogo à Seneca, sed à Galeno lib. de Hist. Philos. ac Eusebio loco aliquoties citato, recenseri. Intelligendus autem est Zeno Eleates, ut expresse à Seneca & Galeno vocatur, nec temere confundendus cum Citiæo Stoicæ familiæ principe; is enim Academicorum Scepsi faventium infestissimus adversarius fuit, ut liquet ex Ciceronis Lucullo. Hos duos, posteriores potissimum, per aliquos illos los intélligere videtur Philosophus, quando lib. 1. Analyt. Post. in vestibulo capitis tertij dicit; Quibusdam visum est nullam omnino scientiam esse. Nausiphanes denique, quem duum viris his Seneca conjungit, Pyrrhonis discipulus fuit, ut infra exLaertio ostendetur; & quia inter eos celebrior, præ alijs citatur.
units.tr: Now and then Empedocles seems to me to rage: all things are hidden, we perceive nothing, we discern nothing, and we are unable to find out at all what anything is like. But since the question whether Heraclitus and Empedocles were approaching Scepticism was debated long ago, Tertullian speaks with great caution in De Anima, ch. 17, when he says: The Academics condemn these [namely the senses] more harshly; according to some, Heraclitus, Diocles and Empedocles do too. One may reasonably doubt whether the old man of Samos, the great Pythagoras, should also be counted in this class. If anyone is willing to trust Heraclides of Pontus in the Preface of Laertius, he seems to have taught that there is no wise man; but who would infer from this that he did the same as Empedocles? For just as modesty led him to embrace the title of philosopher rather than the name of wise man, so he thought the same of others as he freely confessed of himself. Next comes Parmenides, whom Eusebius, in Praeparatio Evangelica 14, ch. 7, lists not only among the forerunners of the Sceptics, but Diogenes also: for in book 9 he hints that the senses are less fit for judging. Indeed, if Theodoret in Graecarum Affectionum Curatio, book 2, is to be believed, he declared that the judgement of the senses is to be valued at nothing. Of the most ancient philosophers, Xenophanes survives, whose champion of Scepticism is mentioned not only by Cicero, who summoned him to the cause from Lucullus above, but also by Eusebius, where he counts this Xenophanes of Colophon among those who called the judgement of the senses into doubt. Before we go on to list the ancient founders of Scepticism, I think we should note about those already mentioned [excepting Heraclitus and Gorgias] what Cicero remarks in the Lucullus: For the most part, it seems to me, all these men affirm some things too positively, and profess to know more than they know. But if they hesitated then, as it were in new matters just coming into being, do we think that nothing has been explained in so many centuries by the greatest minds and the greatest labours? By these words Lucullus [for he is there disputing against the Academics] means that these men, when stuck in the mud, speak like the Academics from time to time, but elsewhere admit that they know more than they are ignorant of; so that they are not to be counted in every respect as one with the Academics or the Sceptics. It is a different matter with Protagoras, Nausiphanes and Zeno of Elea, of whom Seneca says in Epistle 88: Protagoras says that on every matter one can argue on both sides, and equally on this very question, whether every matter can be argued on both sides. Nausiphanes says that of the things which seem to exist, none is more existent than non-existent. Zeno of Elea dismissed every business from business and said that nothing exists. As for Protagoras, he was commonly called Sophia [σοφία], or wisdom, according to Diogenes, or, as occurs in Suidas, logos [λόγος] or logos emmisthos [λόγος ἔμμισθος]. Besides Seneca, Plato in the Theaetetus also bears witness about him, that he laid down that nothing at all exists; and Laertius adds in book 9 that a certain book of his began with these words: I cannot determine concerning the gods, whether they exist or do not exist. For there are very many things that prevent our knowing this, both the obscurity of the matter and the brevity of human life. Above all others, however, Ammonius recounts his opinion distinctly in his commentary on the Categories, where he testifies that he held that nature has no fixed character, and that nothing is simply true or false, but only that is true which appears to be so; and that, according to the diversity of opinions, things are true or false in different ways: since the opinions of men are various and uncertain, the sciences too are various and uncertain, and therefore there is no certain science or truth of things. Zeno, because he was a fellow-citizen and disciple of Parmenides, or, as Laertius puts it, heard Parmenides, or, as Sextus Empiricus says, was known to him, not only imbibed his master's doctrines but also propagated them in such a way that he deserved to be listed not only in this catalogue by Seneca, but also by Galen in his book on the History of Philosophy, and by Eusebius in the passage cited several times. But Zeno of Elea must be understood, as Seneca and Galen expressly call him, and he is not to be rashly confused with Zeno of Citium, the head of the Stoic school; for the latter was the most hostile opponent of those who favoured the Scepsis of the Academics, as is clear from Cicero's Lucullus. The Philosopher seems to mean these two, especially the latter, by certain persons when, in the preface to chapter 3 of book 1 of the Posterior Analytics, he says: It has seemed to some that there is no science at all. Finally, Nausiphanes, whom Seneca joins with these two men, was a disciple of Pyrrho, as will be shown below from Laertius; and because he was more famous among them, he is cited before the others.

units.la: CAPUT SECUNDUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWO.

units.la: Socrates & Plato videntur haut alieni quoque a Scepsi fuisse, quam ut cum ratione in quibusdam foverunt, ita Sceptici perfecti nequaquam haberi debent.
units.tr: Socrates and Plato seem not to have been far removed from skepticism either, insofar as they sometimes cherished it along with reason; but they ought not to be regarded as perfect Skeptics.

units.la: SCepticismi autores perduximus ad Socratem, sejusque celeberrimum discipulum Platonem.
units.tr: We have traced the authors of skepticism back to Socrates and to his most famous disciple, Plato.

units.la: De utroque autem jam olim quæsitum fuit, an cum ratione Scepticismi architecti haberi queant. Quod ad Socratem, quem Delphicus Apollo omnium hominum sapientissimum esse judicavit, dicere solet, Laërtio lib. 2. teste, se scire nihil praeter hoc ipsum, quod nihil sciret. Quod ne forte quis soli modestiæ imputet, amplius apud Ciceronem in Lucullo proclamat; nihil cognosci, nihil percipi, nihil sciri, angustos sensus, imbecilles animos, brevia curricula vitæ, opinionibus & insomniis omnia teneri, nihil veritati relinqui, & omnia tenebris circumfusa esse. Et ut Sextus testatur adversus Mathematicos, mancipis manens in consultatione dubitavit, dicens se ignorare quidnam ipse sit, & quemadmodum se habeat ad universitatem. Ego enim, inquit, nescio an sim homo, an aliqua alia fera Typhone magis multiplex & varia. quę posteriora verba desumpta sunt ex Platonis Phædro modo ad partes vocando. Ut non sine ratione dicat Lucianus in Hermotimo: Socrates omnium testimonio professus est, se non tantum omnia, sed in universum nihil nosse, aut hoc tantum se scire, quod nesciret. Socratis discipulus Plato [ ut recte observatum est à Tertulliano lib. 3. de Anima cap. 17. ] suam quoque sententiam sub præceptoris nomine clarissime in Theæteto propositi, quando ita loquentem introducit: Illud peraque ac obstetricibus mihi inest: nulla nimirum sapientia valeo fatura, & quod jam dudum complures mihi exprobrant, me alios quidem interrogare, me vero nihil nulla de re respondere, quippe qui nulla præditus sim sapientia, vere profecto exprobrant. Hujus vero rei hæc est causa: Deus me quidem cogit obstetricari, at me prohibuit aliquid generare. Et iterum sub ejusdem Socratis persona sententiam suam proponens in Phædro dicit: Quoniam nondum queo, prout imperat Delphicum elogium, me ipsum cognoscere: ridiculum autem mihi videtur, me, quamdiu ignoretur quæ ad me proxime pertinent, in alienis exquirendis anxie versari. Et in Phædone moxmoriturus Socrates veritatis sententiam post mortem differt, elegantissimaque comparatione hoc declarat : inquiens, ac si quis in medio profundi pelagi habitans putet se altiora maris incolere : atque solem caeteraque astra per mare prospiciens, mare ipsum esse caelum existimet: Propter tarditatem autem imbecillitatemque nunquam ad summum maris evaserit, neque caput undis extulerit, planeque aspexerit quanto hic locus profundo illo purior pulchriorque sit, quin etiam neque ab illo, qui hunc intuitus sit, acceperit. Hoc igitur idem & nobis accidere, qui in quadam orbis terreni concavitate habitantes, altam incolere superficiem arbitremur, atque aërem nominemus caelum, ut qui per ipsum quasi caelum astrorum motus intueamur. Idque nobis accidere propterea quod propter imbecillitatem tarditatemque ad supremum usque aërem ascendere nequeamus. Quod si quis ad summum evaderet, vel alijs fretis eo volaret, quemadmodum pisces emergentes e mari, nostra haec aspiciunt: sic ea, quae illic sunt, aspiceret. Ac si natura ad inspiciendum sufficeret, cognituram protinus caelum illud esse verum, veramque lucem. Quid vero de sensuum judicio exististimaverit, indicat idem Tertullianus loco dicto: Certe Plato in Timaeo irrationalem pronunciat sensualitatem & opinioni complicitam; non renuente ipso Platone, qui in nobilissimo illo Dialogo sic de sensibus loquitur: Adversis motibus sibi invicem animam, totamque ejus substantiam diverse distrahentes; ut una quidem feratur, cum confirmationis suae nixibus, verum sine ratione, utpote motibus discordantibus, & depravante rectum iter sensuum illecebra. Propterea varias inclinationes animæ existere, & obliquas, & contrarias, item resupinis casibus similes: Vt si quis naturalem membris regionem mutans, caput pro pedibus solo figat; pedes in altum pro capite suspollat: tunc opinor, tam ejus qui patitur, quam eorum qui expectant, dextra quidem partes sinistra, sinistra vero dextra videntur. Invicem ad ipsum quoque animæ circuitus patiuntur. Propterea errant in ejusdem diversique generis contemplatione: cum quod diversum,idem: & quod idem est, diversum, imbecillitate discernendi autumant. Estque hæc plena erroris & falsitatis opinio, orta ex depravatione sensuum: nec habet ullum certum ducem talis peragratio. Cumque extra positi sensus pulsarint animam vehementius, omnemque eam possederint, tunc illa subjugata & serviens, pontificium quid potestatemque retinere falso putatur. Eademque passionibus agra, & initio cum incorporata est, & quandiu perinde afficietur, amens erit. Item in Phædro Socratem sic loquentem introducit: Quare his (sensibus) dimissis, atque existimationi, quam de his paulo ante narrabam, fide adhibita, non ipsa quidem, sed me ipsum consīdero, utrum sim bellua aliqua Typhone multiplicior, ardentiorque & furiosior, sive placatius quoddam & simplicius animal divina cinjusdam mitisque fortis naturâ particeps. Ejus notæ sententiæ è Platonis scriptis plures citari possent, si liberet ijs lectorem brevitatis studiosum onerare. Nec tamen cum ratione quis hinc colligere potest, Academiæ patrem Scepticum per omnia esse. Ut enim Sextus Empiricus lib. 1. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. 33. dicit de eo; Etiamsi quadam Scepticorum more pronuntiat, quum, ut ajunt, se exercet, non ideo erit Scepticus. Nam qui de uno aliquo dogmatice pronunciat, aut phantasiam phantasiæ præfert ullo modo ad fidem impetrandam aut non impetrandam de aliqua re incerta, dogmaticum sequitur characterem. Idem de Philosophorum Homero existimat Lucullus apud Ciceronem: cum tamen eo loco ipsi Ciceroni contrarium visum suerit, quando contra Lucullum disputans sic loquitur: Ab his (Scepticismi scilicet patronis) ajebat removendum Socratem & Platonem? an de ullis certius possum dicere vixisse cum his equidem videor: ita multi sermones perscripti sunt, à quibus dubitari non potest, quin Socrati nihil sit visum sciri posse. Excipit unum tantum scire se, nihil se scire: nihil amplius. Quid dicam de Platone; qui certe tam multis libris hæc persecutus non esset, nisi probavisset, ironiam enim alterius, perpetuam præsertim, nulla fuit ratio persequi. Conciliare hæc forte quis posset, si statuat Socratem & Platonem circa quædam scepsin fovisse, è quibusquidam, non attendentes ad ea, quæ dogmatice ab ijs tradita erant, minus commode collegerint eos per omnia nouis Academicis similes esse; Ad hoc eos voluisse, ut supra circa alios quoque notatum est, contundere sciolorum supercilium, qui dum per sensuum praesidium, omnium rerum perfectam cognitionem assequi se jactabant, risum debuere illis, quibus fallaciae, sensibus ex accidente obvenientes, non minus exploratae erant, atque angusti scientiae termini. Denique & hoc dici potest, quod observatum quoque est ab Augustino in opere adversus Academicos, Socratem & Platonem non tam negasse ullam dari scientiem, quam eam vulgo denegasse. Unde & idem Augustinus lib. 2. adversus Academicos cap. 10. testatur, illos sibi videri graves & prudentes viros fuisse.
units.tr: Both men were questioned long ago on whether they can rightly be counted among the architects of skepticism. As for Socrates, whom the Delphic Apollo judged the wisest of all men, he used to say, as Laertius reports in book 2, that he knew nothing except this very fact, that he knew nothing. Lest anyone attribute this to mere modesty, he declares more fully in Cicero's Lucullus: nothing can be known, nothing perceived, nothing understood; our senses are narrow, our minds feeble, our course of life brief; everything is held fast by opinions and dreams; nothing is left to truth, and all things are wrapped in darkness. And as Sextus testifies in his work against the Mathematicians, he remained in lasting doubt, saying that he did not know what he himself was, or how he stood in relation to the whole. For I, he said, do not know whether I am a man, or some other creature more manifold and varied than Typhon. These last words are taken from Plato's Phaedrus, though quoted here out of context. So Lucian says, not without reason, in the Hermotimus: Socrates, by the testimony of all, professed that he knew not merely everything, but altogether nothing, or only this, that he knew what he did not know. Socrates' disciple Plato (as Tertullian rightly observes in book 3 of On the Soul, chapter 17) also set out his own opinion very clearly in the Theaetetus, under the name of his teacher, when he introduces him speaking thus: This is inherent in me, as in midwives: I am clearly barren of wisdom, and the charge that many have long made against me is true, that I question others but never answer anything myself on any subject, because I possess no wisdom. The cause of this is as follows: God compels me to act as a midwife, but has forbidden me to bring forth anything. Again, in the Phaedrus, putting forward his opinion in the person of the same Socrates, he says: Since I cannot yet, as the Delphic inscription commands, know myself, it seems ridiculous to me to busy myself anxiously with investigating things foreign to me while I am ignorant of what lies nearest to me. And in the Phaedo, Socrates, about to die, puts off the verdict of truth until after death and makes this clear by a most elegant comparison, saying: It is as if someone living in the depths of the sea were to think that he dwelt on the heights, and seeing the sun and the other stars through the sea, were to suppose that the sea itself is the sky. Because of his slowness and weakness he never rises to the surface of the sea, nor lifts his head out of the waves, and so never plainly sees how much purer and more beautiful this place is than that deep, nor even learns it from anyone who has seen it. This same thing happens to us as well, who dwell in some hollow of the earthly globe and think we inhabit its upper surface, and call the air the sky, as if through it we observed the motions of the stars. And this happens to us because, through our weakness and slowness, we cannot rise to the highest air. But if anyone were to reach the top, or fly thither on some other support, as fishes emerging from the sea look upon our world, so he would look upon those things that are there. And if our nature were sufficient for such viewing, he would at once know that that heaven is true heaven and that light is true light. What Plato thought of the judgment of the senses is shown by the same Tertullian in the passage cited: Certainly Plato in the Timaeus pronounces sense irrational and bound up with opinion; and Plato does not deny it, for in that noble dialogue he speaks of the senses thus: With conflicting motions, dragging the soul and its whole substance in different directions, so that one motion carries it along, with the efforts of its own support, yet without reason, since it is driven by discordant motions, and the enticement of the senses corrupts the straight path. Hence there arise various inclinations of the soul, oblique and contrary, and likewise like those of people overturned on their backs: as when someone, changing the natural position of his limbs, fixes his head to the ground and lifts his feet high in place of his head. Then, I suppose, both the one who suffers this and those who look on see the right side as left and the left as right. The circuits of the soul itself suffer in the same way towards one another. Hence they err in the contemplation of the same and the different: taking the different for the same, and the same for the different, through weakness of discernment. And this opinion is full of error and falsehood, arising from the corruption of the senses, and such a wandering has no certain guide. And when the senses placed outside the soul have struck it more violently and taken full possession of it, then the soul, subjugated and in servitude, is falsely thought to retain some power of its own. And the same soul, sick with passions, from the time it is first embodied and as long as it is so affected, will be out of its mind. Likewise, in the Phaedrus, he introduces Socrates speaking thus: Setting aside these senses, and putting faith in that opinion which I was describing a little while ago, I consider not them but myself, whether I am some beast more manifold than Typhon, and fiercer and more raging, or a gentler and simpler creature, partaking by nature in some divine and mild lot. Many more such sayings could be cited from Plato's writings, if it pleased us to burden a reader who values brevity with them. Yet no one can rightly conclude from this that the father of the Academy was a Skeptic in every respect. For as Sextus Empiricus says of him in book 1 of the Outlines of Pyrrhonism, chapter 33: Even if he pronounces in the manner of the Skeptics, when, as they say, he is exercising himself, he will not on that account be a Skeptic. For whoever pronounces dogmatically on any one thing, or in any way prefers an appearance to an appearance in order to win or withhold assent about some uncertain matter, follows the character of a Dogmatist. Lucullus in Cicero holds the same view about Plato, the Philosopher's Homer; yet in that very passage Cicero himself judged the opposite, when, disputing against Lucullus, he speaks thus: Lucullus said that Socrates and Plato should be removed from the ranks of the Skeptics. But can I say anything more certain about anyone than that I seem to have lived with these two? So many discourses have been written down by them, from which no one can doubt that Socrates thought nothing could be known. He excepts only one thing, that he knows that he knows nothing, and nothing more. And what shall I say of Plato, who certainly would not have pursued these matters through so many books, unless he had approved of them? For there was no reason to pursue irony for so long, especially one that was perpetual. Perhaps someone could reconcile these things if he holds that Socrates and Plato cherished a certain skepticism about some matters, but those who, not attending to what was delivered dogmatically by them, have too hastily gathered that they were in all respects like the New Academics. It was their purpose, as has been noted above concerning others too, to humble the pride of the half-learned, who, while boasting that they could attain a perfect knowledge of all things through the protection of the senses, deserved to be laughed at by those for whom the deceptions that come to the senses by chance were no less well known, and the limits of knowledge no less narrow. Finally, this too may be said, which Augustine also observed in his work against the Academics: that Socrates and Plato did not so much deny that any knowledge exists as deny that it is commonly possessed. Hence Augustine too, in book 2 against the Academics, chapter 10, testifies that they seemed to him men of weight and prudence.

units.la: CAPUT TERTIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER THREE.

units.la: De Arcesila, ab aliis Arcesilao dicto, media Aca- demia conditore, itemque de Epocha Sceptico- rum, quam primus in Academiam traduxit.
units.tr: On Arcesilas, called Arcesilaus by others, founder of the Middle Academy, and likewise on the suspension of judgment (epoche) of the Sceptics, which he first brought into the Academy.

units.la: SOcratis, Platonisque mentem cum per omnia exploratam non haberet Arcesilas (Parmenonis discipulus ut docet Sextus lib. 1. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. 33. aut ut vult Laërtius Crantoris, successor autem Parmenonis, docente Augustino lib. 19. de civit. Dei cap. 1.) quum ingenio suo indulgcdulgere, novæque familiæ pater haberi posset, omnia alta ignorantiæ caligine involvere cœpit,& ut Lucullus apud Ciceronem loco modo laudato dicit; cum jam Philosophorum disciplinæ gravissimæ constituissent, exortus est, ut in optima repub. Tiberius Gracchus, etc. ut constitutam Philosophiam everteret & in eorum authoritate delitesceret, qui negarent quicquam sciri, aut percipi posse. Quid docuerit vero, idem docet lib. 3. de Oratore; Arcesilas primum qui Platonem audierat, ex variis Platonis libris sermonibusque Socraticis, hoc maxime arripuit nihil esse certi, quod aut sensibus aut animo percipi possit. A Laërtio in proœmio & passim lib. iv. ubi ejus vitam describit, Arcesilaus vocatur; quod imitatus est Plutarchus in Opusc. de discernendo amico ab adulatore; & Seneca lib. 2. de Benef. cap. 10. ubi hanc notatu dignam historiam de eo refert, Arcesilaus, ut ajunt, amico pauperi, & pauperta tem suam dissimulanti, ægro autem, & ne hoc quidem dcesse sibi confitenti insumptum ad necessarios usus, cum clam succurrendum judicasset, pulvino ejus ignorantis sacculum subjecit, ut homo inutiliter verecundus, quod desiderabat, inveniret potius quam arriperet. Conditor autem fuit Academiæ, quæ media dicebatur. Laërtius lib. 4. Primus hic mediam invexit Academiam, negationes continens propter sermonum contrarietatem: quam scientiæ incertitudinem ut plausibiliori ratione confirmaret, contra, quam ab alijs vulgo Philosophis factum erat, nulla ingenij sui monumenta relinquere instituit. Laërtius l. d. Nullum librum scripsit, quod aque de omnibus sententiam suspenderet. Imo hoc egit, ut omnis scientia submoveretur; in quo per omnia ei cum Pyrrhonijs convenit. Ex re est audire Sextum, loco aliquoties hoc capite citato: At vero Arcesilaus, quem mediæ Academiæ dicebamus præsidem fuisse & authorem, magnâin mihi videtur cum Pyrrhoniorum verbis affinitatem habere: adeo ut una sit promodum disciplina. Neque enim de existentia aut inexistentia rei cujusquam pronuntiare comperitur, neque alterum alteri ad fidem obtinendam aut non obtinendam præferre: sed de omnibus assensum retinet, & finem esse dicit Epochaм: cum qua simul ingredi imperturbatum mentis statum dicebamus. Vult præterea esse quidem bona particulares Epochas, mala autem particulares assensiones.Quare non sine ratione à Lactantio lib. 3. Divin. Instit. cap. 6. Ignorantiæ Magister vocatur. Quia vero disertissimi inter Latinos Patres locus luculentus admodum est, integrum ascribere non pigebit: Arcesilas ignorantiæ magister, cum Zenoni obtrectaret principi Stoicorum, ut totam Philosophiam everteret; authore Socrate suscepit hanc sententiam, ut affirmaret nihil sciri posse. Itaque æstimationem Philosophorum, qui putarent ingenijs suis erutam esse atque inventam veritatem: Videlicet quia mortalis fuerat illa sapientia, paucisque ante temporibus instituta, ad summum jam incrementum pervenerat, ut jam necessario consenesceret, ac periret, repente exitit Academia tanquam senectus Philosophiæ, quæ illam conficeret jam defloresceentem. Reliqueque vidit Arcesilas, arrogantes vel potius stultos esse, qui putent scientiam veritatis conjectura posse comprehendi. Sed tamen falsa dicentem redarguere non potest, nisi qui scierit ante quid sit verum. Quod Arcesilas veritate non cognita facere conatus : introduxit genus Philosophiæ αφυσιατον, quod Latinè instabile sive inconstans possumus dicere : ut enim nihil sciendum sit, aliquid sciri necesse est. Hactenus Lactantius. Arcesilaum penitius si quis cognoscere velit, audiat Eusebium, qui lib. 14. de Præpar. Evang. cap. 2. hæc amplius de eo perhibet : Hic subtilitatibus Diodori, qui acutus Dialecticus, & Pyrronis ratiocinationibus Platonicam eloquentiam fœdavit, & modo hoc modo aliud dicens, hinc illo, & illinc huc facile tanquam nihil sciens volvebatur, scire tamen multa eloquentia umbra videbatur, nec unquam fuit in eo, ut unum & idem bis diceret, nec putabat ingeniosi esse viri in eisdem permanere. Cavillator igitur summus vocabatur, cum ita se his quæ dicebantur dare adaptareque semper fuerit præmeditatus, ut cum ipse nihil sciret, nec alios scire quicquam pateretur. Terrebat enim omnes turbabatque sophismatibus, gaudebatque ac gloriabatur fœditate illa mirifice, quia nihil turpe, nihil honestum, nihil bonum, nihil malum cognosceret: sed se quod primo turpe dixerat, repente commutatus, pluribus conabatur rationibus, quae prius aestruxerat confutare. Erat igitur Hydra capita sua proprio ense amputans, nec aliquid habens utile, nisi quod libenter & audiretur, & videretur. Nam & facie benigna, & ore rotundo, & suavibus erat oculis praeditus, quae non repente arripuit, sed aptus ad hac natura, exercitatione quoque ab initio firmavit. Haec ibi Eusebius. Porro decantata illa Epocha quae tantopere quoque Pyrrhoni placuit & omnibus post eum Scepticis, primum ab Arcesilao in Academiam traducta est. Dicitur vero ut a Sexto annotatum fuit σχόν τǿ ἐποχής τǿν σκεπτικων. Cicero interpretatur assensionis retentionem; & vim verbi explicans in Lucullo dicit: Contineo igitur me ne incognito assentiar. Agellius lib. II. Noct. Att. cap. 5. verbum ipsum videtur voluisse interpretari per cunctari, & insistere, ita scribens: Ac ne videre quidem plane quicquam, neque audire sese putant: sed ita pati afficique quasi videant vel audiant. Eaque ipsa quae affectiones istas in sese efficiant, quanta & cuiusmodi sint, cunctantur atque insistunt. Alias apud Sextum Epocha dicitur σχέσης αποχή & apud Galenum vocis pomoerijs aliquantum dilatatis, ἐπέχειν.
units.tr: Since Arcesilas did not have a full grasp of the mind of Socrates and Plato (he was a pupil of Parmenon, as Sextus teaches in Pyrrhonian Outlines book 1, chapter 33, or, as Laertius would have it, Crantor's successor and Parmenon's successor, according to Augustine in De civitate Dei book 19, chapter 1), and since he could indulge his own talent and could be regarded as the founder of a new school, he began to wrap everything in the thick darkness of ignorance. As Lucullus says in Cicero, in the passage quoted above: when the philosophers had already established the most serious disciplines, there arose, as Tiberius Gracchus did in the best republic, and so on, to overthrow the established philosophy and to hide behind the authority of those who denied that anything could be known or perceived. What he taught, Cicero says in the same place in book 3 of De oratore: Arcesilas, who first heard Plato, took from the various books of Plato and from the Socratic conversations above all this: that nothing is certain which can be perceived either by the senses or by the mind. Laertius, in his preface and throughout book 4 where he describes his life, calls him Arcesilaus; Plutarch imitated this in his tract on distinguishing a friend from a flatterer; and Seneca, De beneficiis book 2, chapter 10, where he relates this notable story about him: Arcesilaus, as they say, when he judged that help must be given secretly to a poor friend who hid his poverty, and to a sick man who admitted that he lacked not even this, the money for necessary expenses, slipped a purse under the pillow of the sick man, who knew nothing of it, so that this man, uselessly bashful, would find what he wanted rather than seize it. He was the founder of the Academy which was called the Middle. Laertius, book 4: He was the first to introduce the Middle Academy, which contains denials because of the contrariety of arguments: and, in order to confirm this uncertainty of knowledge by a more plausible reason, he resolved, contrary to what the other philosophers commonly did, to leave behind no monument of his own talent. Laertius, in the same place: He wrote no book, since that would equally settle an opinion about everything. Indeed he aimed at this, that all knowledge should be removed; in this he agreed with the Pyrrhonists in every respect. It is worth hearing Sextus, whom I have cited several times in this chapter: But Arcesilas, whom we called the leader and founder of the Middle Academy, seems to me to have a great affinity with the words of the Pyrrhonists, so that the discipline is almost one and the same. For he is not found to pronounce on the existence or non-existence of anything, nor to prefer one thing to another so as to win or not to win belief; but he withholds assent about everything and says that the end is suspension of judgment, with which, we said, a state of mind undisturbed comes in at the same time. He holds further that particular suspensions are indeed good, but particular assents are bad. Therefore not without reason Lactantius, Divine Institutes book 3, chapter 6, calls him the master of ignorance. Since the passage in Lactantius, the most eloquent of the Latin Fathers, is quite splendid, I shall not hesitate to transcribe it in full: Arcesilas, the master of ignorance, when he disputed with Zeno, the prince of the Stoics, in order to overturn all philosophy, took up this opinion on the authority of Socrates: that he affirmed that nothing can be known. Thus, against the estimation of the philosophers who thought that truth had been dug out and discovered by their own talents, namely because that wisdom was mortal and had been established only a short time before, and had already reached its full growth, so that it must necessarily grow old and perish, the Academy suddenly arose like the old age of philosophy, to bring to an end a philosophy that was already withering. And Arcesilas saw, that those are arrogant, or rather foolish, who think that the knowledge of truth can be grasped by conjecture. Yet one who says false things cannot be refuted unless he has known beforehand what is true. Since Arcesilas, having not known the truth, tried to do this, he introduced a kind of philosophy, aphysiaton [ἀφυσιάτον], which we may call in Latin unstable or inconstant: for just as nothing must be known, something must necessarily be known. So far Lactantius. If anyone wishes to know Arcesilas more thoroughly, let him hear Eusebius, who in book 14 of Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 2, adds this about him: He, with the subtleties of Diodorus, who was a sharp dialectician, and with the reasonings of Pyrrho, defiled Platonic eloquence; and saying now this, now that, he was easily turned hither and thither, and thither and hither, as if knowing nothing, yet he seemed by the shadow of eloquence to know many things, and he never said the same thing twice, nor did he think it the mark of a clever man to remain in the same position. Therefore he was called the supreme trickster, since he had always premeditated so adapting and fitting himself to what was said that, while he himself knew nothing, he did not allow others to know anything either. For he terrified and disturbed everyone with sophisms, and he rejoiced and gloried wondrously in that filth, because he recognised nothing shameful, nothing honourable, nothing good, nothing bad; but, having suddenly changed what he had first called shameful, he tried with many arguments to refute what he had previously built up. He was therefore a Hydra cutting off its own heads with its own sword, and he had nothing useful about him, except that he was gladly heard and gladly seen. For he was endowed with a kindly face, a round mouth and pleasant eyes; these he did not seize suddenly, but his nature was suited to them, and from the beginning he also strengthened them by practice. So far Eusebius. Moreover, that celebrated epoche, which pleased Pyrrho so greatly and all the Sceptics after him, was first brought into the Academy by Arcesilas. It is called, as Sextus has noted, the aim of the Sceptics' suspension [σκοπὸν τῆς ἐποχῆς τῶν σκεπτικῶν]. Cicero translates it as the retention of assent, and explaining the force of the word in Lucullus he says: I therefore restrain myself from assenting to what is unknown. Gellius, book 2 of Attic Nights, chapter 5, seems to have wished to render the word itself by to hesitate and to dwell upon, writing thus: Nor do they think that they see or hear anything clearly; but they are so affected and moved as if they saw or heard. And as to what these affections produce in them, how great and of what kind they are, they hesitate and dwell upon it. Elsewhere in Sextus the epoche is called abstention from relation [σχέσεως ἀποχή], and in Galen, with the boundaries of the word somewhat extended, to suspend judgment [ἐπέχειν].

units.la: CAPUT QUARTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FOUR.

units.la: De nova Academia, & quis eam instituerit, itemque in quibus diversa fuerit a Veteri & Media. An quarta constituenda sit Academia.
units.tr: On the New Academy, and who founded it, and in what respects it differed from the Old and the Middle Academy. Whether a fourth Academy should be posited.

units.la: Vnde dum media Academia, duce Arcesilao, lacertos movere coeperat; aut exorta est, auspiciis prae caeteris Carneadis, nova Academia, quae emolliens asperiorem prioris familiae sententiam, pro invidioso illo NIL SCIRE, substituit DUBITARE. Fundamenta illius antea jecerat Lacydes, qui proinde vulgo quoque nova Academiae conditor habetur. Laert. in Proem. Lacydes nova Academia Philosophus. Sed auspicatus solum est, quod Carneades cum Clitomacho perfecit. Hinc ita Sextus lib. 1. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. 33. Tertia & nova Academia Carneadis & Clitomachi. Quid docuerint, qui ex hac familia fuerunt; prae aliis Cicero docet lib. 3. de Orat. Nova Academia nihil affirmabat, verum rem propositam in utramque partem versabat, semper dubitabunda & incerta, verisimilium consectatrix, aliorum rationes adversa subvertens argumentatione. Quo respiciens Seneca lib. de Brev. Vitae cap. 14. dicit: Disputare cum Socrate licet, dubitare cum Carneade. Opinionis hujus sectatores, quia Academiam obtinuerunt, in eaque, exclusis aliis, dominabantur, soli Academici dicti fuerunt. Ex quorum sensu haud male Lactantius lib. 3. Divin. Instit. cap. 6. Academici contra Physicos ex rebus obscuris argumentati sunt, nullam esse scientiam, & exemplis paucarum rerum incomprehensibilium contenti, amplexi sunt ignorantiam: tanquam scientiam totam sustulisset, quia in parte sustulerant. Quanquam enim novae Academiae sectatores, non tam ignorantiam, quam dubitationem amplexi fuerunt, recte tamen Lactantius, respiciens dubitationis effectum (ut infra pluribus illud declarabimus) ignorantiam illis tribuit. Dubitans enim, imo opinans, ignoranti similis est. Augustinus lib. 19. de Civ. Dei cap. 1. Ob hoc distinguit ab Academicis novis, quibus incerta sunt omnia. & paulo post: Cum quaeritur de Academicis novis, quibus incerta sunt omnia. Quando autem eodem loco, Hipponensis Episcopus novae Academiae originem ad Arcesilam refert, mediam Academiam cum nova confundit. Quod & ab Hieronymo factum Apol. ult. adv. Rufinum: Arcesilaum aut Carneadem putes, qui omnia incerta pronuntiant, licet & illos superet cautione. Illi enim omnium Philosophorum invidiam non ferentes, quod vitam e vita tollerent, verisimilia repererunt, ut ignorantiam rerum probabili assertione temperarent. Non sine ratione vero Tertullianus lib. 3. de Anima cap. 17. talibus Academiae mangonibus procaciam tribuit, quando ait: Quid agis Academice procacissime? Novi hi Academici postquam sectam constituere coeperunt, & soli Academiam obtinere, non tam ut Academici in genere considerati, quam ut Philosophi in universum spectati (uti ante ex Cicerone & Lactantio discere licuit) divisi sunt in Academicos & Physicos. Clare supra Cicero: Primum mihi videmini (vos novæ scilicet Academiæ alumni) cum veteres (tum Academicos, tum antiquos Philosophos) Physicos vocatis, etc. & Galenus in libello de Optimo docendi genere: Verum si nobis Physicis, concedant, ut oportet, sensum. item Lactantius lib. 3. cap. 6. Academici contra Physicos ex rebus obscuris argumentati sunt, nullam esse scientiam. Ideo credo, quod Thaletis exemplo (qui naturalem Philosophiam præ aliis excoluit, primusque Physicorum parens exstitit, docente Sexto adversus Mathematicos) Physiologiam sic excolerent, ut circa res naturales veras conclusiones cum certo animi assensu amplecterentur: alias Physicus qui secundum Ciceronem venator speculatorque naturæ est, Laërtio teste, proprie dicitur qui naturæ negotia tractat, quod circa naturam occupetur, docendo scil. & scribendo. An vero triplici huic Academiæ quarta quoque conjungi debeat, non sine ratione quis quærat? Eam certe agnoscere videtur Eusebius lib. ult. de Præpar.
