Evang. cap. 2. sed contra Ciceronem, Laërtium, & Augustinum, qui diligentissime Academiæ descripserunt historiam, non tamen contra Sextum Empiricum, uti alibi ostendemus.
units.tr: While the Middle Academy, under the leadership of Arcesilaus, had begun to stir its limbs, the New Academy arose, chiefly under the auspices of Carneades. It softened the harsher doctrine of the earlier school and in place of the notorious NOTHING IS KNOWN put TO DOUBT. Lacydes had earlier laid the foundations for this, and so he is commonly regarded as the founder of the New Academy. Laertius, in the Proem: Lacydes, a philosopher of the New Academy. But he only began the work, which Carneades completed together with Clitomachus. Hence Sextus, in the first book of the Pyrrhonian Hypotyposes, chapter 33: The third, the New Academy, of Carneades and Clitomachus. What those who belonged to this school taught, Cicero shows above all others, in the third book of De Oratore: The New Academy affirmed nothing, but argued each proposed matter on both sides, always doubting and uncertain, pursuing the probable, and overturning the arguments of others by refutation. Looking to this, Seneca in De Brevitate Vitae, chapter 14, says: One may debate with Socrates, but one may doubt with Carneades. The adherents of this opinion, because they held the Academy and ruled in it to the exclusion of others, alone were called Academics. Lactantius, in the third book of the Divine Institutes, chapter 6, speaks well of their view: The Academics argued against the Physicists from obscure matters that there is no science, and, content with examples of a few incomprehensible things, they embraced ignorance, as though they had removed all science because they had removed it in part. Although the followers of the New Academy embraced not so much ignorance as doubt, Lactantius rightly attributes ignorance to them, looking to the effect of doubt (which we will explain at greater length below). For one who doubts, or even one who opines, is like one who is ignorant. Augustine, in the nineteenth book of The City of God, chapter 1: On this account he distinguishes them from the New Academics, for whom all things are uncertain. And a little later: When one inquires about the New Academics, for whom all things are uncertain. But in the same place the Bishop of Hippo traces the origin of the New Academy back to Arcesilaus, and so confuses the Middle Academy with the New. Jerome did the same in the last Apology against Rufinus: You would take them for Arcesilaus or Carneades, who pronounce all things uncertain, although they surpass those men in caution. For those men, not bearing the hatred of all philosophers because they removed life from life, found probable things, so that they might temper ignorance of things with probable assertion. Not without reason, however, Tertullian, in the third book On the Soul, chapter 17, ascribes boldness to such hucksters of the Academy when he says: What are you doing, most insolent Academic? These New Academics, after they began to form a sect and alone held the Academy, were divided, not so much as Academics considered in general, but as philosophers viewed in general (as we have already learned from Cicero and Lactantius), into Academics and Physicists. Cicero above makes this plain: First, you seem to me (you, of course, the pupils of the New Academy) to call the old (both the Academics and the ancient philosophers) Physicists, and so on. And Galen, in his little book on the best method of teaching: But if they grant us Physicists, as they ought, the sense. Likewise Lactantius, in the third book, chapter 6: The Academics argued against the Physicists from obscure matters that there is no science. I think this is why, following the example of Thales (who cultivated natural philosophy before others and first became the parent of the Physicists, as Sextus teaches against the Mathematicians), they cultivated physiology in such a way that they embraced true conclusions about natural things with firm assent of mind. Otherwise, a Physicus, who according to Cicero is a hunter and observer of nature, is properly, as Laertius testifies, one who handles the affairs of nature, because he is occupied with nature, teaching and writing, that is. But may someone reasonably ask whether a fourth Academy should also be joined to this threefold one? Eusebius, in the last book of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 2, certainly seems to acknowledge it, but against Cicero, Laertius and Augustine, who described the history of the Academy most carefully, and not, however, against Sextus Empiricus, as we shall show elsewhere.

units.la: CAPUT QUINTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FIVE.

units.la: De Scepticis, & eorum parente Pyrrhone, ejus- que occasione de Megaricis.
units.tr: On the Sceptics and their founder Pyrrho, and on the occasion of the Megarians.

units.la: AB Academicis ad Scepticos, ejusdem prope notæ Philosophos, transimus, de quorum patre Pyrrhone priusquam agimus, præceptores illius considerare debemus. Ut varij autem Philosophi à patria cognomentum traxerunt, ita quidam Megarici à Megara dicti sunt, teste Laërt. in procem. inter quos præ alijs excelluit Stilpo, qui tantam ex Græcia caterva m ad se pertraxit, ut diceretur tota Græcia μεγαρεῖσαι secundum Laërt. lib. 3. De eodem hoc Euseb. lib. 14. de Præp. Euang. cap. 7. Stilpo, inquit, & Megarici, qui dicebant unum esse quod est, & quod diversum esse videtur diversum non esse, nec gigni quicquam, nec corrumpi, nec moveri. Filius ejus Dryso ut à Laërtio lib. 9. traditum est, præceptor fuit Pyrrhonis, qui præter Drysonem audivit & diu sectatus est Anaxarchum, teste non solum Laërtio, sed Galeno quoque in Historia Philosophorum, ubi hæc occurrunt: Phaedonem Elienfem Anaxarchus Abderita sectatus est, qui Pyrrhonem docuit Sceptica Philosophiæ authorem. Anaxarchi præceptores & Sectatores, longa serie Eusebius loco modo laudato recenset. Xenophanis vero, inquit, auditor fuit Parmenides, illius Melissus, Melissi Zeno, Zenonis Leucippus, Leucippi Democritus, Democriti Protagoras & Nessas, Nessa Diogenes, Diogenis Anaxarchus. Ab Eusebio aliquantum recedit Laërt. lib. 9. in Anaxarchi vita, quando ita Latine loquitur: Anaxarchus Abderites Diomenis Smyrnæi auditor fuit, alij Metrodori Chij auditorem tradunt. PorroMetrodorum alij Nausam Chium, alij Democritum audisse tradunt. Quem hoc ipso in loco Eusebius Diogenem vocat, à Laërtio Diomenes dicitur: &, si antiquis Codd. MSS. quæ fides deferenda: Nessas Eusebij, Naşas Laërtij fuerit. Cum verò de plerisque ex his distincte egerimus, de solo Anaxarcho verbo quid ex Laërtio annotandum. Ita autem de eo :Hic ne se id quidem scire dicebat, quod nihil sciret. Eadem occurrunt apud Hesychium lib. de Sapientibus. Ita ut neque à Stilpone, ejusque filio Dryfone, neque ab Anaxarcho Pyrrho Elienfis per omnia recesserit, cumteste Aristocle apud Eusebium l. d. doceret: Res ex æquo indifferentes, incertas, injudicabilis, ideo nec sensus, nec opiniones nostras verum aut falsum dicere. Ergo nec ipsis fidem habendam, nec opinationis expertes manere nos debere sine inclinatione, sine motione: de quaque singulari re dicentes: Non magis est, quam non est: itemque, est, non est, neque non est. Qua vero occasione ad has furoris lineas accesserit, prae aliis Aristocles docet, cujus verba non pigebit affcribere: Pyrrho igitur Anaxarchi cujusdam discipulus fuit, qui primo quidem pictor erat, non adeo felix artifex, deinde vero cum Socratis libros legisset, nihil boni nec excogitavit, nec scripsit. sed omnes Deos & homines maledictis prosecutus est: Ipse vero cum hunc saltum assumpsisset, quamvis vocaret se a saltu alienum, nihil literarum monumentis mandavit. Recte autem Aristocles notat, Pyrrhonem praeter rationem semet a fastu remotu vocasse, &alijsPhilosophis fastum, quem Timon apud eundem in versibus vana opinione vocat, tribuisse. Quis enim modestum eum vocet, qui pronunciare audet, omnes ad unum sapientes nihil scire, & quotquot disciplinas perficere laborarunt, pariter omnes oleum & operam perdidisse. Ab hoc Pyrrhone descendit illa haeresis sive Secta, quae Pyrrhonica dicta est, teste Laërt. in proem. vulgoque Sceptica vocatur. Quamvis vero Generale nomen sit Sceptica; eoque insigniri consueverit ipsa quoque Secta Academica; uti ex variis testimoniis infra adducendis liquere poterit: prae caeteris tamen Pyrrhonis familia, hunc titulum ferre consuevit, non solum eminenter, uti loquuntur, sed proprie. Cujus nōjus nominis rationem priusquam reddimus, expendendum, quod ex Theodosio in Scepticis capitulis retulit Laërtius in Pyrrhonis vita, contendebat autem ille; Scepticam Pyrrhoniam minime appellari oportere. Nam siquidem, ait, motus & agitatio mentis alterius comprehendi à nobis non potest, professo Pyrrhonis affectum ignorabimus. At si illum ignoremus, Pyrrhonij haut quaquam dicemur, praterquam quod neque Pyrrho primus Sceptices inventor fuerit, neque ea dogma aliquod habeat, rectius autem diceretur Pyrrhonis moribus similis. Non movit tamen hoc Sextum Empiricum, sic enim lib. 1. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. 3. loquitur: Quoniam solidius & apertius Scepsin tractavisse Pyrrhonem existimamus, quam eos, qui ante illum praecurrerunt, ab ejus nomine Pyrrhonia nuncupatur: nec sine ratione. Ut enim Galenus in Hist. Philosophorum loquitur: Scepticos fuisse tradunt Zenonem Eleatensem, Anaxarchum Abderitem, & Pyrrhonem, quem exactissimum in hoc genere fuisse dicunt. Si Pyrrho in Scepsi exactissimus fuit, nae dignus est, a quo nomen ferant omnes Scepticorum familiae.
units.tr: Having passed from the Academics to the Sceptics, philosophers of nearly the same reputation, we must first consider the teachers of Pyrrho, their founder, before we treat of him. Just as various philosophers took their surname from their homeland, some were called Megarians from Megara, as Laertius says in his preface. Among them Stilpo excelled above the rest, and drew to himself so great a crowd from Greece that all Greece was said to be "Megarizing" [μεγαρεῖσαι], according to Laertius, book 3. Of this same man, Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book 14, chapter 7: "Stilpo," he says, "and the Megarians, who taught that what is is one, that what seems to be different is not different, and that nothing comes into being, nothing perishes, and nothing moves." Stilpo's son Dryso, as Laertius reports in book 9, was the teacher of Pyrrho. Pyrrho, besides Dryso, heard Anaxarchus and followed him for a long time, as not only Laertius attests but also Galen in his History of the Philosophers, where these words occur: "Anaxarchus of Abdera followed Phaedo of Elis, who taught Pyrrho, the founder of the Sceptical philosophy." Eusebius, in the passage already cited, lists at length the teachers and followers of Anaxarchus: "Parmenides," he says, "was the pupil of Xenophanes, Melissus of Parmenides, Zeno of Melissus, Leucippus of Zeno, Democritus of Leucippus, Protagoras and Nessas of Democritus, Diogenes of Nessas, and Anaxarchus of Diogenes." Laertius, book 9, in the life of Anaxarchus, departs somewhat from Eusebius when he writes in Latin: "Anaxarchus of Abdera was a pupil of Diomenes of Smyrna; others report that he was a pupil of Metrodorus of Chios. Moreover, some report that Metrodorus heard Nausas of Chios, others Democritus." In this very place Eusebius calls Diogenes the man whom Laertius calls Diomenes; and, if we may trust the old manuscripts, Eusebius's Nessas is Laertius's Naşas. But since we have treated most of these men separately, only one thing about Anaxarchus alone need be noted from Laertius. He is reported thus: "He used to say that he did not even know this, that he knew nothing." The same occurs in Hesychius, On the Wise Men. So Pyrrho of Elis did not depart in all things from Stilpo, his son Dryso, or Anaxarchus, since, as Aristocles reports in Eusebius (loc. cit.), he taught: "Things are equally indifferent, uncertain, and incapable of judgement; therefore neither our senses nor our opinions say what is true or false. Hence we ought not to trust them, but to remain without opinion, without inclination, without motion, saying of each single thing that it no more is than is not, or that it both is and is not, or that it neither is nor is not." Aristocles, more than others, shows by what occasion he came to these lunatic notions, and I will not hesitate to quote his words: "Pyrrho, then, was a pupil of a certain Anaxarchus. At first he was a painter, not a very successful artist; then, having read the books of Socrates, he neither devised nor wrote anything good, but attacked all gods and men with abuse. Yet he himself, having assumed this lofty pose, though he called himself remote from arrogance, left nothing committed to the written record." Aristocles rightly notes that Pyrrho, without reason, called himself free from arrogance, and attributed arrogance to other philosophers, which Timon, in the same author, calls "vain opinion" in verse. For who would call that man modest who dares to pronounce that all the wise, without exception, know nothing, and that all who have laboured to perfect the disciplines have equally wasted their oil and their effort? From this Pyrrho descended that heresy or sect which was called Pyrrhonian, as Laertius reports in his preface, and which is commonly called Sceptical. Although "Sceptical" is a general name, and the Academic sect too has been commonly designated by it, as will be clear from the various testimonies to be cited below, nevertheless the school of Pyrrho has been accustomed to bear this title above all others, not only eminently, as they say, but properly. Before we give the reason for this name, we must weigh what Laertius, in the life of Pyrrho, reports from Theodosius in his Sceptical Chapters. Theodosius contended that "the Sceptical school ought by no means to be called Pyrrhonian. For, he says, if the motion and agitation of another mind cannot be grasped by us, then, since Pyrrho professed his state of mind, we shall not know it; and if we do not know it, we shall not be called Pyrrhonians at all. Besides, Pyrrho was not the first inventor of Scepticism, and it has no doctrine of its own; it would rather be called one that resembles Pyrrho's manner." Yet this did not move Sextus Empiricus, for he speaks thus in book 1 of the Pyrrhonian Outlines, chapter 3: "Since we think that Pyrrho treated Scepsis more solidly and more openly than those who ran before him, it is named Pyrrhonian after his name." Nor is this without reason. As Galen says in his History of the Philosophers: "They report that Zeno of Elea, Anaxarchus of Abdera, and Pyrrho were Sceptics, and they say that Pyrrho was the most exact in this kind." If Pyrrho was the most exact in Scepsis, then he is surely worthy to give his name to all the families of the Sceptics.

units.la: CAPUT. SEXTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SIX.

units.la: Pyrrhonis cur dicti fuerint Sceptici: ipsa vero secta [Greek]
units.tr: Why the Pyrrhonists were called Sceptics, and the sect itself [Greek]

units.la: NOnsolum à Pyrrhone denominati fuerunt, quotquot de omnibus dubitando, pretiosissimam fiffimam scientiæ possessionem homini ad veritatis investigationem nato eripere voluerunt, sed alia etiam nomina tulerunt, occurrentia partim apud Laërtium lib. 9. in Pyrrhonis vita, partim apud Sextum lib. 1. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. 3. Usitatissime autem tota secta Sceptica dicta est, à σκέψις: quid vero vocabulum hoc sibi velit, præ aliis docet Gellius lib. 11. Noct. Att. cap. 5. Quos Pyrrhonios Philosophos vocamus, ij Græco cognomento Sceptici appellantur: id ferme significat quæsitores & consideratores: nihil enim decernunt, nihil constituunt; sed in quærendo semper considerandoque sunt, quidnam sit omnium rerum de quo decerni constituique possit. Ac ne videre quoque plane quicquam nec audire putant, sed ita pati afficique quasi videant vel audiant. eaque ipsa quæ affectiones ipsas in se efficiant, qualia & cujusmodi sint, cunctantur atque insistunt. Cæterum observandum verbum hoc, cum ad Scepticorum familiam refertur, non dici de quacunque commentatione; sed ad illam restringi, quæ est hominis responsionem ad quæstinem, de qua interrogatus fuerat, meditantis, eamque aut affirmativam, aut negativam. Ejus autem notæ responsionem nemo ullis machinis Sceptico alicui extorserit, eo quod dum Scepsi vacat dicit sibi omnia contraria circa idem videri, ideoque omnia talia apparere, ut æquum pondus tum ad fidem, tum ad dubitationem habeant: quare neque ultra Scepsin progredietur, sed in eâ perpetuò defixus manebit. Sic apud Xenophontem Διαπορέω dicitur, qui aliquid consideret, de quo interrogatus est, ἀπορίσεως ponsionem ad id meditans: pro quo etiam σχέψις τεθεὶς dicitur, quo Scepticus quidam apud Lucianum, huic hominum generi valde præ aliis infestum, sane eleganter utitur in Icaro Menippo; idem ipse hoc vocabulum Pyrrhoni tribuit. Cur autem Gellius Scepticos appellatos dixerit, quasi quæsitores, rationem vix video. Budæus in Comment. de Asse, rectius eos dictos vult, quasi cunctatores & hæsitatores: & tamen Gellio astipulari videtur Laertius, modò ad partes vocandus. Alias eadem hæc Secta dicta est Setetica, Ephectica, & Apotetica. Sextus Lib. 1. Pyrrho. Hypoth. Cap. 3. Sceptica igitur institutio, vocatur etiam quæsitoria, ab ipsa actione, quæ est in quærendo & utendo Scepsi. Appellatur etiam Ephectica, ab ea affectione, quæ in eo est, qui Scepsi utitur, deducto nomine. Dicitur & dubitatoria, aut inde quod de omni re dubitet, & quarat, ut nonnulli volunt: aut propterea, quod hæsitans suspensio sit ad assentiendum aut repugnandum animo. Gellius. l. d. Vtrique enim [Academici & Sceptici] dicuntur; quoniam utrique nihil affirmant, nihilque comprehendi putant. Et Laërtius libro. 9. in vita Pyrrhonis: Hi omnes à magistro quidem Pyrrhone, caeterum à dogmate mate aporetici & sceptici, praetereaque & ephectici, & Zetetici appellabantur. Est enim Zetetica Philosophia sic dicta, quod semper in veritatis inquisitione versetur. Porro Sceptica, quod semper quaerat, & nunquam inveniat. Ephectica autem dicitur ab eventu, quod post inquisitionem ambigatur itidem: Aporetica vero quod ejus sectatores semper addubitent. Haec Laërtius.
units.tr: Those who wished to strip humanity, born to investigate the truth, of the most precious possession of knowledge by doubting everything were not named only after Pyrrho. They also bore other names, which occur partly in Laertius, book 9, in the life of Pyrrho, and partly in Sextus, book 1 of the Pyrrhonian Outlines, chapter 3. The whole sect is most commonly called Sceptical, from σκέψις [skepsis]. Gellius, Attic Nights, book 11, chapter 5, explains better than others what this word means: Those whom we call Pyrrhonian philosophers are called in Greek Sceptics. The word roughly signifies inquirers and considerers. For they decide nothing and settle nothing, but are always inquiring and considering what there might be among all things that can be decided and settled. Nor do they think that they plainly see or hear anything, but they are affected and moved as if they were seeing or hearing. And they hesitate over and dwell upon these very affections themselves, what they are and of what kind. However, this word, when it is applied to the Sceptical school, should be noted as not being used of any kind of study, but restricted to that thinking which is a person's reply to a question about which he has been asked, and which is either affirmative or negative. No one could, by any devices, extract a reply of this kind from a Sceptic, because while he is at leisure in Scepsis he says that everything seems to him contrary about the same thing, and so everything appears such that it has equal weight both for belief and for doubt. Therefore he will not advance beyond Scepsis, but will remain fixed in it forever. Thus in Xenophon διαπορέω [diaporeō] is used of someone who considers something about which he has been asked, thinking over a reply to it. Instead of this, σχέψις τεθεὶς [skepsis tetheis] is also used, which a certain Sceptic in Lucian, in the Icaromenippus, uses quite elegantly; Lucian, who was very hostile to this kind of men beyond others. He himself also attributes this word to Pyrrho. But I hardly see the reason why Gellius said the Sceptics were so called, as if they were inquirers. Budé, in his Commentary on the As, wants them to be called more rightly hesitators and waverers. Yet Laertius seems to agree with Gellius, if he is called to that side. This same school was also otherwise called Zetetic, Ephectic, and Aporetic. Sextus, book 1 of the Pyrrhonian Outlines, chapter 3: The Sceptical teaching is therefore also called Zetetic, from the very activity which consists in inquiring and in using Scepsis. It is also called Ephectic, from the state of mind which is in the one who uses Scepsis, the name being derived from that. It is also called Dubitative, either because it doubts and inquires about everything, as some wish, or because the suspension of the mind, hesitating, is toward assenting or dissenting. Gellius, in the place cited: For both [the Academics and the Sceptics] are called so, since both affirm nothing and think that nothing can be grasped. And Laertius, book 9, in the life of Pyrrho: All these were called, indeed, from their master Pyrrho, but from their doctrine Aporetics and Sceptics, and besides these Ephectics and Zetetics. For the philosophy is called Zetetic because it is always engaged in the search for truth. It is called Sceptic because it always seeks and never finds. It is called Ephectic from its outcome, because after inquiry one is likewise left in doubt. It is called Aporetic because its followers are always in doubt. So Laertius.

units.la: CAPUT SEPTIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SEVEN.

units.la: De successoribus Arcesilae & Pyrrhonis: Pyrrhoniorum nonnulli scriptis grassati sunt in famam reliquorum Philosophorum, alij vero a scribendo abstinuerunt, paulatimque omnes defecerunt.
units.tr: On the successors of Arcesilaus and Pyrrho: some of the Pyrrhonists attacked the reputation of other philosophers in their writings, while others abstained from writing, and gradually all of them died out.

units.la: DEinde successores Academicorum pariter, & Pyrrhoniorum enumerare convenit. Cum vero, eodem prope saeculo, Arcesilas Academiam in ignorantiae scholam transformare instituerit, & Pyrrho hominem potissima possessione exuere; ad hoc Arcesilas, ut fuse ostendit Eusebius lib. 14. de Praep. Evang. cap. 2. praeceptorem habuerit Pyrrhonem; conjunctim hoc capite de eorum successoribus & discipulis agemus, conjungendo etiam Megaricos & Eretricos; [hi sic dicti sunt à Menedemo Eretriensi] si modo qui extra Pyrrhonios in ordine eorum Scepsin amplexi fuerint; ut indicare videtur Seneca epist. 89. Circa eadem fere Pyrrhonij versantur, & Megarici, & Eretici, & Academici, qui novam induxerunt scientiam, Nil scire. Voluissem Stoicæ familiæ princeps nomina pariter, quorundam Megaricorum & Eretricorum prodidisset: apud Lærtium enim aliosque altum silentium. Quod ad Arcesilæ autem successores, illi ut degenerarunt constituendo novam Academiam; ita numero valde pauci sunt: post Lacydem siquidem Arcesilai successorem, primumque novæ Academiæ auspicem, quatuor hi solum occurrunt; Evander, Hegesinus Pergamenus, [à Clemente Hegesilaus vocatus] Carneades Cyrenæus, & Clitomachus Carthaginensis: quod ad Philonem enim & Charmidam; illi quartam Academiam constituerunt, ut quintam Antiochus, fidem faciente Sexto Empirico lib. 1. Pyrrh. hypoth. cap. 33. videnturque ad veterem Academiam redijsse. Postea vero plures hanc cum Arcesilao ignorantiæ doctrinam non fuisse professos, liquere videtur ex Seneca lib. 7. Nat. Quæst. cap. ult. Tot familiæ, inquit, Philosophorum sine successore deficiunt. Academici & veteres & minores nullum antistitem reliquerunt. Quo loco ut duplicem Academiam agnoscit, ita per Minores Academicos, omnes Sectæ posi post Platonis excessum constitutas intelligit. Mirum vero, quod Annaeus Ciceronum nusquam in hac classe meminerit: teste Augustino enim lib. 3. adversus Academ. cap.7. libros Academicarum Quaestionum[ ex quibus quartus solum integer, & primus magna sui parte mutilus supererat] in hujus caussa( Academicę scil.) patrocinium scripsit. & quanquam multis in locis Platonicorum dogmata tueri videtur, genuinum tamen Academicum fuisse patet ex initio lib. II. & IV. Tusc. Q. & I. de Nat. Deorum, ex ejusque Hortensio refert Augustinus ib. cap. 14. Se ipsum magnum esse opinatorem. Pyrrhonis discipuli hi potissimum a Laërtio nominantur, Eurylochus, Hecataeus Abderites, Timon Phliasius, Naufiphanes Tejus, Aenesidemus, Antiochus Laodicenus, Apelles, & Zeuxis Aenesidemi discipulus. Ex his quidam nihil exemplo praeceptoris Pyrrhonis scripserunt, alij vero scriptis, Philosophorum alias summorum famam traducere instituerunt, ut Timon, qui Sillos scripsit, & de quo post Diogenem sic Suidas: Timon Phliasius & ipse Philosophus ex familia Pyrrhonis scripsit tres libros, vocatos Sillos, sive vituperationes Philosophorum. Idem hic Timon aliquoties a Laërtio laudatur, nec non a Stephano alicubi in Comm. de Urbib. Subsequentibus seculis pauci Pyrrhonis decreta amplexi sunt, quod innuere videtur Seneca, quando loco postremo laudato exclamat: Quis est qui tradat præcepta Pyrrhonis? Post ætatem enim illius vix alium invenias sectæ hujus asseclam, quam Favorinum, contra quem Galenus scripsit opusculum de optimo genere docendi, cujusque decem libros Pyrrhonicarum Definitionum ad partes vocat Aulus Gellius lib. II. Noct. Att. cap. 5. Nâm de Theodosio, quem in Scepticis capitulis citat Laertius; jure meritoque ambigas. Meminit illius quoque Suidas, ac præter Scep-tica Capitula recenset ejus Sphærica, item Commentarios de diebus & noctibus, nec non Delineationes ædium. Ambigo an non sit ille, cujus meminit Strabo lib 14. Geographiæ. Ob doctrinam memorabilem in Bithynia exstiterunt, Xenocrates philosophus, Dionysius Dialeƈticus, Hipparchus, ac Theodosius, & filij ejus Mathematici, Cleophanes. Myrleanus Rhetor, Asclepiades Prusiensis medicus. Pari ratione circa Callium hæreas, quem non ignobilem Pyrrhonium fuisse innuit Galenus lib. de Suffigur. Empir. De Sexto Empirico, quoniam ad hunc catalogum non pertinet, dicemus capite sequenti.
units.tr: Next, it is fitting to list the successors of both the Academics and the Pyrrhonists. Since, in roughly the same century, Arcesilaus set about turning the Academy into a school of ignorance, and stripped Pyrrho of the chief possession, and since, as Eusebius shows at length (Preparation for the Gospel, book 14, chapter 2), Arcesilaus had Pyrrho as his teacher, in this chapter we shall deal together with their successors and disciples, including also the Megarians and the Eretrians [who were so named from Menedemus of Eretria], provided they are those who, outside the Pyrrhonists, embraced Scepsis in that order. Seneca, Letter 89, seems to indicate this: The Pyrrhonists, and the Megarians, and the Eretrians, and the Academics, who introduced the new science of knowing nothing, deal with roughly the same matters. I would have wished that the leader of the Stoic family had also named some of the Megarians and Eretrians, but Laertius and others are silent on this. As for the successors of Arcesilaus, they degenerated by establishing a New Academy, and they are very few in number. For after Lacydes, the successor of Arcesilaus and the first founder of the New Academy, only these four occur: Evander, Hegesinus of Pergamum [called Hegesilaus by Clement], Carneades of Cyrene, and Clitomachus of Carthage. As for Philo and Charmidas, they established a fourth Academy, as Antiochus did a fifth, as Sextus Empiricus vouches (Pyrrhonian Outlines, book 1, chapter 33), and they seem to have returned to the Old Academy. Afterwards it seems clear from Seneca, Natural Questions, book 7, last chapter, that many did not profess this doctrine of ignorance along with Arcesilaus: So many schools of philosophers, he says, die out without a successor. The Academics, both old and younger, have left no leader. In this passage, just as he recognises a double Academy, so by the Younger Academics he understands all the sects established after the death of Plato. It is surprising, however, that Cicero is nowhere mentioned by Seneca in this class. For, on the testimony of Augustine (Against the Academics, book 3, chapter 7), he wrote the books of the Academic Questions [of which only the fourth survived whole and the first largely mutilated] in defence of this cause, that is, of the Academy. And although in many places he seems to defend the doctrines of the Platonists, it is nevertheless clear that he was a genuine Academic, from the beginning of book 2 and book 4 of the Tusculan Disputations and of the first book On the Nature of the Gods. Augustine also reports from his Hortensius, in the same work, chapter 14, that he thought himself a great opiner. The disciples of Pyrrho named by Laertius are chiefly these: Eurylochus, Hecataeus of Abdera, Timon of Phlius, Nausiphanes of Teos, Aenesidemus, Antiochus of Laodicea, Apelles, and Zeuxis, a disciple of Aenesidemus. Of these, some wrote nothing, following the example of their master Pyrrho, while others, through their writings, set about disparaging the fame of other, very eminent philosophers. Such was Timon, who wrote the Silloi, and of whom Suidas says, after Diogenes: Timon of Phlius, himself also a philosopher of the school of Pyrrho, wrote three books called the Silloi, or reproaches of the philosophers. This same Timon is praised several times by Laertius, and also by Stephanus in some place in his work On Cities. In later centuries few embraced the decrees of Pyrrho, which Seneca seems to hint at when, in the last passage cited, he exclaims: Who is there who hands down the precepts of Pyrrho? For after his time you would hardly find another follower of this sect besides Favorinus, against whom Galen wrote a little work on the best kind of teaching, and whose ten books of Pyrrhonian Definitions Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 2, chapter 5, cites as authoritative. But as to Theodosius, whom Laertius cites among the Sceptical chapters, you may rightly doubt. Suidas also mentions him, and besides the Sceptical Chapters he lists his Spherics, likewise commentaries on days and nights, and also Outlines of Buildings. I wonder whether he is not the one whom Strabo mentions in book 14 of the Geography: On account of their memorable learning there lived in Bithynia the philosopher Xenocrates, the dialectician Dionysius, Hipparchus, and Theodosius, and his sons, the mathematicians, Cleophanes, the rhetorician of Myrlea, and Asclepiades of Prusa, the physician. By the same reasoning you may also suspect Callias, whom Galen, in his book on the Sphygmic... on the Empiricists, hints was a Pyrrhonist of no little note. Sextus Empiricus, since he does not belong to this catalogue, we shall discuss in the following chapter.

units.la: CAPUT
units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: CAPUT OCTAVUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER EIGHT.

units.la: De Empiricis Scepticorum cognatis, ubi & fusè de Sexto Empirico.
units.tr: On the Empirics, the Kindred of the Sceptics, Including a Lengthy Account of Sextus Empiricus.

units.la: Proxime de Empiricis Scepticorum quasi contubernalibus agere debemus: saepe enim Galenus eos cum Scepticis componit, nominatim in lib. de Simplic. Medicament. Facult. cap. I. Quae sit facultatis essentia, quidam certe non posse agnosci existimant, quales sunt Sceptici Philosophi, & qui inter medicos vocati sunt Empirici. Item de suffigur. Empir. cap. 13. Praterea sermonis multitudinem longitudinemque aspernabitur, sed pauca & raro loquetur, quemadmodum Pyrrho Scepticus facere solebat: hic enim desperata veritatis inventione, quam diu frustra quaesierat, in singulis haesitabat, nec amplius agendorum rationem quaerebat, sed evidentia sectabatur, ut qualis in omnibus vitae muneribus Scepticus, talis in Medicina Empiricus sit, minime superbus aut ambitiosus, neque gloriae inhians, non composite ambulans, non fucatis gestibus, sed interius exteriusque totus integer, qualem Timon ait fuisse Pyrrhonem. Ex quibus liquet, eos, qui vulgo Empirici dicti fuerunt. Galeno si credimus, in Medicina haut aliter Sceptin fovissent, atque in omnibus alijs disciplinis, qui proprie Sceptici vocabantur. Pater & antecessor horum quis fuerit, idem scriptor in vestibulo operis de Suffigurat. Empir. docet: Omnes Empirica cultores cognomen ab Hippocrate ductum renuentes, se ab animi affectu denominari maluerunt, quem admodum Philosophi, quos, quia in singulis haerent, Scepticos Graeco nomine appellant. Ergo non sunt sicut ceteri Hippocratici aut etiam Asclepiadei, Praxagorei, Erasistratei, ita ipsi Acronei ab Acrone primo Empirica disciplina scriptore, vel a Critone, Philistione, Serapione cognomenta traxere, qui Acrone quidem juniores, reliquis autem Empiricis vetustiores habentur. & clarius in Introd. cap. 4. Quem locum, quoniam in eo Sexti fit mentio, quem saepe in hoc opusculo ad partes vocabimus, integrum, sed Latine, exhibebimus. Sic ergo ibi Pergamenus: Empiricae praefuit Philinus Cous, qui primus eam a rationali separavit, occasione ab Herophilo praeceptore suo accepta. Cum autem suam haeresin principem esse vellent, Acronem Agrigentinum, quo rationali esset vetustior, ei dedisse initium dixerunt. Post Philinum Serapion Alexandrinus in ea secta floruit. Dein Apollonij duo pater & filius Antiocheni. Hos secuti Menodotus & Sextus exacte eam corroborarunt. Per Sextum intelligere convenit SextumEmpiricumPyrrhoniarum Hypothesium scriptorem; non vero Sextum Chaeronensem MarciPhilosophi praeceptorem & magni Plutarchi e sorore nepotem: fuit enim hic coaetaneus Galeno; & quia Suidas Grammaticus testatur eum fuisse non solum ex familia Pyrrhonia, sed etiam Scepticorum libros decem reliquisse, viri docti crediderunt eundem illum esse, cujus hodie extant Pyrrhoniarum Hypothesium libri tres, & adversus Mathematicos libri decem: cum tamen cognomen Empirici quod constanter in omnibus Codicibus Græcis Manuscriptis occurrit, contrarium doceat, & eum esse evincat, cujus in Empiricorum catalogo Galenus mentionem facit. Quid quod ipse Antoninus alterum Sextum dogmaticum fuisse testatur, quando de eo scribit, doctum se ab illo, talia dogmata per quae, ea quae in vita necessaria occurrebant, moderari poterat. Nec contrarium suadere potest Suidas Grammaticus, haut raro circa nomina falsus; cujus etiam testimonium si admitteretur, dici posset Sextum Chæronæum historice solum Pyrrhonia tractavisse instar Laërtij; cum ex singulis Sexti Empirici capitibus pateat, eum ipso sensu & sententia Scepticum fuisse. Sed ut ad Empiricos redeamus, Sextum, qui in ordine eorum celebris fuit, si audiamus, distincti multis modis a Scepticis fuerunt; nec ulla omnino ratione, uti a multis perperam factum fuit, cum ijs confundi possunt. Hæc enim ejus verba sunt lib. 1. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. 34. Quoniam experientiam, quae circa Medicinam versatur, eandem nonnulli esse jaejunt, cum Scepticapbilosophia: Scire nos oportet, experientiā illam, si afferat incerta comprehendi non posse, neque eandem esse cum Scepsi. Sed necSceptico convenientem ejufmodiSectam esse. Prop-ius ad Scepticos accessere, qui in ordine Medicorum Methodici dicti sunt, quorumque institutum fuit, signis contemptis, nec caussis multum inspectis, ad duas communitates, quas laxum & strictum vocabant, præ cæteris attendere. Fidem facit Sextus loco modo citato ita loquens: Methodus una ex omnibus medica artis sectis, in incertis quidem temerarie se non gerere videtur, nec tantum sibi arrogare ut comprehensibilia sint ea, nec ne, pronunciet: sed apparentia sequens, ex ijs quod utile videatur, accipere, eandem quam Scepticî insistens viam. Dicebamus enim antea, vitam communem, qua etiam Scepticus utitur, quadruplicem esse: quæ videlicet partim in natura instructione versetur, partim in coactu passionum, partim in constitutione legum & consuetudinum, partim in traditione artium. Quemadmodum igitur ex coactu passionum Scepticus à siti quidem ad potum deducitur, & à fame ad cibum, & ad aliquid ex ijs itidem: sic & Methodicus, medicus à passionibus ad consentanea & congrua dirigitur: à consspissatione quidem & condensatione ad laxationem, etc. & vice versa à laxatione & effluvio, ad ejus repressionem. &c. Ea autem quæ natura sint aliena, ad ea, quæ secundum naturam cogere eum venire, vel hinc patet, quod etiam canis, simulac impegerit ei aliquis palum, ad eum extrahendum festinet. Ac ne singula enumerans, fines hypotyposis prætergrediar, omnia puto quæ à methodicis ita dicuntur, referri posse ad coactum illum, eamque vim, quam afferunt nobis passiones, & ea quae secundum naturam, & ea quae praeter naturam sunt. Sed & in his conveniunt inter se hae duae institutiones, quod utraque opinationem omnem à se removeat, utraque indifferenter verbis utatur. Quemadmodum enim Scepticus utitur hac voce, Nihil definio: hac item, Nihil comprehendo: ita & Methodicus usurpat communionem & vocem inquirere ac similes indifferenter, sic ergo & hoc nomen monstratio citra opinationem accipit pro ea actione, qua nos à passionibus apparentibus, & quae secundum & quae praeter naturam sunt, ad ea, quae consentanea & congrua esse videntur, deducimur. Vnde liquet prosessionem eorum, qui in Medica arte Methodici dicuntur, majorem cum Scepsi affinitatem habere, quam ullas alias sectas medicae artis. Haec Sextus. Per quos haec secta Methodicorum constituta fuerit, & quinam in ea floruerint, ignorare nos non finit Galenus, quando loco postremo citato ita loquitur: Methodicen Themison Laodicenus Syrus incepit, qui ab Asclepiade rationali occasiones nactus, ad Methodicae Sectae inventionem se contulit. Thessalus Trallianus eam absolvit. Post hos Mnaseas, Dionysius, Proclus, Antipater. In ea autem de quibusdam differenter, Olympiacus Milesius, Menemachus Aphrodisseus, & Soranus Ephesius. Ductoris hujus familiae, Themisonis nempe, meminit quoque Plinius lib. 29. Nat. Hist. cap. 1. & clariusSenecaEpist. 95. Alia est Hippocratis Secta, alia Asclepiadis, alia Themisonis.
units.tr: Next we must treat of the Empirics, who are, as it were, the companions of the Sceptics. Galen often pairs them with the Sceptics, notably in his book On the Simple Medicines and Faculties, chapter 1: Some certainly think that the essence of a faculty cannot be known, as do the Sceptic philosophers and those who are called Empirics among the physicians. Likewise in On the Empirical Subfiguration, chapter 13: Moreover, he will shun a multitude and length of words, but will speak few words and rarely, as Pyrrho the Sceptic was accustomed to do. For he, having despaired of finding the truth, which he had long sought in vain, hesitated over each thing and no longer sought the rationale of his actions, but followed what was evident. So, as the Sceptic is in all the duties of life, so the Empiric is in medicine: by no means proud or ambitious, not greedy for glory, not walking affectedly, not with artificial gestures, but wholly sound within and without, such as Timon says Pyrrho was. From these words it is clear that those who were commonly called Empirics, if we believe Galen, cherished the same views in medicine as those who were properly called Sceptics did in all the other disciplines. Who was the father and forerunner of these men, the same writer teaches in the preface of his work On the Empirical Subfiguration: All the cultivators of the Empirical method, refusing the name derived from Hippocrates, preferred to be named from a state of mind, just as the philosophers, because they cling to each thing, are called Sceptics in Greek. Therefore they are not named after Acron, the first writer of the Empirical discipline, or after Criton, Philistion or Serapion, as the other Hippocratics, or the Asclepiadeans, Praxagoreans and Erasistrateans, took their names from their founders. Acron is regarded as the earliest, and the others as later than he. And more clearly in the Introduction, chapter 4. Since in that passage Sextus is mentioned, whom we shall often call to our side in this little work, we shall set out the whole passage, though in Latin. Thus Pergamenus says there: Philinus of Cos, who first separated it from the rational school, presided over the Empirical school, having taken the occasion from his teacher Herophilus. But when they wished their heresy to be regarded as the first, they said that it began with Acron of Agrigentum, who was older than the rational school. After Philinus, Serapion of Alexandria flourished in this sect. Then the two Apollonii, father and son, of Antioch. Following these, Menodotus and Sextus strictly strengthened it. By Sextus we must understand Sextus Empiricus, the writer of the Outlines of Pyrrhonism, not Sextus of Chaeronea, teacher of Marcus the philosopher and nephew of the great Plutarch through his sister. For this man was a contemporary of Galen. And since Suidas the grammarian testifies that he was not only of the Pyrrhonian school but also left behind ten books of the Sceptics, learned men have believed that he is the same man whose three books of Pyrrhonian Outlines and ten books Against the Mathematicians survive today. Yet the surname Empiricus, which constantly occurs in all the Greek manuscripts, shows the contrary, and proves that he is the man whom Galen mentions in his catalogue of the Empirics. Moreover, Antoninus himself testifies that the other Sextus was a dogmatist, when he writes that he had been taught by him such dogmas, through which he could regulate the things that were necessary to occur in life. Nor can Suidas the grammarian, who is not infrequently wrong about names, persuade us of the contrary; and even if his testimony were admitted, it could be said that Sextus of Chaeronea treated the Pyrrhonian matters only historically, like Laertius. For it is plain from the individual chapters of Sextus Empiricus that he was a Sceptic in his very feeling and opinion. But to return to the Empirics: if we listen to Sextus, who was famous in their ranks, they were distinguished from the Sceptics in many ways, and by no means can they be confused with them, as many have wrongly done. For these are his words in the first book of the Pyrrhonian Outlines, chapter 34: Since some assert that the experience which is concerned with medicine is the same as Sceptic philosophy, we must know that this experience, if it says that uncertain things cannot be grasped, is not the same as Scepticism. But nor is such a sect suitable to the Sceptics. Closer to the Sceptics are those who in the order of physicians were called Methodists, whose method was, the signs being disregarded and the causes not much examined, to attend above all to two communities, which they called the loose and the tight. Sextus, speaking in the place just cited, confirms this: Of all the sects of the medical art, the Method alone seems not to act rashly in uncertain matters, nor to claim so much for itself as to pronounce whether those things are comprehensible or not; but following appearances, it takes from them what seems useful, pursuing the same path as the Sceptics. For I said before that common life, which the Sceptic also uses, is fourfold: namely, it consists partly in instruction by nature, partly in the compulsion of the passions, partly in the establishment of laws and customs, and partly in the transmission of the arts. Just as, therefore, from the compulsion of the passions the Sceptic is led from thirst to drink, and from hunger to food, and to something of the same kind, so also the Methodist physician is directed from the passions to what is fitting and suitable: from constriction and condensation to relaxation, and so on, and conversely from relaxation and discharge to its restraint, and so on. That those things which are contrary to nature drive us to those which are according to nature is shown even by this, that a dog, as soon as someone has struck it with a stake, hastens to pull it out. And, not to enumerate each thing and go beyond the limits of an outline, I think that all the things which the Methodists call so can be referred to that compulsion, and to that force which the passions bring upon us, both those which are according to nature and those which are against nature. But in these matters the two schools also agree with each other, in that each removes from itself all opinion, and each uses words indifferently. For just as the Sceptic uses this expression, I define nothing, and likewise this, I comprehend nothing, so also the Methodist uses to enquire into the common and the like words indifferently. So too the Methodist takes this word demonstration, without opinion, for that action by which we are led from the apparent passions, both those according to nature and those against it, to those which seem fitting and suitable. Whence it is clear that the profession of those who are called Methodists in the medical art has a closer affinity with Scepticism than any other sect of the medical art. These are Sextus' words. By whom this sect of the Methodists was founded, and who flourished in it, Galen does not let us remain ignorant, when in the last passage cited he speaks thus: Themison of Laodicea in Syria began Methodism, who, having taken occasion from Asclepiades the rationalist, betook himself to the invention of the Methodist sect. Thessalus of Tralles completed it. After these came Mnaseas, Dionysius, Proclus, Antipater. Among those who differed in some points were Olympiacus of Miletus, Menemachus of Aphrodisias, and Soranus of Ephesus. Pliny also mentions the founder of this family, namely Themison, in book 29 of the Natural History, chapter 1, and more clearly Seneca, Letter 95: The sect of Hippocrates is one thing, that of Asclepiades another, that of Themison another.

units.la: Dubito an eum in animo habuerit Juvenalis Satira X.
units.tr: I doubt whether Juvenal had him in mind in Satire X.

units.la: Quot Themison agros autumno occiderit uno.
units.tr: How many fields Themison destroyed in one autumn.

units.la: Videtur sic quidem Medico incomparabili Joanni Huernio lib. 1. Instit. Medic. cap. 1. sed poëtæ scopus obstare videtur, Themisoni alios enim quosdam, sua ætate, flagitiis etiam celebres conjungit. Astipulatur Vetus Scholiastes, qui ad præsentem versum hæc habet: Themison archiater illius temporis, cui detrahit. Quantus autem Themison, de quo loquimur, fuerit, docet Athenæus lib. 7. Deipnos. Themison Antiochi regis deliciæ, non solum in publicis hominum conventibus ac celebritatibus voce præconis renunciabatur, Themison Macedo, Antiochi regis Hercules, verum indigena sacra illi omnes faciebant, acclamantes, Themisoni Herculi: & quoties ex illustribus viris quisquam sacrificabat, aderat ille, seorsim in lecto cubans, leonis pelle vestitus, arcum Scyticum ferens, clavamque tenens. Alios, quorum Galenus meminit, prolixius non examinamus; factum hoc sæpius ab ijs, qui Medicorum historiam scripserunt; ad hoc Methodici non fuerunt.
units.tr: This seems indeed to be the view of the incomparable physician Johannes Heurnius, in book 1 of the Institutions of Medicine, chapter 1. But the poet's aim seems to stand in the way, since he links with Themison certain others of his own age, notorious even for their crimes. The old scholiast agrees, who on this line has this: Themison, the chief physician of that time, whom he disparages. How great Themison, of whom we speak, was, Athenaeus teaches in book 7 of the Deipnosophists: Themison, the darling of King Antiochus, was proclaimed by a herald's voice not only in public gatherings and celebrations of men, Themison the Macedonian, Hercules of King Antiochus, but all the natives performed sacred rites for him, shouting, To Themison Hercules. And whenever any of the illustrious men sacrificed, he was present, reclining apart on a couch, clothed in a lion's skin, carrying a Scythian bow and holding a club. We do not examine at length the others whom Galen mentions; this has been done more often by those who wrote the history of physicians; but the Methodists did not belong to this.

units.la: CAPUT NONUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Quis finis Scepticismi fuerit. Vbi etiam de Ataraxia agitur.
units.tr: What the end of Scepticism was. Where ataraxia is also discussed.

units.la: CUm vero omnia propter finem fiant, eumque quelibet professio ac disciplina sibi proprium, ac ultimo assequendum, propositum habeat, Sceptici quoque & Pyrrhonis Sectatores, Scopum sibi propositerunt; in quem collinearent & ad quem assequendum omnia destinarent. Is fuit ataraxia, quæ à Sexto Empirico lib. 1. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. 4. definitur, vacuitas perturbationis in animo & tranquillitas. Quam quomodo Pyrrhonius assequatur, ex re est discere ex eodem Sexto libro laudato cap. 12. ubi ita loquitur: Dicimus etiamnum finem esse Sceptici imperturbatum mentis statum, circa ea quæ ad opinationem spectant, & in coactis moderationem in ferendis affectionibus. Incipiens enim Philosophari, ad phantasias discernendas & comprehendendas, quanam sint veræ, quæ falsæ, ut perturbatione mentis careret, incidit in æqualia contrariis in partibus momenta rationum: quæ quum dijudicare non potuissent, assensum retinuerunt: etc. at hanc assensus retentionem, quasi fortuito imperturbatus mentis status consequutus est, tanquam umbra corpus. Scepticis Pyrrhonisque familiaribus, præiverant
units.tr: Since all things are done for the sake of an end, and every profession and discipline has its own aim, to be finally attained, the Sceptics and the followers of Pyrrho also set before themselves a goal, at which to aim and toward which to direct everything. This was ataraxia, which Sextus Empiricus, in Book 1 of the Pyrrhonian Outlines, chapter 4, defines as freedom from disturbance in the soul and tranquillity. How the Pyrrhonist attains it we learn from the same Sextus, in the book already cited, chapter 12, where he speaks thus: We say that the end of the Sceptic is an undisturbed state of mind concerning those things that belong to opinion, and moderation of feelings in matters that are forced upon us. For when he began to philosophise, in order to distinguish and grasp the appearances, which are true and which false, so as to be free from disturbance of mind, he fell upon equal weights of arguments on opposite sides; and since they could not judge between them, they withheld assent: etc. But this retention of assent was followed, as if by chance, by an undisturbed state of mind, as a shadow follows a body. The Academics had gone before the Sceptics and Pyrrhonists, and were familiar to them.

units.la: Academici, qui pariter diu antea ataraxian intenderant, sibique propositerant. Ignorare nos non finit Cicero itain Lucullo scribens: Sed quaero quando ista fuerint in Academia vetere decreta, ut animum sapientis commoveri & conturbari negarent. & ibidem de Academicis veteribus loquens dicit: Mediocritates illi probant,& in omni permotione naturalem volebant esse quendam modum. Quibus verbis exprimere videtur Sexti moderatam passionem: omnium vero mortalium beatissimi fuissent Academici pariter atque Sceptici, testibus quoque poëtis, & inter eos Menandro atque Philemone, si quod intendebant, & per accidens, ut Sextus modo innuit, assequebantur, semper atque in omnibus indipisci potuissent. Sed quam animo fluctuaverint in iis quoque, in quibus securi atque tranquilli maxime esse debuissent, idem Sextus innuit, quando loco jam saepius citato ita loquitur: Neque tamen omnino quietum esse & ab omni molestia abesse Scepticum existimamus, sed externorum quorundam impulsu inquietari dicimus. Nam algere nonnunquam eum, & sitire, & huiusmodi alia pati videmus. Difficile enim esse hominem exuere, suo exemplo docet ipse Pyrrho apud Laërtium. Quanquam enim medicamenta putria & sectiones, atque ustiones ulceri cuidam suo adhibitas tanta tulit constantia, ut, ne quidem supercilia contraxerit; itemque navigans, cum tempestate acti dejecti-ores ores essent, ipse tranquillo animo porcellum in navi edentem ostenderit, dicendo sapientem imitari debere hanc illius securitatem: cum alias tamen à cane invaderetur, repellere eundem instituit, eique, à quo arguebatur, dixit: Quam difficile est penitus hominem exuere; teste, post Androclem apud Eusebium, Diogene Laërtio. Quod cum sectatores, Pyrrhonij ab eo dicti, diligentius ad animum revocassent, pro duplici imperturbatione duplicem finem sibi proposuerunt: moderatam scil. & proprie dictam imperturbationem: Illa intendebatur in illis, quae ex opinatione pendebant, haec vero in coactis.
units.tr: The Academics, who likewise had long before aimed at ataraxia and set it before themselves, go before them. Cicero, writing to Lucullus, does not let us remain ignorant: But I ask when these things were decreed in the Old Academy, that they denied the mind of the wise man could be moved or disturbed. And in the same place, speaking of the older Academics, he says: They approved of moderation, and wanted in every agitation some natural measure. By these words he seems to express Sextus's moderate passion. Indeed, the Academics and Sceptics alike would have been the most blessed of all mortals, as the poets also attest, among them Menander and Philemon, if they could have attained, and by accident (as Sextus just now hints), whatever they aimed at, and always and in all things been able to obtain it. But how their minds fluctuated even in those matters in which they ought most of all to have been secure and tranquil, the same Sextus hints, when he speaks thus in the passage already cited so often: Yet we do not think that the Sceptic is altogether quiet and free from all discomfort, but we say that he is disturbed by the force of certain external things. For we see him sometimes shiver with cold, and thirst, and suffer other such things. That it is difficult to strip off the human being, Pyrrho himself teaches by his own example, as reported in Laertius. For although he endured applied medicines, cuttings and burnings to a certain ulcer of his with such constancy that he did not even raise an eyebrow; likewise, when sailing in a storm, while the others were more afraid, he showed a piglet eating in the ship with a calm mind, saying that the wise man ought to imitate this security of his; yet when at another time a dog attacked him, he set about driving it off, and said to the man who had reproached him: How difficult it is to strip off the man completely; this is reported by Diogenes Laertius, after Androcles, in Eusebius. When his followers, the Pyrrhonists so called after him, had brought this to mind more carefully, they set before themselves a twofold end for a twofold imperturbability: namely moderate imperturbability and imperturbability properly so called. The former was aimed at in those things that depend on opinion, the latter in those that are forced upon us.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM. De vocibus ac formulis, quae familiares solent esse Pyrrhoniis & Scepticis.
units.tr: CHAPTER TEN. On the words and formulas that were customarily familiar to the Pyrrhonists and Sceptics.

units.la: EX re quoque est, cum circa Pyrrhonios & Scepticos occupemur, varias formulas, vocesque ijs peculiares, explicare. Ergo primo ut ex Sexto & Laërtio liquet, ijs valde frequenter in ore fuit illud non magis, aut, quod eodem redit, nihil magis: quae locutio est elliptica, ut abunde innuit Agellius, quando lib. 11. Noct. Att. cap. 5. ita scribit: Omniumque rerum fidem veritatemque confusisque signis veri atque falsi ita incomprehensibilem videri ajunt, ut quisquis homo est non praeceps, neque judicij sui prodigus, his verbis uti debeat, quibus authorem Philosophiae istius Pyrrhonem usum esse tradunt: Haud magis sic se hoc habet, quam illo habet modo, aut quam neutro. Cicero simile quid ab Academicis usurpatum fuisse innuit, quando sic in Lucullo scribit: Non eorum, qui clamant nihilo magis vera esse, quam falsa. Ut vero ex Sexto lib. 1. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. 19. constat, solent Scepticorum filij vocem hanc suam proferre, non affirmantes ipsam omnino veram atque indubitatam esse, sed solum secundum illud quod ijs apparebat. Recte amplius observavit Laërtius, eosdem Scepticos locutionem hanc nunquam positive, sed semper negative accipere. Secundo peculiaris quoque Scepticorum vox fuit àphasia, recte eodem Sexto libro jam laudato: quanquam autem Aristocles apud Eusebium eam accipere videtur pro Epocha, teste tamen Sexto est discessus ab ea, quae generaliter phasis dicitur. Sumitur enim apud Scepticos Phasis duobus modis, Generaliter & Specialiter. Illo modo sumpta, est vox quae poni aut tolli quid significat, hoc vero modo considerata, est vox quae aliquid ponit tantum significat. Tertio frequenter Scepticis in ore esse solet illud, Nihil definio, quod cum ex Pyrrhonijs quis proferret, tantundem teste Sexto volebat innuere, ac si sic diceret: Ego ita nunc affectus sum, ut nihil eorum, quae sub hanc quaestionem cadunt ponam dogmatice aut tollam; quod cum dicit, quid sibi appareat de rebus propositis, non enunciative cum persuasione pronunciat, sed solum affectionem suam exprimit. Ex eo autem quod nihil definiebat Scepticus, existebat arrepsias pathos, ut eleganter loquitur Laërtius. Est vero arrepsia proprie cum neutram in parte mentem vergimus aut inclinamus. Nam Répo, ut Græcæ linguæ peritis ignotum esse non potest, vergo est, quomodo & non uno loco à Cicerone redditur; huic proxima est doriftia, quam quanquam Galenus initio libelli, qui de optima disciplina inscribitur, idem valere censet, atque Epocham; à Sexto tamen definitur; Passio intellectus secundum quam nec ponimus quid nec tollimus eorum, quæ dogmatice quæruntur. Quarto inter eosdem Scepticos sæpissime & hoc audiebatur; non comprehendo: item; Omni orationi oratio æqualis opposita est. Quinto usitatissimæ quoque ijsdem erant sequentes dubitandi formulæ: fortasse & non fortasse: licet & non licet: fieri & non fieri: de quibus cum prolixius agat Sextus libro primo, pluribus ijs immorari nolumus. Laërtius Scepticis amplius adiaphorian tanquam peculiarem vocem tribuere videtur. Cæterum in eadem narratione rectius Aristocles substituit apatheian. Adiaphoria enim Zenoni erat propria, ut Pyrrhonis affectis apatheia. Ignorare non sinit Cicero, cujus verba ex Lucullo notatu dignissima sunt: Zenoni summum bonum est in his rebus neutram in partem moveri, quæ ἀδιαφορία dicitur ab ipso: Pyrrho autem ea ne sentire quidem sapientem, quæ ἀπάθεια nominatur.
units.tr: It is also worth explaining, since we are dealing with the Pyrrhonists and Sceptics, the various formulas and expressions peculiar to them. First, as is clear from Sextus and Laertius, the phrase non magis (or, which comes to the same thing, nihil magis, "nothing more") was on their lips very often. It is an elliptical expression, as Aulus Gellius clearly indicates in book 11, chapter 5, of the Attic Nights, where he writes: They say that the trustworthiness and truth of all things appear so incomprehensible, with the signs of true and false confused, that whoever is a man, not rash and not prodigal of his judgment, ought to use those words which they report the author of this philosophy, Pyrrho, used: "It is no more so than it is otherwise, or than neither." Cicero suggests that the Academics used something similar, when he writes in the Lucullus: Not of those who cry out that nothing is more true than false. As is clear from Sextus, book 1 of the Pyrrhonian Outlines, chapter 19, the sons of the Sceptics are accustomed to utter this phrase of theirs, not affirming that it is altogether true and beyond doubt, but only according to how it appeared to them. Laertius further observed rightly that these same Sceptics never took this expression positively, but always negatively. Second, aphasia [ἀφασία] was also a word peculiar to the Sceptics, as Sextus rightly says in the book already cited. Although Aristocles in Eusebius seems to take it to mean epochē (suspension), yet, according to Sextus, it is a departure from what is generally called phasis (assertion). For among the Sceptics phasis is taken in two ways, generally and specifically. In the first sense it is a word signifying that something is posited or removed; in the second sense it is a word that merely signifies that something is posited. Third, the phrase I define nothing (nihil definio) was frequently on the lips of the Sceptics. When one of the Pyrrhonists uttered it, according to Sextus he meant as much as if he had said: "I am now so affected that I neither posit nor remove dogmatically any of those things that fall under this question." When he says this, he does not pronounce in an assertive manner with conviction about what appears to him concerning the matters proposed, but merely expresses his own state. Now from the fact that the Sceptic defined nothing there arose arrepsias pathos [ἀρρεψίας πάθος] (a state of not being inclined), as Laertius elegantly puts it. Arrepsia properly means when we do not incline or lean the mind to either side. For repo, as is not unknown to those skilled in the Greek language, means "to incline," as Cicero also renders it in more than one place. Closest to this is doriftia [δωρίφτια?], which Galen, at the beginning of the little book entitled On the Best Teaching, thinks means the same as epochē; yet Sextus defines it thus: a state of the intellect according to which we neither posit nor remove anything of those things which are dogmatically inquired into. Fourth, among these same Sceptics the following was also very often heard: I do not comprehend; likewise: To every argument an equal argument is opposed. Fifth, the following formulas of doubt were also in very common use among them: perhaps and perhaps not; it is permitted and it is not permitted; it happens and it does not happen. Since Sextus treats these at greater length in book 1, we do not wish to dwell on them more. Laertius seems to attribute to the Sceptics also adiaphoria as a word peculiar to them. Elsewhere in the same account Aristocles more correctly substitutes apatheia (freedom from feeling). For adiaphoria was proper to Zeno, as apatheia was to the disposition of Pyrrho. Cicero does not allow us to be ignorant of this; his words from the Lucullus are most worthy of notice: For Zeno, the highest good is to be moved in neither direction in those things which he calls adiaphoria [ἀδιαφορία]; but Pyrrho says that the wise man should not even perceive those things which are called apatheia [ἀπάθεια].

units.la: CAPUT UNDECIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER ELEVEN.

units.la: Proponuntur decem modi, quibus antiqui Sceptici niti solent, ut ad suam tum Epocham, tum ataraxian pervenirent.
units.tr: The ten modes which the ancient Sceptics were accustomed to rely on, in order to reach both their epoché and their ataraxia.

units.la: CUM vero Sceptici antiqui ad suam ataraxiam pervenerint per Epocham, quæ erat assensus retentio, propter parem vim, aut paria momenta in oppositis rebus, seu in utraque contradictionis parte; non possumus non, ex Sexto Empirico breviter ostendere quomodo Pyrrhonia familia Epocham astruere conata fuerit. Fecit autem hoc per modum Epochæ (alias etiam lógos, sive tópos dicitur) qui nihil aliud erat, quam methodus qua utebatur, ad inhibendam omnem assensionem, præter eam, per quam inclinabatur ad Phantasiam determinatam. Quos modos quo distincte atque dilucide proponere queamus, pro variarum partitionum ratione, varie expendemus. Omissis autem modis specialibus, generales secundum Sextum, sunt aut veteres aut novi; illi vi; illi antiquis, hi vero recentioribus Scepticis in usu fuerunt. Antiquis decem modi familiares erant, de quibus hoc capite ordine. Primus antiquorum modus desumebatur ex animalium varietate: quoniam enim varia animalium temperamenta sunt, Scepticus quoque colligebat varias esse phantasias atque affectiones, ita ut quod videtur uni insuave atque noxium, illud alteri sit suave atque utile; cumque nulla ratio sit cur hominis phantasia aliorum animalium phantasiæ præferatur, pariter inferebat, assensum circa rerum naturas suspendendum esse. Secundus modus desumptus est ex hominum differentia: quandoquidem enim dissimilia sunt hominum judicia de rebus eadem, propter varietatem regionis, ætatis, valetudinis, atque temperamenti, colligit Scepticus inducendam esse Epocham. Tertius modus petitus est à diversa dispositione ejusdem etiam sensus organi: nam cum modo hoc, modo ejus contrarium gratum aut ingratum palato sit, infert Scepticus Epocham circa externa subjecta inducendam esse. Quartus modus oritur, ex varia dispositione sensus ejusdem, servato etiam eodem temperamento, quod accidit v. c. ex somno & vigilia, motu & quiete, audacia & timore, omnique affectu vario. Sic oculus dum in navi movetur, judicat rem moveri, quæ eidem quiescenti quiescere videtur, simulque dormiens exiguum strepitum ingentem fragorem existimat, etc. quæ omnia apud se expendens Scepticus,confugit ad suam Epochàm, circa externorum subjectorum naturam. Quintus modus notabatur in diversa ratione intervallorum, locorum, ac positionum. Sic quippe Scepticus aliquis apud se ratiocinari solet: res una eademque quæ eminus exigua apparet, propius intuenti magna videtur, proque situ vario, nullo etiam discrimine ratione intervalli obveniente, varios induit colores; sed cum hæc uni eidemque rei accidant, quis non potius circa eam Epochàm foveat, quam temeraria atque præcipiti assertione deridendum sese ipsi vulgo propinet? Sextus modus existit per mixtiones rerumque confusiones. Scepticus scil: Epochàm, ut compendiosissimam ad ἀταραξίαν viam ampleƈtitur, quia nihil purum sub sensum cadit, & omnia confusa sunt, incertumque est unde species atque apparentia prodeant: ad hoc longo usu didicit, unam eandemque rem aliis atq; aliis rebus conjunƈtam, pro diversitate rerum, quibus conjungitur, diversimode sensum affecre. Septimus oritur à quantitatibus & diversis constitutionibus rerum sensibilium. Quoniam enim Scepticus cognoscit v. c. ramenta cornu caprini apparere alba, eadem vero conjunƈta videri nigra; itemque telam madidam uno modo nigriorem, altero vero candidiorem apparere, ad hoc pro vario si-tu ue quantitate res aliter atq; aliter apparere
units.tr: WHEN the ancient Sceptics reached their ataraxia through epoché, which was the holding back of assent because of an equal force, or equal weight, in opposed matters, that is, in either side of a contradiction, we cannot fail to show briefly, from Sextus Empiricus, how the Pyrrhonian school tried to establish epoché. It did this by means of a mode of epoché (also called a logos or topos), which was nothing other than the method it used to check all assent, except that by which it was inclined toward a determinate impression. We shall weigh these modes in various ways, according to the arrangement of the various divisions, so that we may set them out distinctly and clearly. Setting aside the special modes, the general modes, according to Sextus, are either old or new. The old ones were in use among the ancients, the new among the more recent Sceptics. The ancients had ten familiar modes, which are discussed in this chapter in order. The first mode of the ancients was derived from the variety of animals. Since the temperaments of animals differ, the Sceptic also inferred that impressions and affections differ, so that what seems unpleasant and harmful to one thing seems pleasant and useful to another. And since there is no reason why the impression of man should be preferred to the impressions of other animals, he likewise concluded that assent about the natures of things must be suspended. The second mode is taken from the difference among men. For since human judgments about the same things are unlike, on account of differences of region, age, health and temperament, the Sceptic concludes that epoché must be induced. The third mode is drawn from the differing disposition of the same sense-organ. For since at one time a thing is pleasing to the palate and at another time its opposite is, the Sceptic infers that epoché must be induced concerning external objects. The fourth mode arises from the varying disposition of the same sense, even when the same temperament is kept, as happens, for example, from sleep and waking, motion and rest, boldness and fear, and every varying affection. Thus the eye, while it is moving in a ship, judges that the thing is moving which seems to be at rest to the same eye when it is at rest; and likewise a man asleep thinks a faint sound a huge crash, and so on. The Sceptic, weighing all these things within himself, takes refuge in his epoché concerning the nature of external objects. The fifth mode was noted in the different relations of intervals, places and positions. For a Sceptic is accustomed to reason with himself in this way: one and the same thing, which appears small from a distance, seems large to one who looks at it closely, and it takes on various colours according to its varying position, although no difference arises from the interval itself. But since these things happen to one and the same thing, who would not rather cherish epoché about it than expose himself to the crowd's ridicule by a rash and headlong assertion? The sixth mode exists through mixtures and confusions of things. The Sceptic, that is, embraces epoché as the shortest way to ataraxia, because nothing pure falls under the senses, all things are confused, and it is uncertain whence the species and appearances proceed. To this he has learned by long experience that one and the same thing, joined with different things according to the variety of those things with which it is joined, affects the sense in different ways. The seventh arises from the quantities and diverse constitutions of sensible things. For since the Sceptic knows, for example, that the filings of goat's horn appear white but look black when they are mixed together, and likewise that a wet cloth appears blacker in one way and whiter in another, and that, according to the varying position or quantity, things appear differently, and some things seem to harm and others to benefit, he thinks he is driven by a certain necessity to epoché.

units.la: {y} parare, & videri modo nocere, modo prodesse; existimat se necessitate quadam adigi ad Epocham. Octavus modus pertinet ad relationem: quoniam Scepticus unam eandemque rem videt, prout ad aliud atque aliud refertur, modo magnam modo parvam, albescentem & nigrescentem, meliorem ac deteriorem, etc. videri, quo mente quieta fruatur, putat sibi confugiendum esse ad sacram Epochæ anchoram. Nonus modus consistit in raro ac crebro contingentibus: quandoquidem enim Scepticus, in rerum pretijs censendis occupatus, videt frequentiam earum illa jam minuere, & succedaneam raritatem mox iterum augere, certo sibi persuadere incipit, rerum neque pretium neque naturam certo explorari posse. Decimus modus, qui pertinet maxime ad moralia, consideratur in diversis institutis, moribus, legibus, persuasionibus, atque decretis Sectarum inter Philosophos: nam præter Epochàm Scepticus, in quo acquiescat, nihil invenire potest, quando videt unum idemque censeri tum urbanum tum inurbanum, justum & injustum, turpe & honestum, credibile & incredibile, etc. Tantum quidem de decem antiquorum Scepticorum modis, per quos ad Epochàm præ cæteris visi fuerunt duci, aut saltem inclinari.
units.tr: ...to prepare, and to seem at one time harmful and at another beneficial; he thinks he is driven by a certain necessity to epoché. The eighth mode pertains to relation. For since the Sceptic sees one and the same thing appear, according as it is referred to one thing or another, now large and now small, whitish and blackish, better and worse, and so on, he thinks that to enjoy a quiet mind he must take refuge in the sacred anchor of epoché. The ninth mode consists in things that happen rarely and frequently. For when the Sceptic, busy in estimating the prices of things, sees that their abundance now diminishes them and their scarcity soon increases them again, he begins to persuade himself firmly that neither the price nor the nature of things can be surely determined. The tenth mode, which pertains chiefly to moral matters, is considered in the diverse institutions, customs, laws, beliefs and decrees of the sects among the philosophers. For, apart from epoché, in which he may rest, the Sceptic can find nothing when he sees that one and the same thing is judged both courteous and discourteous, just and unjust, base and honourable, credible and incredible, and so on. So much concerning the ten modes of the ancient Sceptics, by which they were seen to be led, or at least inclined, to epoché above all others.

units.la: CAPUT DUODECIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWELVE.

units.la: Quo proponuntur quinque alij modi, quibus re- centiores Sceptici usi sunt.
units.tr: In which five other modes are set out, which the more recent Sceptics used.

units.la: Recentiores Sceptici, cum compendio studerent, omnibusque modis discipulis suis succurrere laborarent, pro decem modis praecedenti capite propositis, quinque supposuerunt. Primus ergo recentiorum Scepticorum modus desumptus fuit a multiplici Philosophorum dissidentia. Ita enim secum Scepticus ratiocinari solet, quomodo veri quid in rebus Philosophicis cognosci posset, cum circa unam eandemque rem tot vulgo inveniantur sententiae, quot capita, Philosophique, non tantum ab alijs, verum etiam a se invicem multoties dissideant; praestat proinde nihil definire. Secundus modus est ille, qui in infinitum rejicit. Pyrrhonius quia probationis probationem petit, idque in infinitum, primaque principia, quae indemonstrabilia esse solent, sibi demonstrari vult; mavult Epochae amplecti, quam acquiescere in tali scientia, quae in infinitum extendi non possit, demonstrationesque suppeditare eorum, quae omnium Philosophorum calculo indemonstrabilia haberi solent. Tertius modus petitus a relatione, haud longe recedit ab octavo modo superiori capite propósito, nisi quod relatio a recentioribus ecentioribus Pyrrhonijs fuerit restricta & limitaa: quoniam enim videbant relationem à natura rarijs modis mutari posse, per relationes secundum ios, eoque modo magnam exoriri incertitudinem, assensum circa omnia suspendere cœperunt. Quartus modus à familia hac vulgo vocari solet hypotheticus, seu suppositorius: propterea enim dogmata pleraque rejicere, aut saltem circa illa nihil definire Sceptici filius solet, quod judicet illa inniti suppositioni, sive propositionibus minime probatis, aut demonstratis. Quintus modus ab ipsis Pyrrhonijs communiter vocari solet diállelos, sive alternatorius. Si enim Sceptico confirmaveris solem lucere, quia dies est: mox respondebit, hanc probationem similiter confirmatione indigere à sole petita, ut sint ejusdem ordinis atque conditionis duæ hæ propositiones: Est dies, quia sol lucet: & Sol lucet, quia est dies. Et tantum quidem de quinque modis ad Epocham ducentibus, quas recentiores Sceptici compendij ergo invenisse, suisque Sectatoribus proposuisse videntur. Idem hi, ut Sextus innuit lib. 1. Pyrrho. Hypoth. cap. 16. duos amplius modos communissimos ac valde generales habuerunt. Nam cum omne quod comprehenditur, aut ex se ipso, aut ex alio comprehendatur; primo habuerunt modum, quo instituerunt nihil posse ex se ipso comprehendi. Sic enim colligere solent: Cum controversia de sensibilibus & intellectualibus, qua quæritur utrum sensui potius, quam ratiocinationi credenum sit per omnia sit injudicabilis, liquet neque sensui neque ratiocinationi credendum esse.Non datur enim aut judex tertius, aut criterium cui credere possis, nullusque potest esse judex in propria sua causa. Deinde nihil quoque comprehendi posse ex alio, ita visi sunt colligere. Si ex alio quid cognoscitur,aut deveniendum est in infinitum, aut deveniendum est ad aliquid, quod ex se ipso comprehendatur: sed cum utrumque absurditatem implicet, tutissimum est subsistere, & nihil definire.
units.tr: The more recent Sceptics, wishing to be brief, and labouring in every way to help their disciples, added five modes to the ten proposed in the preceding chapter. The first mode, then, of the more recent Sceptics is taken from the manifold disagreement of the philosophers. For the Sceptic is accustomed to reason thus: how could anything true be known in philosophical matters, when about one and the same thing there are as many opinions as there are heads, and the philosophers disagree not only with others but very often with one another? It is better, therefore, to define nothing. The second mode is that which rejects things to infinity. The Pyrrhonist, because he asks for a proof of the proof, and that without end, wants even the first principles, which are commonly held to be indemonstrable, to be demonstrated for him; he prefers to embrace suspension of judgement rather than to rest in a science which cannot be extended to infinity, and which cannot supply demonstrations of those things which by the reckoning of all philosophers are regarded as indemonstrable. The third mode, drawn from relation, does not depart far from the eighth mode proposed in the superior chapter, except that the relation was restricted and limited by the more recent Pyrrhonists; for, seeing that relation can be changed in many ways by nature, through relations according to individuals, and that in this way a great uncertainty arises, they began to suspend assent about all things. The fourth mode is commonly called by this school the hypothetical, or suppositional: for the Sceptic is accustomed to reject most dogmas, or at least to define nothing about them, because he judges that they rest on a supposition, that is, on propositions that have not been proved or demonstrated. The fifth mode is commonly called by the Pyrrhonists themselves the diallelus, or alternating. For if you should assert to a Sceptic that the sun is shining because it is day, he will presently reply that this proof likewise needs confirmation drawn from the sun, so that these two propositions are of the same order and condition: It is day, because the sun shines; and the sun shines, because it is day. And so much for the five modes leading to epochē, which the more recent Sceptics seem to have discovered for the sake of brevity and proposed to their followers. The same men, as Sextus hints in book 1 of the Pyrrhonian Hypotyposes, chapter 16, also had two further very common and very general modes. For since everything that is comprehended is comprehended either from itself or from another, first they had a mode by which they established that nothing can be comprehended from itself. For they are accustomed to conclude thus: since the controversy about sensible and intellectual things, in which it is asked whether the senses or reasoning are to be trusted rather than the other, is wholly undecidable, it is clear that neither the senses nor reasoning are to be trusted. For there is neither a third judge nor a criterion in which you could put your trust, and no one can be judge in his own cause. Next, they seem to have concluded that nothing can be comprehended from another. If something is known from another, either one must proceed to infinity, or one must arrive at something which is comprehended from itself; but since both imply absurdity, it is safest to stop and define nothing.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM TERTIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER THIRTEEN.

units.la: Quæ Scepticorum fuerit sententia distincte ostenditur, speciatimque docetur, quid circa phænomena statuerint.
units.tr: The opinion of the Sceptics is set out distinctly, and it is shown in particular what they held concerning phenomena.

units.la: Deinde quæ Scepticorum (sub quibus hic Academicos non minus quam Pyrrhonios comprehendimus) sententia fuerit, aliquanto diligentius inquirendum.
