Doctissimus Gassendus, in eximio opere, quoante annos paucos exist imationem suam adversus Renati Cartesij insultus asseruit, existimare videtur, Pyrrhonem, & quot quot ipsum imitati sunt, inter actiones vitæ, & inquisitionem quisitionem veritatis ita distinxisse, ut quod ad vitae actiones spectaret, non esse habendam indifferentiam censuerint, sed obtemperandum patriis legibus, necessitatibus consulendum, exhibenda officia, unoque verbo omnia agenda, quae seu privatim, seu publice, boni & viri & cives agunt. Quod ad inquisitionem autem veritatis, ita distinxerint, ut discrimen statueretur inter phænomena ea quae sensibus apparent, cujusmodi sunt calor ignis, dulcedo mellis, universe, catera; & nomina ea, quae mente intelliguntur, ut sunt quae dicuntur natura, causae externae atque proxima, & proprietates earundem rerum. Denique cum incerta haberent, quae posterioris sint generis: admiserint tamen quae prioris sunt, nisi si quando animi gratia, facere libuit dogmaticis insolentibus negotium. In summa eorum dubitationes solum de rebus revera incertis, & quas disquirere esset operae pretium, non vero de rebus apparentibus, & de quibus facere controversiam nihil prodest.
units.tr: Next, what the opinion of the Sceptics was (under which name we include the Academics no less than the Pyrrhonists) must be examined somewhat more carefully. The most learned Gassendi, in his excellent work, which a few years ago defended his own opinion against the attacks of René Descartes, seems to think that Pyrrho, and all who imitated him, drew the distinction between the actions of life and the inquiry after truth in such a way that, as regards the actions of life, they judged that indifference should not be held, but that one should obey the laws of one's country, attend to needs, perform duties, and, in a word, do all the things which good men and citizens do, whether in private or in public. As for the inquiry after truth, they drew the distinction so that a difference was set up between phenomena, which appear to the senses, such as the heat of fire, the sweetness of honey, and the like, and those notions which are understood by the mind, such as what are called nature, external and proximate causes, and the properties of the same things. Finally, since they held the latter kind to be uncertain, they nevertheless admitted the former kind, unless perhaps, when they wished to amuse themselves, they chose to give trouble to the dogmatists. In sum, their doubts concerned only things that are really uncertain and that it would be worth the trouble to investigate, not apparent things, and it is of no use to raise controversy about those.

units.la: Sed quod pace viri in Philosophia exercitatissimi dictum sit, haec per omnia haut vera videntur: quanquam enim concedimus ea, quae circa actiones notat, ut alibi ostendemus: quae tamen de apparentibus observat, per omnia probare non possumus. Illi enim, qui nomen Scepticorum tulerunt, sic de omnibus dubitarunt, ut pariter etiam quaestionem moverint de iis, quae vulgo Phenomena dicuntur, ut non solum ex ipso Laertio & Sexto, postea ad partes vocandis liquet, sed ex omnibus quoque illis, qui jam olim eos,ut in naturam ipsam injurios,insectati fuerunt.Seneca ep. 88.Circa eadem fere Pyrrhonij versantur & Megarici, & Eretrici, & Academici, qui novam induxerunt scientiam nihil scire.Hac omnia in illum supervacuum studiorum gregem conijce.Illi mihi non profuturam scientiam tradunt, hi spem omnis scientiae eripiunt: satius est supervacua scire, quam nihil.Illi non proferunt lumen, per quod acies dirigatur adverum: hi oculos mihi effodiunt.Epictetus apud Arrianum lib. 1. c. 5. disputationem adversus Academicos ita auspicatur:
units.tr: But, with all respect to a man so skilled in philosophy, what has been said seems in every respect not quite true. For although we concede what he notes about actions, as we shall show elsewhere, what he observes about apparent things we cannot prove in every respect. For those who bore the name of Sceptics doubted all things in such a way that they also raised the question about those things which are commonly called phenomena, as is clear not only from Laertius and Sextus, who are to be brought forward later, but also from all those who long ago attacked them as injurious to nature itself. Seneca, letter 88: The Pyrrhonists, the Megarians, the Eretrians and the Academics concern themselves with almost the same things, those who introduced the new science of knowing nothing. Throw all of these into that useless crowd of scholars. The former offer me a science that will not profit me, these snatch away all hope of any science: it is better to know useless things than nothing. The former do not hold forth a light by which the eye may be directed towards the truth; these gouge out my eyes. Epictetus, in Arrian, book 1, chapter 5, begins his disputation against the Academics thus:

units.la: Si quis,inquit, disputando se opponit impendio perspicuis, contra illum adferre rationes, non est facile, quibus diversum ei persuadeatur. Ille dicit Pyrrhonios spem omnis scientiae eripere; hic de Academicis, quod opposuerint se impendio perspicuis. Eadem perhibent Christiani Doctores, antiqui Patres. Clemens Alexandrinus lib. 8. Stromat. Apud Pyrrhonios est epocha, quae nihil vult esse firmum & stabile. Tertullianus lib. 3. de Anima cap. 17. Quid agis Academice procacissime? totum vitae statum evertis, omnem naturae ordinem turbas, ipsius Dei providentiam excaecas, qui cunctis operibus suis intelligendis, incolendis, dispensandis, fruendisque fallaces & mendaces dominos praefecerit sensus. Lactantius lib. 3. cap. 5. de Arcesila, mediae Academiae conditore loquens, ait: Doctrina ejus est nihil scire.etc.Cum aut nihil sciat, quae perversitas, quaeve insolentia est, ob id ipsum se Philosophum constituere, propter quod cæteros tollat? Augustinus lib. 19. De civitate Dei cap.ult. Academicis novis incerta sunt omnia. Eadem occurrunt apud Eusebium, ut ante cum de Pyrrhone egeremus, adductis ejus verbis, ostendimus. Fateor Sextum & Laertium, docere quidem genuinos Scepticos contendisse Phænomena à se admitti; sed ijdem addunt, eos volentes nolentes ea admisisse, sibique voluisse libertatem relinqui ambigendi & assensum suspendendi circa omnia, quæ de illis enunciabantur. Sic enim Laertius in Pyrrhonis vita: Nam quum se nihil definire ajunt; omniq; rationi contrariam obiectam esse rationem, ea ipsa, & definiunt & proferunt. Adversus quos illi respondent. Atque ea, quæ patimur, ut homines fatemur. Nam & quod dies sit, quod sit generatio, quodq; viväimus, & cætera in hunc modum, quæ in vita nostra manifesta sunt, scimus: cæterum in iis quæ dogmatici asserunt, ea se ratione comprehendere dicentes, velut de incertis, neutiquam consentimus, solas vero passiones (liberter) agnoscimus. Nam & nos videre confitemur, nosque intelligere scimus, verum quo pacto videamus aut intelligamus, ignoramus. Quin quod hoc album videatur narrando dicimus, non asserendo an revera ita sit. & iterum eodē loco: Rursus illos dogmatici vitam etiam tollere asserunt, dum omnia ex quibus vita constat, evertunt. Ac contra eos illi mentiri asseverant: non enim visum se auferre, sed quomodo se habeat vis videndi ignorare. notare se dicunt. Atque quod apparet, ponimus, non quod tale, quale cernitur, &c. Nam quod urit ignis, sentimus, verum an habeat incendendi naturam, non pronuntiamus: quodque moveatur quispiam, & quod pereat, videmus, verum ista quo pacto fiant, ignoramus. Similia occurrunt apud Sextum lib. 1. Pyrr. Hypoth. cap. 10. Qui autem ajunt Scepticos tollere apparentia, ea quae a nobis duci solent, audrvisse mihi non videntur. Non enim ea evertimus, quae per phantasiam patientem invitos nos ad assensionem adducunt; ea autem sunt apparentia. Sed cum quaerimus an tale sit ipsum subjectum, quale apparet, apparere quidem concedimus: quaerimus autem & ambigimus non de ea re, quae apparet, sed de ea, quod dicitur de re apparente: hoc autem aliud est, quam quaestionem movere de ipsa re apparente. Verbi gratia apparet nobis mel dulce: dulcedinem enim ipsam sensu percipimus: sed quod dulce sit quod ad rationem & intelligentiam attinet, ambigimus. Quod si etiam aperte circa apparens quaestiones moveamus, non ita has movemus, quasi apparentia avertere velimus: sed Dogmaticorum Philosophorum temeritatem arguentes. Si enim tales sunt rationis impostura, ut etiam apparentia tantum oculis mostris surripiat, quomodo non in incertis suspectam eam habere debemus, ne eam sequamur, in temeritatem labamur?
units.tr: If anyone, he says, in disputing sets himself against things that are most evident, it is not easy to bring arguments against him by which he might be persuaded otherwise. The one says that the Pyrrhonists snatch away all hope of knowledge; this one says of the Academics that they have set themselves against things that are most evident. The Christian teachers, the ancient Fathers, say the same. Clement of Alexandria, Stromata book 8: Among the Pyrrhonists there is suspension of judgement, which wishes nothing to be firm and stable. Tertullian, On the Soul, book 3, chapter 17: What are you doing, most shameless Academic? You overturn the whole state of life, you throw the whole order of nature into confusion, you blind the providence of God himself, who has set deceitful and lying senses as masters over all his works to be understood, inhabited, arranged and enjoyed. Lactantius, book 3, chapter 5, speaking of Arcesilaus, founder of the Middle Academy, says: His doctrine is to know nothing. etc. Since he knows nothing, what perversity or what insolence is it that, for that very reason, he sets himself up as a philosopher, on account of which he disparages the rest? Augustine, On the City of God, book 19, last chapter: For the New Academics everything is uncertain. The same things occur in Eusebius, as we showed before when we dealt with Pyrrho, by citing his words. I grant that Sextus and Laertius teach that the genuine Sceptics contended that phenomena were admitted by them; but the same authors add that they admitted them whether willing or unwilling, and that they wished freedom to be left to them to doubt and to suspend assent about all those things which were asserted about them. For thus Laertius in the life of Pyrrho: For when they say that they define nothing, and that every argument is opposed by an argument of equal weight, they themselves both define and propose these very things. Against these the others reply. And what we undergo, we admit as men. For we know that it is day, that there is generation, that we live, and other such things which are manifest in our life; but in those things which the dogmatists assert, claiming to grasp them by reason, as if they were uncertain matters, we by no means agree; we acknowledge only the passions (gladly). For we too confess that we see, and we know that we understand, but how we see or understand, we do not know. Indeed, when we say in narrating that this appears white, we do not assert whether it really is so. & And again in the same place: Again, the dogmatists assert that they even abolish life, while they overturn all the things of which life consists. And against them the others affirm that they lie: for they do not take away sight, but are ignorant of how the power of seeing stands. They say they take note. And we posit what appears, not that it is such as it is perceived, etc. For we feel that fire burns, but whether it has the nature of burning we do not pronounce; and we see that someone is moved and that someone perishes, but how these things come about we do not know. Similar things occur in Sextus, book 1 of the Outlines of Pyrrhonism, chapter 10. Those who say that the Sceptics abolish appearances, which are usually brought forward by us, seem to me not to have heard correctly. For we do not overturn those things which, through a passive impression, lead us unwilling to assent; and those are appearances. But when we ask whether the subject itself is such as it appears, we concede indeed that it appears; but we ask and doubt not about the thing which appears, but about what is said of the apparent thing, and this is something other than to raise a question about the apparent thing itself. For example, honey appears sweet to us: for we perceive the sweetness itself by sense; but as to whether it is sweet as far as reason and understanding are concerned, we doubt. And if we do openly raise questions about what appears, we do not raise them as if we wished to overturn appearances, but in arguing against the rashness of the dogmatic philosophers. For if reason's deceit is such that it snatches away even appearances from our eyes, how should we not hold it suspect in uncertain matters, lest by following it we slip into rashness?

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM QUARTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FOURTEEN.

units.la: De ætiologia, quam Onesidemus primo excogitavit.
units.tr: On the aetiology which Onesidemus first devised.

units.la: Cum vere omnis scientia incumbat ætiologiæ seu causæ reddltioni, dirutaque ætiologia necessum sit ipsam scientiam corruere: Onesidemus, teste Sexto Empirico, octo modos adinvenit, quibus dogmatica æftiologia refellatur, funditusque evertatur Philosophia, quæ se causæ indagatricem profitetur. Excogitavit autem Onesidemus octo modos æetiologicos: inter duos primus hic erat, quæ non apparent haut satis comprehendi possunt per ea quæ apparent: quomodo nova Roma, etiam apud eos, qui statuunt quid comprehendi posse, minus commode comprehenditur & cognoscitur per antiquam Romam. Secundus, ex variis causis atque rationibus, quæ proferri possent atque deberent, ut plurimum non nisi unica profertur: effectus vero si similis causæ est, cuivis similis, non vero uni tantum, judicio ipsorum Dogmaticorum. Tertius modus respicit illa, quæ fiunt ordinate: in iis enim, cum causæ, quæ afferuntur, non ostendant ordinem, causarum sufficientium loco censeri haut quaquam possunt: quoniam fatentibus ipsis Dogmaticis, non satis est nosse causas, nisi pariter ordo, qui inter illas intercedit, cognoscatur. Quartus
units.tr: Since all true knowledge rests on aetiology, that is, on the giving of causes, and once aetiology is overthrown the science itself must necessarily collapse, Onesidemus, according to Sextus Empiricus, devised eight modes by which dogmatic aetiology is refuted and Philosophy, which professes to investigate causes, is utterly overturned. Onesidemus devised eight aetiological modes. The first of these was this: things that do not appear cannot be sufficiently grasped through things that appear, just as the new Rome, even for those who hold that something can be grasped, is less conveniently grasped and known through the old Rome. Second, of the many causes and reasons that could and should be offered, usually only one is offered; yet if an effect is similar to a cause, it is similar to anything, not to one cause only, by the judgement of the Dogmatists themselves. Third mode concerns those things that happen in an orderly way: in these, since the causes that are offered do not show the order, they can by no means be counted as sufficient causes, since, as the Dogmatists themselves admit, it is not enough to know the causes unless the order that lies between them is also known. Fourth

units.la: est hic; non possunt caussæ, quæ vulgo tanquam sufficientes adferri solent, admitti, quia nescimus utrumque;& quæ non apparent,ac nunquam sunt conspecta, eodem modo se habent, quo apparent, itemque an eodem modo affecta sint aliena, quo nostra. Quintus occupatur in evertendis suppositionibus vulgo quidem receptis, cæterum dubijs atque incertis, maxime in labefactandis duobus his axiomatibus: Omnia appetunt bonum. Quæ sunt æqualia uni tertio, illa inter se æqualia sunt. Sexto ita ad suam Epocham per caussarum eversionem contendebat Onesidemus: Supponuntur in suppositionibus sæpe numero illa, quæ facile ubique, & à quovis deprehendi possunt: sed præmittuntur quæ ijs repugnant, quamvis æque probabilia fuerint. Dein sæpe non proseruntur rationes atque conjecturæ nisi in unam partem, cum tamen in utramque æque probabiliter adferri possint. Septimo ita progredi solent plerumque: rationes particulares, quæ afferuntur, repugnant tum hypothesibus, tum phænomenis, sive illis, quæ apparent: adhoc apud Philosophos nonnullos aliquando propositio universalis credibilior est, quam particularis, aliquando vero contra. Octavo atque postremo, cum dubia fere strui consueverint per æque dubia, concludebat Onesidemus nihil æque mentem tranquillare, atque decantatam ac tutissimam Epocham: & tantum quoque de modis ætiologicis, Onesidemo à Sexto Empirico attributis.
units.tr: is this: the causes that are commonly offered as sufficient cannot be admitted, because we know neither of the two things; and things that do not appear and have never been observed are not necessarily in the same condition as those that appear, nor is it certain whether they are affected by other things in the same way as ours are. Fifth is concerned with overturning suppositions that are commonly accepted but are doubtful and uncertain, chiefly by weakening these two axioms: All things seek the good; things that are equal to a third thing are equal to one another. Sixth, Onesidemus pressed towards his Epoche by overturning causes in this way: in suppositions, things are often assumed that can easily be detected everywhere and by anyone, while things that contradict them are put forward, though they are equally probable. Then, often, reasons and conjectures are advanced only on one side, although they can be brought forward with equal probability on the other. Seventh, arguments generally proceed in this way: the particular reasons that are advanced contradict both the hypotheses and the phenomena, that is, those that appear; moreover, among some philosophers a universal proposition is sometimes more credible than a particular one, and sometimes the reverse. Eighth and last, since doubtful matters are usually built up from equally doubtful ones, Onesidemus concluded that nothing calms the mind so much as the celebrated and most secure Epoche; and so much on the aetiological modes ascribed to Onesidemus by Sextus Empiricus.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM QUINTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: An Scepticisti Sectam constituere Possint?
units.tr: Can the Sceptics Constitute a Sect?

units.la: EX illis, quæ præcedentibus capitibus proposita sunt, liquere arbitror, quæ Pyrrhoniorum, Scepticorum primipilarium, sententia fuerit, antequam eos ab Academicis destinctum imus, subsistendum aliquantum circa quæstionem, quæ jam olim quoque controversa inter eos fuit, Philosophos per certas familias sive sectas distribuere studuerunt. Cum ergo nulla dogmata secta Pyrrhoniorum habeat, [contenta quippe vivit bella sua epocha] quæsitum fuit, an possint Pyrrhonii certam quam sectam aut Philosophantium classem constituere. Varias opiniones innuit circa hoc quæsitum Laërtius in proœm. operis de vitis Philosophorum, quando ita per interpretem suum loquitur: Ea vero (Secta) quæ Pyrrhonia dicitur, propter obscuritatem à plurimis repudiatur. Hanc ipsam tamen plerique ex parte Sectam esse dicunt, ex parte negant. Eam denique Sectam dici ajunt, quæ ratione aliquam juxta id quod apparet & in promptu est, sequitur aut sequi videtur: juxta quod & Scepticam non incongrue Sectam appellabimus. Verum si Sectam intelligimus appellationem ex his dogmatibus constantem non jam appellabimus Sectam: neque enim dogmata habet. Hactenus Laërtius: cujus verba si diligenter expenderimus atque contulerimus cum ijs, quæ occurrunt apud Sextum Empiricum lib. 1. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. 8. per distinctionem erit respondendum. Dupliciter enim nomen hæresios sive Secta, quo Laërtius pariter atque Sextus utuntur, accipi potest. Vel enim est comprehensio plurium dogmatum inter se consonantium ut definitur à Galeno, aut ut loquitur Clemens Alexandrinus lib. 8. Stromat. consecutio dogmatum: pro quo Laërtius dicit, consecutio in dogmatibus. & Sextus consecutio secundum plura dogmata, secundum se invicem & apparentia, & consequentiam habentia. & sic Scepticus Sectam nequaquam constituere potest, cum nulla dogmata habeat, sed circa omnia atque singula Epocham foveat; imo non potest aut Scepticus ad Philosophiam referri, aut Scepticus Philosophi nomen ferre, unde & recte Aristocles apud Eusebium dicit; Ego quidem existimo eam tioni mereri nomen Philosophiæ, quæ tollit Philosophiæ principia: eoque respiciens Sextus lib. 1. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. 2. valde circumspecte dicit, quomodo sceptici distinguatur à Philosophandi modis, qui sunt ei si nitimi Si vero nomen Sectæ latius accipiatur, & ut Sextus loquitur, sit institutio quæ secundum Phainomena rationi alicui adhæreat, illa ratione monstrante quomodo recte vivere videri possimus [illud recte non solum ad virtutem referendo, sed simplicius dictum intelligendo] & ad assensus retentionem tendente, Sceptica potest dici Sectam constituere: adhæret enim rationi cuidam, quæ secundum id quod apparet, atque sub sensum se profert, demonstrat vivere non solum secundum patrios ritus atque leges, verum etiam secundum proprias affectiones. Latioris hujus notationis ratione habita, Sextus cap. 2. jam ante laudato, Scepsin Philosophiæ nomine condecorat, quam cap. 9. ejusdem, Scepticam facultatem vocat.
units.tr: I think it is clear from what has been set out in the preceding chapters what the view of the Pyrrhonists, the chief Sceptics, was. Before we distinguish them from the Academics, we must dwell for a while on the question, long disputed among them, of whether philosophers ought to be distributed into definite families or sects. Since the Pyrrhonist sect holds no dogmas [for it lives content with its own epoche], the question has been raised whether the Pyrrhonists can constitute a definite sect or class of philosophers. Laërtius, in the preface to his work on the lives of the philosophers, hints at various opinions on this question when he speaks through his translator as follows: The sect called Pyrrhonian is rejected by most people on account of its obscurity. Yet many say that it is in part a sect and in part not. Finally, they say it is a sect that follows, or seems to follow, some rational principle in accordance with what appears and lies at hand; and by this we may not inappropriately call it the Sceptical sect. But if we understand a sect as a body of doctrines, then we shall not call it a sect, for it has no doctrines. So far Laërtius. If we weigh his words carefully and compare them with what Sextus Empiricus says in book 1 of the Pyrrhonian Outlines, chapter 8, the answer must be given by a distinction. For the name hairesis or sect, which Laërtius and Sextus alike use, can be taken in two ways. Either it is a combination of several mutually consistent dogmas, as Galen defines it, or, as Clement of Alexandria says in book 8 of the Stromata, a sequence of dogmas; for which Laërtius says a sequence in dogmas, and Sextus a sequence according to several dogmas, related to one another, to appearances, and to consequence. In this sense the Sceptic can by no means constitute a sect, since he has no dogmas but maintains epoche concerning all things, each and every one. Indeed, the Sceptic can be referred neither to philosophy nor be called a philosopher. Hence Aristocles, quoted by Eusebius, rightly says: I think that only that which abolishes the principles of philosophy deserves the name of philosophy. With this in view, Sextus, in book 1 of the Pyrrhonian Outlines, chapter 2, very carefully says how the Sceptic is distinguished from the modes of philosophizing that are opposed to him. But if the name of sect is taken more broadly, and, as Sextus puts it, is a teaching that adheres to some reasoning in accordance with appearances, that reasoning showing how we may seem to live rightly [where "rightly" is referred not only to virtue but is understood in a plainer sense] and tending to the suspension of assent, then Scepticism may be said to constitute a sect. For it adheres to a certain reasoning which, in accordance with what appears and is presented to the senses, demonstrates that we should live not only according to ancestral customs and laws, but also according to our own feelings. Taking account of this broader meaning, Sextus in the chapter already cited, chapter 2, honours Scepsis with the name of philosophy, while in chapter 9 of the same work he calls it the Sceptical faculty.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM SEXTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SIXTEEN.

units.la: In quibus Academici à Pyrrhonijs distincti fue- rint?
units.tr: In what respects the Academics were distinguished from the Pyrrhonists?

units.la: Dein expendere convenit, an, & in quibus Phyrrhonij distincti fuerint ab Academicis.
units.tr: Next we should consider whether the Pyrrhonists were distinguished from the Academics, and in what respects.

units.la: Quanquam enim illos cum omnibus ijs componere possemus exemplo Sexti, quos ad Scepsin viam stravisse, aut, eam quocunque modo fovisse constat, nominatim cum Cyrenaicis & Megaricis; sufficit tamen eos comparasse cum solis Academicis, tanquam inter Scepticos præ alijs celebrioribus. Differentiam paucis verbis proponit Aulus Gellius, quando lib.11. Noct.
units.tr: Although we could compare the Pyrrhonists with all those whom Sextus' example shows to have paved the way to skepticism, or to have fostered it in some manner (among them, by name, the Cyrenaics and the Megarians), it is enough to compare them with the Academics alone, as the most famous of the Sceptics among the others. Aulus Gellius sets out the difference in a few words, when in book 11 of the Attic Nights, chapter 5, he speaks thus: The Academics indeed hold that it cannot be grasped that anything can be grasped, and that nothing can be decided, though they do decide it; the Pyrrhonists say that it does not even seem true in any way that nothing seems to be true.

units.la: Att. cap. 5. ita loquitur: Academici quidem ipsum illud nihil posse comprehendi, quasi comprehendunt, & nihil posse decerni quasi decernunt: Pyrrhonij ne id quidem ullo pacto videri verum dicunt, quod nihil esse verum videtur. Accuratius, pleniusque momenta hujus differentiae persequitur Sextus lib. 1. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. 33. quo loco ut cum ratione annotat, exiguum discrimen intercessisse inter mediam Academiam, quam Arcesilas constituit, & Pyrrhoniam familiam, ita novam Academiam a Pyrrhonia secta in tribus potissimum differre atque dissentire observat. Nam primo Academici novi aliquid non solum melius & pejus esse statuerunt, verum etiam verosimilius: Sceptici contra, indifferentiae patroni, nihil aut bonum aut malum agnoscere voluerunt, existimantes unum prae alio probabilius esse non posse, vitamque solum, ne viderentur nihil agere, sine ulla opinatione instituerunt. Secundo novi Academici phantasiarum verisimilium gradus constituerunt, alias dicendo verisimiles tantum esse; alias verisimiles & probabiles, atque denique verisimiles & probabiles, sed cum quadam mentis distractione: Sceptici contra crediderunt omnes eas aequales esse, ad fidem obtinendam vel non obtinendam. Academici, tertio in vita hac verosimili utebantur, quod a Scepticis viventibus citra ullam opinationem, atque eo modo sequentibus leges, consuetudines, atque affectiones, acerrime oppugnabantur. oppugnatum fuit. Et hæc quidem à Sextò annotantur circa differentiam, quę inter novos Academicos & Scepticos intercessit, cum vero is brevitatis studio plura non subjecerit, nos ejus exemplo, prolixius non inquiremus in illa, per quæ nova Academia à Pyrrhonis familia divisa fuit.
units.tr: Sextus, in book 1 of the Pyrrhonian Hypotyposes, chapter 33, follows the points of this difference more exactly and fully. There, as he sensibly notes, only a slight distinction lay between the Middle Academy, which Arcesilaus founded, and the Pyrrhonian school. He observes that the New Academy differed and dissented from the Pyrrhonian sect chiefly in three respects. First, the New Academics held that some things are not only better or worse but also more probable, whereas the Sceptics, the advocates of indifference, would acknowledge nothing as either good or bad. They thought that one thing could not be more probable than another, and they arranged their life without any opinion, only so that they would not seem to do nothing. Second, the New Academics set up degrees of probable appearances: some they called merely probable, others probable and persuasive, and finally probable and persuasive but with a certain distraction of the mind. The Sceptics, on the contrary, believed that all of these were equal in winning or not winning assent. Third, the Academics followed probable life in living, whereas the Sceptics, who lived without any opinion and followed laws, customs and feelings in that way, were most fiercely attacked for it. These are the points which Sextus notes about the difference between the New Academics and the Sceptics. Since, in his zeal for brevity, he did not add more, we, following his example, will not inquire at greater length into those matters by which the New Academy was divided from the school of the Pyrrhonists.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM SEPTIMUM
units.tr: CHAPTER SEVENTEEN

units.la: Sceptici publice ludibrio habiti fuerunt.
units.tr: The Sceptics were held up to public ridicule.

units.la: ULterius priusquam pergimus dissimulare non possumus, Academicos non minus atq; Pyrrhonios, quod vulgo persuasum esset eorum vivendi rationem respondere ijs, quæ perpetuo ad aliorum fastum contundendum (ut dicebant) in ore habebant; publicum ludibrium & fabulam fuisse. Plutarchus in eximio opusculo, quod Colotes inscribitur, meminit male feriati cuiusdam ac petulantis hominis, qui Socrati, cum diceret se nihil certo scire, fœnum loco panis obtulit, sarcastice amplius ex barbato magistro sciscitando, cur cibum potius in os, quam aurem imponeret. Quam vulgo etiam ridiculus fuerit Scepticus, vix uno asse dignus, egregie ostendit Lucianus sub finem elegantissimi dialogi, qui inscribitur vitarum auctio; ut haut mirandum sit Arrianum in Commentario ad Epictetum professione Stoicum, ex mente Stoicorum, qui Scepticis infestissimi esse solent, Academicos false ridere atque traducere. Verba eius, quoniam notatu digna sunt ex lib. 5. Differt. Epist. cap. 28. hic Latina ex versione Schegkij exhibemus: Bone vir quid agis? Quotidie vis te ipsum confutare, ac non tandem missa facis frigida haec & ieiuna epicheremata. Quando vesceris, quonam admoves panem? ad os scilicet, & non ad oculum. Lavans quo descendis? Ollam, quando unquam appellasti craticulam? Aut tudiculam, veru? Quod si horum alicuius effem servus, etiamsi me quotidie verberibus excoriaret, nihilominus hoc tormento ipsum excruciarem. Age puer oleum affer in balneum, ego vero garum apponerem. Veni, infunde capiti. Quid hoc? Ah quam simillimum istud fuit oleo, nec internosci species potuit, ita te Dij servent Porrige huc ptisanam. Afferrem paropsidem plenam oxygaro. Nonne petij ut dares ptisanam. Ita, ita Domine. Est illud ptisana, & non potius oxygarum? quid illud aliud esset quam ptisana, cape, subodorare, accipe & degusta. Unde discrimen, mihi here, nosti, siquidem sensus nostri fallantur. Tres aut quatuor consentientes si haberem famulos, citius efficerem, ut ipse se suspenderet aut rumperetur prae moleslia, quam sententiam relinqueret aut mutaret. Nunc vero per libidinem nobis illudunt omnibus a natura concessis, rebus ut entitentes, verbis tamen & oratione pro nullis habentes. Non ingratum autem fore Lectori credo, si ex Numenio, lepidam hestoriam unice huc facientem retuleo: ex ea enim clare liquet Scepticum aliter domi vivere, aliter docere in Schola. Ita ergo Numenius, citatur quoque a Canterolib. 6 Nov.Lect.cap.18. Latine loquitur: Cum Lacydes Archesilai sectator esset paulo sordidior, penarij sui curam inter alia gerebat diligenter, ita ut nemini praeter ipsum id nec aperire liceret nec claudere: quum autem clauem suam circumferre nollet, eam solebat, postquam penarium clausisset, in concava quadam tabella reponere, & eam cum anulo obsignasset, rursum devolvere. Quam astutiam cum servi animadvertissent, simulac foras ille prodierat, ipsi quoque penario aperto, postquam quantum voluerant, comederant, biberant, atque abstulerant, clamdebant, obsignabant, anulum, non secus atque ille, devolvebant. Lacydes vero cum vasa, quę discedens plena reliquerat, post reditum vacua reperiret, nec quid hoc sibi vellet, scire posset: postquam audivit Arcesilaum acatalepsiam asterere, hoc ipsum sibi in penu contingere arbitratus est. Hac igitur arrepta occasione: Arcesilaum sectabatur, atque ejus opinionem contra Zenonem & Stoicos [ nam hi contrariam tuebantur sententiam ] defendebat strenue: cumque aliquādo quendam ex condiscipulis ad se deduxisset, re-
units.tr: Before we go on, I cannot pass over the fact that the Academics, no less than the Pyrrhonists, were commonly held to be a public laughing-stock and a joke. It was widely believed that their way of life did not match the things they constantly had on their lips to crush the pride of others (as they said). Plutarch, in his excellent little work entitled Colotes, mentions a certain idle and impudent fellow who, when Socrates said he knew nothing for certain, offered him hay instead of bread, sarcastically asking the bearded teacher why he put food into his mouth rather than his ear. Lucian shows at the end of his most elegant dialogue, Vitarum auctio, how generally ridiculous the Sceptic was, scarcely worth a single as. So it is no wonder that Arrian, in his Commentary on Epictetus, though a Stoic by profession, and following the mind of the Stoics, who are usually most hostile to the Sceptics, mocks and misrepresents the Academics as false. Since his words are worth noting, I give them here in Latin, from the fifth book of the Dissertations, chapter 28, in the version of Schegk: Good man, what are you doing? Every day you want to refute yourself, and yet you have not put aside these cold and empty arguments. When you eat, where do you bring the bread? To your mouth, surely, and not to your eye. When you go down to bathe, what do you call the pot? Have you ever called a gridiron a pot, or a spit a skewer? If I were the slave of any one of these men, even if he flayed me with blows every day, I would still torment him in return. Come, boy, bring the oil to the bath; I will bring the fish sauce. Come, pour it on my head. What is this? Ah, how very like oil it is, and one could not tell the difference. So may the gods keep you safe. Hand me the barley drink here. I would bring a dish full of oxygarum. Did I not ask you to give me barley drink? Yes, yes, sir. Is it barley drink, and not rather oxygarum? What else could it be but barley drink? Take it, smell it, receive it and taste it. Where is the difference, my good man, you know, if indeed our senses are deceived? If I had three or four servants who agreed with me, I would soon bring it about that he hanged himself or burst from vexation rather than give up or change his opinion. But now they mock us with their desires, in every matter given to us by nature, pretending to be concerned with things, yet holding them as nothing in word and speech. I think it will not be unwelcome to the reader if I relate from Numenius a charming story which bears on this point alone, for from it it is clear that the Sceptic lives one way at home and teaches another way in the school. Numenius, who is also quoted by Canter, Novae lectiones, book 6, chapter 18, speaks in Latin as follows: Lacydes, a follower of Arcesilaus, was somewhat careless in his habits, yet he took diligent care of his storeroom among his other concerns, so that no one but himself was allowed to open or lock it. Since he did not wish to carry his key about with him, he used, after locking the storeroom, to place it in a certain hollow tablet, seal it with his ring, and hide it away again. When the slaves noticed this trick, as soon as he had gone out they too opened the storeroom, and after they had eaten, drunk and carried off as much as they wanted, they locked it, sealed it and hid the ring away again, just as he did. But when Lacydes, returning, found the vessels he had left full now empty, and could not tell what this meant, he judged, after hearing that Arcesilaus denied that anything could be comprehended, that this very thing had happened to him in his storeroom. Seizing this occasion, he followed Arcesilaus and vigorously defended his opinion against Zeno and the Stoics, who maintained the opposite view. Once he had brought a certain fellow pupil to his house, he tried to demonstrate the truth of his opinion by the actual fact itself. For he had not received its confirmation from others, but had learned it by his own experience: "I," he said, "lock it, I seal it, I hide the ring, and after I have opened it again I find the ring but nothing else. Why should I not think so, and bid farewell to Zeno and his followers? For I would not say that anyone has entered, since the ring is still inside." Then the other man, when he understood the whole matter, noticed the trick, laughed heartily, and at the same time by laughing exposed the vanity of Lacydes. So from then on Lacydes no longer hid the ring, nor did he believe that his senses were deceived, but rather that he was truly suffering loss, and he seemed to have philosophized to no purpose. Yet his slaves were not so stupid that, once they knew his heresy, they did not openly break the seal, and then put back now one thing, now nothing, thinking that either would suit his opinion. But when he came in and offered a tablet that was unsealed, or sealed in another way, he scolded them; and when they insisted that it was sealed, and that they themselves could see the seal, he showed the contrary; or if the seal was missing, they maintained that he had forgotten to seal it. He declared that he had certainly sealed it and remembered doing so, and that they were mocking him. Then they in turn said that he was mocking them. And when he had removed his opinion, he would also abolish his memory, for that was what his opinion amounted to. While he argued fiercely against these things, they went to a certain Academic and learned what answer they should give. So every day there was a dispute between the slaves and their master, the slaves arguing in the Stoic manner and he in the Academic. Meanwhile nothing was left: not the vessels, not what was in the vessels, nor anything else in the house. At last Lacydes, seeing that he made no progress, sat down himself in front of the storeroom to guard it. And when even so he could not sufficiently protect his goods, he finally said openly: "Boys, we dispute one way in the school, and we live another way." Thus far Numenius.

units.la: ipsa re ipsa opinionis suæ veritatem demonstrare conabatur: quippe cuius confirmationem non ab aliis accepisset, verum ipse expertus didicisset: & quoniam inquiebat, ipse claudo, ipse obsigno, ipse anulum devolvo, ipse postquam iterum aperui, anulum quidem, non etiam alia invenio, quid ni sic sentiam, & Zenonem cum suis valere iubeam? nec enim furem ingredi quemquam dixero, cum sit intus anulus. Tum alter ille, ut rem totam intellexit, animadversa fraude, risit effusissime, simulque ridendo vanitatem eius coarguit. Ita deinceps anulum non devolvebat Lacydes, nec sensus suos falli credebat potius, quam verum sentiebat damnum, frustraque philosophatus videbatur. Veruntamen, nec servi eius tam stupidi erant, ut non, cum eius hæresin cognovissent, aperte iam sigillum rumperent, & nunc aliud, nunc nullum reponerent: quod existimabant utrumque fore ipsius opinioni congruum. At ille cum ingressus non signatam, vel aliter signatam offerret tabellam, eos increpabat: cumque illi vel signatam esse affirmarent, ac sese quidem sigillum conspicere, contra demonstrabant: vel si deesset, ipsum obsignare oblitum suisse contenderent: probe se cum obsignasset, meminisse aiebat, ac se ab ipsis ludi affirmabat. Tum illi vicissim se ab ipso ludi aiebant: qui cum opinionem sustulisset, memoriam quoque aboleret. Hanc enim esse opinionem. Contra quae cum ipse disputaret acriter, ipsi ad Academicum quendam itantes, quid essent responsuri discebant. Itaque disputabatur inter servos ac dominum quotidie, ab illis Stoice, ab his Academice: nec quicquam interim relinquebatur, non vasa, non quae in vasis erant, non aliud quicquam domesticum. Denique Lacides, cum nihil se proficere videret, ante penarium ipse custodiae causla consedit. Cumque nec sic satis tueri sua posset, aperte tandem; Aliter, pueri inquit, haec in schola disputamus, aliter vivimus. hucusque Numenius.
units.tr: Lacydes was not confident in the truth of his opinion on the basis of reasoning alone; he tried to prove it by the very thing itself, the actual event. He had not received the confirmation of his view from others, but had learned it by his own experience. "I," he said, "lock it, I seal it, I put the ring away, and when I open it again I find the ring but nothing else. Why should I not think as I do, and bid Zeno and his followers farewell? For I cannot say that anyone has entered, since the ring is still inside." Then the other man, when he grasped the whole matter, noticed the trick, laughed very loudly, and by laughing at him exposed his vanity. So from then on Lacydes no longer hid the ring away, nor did he believe that his senses were deceived, but rather that he truly suffered loss, and he seemed to be philosophizing to no purpose. Yet his slaves were not so stupid that, once they had learned his heresy, they did not openly break the seal, and then put back now one thing, now nothing, thinking that either would suit his opinion. But when he came in and offered a tablet that was unsealed, or sealed in some other way, he scolded them; and when they insisted that it was sealed, and that they themselves could see the seal, he showed the contrary; or if the seal was missing, they maintained that he had forgotten to seal it. He declared that he had certainly sealed it and remembered doing so, and that they were mocking him. Then they in turn said that he was mocking them. And when he had removed his opinion, he would also abolish his memory, for that was what his opinion amounted to. While he argued fiercely against these things, they went to a certain Academic and learned what answer they should give. So every day there was a dispute between the slaves and their master, the slaves arguing in the Stoic manner and he in the Academic. Meanwhile nothing was left: not the vessels, not what was in the vessels, nor any other household goods. At last Lacydes, seeing that he gained nothing, sat down himself in front of the storeroom to guard it. And when even so he could not sufficiently protect his goods, he finally said openly: "Boys, we dispute one way in the school, and we live another way." Thus far Numenius.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM OCTAVUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER EIGHTEEN.

units.la: An Sceptici ingenio superarint omnes alios Philoso- phos.
units.tr: Whether the Sceptics surpassed all other philosophers in ability.

units.la: Corculum eruditorum Iustus Lipsius lib.2. Manud.ad Philos. Stoicam Diffiert.4. de Scepticis agens pronunciat eos, labore, ingenio, memoria, supra omnes pene philosophos fuisse: Et ne quis dubitet, hanc rationem subijcit: Quid nonne omnia aliorum scita tenere debuerunt & inquirere, si potuerunt refellere? res dicit.Nonne rationes varias, rari, subtiles invenire ad tam receptas, claras, certas, (ut videbatur) sententias evertendas? Nonne & in promtu, ac velut numerato, habere quicquid scripsissent scripsissent tot diversi autores, aut dixissent? Ego vero, quod pace viri doctissimi dictum sit, in alia omnia discedere cogor. Cum enim ex Sexto constet, ijsque quae ante ex illo a nobis allata sunt, generales modos genuinos Scepticos habuisse, quibus oppugnabant omnes disciplinas & quicquid scientiae rationem habere videbatur, in proclivi fuit machinas illas admovere ijs etiam disciplinis, quas a limine non salutaverant, simulac aliquid ad eas pertinens objiceretur: neque enim necesse fuit Scepticoin numerato habere quicquid hac aut illa de re ab aliquo scriptum erat, cum scientiae certitudinem non solum labefactare studuerit, per dissentientium circa hanc illamve thesin multitudinem, verum per multos etiam alios modos antea enumeratos. Ad hoc haut necessarium cuique semper, tanquam digitos explorata habere scita, quae refellere studet; cum multum interfit inter solidam & cum ratione institutam refutationem, atque insectationem & qualemcunque labefectationem, qualis Scepticorum esse solet. Ex Apostoli Judae Epistola notum est, multos, quaecunque non noverunt, vituperare consuevisse. Sceptici omnes alios Philosophos cum scitis atque dogmatibus suis rejiciebant, ignotos licet, quod existimarent ab ijs nihil proponi posse, quod verae liquidaeque scientiae rationem mereretur. Illos enim praecipites fuisse in aliorum sententijs jugulandis, vel ex solo Sexto Empirico constare potest. Quid quod ijsdem familiare fuit, loco argumentorum, convitijs reliquos Philosophos conscindere: eruditionem vero profundam maledicta non arguiunt, sed potius impudentiam. Notum est quod de Timone Suidas perhibet. Verba ejus hæc sunt: Timon Phliasius, & ipse Philosophus fuit, ex secta Pyrrhonis, libros tres scripsit, quos inscripsit Sillos sive Philosophorum vituperationem. Non dicam, quod cum Scepticorum institutum esset scientiæ certitudinem tollere, & sensuum fidem sublevare; simul visi fuerint negare, non solum quæ eruditis omnibus quam explorata sunt, verum etiam quæ certo cognoscuntur ab illis, qui ære nondum lavantur. Arrianus in Dissertationibus Epicteti loco antea laudato: Grati scilicet homines & verecundi, qui cum quotidie pane vescantur, audent negare se scire utrum sit Ceres, aut Proserpina, aut Dis, ut ne dicam, dum fruuntur noctis diesque vicibus alternis, & tempestatibus annii, præterea astris, mari & terra, hominumque opera, ab horum nullo afficiuntur tamen ne minimum quidem, sed duntaxat occasiones ad eoimendam quæstiunculam suam captant, & stomacho suo satisfacere, dum ad balnea se conferunt, student. Ubi cum Stoicus Scepticorum quæstionem, problematis nomine condecoret, abunde ostendit, eorum dogmata & disputandi modum eruditionem præ cæteris excellentem non arguisse. Nisi forte quis Epicteti,
units.tr: Justus Lipsius, in the fourth Dissertation of the second book of his Manuductio ad Philosophiam Stoicam, where he treats of the Sceptics, declares that they were, in labour, in intellect and in memory, almost superior to all philosophers. And lest anyone doubt it, he gives this reason: Must they not have held and examined all the opinions of others, if they were to refute them? Must they not have found various, rare and subtle arguments for overturning such accepted, clear and certain (as it seemed) opinions? And must they not have had at hand, as it were counted out, whatever so many different authors had written or said? I am compelled, with all respect to that most learned man, to say something quite different. For it is established from Sextus, and from what has been cited above from him, that the genuine Sceptics had general modes by which they attacked all disciplines and whatever seemed to have a rational basis of knowledge; so it was easy to bring those engines to bear even on those disciplines which they had not greeted from the threshold, as soon as something pertaining to them was put forward. For the Sceptic did not need to have counted out whatever this or that man had written on this or that subject, since he aimed to shake the certainty of knowledge not only through the multitude of those who disagree about this or that thesis, but also through the many other modes listed earlier. Nor is it always necessary to have at one's fingertips, as it were, the opinions one is trying to refute; for there is a great difference between a solid refutation founded on reason and the attack and carping and whatever sort of undermining the Sceptics are wont to make. From the Epistle of the Apostle Jude it is known that many are accustomed to rail at whatever they do not know. The Sceptics rejected all other philosophers together with their tenets and doctrines, although they were unknown to them, because they thought nothing could be put forward by them that deserved the name of true and clear knowledge. That they were rash in demolishing the opinions of others can be established from Sextus Empiricus alone. And what of the fact that it was familiar to the same men, instead of arguments, to tear the remaining philosophers apart with insults? Yet profound learning is not shown by abuse, but rather by impudence. What Suidas reports of Timon is well known. His words are these: Timon of Phlius was himself also a philosopher, of the school of Pyrrho; he wrote three books, which he entitled Silloi, or the Reviling of the Philosophers. I will not say that, although it was the aim of the Sceptics to remove the certainty of knowledge and to undermine trust in the senses, they were at the same time seen to deny not only what is as well established as anything to all the learned, but even what is known with certainty to those who are not yet washed in the bath. Arrian, in the Dissertations of Epictetus cited above in another place: Surely they are thankful and modest people, who, though they eat bread every day, dare to deny that they know whether it is Ceres or Proserpina or Dis; not to mention that, while they enjoy the alternation of night and day, the changes of the year, moreover the stars, sea and land, and the works of men, they are not in the least affected by any of these, but only seek occasions to pick at their little question and strive, as they go to the baths, to satisfy their stomach. Here the Stoic, by dignifying the Sceptics' question with the name of a problem, amply shows that their doctrines and manner of disputing did not argue a learning surpassing all others. Unless perhaps someone thinks that the testimony of Epictetus, as enemies of the Sceptics, should be rejected. This is certain, and will become clearer later, that the arguments with which the dogmatists are wont to be attacked by the Sceptics are not of such a kind and quality that they could furnish evidence of rare and astonishing learning.

units.la: Epicteti, ut inimici Scepticorum te stimonium reijciendum putet. Hoc certum, & postea liquebit, argumenta, quibus dogmaticos Sceptici oppugnare solent, ejus notae ac commatis non esse, ut indicium rarae atque stupendae eruditionis facere potuerint.
units.tr: Epictetus, as enemies of the Sceptics... (see above; this unit continues the preceding paragraph and is given in full there).

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM NONUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER NINETEEN.

units.la: Quinam subsequentibus seculis jure, sive iniuria, Sceptici habiti fuerint.
units.tr: Who were regarded as Sceptics in the following centuries, rightly or wrongly.

units.la: Consideravimus hactenus Scepticos per varias familias divisos, deinceps videndum quando desierint, quisque eorum errores aut universim aut ex parte resuscitaverint. Seneca iam suo aevo{ videre est apud eum lib.7.Nat. Quaest. cap.ult.} exclamavit; Quis est qui tradat praecepta Pyrrhonis? cum enim omnes homines natura scire desiderent, non nisi paucissimi a se impetrare potuerunt, ut destinato consilio ad ignorantiae praecipitium properarent; multique ingenij maluerunt excrementa adorare, pertinaciterq; defendere, quam se nihil scire profiteri. Et tamen quidam post Senecam, cuius aetate prope compositum fuisse Scepticorum nomen videtur, Sceptices professores esse sustinuerunt. Inter eos principem locum obtinet Ptolemaeus Astronomorum alpha, qui ut recte quoque animadvertit Celius Rhodigin.lib.26. Antiq Lect.cap.14.fi nō genuinus Scepticus extitit, Scepticorum tamen opinioni quam vicinus fuit. Theologiam enim & Physicam, scientiarum reliquarum dominas, contemptui habuit: quod illam præ insigni rerum excellentia humana imbecillitas consequi non queat; hæc vero ob inconstantem perpetuoque fluentem materiam capi minime possit. Ulterius ex recentioribus progressus est Cardinalis Crescentius in libro de docta ignorantia: ac præ alijs Franciscus Sanchez in opusculo, quod inscripsit de multum nobili & prima universali scientia, quod nihil scitur, in quo antiquorum Scepticorum deliria non solum ab ovo revocavit, sed etiam classes, ex quibus argumenta sua petere solent, undiquaque advocato lumine illustrare conatus est, quemadmodum deinceps sigillatim ostendemus. Ut vero hoc seculo peiores quam meliores libri sæpius recudi solent, typographiis uni avaritiæ studentibus, hominumque vitijs servientibus; ita nuper admodum, & quidem in ipsa Hollandia sacrum hoc opusculum ex Sexto collectum recusum suit. Accenseri his cum quibusdam posset Henricus Cornelius Agrippa nisi in Cynica Declamatione de incertitudine ac vanitate scientiarum, post labefactatas omnes disciplinas, contenderet nusquam certi quicquam, perpetui, & divini occuroccurrere, in solidis. Dei eloquiis, atque eminentia verbi divini Aliter de eo existimat maximus Melancthon in epist. editis Leidę anno 1647. in quibus pag. 10. sic scribit: Heri huc venit Tridentinus Cardinalis iturus in Belgium. Ex eius comitatu duo ad me Itali accesserunt, quorum alter mihi librum exhibuit à se scriptum, [dubium quod ei nomen] in quo false & insulse contendit Philosophiam totam, Physicam, & Ethicam incertam esse. Talis est vanitas huius temporis damnare artes, quæ sunt dona Dei, & testimonia de Deo. Scripserat Cornelius Agrippa magus similes artium vituperationes, & in multis Germania locis indocti similibus clamoribus abducunt iuventutem à studijs ut confirment idola. Inter Scepticos à Bellarmino refertur quoq; Erasmus, at per calumniam: quanquam enim alicubi in N.T. ait se toto vitæ tempore nihil aliud didicisse, quam se nihil scire; non tamen eo negat veritatem ullam dari, sed solum eam repertu difficillimam esse, virosq; summos ac doctissimos nullam eruditionem suam æstimare, si illud quod cognoscunt, componant cum ijs, quod ignorant. Ex horum numero ipse quoque Augustinus est, in conclu-sione enim operis, quod contra Academicos scripsit, fatetur se tum agentem trigesimū tertium suę ætatis annum, nondum quicquam percepisse de humana scientia nec tamen desperare. Propius ad Scepticismum vergunt qui disciplinas humana distinguunt in consectarias & demonstrativas; quam distinctionem ut suo loco examinabimus, ita illius authores prodemus, inter quos praeter H.Cardanum, eximius etiam medicus atque Philosophus Fr. Vallesius nomen suum profitetur, ut patet ex eius libro de Sacra Philosophia cap.64.Haut mirandum vero si pauciores Scepticismum in vulgus propalent ac profiteantur: amant enim latere, probantque Arcesilae ac Pyrrhonis institutum, qui, teste Laertio, nullum unquam librum aut scripserunt aut evulgarunt: ad hoc omnibus modis interpolare ac circumscribere ipsam scepsin laborant, atque in statione Semiscepticorum subsistere: ut suo loco, prodendo varios qui hoc agunt, prolixius ostendemus.Quid vero de eximio Philosopho Gassendo exististimandum sit, ambigo.Certe delineans argumentum libri secundi contra Aristotelicam Philosophiam, haec postremo loco dicit: Atque hic praecipuum est, ubi cognitio, scientiaque humana arguitur infirmitatis, ac incertitudinis.Hic est, ubi praecipua iaciuntur Pyrrhonismi fundamenta, stabiliturque maxime illud, NIHIL SCIRI.Quoniam liber, qui diu in exspectatione fuit, nondum prodiit, malo nihil, quam quid temere definire.
units.tr: So far we have considered the Sceptics divided into their various schools; next we must see when they ceased, and who revived their errors, wholly or in part. Seneca, already in his own age (it may be seen in him, book 7 of the Natural Questions, last chapter), exclaimed: Who is there who hands down the precepts of Pyrrho? For although all men by nature desire to know, only a very few could be persuaded to hasten, with a settled purpose, down the precipice of ignorance; and many of unsound mind have preferred to admire their own dregs and stubbornly defend them rather than profess that they know nothing. Yet some after Seneca, in whose age the name of Sceptic seems to have nearly died out, did venture to profess Scepticism. Among them the chief place is held by Ptolemy, the first of the astronomers, who, as Caelius Rhodiginus rightly observes (book 26 of the Antiquae Lectiones, chapter 14, near the end), was not a genuine Sceptic, yet was close to the Sceptical opinion. For he held theology and physics, the mistresses of the other sciences, in contempt, because human weakness cannot attain the former on account of the surpassing excellence of its objects, and the latter cannot be grasped at all on account of its inconstant and perpetually flowing matter. Further on among the more recent writers went Cardinal Crescentius, in his book on learned ignorance; and above all Francisco Sanchez, in the little work entitled On the Most Noble and First Universal Science, which is that Nothing Is Known, in which he not only recalled the follies of the ancient Sceptics from the egg, but also tried to illuminate, with light summoned from every quarter, the classes from which they are accustomed to draw their arguments, as we shall show in detail later. Now, just as in this age the worse books are more often reprinted than the better, since printing houses serve only avarice and cater to human vices, so quite recently this little sacred work, collected from Sextus, was reprinted, and that in Holland itself. Henry Cornelius Agrippa could be counted among these, except that in his Cynical Declamation on the Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences, after overturning all disciplines, he contends that nowhere is there anything certain, perpetual and divine, except in the solid utterances of God and the eminence of the divine Word. The great Melanchthon judges him otherwise, in the letters published at Leiden in 1647, where on page 10 he writes thus: Yesterday there came here a Cardinal of Trent on his way to Belgium. Two Italians from his retinue approached me, one of whom showed me a book written by himself, [the name of which is uncertain] in which he falsely and foolishly contends that the whole of philosophy, physics and ethics, is uncertain. Such is the vanity of this age, to condemn the arts, which are gifts of God and testimonies concerning God. The magician Cornelius Agrippa had written similar disparagements of the arts, and in many places in Germany the unlearned, with similar outcries, draw young people away from their studies so that they may confirm idols. Among the Sceptics Bellarmine also lists Erasmus, but by calumny; for although somewhere in the New Testament he says that he had learned nothing else in the whole course of his life than that he knew nothing; he does not deny that any truth is given at all, but only that it is very hard to find, and that the greatest and most learned men value none of their learning if they weigh what they know against what they do not know. Among these too is Augustine himself; for at the conclusion of the work he wrote against the Academics, he confesses that he, then in his thirty-third year, had not yet grasped anything of human knowledge, yet did not despair. Nearer to Scepticism lean those who divide human disciplines into consectary and demonstrative; this distinction we shall examine in its place, and so we shall also name its authors, among whom, besides H. Cardan, the distinguished physician and philosopher Francisco Vallesio also professes his name, as appears from his book On Sacred Philosophy, chapter 64. Yet it is no wonder if fewer make Scepticism public and profess it openly: for they love to lie hidden, and approve the practice of Arcesilaus and Pyrrho, who, as Laertius testifies, never either wrote or published a book. Moreover, by every means they labour to water down and circumscribe scepticism itself, and to remain in the position of the half-Sceptics; as we shall show at greater length in its place, by naming the various men who do this. What exactly is to be thought of the distinguished philosopher Gassendi, I am uncertain. Certainly, when outlining the argument of the second book against Aristotelian philosophy, he says at the end: And here is the chief point, where human knowledge and science is charged with weakness and uncertainty. Here are laid the chief foundations of Pyrrhonism, and that principle is most firmly established: NOTHING IS KNOWN. Since the book, which has long been awaited, has not yet appeared, I prefer to define nothing rashly.

units.la: CAPUT
units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: Caput Vigesimum.
units.tr: Chapter Twenty.

units.la: An disputandum sit cum Scepticis?
units.tr: Whether one should dispute with the Sceptics?

units.la: Priusquam subsequentibus libris Scepticos confutare, eorumq; rationes exarmare instituimus, in anteceßum constare debet, an cum ijs congrediendum ac disputandum sit. Quæstio illa iam olim Academicorum occasione mota est apud Marcum Tullium Ciceronem lib. II. Acad. Quæst. ubi ita disertissimum os loquitur: Sed quod nos facere nunc ingredimur, ut contra Academicos disseramus: id quidam à Philosophis & ij quidem non mediocres, faciendum omnino non putabant: nec vero esse ullam rationem disputare cum ijs, qui nihil probarent: Antipatrum, Stoicum, qui multus in eo fuisset, reprehendebant, etc. Interim, ad illam quæstionem, ut liquet ex filo totius illius disputationis, respondetur ibidem affirmative, deserunturque qui existimabant cum Academicis disputandum non esse. Quanquam enim Academicorum & Scepticorum, quasi Philosophorum magis quam Philosophorum pullicies, risu potius excipienda, quam scrupulose confutanda videtur: si quis tamen argumenta in speciem subtilia, quibus rudiores & minus in sacris his exercitatos illaqueare student, paulo accuratius expenderit, notaritque ijs immota disciplinarum atque adeo ipsius S.S. Theologiæ fundamenta concuti, non frustra exemplo Tertulliani, ani, Lactantij, Augustini, aliorumque recentiorum cum ijs disputari, iudicabit. Quanquam autem prima fronte difficillimus cum ijs conflictus videtur, quod nulla agnoscant principia, ex quibus disputando cum ijs congrediaris, tamen ad incitas non difficulter eos adegeris, si ea ipsa effata arripias, quibus absonam suam sententiam, profundamq; ignorantiam complecti laborant. In congressu autem cum ijs, non tam ipsorum quam aliorum quibus imponere possent, habenda ratio. Ipsi enim cum septemplici inexpugnabilis pertinaciæ scuto animum obfirmatum munierint, neque rationibus, neque orationibus, ut ut ad persuadendum idoneis, à sententia sua dimoveri possunt, quod certo apud se statuerint thesin suam non deserere: quare abunde nobis munere nostro perfuncti videbimur, si non tam eos ipsos ab afsectata ignorantia, quam tanquam claudi pilam retinent, ad scientiæ amœnitatem perduxerimus, quam alios ad sciendum excitaverimus, scientiæque amorem exsuscitaverimus, confirmata ejusdem certitudine.
units.tr: Before we undertake, in the following books, to refute the Sceptics and disarm their arguments, it must first be settled whether one ought to engage and dispute with them at all. That question was raised long ago by the Academics, and Marcus Tullius Cicero discusses it in Book II of the Academica Quaestiones, where that most eloquent mouth speaks thus: But what we are now undertaking, namely to argue against the Academics, some philosophers, and not unimportant ones, thought should not be done at all; there is no reason to dispute with those who prove nothing; they reproached Antipater the Stoic, who had spent much effort on this, etc. Meanwhile, as is clear from the thread of that whole discussion, the question is answered there in the affirmative, and those who thought one should not dispute with the Academics are set aside. Although the Academics and Sceptics, a sort of brood of philosophers rather than true philosophers, seem better met with laughter than with a painstaking refutation, yet if anyone weighs somewhat more carefully the arguments, subtle in appearance, with which they try to ensnare the cruder and those less practised in these sacred matters, and notes that by them the unshaken foundations of the disciplines, and indeed of Holy Theology itself, are shaken, he will judge that it was not in vain that, after the example of Tertullian, Lactantius, Augustine and other more recent writers, they were disputed with. Although at first sight the conflict with them seems most difficult, since they acknowledge no principles from which you could argue with them, yet you will not find it hard to drive them into a corner if you seize upon the very words by which they labour to embrace their absurd opinion and profound ignorance. In the encounter with them, however, regard must be had not so much to them as to others whom they could deceive. For they, having fortified their minds with the sevenfold shield of unconquerable obstinacy, cannot be moved from their opinion by arguments or speeches, however suited to persuasion, since they have firmly resolved in themselves not to abandon their thesis. Therefore we shall seem to have discharged our task sufficiently if we bring not so much those who cling to their affected ignorance, as if holding a lame ball, to the pleasantness of knowledge, as if we rouse others to know and kindle a love of knowledge, with the certainty of knowledge having been confirmed.

units.la: CAPUT VIGESIMUM PRIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWENTY-FIRST.

units.la: Quinam scripserint contra Scepticos?
units.tr: Who have written against the Sceptics?

units.la: QUum ex Superiori capite pateat, contra Scepticos cum ratione & non sine spe emolumenti disputari posse, antequam coronidem huic libro imponimus, breviter expendere convenit, quinam maxime cum his quasi Philosophis tum olim, tum hodie congressi fuerint. Olim quidem infestissimi prae aliis, Academicis, nec non Pyrrhonijs Stoici fuerunt: ut non tantum patet ex illis, quae de Epicteto Arrianus in Dissertationibus perhibet, sed maxime ex illo conflictu, qui inter Stoicae familiae patrem Zenonem, atque Arcesilaum intercesssit: quem quoniam distincte prae caeteris retulit Eusebius lib. 14. de Praepar.Evang.cap. 2. non pigebit locum totum, licet prolixiorem, prout ab interprete Latine redditus est, hoc loco exhibere. Ita ergo eo loco Eusebius: Magna igitur pugna inter Archesilaum atque Zenonem fuit, & alter in alterum & dicendo & scribendo impudenter ferebantur: quam vis Zeno non melius faceret, quam Cophisidorus orator, qui cum graviter ferret Isocratem, quem audiebat ab Aristotele premi, dicebat scribebatque non in Aristotelem quidem, ut putabat, sed in Platonem, a quo alienus non erat. Nam cum Aristotelem nullo modo intelligeret, putaret autem, quoniam Platonem Aristoteles audiverat, Platonicum illum esse, bellum quidem indixerat Aristoteli, Platonem vero & eius dogmata, quae tamen nesciebat, reprobare conabatur, putans non Platonis dogmata, sed Aristotelis refutare. ita magnus iu s ille orator non eum percutiebat, cui bellum ndixerat, sed eum quo cum pacem habebat. Sic gitur & Zeno cumArchefilao pugnans, Platonem acerabat,non enim erat forsan nescius eorum quæ Archesilaus dicebat: Platonica vero penitus ignorabat, ut è libris suis manifesto colligitur, ita quem non debebat, impudenter exagitabat, & quem debebat, minime tangebat. Et certe si Platonica non oppugnasset dogmata, bonus meo iudicio fuisset Philosophus. Sed de hac re latius si ocium erit: utinam autem nunquam mihi tantum sit ocium, ut ad hujusmodi res non joco, sed serio revertar. Studebat igitur Zeno Archesilai omnia dicta refutare, ac maxime incomprehensibilitatem quibuscunque poterat argumentis aggrediebatur, quocum Archesilaus alia depellebat, alia succidebat, alia supplantabat: ita contradicens deiiciebat, & auditores in stuporem vertebat, facile putantes, non verbum non operam, non passionem, non quicquam aliud esse n agnum aut parvum, nisi quod Pitanæus Archesilao videretur: illi vero nil prorsus videbatur, nec affirmabat quicquam, sed verbis solummodo pronunciando terrebat, Hactenus Eusebius. Præter Stoicos, vix ulli inter antiquos occurrunt, qui ex professo cum hac Philosophantium pullicie congressi sunt; si excipias unum Galenum, qui in libello de optimo docendi genere, Favorinum professione Academicum, ut supra ostendimus, nominatim aggreditur. Ex Patribus preter Lactantium, Eusebium, & Clementem Alexandrinum, qui incidéter & aliud quasi agendo contra eos disputant; ex professo Aurelius Augustinus Latinorum patrum doctissimus, oppido licet iuvenis, Academicorum dogmata, tribus ad hoc evulgatis libris, oppugnavit. Ex recentioribus multi quidem pro re nata in Scepticos insurrexere, [inter quos præcipuus est Franciscus Picus Mirandulæ Comes in eximio opere de vanitate doctr. Gentium] nulli autem plane omnia, quæ de ijs, atque eorum qualibuscunque dogmatis [si modo ita vocari debeant] dici possent, proponere instituerunt. Quod hactenus autem ab alijs, cum quibus tamen tenuitatis nostræ nobis conscij nos componere non audemus, neglectum est; subsequentibus libris, pro exiguo eruditionis nostræ dimenso agere conabimur.
units.tr: Since it is clear from the previous chapter that the Sceptics can be disputed against by reason, and not without hope of benefit, before I place a crown upon this book it is fitting to consider briefly who, both in former times and today, have most engaged with these men as if they were philosophers. In former times the Stoics were the most hostile of all to the Academics and the Pyrrhonists, as is shown not only by what Arrian reports of Epictetus in his Dissertations, but above all by that conflict which took place between Zeno, the father of the Stoic school, and Arcesilaus. Since Eusebius, in book 14 of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 2, relates this conflict more clearly than others, I shall not mind setting out the whole passage here, though it is rather long, as it has been rendered into Latin by the translator. Eusebius says the following in that place: "There was therefore a great fight between Arcesilaus and Zeno, and each of them was shamelessly attacked by the other, both in speech and in writing. Yet Zeno did no better than the orator Cephisodorus, who, being angry that Isocrates, whom he attended, was being pressed by Aristotle, spoke and wrote against not Aristotle, as he thought, but Plato, from whom Isocrates was not far removed. For since he did not understand Aristotle at all, but supposed that Aristotle, having heard Plato, was himself a Platonist, he declared war on Aristotle, yet tried to refute Plato and his doctrines, which he did not know, thinking he was refuting not the doctrines of Plato but those of Aristotle. So that great orator did not strike the man against whom he had declared war, but the man with whom he was at peace. In the same way Zeno, fighting with Arcesilaus, attacked Plato, for he was perhaps not ignorant of what Arcesilaus was saying, yet he was entirely ignorant of Platonic doctrines, as is clear from his own books. Thus he shamelessly assailed the one he ought not to have, and hardly touched the one he ought to have. And certainly, if he had not attacked the doctrines of Plato, he would in my judgement have been a good philosopher. But I shall treat this matter more fully if I have leisure; would that I might never have so much leisure that I return to such things not in jest but in earnest. Zeno therefore set himself to refute all the sayings of Arcesilaus, and above all he attacked incomprehensibility with whatever arguments he could muster, while Arcesilaus repelled some of them, cut down others, and undermined others. So by contradicting, Zeno overthrew and stunned his hearers, who easily supposed that nothing was great or small, no word, no action, no feeling, nothing else, except what seemed so to Arcesilaus of Pitane. Yet Arcesilaus himself seemed to hold nothing at all, nor did he affirm anything, but only frightened his opponents by pronouncing words." Thus far Eusebius. Apart from the Stoics, hardly any of the ancients are found who engaged expressly with this rabble of philosophers, except Galen, who, in his little book on the best method of teaching, expressly attacks Favorinus, a professed Academic, as we have shown above. Among the Fathers, besides Lactantius, Eusebius and Clement of Alexandria, who dispute against them incidentally while doing something else, Augustine, the most learned of the Latin Fathers, though still quite young, expressly assailed the doctrines of the Academics in three books published for this purpose. Among the more recent writers, many have indeed risen against the Sceptics as occasion arose, [among whom the most outstanding is Francesco Pico, Count of Mirandola, in his excellent work on the vanity of the teaching of the Gentiles], but none has undertaken to set out fully everything that could be said about them and about whatever doctrines they hold [if indeed they ought to be called that]. Since this has hitherto been neglected by others, with whom, however, aware of our slenderness, we do not dare to compare ourselves, we shall try in the following books to deal with it as far as the modest measure of our learning allows.

units.la: LIBER
units.tr: BOOK

units.la: LIBER SECUNDUS DE SCEPTICISMO
units.tr: BOOK TWO, ON SCEPTICISM

units.la: CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER ONE.

units.la: Nonnulli ex antiquis Philosophis omnia nihil esse contenderunt. Fanaticos illos fuisse, & vix dignos cum quibus disputetur, ostenditur.
units.tr: Some of the ancient philosophers contended that all things are nothing. It is shown that those men were madmen, hardly worth disputing with.

units.la: UT ad rem accedamus, & Scepticorum absona effata excutiamus, primo despiciendum erit, quomodo probetur inveniri ens aliquod reale. Eo enim processit Scepticorum insolentia, ut ausi fuerint omnia tollere & ad nihili profunda usque praecipitare. De Gorgia Leontino expresse illud testatur Sextus lib. 7. adv. Mathem. Gorgias, inquit, Leontinus fuit ipse quoque ex ordine eorum, qui sustulerunt id quod indicat, etc. nam in libro, qui inscribitur, de eo quod non est, aut de natura, tria ordine constituit capita. Unum quidem & primum quod nihil sit: secundum autem, quod etsi sit, ab homine non possit comprehendi: tertium, etsi possit comprehendi, enunciari tamen & explicari non possit proximo. et si Senecae ep. 89. fides adhibenda, idem docuit Zeno Eleates, qui omnia negotia de negotio dejiciens, dixit, Nihil esse. Pyrrhonios quoque haut alienos ab hac sententia fuisse, inde liquet quod negarint intellectum esse. Docet Sextus lib. 2.
units.tr: So that we may come to the matter and examine the absurd sayings of the Sceptics, we must first consider how it is proved that some real being exists. For the Sceptics' insolence went so far that they dared to remove everything and cast it down into the depths of nothingness. Sextus expressly bears witness to this about Gorgias of Leontini, in book 7 Against the Mathematicians: Gorgias of Leontini, he says, was also one of those who abolished what is indicated... for in the book entitled On What Is Not, or On Nature, he laid down three heads in order. The first, and indeed the chief, that nothing is; the second, that even if something is, it cannot be comprehended by man; the third, that even if it can be comprehended, it cannot be stated and explained to a neighbour. And if Seneca's letter 89 is to be trusted, Zeno of Elea taught the same thing, who casting down all business from its business, said: Nothing is. That the Pyrrhonists were not far removed from this opinion is clear from the fact that they denied there is any understanding. Sextus teaches this in book 2.

units.la: 2.Pyrh.Hypoth.cap.6.quando ita loquitur: igitur censent intellectum solum sequendum esse in iudicatione rerum, primum quidem demonstrare non poturunt esse intellectum.Porro effatum Zenonis; omnia nihil sunt, tolerari posset, si per nihilum notaretur vanitas, cui per lapsum, teste Apostolo ad Rom. 8.v.10.omnia quae in mundo occurrunt, obnoxia sunt.Non infrequenter enim vox nihili in omnibus linguis sic accipi solet, quemadmodum discurrendo per singulas linguas, adducto per quam prolixo exemplorum syrmate, hoc ipsum hoc loco ostendi posset, nisi ipsis tironibus notum foret. Audiri quoque possent, si per nihil res caducae distinguere voluissent a Deo, qui solus expers est omnis mutabilitatis; aut ipsum Deum, qui nihil rerum creatarum est, super eas evehere. Quo sensu non male Psellus dixit, Deum alloquens: Tu finis es omnium, & unus es, & omnia, & nihil. Excelsus enim Deus, qui inhabitat lucem inaccessam, 1.Tim.6.v.16. nihil earum rerum est, de quibus nos cogitare possumus.Unde & recte Thomas p. 1.q.3.art.3.Deus in nullo rerum genere est, vel proprie, vel reductive: iniuste item redargui eos stat-tuerem, si per nihil intellexissent ens incomplettum, quale v.c.materia prima est: quam, ut & angelos, Augustl.lib.12.Confes.cap.7.cum Deus comparans, subtiliter prope nihil vocat, cum dicit Fecisti duo quaedam, unum prope te, alterum prope nihil unum unum quo superior tu esses, alterum quo inferius nihil esset.Idem dicerem si per nihil intellexissent non ens comparate acceptum, quomodo Scal. Exer. 307.Sect.24. accidens non ens vocat: & eodem sensu Augustinus lib.8.de Civ.Dei cap.11.Quae creata sunt, etsi videntur esse, non sunt tamen.Nam ut idem ait lib.7.Conf.cap.11.Id vere est quod incommutabiliter manet.Quod uni Deo convenit Malach.3.v.6. At quia per nihil non ens, quod vulgo a Metaphysicis negativum vocatur, intellexisse videntur, exclamamus cum Seneca ex epist.98. Quid ergo nos sumus? quid ista, quae nos circumstant, dicunt, sustinent? Tota rerum natura umbra est, aut inanis aut fallax? Non facile dixerim, utrum magis irascor illis, qui nos nihil scire voluerunt, an illis, qui ne hoc quidem nobis reliquerunt, Nihil scire.Cum ratione autem Stoicus Romanus sic exclamat: furor, siquidem est omnia velle ad nihilum redigere, omniumque entium essentiam evertere; quique hoc pertinaciter urgent, Medico magis, quam Philosopho indigent: ut mirer viros alioquin doctos & subtiles, velle in Philosophia primo probari esse aliquid; seque fatigare in argumentis, quibus hoc probetur: cum hoc sit ex ijs, quae non probare, sed praesupponere debet Philosophia: ut enim est habitus, praesupponit praeviam potentiam naturalem, cum qua uni subiecto insit: quod ut cum ipsa potentia est extra nihil,
units.tr: 2 Pyrrhonian Outlines, ch. 6, where he speaks thus: therefore they think that the understanding alone is to be followed in judging things; but first they will not be able to demonstrate that there is understanding. Further, Zeno's saying all things are nothing could be tolerated if by nothing were signified vanity, to which, as the Apostle witnesses in Rom. 8.10, all things that occur in the world are subject through the Fall. For the word nothing is not infrequently understood in this way in all languages; this could be shown here by running through the individual languages and adducing a rather long string of examples, were it not known to beginners themselves. Their view could also be heard if by nothing they wished to distinguish transient things from God, who alone is free from all mutability; or if they meant to raise God himself, who is nothing of created things, above them. In this sense Psellus did not badly say, addressing God: You are the end of all, and you are one, and all things, and nothing. For God, who dwells in unapproachable light (1 Tim. 6.16), is none of those things that we can think of. Hence Thomas also rightly says, Part 1, question 3, article 3: God is in no genus of things, either properly or by reduction.
