Likewise they would be unjustly refuted if by nothing they understood an incomplete being, such as prime matter is; and Augustine, in book 12 of the Confessions, chapter 7, when comparing God with it and with the angels, subtly calls it almost nothing, when he says: You made two things, one close to you, the other close to nothing: one, by which you would be above, the other, by which it would be below nothing. I would say the same if by nothing they understood a non-being taken comparatively, as Scaliger, Exercise 307, section 24, calls an accident a non-being; and in the same sense Augustine, book 8 of The City of God, chapter 11: Things that are created, though they seem to be, nevertheless are not. For, as he says in book 7 of the Confessions, chapter 11: That truly is which remains unchangeably, which belongs to God alone (Mal. 3.6). But because they seem to have understood by nothing a non-being, which is commonly called a negative by the Metaphysicians, we cry out with Seneca in letter 98: What then are we? What do these things that surround us say and bear? Is the whole nature of things a shadow, either empty or deceptive? I could not easily say whether I am more angry with those who wished us to know nothing, or with those who did not even leave us this, to know nothing. Rightly, too, a Roman Stoic cries out: it is madness, indeed, to wish to reduce all things to nothing and to overturn the essence of all beings; and those who press this stubbornly need a physician rather than a philosopher. So I marvel that men otherwise learned and subtle wish to be proved in philosophy, first, that something is, and tire themselves with arguments by which this is proved, since this is among those things which philosophy ought not to prove but to presuppose. For as a habit presupposes a prior natural power, in which it inheres in one subject, so, as that power itself is outside nothing,

units.la: consequenter verum atque reale ens ; sic abunde cognoscere potest Philosophia, certum esse, aliquod ens esse, cum ne ipsa quidem concipi & nasci possit, nisi præexistente ente tum substantiali tum accidentario. Nescio vero quid de novis his Philosophiæ Reformatoribus existimandum sit, qui tantopere se fatigant in probando illo, quod ab omnibus, qui homines sunt, citra ullam hæsitationem admittitur, atque ut certum creditur, si dicant ad Philosophiæ absolutionem pertinere, progredi à primis principiis atque elementis, probandumque ante esse, dari entia constituta extra nihil, quam eorum investigentur essentiæ, implicant se difficultati ex qua nunquam expedire se poterunt. Si enim volunt omnia ex proprijs probari principijs, atque à priori demonstrari esse aliquod ens reale, vergunt ad infinitum : cum tamen subsistendum sit in aliquo tanquam primo, & tandem deveniatur ad ea principia, quæ sic suprema sunt, ut supra se nulla alia tanquam principia habeant. Demonstrationem à posteriori si sufficere dicant, eo ipso ostendunt otiosum esse hoc in ipso limine Philosophiæ probare, cum ipsa ratio subsidijs omnium habituum destituta ultro hoc admittat, & quæcunque dein præcepta sunt adferenda, illud ipsum, quod tam anxie laborant investigare, inferant. Nec est quod de Scepticis hic sint solliciti, siquidem ne ipsi quidem Pyrrhonij, in hac familia hesitabunda præcipui, eo usque accesserunt, ut entibus realibus. omnem realitatem voluerint eripere: utque Philosophia, & omnes habitus, qui potentiam aliquam naturalem perficient, non eam præsupponunt tantum tanquam primam, sed maxime tanquam secundam; sic nulla ratio habenda eorum est, qui potentiam tantum primam ad Philosphiam habent, aut ex morbo, aut per accersitam insaniam. hoc enim existimandum de ijs, qui in initio huius capitis pro sententia hac, cum qua deinceps congredeemur, fuere adducti. Enimvero ut Psal.xiv.regius Propheta non conquirit argumenta, quibus probet Deum esse, sed contentus est insipientem eum vocasse, qui hoc in corde suo negat: sic neque argumenta ijs adhibenda, sed Hippocratis potius fomenta& vincula, qui entia sua realitate exuunt, nullumque discrimen inter ea atque nihilum agnoscere volunt. Insaniunt enim ultra Atheos, in quos David incidit. Ne quis tamen ex novis Flavijs existimet, nobis nulla ad manum esse argumenta, quibus grande hoc arcanum astruamus, primo argumentorum nostrorum aciem instruemus; dein aliorum librabimus argumenta, alio loco ijs, quæ à fanaticis in contrarium vulgo adferuntur, breviter occursuri.
units.tr: and consequently a true and real being, so philosophy can sufficiently recognise that it is certain that some being exists, since not even the power itself can be conceived and born unless a being, both substantial and accidental, pre-exists. I do not know what to think of these new Reformers of philosophy, who tire themselves so greatly in proving that which is admitted without any hesitation by all who are human, and is believed as certain. If they say that it pertains to the completion of philosophy to proceed from first principles and elements, and that it must be proved, before their essences are investigated, that there are beings constituted outside nothing, they entangle themselves in a difficulty from which they will never be able to extricate themselves. For if they want everything to be proved from its own principles, and that some real being is demonstrated a priori, they tend toward infinity; yet one must stop at something as first, and at last one arrives at those principles which are so supreme that they have no other principles above themselves. If they say that a demonstration a posteriori suffices, they show by that very fact that it is idle to prove this at the very threshold of philosophy, since reason itself, destitute of the aids of all habits, admits this of its own accord, and whatever precepts are afterwards to be brought forward will infer that very thing which they labour so anxiously to investigate. Nor is there any reason for them to be concerned about the Sceptics here, since not even the Pyrrhonists, the chief men in this hesitating school, went so far as to wish to snatch all reality from real beings. And just as philosophy and all habits which perfect some natural power do not presuppose it only as first but especially as second, so no account is to be taken of those who have only the first power for philosophy, either from disease or through acquired madness. For this is what must be thought of those who were brought forward at the beginning of this chapter in support of this opinion, with which we shall afterwards contend. Indeed, just as the royal Prophet in Psalm 14 does not seek arguments by which to prove that God exists, but is content to have called insipid the one who denies this in his heart, so arguments are not to be applied to these men, but rather the poultices and chains of Hippocrates, who strip beings of their reality and wish to acknowledge no difference between them and nothing. For they are mad beyond the atheists whom David encountered. Yet lest anyone among the new Flavii think that we have no arguments at hand by which to establish this great mystery, we shall first arrange the line of our arguments; then we shall weigh the arguments of others, and in another place briefly meet those things which are commonly brought forward on the contrary side by the fanatics.

units.la: CAPUT SECUNDUM
units.tr: CHAPTER TWO

units.la: Adferuntur quinque argumenta, quibus iis, qui à Scepticismo alieni sunt, solidissime astruitur, quam fanaticos se quidam ex Scepticis prabuerint, cum omnia ad Nihilum redigerent.
units.tr: Five arguments are offered, by which it is most solidly established, for those who are not of the Sceptical persuasion, how some of the Sceptics showed themselves to be fanatics, when they reduced everything to Nothing.

units.la: UT cum fructu quis contra Scepticos disputare queat, anquisite observare debet, aliis argumentis utendum esse apud eos, qui à Scepticismo alieni sunt, alijs vero adversos ipsos Academicos & Pyrrhonios: cum enim hi toti in hoc sint, ut omnia subvertant, apertoque capite ipsa indubitatæ veritatis principia negare ausint, nemo eos constringere poterit, nisi è paucis illis principijs, quæ volentes nolentes, & quasi contra animi sui sententiam admittere coguntur, ad eos illaqueandos progrediatur, quod ut ubique attendemus, ita circa primum hoc dubium haut quaquam negligemus. Quo ergo ante omnia satisfaciamus ijs, quibus nullum cum Pyrrhonijs est commercium, quinque potissimum argumenta præ alijs solidiora esse videntur. Primo, præterquam quod furori huic [sic enim vocare iam lubet] verbum Dei adversatur: quod testatur Gen. 1. in initio temporis Deo loquente, omnia esse ac existere incepisse, ac ex invisibilibus ea quæ cernimus, facta esse, Heb. 11. v. 3. Illo vocante quæ non sunt, tanquam essent, Rom.4.v. 17.atque e tenebris lucem educente2. Cor 4.v.6. & consequenter de nihilo producendo omnia quæ sunt: non ut de materia, sed ut à non termino subiectivo ad terminum realem, ut docet Thomas 1.p.q.43.art.3.fugandoque tenebras & nihil, ut esset lux & aliquid. Est enim revera ipsum Nihil profundissima quædam tenebrarum abyssus, ut eleganter Corn.Martini in Metaphys. p.39.loquitur: amplius secundo, experientiæ omnium seculorum, imo omnium hominum, Sceptici oblocuti fuerunt. Experientia sola est omnium certissimus index, secundum Gal.lib.1.de simpl. medicam. facultat. cap.ult. Tertio si omnia nihil sunt, nulla erit differentia, imo nulla cogitari poterit inter res maximè distinctas & contrarias. Malum erit bonum, album nigrum, homo bellua, & sic vicissim. Quod enim discrimen erit nihili, in quo nihil reale, ne quidem potentia, quam ipsa materia prima, ignobilissimæ alias entitatis, habet? Nec poterit concipi tanquam aliquid, quomodo enim nihil (ipse homo scilicet, qui cum intellectu suo ijs quoque nihil fuit) nihil intelliget ut aliquid? Quarto, sibi ipsis contra dixerunt dicendo omnia esse nihil? quomodo enim potest idem esse & non esse? si enim per hæc omnia intelligas ea quæ existtunt, etenim sunt aliquid, & quia convenit illi esse, non potest de ijs prædicari non esse. Nisi forte hæc omnia crediderint Chimeras & Centauros esse, nullamque differentiam intercedere inter esse & non esse. Sic enim videntur philosophati esse: sed tamen se ipsos redarguunt; si enim idem est esse ac non esse, falsi fuerunt: æque enim staruere potuerunt omnia esse ac non esse, & tam dicere omnia esse aliquid, quam esse nihil. Quinto, si omnia sunt nihil, viventia non morientur, aut quid interitui aut corruptioni poterit esse obnoxium, quod enim iam revera nihil negativum est, quomodo poterit in nihilum magis redigi. Tale nihil nullos habet gradus aut etiam habere potest: imo in eo cogitari non possunt. Nam quomodo mens nostra, cuius objectum est ens, quid de eo percipiat, quod omnis entis est expers, cum illud ipsum percipere non possit, nisi saltem consideret ut ens rationis, aut non ens privativum, ut Plato animadvertit quoque in Sophista. Quo loco prolixam adversus Parmenidem disputationem hac coronide obsignat: Nos autem non tantum quae non sunt, ut sunt, demonstratimus: sed etiam eam speciem quae est ejus quod non est, ostendimus. Nam quum doceremus, alterius naturam existere, & per omnes res quae vere sunt, mutua quadam communitate in minimas partes distributam, illa ipsius [natura] pars, quae singularum rerum, quae vere sunt, ratione, sane opponitur: illud vero ipsum est esse revera. Id quod non est, aut sum appellare.
units.tr: To dispute against the Sceptics with profit, one must carefully observe that different arguments are to be used with those who are not Sceptics and with the Academics and Pyrrhonists themselves. Since these men are wholly intent on overturning everything, and openly dare to deny the very principles of indubitable truth, no one can constrain them except by means of those few principles which they are forced, willing or unwilling, and as if against the judgment of their own minds, to admit. By these they can be ensnared. We shall attend to this throughout, and we shall by no means neglect it in regard to this first doubt. So, to satisfy first of all those who have no dealings with the Pyrrhonists, five arguments seem chiefly and above the rest to be the more solid. First, besides the fact that this madness (for so I now choose to call it) is opposed to the Word of God, which testifies in Gen. 1 that at the beginning of time, when God spoke, all things began to be and to exist, and that what we see was made from things invisible (Heb. 11:3); "by calling those things which are not as though they were" (Rom. 4:17); and who "out of darkness caused light to shine" (2 Cor. 4:6). Consequently, all things that are were produced out of nothing: not as out of matter, but as from a non-subject term to a real term, as Thomas teaches (1 p. q. 43 art. 3), dispelling darkness and nothing, so that there might be light and something. For Nothing itself is truly a most profound abyss of darkness, as the elegant Cornelius Martini puts it in his Metaphysics (p. 39). Second, the Sceptics have contradicted the experience of all ages, indeed of all men. Experience alone is the most certain judge of all things, according to Galen, On the Simple Medicines, book 1, last chapter. Third, if all things are nothing, there will be no difference, indeed no difference at all can be conceived, between things most distinct and contrary. Evil will be good, white black, man a beast, and so on in turn. For what difference will there be in nothing, in which there is nothing real, not even the potency which even prime matter, a most lowly entity otherwise, possesses? Nor can it be conceived as something: for how can nothing (namely man himself, who with his intellect is also nothing) understand anything as something? Fourth, have they not contradicted themselves in saying that all things are nothing? For how can the same thing both be and not be? If by "all these things" you understand those things which exist, then since they are something, and since being belongs to them, it cannot be predicated of them that they are not. Unless perhaps they believed that these things are chimeras and centaurs, and that there is no difference between being and not being. For so they seem to have reasoned; but they refute themselves nonetheless. If being and not-being are the same, they were wrong: for they could just as well have maintained that all things both are and are not, and to say that all things are something is as much as to say that they are nothing. Fifth, if all things are nothing, living things will not die, nor will anything be subject to perishing or corruption. For what is already truly a negative nothing, how can it be reduced further to nothing? Such a nothing has no degrees, nor can it have any; indeed, in it no such thing can be thought. For how can our mind, whose object is being, perceive anything of that which is free of all being, since it cannot perceive that very thing unless it considers it at least as a being of reason, or a privative non-being, as Plato also observed in the Sophist. In that passage, he closes his lengthy disputation against Parmenides with this crowning remark: We have shown not only that things which are not, are, but also that form which belongs to what is not. For when we taught that the nature of the other exists, and that it is distributed into the smallest parts through all things which truly are, by a certain mutual communion, that part of it which is opposed to the account of each of the things which truly are, is surely itself truly being. That which is not, we call not-being.

units.la: CAPUT TERTIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER THREE.

units.la: Argumento, quo usus quoque est Augustinus, confunditur fanaticorum pertinacia.
units.tr: An argument that Augustine also used refutes the obstinacy of the fanatics.

units.la: QUanquam argumenta superiori capite adducta sufficere possunt ei, qui meminit se ratione praeditum esse, nec animum praefracta pertinacia contra veritatem armavit; aliter agendum tamen est contra obstinatos Scepticos, quibus si quis argumenta proxime adducta, velut machinas aliquas opponat, aut nihil, aut parum proficiet, cum mox dicturi sint, ea sibi videri incongrua, aut sese existimare ea, si non falsa, saltem fallacia esse. Eoque, duro huic nodo alius adhibendus est cuneus, & arripiendum illud ipsum, quod Scepticus volens nolens concedere cogitur. Ideo vero tum praecedentibus argumentis, tum aliis, quae illis amplius addi possent, expugnari se non patitur, quia de iis aut dubitat, aut iis sese circumveniri existimat; aut, saltem subtiliter apud se, metuens ne fallatur. Quocunque autem modo animum componit, aut eum affectum esse existimat, captus est. Si enim aut dubitare se dicat, aut falli, aut inquirere ulteriorem probationem, fateri debet se esse: cum neque dubitare, neque falli, neque ulteriorem probationem inquirere possset, nisi esset. Posset quidem quis apud se
units.tr: The arguments adduced in the previous chapter may be enough for anyone who remembers that he is endowed with reason and has not armed his mind with stubborn obstinacy against the truth. Yet one must proceed differently against the obstinate Sceptics. If someone opposes them with the arguments just adduced, as though they were siege engines, he will achieve nothing or very little, for they will soon say that these arguments seem to them incongruous, or they will think them, if not false, at least fallacious. Therefore another wedge must be applied to this hard knot, and we must seize on the very thing that the Sceptic is forced to concede whether he likes it or not. He does not allow himself to be overcome either by the preceding arguments or by others that could be added to them, because he either doubts them or believes himself to be deceived by them, or at least, privately and cautiously, fears being deceived. However he settles his mind, if he thinks himself affected in this way, he is caught. For if he says that he doubts, or that he is deceived, or that he seeks further proof, he must admit that he exists, since he could not doubt, be deceived, or seek further proof unless he existed. One might indeed ask himself whether

units.la: [The lower lines of the page are overprinted with show-through and stains and are not fully legible.] se ambigere, an non dubitare idem sit, atque falli, & contra. Sed quicquid sibi Scepticus hic saltem fingat, si argumentis, quibus alij moventur, assentiri nolit, aut quia dubitat, aut quia falli sese existimat, volens nolens in quascunque quoq; formas se converterit, fateri cogitur sese esse re aut dubitantem, aut eam quæ fallitur. Poterit quidem ambigere, an secundum illam affectionem mentis, si alijs videatur dubitare, sit etiam res dubitans, aut quando fallitur, sit illud quod fallitur: haut quaquam tamen negare poterit sese esse aut alterutrum, aut saltem aliquid, quod sentit commotionem mentis, quo minus argumentis, quibus alij moventur, moveri possit. Atque hoc sufficit ad hoc, ut Scepticus fateatur, aut se, aut in se, aut circa se esse aliquid, quod extra nihil est. Similí argumento contra Academicos usus quoque fuit Augustinus de Civ. Dei l. xi. cap. 26. Nulla, inquit, in his veris Academicorum argumenta reformido dicentium: Quid si falleris? Si enim fallor, sum. Nam qui non est, utique nec falli potest: ac per hoc sum, si fallor. Quia ergo sum qui fallor, quomodo esse me fallor, quando certum est esse me, si sallor. Qui igitur essem, qui fallerer, etiamsi fallar, procul dubio in eo quod me novi esse, non fallor. Eodemque prorsus modo de Libero Arbitrio l. ii, c. 3. Ubi probaturus Dei existentiam, sic infit: Prius obs te quaero [ut de manifestissimis capiamus exordium] uirutrum tu ipse sis? An tu forta sse metuis, ne in hac interrogatione fallaris! cum utique, si non esses, falli omnino non posses.
units.tr: [The lower lines of the page are overprinted with show-through and stains and are not fully legible.] to doubt and to be deceived are the same thing, and conversely. But whatever the Sceptic may pretend to himself, if he is unwilling to assent to the arguments by which others are moved, because he doubts or believes himself deceived, then whether he wills it or not, he turns himself into whatever form he likes, and he is compelled to confess that he is either one who doubts or one who is deceived. He may indeed wonder whether, in accordance with that state of mind, a thing is also doubting if it seems to others to doubt, or whether, when it is deceived, it is the thing that is deceived. Yet he can by no means deny that he is either one or the other, or at least something that perceives the disturbance of mind which keeps him from being moved by the arguments by which others are moved. And this is enough to make the Sceptic admit that he, or something in him, or something about him, exists, which is not nothing. Augustine also used a similar argument against the Academics, De Civitate Dei 11.26: "I am not afraid of the Academics' arguments in these matters of truth, who say: 'What if you are deceived?' For if I am deceived, I am. For one who does not exist cannot in any way be deceived; and therefore I am, if I am deceived. Since, then, I am the one who is deceived, how am I deceived in my existence, when it is certain that I exist, if I am deceived? Therefore, even if I am deceived, I who would be deceived, undoubtedly am not deceived in that which I know that I am." In the same way, in De Libero Arbitrio 2.3, where he is about to prove the existence of God, he begins thus: "First I ask you [so that we may take our beginning from the most manifest things], man: whether you yourself exist? Or are you perhaps afraid lest you be deceived in this question? For surely, if you did not exist, you could not be deceived at all."

units.la: CAPUT QUARTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FOUR.

units.la: Quorundam recentiorum argumentum eidem Scepticorum furori oppositum examinatur.
units.tr: The argument of certain recent writers, set against this same madness of the Sceptics, is examined.

units.la: EX recentioribus quidam, qui videri volunt cornici oculos secundum vulgatum verbum, argumentum, Augustino quoque notum, tanquam à se primo inventum, non solum quasi Archimedis inventum jactant; sed, quod deplorandum quam maxime, multis modis à se debilitatum atque deturpatum, quasi Delphici Apollinis responsum agnosci volunt. Ita scilicet argumentantur, quo Scepticismo iugulum præcidatur: Cogito, ergo sum: vel, ut alij, ignari tamen methodi disputandi contra Scepticos, cæterum exercitatiores in syllogistica idem argumentum proponunt: Cogito ergo sum res cogitans; & consequenter, etiam sum. Sed, utro etiam modo argumentum proponatur, illi, qui obsirmati sunt Sceptici, (quales eos esse, quibuscum hic nobis negotium, præsupponimus) neutiquam eo, (quicquid multis etiam visum fuerit) moveri poterunt. Quis enim Sceptico hoc extorserit, sc rit se cogitare? Argumenti hujus putatij fabri illud suum cogito latissime quidem extendunt, caeterum qualcunque etiam significationes illi aptaverint, non tamen Scepticos ad incitas adegerint, ijsque hanc confessionem expresserint, ideo eos debere fateri, sese esse, quod cogitent; (qualiscunq; etiam cogitationis fingatur significatio) cum aeque incertum ijs videatur, quod cogitent, ac quod sint. Stringere talis conse quentia posset; si illud cogito, aut saltem illud quod sub eo (qualecunque etiam id fuerit) intelligi Flavij volunt, Scepticos moveret, quo minus admittere volunt ea argumenta, quibus alij moventur. tantum vero abest, ut in illo ipso cogito, ad cuiuscunque quoque significationis cothurnum exacto, quid occurrat, quod pertinaces hos Philosophos movere possit, semper recurrent ad familiarem suum circulum, petentque ut probetur quod cogitent, sive cogitario haec intellectus, sive voluntatis, sive phantasiae statuatur actio. Verum quidem est cogitationem esse opus animae; sed non credit hoc Scepticus, qui quoniam non dederit facile se esse, non concesserit etiam in se esse animam, qua cogitare possit. Deinde dato Scepticum fateri se cogitare, non tamen admittere poterit hanc consequentiam, quod inde sequatur eum esse. Nam 1. quae ratio compellet, ut statuat illud cogitare esse quid infe;
units.tr: Some of the more recent writers, who want to look as if they have the eyes of a crow (to use the common saying), not only boast of an argument known to Augustine as though it were a discovery of their own, as if it were Archimedes' invention. What is most deplorable is that, after weakening and disfiguring it in many ways, they want it accepted as the oracle of the Delphic Apollo. They argue in this way, to cut the throat of Scepticism: I think, therefore I am; or, as others do, who are ignorant of the method of disputing against the Sceptics but are more practised in syllogistic, they put forward the same argument as: I think, therefore I am a thinking thing, and consequently I also am. But in whatever form the argument is put, those who are hardened Sceptics (whom we presuppose to be the kind of people we have to deal with here) will by no means be moved by it, whatever many have thought. For who could wring from a Sceptic the admission that he knows he thinks? These makers of the supposed argument stretch their "I think" very widely, but however many meanings they fit to it, they have not driven the Sceptics into a corner or forced from them the confession that they ought to admit they exist because they think (whatever meaning of thinking is invented), since it seems to them just as uncertain whether they think as whether they exist. Such a consequence could be pressing if that "I think", or at least what the Flavians want to be understood by it (whatever that may be), would move the Sceptics to be less willing to admit those arguments by which others are moved. But it is so far from the case that, in that very "I think", raised to the buskin of whatever meaning, there is anything that could move these stubborn philosophers, that they always return to their familiar circle and ask that it be proved that they think, whether this is taken to be an act of the intellect, of the will, or of the imagination. It is true that thinking is an operation of the soul, but the Sceptic does not believe this. Since he has not readily granted that he exists, he does not concede that there is in himself a soul by which he could think. Then, granting that the Sceptic admits he thinks, he will still not be able to accept the consequence that it follows from this that he exists. For (1) what reason will compel him to hold that this thinking is something within

units.la: [Marginal notes at left are damaged and illegible.] in se; cum in somnio, aut extasi à Genijs, aut spiritibus sibi extinsecus abstantibus suggeri aliquid queat, quod videatur esse cogitantis, cum revera tamen sit externi illius motoris, qui quod suggerit, tanquam causa moralis forte, sibi magis, quam subjecto temere hoc arripienti imputari velit.2. Ex Sceptici principiis, non major consequentia intercedit inter cogitare & esse, atque inter edere, aut scribere, & esse.Si enim Scepticus quando scit se cogitare, inde colligere potest, quod sit: etiam quando se edere aut scribere novit, inferre potest quod sit: quum æque necessum sit eum esse, quando aut scribit, aut edit;atq;cum cogitat.3. Quo procedat illud ex mente Sceptici: Cogito, ergo sum:necessario mens in se ipsam reflecti debet.Novit autem Scepticus, quantum erroris subsit simplici atque directæ actioni mentis, multo magis ergo suspectare debet actionem ejusdem reflexam.Nec hæc altera consequentia dubium omne expedit: Cogito, ergo sum res cogitans.quanquam enim propterea melior haberi debet, quoniam vult Scepticum colligere quod sit, ex eo, quando collegit se esse rem cogitantem: tamen in hoc ipso primo progressu: Cogito ,ergo sum res cogitans;necessario mens in se ipsam reflecti debet,quod non potest non suspectum admodum Sceptico esse, ut modo ostensum fuit.4.Qui de hocargumento tantopere gloriantur, atque ap-plau plausum apud omnes ordines quÿrunt: concedunt dubitari posse de hac aut simili connexione: Totum est maius quacunque sui parte: Bis bina efficiunt quatuor. quanto non magis ergo homo ad dubitandum factus, & in palestra Pyrrhonica exercitatissimus, hanc definitam consequentiam, [cogito, ergo sum] non sibi solum, sed multis aliis extra Pyrrhonismum dubiam, in dubium vocare poterit? Dicunt quidem: nullam in nobis esse cogitationem, cuius eodem illo momento, quo in nobis est, conscij non sumus. Sed 1. ut iam ante saepius ostendimus, non valet consequentia a nobis, vel aliis a Scepticismo remotis ad ipsos Scepticos. hi quoniam de omnibus dubitant, non possunt moveri nisi argumentis, quę ipsi ab omni dubio remota volentes nolentes concedere coguntur. 5. Quis concesserit mentem in statu corruptionis conscium esse omnium cogitationum suarum? certe non dederit illud Ieremias Propheta, quando cap. 17. v. 9. exclamat: Fraudulentum cor ipsum supra omnia, & morti ferum est, quis cognoscat ipsum? Deinde certissimum est, mentem inter dormiendum otiosam esse, millenasque species a phanthasia ei exhiberi, quarum soluto somno ne unam tamen nominare potest. Scepticus autem, quod omnia tuta timeat, se vigilantem, nec non praesentem atque videntem, cum somniante componere solet. 3. Qui hoc ipso argumento contra Scepticos utuntur, alias monent, seduloque inculcant: Nos nunquam plus æquo diffidentia indulgere posse. Quod si verum, næ multo magis Scepticus, circa cogitationes suas, quod illæ sæpe subrepant, nec ab eo animadverti possint, diffidere debet. Ut vero pertinaces huius argumenti patroni, quibus cum genuinis Scepticis nunquam res fuit, liquido cognoscant, quam invalidum hoc contra illos telum sit, lubet adducere confessionem Francisci Sanchez Scepticissimi Doctoris, qui in opusculo quo expresse docere laborat, quod nihil sciatur, pag. 83. ita de se ipso: Certus quidem sum, me nunc hæc, quæ scribo, cogitare velle scribere, & optare ut vera sint, & ut à te approbentur: nec tamen nimis curare: sed cum considerare nitor, quid sit hæc cogitatio, hoc velle, hoc optare, hoc non curare, sane deficit cogitatio, frustratur voluntas, incessit desiderium, augetur cura. Nil video quod captare aut comprehendere possim. Ut vero hoc argumento parum moveri possunt Scepticî, ita neque eos educere potest ex puteo ignorantiæ, & Labyrintho dubitationis; quicunque omnibus sententijs, & præiudicijs semet multant, nullamque aliam veritatem ante hanc ipsam admittunt, quod reliqua sint aut dubia, aut falsa, eique, tanquam primo principio omnia alia dogmata superstrui debeant. Quod cum luculenter & solidissime ostensum fuerit à Cl. Gassendo in disquisitionibus Metaphysicis pag. 38. & seqq. non pigrpigebit illius vitula hic arare. Ita vero loquitur: Ego cogito, inquis, sed quid cogitas? siquidem omnis cogitatio alicuius rei cogitatio est. An cælum? an terram? an quid vis aliud? an te ipsum? Omnia iam reputasti falsa, neque mutasti sententiam; quamobrem quicquid cogites, falsum cogitas, ac proinde est tua cogitatio falsa. Igitur & omnes, quas consequenter elicies cogitationes, falsæ erunt. Rursus, Ego cogito, inquis: At cum dicis Ego, nosti ne te ipsum, an non? nosti dubio procul, nam te alioquin non nominares. Nostine vero te esse, an non? Si nosti te esse, igitur præiudicium habes, quod adversatur suppositioni, si non nosti te esse, ergo neque nosti te agere, quoniam agere, ut loquuntur, præsupponit esse. Igitur neque nosti te cogitare, quoniam cogitare est agere; igitur cum dicis Ego cogito, ignoras quod dicis; atque adeo quicquid deinde cognoscis, aut inferes, ignorato plane principio nitetur. Ad hæc cum dicis, Ego cogito, enuncias aliquid de te, ac in præsenti tempore quidem; Igitur idem est, ac si diceres, Ego sum cogitans, tu nimirum subiectum es, & cogitatio attributum; Atqui non potes dicere te esse cogitantem, quin dicas te esse? idque declarant Dialectici, cum docent verbum ad significandum tempus, quod est nunc esse: Igitur cum dicis Ego cogito, dicis ego sum; & dicens deinde in consequente igitur Ego sum sum, nihil aliud infers, quam quod presupposuiti; sicque idem per idem probas. Præterea quoniam quando dicis Ego cogito, igitur ego sum, Enthymema est, neque probationis vim habet, nisi vigore consequutionis firmitudine habentis ex illo principio, etc. Qui cogitat est; ideoque contexendus necessario syllogismus est, aut in forma primæ perfectæque figuræ hoc modo: Quicunque cogitat est; Ego cogito; Igitur ego sum. Aut forma quartæ vulgo improbatæ, & quam dicunt Galenicam, hoc modo: Ego cogito; Qui cogitat est; Igitur ego sum. At utrovis modo ruina. Nam si priore forma concludas, propositio illa, Qui cogitat est, præiudicium est, antecedens illud, quod tu vis statuere iudiciorum primum. Si posteriore, cum Assumptio illa Qui cogitat est; iudicium est, quod neque dependet à tua propositione Ego cogito, neque sequitur tuam conclusionem, Ego sum, ex qua vis omnia iudicia præter illud Ego cogito, dependere. Hactenus Gassendus, cui hactenus nemo ex patronis huius argumenti, cum ratione respondere potuit.
units.tr: [The marginal notes at the left are damaged and illegible.] himself, since in a dream, or in ecstasy, something can be suggested to him by genii or spirits standing outside him, which seems to belong to a thinker, when in truth it belongs to that external mover, who, perhaps as a moral cause, wishes what he suggests to be imputed to himself rather than to the subject who rashly seizes it? (2) On the principles of the Sceptic, there is no stronger connection between thinking and being than between publishing or writing and being. If the Sceptic, when he knows that he thinks, can gather from this that he is, then when he knows that he publishes or writes, he can infer that he is, since it is equally necessary that he exists when he writes or publishes as when he thinks. (3) Where that argument I think, therefore I am leads, according to the mind of the Sceptic, the mind must necessarily be turned back upon itself. But the Sceptic knows how much error lies in the simple and direct action of the mind, so he ought all the more to suspect its reflexive action. Nor does this second consequence clear away all doubt: I think, therefore I am a thinking thing. For although it is for this reason thought to be better, because it wants the Sceptic to gather that he is from the fact that he has gathered that he is a thinking thing, yet in this very first step, I think, therefore I am a thinking thing, the mind must necessarily be turned back upon itself, which cannot but be very suspect to the Sceptic, as has just been shown. (4) Those who boast so greatly of this argument, and seek applause from all classes, concede that doubt can be raised about this or a similar connection: The whole is greater than any of its parts; twice two make four. How much less, then, can a man who was made for doubting, and is most thoroughly trained in the Pyrrhonian arena, call into doubt this settled inference [I think, therefore I am], which is doubtful not only to himself but to many others outside Pyrrhonism? They say indeed: there is no thought in us of which we are not aware at the very moment it is in us. But (1), as we have often shown before, the inference from us, or from others remote from Scepticism, does not hold for the Sceptics themselves. Since they doubt everything, they cannot be moved except by arguments which, willy-nilly, they are forced to grant as free from all doubt. (5) Who would grant that a mind in a state of corruption is aware of all its thoughts? Certainly the prophet Jeremiah would not grant it, when at chapter 17 verse 9 he cries out: The heart is deceitful above all things and desperately wicked; who can know it? Again, it is most certain that the mind is idle during sleep, and that countless images are presented to it by the imagination, of which, once sleep is over, it cannot name even one. The Sceptic, however, because he fears everything, is accustomed to set himself awake, alert and present, and seeing, against the one who is dreaming. (3) Those who use this very argument against the Sceptics warn others, and diligently impress on them: We can never indulge in diffidence more than is right. If this is true, then the Sceptic, much more, ought to be diffident about his own thoughts, since they often creep in unnoticed and cannot be observed by him. But so that the obstinate defenders of this argument, who have never had dealings with genuine Sceptics, may clearly see how weak this weapon is against them, let me cite the confession of Francisco Sanchez, a most sceptical doctor, who, in the little work in which he labours to teach expressly that nothing can be known, says of himself at page 83: I am certainly sure that I now wish to write these things that I am writing, to think them, and to hope that they are true and that they will be approved by you; yet I do not care too much. But when I try to consider what this thought is, what this wishing, this hoping, this not caring is, then indeed thought fails, the will is frustrated, desire falters, anxiety grows. I see nothing that I can grasp or comprehend. But just as Sceptics can be moved little by this argument, so neither can it lead them out of the well of ignorance and the labyrinth of doubt. Those who burden themselves with all opinions and prejudices, and admit no other truth before this one, because the rest are either doubtful or false, and who think all other doctrines must be built upon it as a first principle: this is what the most illustrious and most solid Gassendi has clearly and thoroughly shown in his Metaphysical Disquisitions, page 38 and following. I shall not hesitate to plough with his heifer here. He speaks thus: "I think," you say. But what do you think? For every thought is the thought of some thing. Heaven? Earth? Or what else do you want? Or yourself? You have already considered all these false, and you have not changed your opinion. Therefore whatever you think, you think falsely, and so your thought is false. Therefore also all the thoughts which you afterwards derive will be false. Again: "I think," you say. But when you say "I", do you know yourself or not? Undoubtedly you know, for otherwise you would not name yourself. But do you know that you are or not? If you know that you are, then you have a prejudgment which contradicts the supposition; if you do not know that you are, then you do not know that you act, since to act, as they say, presupposes being. Therefore you do not know that you think either, since to think is to act; therefore when you say "I think", you do not know what you are saying, and so whatever you then recognise or infer will rest on a principle entirely unknown. Moreover, when you say "I think", you pronounce something about yourself, and in the present tense. Therefore it is the same as if you said "I am thinking", where you are plainly the subject and thinking the attribute. But you cannot say that you are thinking without saying that you are; and the dialecticians declare this when they teach that the verb which signifies time, which is "to be now", is used. Therefore when you say "I think", you say "I am"; and then, saying in the consequent "therefore I am I am", you infer nothing other than what you presupposed, and so you prove the same by the same. Besides, since when you say "I think, therefore I am" it is an enthymeme, and has no force of proof unless by the power of a consequence which has firmness from that principle, namely "whoever thinks is", the syllogism must necessarily be constructed either in the form of the first and perfect figure, thus: Whoever thinks is; I think; therefore I am. Or in the form of the fourth figure, commonly disapproved and called Galenic, thus: I think; whoever thinks is; therefore I am. But in either form it collapses. For if you conclude in the first form, the proposition "whoever thinks is" is a prejudgment, being that antecedent which you want to set up as the first of your judgments. If in the second form, the assumption "whoever thinks is" is a judgment which depends neither on your proposition "I think" nor follows from your conclusion "I am", from which you want all judgments except that one, "I think", to depend. So far Gassendi, to whom no defender of this argument has so far been able to reply with reason.

units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: CAPUT QUINTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Iterato inquiritur in hoc principium; Cogito, ergo sum; obviamque itur ijs, qui contendunt primam veritatem esse.
units.tr: Again the inquiry is made into this principle, I think, therefore I am; and one meets those who maintain that this is the first truth.

units.la: AT interim secundum nonnullos, quibus antiqua sordent, hæc prima & certissima veritas est, cogito, inquiro, dubito ergo sum: nec certa rei existentia inferri potest in conclusione ex medio incerto, aut incertæ existentiæ. At hi actus loquendi ambulandi, videndi, incertum est ac dubium, an sint. Contra actus inquirendi, cogitandi, dubitandi, certum est & indubium, quod sint. Audio quidem hæc, & ingeniose excogitata fateor, non tamen ulla ratione à me impetrare possum, ut ijs movear. Nam 1. quomodo hæc prima veritas esse potest, quandoquidem cogitatio aut dubitatio non potest menti oboriri de re, nisi antea præcesserit apprehensio illius rei, ut existentis, de qua dubitatur. 2. Incertum quidem est, an actus videndi, & ambulandi sint tales actus, quales secundum suam formalitatem vulgo censentur; non tamen incertum pariter esse potest intellectui an sint. Nisi enim fuerint, & exstiterint quomodo de ijs cogitari, aut dubitari poterit? Quæ ratio quod cæcus à nativitate, cui à nullo explicata fuit colorum ratio, nunquam aut cogitat, aut dubitat de coloribus loribus? nulla alia omnino, quam quoniam nunquam colores apprehendit ut existentes. Eoque si eleemosynas collegerit,& existimet sibi aliquot asses subductos esse, dubitat an definitum eorundem numerum habeat, quandoquidem iam ante asses, certo numero definito, ut existentes solum, apprehendit, perpetuo interim eodem dubitante de qualitate, atque valore eorundem assium. 2. Non debent confundi quæstiones hæ duæ an res sit, & qualis eadem sit. Dubitamus quidem sæpe an videamus; sed tamen ut dubitemus, necessum est apprehendamus visionem, saltem ut possibilem. Non potest in nobis occurrere cogitatio, seu dubitatio, citra rationem alicuius objecti. Quis enim dicere queat se cogitare, aut dubitare, quando nullum obiectum suæ sive cogitationis, sive dubitationis indicare potest? 4. Eoque concedo hactenus quidem (non tamen apud Scepticos, ut ex superiori capite patuit] bonam esse hanc illationem: Quicunque cogitat, aut dubitat, ille est. Ego cogito, ergo sum. Non potest tamen censeri hæc prima veritas esse; siquidem nec cogitatio, nec dubitatio est, nisi præcesserit apprehensio rei ut existentis, quæ cogitetur. Sed ex hypothesi eorum qui hoc argumento utu ntur, omnia supponuntur ut incerta, aut falsa esse, imo tanquam non esse. Sic enim loquuntur alibi: Actus loquendi, ambulandi, videndi, ut sunt sive cogitationis, sive dubitationis, sive cujuscunque alterius actus intellectualis, debebit necessario esse apprehensio rei alicujus ut existentis. Sed sive ipse cogitans apprehenderit se existere, sive aliud extra se existere, jam datur apprehensio certa rei existentis, quæ prior sit hac veritate cogito, sive dubito, ergo sum: non potest enim aut cogitatio, aut dubitatio esse de ulla re, nisi præcesserit apprehensio rei existentis: non dico hujus, illusve rei ut existentis; circa quam ut ratione definitæ naturæ & formalitatis potest mens fluctuare, ita non potest in sua sive cogitatione, sive dubitatione, quo inde procedatur ad existentiam cogitantis, seu dubantis, sibi constare, & statui primæ & certæ veritatis lineis insistere, nisi ante pro illa cogitatione seu dubitatione præcesserit non solum res existens, sed etiam apprehensio illius, ut possibilis saltem existere. Atque hoc sufficit, ut hæc illatio, cogito ergo sum, ne quidem ex fautorum illius sententia, sit prima veritas. An vero certitudo quædam plus quam vulgaris, huic argumento conveniat, proximo capite examinabimus.
units.tr: Meanwhile, according to some who despise the ancient writers, this is the first and most certain truth: I think, I inquire, I doubt, therefore I am. A certain existence of a thing cannot be inferred in the conclusion from an uncertain middle term, or one of uncertain existence. But the acts of speaking, walking and seeing are uncertain and doubtful as to whether they exist. On the other hand, the acts of inquiring, thinking and doubting are certain and undoubted as to whether they exist. I do hear these things, and I admit they are ingeniously devised; yet by no reasoning can I bring myself to be moved by them. For (1) how can this be the first truth, since thought or doubt cannot arise in the mind about a thing unless an apprehension of that thing, as existing, has gone before, about which it is doubted? (2) It is indeed uncertain whether the acts of seeing and walking are such acts as are commonly held to be, according to their formal nature; yet it cannot equally be uncertain to the intellect whether they exist. For unless they existed and had been, how could one think or doubt about them? Why does a man blind from birth, to whom no one has explained the theory of colours, never think or doubt about colours? For no reason at all except that he has never apprehended colours as existing. And so if he has collected alms and believes that some asses have been taken from him, he doubts whether he has a definite number of them, since he had already apprehended the asses before, as existing in a definite number, while all the time he doubts about the quality and value of the same asses. (3) These two questions, whether a thing is and what it is, must not be confused. We often doubt whether we see; yet in order to doubt, we must necessarily apprehend the vision, at least as possible. Thought or doubt cannot arise in us without some object. For who could say that he thinks or doubts when he can point to no object of his thought or doubt? And so I concede this much (though not among the Sceptics, as appeared from the previous chapter): this inference is good, that whoever thinks or doubts, is; I think, therefore I am. Yet this cannot be regarded as the first truth, since there is neither thought nor doubt unless the apprehension of a thing as existing, which is then thought about, has gone before. But on the hypothesis of those who use this argument, everything is supposed to be uncertain or false, indeed as though it did not exist. For they speak elsewhere thus: "The acts of speaking, walking and seeing, as they are acts of thought, or of doubt, or of any other intellectual act, must necessarily involve an apprehension of something as existing. But whether the thinker has apprehended that he himself exists, or that something else exists outside himself, there is already a certain apprehension of an existing thing, which is prior to this truth: I think or I doubt, therefore I am. For neither thought nor doubt can be about anything unless an apprehension of an existing thing has gone before; I do not mean of this or that thing as existing, about which the mind may waver according to the definite nature and formality of the thing; nor can it, in its thinking or doubting, be sure of its own existence as the thinker or doubter, and so proceed to stand upon the lines of the first and certain truth, unless before that thinking or doubting there has gone before not only an existing thing but also an apprehension of it as at least capable of existing." This is enough to show that this inference, I think therefore I am, is not the first truth, not even on the view of its own supporters. Whether a certainty somewhat greater than the ordinary belongs to this argument, we shall examine in the next chapter.

units.la: CAPUT SEXTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SIX.

units.la: Idem hoc sciendi principium tam certum non est atque ij contendunt, qui pro eo, tanquam fundamentali axiomate omnis cognitionis digladiantur.
units.tr: This principle of knowing is not as certain as those who fight over it, as the foundation of all knowledge, claim.

units.la: Principium axiomaticum, superioribus capitibus examinatum, neque Scepticis multum prodesse, neque etiam habendum esse pro principio primo abunde quivis colligere poterit ex ijs, quæ jam antea observata fuerunt. Nec hoc, sepositis ipsis Scepticis, adeo certum esse, ut certius nihil esse queat, gratis potius assumi, quam solide probari, hoc ipso capite evincemus. Veram hanc illationem esse (non tamen circa eam audiendo Scepticos) Cogito, ergo sum, iam antea concessimus, adducendo non solum pro nobis authoritatem Gassendi viri eximij; sed potius audiendo hanc rationem: Omnis actio præsupponit suum suppositum, cogitatio est actio immanens mentis: ergo ut præsupponit necessario suum suppositum, quod agere dicitur, ita convenienter a posteriori procedit hæc illatio: Cogito sive cogitandi actum exerceo, ergo debeo esse res, sive suppositum cogitans. Sed ut vera est hæc illatio, ratione illius individui, sive personæ, quæ sic inferre instituit, ita hanc pariter principaliter certam esse, imo certiorem omnibus aliis argumentis, quis, cui ratio modo superest, concedat? Nam I.Illa illatio est vera, & certissima, quae ex certissimis atque extra omnem dubij aleam positis principijs inferre instituit conclusionem.Haec vero argumentatio, sive illatio, talis neutiquam censeri potest: siquidem conclusionem, quam inferre laborat, in utraque praemissa tanquam veram supponere debet.Conclusio est,ego sum,ac tantummodo eum ipsum,qui cogitandi actu exercet, esse supponit: quum tamen tirones Logici norint, de subiecto in syllogismo demonstrativo semper praesupponendum esse quod sit. Minor est, ego cogito: in qua iterum supponitur existentia subiecti, tam operose per hunc quasi syllogismum probanda, nisi enim exstiterit ipse cogitans, atque de eo verum sit, quod sit, quomodo ulla ratione actum cogitandi edere poterit? Sane nullus mortalium perceperit, aliquem cogitare posse, nisi ante convenerit ei esse.II.Si certa haec est illatio, imo certior omnibus aliis illationibus, antecedens id, e quo conclusio lepida infertur, certum & probe exploratum ei debet esse, qui eandem inferre laborat.Quis enim ex antecedente ignoto, obscuro, nec probe explorato exist(imet inferri posse conclusionem certissimam? Sed antecedens adeo obscurum est inferenti, ut ipsi patroni hujus argumenti, promiscue dubitationem cum cogitatione, atque ipsam cogitationem cum dubita-tione confundant. Certe eos ipsos, quos volunt ex profundo ignorantię emergere, atque accipere hanc quasi primam tabulam, cogito, ergo sum; certissimum est cum ignarissimis nescire quis qualisve actus sit, quem sic exercere instituant, ut inde progrediantur ad hanc conclusionem, tanto apparatu inferendam: Ergo ego sum. Et tamen certissimum, & quasi primum principium agnoscidebet hic syllogismus ex ignorato antecedente illatus? III. Quum hæc argumentatio à posteriori procedens, solummodo vera sit, inferens existentiam suppositi agentis, nulla major certitudo eidem assignari potest, atque sexcentis similibus, procedentibus ab actione quacunque alia, ad illationem suppositi agentis. Quando enim Mopsus latrat, æque certo inferre hoc modo licet: Quicunque latrat, ille est; Mopsus latrat, ergo Mopsus est. Nec quicquam ad rem facit, quod aliquis circa latratus perceptionem sæpe deceptus fuerit: pluries idem ipse, qui suas hic adducit fallacias, deceptus est ratione suarum sive cogitationum, sive dubitationum; atque uti progrediendo à sua aut cogitatione, aut etiam dubitatione, solummodo existimat se inde certo argumentari posse ad sui existentiam; sic admisso Mopsi actu & revera latrantis latratu [dubio licet] inde solummodo infertur eum ipsum, qui ejusmodi actionem edit, revera debere existere. Cum rei non existentis nulla prorsus notari queat actio, incerta ac controversa licet quod ad specificationem.Nec est quod clament nobis magis liquere quid sit cogitatio, aut dubitatio, quod cum circa alia fallamur, circa hæc tamen nunquam decipiamur.Nam gratis hoc dicitur, nec Scepticus, imo nec alius aliquis extra hanc familiam, quem hoc argumento moveri volunt, unquam explicaverit, quid cogitatio, aut dubitatio sit; dato siquidem eum colligere ex hoc ipso actu seu cogitationis, seu dubitationis sese esse: non poterit tamen, ut certum, talis ratiocinium a parte quoque ipsius Scepticì censeri, cum incertum eidem sit, quid aut cogitatio, aut dubitatio sit.Non dicam iam 4. contingens omnino esse, ut aliquis, cui hoc argumentum, velut generale remedium praeratur pariter aut cogitet, aut dubitet; potest siquidem mente adeo obfirmata, & roborata esse, circa omnia quæ occurrunt, ut fidem habendo suis sensibus, & ipsi rationi sensus dirigenti & ordinanti, necproprie cogitet, nec dubitet.At discere velim, quomodo ex præmissis mere contingentibus colligi possit conclusio certissima, imo certitudine provocans quæcunque axiomata.Nec quicquam patronos hujus argumenti iuvare potest, quod nos cap.quarto hujus libri, videamur eodem modo argumentari: neque enim nos, exprincipijs ipsorum Scepticorum progrediendo, definimus aliquid tanquam certum, ipso Sceptico fatente, præ omnibus alijs, quæ aut falsa, aut dubia, aut incerta sunt; sed, tantummodo optionem damus Sceptico, qui postquam in omnes formas se vertit, ut ut Proteus esse velit, unam tamen præ omnibus alijs apprehendere debet, quæ ab eo assumpta, hactenus sufficit ad eum ipsum, mille elabendi licet artes noverit, illaqueandum: cum contra fautores hujus argumenti, formam hanc ipsam definitam & signatam esse contendant nota cogitationis, aut dubitationis, quod hæc actio sola ut certa à Sceptico agnosci debeat ad illationem hujus conclusionis; Ergo sum.Multo minus fautoribus hujus argumenti prodesse potest nostra concessio. Fatemur quidem ratione argumentantis & inferentis personæ certam esse hanc illationem: Cogito, ergo sum.Sed cogitatio haut magis distincte hic admittitur, atque quæcunque alia actio sive mentis, sive corporis, in quam si consenserit Scepticus, jam adeo certo tenetur, ut rima non occurrat, per quam elabatur.
units.tr: Anyone can gather, from what has already been noted, that the axiomatic principle examined in the earlier chapters does little good for the Sceptics, and that it cannot be regarded as a first principle. In this chapter we will show that, even setting the Sceptics aside, it is assumed without warrant rather than solidly proved, and that nothing is more certain than it. We have already conceded that the inference I think, therefore I am is true (though not for the sake of listening to the Sceptics on this point). We did so by citing the authority of the distinguished Gassendi, and by appealing to this reasoning: every action presupposes its subject, and thinking is an immanent action of the mind. So just as it necessarily presupposes the subject said to act, this inference proceeds rightly from effect to cause: I think, or I exercise the act of thinking, therefore I must be a thing, a subject that thinks. But even if this inference is true with respect to the individual person who sets out to draw it, who would grant that it is equally certain in principle, indeed more certain than all other arguments, provided he still has his reason? For (I) an inference is true and most certain when it sets out to draw its conclusion from principles that are most certain and beyond all chance of doubt. But this argument or inference can by no means be judged of that kind. The conclusion it labours to reach, namely I am, it must assume as true in both premises. The conclusion ego sum presupposes only that the very person who exercises the act of thinking is; yet novice logicians know that in a demonstrative syllogism the subject must always be presupposed to exist. The minor premise is ego cogito, in which the existence of the subject is again presupposed, though it is laboriously to be proved by this quasi-syllogism. For unless the thinker exists, and it is true of him that he is, how could he in any way perform the act of thinking? Certainly no mortal has ever perceived that anyone can think unless it has first been granted that he exists. (II) If this inference is certain, indeed more certain than all other inferences, then the antecedent from which the neat conclusion is drawn must be certain and well tested for the one who labours to draw it. For who could suppose that a most certain conclusion can be inferred from an unknown, obscure, and untested antecedent? Yet the antecedent is so obscure to the one inferring that the very advocates of this argument confuse doubt with thinking, and thinking with doubt, indiscriminately. Indeed, those whom they wish to rise out of the depths of ignorance and take up this, as it were, first plank, I think, therefore I am: it is most certain, even to the most ignorant, that they do not know what sort of act it is that they set out to perform, so as to proceed from it to this conclusion, introduced with such display: therefore I am. And yet should this syllogism, drawn from an unknown antecedent, be acknowledged as the most certain and, as it were, first principle? (III) Since this argument, proceeding from effect to cause, is true only insofar as it infers the existence of the acting subject, no greater certainty can be assigned to it than to six hundred similar arguments that proceed from any other action to the inference of the acting subject. When Mopsus barks, one may infer with equal certainty in this way: whoever barks is there; Mopsus barks, therefore Mopsus is there. Nor does it help that someone is often deceived about his perception of barking. The very man who here brings forward his deceptions has often been deceived about his thoughts or his doubts. And just as by proceeding from his own thinking or doubting he thinks he can argue with certainty to his own existence, so, granting that Mopsus performs an act, and that he really barks, even if the bark is doubtful, it is inferred only that he who produces such an action must really exist. For no action at all can be noted of a thing that does not exist, however uncertain and disputed its specific nature may be. Nor should they insist that we understand better what thinking or doubting is, and that although we are mistaken about other things, we are never mistaken about these. This is said without warrant. Neither the Sceptic, nor anyone outside this circle whom they wish to move by this argument, has ever explained what thinking or doubting is. Granting that he can gather from this very act, whether of thinking or of doubting, that he exists, still such reasoning cannot be counted as certain on the part of the Sceptic, since it is uncertain to him what thinking or doubting is. I need not add that it is entirely possible for someone to whom this argument is offered as a general remedy to think or doubt at the same time. For his mind may be so fixed and strengthened about everything that comes before him, trusting his senses and reason itself, which directs and orders the senses, that he neither properly thinks nor doubts. Yet I would like to learn how a most certain conclusion, indeed one that outdoes every axiom in certainty, can be drawn from premises that are merely contingent. Nor can the advocates of this argument be helped by the claim that in the fourth chapter of this book we seem to argue in the same way. For we do not, proceeding from the Sceptics' own principles, define something as certain, with the Sceptic himself admitting it, above all others that are false, doubtful, or uncertain. We only give the Sceptic a choice. Though he turns himself into every form, and wishes to be a Proteus, he must still grasp one thing above all others, and once he has assumed it, that is enough to catch him, however many arts he knows for slipping away. Whereas the advocates of this argument contend that this very form is defined and marked by the sign of thinking or doubting, so that this act alone must be acknowledged by the Sceptic as certain for the inference of this conclusion: therefore I am. Still less can our concession help the advocates of this argument. We admit that, from the standpoint of the person arguing and inferring, this inference is certain: I think, therefore I am. But thinking is not admitted here more distinctly than any other action of mind or body. And if the Sceptic has granted any such action, he is already held so firmly that no crack is left through which he might slip.

units.la: LIBER SECUNDUS. CAPUT SEPTIMUM
units.tr: Book Two, Chapter Seven

units.la: In quo statu considerari debeat homo, de quo quæritur an scientiam acquirere possit ?
units.tr: In what state the man should be considered, concerning whom it is asked whether he can acquire knowledge?

units.la: Omisso vero præcedenti tum argumento, tum thesi, ulterius progredimur, expensuri an scientia in hominem cadere possit: quod ut legitime à nobis fieri queat, ante omnia constare debet, secundum quem statum homo considerari debeat. Ergo ex Theologia revelata constat, hominem in triplici potissimum statu considerari posse: Integritatis, corruptionis, & gloriæ. Quod quanquam ex solo libro Scripturæ constat, sana tamen Philosophia, quæ Theologiæ nunquam adversari potest, ambabus ulnis amplectitur. Quod ad hominem in primo statu consideratum, sub eo, cum ornatus esset divina imagine, maximam non tantum rerum divinarum, sed etiam naturalium cognitionem habebat (quicquid Socinianis videatur) quemadmodum liquido patet ex impositione nominum [de qua Genes. cap. 2.] quam Deus ratam habuit utpote cum natura eorum convenientem. Quanquam autem Scriptura Senecdochice in una solum re primo homini sapientiam assignat, recte tamen ei per Analogiam in similibus rebus assignare licet. Nec tamen hæc congenita Adamo cognitio sic perfecta fuit, quin colla
units.tr: Having now set aside the previous argument and thesis, we go on to examine whether knowledge can fall to man. For this to be done properly by us, we must first establish according to which state man ought to be considered. Revealed theology teaches that man can be considered chiefly in three states: of integrity, of corruption, and of glory. Although this is known from Scripture alone, sound philosophy, which can never be opposed to theology, embraces it with both arms. As for man considered in the first state, while he was adorned with the divine image he had not only the greatest knowledge of divine things but also of natural things (whatever the Socinians may think). This is clear from the imposition of names [see Gen. 2], which God approved as suited to their nature. Although Scripture, by synecdoche, assigns wisdom to the first man in only one matter, we may rightly assign it to him by analogy in similar matters. Nor was this knowledge innate in Adam so perfect that it could not be called imperfect when compared with the knowledge God has of the same things.

units.la: colla collàta cum ea cognitione, quam de ijsdem rebus Deus habet, imperfecta dici potuerit: imo sic perfecta fuit, ut ipse homo paulatim eam perfectiorem reddidisset: 1.cognoscendo novas rerum formas, quæ subinde exortæ fuissent, aut ex putri materia, aut ex diversarum specierum commixtione. 2.Cognitione individuorum cujusque speciei, quæ quia ratione hominis innumerabilia, per partes cognovisset. 3.Secundum modum sciendi, cum enim Adam initio omnium rerum cognitionem tantum speculativam haberet, ea deinceps in eo facta fuisset clarior, & tum experientia, tum sensuum judicio magis at magis confirmata. Videatur Dn. Pareus inComm. ad cap.
units.tr: Indeed it was so perfect that man himself would gradually have made it more perfect: (1) by coming to know the new forms of things that arose from time to time, either from putrid matter or from the mixing of different species; (2) by knowing the individuals of each species, which, given the human mind, he would have known one by one, though they are innumerable; (3) by the mode of knowing. For although Adam at first had only speculative knowledge of all things, that knowledge would afterwards have become clearer in him and been more and more confirmed, both by experience and by the judgement of the senses. See Pareus in his Commentary on Gen. 2.

units.la: 2. Gen.v.20.Si quis vero quærat, quænam scientiæ hujus prærogativæ fuerint præ ea, quam nos post lapsum de rebus naturalibus habemus: notet privilegiorum momenta .1.Prærogativa gavisus est Adam in ipso habitu, qui perfectissime illi à Deo cum speciebus intelligibilibus infusus est. 2. In actu & exercitio, quia commodius uti poterat scientia quam nos, cum nullam inordinatam affectionem aut impedimentum corporis haberet, quale nos habemus. 3.In amplitudine, quia scie bat omnes res naturales, quæ ab homine cognosci possunt: quod nobis nequaquam licet: quia vel non vivimus tanto tempore, ut possimus acquirere omnium naturalium rerum scientiam, vel vel non applicamus animum ob alias occupationes. 4. In modo sciendi, quia ille sciebat quamq; rem per propria s causas, ea perfectione, quæ in hominem tum cadere poterat: nos vero pleraque scimus tantum p r suos effectus. 5. In firmitate, quia ille non poterat amittere scientiam, quam nos sæpe amittimus vel propter longam cessationem ab exercitio; vel propter læsionem phantasiæ per morbum, vel propter fallacem ratiocinationem, vel deceptionem: quæ in statu innocentiæ nequaquam locum habebant. Quoniam vero homo possessione omnium harum prærogativarum excidit, frustra sunt, quicunque ei in altero statu (sub lapsu nempe) considerato, aut omnia hæc privilegia, aut saltem quædam ex ijs, propria industria ac diligentia, quod ad rerum naturalium cognitionem, contingere posse existimant. Quanquam enim per lapsum omnes scintillulæ imaginis divinæ penitus extinctæ non fuerunt, sed tenues remanserunt reliquiæ; quarum subsidio accedente peculiari quo Spiritus Sancti lumine, Philosophia primo exuscitari, & paulatim magis ac magis perfici potuit; non potest tamen earum præsidio, homo, ne quidem regenitus, de quo Apostolus testatur Col. 3. v. 10. quod renovetur in agnitionem congruentem imagini ejus qui ipsum condidit, pervenire ad perfectionem illam scientiæ, qua ante lapsum coruscabat: quia quamdiu in hac vitata degit ex parte solum {ut idem Apostolus loquitur 1.Cor.13.v.9.} cognoscit: quod non verum tantum ratione rerum spiritualium ac divinarum, verum & naturalium. Nec contrarium evincit Salomonis exemplum. Quod enim de ejus sapientia dicitur (ut recte animadvertit Cl. Rivetus Exerc. 22. in Genef. quæ omnium sapientiæ præfertur 1. Reg. 3.) qui fuerunt, vel futuri sunt; intelligendum est comparatione facta ad omnes homines post corruptionis statum, non ad Adamum ante peccatum. Addere possumus triplici solum modo Salomonem omnibus hominibus post lapsum sapientiorem fuisse. Primo si conferatur cum illis qui proprio studio & labore scientiam acquisiverunt. Secundo si componatur cum regibus, qui vel ante, vel post eum in Hierusalem fuerunt: ut ipse innuere videtur Eccl. 1. v. 16. Tertio si sermo sit non tam de rerum naturalium scientia, quam de prudentia regendi populum, quam speciatim à Deo expetiverat, 1. Reg. 3. v. 9. In tertio gloriæ statu quoniam ratione electorum adveniet quod persectum est, illud quod aliquatenus est, ex parte tolletur, docente Apostolo 1.Cor. 13. v. 10. Ipsiqne amplius cognoscent, prout amplius edocti fuerint, ib. v. 12. Quod an complementum etiam habiturum sit ratione cognitionis rerum naturalium, cum Scripturæ definire non placuerit, exemplo quorundam Scholasticorum rimari non audemus: Sufficit ex ea liquere, hominem ante lapsum perfectiorem rerum naturalium habuisse cognitionem, quam post eum assequi potest. Quod nobis magno usui futurum est, non tantum contra inflatos sciolos, sed & quosdam recentiores, qui majorem Philosophiae, quam cudere moliuntur, persectionem praeconcipiunt, quam in hominem aliquem post lapsum cadere potest. Quanquam autem hi a Scepticismo alienissimi videntur, ad nihil scire tamen viam expeditissimam faciunt, dum omne scire prae suo scire nihil putant; quod tamen si penitius excutiatur ipsis ineptiis ineptius deprehendetur. Sed hac de re pluribus libris subsequentibus: hic tantum ex iis, quae dicta sunt, notetur, quando a nobis disputatur de perfectione scientiae Philosophice perfectae, considerari scientiae hujus subjectum hominem, quatenus post lapsum destitutus est imagine Dei.
units.tr: If anyone asks what the advantages of this knowledge were over the knowledge of natural things that we have after the fall, let him note the following points of privilege. (1) Adam enjoyed a prerogative in the habit itself, since it was infused into him by God most perfectly, together with intelligible species. (2) In the act and exercise, since he could use his knowledge more conveniently than we can, having no disordered affection or bodily impediment such as we have. (3) In its extent, since he knew all the natural things that can be known by a man, which we by no means can do: either because we do not live long enough to acquire knowledge of all natural things, or because we do not apply our minds, being occupied with other things. (4) In the mode of knowing, since he knew each thing through its proper causes, with that perfection which could then fall to a man, whereas we for the most part know things only through their effects. (5) In firmness, since he could not lose the knowledge, which we often lose, either through long disuse, or through injury to the imagination by disease, or through faulty reasoning, or through deception; none of which had any place in the state of innocence. But since man lost possession of all these prerogatives, those who think that, in the second state (that is, under the fall), a man can attain by his own industry and diligence either all these privileges or at least some of them, as far as knowledge of natural things is concerned, are wasting their effort. For although the sparks of the divine image were not entirely extinguished by the fall, but faint remnants remained, with whose help, and with the special light of the Holy Spirit added, philosophy could first be roused and gradually made more and more perfect, yet by these remnants man cannot attain that perfection of knowledge which shone before the fall, not even when he has been regenerated. The Apostle testifies that he is renewed unto knowledge after the image of him that created him (Col. 3:10); but as long as he lives in this life, he knows only in part (as the same Apostle says, 1 Cor. 13:9). This is true not only of spiritual and divine things but also of natural things. Nor does the example of Solomon prove the contrary. What is said of his wisdom, that it surpassed the wisdom of all who were or will be (as the illustrious Rivet rightly observes, Exerc. 22 on Genesis, citing 1 Kings 3), must be understood as a comparison made with all men after the state of corruption, not with Adam before the sin. We may add that Solomon was wiser than all men after the fall in only three ways: first, if he is compared with those who acquired knowledge by their own study and labour; second, if he is compared with the kings who were in Jerusalem before or after him, as he himself seems to hint at Eccl. 1:16; third, if the discussion concerns not so much the knowledge of natural things as the prudence of ruling the people, which he especially asked of God, 1 Kings 3:9. In the third, glorious state, since with the elect that which is perfect will come, that which is in part will be taken away, as the Apostle teaches (1 Cor. 13:10). They will know even more, as they have been more fully taught (ibid. v. 12). Whether this will also have a completion with respect to knowledge of natural things, since Scripture has not chosen to define it, we do not dare to probe by the example of certain Scholastics. It is enough that it is clear from Scripture that man before the fall had a more perfect knowledge of natural things than he can attain after it. This will be of great use to us, not only against the puffed-up half-learned, but also against some more recent writers, who conceive in advance a greater perfection of philosophy than can fall to any man after the fall. Although these men seem very far from scepticism, they make the way to knowing nothing very easy, while they think that all knowing is nothing compared with their own knowing; yet if this is examined more closely, it will be found to be as foolish as their follies. But we will discuss this matter in more books to follow. Here let us only note, from what has been said, that when we dispute about the perfection of perfect philosophical knowledge, the subject of this knowledge is considered to be man as far as, after the fall, he has been deprived of the image of God.
