units.la: Quid sit scientia, & quaenam illius attributa?
units.tr: Quid sit scientia, & quaenam illius attributa?

units.la: Sed dein quaerendum quid sit scientia; quod ut commode fieri queat, removendae vocis significationes aliquae sunt, instituto nostro minus convenientes. Neque enim primo hic vox latissime accipitur pro quacunque cognitione, sive certa & evidente, sive incerta& obscura, sive intellectiva, sive etiam sensitiva: quomodo etiam ea quæ aut fide credimus, aut fide percipimus, scire dicimur. Neque secundo minus improprie accipitur pro cognitione intellectiva& certa,quatenus ea ab opinione distinguitur; sive sit clara ac evidens, sive obscura & inevidens, quo sensu non tantum comprehendit scientiam proprie dictam, verum etiam fidem. Neque tertio sic vocem accipimus, quatenus proprie magis, quamcunque cognitionem intellectivam certam & evidentem notat, sive ea per causam, sive sine causa sit: quo sensu in se etiam comprehendit cognitionem principiorum, alias intelligentiam dictam. Neque postremo vocem scientiæ tam rigorose accipimus, prout accipi solet à Philosophi interpretibus ad lib. 2. post. Anal. & lib. 6. Eth. cap. 3. Quatenus opponitur quatuor aliis habitibus intellectualibus, arti nempe, prudentiæ, sapientiæ, & intelligentiæ. Concedimus libenter secundum Philosophum, Scholæque Peripateticæ praxin, talem scientiam, perfectissimam, & quasi eminenter scientiæ rationem habere, sed tamen nobis, qui hoc loco contraScepticos disputamus, hæc propriissima notatio admodum usui non est. Consideramus enim hic scientiam, quatenus accipitur pro cognitione intellectiva certa & evidenti, nec anxie inquirimus, sitne illud quod proprie rie solum,sciri potest universale & necessarihabeaturve vel per demonstrationem tan-, vel per definitionem, vel per utrumque. ntiae autem hoc modo consideratę tria accit, quae ab ea separari nulla ratione possunt: itas, perspicuitas, & certitudo. Primo conratur circa eam veritas: eaque tum ratione ecti, quia mens est perficienda rerum veran perfectione; tum ratione instrumentorum quae acquiritur, sive illa sint demonstratios, sive quid aliud eorum loco; tum ratione ionis rei obiectae, & intellectus, quatenus eam vera, & non tantum existimata comprensione comprehendit. Secundo perspicuitas, ię considerata in re obiecta est magna intelligilitas, in notitia vero est claritas, profluens ex telligibilitate rei, & ipsa intellectus intellectio-. Tertio certitudo, quae ratione ipsarum reim considerata, earum constantia est; ratione item scientiae, hic tantum consideraբilis, est firma ientis adhaesio, quae ut talis sit, qualis habetur, riri debet a perspicuitate, a qua nisi originem rahat, conjuncta potest esse cum falsitate, haebitque rationem non tam certitudinis, quam ertinaciae. Ratione trium harum conditionum cientia, prouta nobis hic consideratur, non incomnode definiri potest: Cognitio intellectiva rei vera et perspicua.
units.tr: But next we must ask what science is. So that this can be done conveniently, some meanings of the word that are less suited to our purpose must first be set aside. For, first, the word is not taken here in its widest sense, for any cognition whatever, whether certain and evident or uncertain and obscure, whether intellectual or even sensory; in this way we also say that we "know" things which we believe by faith or perceive by faith. Nor, secondly, is it taken, no less improperly, for intellectual and certain cognition as distinguished from opinion, whether it be clear and evident or obscure and unevident; in this sense it comprises not only science properly so called but also faith. Nor, thirdly, do we take the word in the sense in which it more properly denotes any certain and evident intellectual cognition, whether it is through a cause or without a cause; in this sense it also includes the cognition of first principles, otherwise called understanding. Nor, lastly, do we take the word "science" so rigorously as it is commonly taken by the interpreters of the Philosopher on the second book of the Posterior Analytics and the sixth book of the Ethics, chapter 3, namely as opposed to four other intellectual habits: art, prudence, wisdom, and understanding. We willingly concede, following the Philosopher and the practice of the Peripatetic school, that such science has the most perfect and, as it were, eminent character of science; but for us, who in this place dispute against the Sceptics, this most proper notation is of little use. For we consider science here as far as it is taken for certain and evident intellectual cognition, and we do not anxiously inquire whether that which can be known strictly as universal and necessary is to be held to be so by demonstration alone, or by definition, or by both. Science considered in this way has three attributes which can in no way be separated from it: truth, perspicuity, and certainty. First, truth is concerned with it; and this is required both on account of the mind, which is to be perfected by the truth of things, and on account of the instruments by which it is acquired, whether these are demonstrations or something else in their place, and on account of the object known, and the intellect insofar as it comprehends that object with a true and not merely supposed understanding. Second, perspicuity: considered in the object, it is great intelligibility; in the knowledge, it is clarity, flowing from the intelligibility of the thing and from the intellect's own act of understanding. Third, certainty: which, considered in regard to the things themselves, is their constancy; and, in regard to science, which alone is considered here, is a firm adherence of the mind, which, in order to be such as it is held to be, ought to arise from perspicuity. Unless it arises from that, it may be joined with falsity, and it has the character not so much of certainty as of obstinacy. By these three conditions science, as it is considered by us here, can conveniently be defined: an intellectual cognition of a thing that is true and perspicuous.

units.la: CAPUT NONUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER NINE.

units.la: Quomodo scientia ab opinione distinguatur.
units.tr: How science is distinguished from opinion.

units.la: SCientia ex nostra mente descripta, videndum deinceps quomodo ab opinione distinguatur. Scepticorum enim effatum est apud Sext.Empiric. adverf. Mathem. Per caussam de nulla re quicquam scimus, sed est singulis opinio ut affluxus.Inde & Xenophanis Colophonij vox apud eundem lib.2. Pyrrh.Hypoth. Opinio est in omnibus. Ut vero liquido differentiæ momenta cognosci queant, exploratum ante esse debet, quid opinio sit. Observandum ergo eam pertinere ad habitus illos qui à Philosophi interpretibus ad lib. 6. Eth. cap. 3. inevidentes vocari solent: quibus opponuntur habitus evidentes, Intelligentia, scientia, & sapientia. Quia autem inevidentes habitus collati cum evidentibus, secundariorum habituum, & ut loquuntur, habituum secundum modum, rationem habent, inde opinionem habitum verum esse negant, eamque malunt per affectionem aut dispositionem definire, quam per habitum: quorum opinioni nos applaudentes definimus opinionem, quod sit: Dispositio inclinans intellectum ad assentiendum alicui rei, vel ex terminis, vel ob rationem probabilem, cum formidine partis oppositæ. Per hanc definitionem opinionem à fide humana distinguimus, ei enim necessario non adest formido, quæ ab opinione inseparabilis est. Qando autem fit mentio formidinis partis oppositæ, notandum eam duplicem esse. Alia enim est ex parte potentiæ intellectivæ, sive subjecti, & est nihil aliud quam vacillatio ipsius intellectus in assentiendo. Alia autem est ex parte ipsius actus sive cognitionis: estque talis formido per quam ipsa cognitio secundum se (& dempto judicio intellectus vel formidantis, vel sibi tenaciter persuasum habentis) ita afficitur, ut possit ei subesse falsum. Hæc posterior formido prorsus requiritur ad rationem opinionis, quia id postulat discrimen scientiæ & opinionis. Prior vero formido, quæ existit ex parte potentiæ intellectivæ, non est opinioni necessaria, ut apparet per cujusvis experientiam: nemo enim est ex omni doctorum numero, qui non opinetur quandoque, verissimam se tueri sententiam, eique mordacissime adhæreat, citra ullam partis oppositæ formidinem; cum nihilominus progressu temporis discat, notitiæ suæ falsum sub fuisse, & eam non habuisse rationem scientiæ, sed opinionis. Potest ergo opinio carere actuali vacillatione intellectu sad assentiendum: ut & Aristoteles docet lib. 7. Eth. cap. 3. ubi testatur; Nonnullos opinantium non ambigere, sed certo se scire putare. Conferatur Cajetanus 2. 2. q. a. 5. & part. 3. q. 5. 3. Notandum notandum hoc non tantum contra multos exrecentioribus Philosophis, verum etiam contra Pyrrhonios, qui cum existimarent, opinionem omnem vacillantem, ipsi intellectui, & proinde opinanti quam crucem figere [ut liquet ex Sexto I.3.Pyrrh.hypoth.cap.14.]laborabant vivere citra ullam opinionem.Definita ergo hunc in modum opinione, videndum, quomodo à scientia, prout eam superiori capite consideravimus, distinguatur. 1.Scientia & opinio differunt ratione generis.Scientiæ enim genus est verus habitus, opinionis vero dispositio. 2.Ex parte certitudinis, scientia est certa ac infallibilis cognitio, opinio vero dubia, incerta, & fotmidolosa. 3.Ex parte claritatis, nam de ratione scientiæ est evidentia, de ratione vero opinionis, inevidentia & obscuritas.Habet vero scientia evidentiam non perse, sed ab evidentia principiorum participatam: unde major evidentia ipsis principijs inésse debet, quam conclusionibus scientiarum, ut recte colligit Philosophus lib. 1.Poster.Anal. cap. 2. Ut non audiendi sint quidam recentiores, qui eandem evidentiam scientiarum & principiorum esse volunt; ac proinde omnia tam liquido sciri, quam ab omnibus terminorum non ignaris cognoscitur, bis bina efficere quatuor.
units.tr: Having described science as it lies in our mind, we must next consider how it is distinguished from opinion. For the saying of the Sceptics is reported in Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians: Through cause we know nothing of any thing, but opinion is for each person like an influx. Hence also the saying of Xenophanes of Colophon in the same author, book 2 of the Pyrrhonian Outlines: Opinion is in all things. But so that the grounds of difference may be clearly known, it must first be established what opinion is. We must observe, therefore, that it belongs to those habits which the interpreters of the Philosopher, on book 6 of the Ethics, chapter 3, are accustomed to call inevident. Opposed to them are the evident habits: understanding, science, and wisdom. Since, however, inevident habits, compared with evident ones, have the character of secondary habits, or, as they put it, of habits according to a mode, they deny that opinion is a true habit, and prefer to define it by an affection or disposition rather than by a habit. Applauding their view, we define opinion as follows: A disposition inclining the intellect to assent to some thing, either from its terms or on account of a probable reason, with fear of the opposite part. By this definition we distinguish opinion from human faith, for fear, which is inseparable from opinion, is not necessarily present in faith. When mention is made of fear of the opposite part, it should be noted that this fear is twofold. One lies on the side of the intellective power, or the subject, and is nothing other than the wavering of the intellect itself in assenting. The other lies on the side of the act or cognition itself, and is such that through it the cognition, considered in itself (setting aside the judgement of the intellect, whether fearful or firmly persuaded of its view), is so affected that falsity may underlie it. This latter fear is entirely required for the definition of opinion, since it is what marks the difference between science and opinion. The former fear, which exists on the side of the intellective power, is not necessary for opinion, as anyone's experience makes plain. For there is no one among all the learned who does not sometimes suppose that he upholds the truest view, and clings to it most tenaciously, without any fear of the opposite part; yet with the passage of time he learns that his knowledge was false, and that it had the character not of science but of opinion. Opinion can therefore lack actual wavering of the intellect in assenting, as Aristotle also teaches in book 7 of the Ethics, chapter 3, where he testifies: Some of those who opine do not doubt, but think they know for certain. Compare Cajetan, on 2.2 q. a. 5, and part 3 q. 5 art. 3. This must be noted not only against many of the more recent philosophers, but also against the Pyrrhonists, who, thinking that every opinion wavers and so inflicts torment on the opining intellect itself (as is clear from Sextus, Pyrrhonian Outlines 1.3, chapter 14), laboured to live without any opinion. Having defined opinion in this way, we must see how it is distinguished from science, as we considered science in the previous chapter. 1. Science and opinion differ in respect of genus: the genus of science is a true habit, but the genus of opinion is a disposition. 2. On the side of certainty, science is certain and infallible cognition, while opinion is doubtful, uncertain, and fearful. 3. On the side of clarity, evidence belongs to the nature of science, while inevidence and obscurity belong to the nature of opinion. Science does not have evidence in itself, but participates in the evidence of its principles; hence the principles themselves must have greater evidence than the conclusions of the sciences, as the Philosopher rightly infers in book 1 of the Posterior Analytics, chapter 2. Certain more recent writers are not to be listened to, who want the evidence of the sciences and of their principles to be the same, and so hold that everything is known as clearly as it is known by all who are not ignorant of the terms, that twice two makes four.

units.la: Quomodo scientiæ, jam antea definitæ, perse- ctio accidere queat.
units.tr: How the perfection of science, already defined above, may come about.

units.la: Distincta opinione à scientia, videndum quo- modo huic perfectio accidat. Non quidem tam propter Scepticos hoc cognoscendum, quam propter ea, quæ subsequentibus libris fusius & distinctius disputanda erunt, quamvis & cognoscì debeat, quo commodius Scepticorum ar- gumentis occurri queat. Potest ergo scientiæ per- sectio oboriri, aut ab objecta materia, scibili nempe, aut à causis, aut ab affectionibus; aut denique ab omnibus. Quantum autem ad primum modum perfectionis advenientem ab objecto, notandum scibile sex habere conditiones, de quibus duæ priores tam absolute ad illud pertinent, ut separari non possint: quatuor vero posteriores concernunt perfectionem. 1. Scibile ita affectum debet esse, ut disci ac doceri possit. Unde non valet quorundam Scepticorum argumentum ab ignorantia quarundam rerum, quæ ab homine in statu apsus consideràto, perfecte cognosci non possunt aut ob summam perfectionem, aut ob imperfectionem, ad eversionem omnis, qualiscumque etiam, scientiæ. 2. Scibile debet habere causas, ut Philosophus quoque innuit secundo
units.tr: Having distinguished science from opinion, we must consider how perfection comes to science. We need to know this less for the sake of the Sceptics than for the sake of what will be disputed more fully and distinctly in the following books, although it ought also to be known so that the Sceptics' arguments can be met more conveniently. The perfection of science can therefore arise either from the object matter, namely the knowable, or from causes, or from affections, or finally from all of these. As for the first mode of perfection, which comes from the object, it should be noted that the knowable has six conditions. The first two pertain to it so absolutely that they cannot be separated from it, while the last four concern its perfection. 1. The knowable must be such that it can be learned and taught. Hence the argument of some Sceptics from the ignorance of certain things, which a man in his present state cannot know perfectly, either because of their supreme perfection or because of their imperfection, does not hold, and it does not overturn every science, however slight. 2. The knowable must have causes, as the Philosopher also hints in the second book of the Metaphysics and the first book of the Posterior Analytics.

units.la: Metaphyf.& primo posteriorum. Hæ conditiones simpliciter sunt necessariæ ad scientiam proprie dictam. Ratione objecti reliquæ quatuor serviunt perfectioni; ergo. 3. scibile synonymum, vel saltem analogum est: à qua lege cum quibusdam non male unus Deus excipitur. 4. Est unum, & quidem vel genere, vel specie, vel proportione, vel attributione. 5. Est ens per se, non vero per accidens. 6. Est necessarium, æternum, immutabile. Quæ postrema conditio non tantum à Philosopho adfertur lib. 1. Post. Anal. verum etiam lib. 6. Eth. cap. 3. Quanquam vero plerique Philosophi Interpretes, ad scientiam proprie dictam, quatuor etiam posteriores conditiones, & præcipuè sextam requiri existimant, nos tamen dicere malumus, pertinere ad scientiam perfectissimam: & Aristotelem in libb. Posteriorum, non tam agere de scientiæ propriè sumptæ conditionibus, quam perfectissimæ. Communi Interpretum sententiæ quicunque adhærent; si cum Scepticis disputare debeant, concedere illis debebunt, dari tantum eorum scientiam, quorum datur demonstratio, disputationisque filum eo deduceturs, ut manear solum in controversia an detur demonstratio; quam si everterit Scepticus, simul etiam submoverit omnem scientiam. Deinde secundo scientiæ perfectio oboritur à causis. Per causas potissimum intelligimus finalem & efficientem. Quantum ad illam ea respicit aut finem primarium scientiæ, aut fines secundarios sive primarij finis usus.Ratione finis primarii nulli diversæ perfectionis gradus scientiæ accidere possunt.Omnis enim scientiæ finis est scire.Quanquam autem scire, ut & scientia, multiplex est; diversosque perfectionis gradus habet, non tamen ratione hujus finis potissimum in intentione considerandi, diversitas oboriri potest.Omnis enim scientia intendit scire perfectum, quod si attingere semper non possit,mediis imputandum est. Respectu nihilominus finium secundariorum,sive usus multiplicis,multiplex diversitas scientiis accidere potest; ut enim illud scire est melius, cujus plures & simul meliores usus sunt: ita etiam illa scientia perfectior habenda est, cujus scire ejusmodi usus comitantur.Sed ex caussis præcipue efficiens perfectionem scientiæ confert: quod ut intelligi possit [cū summum contra Scepticos usum habeat] ante paulo uberius de caussis scientiæ efficientibus agendum est.Distribuimus autem easin principales, & minus principales sive organicas. Principalis, iterum aut universalis, ut Deus: aut particularis est, quæ ipsa hominis mens.Organicæ sive instrumentariæ iterum in duplici differentia: aut enim menti inserviunt in investigatione scientiarum, aut scientiam investigatam per partes, totam in mente progenerant.Prioris notæ instrumentariae caussae multae sunt. 1. Pietas, ejusq; exercitium, quae primae causae opem conciliant. 2. Sensus, unde mens quasi emendicat, quod intelligit. 3. Memoria, a qua nascitur experientia: quae gignitur ex multis recordationibus unius ejusdemque attributi, observati aut in pluribus, aut in uno saepius: ut v. c. quando quis meminit rhabarbarum profuisse Titio, Sempronio, &c. ubi saepius illud deprehensum est, tandem fit experientia & inductio. Porro etiam atque etiam notandum, experientiam duplicem esse, unam sensuum, quae in bestiis locum habere potest, & alteram accuratam, quae solius mentis est, quatenus ut alio in loco indicatum est, mentis in homine officium est, non tantum sensuum judicium a fallacia, quantum fieri potest, afferere, verum etiam ordinare. Ratio enim ut potest sensus errantes corrigere, sic potest quoque dirigere. Quod docere videtur Philosophus lib. 3. de Gener. Anim. cap. 10. Quoniam vero experientia inservit vel ad apprehendendum, vel ad assentiendum: ut apprehendamus sufficit prior experientia: habetque hic locum quod vulgo dicitur, Nihil unquam in mente est, nisi prius in sensu fuerit: ut vero assentiamur & non temere, requiritur accurata experientia, sive mentis: quod sedulo contra recentiores quosdam experientiae blaterones est notandum, quibus assiduo in ore, Veni & Vide: & interim non expendunt, an nonsensioni, ad quam provocant, ob conditionis alicujus defectum ( quemadmodum prolixe alio in loco ostendimus ) error subesse possit, quem ut sola mens in homine potest castigare, sic sensuum judicium unius mentis moderamine indiget. Porro ad causas scientiæ instrumentales etiam pertinet species intentionalis, quodque eam facit, 5. dispositio organi, cerebri nempe, congruens. Ob cujus pravam dispositionem multi ad Philosophandum, nedum perfecte, maxime inhabiles & inidonei sunt. Et tantum de caussis organicis, quæ causæ principales particulai scientiam generanti inserviunt. succedunt organa per quæ scien-tia tota, per partes ante investigata, in mente progenerätur. Illud autem non unicum tantum est, utquibusdam recentioribus visum est, sed geminum: Definitio & Demonstratio, ut non tantum ex Aristotele colligi potest, si accuratè sequentia ejus loca conferantur: 1. de Anim. t. 11. 8. Phys. c. 3. lib. 1. Met. cap. ult. verum etiam suadet ratio: Scitur enim aut rei essentia, per definitionem scilicet: aut proprietas, & energit Demonstratio. Demonstratio autem quæ scientiam gignit, ea aut per caussam, aut per effectum instituitur. Definitio vero quæ ali quid ad scientiæ perfectionem conferet, constare debet genere& differentia, aut saltem loco differentiæ, proprietate. Queri hic solet utrum ex duobus his instrumentis nobilius habendum sit? Nos omnibus rite expensis, definitioni perfectæ sive essentiali cum Averroë primas concedimus, moti præcæteris his rationibus. (1.) Quia præstat scire quid res sit, quam qualis: 3. Metaph. cap. 1. & 7. Metaph. cap. 5. definitio autem docet quid res sit, demonstratio qualis. (2) Ex definitione facile proprietates colliguntur: lib. 4. Phys. cap. 5. Non autem ex demonstratione æque facile rei essentia. (3) Quia definitio magis substantiæ congruit, demonstratio autem accidentibus (4.) Quia definitione scientia nobilior paratur, quod apparebit, sive spectetur præstantia materiæ: definitur quippe substantia, demonstratur autem affectio; sive etiam certitudo spectetur, est enim definitio demonstrationis elementum ac proinde etiam certior. Quibus prælibatis, facile cuique liquere poterit, quomodo à caussis tum principalibus tum etiam instrumentariis perfectio scientiæ accedere possit. Præcipue autem illa consideratur ratione instrumentorum totam in mente generantium, pro quorum diversa ratione, diversisque perfectionis gradibus plurimum etiam variat. Omnium perfectissima scientia in ordine ad demonstrationem, quæ habetur per demostrationem propter quid: in ordine vero ad definitionem, quæ acquiritur per definitionem constantem generere &c. nere & differentia specifica. Ipsa instrumenta hæc si inter se conferantur, perfectior erit habenda scientia, quæ comparata est per definitionem essentialem, quam per demonstrationem, ut liquet ex precedentibus. Tertio & postremo scientię perfectio contingit ab affectionibus, ijs nempe, de quibus locuti fuimus antea. Veritate, perspicuitate, & certitudine, quorum gradus eminentior eminentiorem perfectionem, eminentissimus autem summam perfectionem scientiæ conciliat. Ex his quæ de scientiæ perfectione dicta sunt, liquet primo quid opinandum sit de sententia eorum, qui nullam aliam scientiam agnoscunt præter intuitivam, eam scilicet quæ omnia tam liquido ostendit, ut manibus quasi palpari possint, habetque tantam certitudinem, quam sensuum dicium. Quasi vero nulla differentia in erredat inter scientiæ instrumentum, experientiam sensuum, & scientiam perfectam, quæ universalium est. Certitudo scientiæ non potest citra grandem errorem confundi cum certitudine sensuum. Nam [1] si eadem est certitudo scientiæ quæ sensuum, idem deberet esse objectum: & consequenter scientia tantum dabitur accidentium singularium. [2] a quę sub sensum cadere non possunt, sciri quoque non poterunt: quoniam fautores huius de hanc scientiæ persectionem à solis sensibus obvenire volunt. Quid ergo
units.tr: These conditions are simply necessary for science properly so called. The remaining four serve the perfection of the object; therefore: 3. The knowable is univocal, or at least analogous, though some not unreasonably except the one God from this rule. 4. It is one, either by genus, by species, by proportion, or by attribution. 5. It is a being per se, and not per accidens. 6. It is necessary, eternal and immutable. This last condition is set down not only by the Philosopher in the first book of the Posterior Analytics but also in the sixth book of the Ethics, chapter 3. Although most interpreters of the Philosopher think that the last four conditions, and especially the sixth, are required for science properly so called, we prefer to say that they pertain to the most perfect science, and that Aristotle, in the books of the Posterior Analytics, treats not so much of the conditions of science properly taken as of those of the most perfect science. Whoever adheres to the common opinion of the interpreters, if they must dispute with the Sceptics, will have to concede to them that there is science only of those things of which there is demonstration, and the thread of the dispute will lead them to this: that the only question left is whether demonstration exists at all. If the Sceptic overturns this, he will at the same time remove all science. Next, secondly, the perfection of science arises from causes. By causes we chiefly understand the final and the efficient cause. As regards the final cause, these concern either the primary end of science or the secondary ends, that is, the uses of the primary end. In respect of the primary end, no different degrees of perfection can arise in science, for the end of every science is to know. Although knowing, like science itself, is manifold and has different degrees of perfection, the difference cannot arise chiefly from consideration of this end in intention. For every science intends to know perfectly, and if it cannot always attain this, the blame must be laid on its means. Nevertheless, with respect to the secondary ends, or the manifold uses, a manifold difference can arise among sciences. For just as that knowing is better whose uses are more numerous and at the same time better, so that science is to be held more perfect whose uses of this kind accompany it. But the efficient cause chiefly confers perfection on science. So that this can be understood [since it has the greatest use against the Sceptics], we must first treat a little more fully of the efficient causes of science. We divide them into principal and less principal, or instrumental, causes. The principal cause is again either universal, as God, or particular, as the human mind itself. The instrumental or organic causes come in a twofold distinction: for they either serve the mind in the investigation of the sciences, or they bring forth in the mind the science that has been investigated part by part, as a whole. Of the first kind there are many instrumental causes: 1. piety and its exercise, which win the help of the first cause; 2. the senses, from which the mind as it were begs what it understands; 3. memory, from which experience is born, which arises from many recollections of one and the same attribute, observed either in many instances or often in one: as when someone remembers that rhubarb benefited Titius, Sempronius and others, and when this has been observed often, experience and induction finally come about. Moreover, it must be noted again and again that experience is twofold: one of the senses, which can take place in beasts, and another accurate experience, which belongs to the mind alone. As has been indicated elsewhere, it is the office of the mind in man not only to correct the judgment of the senses from error as far as possible, but also to put it in order. For reason can direct as well as correct erring senses. The Philosopher seems to teach this in the third book of On the Generation of Animals, chapter 10. Since experience serves either to apprehend or to assent, the earlier experience suffices for apprehending, and here what is commonly said applies: Nothing is ever in the mind that was not first in the sense. But to assent, and not rashly, accurate experience, that is, of the mind, is required. This must be carefully noted against certain recent babblers of experience, always having on their lips, Come and see, and in the meantime do not consider whether error may lie in the sense to which they appeal, owing to the lack of some condition (as we have shown at length elsewhere). Just as the mind alone in man can correct this error, so the judgment of the senses needs the moderation of the mind. Moreover, the intentional species also belongs to the instrumental causes of science, and so does the fifth factor, the disposition of the organ, namely a suitable brain. Because of a bad disposition of it, many people are not only unable to philosophize perfectly, but are altogether unfit and unsuited for it. And this is enough about the organic causes, which, as the principal causes of the science being generated, serve the particular mind. Next come the organs through which the whole science, investigated beforehand part by part, is brought forth in the mind. This is not only one, as seemed to some recent writers, but twofold: definition and demonstration. This can be gathered not only from Aristotle, if his passages that follow are carefully compared (On the Soul, book 1, text 11; Physics 8, chapter 3; Metaphysics 1, last chapter), but reason also persuades us of it: for a thing is known either by its essence, namely through definition, or by its property and affection, namely through demonstration. Now the demonstration that generates science is set up either through the cause or through the effect. A definition that will contribute something to the perfection of science must consist of genus and difference, or at least, in place of the difference, of a property. It is customary to ask here which of these two instruments is to be considered the more noble. We, having weighed everything properly, grant the first place to the perfect or essential definition, along with Averroës, moved by the following reasons. (1) Because it is better to know what a thing is than what sort it is (Metaphysics 3, chapter 1, and Metaphysics 7, chapter 5); now a definition teaches what a thing is, a demonstration what sort it is. (2) From the definition the properties are easily gathered (Physics 4, chapter 5), but the essence of a thing is not as easily gathered from a demonstration. (3) Because a definition fits substance more, a demonstration fits accidents. (4) Because science is obtained more nobly by definition, as will be clear whether we look at the excellence of the matter (for substance is defined, but an affection is demonstrated) or at certainty (for a definition is an element of demonstration and therefore also more certain). Having set down these points, it will be easy for anyone to see how perfection can come to science from the principal causes and also from the instrumental causes. But it is considered especially in respect of the instruments that generate the whole science in the mind, and according to their different nature it also varies greatly in its degrees of perfection. The most perfect science, in relation to demonstration, is that held through demonstration of the reason why, but in relation to definition, it is that acquired through definition by genus and specific difference. If these instruments are compared with one another, the science acquired through essential definition will be held more perfect than that acquired through demonstration, as is clear from what has gone before. Third and last, the perfection of science comes from affections, namely those of which we spoke earlier: truth, perspicuity and certainty. The higher degree of each gives a higher perfection, and the highest gives the supreme perfection to science. From what has been said about the perfection of science, it is clear first what must be thought of the opinion of those who acknowledge no science except intuitive science, namely that which shows everything so clearly that it can almost be touched with the hands, and has as much certainty as the judgment of the senses. As if there were no difference at all between the instrument of science, experience of the senses, and perfect science, which is of universals. The certainty of science cannot be confused with the certainty of the senses without great error. For (1) if the certainty of science were the same as that of the senses, the object would have to be the same, and consequently there would be science only of singular accidents; (2) things that cannot fall under the senses could not be known either, since the supporters of this view want the perfection of science to come only from the senses. What then

units.la: [1] si: the mark is partly obscured by a damaged patch in the scan. ergo fiet animæ rationali, quid reliquis formis substantialibus, nisi forte novis hisce Flaviis, omnia, excepta sola anima rationali & corporea materia, accidentibus accensere placeat? Secundo, falluntur quotquot disciplinas in Conjecturales & demonstrativas distinguunt: illis accensendo Physicam & Medicinam, his autem Theologiam & Mathesin. Nulla enim ratione sententia hæc subsistere potest. Si enim disciplinis, quæ coniecturales vulgo vocantur, scientiæ conditiones accidere possunt, imo ea per quæ perficiuntur, cur non scientiarum quoque loco habebuntur? Hæc autem denegari iis nulla ratione posse, deinceps in hypothesi ostendemus. Tertio, summo errore de scientiæ aut perfectione aut impersectione ratione certorum individuorum pronunciatur. Quasi vero, ut rem exemplo declaremus, propterea formarum substantialium non detur scientia, quia hic qui deliris somniis dementatus est, hoc credere non potest, aut moveri argumentis, quæ alii in palæstra Philosophiæ exercitatissimi, ut certissima amplectuntur.
units.tr: ...what will become of the rational soul, or of the other substantial forms, unless perhaps, with these new Flavii, one is pleased to count everything except the rational soul and corporeal matter among the accidents? Second, those are mistaken who divide the disciplines into conjectural and demonstrative, counting physics and medicine among the former and theology and mathematics among the latter. For this opinion cannot stand on any ground. If the conditions of science can belong to the disciplines commonly called conjectural, indeed the very things through which they are perfected, why will they not also be counted in the place of sciences? That these cannot be denied to them on any ground we will show later in the hypothesis. Third, with the greatest error a judgment is pronounced on the perfection or imperfection of a science by reference to certain individuals. As if, to make the matter plain by an example, there were no science of substantial forms because a man who is crazed by delirious dreams cannot believe this, or be moved by arguments which others, most practised in the arena of philosophy, embrace as most certain.

units.la: CAPUT UNDECIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER ELEVEN

units.la: Proponitur argumentum ab Augustino, Lactantio, & Clemente Alexandrino quoque usurpatum, quo validissime contra Scepticos evincitur aliquid sciri.
units.tr: The argument used by Augustine, Lactantius and also Clement of Alexandria is set out, by which it is most forcefully proved against the Sceptics that something can be known.

units.la: EXplicata scientiæ ratione, eaque pariter distincta ab opinione, consequens deinceps est, contra Scepticos, atque universam eorum sobolem, probemus aliquid posse sciri, secundum eas scientiæ regulas, quas jam antea definivimus. Quam vero methodum nobismet ipsis jam antea præscripsimus, in probatione quæstionis hujus, inter Dogmaticos atque Scepticos admodum controversæ, anquisite in universa ipsius tractatione observabimus. Eoque priusquam ulla argumenta adducimus, quæ satisfacere possint iis, qui in Dogmaticorum ordine censentur, pauca quædam argumenta proponere debemus, quod obfirmatis, atque in pertinaciæ palæstra præ omnibus aliis exercitatis Scepticis, volentibus atque nolentibus licer, assensum extorqueant. Hoc capite unum, proximis alia quædam, quod cujusdem ponderis existimemus, adducemus. Initio quoniam Scepticorum gens dura, atque nescia cedere est [sicut jam antea ostendimus] non potest quoque cum ratione invadi & expugnari, nisi ibi, ubi infirmitatem suam, atque animum cedere paratum exhibet, utrumque vero ostentat tum, quando pertinaciam suam proponit & urget; eam vero tum maxime proponit, quando sive pro sua epocha, sive pro dubitatione, sive fallacia, sive quocunque alio placito, quod aduersus Dogmaticos propugnare contendit, certitudinem conjunctam evidentiae, ex suo quasi sensu urget. Fateatur enim Scepticus, aut omnia opinionibus plena esse, aut nullum esse judicium, aut nihil sciri, aut de omnibus dubitandum esse, aut de evidentibus aequalia momenta cum inevidentibus menti offerri, aut nihil sciri ab aliis, aut nullos sapientes, esse aut simile quid: eo ipso, quod fatetur vel virum ex his a se cognosci, sibique prae omnibus aliis Dogmaticorum placitis certum esse fatetur, vincitur. Nam, si hoc suo assensu approbat, atque e sua sententia verum ac certum esse concedit, neque pariter concedere debet, a se, ut ut infesto omni omnino scientiae, aliquid cognosci; quod verum atque certum sit. Si nolit tale haberi, & aeque dubium cum aliis dogmatibus esse pronunciet, ridiculum se exhibet. Quae enim ratio, quod pro hoc dogmate, quod dubium esse concedit, omnes animi sui nervos intendat, illiusque ratione, haud aliter atque seditiosus aliquis Tribunus plebis, omnes non solum Philosophorum familias, verum reliquorum quoque aut ex eruditis, aut eruditionis candidatis, classes inquietet pariter atque turbet. Argumentum, quod propono, antiquum est, suoque calculo probat Augustinus lib.3. adversus Academicos cap.11.quod cum integrum hic exhibere possem, nolo tamen, ne lectorem meum avertam a tanti tum Theologi, tum Philosophi lectione. Argumentum ponderis maximi pluribus in locis idem Augustinus proponit, speciatim lib. 2.de lib.Arbitrio cap.3.verba, licet ex parte propositá jam antea hoc libro, iterato exhibeo. Probaturus ergo Deum esse, sic progreditur: Prius ante quaero [ut de manifestissimis capitibus exordium]utrum tu i-se sis? An tu fortasse metuis, ne hac interrogatione fallaris? cum utique, si non esses, falli omnino non posses. Ac deinde: Ergo, quoniam manifestum est esse te; nec tibi aliter manifestum nisi viveres; id quoque manifestum est, & te vivere. Intellegisne ista duo esse verissima. Respondet Evodius: Prorsus intelligo. Unde Augustinus concludit: Ergo etiam hoc tertium manifestum est, hoc est, intelligere te. Pari fere ratione contra Scepticos, obfirmatosque Academicos progrediendum esse jam antea ostenderat Lactantius, quem, utpote Ciceronem Christianum, non possum non, integro illius capite [alia licet argumenta quoque habeat] adducto, hic ad suffragium vocare. Ita ergo lib.3. Divin.Instit.cap.5 loquitur: Sunt enim multa, quae natura ipsa nos scire & usus frequens, & vitæ necessitas cogit. Itaque pereundum est, nisi scias quæ ad vitam sunt utilia, eaq; appetas: quæ periculosa, ut fugias & vites. Præterea multa sunt, quæ usus invenit. Nam solis ac lunæ varij cursus, & meatus siderum, & ratio temporum deprehensa est, & natura corporum à medicis, herbarumque vires; & ab agricolis natura terrarum, nec non imbrium futurorum ac tempestatum signa collecta sunt. Nulla denique ars est, quæ non scientia constet. Debuit ergo Arcesilas, siquidem saperet, distinguere, quæ sciri possent, quæve nesciri. Sed si id fecisset, ipse se in populum redegisset. Nam vulgus interdum plus sapit: quia tantum quantum opus est sapit. A quo si quæras, utrum sciat aliquid an nihil? dicet se scire, quæ nesciat. Recte ergo aliorum sustulit disciplinas, sed non recte fundavit suam: ignoratio enim rerum omnium non potest esse sapientia, cujus est scire proprium. Ita cum Philosophos expugnaverit, ac docuerit eos nihil scire, ipse quoque nomen Philosophi perdidit: quia doctrina ejus est, nihil scire. Nam qui alios reprehendit quod nesciant, ipse debet sciens esse: cum autem nihil sciat, quæ perversitas, quæve insolentia est, ob id ipsum se Philosophum constituere, propter quod cæteros tollat? Possunt enim sic respondere: Si nihil nos scire conviceris, & ideo non esse sapientes, quia nihil sciamus: ergo ne tu quidem es sapiens, quia quoq; confiteris te nihil scire? Quid ergo promovit Arcesilas, nisi quod confectis omnibus Philosophis, se ipsum eodem mucrone transfixit.Hactenus Lactantius. Eodem modo ante ipsum Lactantium instituerat oppugnare Scepticos Clemens Alexandrinus, lib.8.Stromat. per suum interpretem hunc in modum differens: Apud Pyrrhonios est assensionis sustentatio, quae vult nihil firmum esse & stabile. Ea si a se ipsa inceperit, arum, quod primum se ipsum infirmabit. Aut ergo dat aliquid esse verum, & non est de omnibus sustinenda assensio: aut persistit dicens nihil esse veri, & est perspicuum quod nec ipsa prius verum dicet: aut enim ipsa verum dicit, aut non. Sed si verum quidem dicit, concedit vel invita esse aliquid veri: sin autem non verum dicit, vera ea relinquit, quae volebat tollere de medio. Nam quatenus falsa ostenditur, quę perimit epoche, eatenus vera esse ostenduntur ea, quae perimuntur, quomodo somnium, quod omnia somnia dicit esse falsa: nam cum se ipsum perimat, confirmat alia. Et in summa, si est vera, ducet a se ipsa principium, cum non sit alicujus alterius sustentatio assensionis, sed primum sui ipsius. Deinde si comprehendit quod sit homo, vel quod sustinet assensionem, est perspicuum cum non sustinere assensionem. Quomodo autem respondit etiam ad rogatum? nam clarum est est eum de hoc non suf-tinere assensionem. At qui se sustinere assensionem pronunciat, quod sequendo, si oporteat nos de rebus omnibus sustinere assensionem, de ipsa afsensionis sustentatione assensionem primum sustinebimus, sitne ei credendum, an non. Præterea si hoc ipsum verum est, eum verum nescire, neque omnino veri quicquam ab illo datur: si autem hoc quoque dicet dubitabile verum ignorare, eo ipso dat verum cognosci posse, quod suam de ipsa assensionis sustentatione sustentationem videatur non confirmare. Hac eo loco doctissimus Clemens.
units.tr: Having explained the nature of knowledge, and distinguished it from opinion, the next task is to prove against the Sceptics, and their whole brood, that something can be known according to those rules of knowledge which we have already defined. In proving this question, which is much disputed between the Dogmatists and the Sceptics, we will observe in our whole treatment of it the method we prescribed for ourselves earlier. Before we bring forward any arguments that might satisfy those who are counted among the Dogmatists, we must first set out a few arguments which can wring assent even from the obstinate, and from Sceptics who are practised in stubbornness above all others, whether they like it or not. In this chapter I shall adduce one argument, and in the next some others which I judge to be of some weight. First, since the Sceptic breed is hard and unyielding, as we have shown above, it cannot be attacked and overcome by reason unless it is found where it displays its weakness and readiness to give way. It displays both when it sets forth its obstinacy and presses it. It displays this most of all when, whether from its own suspension of judgement, its doubt, its fallacy, or any other tenet which it strives to defend against the Dogmatists, it insists, as if from its own feeling, on a certainty joined to evidence. For let the Sceptic admit either that everything is full of opinions, or that there is no judgement, or that nothing can be known, or that everything must be doubted, or that evident and non-evident matters present equal weight to the mind, or that nothing can be known by others, or that there are no wise men, or something similar. By the very fact that he admits that he knows at least one man of this kind, and admits that this tenet is certain to him above all the other tenets of the Dogmatists, he is overcome. For if he approves it by his assent, and concedes that it is true and certain by his own judgement, he must in the same way concede that something can be known by him, and that it is true and certain, even though he is hostile to all knowledge. If he does not want it to be held as such, and declares it to be as doubtful as the other dogmas, he makes himself ridiculous. For what reason is there that he should strain every nerve of his mind for this dogma, which he admits to be doubtful, and, like some seditious tribune of the plebs, disturb and trouble not only the schools of the philosophers but also the classes of the learned, and of those who aspire to learning? The argument which I propose is ancient, and Augustine proves it with his own reckoning in book 3 of Against the Academics, chapter 11. Although I could set it out here in full, I do not wish to turn my reader away from reading so great a theologian and philosopher. Augustine sets out the same argument of very great weight in several other places, especially in book 2 of On Free Choice of the Will, chapter 3. I repeat the words here, although part of them has already been set out earlier in this book. Thus he proceeds, intending to prove that God exists: "First of all I ask you (as a beginning from the most obvious matters): are you yourself? Or perhaps you fear that you may be deceived by this question? For if you did not exist, you could not be deceived at all." And then: "Therefore, since it is evident that you exist, and it would not be evident to you unless you were living, it is also evident that you are living. Do you understand that these two things are most true?" Evodius replies: "I understand them entirely." From this Augustine concludes: "Therefore this third thing is also evident, namely that you understand." Lactantius had already shown that one must proceed in almost the same way against the Sceptics and the stubborn Academics. As he is a Christian Cicero, I cannot help calling him here as a witness, quoting his whole chapter, although he has other arguments as well. In book 3 of the Divine Institutes, chapter 5, he speaks thus: "For there are many things which nature itself and frequent experience and the necessity of life compel us to know. Thus we must perish unless we know what is useful for life and seek it, and what is dangerous, so that we may flee from it and avoid it. Besides, there are many things which experience has discovered. For the varying courses of the sun and moon, the movements of the stars, and the reckoning of times have been grasped; the nature of bodies and the powers of herbs have been learned by physicians; and the nature of lands, and the signs of coming rains and storms, have been gathered by farmers. In short, there is no art which does not rest on knowledge. Arcesilas ought therefore, if he were wise, to distinguish what can be known from what cannot. But if he had done this, he would have reduced himself to the level of the common people. For the common people are sometimes wiser, because they are wise to the extent that they need to be. If you ask them whether they know something or nothing, they will say that they know what they do not know. Arcesilas therefore rightly overturned the teachings of others, but he did not rightly found his own; for ignorance of all things cannot be wisdom, since knowing is its proper function. Thus, when he had overcome the philosophers and taught that they know nothing, he also lost the name of philosopher himself, because his doctrine is that nothing can be known. For he who reproaches others for not knowing ought himself to be a knower; but since he knows nothing, what perversity or what arrogance is it that he sets himself up as a philosopher on the very ground on which he removes all others? For they can answer him thus: 'If you convict us of knowing nothing, and therefore of not being wise, because we know nothing, then are you not wise either, since you also confess that you know nothing?' What, then, did Arcesilas achieve, except that, having destroyed all the philosophers, he pierced himself with the same sword?" So far Lactantius. In the same way, before Lactantius, Clement of Alexandria had set about attacking the Sceptics in book 8 of the Stromata, speaking through his translator in this manner: "Among the Pyrrhonists there is a suspension of assent which holds that nothing is firm and stable. If it begins from itself, it will first weaken itself. Either it therefore grants that something is true, and assent must not be suspended about everything; or it persists in saying that there is no truth, and it is plain that it will not even say first that this is true. For either it says that something is true, or it does not. But if it says that something is true, it concedes, even against its will, that some truth exists; but if it does not say that something is true, it leaves standing those very things which it wished to remove from the middle. For insofar as the suspension of judgement shows that the things it destroys are false, to that extent those things which it destroys are shown to be true, just as a dream which says that all dreams are false: for in destroying itself it confirms the others. And in sum, if it is true, it will derive its principle from itself, since it is not the support of some other assent but is primary in itself. Next, if it comprehends that it is a man, or that it sustains assent, it is plain that it does not sustain assent. And how does it answer even when questioned? For it is clear that it does not sustain assent about this. But if it declares that it sustains assent, then, following this reasoning, if we ought to sustain assent about all things, we shall first have to sustain assent about the very suspension of assent, namely whether it is to be believed or not. Moreover, if this very thing is true, namely that it does not know the truth, then nothing of the truth is given by it at all; but if it also says that this doubtful truth is unknown, then by that very fact it grants that truth can be known, since it seems not to confirm its own suspension of assent about the suspension itself." So far the most learned Clement.

units.la: Caput Duodecimum.
units.tr: Chapter Twelve.

units.la: Proponitur secundum argumentum, à reminiscentia desumptum, æque sufficiens ad convincendos Scepticos, ad hoc ut fateantur aliquid sciri posse.
units.tr: The second argument is put forward, drawn from recollection, and it is equally sufficient to convince the Sceptics, so that they admit that something can be known.

units.la: QUum, uti ex antecedentibus liquet, Sceptico obstirmato adversus Dogmaticos, & ea quæ Dogmaticorum sunt, extorqueri invito quasi debeat hæc confessio, aliquid sciri posse, nullis certis scientiæ notis consideratis; præter argumentum superiori capite adductum, alterum à reminiscentia, actu intellectui proprio desumptum occurrit, quod si rite ordineque consideretur, deprehendetur omnino sufficiens esse ad convincendos duros hos, & cedere nescios homines. Reminiscentia siquidem, seu memoria rationalis, non nisi ratione distincta ab ipso intellectu, quatenus ratione actus, quem exercet, consideratur, non est nisi iterata quædam intellectio, ab aliis recordatio dicta, secundum quam mens ea quæ jam antea cognovit, rursum sibi contemplanda cum quodam discursu, secundum quem unum ab altero separat, exhibet atque repræsentat. Quotquot autem inter homines censentur, etiam illi, qui minimum ratione utuntur, hoc fateri debent, quotidie sæpius sibi usu venire, ut quando menti affertur aliqua species, quam velit conremplari, eam removeat ipsa, atque alteram, quam convenientem magis esse credit, apprehendat. Quicquid ratio quoque Sceptico alicui dictaverit, dum ex iis, quas recondidit species, unam præ alia amplectitur, volens nolens agnoscere compellitur eam convenientiorem esse: si cognoscit eam convenientiorem esse, næ pariter hoc ipsum novit quod sit ipsa illa species convenientior: secundum communem errorem atque opinionem si progredi se dicat, pariter etiam agnoscere compellitur, præstare secundum communem etrorem, quam alia sive contraria ratione progredi. Quid quod hæc ipsa inquisitio speciei, quæ recordanti occurrit, quædam intellectio est. nam, uti jam antea monuimus, reminiscentia nihil aliud, quam iterata intellectio censeri potest. Quę dicimus eleganter illustrantur abAugust. lib. 10. Conf. cap. 13. ubi ita: Quid cum ipsa memoria perdidit aliquid, sicut fit cum oblivisci mur, & quærimus ut recordemur? ubi tandem quærimus, nisi in ipsa memoria? & ibi si aliud pro alio forte offeratur, respuimus, donec illud occurrat, quod quærimus, & cum occurrerit, dicimus, hoc est, quod non diceremus nisi agnosceremus, nec agnosceremus, nisi meminissemus. certe ergo obliti fueramus. At non totum exciderat, sed ex parte qua tenebatur, pars alia quærebatur, quia sentiebat se memoria non simul volvere quod simul solebat,& quasi detruncata certitudine claudicans, reddi quod deerat, flagitabat. Tanquam si homo notus sive conspiciatur oculis, sive cogitetur, & nomen eius obliti requiramus, quicquid aliud occurrerit non connectitur, quia non cum illo cogitari consuevit, ideoque respuitur donec illud adsit, ubi simul assuefacta notitia non inæqualiter acquiescat. Et unde adest, nisi ex ipsa memoria? Nam & cum ab illo commoniti recognoscimus inde adest, non enim quasi novum credimus, sed recordantes approbamus hoc esse, quod dictum est. Si autem penitus aboleatur ex animo, nec admoniti reminiscimur. Hæc eo loco Augustinus. In quascunque ergo formas sese converterit. quas aut videtur sensibus suis percepisse, aut quas existimat pariter alio tempore sive dormienti, sive vigilanti, occurrisse, sepositaque differentia omni, itemque distincta cognitione singularum specierum, tamen certum manet, nec ipse insicias ire poterit aliquid exhiberi, quod alias, aut eadem ratione, aut etiam diversa, exhibitum sibi esse existimat: atque si has species aut ipse propulerit, mentem suam ab iis quasi avertendo, aut conciderint, sponte quasi evanescendo, succedent mox alterae, pari ratione cum prioribus afsectae, & quicquid etiam factum fuerit a Pyrrhonio, perpetuo hoc remanebit eum contemplari, atque mente percipere quasdam species, quae respondeant iis, quas alias (falso an vere eodem hic redit) videtur pari aut diversa ratione percepisse. At iterata haec ejusmodi speciem perceptio, quid aliud quam reminiscentia est? Quam si illi (quorum argumentum superioribus capitibus hujus libri examinavimus) per cogitationem (quam ipsi definire non potuerunt) intellexissent, aliquid solidius contra Scepticos, homines ferreae pertinaciae, exhibuissent. Denique ipsa reminiscentia, exhibens intellectionem circa ea, quae in memoriae thesauro latitant, si non Scepticis, saltem aliis, rei perquam admirandae, imo prae omnibus naturae quasi miraculis stupendae, certissimum exhibet exemplar. Noverat hoc magnus
units.tr: Since, as is clear from what has gone before, the confession that something can be known, made without any certain marks of knowledge, is extracted almost against his will from the obstinate Sceptic who opposes the Dogmatists and their positions, there occurs, besides the argument adduced in the previous chapter, another argument drawn from recollection, which arises from the intellect's own activity. If it is considered properly and in order, it will be found wholly sufficient to convince these stubborn men, who do not know how to yield. Recollection, or rational memory, is nothing other than a repeated act of understanding, called recall by others, when considered, as distinct from the intellect itself, in terms of the act it performs. By it the mind again presents and represents to itself, for contemplation, those things it has already known before, with a certain reasoning process by which it separates one thing from another. All who are counted among men, even those who use reason very little, must admit that this happens to them daily and often: when some image is brought to the mind which it wishes to contemplate, the mind sets it aside and grasps another, which it believes more suitable. Whatever reason has dictated to the Sceptic too, while he embraces one of the images he has stored away in preference to another, he is compelled, willing or unwilling, to recognise that this one is the more suitable. If he knows that it is the more suitable, then he equally knows this very thing, that this image is the more suitable. If he says that he proceeds according to common error and opinion, he is equally compelled to acknowledge that it is better to proceed according to common error than by some other or contrary method. Moreover, this very search for the image which presents itself to the one recollecting is itself a kind of understanding; for, as we said before, recollection can be regarded as nothing but a repeated understanding. These points are elegantly illustrated by Augustine, Confessions book 10, chapter 13, where he says: "What happens when the memory itself has lost something, as happens when we forget and seek to recall? Where do we finally seek, unless in the memory itself? And there, if something else is perhaps offered in place of what we want, we reject it until that which we seek comes to mind; and when it has come, we say, 'This is it,' which we would not say unless we recognised it, nor would we recognise it unless we remembered it. Certainly, then, we had forgotten. But it had not wholly fled; part of it was still held, and the other part was being sought, because the memory felt that it did not keep together what it was accustomed to keep together, and, as if its knowledge had been cut short and limping, it demanded what was lacking. As when a man we know is seen with the eyes, or is thought of, and we seek his name, having forgotten it: whatever else occurs is not connected, because we are not used to thinking of him with it, and so it is rejected until the right name is present, when the knowledge, now joined together, rests with equal ease. And whence is it present, unless from the memory itself? For even when we recognise it on being reminded by another, it comes from there; we do not believe it to be new, but on remembering we approve that this is what was said. But if it has been entirely wiped out of the mind, we do not recall it even when reminded." Thus far Augustine in that place. Therefore, into whatever forms the Pyrrhonist turns himself, whichever ones he seems to have perceived by his senses, or which he thinks have presented themselves to him at another time, whether asleep or awake, with every difference set aside and each individual image distinctly known, it nonetheless remains certain, and he will not be able to deny that something is set before him which he thinks has been set before him at other times, either in the same way or in a different way. And if he himself drives these images away, turning his mind from them, or if they fade away of their own accord, others will soon follow, affected in the same way as the former; and whatever the Pyrrhonist may have done, he will continually remain contemplating these images and perceiving with his mind certain forms which correspond to those he seems to have perceived at other times, in the same or a different way (whether falsely or truly, it comes back to the same point here). But this repeated perception of such images, what else is it but recollection? If those men, whose arguments we examined in the earlier chapters of this book, had understood it through thought (which they were unable to define), they would have offered something more solid against the Sceptics, men of iron obstinacy. Finally, recollection itself, which provides an understanding of the things that lie hidden in the storehouse of memory, offers a most certain example, if not to the Sceptics, at least to others, of a thing most wonderful indeed, and marvellous above all, as if one of nature's miracles. The great man knew this.

units.la: I
units.tr: I

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUMTERTIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER THIRTEEN.

units.la: Proponitur tertium argumentum, a conscientia, quae in omnibus hominibus, desumptum sufficiensque ad confundendos Scepticos.
units.tr: The third argument is put forward, from conscience, which is found in all men, is drawn from them, and is sufficient to confound the Sceptics.

units.la: SEd & alius aries occurrit, quo si convenienter Sceptici oppugnentur, pariter confundi debent; ad hoc ut manus veritati dent. Quotquot inter homines referri merentur, domestieum habent indicem, paratis ad hoc testibus sic examinantem omnia facta cuiusque, ut pariter secundum leges, neque eburneis neque æneis tabulis, sed ipsi cordi inscriptas, sententiam sive ad condemnationem, sive ad absolutionem ferat. Leges illæ sunt reliquiæ imaginis divinæ, post lapsum in homine superstites, ad hoc ut ipse homo, agnoscendo quod rectum & justum est, non solum foret habilis ad humanam societatem conservandam, verum præcipue per has quasi scalas ad Deum creatorem suum deveniret. Fingit quidem Lucianus in Menippo, umbras comitari corpora nostra in hac vita, atque homines apud Inferos accusare; cæterum sub hac fabula, atque per eam, intelligere oportet vim conscientiæ, quam nemo hominum, quisquis quoque fuerit, possit excutere, quin perpetuo bona facta comitetur bona conscientia, quemadmodum scelera & flagitia mala conscientia, quocunque carnifice inclementior) haut aliter atque umbra adhæret corpori in sole posito. Cum ergo nullus ex Scepticis, imo nullus Atheus, (ut ut omnia quoque agat) effurcillare penitus possit conscientiam, [licet ea aliquando sopiatur & quasi brutescere videatur] atque si bene aliquid fecerit, sensum gaudij percipiat, tristitiæ contra & doloris, si perverse ac flagitiose sa gerere instituerit, jure meritoque ad eum arguendum argumentari licet à conscientia. At, uti circa conscientiam, tanquam syllogismum practicum, duę notantur præmissę, quibus conclusio annectitur; ita, ut ut omnia quoque egerit Scepticus, tum certitudinem præmissarum, tum conclusionis quoque è præmissis illis collectæ, agnoscere compellitur. Atque incipiendo à majore propositione, eam suppeditat lex naturæ, ipsorum Gentilium cordibus inscripta, teste Apostolo Paulo, qui ad Romanos cap. 2. v. 14. de gentilibus testatur, quod ostendant opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis. Theologi vulgo synteresin, seu habitum principiorum practicorum vocant. deveniendo autem ad jus naturæ, de eo agens Aristoteles lib. 5. Ethic. cap. 7. dicit: Ius naturale est, quod ubique eandem vim obtinet, non autem quia sic videtur, vel non videtur. Et eleganter Cicero lib. 2. de Repub. apud Lactant. lib. 6. Divin. Instit cap. 8. Est quidem vera lex, inquit, recta ratio, naturæ congruens, diffusa in omnes, constans, sempiterna, quæ vocet ad officium iubendo, vetandoà fraude deterreat: quæ tamen neque probos frustra iubet & vetat, neque improbos iubendo aut vetando fovet. Nec vero aut per senatum aut per populum solvi hac lege possumus, nec est quærendus explorator aut interpres ejus alius. Nec erit alia lex Romæ, alia Athenis, alia posthac: sed & omnes gentes & omni tempore una lex, & sempiterna & immobilis continebit: unusque erit communis quasi magister & imperator omnium Deus: ille legis hujus inventor, disceptator, lator: cui qui non parebit, ipse se fugiet, ac naturam hominis aspernabitur: hoc ipso luet maximas pœnas, etiamsi cætera supplicia, quę putantur, effugerit.
units.tr: But there is also another ram that meets us, and if the Sceptics are attacked in a fitting way, they too must be confounded, so that they give their hands to the truth. Whatever men deserve to be called to account has a domestic judge, with witnesses ready for this purpose, who examines all the deeds of each person in such a way that, according to laws inscribed not on ivory or bronze tablets but on the heart itself, he pronounces sentence either of condemnation or of absolution. Those laws are remnants of the divine image, surviving in man after the fall, so that man himself, by acknowledging what is right and just, should not only be fit to preserve human society but, above all, through these as it were ladders should arrive at God his creator. Lucian, in the Menippus, indeed feigns that shades accompany our bodies in this life and accuse men before the dead; but under this fable, and through it, we must understand the force of conscience, which no man, whoever he may be, can shake off: good conscience constantly accompanies good deeds, and bad conscience accompanies crimes and disgraceful acts, more merciless than any executioner, just as a shadow clings to a body placed in the sun. Since therefore no Sceptic, indeed no atheist (however he may act), can wholly strip himself of conscience [although it is sometimes lulled to sleep and seems to grow brutish], and since, if he has done something good, he perceives a sense of joy, but of sorrow and pain if he has set about acting perversely and shamefully, it is rightly and justly permitted to argue against him from conscience. But, just as in conscience, as a practical syllogism, two premises are noted, to which the conclusion is attached, so, however much the Sceptic has acted, he is compelled to acknowledge both the certainty of the premises and of the conclusion gathered from those premises. And beginning with the major proposition, it is supplied by the law of nature, inscribed in the hearts of the Gentiles themselves, as the Apostle Paul bears witness, who says in Romans 2:14 of the Gentiles that they "show the work of the law written in their hearts." Theologians commonly call this synteresis, or the "habit of practical principles." Coming to the law of nature, Aristotle, treating of it in Ethics book 5, chapter 7, says: "Natural law is that which has the same force everywhere, not because it seems so or does not seem so." And Cicero elegantly, in book 2 of the Republic, as quoted by Lactantius, Divine Institutes book 6, chapter 8: "There is indeed a true law," he says, "right reason, agreeing with nature, diffused among all, constant, everlasting, which calls to duty by commanding and restrains from fraud by forbidding; yet it neither commands and forbids the upright in vain, nor indulges the wicked by commanding or forbidding. Nor can we be released from this law by the senate or by the people, nor is there need to seek any other expounder or interpreter of it. There will not be one law at Rome and another at Athens, another hereafter; but one law, eternal and unchangeable, will bind all nations at all times, and one common teacher and ruler of all, God, will be its inventor, arbiter and proposer. Whoever does not obey it will flee from himself and despise his human nature, and by this very fact will suffer the greatest punishments, even if he escapes those other punishments which are thought to be penalties."

units.la: Huc usque Cicero apud Lactantium. Dicunt quidem Sceptici apud Sextum lib. 3. Pyrrh. Hypoth. ea quæ ad justitiam & injustitiam, & quæ ad honestum, quod cum fortitudine conjunctum est, pertinent, variis controversiis egitari: sed controversiæ illæ solummodo pertinent ad applicationem legis naturalis, circa quam varias differentias accidere posse, nullum dubium: cum alias verum sit quod Dionysius Siculus apud Plutarchum in Apothphegm. dicit: legibus civitatis vim facere possum, naturæ legibus non possum. Eoque, in quas formas quoque instar chamæleontis se converterit Scepticus, nullamque cognitionem agnoscere velit, legis tamen iucunda spes perpetuo comitatur, bona senectutis nutrix, ut inquit Pindarus. Eleganter etiam ille ait: Quicunque juste & pie vitam traduxerit, jucunda spes cor ejus fovens, ad felix senium quoddam comitatur: quae maxime multiplices hominum animos gubernat. Quicquid Scepticus quoque fecerit sensum hunc sive doloris, sive gaudii ut excutere non poterit; ita parirer concludere debet, se longe aliter affici, quando bene fecit, quam quando male & perverse actiones suas instituit.
units.tr: Thus far Cicero, as quoted by Lactantius. Indeed the Sceptics, in Sextus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism book 3, say that "those matters which pertain to justice and injustice, and to what is honourable, joined with courage, are debated in various controversies." But those controversies pertain only to the application of the natural law, about which it is beyond doubt that various differences can arise; since it is otherwise true what Dionysius of Sicily says in Plutarch's Apophthegms: "I can do violence to the laws of the state, but I cannot to the laws of nature." And so, into whatever forms the Sceptic may turn himself like a chameleon, and however he may wish to acknowledge no knowledge, nevertheless the joyful hope of the law constantly accompanies him, the good nurse of old age, as Pindar says. Elegantly also that writer says: "Whoever has lived his life justly and piously, a joyful hope warming his heart attends him to a happy old age, which above all governs the manifold minds of men." Whatever the Sceptic does, he will not be able to shake off this sense, whether of sorrow or of joy; so in the same way he must conclude that he is affected far otherwise when he has acted well than when he has set about his actions badly and perversely.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM QUARTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FOURTEEN.

units.la: Ex eo, quod Scepticus Deum cognoscit, concluditur eum aliquid scire. Qua occasione agitur de Theologia naturali insita.
units.tr: From the fact that the Sceptic knows God, it follows that he knows something. On this occasion the discussion turns to natural theology, which is implanted in us.

units.la: Quod aliquis cum ratione summa miretur Scepticorum pertinacissimi, qui de omnibus rebus aut dubitabant, aut in utramque partem disputabant, inconcussam reliquerunt hanc Thesin, Deum esse: quum, ut ex superiori capite constat, conscientiam effurcillare non queant, non possunt non quoque pariter aliquem numinis sensum retinere: siquidem conscientia non foret illud, quod est, nisi intellectui persuasum esset aliquem omniscium & omnipotentem omnium actionum nostrarum judicem esse, cui aliquando ratio cujuscunque etiam otiosi verbi reddi debeat. Hinc ipsi Pyrrhonij apud Sextum lib. 3. Pyrrh. Hypot. cap. 1. sic loquuntur: Itaque quum Deum efficacissimam esse caussam bona pars eorum (dogmaticorum scil.) pronunciarit, primum de Deo inquiramus: illud præfati, nos vitam communem sequentes, nulli autem opinioni adhærentes, dicere esse Deos, & colere Deos, & providentiam illis attribuere: sed adversus Dogmaticorum temeritatem quadam adferre. Atque hinc ipse Sextus in opere adversus Mathematicos, varijs adductis rationibus, ijsque prægnantibus, probat Deum tum esse, tum eidem honorem deferendum. Sed si exploratum fuit Scepticis, Deum esse, sic ut de ea assertione (licet ignora- verint quis, qualisve Deus esset) ne quidem dubitaverint, næ pariter volentes nolentes fateri debuerunt se aliquid scire, quum cognoverint primum & nobilissimum omnium entium. Verumquidem est, eos disputasse cum Dogmaticis de Dei distincta natura, atque existimasse definire dici non posse, quis qualisve Deus esset: interim quod Deus esset, sive quod esset ens aliquod primum, infinitum, & omnipotens, ne quidem in dubium unquam vocarunt. Atque in hoc distincti fuerunt a Dogmaticis, quibus ex suo saltem sensu, quem de Deo fovebant, liquidum & perspicuum erat, quid Deus esset: cum eatenus accederent his ipsis, eorumque sententiam probarent,in quantum faterentur Deum esse,illud tanquam ens vere proprieque existens agnoscendum. Unde hic ipse Sextus adversus Mathematicos sic scribit: Deorum autem notio & fuit ab æterno, & permanet in æternum, ut cui ea ipsa quæ fiunt, ferant testimonium ut est consentaneum. Verum enimvero si vulgi & imperitorum relinquenda est opinio, credendum est autem viris doctis & præclaris, licet videre Poëticum nihil magnum nec præclarum efferre, in quo non sit Deus, à quo dependet rerum, quæ fiunt, vis & potestas: ut apud Homerum poëtam in bello quod scripsit Græcorum & Trojanorum. Licet autem videre etiam Physicam consonare cum Poetica, Pythagoras enim & Empedocles, & Ionici, Socratesque, & Plato & Aristoteles, & Stoici, & fortasse etiam ij qui sunt ex hortis, ut testantur Epicuri selectæ dictiones, Deum relinquunt. Quomodo ergo si quæreremus de aliquibus, quæ cadunt sub aspectum, merito ijs crederemus, quibus visus est acutissimus: ita considerantes de aliquibus quæ contemplatur ratio, non alijs debemus credere, quam ijs, quibus acutum est ingenium, & perspicax ratio: cujusmodi sunt Philosophi. Sed adversarij respondere solent ad obiectionem.
units.tr: Someone might well wonder how the most stubborn Sceptics, who doubted everything or argued on both sides of every question, left unshaken this one thesis, that God exists. As the previous chapter shows, they could not wipe conscience away, and so they could not help also retaining some sense of a divinity. Conscience would not be what it is unless the intellect were persuaded that there is an all-knowing and all-powerful judge of all our actions, to whom we must one day give an account of every word, even an idle one. Hence the Pyrrhonists themselves speak thus in Sextus (Outlines of Pyrrhonism, book 3, chapter 1): "Since most of the Dogmatists have declared God to be the most effective cause, let us first inquire about God. We, following common life and adhering to no opinion, say at the outset that there are gods, that we worship them, and that we attribute providence to them; but against the rashness of the Dogmatists we bring forward certain arguments." And so Sextus himself, in his work against the Mathematicians, by various arguments, and those very cogent, proves both that God exists and that honour is to be paid to him. But if it was established for the Sceptics that God exists, then, although they did not know who or what sort of being God is, they could not even doubt that assertion. Willing or unwilling, they had to admit that they knew something, since they had come to know the first and most noble of all beings. It is true that they disputed with the Dogmatists about the distinct nature of God, and thought it could not be defined who or what sort of God he is. Yet they never called into doubt that God exists, that is, that there is a first, infinite and omnipotent being. In this they differed from the Dogmatists, for whom at least, from the sense of God that they cherished, it was clear and evident what God is. To that extent they agreed with them and approved their opinion, insofar as they confessed that God exists and must be acknowledged as a being that truly and properly exists. Hence Sextus himself writes in Against the Mathematicians: "The notion of gods both has existed from eternity and remains for eternity, since the things that come to be bear witness to it, as is fitting. But indeed, if the opinion of the common people and the unlearned must be left aside, and we must believe learned and distinguished men, we may see that the poets bring forward nothing great or noble in which God is absent, on whom the power and force of the things that happen depends, as in Homer in the war he wrote between the Greeks and the Trojans. We may also see that physics agrees with poetry: Pythagoras, Empedocles, the Ionians, Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, the Stoics, and perhaps also those of the Garden, as the select sayings of Epicurus attest, all acknowledge God." So, just as in matters that fall under sight we rightly believe those whose sight is keenest, so in considering matters that reason contemplates we ought to believe none but those whose intellect is sharp and whose reason is penetrating, such as the philosophers. But the opponents are wont to reply to this objection.

units.la: Huc usque Sextus.
units.tr: So far Sextus.

units.la: Eodem fere modo Seneca, universalem omnium hominum consensum adducendo, progreditur ep. 117. Multum, inquit, dare solemus praesumptioni omnium hominum. Apud nos veritatis argumentum est aliquid omnibus videri: tanquam Deos esse, inter alia sic colligimus, quod omnibus de Dijs opinio insita est: nec ulla gens usquam est ad eo extra legem moresque rejecta, ut non aliquos Deos credat. Ut ergo latissima omnino differentia intercedit inter quæstionem quare res sit, & quæstionem quod sit; nequaquam existimandum, eos, qui inquirendo se fatigarunt circa Dei naturam, quamque ne quidem attingere potuerunt, pariter falsos fuisse, circa Dei existentiam; utque forte Scepsin & epochiam foverint circa Dei naturam, ita nequaquam sequi eosdem pari ratione debuisse instar Scepticorum fluctuare circa Thesin illis ab ipsis Scepticis concessam. Quamvis enim Socinianî quidam (omnes in eodem sensu non esse alibi oftendo) omnem de Deo insitam cognitionem negare instituerint, certissimum tamen est intellectum humanum, simulac se exercere incipit, atque actus intellectuales edere, devenire secundum prima sciendi principia, eidem ad modum communium notionem insita, ad ens aliquod, pro ratione facultatis illius intelligentis, primum, superiusque omnibus alijs entibus: non quidem dixerim illud ens concipi tanquam Deum, (sic enim axiomatica, eaque distincta cognitio, deberet æque evidens esse atque cognitio simplicis apprehensionis) cum sufficiat concipi tanquam aliquid incomparabile. Naturæ siquidem lumen, (per lapsum hactenus penitus non extinctum) subservīente theoreticæ cognitioni aliquatenus perpetuo conscientia, hominem simulac imperfectissimam quoque functionem intellectualem edere incipit, deducit ad aliquod ens, secundum suum concipiendi modum eatenus non tantum incomparabile, quatenus alteri alicui non existimat æqualem perfectionem attribui posse; verum etiam quod mox apprehendat sese magis ab hoc ipso ente (facit huc conscientiæ testimonium) quam ab ullo alio observari, & quidem tanta cum attentione, ut illi ipsi quoque obligetur ad rationem reddendam omnium eorum, quæ fecerit.
units.tr: Seneca proceeds in much the same way, adducing the universal consent of all men (Letter 117): "We are accustomed," he says, "to give great weight to the presumption of all men. Among us, a sign of truth is that something seems so to all; thus we conclude, among other things, that there are gods, because the opinion of gods is implanted in all, and no nation anywhere is so far cast out of law and custom that it does not believe in some gods." Just as there is a very wide difference between the question why a thing is and the question that it is, we must not think that those who have wearied themselves inquiring into the nature of God, which they could not even reach, were likewise mistaken about God's existence. Even if they held to Scepticism and suspension of judgment about God's nature, it does not follow that for the same reason they ought to waver like Sceptics about the thesis that the Sceptics themselves conceded.
