For although some Socinians (I show elsewhere that they are not all of one mind) have undertaken to deny all innate knowledge of God, it is most certain that the human intellect, as soon as it begins to exercise itself and to put forth intellectual acts, proceeds, according to the first principles of knowing, to the notion implanted in it in common, and so to some being, first and higher than all other beings, according to the capacity of that understanding. I would not say that this being is conceived as God, for then an axiomatic and distinct knowledge would have to be as evident as the knowledge of simple apprehension; it suffices that it be conceived as something incomparable. For the light of nature, which by the Fall has not been wholly extinguished, is always in some measure present to theoretical knowledge, as an awareness. As soon as a man begins to perform even the most imperfect intellectual function, it leads him to some being, which in his manner of conceiving is incomparable, not only in that he does not think any equal perfection can be ascribed to another, but also because he soon perceives that he is observed by this very being more than by any other (conscience bears witness to this), and that with such attention that he is bound to give an account of all that he has done.

units.la: Hoc ita se habere manifesto liquet ex perillustri Pauli loco, ad Rom. cap. 2. v.14.& seq. Quum gentes quæ legem non habent, natura quæ legis sunt, faciant, isti legem non habentes, sibiipsis lex sunt: Ut qui ostendant opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis, una testimonium reddente ipsorum conscientia, & cogitationibus sese mutuo accusantibus aut defendentibus. Quo in loco ut Apostolus testatur gentiles, alie nos à tabulis fœderis, atque promissionibus Evangelicis, natura, sive ex naturæ instinctu, non ipsam quidem legem (hæc siquidem ijs lata non fuit) sed rogatum? nam clarum est est eum de hoc non sustinere assensionem. At qui se sustinere assensionem pronunciat, quod sequendo, si oporteat nos de rebus omnibus sustinere assensionem, de ipsa afsensionis sustentatione assensionem primum sustinebimus, sitne ei credendum, an non. Praete-rea si hoc ipsum verum est, eum verum nescire, neque omnino veri quicquam ab illo datur: si autem hoc quoque dicet dubitabile verum ignorare, eo ipso dat verum cognosci posse, quod suam de ipsa assensionis sustentatione sustentationem videatur non confirmare. Hac eo loco doctissimus Clemens.
units.tr: That this is so is plainly evident from the famous passage of Paul, Romans 2:14ff.: "When the Gentiles, who have not the law, do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves; they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts accusing or else defending one another." In this place, as the Apostle testifies, the Gentiles, though they lacked the tablets of the covenant and the Gospel promises, had the law by nature, or from the instinct of nature. Not that the law itself was given to them (for it was not), but the obligation to give an account of it. For it is clear that he does not suspend his assent about this. But one who declares that he suspends assent: if, following this, we must suspend assent about all things, we shall first have to suspend assent about the very suspension of assent, namely whether he is to be believed or not. Moreover, if this itself is true, that he does not know the truth, then nothing of the truth is given by him. But if he should say that even this, that he does not know the truth, is open to doubt, he thereby grants that truth can be known, since he does not seem to confirm his own suspension of the suspension. So far the most learned Clement.

units.la: CAPUT DUODECIMUM.
units.tr: Chapter Twelve.

units.la: Proponitur secundum argumentum, a reminiscentia desumptum, aeque sufficiens ad convincendos Scepticos, ad hoc ut fateantur aliquid sciri posse.
units.tr: A second argument is put forward, drawn from reminiscence, which is equally sufficient to convince the Sceptics that they must admit that something can be known.

units.la: QUum, uti exantecedentibus liquet, Sceptico obstrmato adversus Dogmaticos, & ea quae Dogmaticorum sunt, extorqueri invito quasi debeat haec confessio, aliquid sciri posse, nullis certis scientiae notis consideratis; praeter argumentum superiori capite adductum, alterum a reminiscentia, actu intellectui proprio desumptum occurrit, quod si rite ordineque consideretur, deprehendetur omnino sufficiens esse ad convincendos duros hos, & cedere nescios homines. Reminiscentia siquidem, seu memoria rationalis, non nisi ratione distincta ab ipso intellectu, quatenus ratione actus, quem exercet, consideratur, non est nisi iterata quædam intellectio, ab alijs recordatio dicta, secundum quam mens ea quæ jam antea cognovit, rursum sibi contemplanda cum quodam discursu, secundum quem unum ab altero separat, exhibet atque repræsentat. Quotquot autem inter homines censentur, etiam illi, qui minimum ratione utuntur, hoc fateri debent, quotidie sæpius sibi usu venire, ut quando menti affertur aliqua species, quam velit contemplari, eam removeat ipsa, atque alteram, quam convenientem magis esse credit, apprehendat. Quicquid ratio quoque Sceptico alicui dictaverit, dum ex ijs, quas recondidit species, unam præ alia amplectitur, volens nolens agnoscere compellitur eam convenientiorem esse: si cognoscit eam convenientiorem esse, næ pariter hoc ipsum novit quod sit ipsa illa species convenientior: secundum communem errorem atque opinionem si progredi se dicat, pariter etiam agnoscere compellitur, præstare secundum communem etrorem, quam alia sive contraria ratione progredi. Quid quod hæc ipsa inquisitio speciei, quæ recordanti occurrit, quædam intellectio est. nam, uti jam antea monuimus, reminiscentia nihil aliud, quam iterata intellectio censeri potest. Quę dicimus eleganter illustrantur abAugust.lib.10.Conf. cap. 13. ubi ita: Quid cum ipsa memoria perdidit aliquid, sicut fit cum obliviscimur, & quęrimus ut recordemur? ubi tandem quærimus, nisi in ipsa memoria? & ibi si aliud pro alio forte offeratur, respuimus, donec illud occurrat, quod quęrimus, & cum occurrerit, dicimus, hoc est, quod non diceremus nisi agnosceremus, nec agnosceremus, nisi meminissemus. certe ergo obli- ti fueramus. At non totum exciderat, sed ex parte qua tenebatur, pars alia quærebatur, quia sentiebat se memoria non simul volvere quod simul solebat,& quasi detruncata certitudine claudicans, reddi quod deerat, flagitabat. Tanquam si homo notus sive conspiciatur oculis, sive cogitetur, & nomen eius obliti requiramus, quicquid aliud occurrerit non connectitur, quia non cum illo cogitari consuevit, ideoque respuitur donec illud adsit,ubi simul assuefacta notitia non in- æqualiter acquiescat. Et unde adest, nisi exipsa memoria? Nam & cum ab illo commoniti recognoscimus inde adest, non enim quasi novum credimus, sed recordantes approbamus hoc esse, quod dictum est. Si autem penitus aboleatur ex animo, nec admoniti reminiscimur. Hæc eo loco Augustinus. In quascunque ergo formas sese converterit quas aut videtur sensibus suis percepisse, aut quas existimat pariter alio tempore sive dormienti, sive vigilanti, occurrisse, sepositaque differentia omni, itemque distincta cognitione singularum specierum, tamen certum manet, nec ipse insicias ire potest aliquid exhiberi, quod alias, aut eadem ratione, aut etiam diversa, exhibitum sibi esse existimat: atque si has species aut ipse propulerit, mentem suam ab iis quasi avertendo, aut conciderint, sponte quasi evanescendo, succedent mox alterae, pari ratione cum prioribus afsectae, & quicquid etiam factum fuerit a Pyrrhonio, perpetuo hoc remanebit eum contemplari, atque mente percipere quasdam species, quae respondeant iis, quas alias (falso an vere eodem hic redit) videtur pari aut diversa ratione percepisse. At iterata haec ejusmodi speciarum perceptio, quid aliud quam reminiscentia est? Quam si illi (quorum argumentum superioribus capitibus huius libri examinavimus) per cogitationem (quam ipsi definire non potuerunt) intellexissent, aliquid solidius contra Scepticos, homines ferreae pertinaciae, exhibuissent. Denique ipsa reminiscentia, exhibens intellectionem circa ea, quae in memoriae thesauro latitant, si non Scepticis, saltem aliis, rei perquam admirandae, imo prae omnibus naturae quasi miraculis stupende, certissimum exhibet exemplar. Nouerat hoc magnus
units.tr: Since, as is clear from what has gone before, the Sceptic, armed against the Dogmatists and against what belongs to the Dogmatists, must be forced to make this admission against his will, that something can be known, even though no certain marks of knowledge have been considered, there occurs, besides the argument adduced in the previous chapter, another drawn from reminiscence, which belongs to the intellect's own activity. If it is considered properly and in order, it will be found wholly sufficient to convince these hard-hearted men, who do not know how to yield. For reminiscence, or rational memory, is nothing other than a repeated act of understanding, distinguished by reason from the intellect itself insofar as it is considered in terms of the act it performs. Others call it recollection. By it the mind, with a certain reasoning by which it separates one thing from another, presents and represents again for its own contemplation what it has already known. Yet everyone who is counted among men, even those who use reason very little, must admit that this happens to them often every day: when some image is brought to the mind which it wishes to contemplate, the mind removes it and grasps another, which it believes to be more fitting. Whatever reason has dictated to any Sceptic, when he embraces one of the forms it has stored away in preference to another, he is compelled, willing or unwilling, to acknowledge that this form is the more fitting. If he knows that it is the more fitting, then he likewise knows that this very form is the more fitting. If he says that he proceeds according to common error and opinion, he is equally compelled to acknowledge that it is better to proceed according to common error than by some other or contrary principle. What is more, this very search for the form that presents itself to the one recollecting is itself a certain act of understanding. For, as we have already observed, reminiscence can be regarded as nothing other than repeated understanding. What we are saying is elegantly illustrated by Augustine, Confessions, book 10, chapter 13, where he says thus: "What happens when memory has lost something, as when we forget and seek to recall? Where do we seek it finally, unless in memory itself? And there, if something else is offered in place of what we want, we reject it until the thing we are seeking comes to mind, and when it comes we say: this is it. We would not say this unless we recognised it, nor would we recognise it unless we remembered it. Certainly, then, we had forgotten. But it had not wholly slipped away; part of it was still held, while the other part was sought, because the memory felt that it did not roll together as one what it was accustomed to hold together, and, as if its certainty were cut short and limping, it demanded back what was missing. It is like a man who is known to us, whether seen with the eyes or thought of, when we seek his name after forgetting it: whatever else comes to mind is not connected, because it was not customary to think of it together with him, and so it is rejected until the right name is present, at which point the knowledge, once more familiar, rests in it with no uncertainty. And whence does it come, unless from memory itself? For even when we recognise it after being reminded by another, it comes from there. We do not believe it to be something new, but in recollecting we approve that it is what was said. If, however, it is entirely wiped out of the mind, we do not recall it even when reminded." So far Augustine in that place. Therefore, into whatever forms the mind turns, forms which it seems to have perceived by its senses, or which it thinks have likewise presented themselves at another time, whether while asleep or awake, and setting aside every difference and every distinct knowledge of the individual forms, it nevertheless remains certain that he cannot deny that something is presented which he thinks has been presented to him at other times, either in the same way or in a different way. And if he himself drives these forms away, turning his mind from them, or if they fade away of their own accord, others will soon follow, affected in the same way as the earlier ones. And whatever the Pyrrhonist has done, he will always continue to contemplate and to perceive in his mind certain forms which correspond to those he seems to have perceived at other times, in the same or a different way (whether truly or falsely, which here comes to the same thing). But what is this repeated perception of such forms, if not reminiscence? If those men whose arguments we have examined in the earlier chapters of this book had understood this through the thinking (which they themselves could not define), they would have produced something more solid against the Sceptics, men of iron obstinacy. Finally, reminiscence itself, which presents an understanding of those things that lie hidden in the treasury of memory, offers a most certain example, if not to the Sceptics, at least to others, of a thing most admirable indeed, and amazing beyond all the marvels of nature. Magnus knew this

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUMTERTIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER THIRTEEN.

units.la: Proponitur tertium argumentum, a conscientia, quae in omnibus hominibus, desumptum sufficiens- que ad confundendos Scepticos.
units.tr: A third argument is put forward, drawn from conscience, which is in all men and is sufficient to confound the Sceptics.

units.la: SEd & alius aries occurrit, quo si convenientes Sceptici oppugnentur, pariter confundi debent; ad hoc ut manus veritati dent. Quotquot inter homines referri merentur, domesticum habent indicem, paratis ad hoc testibus sic examinantem omnia facta cuiusque, ut pariter secundum leges, neque eburneis neque aeneis tabulis, sed ipsi cordi inscriptas, sententiam sive ad condemnationem, sive ad absolutionem ferat. Leges illae sunt reliquiae imaginis divinae, pelt lapsum in homine superstites, ad hoc ut ipse homo, agnoscendo quod rectum & justum est, non solum foret habilis ad humanam societatem conservandam, verum praecipue per has quasi scalas ad Deum creatorem suum deveniret. Fingit quidem Lucianus in Menippo, umbras comitari corpora nostra in hac vita, atque homines apud Inferos accusare; caeterum sub hac fabula, atque per eam, intelligere oportet vim conscientiae, quam nemo hominum, quisquis quoque fuerit, possit excutere, quin perpetuo bona facta comitetur bona conscientia, quemadmodum scelera & flagitia mala conscientia, quocunque carnifice in
units.tr: But there is also another battering-ram, by which, if the Sceptics are assailed together, they must equally be confounded, so that they give up the contest to the truth. Whoever deserves to be brought before men has a domestic judge: witnesses are ready, and the judge examines every deed of each person in such a way that he pronounces sentence, whether of condemnation or of acquittal, according to laws written not on ivory or bronze tablets but on the heart itself. Those laws are remnants of the divine image, surviving in man after the fall, so that man himself, by acknowledging what is right and just, should not only be fit to preserve human society but, above all, by means of these as it were ladders, should come to God his creator. Lucian indeed, in the Menippus, feigns that shadows accompany our bodies in this life and accuse men before the dead; but under this fable, and through it, one must understand the power of conscience, which no man, whoever he may be, can shake off, so that good conscience always accompanies good deeds, just as bad conscience accompanies crimes and shameful acts, whatever the executioner, however merciless. It clings to a man no otherwise than a shadow clings to a body standing in the sun.

units.la: I 2 — signature ce inclementior) haut aliter atque umbra adhæret corpori in sole posito. Cum ergo nullus ex Scepticis, imo nullus Atheus, (ut ut omnia quoque agat) effurcillare penitus possit conscientiam, [licet ea aliquando sopiatur & quasi brutescere videatur] atque si bene aliquid fecerit, sensum gaudij percipiat, tristitiæ contra & doloris, si perverse ac flagitiose se gerere instituerit, jure meritoque ad eum arguendum argumentari licet à conscientia. At, uti circa conscientiam, tanquam syllogismum practicum, duæ notantur præmissæ, quibus conclusio annectitur; ita, ut ut omnia quoque egerit Scepticus, tum certitudinem præmissarum, tum conclusionis quoque è præmissis illis collectæ, agnoscere compellitur. Atque incipiendo à majore propositione, quam suppeditat lex naturæ, ipsorum Gentilium cordibus inscripta, teste Apostolo Paulo, qui ad Romanos cap. 2. v. 14. de gentilibus testatur, quod ostendant opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis. Theologi vulgo syntéresin, seu habitum principiorum practicorum vocant. Deveniendo autem ad jus naturæ, de eo agens Aristoteles lib. 5. Ethic. cap. 7. dicit: Ius naturale est, quod ubique eandem vim obtinet, non autem quia sic videtur, vel non videtur. Et eleganter Cicero lib. 2. de Republ. apud Lactant. lib. 6. Divin. Instit. cap. 8. Est quidem vera lex, inquit, recta ratio, naturæ congruens, diffusa in omnes, constans, sempiterna, quæ vocet ad officium iubendo, vetando à fraude deterreat: quæ tamen neque probos frustra iubet & vetat, neque improbos iubendo aut vetando fovet. Nec vero aut per senatum aut per populum solvi hac lege possumus, nec est quærendus explorator aut interpres ejus alius. Nec erit alia lex Romæ, alia Athenis, alia posthac: sed & omnes gentes & omni tempore una lex, & sempiterna & immobilis continebit: unusque erit communis quasi magister & imperator omnium Deus: ille legis hujus inventor, disceptator, lator: cui qui non parebit, ipse se fugiet, ac naturam hominis aspernabitur: hoc ipso luet maximas pœnas, etiamsi cætera supplicia, quæ putantur, effugerit.
units.tr: Just as a shadow clings to a body standing in the sun. Since therefore no Sceptic, indeed no atheist, however much he may do, can wholly strip away his conscience [although it is sometimes lulled to sleep and seems to grow brutish], and since, if he has done something good, he perceives a sense of joy, but grief and pain if he has set about behaving perversely and shamefully, one may rightly and justly reason from conscience to accuse him. Now, just as in the case of conscience, as in a practical syllogism, two premises are noted to which the conclusion is attached, so the Sceptic, however much he may have done, is compelled to acknowledge both the certainty of the premises and the conclusion drawn from them. And beginning with the major proposition, which is supplied by the law of nature, written in the hearts of the Gentiles themselves, as the Apostle Paul testifies, who says of the Gentiles in Romans 2:14 that they show the work of the law written in their hearts. Theologians commonly call this synteresis [συντήρησιν], or the habit of practical principles. Coming now to the law of nature, Aristotle, treating of it in Ethics book 5, chapter 7, says: Natural justice is that which has the same force everywhere, not because it seems so or does not seem so. And Cicero elegantly, in book 2 of the Republic, as quoted by Lactantius, Divine Institutes book 6, chapter 8: There is indeed a true law, namely right reason, agreeing with nature, diffused among all, constant, everlasting, which calls men to duty by commanding and by forbidding deters them from fraud; yet it neither commands and forbids the good in vain, nor does it favour the wicked by commanding or forbidding. Nor can we be released from this law by the senate or by the people, nor is there need to seek any other expounder or interpreter of it. Nor will there be one law at Rome, another at Athens, another hereafter; but one law, everlasting and unchangeable, will bind all nations at all times, and God will be as it were the common teacher and commander of all, the inventor, judge and proposer of this law. He who does not obey it will flee from himself and despise his human nature, and by this very fact he will suffer the greatest penalties, even if he escapes those other punishments which are thought to be inflicted.

units.la: Huc usque Cicero apud Lactantium. Dicunt quidem Sceptici apud Sextum lib. 3. Pyrrh. Hypoth. ea quæ ad justitiam & injustitiam, & quæ ad honestum, quod cum fortitudine conjunctum est, pertinent, variis controversijs egitari: sed controversiæ illæ solummodo pertinent ad applicationem legis naturalis, circa quam varias differentias accidere posse, nullum dubium: cum alias verum sit quod Dionysius Siculus apud Plutarchum in Apothphegm. dicit :legibus civitatis vim facere possum, naturæ legibus non possum. Eoque, in quas formas quoque instar chamæleontis se converterit Scepticus, nullamque cognitionem agnoscere velit, legis tamen incunda spes perpetuo comitatur, bona senectutis nutrix, ut inquit Pindarus. Eleganter etiam ille ait: Quicunque juste & pie vitam traduxerit, jucunda spes cor ejus fovens, ad felix senium quoddam comitatur: quae maxime multiplices hominum animos gubernat. Quicquid Scepticus quoque fecerit sensum hunc sive doloris, sive gaudii ut excutere non poterit, ita parirer concludere debet, se longe aliter affici, quando bene fecit, quam quando male & perverse actiones suas instituit.
units.tr: So far Cicero, in Lactantius. The Sceptics indeed say, in Sextus, Book 3 of the Pyrrhonian Outlines, that the matters which pertain to justice and injustice, and to what is honourable and joined with courage, are stirred up by various controversies. But those controversies concern only the application of natural law, and there is no doubt that various differences may arise in that application. Otherwise, what Dionysius of Syracuse says in Plutarch's Apophthegms would be false: I can do violence to the laws of the city; I cannot do violence to the laws of nature. And so, into whatever shapes the Sceptic turns himself like a chameleon, and whatever knowledge he is willing to deny, the joyful hope still accompanies the law, the nurse of a good old age, as Pindar says. He also says elegantly: Whoever has lived his life justly and piously, a joyful hope warming his heart accompanies him into a happy old age, and this above all steers the many-minded hearts of men. Whatever the Sceptic may do, he will not be able to shake off this feeling, whether of pain or of joy. So he must conclude in the same way that he is affected quite differently when he has acted well than when he has set about his actions badly and perversely.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM QUARTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FOURTEEN.

units.la: Ex eo, quod Scepticus Deum cognoscit, concluditur eum aliquid scire. Qua occasione agitur de Theologia naturali insita.
units.tr: From the fact that the Sceptic knows God, it follows that he knows something. This occasions a discussion of natural, innate theology.

units.la: Quod aliquis cum ratione summa miretur, Scepticorum pertinacissimi, qui de omnibus rebus aut dubitabant, aut in utramque partem disputabant, inconcussam reliquerunt hanc Thesin, Deum esse: quum, ut ex superiori capite constat, conscientiam effurcillare non queant, non possunt non quoque pariter aliquem numinis sensum retinere: siquidem conscientia non foret illud, quod est, nisi intellectui persuasum esset aliquem omniscium & omnipotentem omnium actionum nostrarum judicem esse, cui aliquando ratio cujuscunque etiam otiosi verbi reddi debeat. Hinc ipsi Pyrrhonij apud Sextum lib. 3. Pyrrh. Hypot. cap. 1. sic loquuntur: Itaque quum Deum efficacissimam esse causam bona pars eorum (dogmaticorum scil.) pronunciarint, primum de Deo inquiramus: illud praefati, nos vitam communem sequentes, nulli autem opinioni adhaerentes, dicere esse Deos, & colere Deos, & providentiam illis attribuere: sed adversus Dogmaticorum temeritatem quaedam adferre. Atque hinc ipse Sextus in opere adversus Mathematicos, variis adductis rationibus, ijsque praegnantibus, probat Deum tum esse, tum eidem honorem deferendum. Sed si exploratum fuit Scepticis, Deum esse, sic ut de ea assertione (licet ignoraverint quis, qualisve Deus esset) ne quidem dubitaverint, nec pariter volentes nolentes fateri debuerunt se aliquid scire, quum cognoverint primum & nobilissimum omnium entium. Verum quidem est, eos disputasse cum Dogmaticis de Dei distincta natura, atque exististimasse definite dici non posse, quis qualisve Deus esset: interim quod Deus esset, sive quod esset ens aliquod primum, infinitum, & omnipotens, ne quidem in dubium unquam vocarunt. Atque in hoc distincti fuerunt a Dogmaticis, quibus ex suo saltem sensu, quem de Deo fovebant, liquidum & perspicuum erat, quid Deus esset: cum eatenus accederent his ipsis, eorumque sententiam probarent,in quantum faterentur Deum esse,illud tanquam ens vere proprieque existens agnoscendum. Unde hic ipse Sextus adversus Mathematicos sic scribit: Deorum autem notio & suit ab æterno, & permanet in æternum, ut cui ea ipsa quæ fiunt, ferant testimonium ut est consentaneum. Verum enimvero si vulgi & imperitorum relinquenda est opinio, credendum est autem viris doctis & præclaris, licet videre Poëticum nihil magnum nec præclarum efferre, in quo non sit Deus, à quo dependet rerum, quæ fiunt, vis & potestas: ut apud Homerum poëtam in bello quod scripsit Græcorum & Trojanorum. Licet autem videre etiam Physicam consonare cum Poëtica, Pythagoras enim & Empedocles, & Ionici, Socratesque, & Plato & Aristoteles, & Stoici, & fortasse etiam ij qui sunt ex hortis, ut testantur Epicuri selectæ dictiones, Deum relinquunt. Quomodo ergo si quæreremus de aliquibus, quæ cadunt sub aspectum, merito ijs crederemus, quibus visus est acutissimus: ita considerantes de aliquibus quæ contemplatur ratio, non alijs debemus credere, quam ijs, quibus acutum est ingenium, & perspicax ratio: cujusmodi sunt Philosophi. Sed adversarij respondere solent ad obiectionem.
units.tr: Someone may well wonder at this: the most obstinate Sceptics, who doubted everything or argued both sides of every question, left unshaken the one thesis that God exists. As the previous chapter shows, they could not rub out their conscience, and so they could not fail to retain some sense of the divinity. Conscience would not be what it is unless the intellect were persuaded that an all-knowing and all-powerful judge of all our actions exists, to whom an account must sometimes be given even of an idle word. So the Pyrrhonists themselves speak this way in Sextus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism, book 3, chapter 1: Since most of the Dogmatists have declared God to be the most effective cause, let us first inquire about God. Let us state beforehand that we, following common life and adhering to no opinion, say that there are gods, worship the gods, and attribute providence to them; but against the rashness of the Dogmatists we bring forward certain arguments. And from this same Sextus, in his work Against the Mathematicians, marshalling various arguments and those of weight, proves both that God exists and that honour is to be paid to him. But if it was established for the Sceptics that God exists, so that they did not even doubt that assertion (though they did not know who or what sort of God he is), then they must also have admitted, whether they liked it or not, that they knew something, since they had recognised the first and most noble of all beings. It is true that they disputed with the Dogmatists about the distinct nature of God, and thought that it could not be stated definitely who or what sort of God he is. Yet they never called into question that God exists, that is, that there is some first, infinite and omnipotent being. In this they differed from the Dogmatists, for whom it was at least clear and evident, from the sense of God they cherished, what God is. Up to a point they agreed with these same men and approved their opinion, insofar as they confessed that God exists and that he must be acknowledged as a being that truly and properly exists. Hence this same Sextus writes in Against the Mathematicians: The notion of the gods both has existed from eternity and remains for eternity, since the things that come to pass bear witness to it, as is fitting. But indeed, if the opinion of the common people and the unlearned is to be left aside, and we must believe learned and distinguished men, we may see that the poet does not put forth anything great or distinguished in which God is absent, on whom the power and force of things that come to pass depends, as in Homer the poet in the war he wrote of the Greeks and Trojans. We may also see that physics agrees with poetry. For Pythagoras and Empedocles, the Ionians, Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, the Stoics, and perhaps also those of the Garden, as the select sayings of Epicurus attest, leave God aside. Just as, if we were inquiring about things that fall under the eye, we would rightly believe those whose sight is sharpest, so, when considering things that reason contemplates, we ought to believe none but those whose intellect is keen and whose reason is penetrating, such as the philosophers. But the adversaries are wont to reply to this objection.

units.la: Hucusque Sextus.
units.tr: Thus far Sextus.

units.la: Eodem axiomatica, eaque distincta cognitio, deberet æque evidens esse atque cognitio simplicis apprehensionis) cum sufficiat concipi tanquam aliquid incomparabile. Naturæ siquidem lumen, (per lapsum hactenus penitus non extinctum) subserviente theoreticæ cognitioni aliquatenus perpetuo conscientia, hominem simulac imperfectissimam quoque functionem intellectualem edere incipit, deducit ad aliquod ens, secundum suum concipiendi modum eatenus non tantum incomparabile, quatenus alteri alicui non existimat æqualem perfectionem attribui posse; verum etiam quod mox apprehendat sese magis ab hoc ipso ente (facit huc conscientiæ testimonium) quam ab ullo alio observari, & quidem tanta cum attentione, ut illi ipsi quoque obligetur ad rationem reddendam omnium eorum, quæ fecerit. Hoc ita se habere manifesto liquet ex perillustri Pauli loco, ad Rom. cap. 2. v. 14. & seq. Quum gentes quæ legem non habent, natura quæ legis sunt, faciant, isti legem non habentes, sibiipsis lex sunt: Ut qui ostendant opus legis scriptam in cordibus suis, una testimonium reddente ipsorum conscientia, & cogitationibus sese mutuo accusantibus aut defendentibus. Quo in loco ut Apostolus testatur gentiles, alienos à tabulis sederis, atque promissionibus Evangelicis, natura, sive ex naturæ instinctu, non ipsam quidem legem (hæc siquidem ijs lata non fuit) sed
units.tr: Likewise, an axiomatic and distinct knowledge ought to be just as evident as the knowledge of simple apprehension, since it suffices to conceive something as incomparable. For the light of nature, which by the fall has not been wholly extinguished, serves theoretical knowledge, and, through a certain continual awareness, as soon as a person begins to perform even the most imperfect intellectual function, it leads him to some being which, according to his mode of conceiving, is incomparable to the extent that he does not think any equal perfection can be ascribed to another. Moreover, he immediately grasps that he is observed by this very being more than by any other (the testimony of conscience bears witness to this), and indeed with such attention that he is bound to give an account of everything he has done. That this is so is plainly evident from the famous passage of Paul, Rom. 2.14ff.: When the Gentiles, who have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves; in that they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts accusing or else excusing one another. In this passage, as the Apostle testifies, the Gentiles, strangers to the tables of the covenant and to the Evangelical promises, show by nature, that is, by the instinct of nature, not indeed the law itself (for this was not given to them), but

units.la: se liquido ostendunt Sociniani, quando hunc Solem obscurare, insitamque de Deo notitiam effurcillare omnium mentibus satagunt. Ita quippe de Barbaris Maximus Tyrius Dissert. 38. Inter Barbaros qui Deos non agnoscat, nemo est. atque distincte magis Ælianus lib. 2. var. Hist. cap. 31. Nemo Barbarorum ad contemptum Deorum unquam accessit: neque in dubium vocant sintne dij, an non sint, & curent ne res humanas, an non. Nemo igitur neque Indus, neque Celta, neque Ægyptius, eam cogitationem in animum induxit, quam vel Evemerus Messenius, vel Diogenes Phryx, vel Hippon, vel Dizagoras, vel Sofias, vel denique Epicurus. (Existimat quidem Ælianus, hos velut Atheos, ipsis Barbaris posteriores esse; at si omnia ad vivum circa singulos resecanda forent, liqueret, hanc opinionem publice de ijs invaluisse, nullam aliam ob caussam, quam quod obloquerentur abominandæ reliquorum gentilium opinioni de Deorum multitudine.) Sed Barbari hi contendunt & esse Deos & nostri curam gerere, & præsignificare sutura per aves, signa, vel omina, vel viscera, & alias quasdam observationes & doctrinas. quæret hic forte aliquis, qui pondus hujus argumenti, à Socinianis licet labefactati, incipiet æstimare, an ergo hæc propositio est Deus, per se nota sit? Non ignoro equidem Scholasticorum certamina circa hoc quæsitum, itemque quid quidam, Recentiores de eodem censuerint: Ego vero existimarem diftinguendum hic accurate esse inter cognitionem rei simplicem, & ejusdem rei notitiam axiomaticam. Quæ priori modo cognoscuntur, solummodo quod sint conceptu quocunque confuso à mente apprehendi possunt: quæ mens, esse quod rei, tum quoque apprehendere censetur, quando eam sic extra nihilum apprehendit, ut distinguat pariter à quocunque alio Ente, etiamsi interim neque cognoscat propriam illius formalitatem, neque etiam formare possit conceptum eidem adæquatum. At quando posteriori modo, sive axiomatice mens aliquid cognoscit, extrema enunciati inter se comparare debet, quo cognoscat aptane sint componi, an vero dividi; quod cum neutiquam fieri possit ni si cognita formalitate ipsorum extremorum, patet multo plus requiri ad cognitionem axiomaticam, quam simplicem. Quibus breviter in Thesi præmissis, dico hanc propositionem hoc est Deus, sive hoc Ens est Deus, neutiquam per se notam esse: nam si proponatur ea quam plurimis, petent illi sibi non solum explicari terminos, ad hoc ut dijudicare possint vera an falsa sit hæc propositio; sed aliqualem quoque descriptionem ipsius Dei, cumque quæstio solummodo sit de esse quod Dei, devenietur ad esse quale ejusdem. Longe vero secus se res habet circa cognitionem simplicem, quatenus nempe ipse Deus, tanquam aliquid secretum ab omnibus aliis Entibus, quibus prius esse menti videtur, apprehenditur: huic siquidem mentis conceptui sua constat ratio, quando modo mens apprehendit rem ipsam, seu Ens aliquod omnibus aliis Entibus (quae pariter apprehendere aut solet, aut potest) excellentius & superius. Atque hoc sensu dici potest per se notum esse quod sit Deus. Nam cum Lex naturae omnium mentibus [quemadmodum ex Apostolo jam antea patuit] sit inscripta, non potest ea ad modum normae a mente apprehendi, quin mox haec ipsa feratur ad Legislatorem, quem uti apprehendit tanquam supremum legis hujus dictatorem executoremque, facit pariter discretionem inter Ens aliquod primum, & reliqua Entia, nec interest, quo sive conceptu Ens illud primum apprehendat, aut quocunque etiam nomine compellet, cum sufficiat apprehendi tanquam primum atque longissime secretum a quibuscunque aliis Entibus. Atque ut haec hoc loco sufficere possunt de insita Dei cognitione; ita eadem antiquis Patribus in primitiva Ecclesia exploratissima fuit. Ex pluribus testimoniis sequentia solummodo adduco. Tertullianus in libro de Spectaculis: Nemo negat quia nemo ignorat, quod ultra naturae suggerit. Deum esse universitatis conditorem, eamque universitatem tam bonam quam homini mancipatam. pata. Sed quia non penitus Deum norunt. nisi naturali jure, non etiam familiari, de longinquo, non de propinquo. Arnob. lib. 1. adv. Gentes: Quisquamne hominum, qui non cum istius Principis notione diem prima nativitatis intraverit, cui non sit ingenitum, non affixum, imo ipsi pene in genitalibus matris non impressum, non insitum, esse Regem ac Dominum, cunctorum quaecunque sunt, moderatorem. Et in vestibulo libri secundi: Deum esse omnes naturaliter scimus. Cyprianus de Idolorum vanitate: Ergo unus est, & ubique diffusus est. Nam & vulgus in multis Deum naturaliter confitetur, cum mens & anima sui Auctoris & Principis admonetur. Hieronym. ad cap. 1. Gal. Ex quo perspicuum fit, natura omnibus inesse Dei cognitionem. Idem in Iob. cap. 36. Per natura bonum notitia creatoris est cordibus hominum, & quamvis aliquis tam pravus sit & frigidus, ut alienus esse studeat a Creatore: nullus tamen est, qui se abscondat a calore ejus. Et denique Damasc. lib. 1. d. fide Orthod. Attamen haud quaquam nos deserut Deus omnimoda sui circumfusus ignorantia: quin imo cunctis cognitio, quod Deus sit, ab ipso naturaliter insita est atque ingenita.
units.tr: the Socinians clearly show themselves when they strive to obscure this sun and to wipe out the innate knowledge of God from all minds. So Maximus of Tyre writes of the barbarians, Dissertation 38: Among the barbarians there is no one who does not acknowledge God. And Aelian more distinctly, Varied History, book 2, chapter 31: No barbarian has ever come to the contempt of the gods; nor do they call into doubt whether there are gods or not, or whether they care for human affairs or not. So no Indian, Celt or Egyptian has ever entertained the thought which either Euhemerus of Messene, or Diagoras the Phrygian, or Hippon, or Diagoras, or Sophias, or finally Epicurus entertained. (Aelian indeed thinks that these men, as atheists, came later than the barbarians themselves; but if everything were to be cut out down to the quick concerning individuals, it would be clear that this opinion about them spread publicly for no other reason than that they opposed the abominable opinion of the other Gentiles about the multitude of gods.) But these barbarians maintain both that there are gods and that they take care of us, and that they foretell future things through birds, signs, omens, entrails, and certain other observations and teachings. Perhaps someone here will ask, as he begins to weigh the force of this argument, which the Socinians, though they have weakened it, still assail: is this proposition God is self-evident? I am not unaware of the disputes of the Scholastics over this question, nor of what some of the more recent writers have held about it. For my part, I think a careful distinction must be made here between the simple knowledge of a thing and the axiomatic knowledge of the same thing. Things known in the first way are known only in that they can be apprehended by the mind under some confused concept; and the mind is judged to apprehend the thing's essence then, when it apprehends it so out of nothing that it distinguishes it likewise from any other being, even though it neither knows the proper formality of that thing nor can form a concept adequate to it. But when the mind knows something in the second way, that is, axiomatically, it must compare the extremes of the proposition with one another, to know whether they are fit to be joined or must rather be separated. Since this cannot be done at all unless the formality of the extremes themselves is known, it is plain that much more is required for axiomatic knowledge than for simple knowledge. With these things briefly laid down as a thesis, I say that this proposition this is God, or this being is God, is by no means self-evident in itself. For if it is put to very many people, they will ask that not only the terms be explained to them, so that they can judge whether the proposition is true or false, but also some description of God himself; and since the question is only about the existence of God, they will come down to the question of what sort of being he is. But the matter stands quite differently with simple knowledge, insofar as God himself is apprehended as something set apart from all the other beings which the mind seems to have known before. For this concept of the mind has its own reason, when the mind apprehends the thing itself, that is, a being more excellent and superior to all other beings, which the mind is wont or able to apprehend in like manner. In this sense it can be said that it is self-evident that God is. For since the law of nature is written in the minds of all (as was already plain from the Apostle), it cannot be apprehended by the mind as a rule without this very thing being carried straight to the Lawgiver. Just as the mind apprehends him as the supreme dictator and executor of this law, so it likewise makes a distinction between a first being and the other beings. Nor does it matter by what concept the mind apprehends that first being, or by what name it addresses it, since it suffices to apprehend it as first and as set farthest apart from any other beings. And as these things may suffice here concerning the innate knowledge of God, so the same was most clearly established among the ancient Fathers in the primitive Church. From many testimonies I adduce only the following. Tertullian, in his book On the Spectacles: No one denies, because no one is ignorant, what nature itself suggests: that God is the creator of the universe, and that this universe has been entrusted to man as good. But because they do not fully know God except by natural right, and not by familiar acquaintance, they know him from afar and not from near. Arnobius, Against the Gentiles, book 1: Is there any man who has not entered upon the day of his first birth with the notion of that Prince, to whom it is not innate, not attached, indeed almost not impressed in the very womb of his mother, not implanted, that there is a King and Lord, the governor of all things whatsoever. And at the beginning of book 2: We all know naturally that God exists. Cyprian, On the Vanity of Idols: Therefore he is one, and is diffused everywhere. For even the common people confess God naturally in many things, when the mind and soul are reminded of their author and prince. Jerome on Galatians, chapter 1: From this it is plain that the knowledge of God is present in all by nature. The same on Job, chapter 36: The knowledge of the Creator is, by the good of nature, in the hearts of men; and although someone be so wicked and cold as to strive to be a stranger to the Creator, yet there is no one who hides himself from his warmth. And finally Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith, book 1: Yet God, who is surrounded on every side by our utter ignorance of him, by no means forsakes us; indeed, the knowledge that God exists is naturally implanted and innate in all.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM QUINTUM
units.tr: CHAPTER FIFTEEN

units.la: An recte statuatur in nobis esse Dei idea, ex qua clare colligere queamus Dei existentiam? Item, an mens se à sensibus subducens, in se inveniat Dei speciem?
units.tr: Whether it is rightly held that an idea of God is present in us, from which we can clearly infer the existence of God? Likewise, whether the mind, withdrawing itself from the senses, finds within itself the image of God?

units.la: Occasione eorum, quæ superiori capite distincte, & tamen perfunctorie, de insita Dei cognitione disputavimus, non possumus non obiter expendere, an recte quidam instituant jactare, in nobis inveniri aliquam ideam, è qua colligere liceat ratiocinio indubitato & perspicuo, actualem Dei qua Dei existentiam. de authore hujus tum disputandi methodi, tum etiam argumenti [quod compositus jam sit] nihil dicere volo, nec etiam omnia, quæ aut ab ipso, aut pro ipso, circa hoc argumentum scripta sunt, quod ab aliis sufficienter hoc præstitum sit, ad examen vocare est animus: solummodo expendendum, aut tolerari qua in Philosophia, qua in Orthodoxa Theologia queat hæc rationativa locutio: Scio me in me habere Dei ideam, ergo Deus existit. Initio dico, quocunque etiam modo nomen ideæ [de cujus significatione acerrime contenditur] hic accipiatur, haut legitimam esse consequentiam: neque enim mox à parte rei formaliter existunt, quæ existunt objectivè
units.tr: Prompted by what we discussed in the previous chapter, distinctly yet cursorily, about the innate knowledge of God, we cannot help examining in passing whether some are right to boast that an idea is found in us from which it is lawful to infer, by indubitable and evident reasoning, God's actual existence as God. I wish to say nothing about the author of this method of arguing, nor about the argument as it has already been put together. Nor do I intend to call into question everything written by him or for him on this subject, since others have sufficiently done that. It is only to be weighed whether this argumentative form of speech, I know that I have in me an idea of God, therefore God exists, can be tolerated either in philosophy or in orthodox theology. First, I say that, in whatever sense the word "idea" is taken here (its meaning is fiercely disputed), the consequence is not legitimate. For things that exist objectively in the intellect do not at once exist formally in the thing itself.

units.la: K parte intellectus. Imo ne quidem ea, quæ citra demonstrationem ullam ab intellectu, ipsis sensibus in partes non venientibus, cognoscuntur, pariter mox à parte rei existunt. Chimæra qua talis,& formaliter sub suo conceptu considerata, nullo sensu aut velut objectum commune, aut etiam proprium percipitur, licet dilucidè atque sub formali sua ratione ab intellectu apprehendatur: à qua tamen conceptione progredi non licet ad ipsius actualem extra intellectum existentiam. Similiter non eris neutiquam à sensibus perceptibile, secundum rationem negationis comparativæ distinctè ab intellectu apprehenditur, quis tamen indè colligat illud pariter à parte rei extra intellectum actualem habere existentiam? Amplius dilucide intellectus percipit hoc axioma: Contradictoria non possunt simul existere: nec tamen quis, nisi Weigelianis delirijs effascinatus, velit inde inferre possibilem in se esse coëxistentiam contradictoriorum. Deinde, quis existentiam rerum existimet considerandam, & censendam esse ratione definitæ scientiæ certi alicujus hominis? Ubi est divina promissio, & obsignans Spiritus sanctus, ibi valet quidem illud scio, usurpatum ab Apostolo Paulo 2. Tim. 1. v. 12. neutiquam vero valere potest extra hunc casum, ob sexcentas fallacias, atque ludibria quæ menti humanæ, sæpe minus compositæ ob turbatas inferiores facultates, oriuntur. Certe cum obstrmatis Scepticis si quis hac ratione agere præsumpserit, risum atque ludibrium iis debebit. Tertio ut ratione Dei, mentî quasi exhibiti, quoad illius existentiam ab apprehensione qualicunque procedatur, quisquis est Christianus, cogitare debeat, quod diabolus, qui vocatur Deus huius seculi. 2. Cor. 4. v. 4. se transfigurët in angelum lucis, 2. Cor. 11. v. 14. fierique possit ut mens, quę hic tanquam sui juris validaque agnosci vult, etiam quando maxime videtur subsistere ad contrarium deflectat. Verum quidem est hanc conclusionem: Ergo Deus existit, adeo certam esse, ut nulla certior ne quidem cogitari queat [Cum enim Deus sit ens necessarium, atque illius esse sit ipsum existere, aliter fieri non potest, quin necessarium sit Deum existere] interim tamen principium e quo illud colligitur certo non tedit ad eam conclusionem: potestque diabolus, Deo permittente, aliquam imaginem, quasi singularem, & cum altera non comparabilem menti objicere, e qua ipsa colligat existentiam primi entis, interim ipsa illa imagine Deo per omnia dissimili, si non contraria existente. Si enim has fallacias diabolus exhibere possit ratione divinorum oraculorum, cur non ratione ipsius Dei pari modo menti ludibrium exhibeat? Sed ut ad illud, quod ingredi debet minorem propositionem huius argumenti, me convertam, illud nunquam ullo ratiocinio hic probari poterit. Audio quidem dici, in mente esse Dei ideam, atque quosdam ita assumere: Dei idea in me est. Sed qua certitudine? nolo iam disputare, proprie an improprie ab authoribus huius argumenti nomen ideae accipiatur, nec notare eorum inconstantiam; [quae vel sola sufficit evortendis illis, quae tanto molimine intellectus extructa sunt] hoc certum, in quascunque formas se converterint, per ideam debere intelligere speciem intellectualem Deo respondentem adaequate [quod & ipsi innuunt, dum per hanc speciem idealem, seu ideam intelligunt claram atque dilucidam Dei notitiam] & quidem eam speciem positive se debere habere, cum mens non possit concipi habere ideam distinctam alicuius rei, nisi ea sit positiva; quum non entis idea, improprie sic dicta, talis solum modo sit a parte intellectus per rationem comparationis, quatenus cogitando ens, quod non habet illud, quod competit ei ut enti, eidem exhibetur formalitas non entis. Sed si sub tali specie positive & adaequate Deus apprehendi poterit, quid fiet Scripturae, quae de Deo dicit quod habitat lucem inaccessam, 1. Tim. 6. v. 16. imo quod, quam diu absumus abeo, cernamus per speculum & aenigma, 1. Cor. 13. v. 12. Utque
units.tr: in the intellect. Indeed, even those things which are known by the intellect without any demonstration, the senses not reaching them, likewise do not at once exist in the thing itself. A chimera, as such, considered formally under its own concept, is perceived by no sense, either as a common or as a proper object, although it is grasped clearly and under its formal character by the intellect. Yet from that conception one may not proceed to its actual existence outside the intellect. Similarly, that which is not perceptible by the senses is distinctly grasped by the intellect under the notion of comparative negation. Yet who would infer from this that it likewise has actual existence outside the intellect? Further, the intellect clearly perceives this axiom: Contradictories cannot exist at the same time. Yet no one, unless bewitched by Weigelian delusions, would wish to infer from this that a possible coexistence of contradictories is in them. Again, who would think that the existence of things is to be considered and judged by the standard of someone's certain and definite knowledge? Where there is the divine promise and the Holy Spirit sealing it, there that "I know", used by the apostle Paul (2 Tim. 1:12), indeed holds. But it can by no means hold outside this case, because of the countless fallacies and delusions which arise for the human mind, often less well composed because its lower faculties are disturbed. Certainly, if anyone presumes to act in this way, he will deserve the laughter and mockery of the Sceptics. Third, if from some apprehension of God, as it were presented to the mind, one proceeds regarding his existence, every Christian ought to consider that the devil, who is called "the god of this world" (2 Cor. 4:4), transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14). It may thus happen that the mind, which here wishes to be recognised as its own master and strong, turns aside to the contrary even when it seems most to stand firm. It is true that this conclusion, "Therefore God exists", is so certain that no more certain conclusion can even be conceived. [For since God is a necessary being, and his essence is to exist itself, it cannot be otherwise than that God's existence is necessary.] Yet meanwhile the principle from which it is inferred does not surely lead to that conclusion. The devil, with God permitting, can present to the mind some image, as if singular and not comparable with anything else, from which the mind infers the existence of the first being, while that very image is wholly unlike God, if not contrary to him. For if the devil can exhibit these fallacies by the reasoning of divine oracles, why could he not in the same way exhibit a delusion to the mind by means of God himself? But to turn to that which must enter as the minor premise of this argument: this can never be proved here by any reasoning. I do indeed hear it said that there is an idea of God in the mind, and some assume it thus: "The idea of God is in me." But with what certainty? I do not now wish to dispute whether the authors of this argument use the name "idea" properly or improperly, nor to note their inconsistency, which alone is enough to overturn what has been built with such effort of intellect. This is certain: however they turn, by "idea" they must understand an intellectual species corresponding adequately to God. (They themselves hint at this when by this ideal species, or idea, they understand a clear and distinct knowledge of God.) And indeed that species must be positive, since the mind cannot be conceived to have a distinct idea of anything unless the idea is positive. The idea of a non-being, so called improperly, is only such a thing on the side of the intellect by way of comparison: by thinking of a being which lacks what belongs to it as a being, the formality of non-being is presented to it. But if God can be grasped in such a positive and adequate species, what will become of Scripture, which says of God that he dwells in unapproachable light (1 Tim. 6:16), and indeed that, as long as we are away from him, we see through a mirror and in an enigma (1 Cor. 13:12)?

units.la: Philosophice agam, intellectus finitus sub proria formalitate concipere debebit ens infinitum: siquidem nulla distincta de Deo potest esse idea, nisi ea pariter fuerit idea & species infinita, cum quicquid in Deo est, sit ipse Deus, & quodlibet attributum Deo ipsi respondens, si adequate concipiatur, pariter implicet adaequatum conceptum infiniti. Nec audio eos, qui dicunt: Si nulla datur idea seu species intelligibilis Dei, non credemus in eum, quia fides est notitia, notitia est per ideam in nobis, ac speciem intelligibilem. nam quamvis verissimum sit nos Deum obscure ex libro naturæ, clarius vero ex libro Scripturæ nosse, non licet tamen inde inferre propterea in nobis esse ideam propriam Dei; siquidem Deum cognoscimus non sub formalitate propria & adequate, sed per conceptus partim comparativos, partim negativos, apprehendendo non tam quid sit, quam quid non sit. Manet vero hæc thesis nobis certa est, Deus: quia quocunque mens se vertit, & quamcunque speciem ut entis speciem apprehendit, per eam ad Deum ducitur. Nec obstat quod dicitur notitia est in nobis per ideam ac speciem intelligibilem: siquidem quædam novimus per se ac per speciem intelligibilem propriam, quædam vero per speciem aliorum cum quibus comparantur, ut modo de non ente dictum. Contrarium quoque non sudet
units.tr: To argue philosophically: a finite intellect, under its own proper formality, must conceive an infinite being. For no distinct idea of God can exist unless it is likewise an infinite idea and species, since whatever is in God is God himself, and every attribute corresponding to God, if conceived adequately, equally involves an adequate concept of the infinite. Nor do I listen to those who say: If no idea or intelligible species of God is given, we will not believe in him, since faith is knowledge, and knowledge is through an idea and intelligible species in us. For although it is most true that we know God obscurely from the book of nature and more clearly from the book of Scripture, it does not follow from this that there is a proper idea of God in us. For we know God not under his proper formality and adequately, but through concepts partly comparative and partly negative, grasping not so much what he is as what he is not. But this thesis remains certain to us: God. For wherever the mind turns, and whatever species of being it apprehends, it is led through it to God. Nor does it stand in the way that is said, "knowledge is in us through an idea and intelligible species". For we know some things through their own proper intelligible species, and some through the species of other things with which they are compared, as has just been said of non-being. The contrary, too, is not hard to show:

units.la: adest Dei cognitio insita, nam ut inde collegeris nobis naturaliter notum esse aliquod Ens, sine socio, atque cum nullo comparabile; ita pariter non licet progredi à simplici Dei ut existentis apprehensione, ad adæquatam illius cognitionem per ideam, sive speciem intelligibilem. Quod qui pertinaciter contendunt, statuunt creaturæ possibile esse, ut Deum secundum essentiam cognoscat: quum tamen illi ipsi hoc Deo uni competere concedere cogantur. Non valet quoque in contrarium, quod dicitur, ideo hanc propositionem, Deus est; esse natura tum notam, tū evidentem, ideo quod pateat ejus cognitio soli intellectui: nam ut concedo lubens esse evidentem intellectui axiomatice ratione immutabilis veritatis, non est tamen evidens ei à parte subjecti: quicquid enim mens sibi finxerit, & quocunque conceptu quod Deum vocat apprehenderit, erit inadæquatus, nec poterit censeri species intelligibilis Deo propria & adæquata. Alij non tam nituntur præcedenti argumento, quam potius provocant ad abductionem intellectus, à rebus omnibus corporeis, existimantque eum in se animadvertere posse Deiipeciem, sive ideam, si modo se à sensibus omnibusque rebus corporeis seiunxerit. Doquidem lubens, intellectum sensibus affixum, & adhærentem rebus corporeis, impediri multis modis in contemplatione eorum, quæ sensibus non sunt perceptibilia; atque cum sui iuris est, melius vacare posse meditationibus rerum diuinarū: interim quocunque modo mens se composuerit, habebit duntaxat de Deo cognitionem partim comparatiuam, partim negatiuam, quam licet intus apud se limare & suo modo perficere queat, neutiquam tamen ut ut in omnes partes se converterit, talem, qualis urgetur, speciem inveniet: nec quando se contemplatur, in se ipsa pariter mens, ut quidam somniarunt, Dei offendit speciem, sic enim ipsa infinita esse deberet. Novi quidem Scholasticos ex Augustini Epist. 112. ratione Dei cognitionis distinguere in visionem apprehensionis, & comprehensionis: cæterum hęc ipsa apprehensionis visio ut consistit in manifestatione veritatis quod Deus sit; ita non efflagitat talem ideam sive speciem, quam homini, imo creaturæ nulli competere posse diximus. Videant vero qui hoc statuunt, quomodo cum Scriptura in gratiam redeant. Ea de omnibus irregenitis testatur, quod ratione intellectus sint tenebrę, Eph. 5. v. 8. cum ipse Deus lux sit 1.Ioh. 1. v. 5. at quæ conuenientia luci cum tenebris? ut usurpem verba Apostoli, 2. Cor. 6. v. 14.
units.tr: that innate knowledge of God is present. For just as you may infer that some Being, without companion and comparable with nothing, is naturally known to us, so likewise it is not lawful to proceed from the simple apprehension of God as existing to an adequate knowledge of him through an idea or intelligible species. Those who stubbornly contend this maintain that it is possible for a creature "to know God according to essence", although they are compelled to concede that this belongs to God alone. Nor is it valid to argue to the contrary that this proposition, "God is", is therefore known by nature and evident because his knowledge lies open only to the intellect. For although I gladly concede that it is evident to the intellect by the axiomatic reason of unchangeable truth, it is not evident to it on the side of the subject. Whatever the mind has fashioned for itself, and whatever concept it has grasped under the name God, will be inadequate, nor can it be judged a species intelligible, proper and adequate to God. Others rely not so much on the preceding argument as urge an abstraction of the intellect from all corporeal things, and think that it can perceive in itself the image or idea of God, if only it has withdrawn itself from the senses and all corporeal things. Indeed I gladly grant that the intellect, fixed to the senses and clinging to corporeal things, is hindered in many ways from contemplating those things which cannot be perceived by the senses, and that when it is its own master it can better be free for meditations on divine things. Yet in whatever way the mind has composed itself, it will have only a knowledge of God partly comparative and partly negative. This, though it can be refined within and perfected in its own way, will by no means find, however it turns in all directions, such an image as is demanded. Nor, when it contemplates itself, does the mind find within itself, as some have dreamed, an image of God, for then that image would have to be infinite. I know indeed that the Scholastics, from Augustine's Epistle 112, distinguish in the knowledge of God a vision of apprehension and of comprehension. But this very vision of apprehension, insofar as it consists in the manifestation of the truth that God is, does not demand such an idea or species as we have said cannot belong to man, nor indeed to any creature. But let those who maintain this see how they agree with Scripture. It testifies of all the unregenerate that in respect of the intellect they are darkness (Eph. 5:8), since God himself is light (1 John 1:5). But what agreement has light with darkness? (2 Cor. 6:14, to use the Apostle's words).

units.la: Duo argumenta proponuntur, haud exiguum pondus habentia apud Dogmaticos, eosque qui extra Scepticorum familiam consistunt.
units.tr: Two arguments are put forward which carry no small weight among the Dogmatists and among those who stand outside the family of the Sceptics.

units.la: QUum supra hasce lineas nobis definivimus, ut dixerimus, nos antea proponere velle illa argumenta, quibus ipsi genuini Sceptici, volentes nolentes expugnari queant, priusquam deveniamus ad ea, quæ apud Dogmaticos duntaxat valent; ex re est, postquam illud egimus, deinceps paucas quasdam rationes, apud hos, si bene examinentur, plurimum valentes, excutiamus. In antecessum vero eas iterum distinguimus, siquidem Dogmatici, quorum hic mentionem facimus, considerari possunt vel ut Scripturæ filii, vel quatenus ab eadem remoti, solis rationibus locum faciunt. Posterioris ordinis Dogmaticos uti prius confiderandos existimamus, ita in eorundem gratiam primo adducimus illud argumentum, quod desumptum est a naturali sciendi desiderio, in omnibus, qui homines sunt, se prodente. Neque enim ullum invenire est hominem, ut ut moribus quoque barbarum, ac ceteroquin ab omni cultu alienum, in quo non inveniatur naturale aliquod studium, quo fertur non tantum ad sciendum, verum etiam ad perfectionem scientiæ circa eam rem, cui cognoscendæ vacat, adhoc omnes animi sui nervos intendendo. Ut non sine ratione ab Aristotele in ipso vestibulo librorum Metaphysicorum dicatur: Omnes homines natura scire appetunt. Et à Cicerone lib. 2. de Finib. Natura, inquit, cuiusdam ingenuit homini veri inveniendi, quod facilime apparet, cum vacui curis, etiam quid in cœlo fiat, scire avemus: frustra vero appetitus hic concessus fuerit homini, creaturarum perfectissimo, atque ab angelis secundo, si ei ipsi appetitui naturaliter indito, satisfieri nulla ratione queat: at notum axioma, quo Deus atque natura nihil frustra facere dicuntur, lib. 2. de Cœlo tex. 50. & 59. lib. 3. de Anima tex. 45. Imo frustra laboraverint viri summi, qui inter difficultates maximas, quibus premebantur, præ sciendi tamen desiderio, studiis sapientiæ vacarunt. Sed quàm argumentum hoc præclare illustratum suerit à Cicerone, lib. 5. de Finib. non possum non integrum ejus locum; licet prolixiorem, hic asscribere. Ita vero loco dicto M. Tullius: Tantus, inquit, est innatus in omnibus hominibus cognitionis amor & scientiæ, ut nemo dubitare possit, quin ad eas res hominum natura nullo emolumento invitata rapiatur. videmusne, ut pueri ne verberibus quidem à contemplandis rebus perquirendisque deterreantur? ut pulsi requirant, & aliquid scire se gaudeant? ut alijs narrare gestiant? ut pompa, ludis, atque hujusmodi spectaculis terreantur, ob eandemque rem & famem & sitim perferant? quid vero, qui ingenuis studijs atque artibus delectantur? nonne videmus eos nec valetudinis, nec rei familiaris habere rationem? omniaque perpeti ipsa cognitione & scientia captos? & cum maximis curis&laboribus compensare eam, quam ex discendo capiant, voluptatem? mihi quidem Homerus hujusmodi quiddam vidisse videtur in ijs, quae de Sirenum cantu finxerit: neque enim vocum suavitate videntur, aut novitate quadam & varietate cantandi revocare eos solita, qui praetervehebantur; sed quia multa se scire profitebantur, ut homines ad earum saxa discendi cupiditate adhaerescerent. Et paulo post: Quem ardorem studij censetis fuisse in Archimede, qui dum in pulvere quaedam describit attentius, ne patriam quidem captam esse senserit? quantum Aristoxeni ingenium consumptum videmus in Musicis? quo studio Aristophanem putamus etatem in literis duxisse? Quid de Pythagora, quid de Platone, aut Democrito loquar, a quibus propter discendi cupiditatem videmus ultimas terras esse peregratas? quae qui non vident, nil unquam magna cognitione dignum amaverunt. Atque hoc loco, qui propter animi voluptates coli dicunt ea studia, quæ dixi, non intelligunt idcirco esse ea propter se expetenda, qu̧e nulla utilitate obiecta delectentur animi, atque ipsa scientia, etiamsi incommoda datura sit, gaudeant? ipsi enim quæramus à nobis stellarum motus, contemplationesque rerum cælestium, eorumque omnium, quæ naturæ obscuritate occultantur, cognitiones quemadmodum nos moveant, & quid historia delectet, quam solemus persequi usque ad extremum, prætermissa repetimus, inchoata persequimur. Nec vero sum inscius esse utilitatem in historia, non modo voluptatem: quid cum fictas fabulas, e quibus utilitas nulla duci potest, cum voluptate legimus? quid cum volumus nomina eorum qui quid gesserint, nota nobis esse, parentes, patriam, multa praeterea minime necessaria? quid quod homines infima fortuna, nulla spe rerum gerendarum, opifices denique delectentur historia? maximeque eos videre possumus, res gestas audire & legere velle, quia spe gerendi absunt confecti senectute. Quocirca intelligi necesse est in ipsis rebus, quæ discuntur & cognoscuntur, invitamenta inesse; quibus ad discendum, cognoscendumque moveamur. Ac veteres quidem Philosophi in beatorum insulis fingunt, qualis natura sit vitæ sapientium, quos cura omni liberaberatos nullum necessarium vitæ cultum aut paratum requirentes, nihil aliud esse acturos putant, nisi ut omne tempus in quærendo, ac discendo in naturæ cognitione consumant: nos autem non solum beatæ vitæ illam oblectationem videmus, sed etiam levamentum miseriarum. Itaque multi cum in potestate essent hostium aut tyrannorum, multi in custodia, multi ex exilio dolorem suum doctrinæ studijs levaverunt. Princeps hujus civitatis Phalereus Demetrius, cum patria pulsus esset injuria, ad Ptolemæum se Regem Alexandriam contulit, qui cum in hac ipsa Philosophia, ad quam te hortamur, excelleret, Theophrastique esset auditor, multa præclara in illo calamitoso otio scripsit, non ad usum aliquem suum, quo erat orbatus, sed animi, cultus ille erat ei quidam humanitatis cibus. Hucusque Cicero. Imo, si nulla detur scientia, nec verum, invitante adhoc ipso naturali appetitu, inveniri posset; inane fuerit non solum Philosophorum studium, verum etiam nomen, quique veritatis investigationi omne suum studium tempusque impendunt, tantundem fecerint, atque illi, qui volantia insequuntur, quemadmodum in materia non admodum absimili loquitur Aristoteles lib. 4. Metaph. cap. 5. At quis hoc credat? Deinde nec hoc altetum argumentum insuper plane habendum esse existimo: Communes veritates, apud cunctos mortales indubitatæ ; concessæque ab omnibus illis, qui modo terminos cognoscere possunt; velut regula & mensura aliorum, quæ cognoscuntur, ab omnibus apprehenduntur, simul ac modo terminos intelligunt: certo argumento i s inesse certitudinem atque veritatem tantam, ut de ijsdem tuto ambigere non liceat. Eo ipso quippe primæ veritates, quæ vulgo generalissima atque indemonstrabilia axiomata vocantur, ab omnibus probantur, quoniam omnes, terminis modo intellectis, certitudini, atque evidenti eorundem veritati assentiuntur. at si omnes, ij quoque qui ab omni humanitate alieni sunt, citra ullam fluctuationem, aut mentis hæsitantiam ijsdem assensum suum concedunt, neque pariter certum est, nec ultra ambigere licet, quin aliquid tanquam verum atque certum intelligi ab humana mente possit. Quod enim omnes omnino homines approbant, & ut certum agnoscunt, illud quoque ut certum cognosci posse, certius est, quam ut ulli homini de eo ambigere liceat. nec quicquam ad rem facit, quod in applicatione primarum veritatum mens sæpe hæsitabunda subsistat, fluctuetque, nescia an primæ veritates certæ & veræ quoque sint; siquidem hoc nullam aliam ob caussam contingit, quam quod mens rerum ad quas fit applicatio, intricata varietate & multitudine confundatur, nec possit illud quod in se ut certum cognoscit, simul qua tale apprehendere cum eo cui applicatur. quomodo mens mox non videt trianguli rectanguli angulũ rectum maiorem esse angulo acuto, quamvis probe alias noñt integrum circuli quadrantem majorem esse parte illius, ex eo quod totum sua parte majus sit. Horum ipsorum vero principiorum certitudo inde elucescit, quod sic cognoscãtur abintellectu, ut nunquã metus contrarii ei sub esse queat, nec unquam axioma, quod contradictorium hisce primis veritatibus existit, verum esse possit. Existimabit quis forte inconvenientem hanc rationem esse, propterea quod primorum principiorum notitia, non censeatur esse scientia, sed intelligentia; quod quamvis concesserim non invitus habita ratione distinctionis, quam Aristoteles agnoscit inter habitus intellectuales: interim, in hac doctrina contra Scepticos, scientię fimbrias latius extendi posse, imo debere, ex iisque antea proposita fuerunt, liquere credo.
units.tr: As I said, I stated above that before turning to those arguments which have force only among the Dogmatists, I wished first to set out those arguments by which the genuine Sceptics themselves can be overcome, whether they like it or not. Having done that, it is now appropriate to examine a few arguments that carry great weight among the Dogmatists, provided they are weighed carefully. First, however, I distinguish the Dogmatists again, since those of whom I am speaking can be considered either as sons of Scripture or as men removed from it who admit only reasons. I think the second group of Dogmatists should be considered first. For their benefit I first adduce the argument drawn from the natural desire to know, which shows itself in all who are human. There is no human being, however barbarous in manners and otherwise removed from all culture, in whom some natural zeal is not found, which drives him not only to know but also to perfect his knowledge of the thing he has set himself to understand, straining all the sinews of his mind to do so. Hence Aristotle rightly says at the very beginning of the books of the Metaphysics: "All men by nature desire to know." And Cicero, in the second book of the De finibus: "Nature," he says, "has implanted in man a love of discovering the truth, which appears most plainly when, free from cares, we desire to know even what happens in the heavens." Yet this desire would be given to man, the most perfect of creatures and second only to the angels, in vain, if the very appetite implanted in him by nature could in no way be satisfied. And there is the well-known axiom that God and nature are said to do nothing in vain (Aristotle, On the Heavens, book 2, texts 50 and 59; On the Soul, book 3, text 45). Indeed, great men would have toiled in vain, who, amid the greatest difficulties that pressed upon them, nevertheless devoted themselves to the pursuit of wisdom out of their desire to know. How splendidly Cicero illustrates this argument in the fifth book of the De finibus I cannot pass over; I must quote his whole passage here, though it is rather long. In that place Marcus Tullius says: "So great is the love of knowing and of learning implanted in all men, that no one can doubt that human nature is drawn to these things without any advantage being held out to it. Do we not see how boys, not even deterred by blows, are kept from contemplating and inquiring into things? How, when driven away, they seek them again, and rejoice to know something? How they are eager to tell it to others? How they are taken up by the procession, the games, and spectacles of this kind, and for the same reason bear hunger and thirst? What of those who delight in liberal studies and arts? Do we not see that they take no account of health or of their family affairs, and that, captivated by knowledge and learning, they endure everything, and balance the pleasure they derive from learning against the greatest cares and labours? Homer seems to me to have seen something of this kind in what he feigned about the song of the Sirens: it was not by the sweetness of their voices, nor by some novelty and variety of singing, that they were accustomed to call back those who sailed past; rather, because they professed to know many things, men clung to their rocks in a desire to learn." And a little later: "What zeal for study do you think there was in Archimedes, who, while drawing figures attentively in the dust, did not notice that his homeland had been captured? How much of Aristoxenus' talent do we see spent on music? With what eagerness do we suppose Aristophanes spent his life on letters? What shall I say of Pythagoras, of Plato, or of Democritus, from whom, because of their desire to learn, we see that the farthest lands were travelled? Those who do not see these things have never loved anything worthy of great knowledge." And here, do those who say that the studies I have mentioned are cultivated for the pleasures of the mind not understand that these are to be sought for their own sake, since the mind delights in them without any useful object, and rejoices in knowledge itself, even if it is going to bring discomforts? For let us ask ourselves how the motions of the stars, the contemplation of heavenly things, and all the knowledge of those things that are hidden by the obscurity of nature move us; and what history delights us with, which we are accustomed to pursue to the end, returning to what we have passed over and pursuing what we have begun. Nor am I unaware that history has utility as well as pleasure. But why do we read with pleasure fictitious tales from which no advantage can be drawn? Why, when we wish to know the names of those who did something, do we also want to know their parents, their country, and many other things that are by no means necessary? What of the fact that men of the lowest fortune, with no hope of doing great deeds, and craftsmen too, take delight in history? We can see especially that old men, worn out with age and cut off from the hope of acting, want to hear and read about deeds done. Therefore it must be understood that there are inducements in the very things that are learned and known, by which we are moved to learn and to know." The ancient philosophers, indeed, in their fables of the islands of the blessed, describe what the life of the wise is like: freed from every care, needing no necessary provision of life or means, they think they will do nothing else but spend all their time in seeking and learning the knowledge of nature. But we see that this delight is not only the pleasure of a happy life, but also a solace for miseries. Thus many, when they were in the power of enemies or tyrants, many when in prison, many in exile, have lightened their grief by the study of learning. The leader of this city, Demetrius of Phalerum, when he had been driven from his country by injustice, went to Ptolemy the king at Alexandria; and since he excelled in that very philosophy to which we exhort you, and was a hearer of Theophrastus, he wrote many excellent works in that wretched leisure, not for any practical use of his own, from which he had been cut off, but because that cultivation of the mind was for him a kind of food of humanity. Thus far Cicero. Indeed, if no knowledge were given, and if the truth could not be found even though this natural appetite invites us to it, then not only the study of the philosophers would be empty, but also the very name of those who devote all their zeal and time to the search for truth would be in vain, and they would have done just as much as those who chase after things that fly, as Aristotle says in a not very dissimilar matter in the fourth book of the Metaphysics, chapter 5. But who could believe this? Next, I do not think that this other argument should be wholly disregarded: common truths, indubitable among all mortals and conceded by all who can merely understand the terms, serve as the rule and measure of other things that are known. Those things are grasped by everyone as soon as they understand the terms. This is a sure sign that there is in these truths such certainty and such truth that it is not allowed to doubt them safely. For by this very fact the first truths, which are commonly called the most general and indemonstrable axioms, are proved by all, since all, once they have understood the terms, assent to the certainty and evident truth of these axioms. But if all, even those who are alien to all humanity, grant their assent to them without any wavering or hesitation of mind, then it is equally certain, and it is not allowed to doubt further, that something can be understood by the human mind as true and certain. For what all men without exception approve and acknowledge as certain, it is more certain that this too can be known as certain than that any man may doubt it. Nor does it matter that in the application of the first truths the mind often hangs back, hesitating and wavering, not knowing whether the first truths are also certain and true. For this happens for no other reason than that the mind is confused by the intricate variety and multitude of the things to which the application is made, and cannot at once grasp, as such, what it knows in itself as certain, together with that to which it is applied. Thus the mind does not immediately see that the right angle of a right-angled triangle is greater than an acute angle, although otherwise it knows well that a whole quadrant of a circle is greater than a part of it, because the whole is greater than its part. Moreover, the certainty of these very principles shines forth from the fact that they are known by the intellect in such a way that no contrary fear can arise in it, and that no axiom which contradicts these first truths can ever be true. Perhaps someone will think this argument inconclusive, because the knowledge of first principles is not reckoned to be science but understanding. Although I grant this, not unwillingly, in view of the distinction Aristotle recognises among the intellectual habits, I believe it is clear from what has been said above that, in this teaching against the Sceptics, the fringes of science can and indeed should be extended more widely.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM SEPTIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SEVENTEEN.

units.la: Proponuntur tria alia argumenta, quibus Dogmaticis astruitur, aliquid certo sciri.
units.tr: Three other arguments are put forward, by which the Dogmatists establish that something is known for certain.

units.la: ARgumentis adductis præsenti hoc capite, tria adhuc succenturiamus.
