Et tertio quidem dicimus, quod si nos, qui homines sumus, certi nihil apprehenderemus, non solum belluis, mutisque pecudibus, verum etiam ipsis rebus inanimatis longe posteriores essemus. Quis vero credat naturæ nobilissimæ, atque ad persectionem ordinatæ ea denegata esse, quæ rebus etiam abiectissimis concessa fuerunt? Ne enim dicam de aviculis minutissimis, quæ remotius licet recesserint à suis nidis, citra errorem tamen ad eos, distinguendo illos ab alienis, redire sciunt; itemque de apibus, quæ circa alvearia sua nunquam fallnntur, aut de formicis, quæ distincte atque definite suas norunt cavernulas: arbores definite & uniformiter norunt folia primo protrudere, dein flores, ac postremo quoque suos fructus sic conformare, ut nullus in tota hac actione error oboriatur: Si dixerit aliquis notitiam hanc esse metaphoricam, regeram eam tamen esse certam, addamque, quod si certitudo denegari non queat ne quidem metaphoricæ cognitioni, multo minus eandem denegandam esse cognitioni proprię: imo si certitudo cognitionis ibi se prodit, ibi ne quidem proxime in ipso subiecto director ordinatorque illius, ratiocinative intelligens occurrit, multo magis ibi agnoscenda erit, ubi ad modum caussæ propinquę adest director illius ratio. Quarto hoc quoque consideratione dignum, quod si intellectus noster non queat assequi scopum suum, atque perpetuo frustrari debeat suo fine, inferior sit futurus manu, instrumento corporeo, nobis ad res corporeas apprehendendas atque continendas concessō. Nam vel pueris notum est, ea, quæ certo & firmiter manu semel apprehenderint, se eadem quoque firmiter complecti & continere, nec dubitant an illa apprehensio reficiens certum atque definitum aliquod corpus fallax sit: quum eo ipso, quod apprehensio illa sit baculi potius, quam lubricę anguillæ, baculum se complecti, non vero anguilla sciant. Mauni non absimilis intellectus, si ea, quæ per definitam speciem videtur apprehendere, non apprehendat, dubiumque eidem esse debeat, an hanc potius quam illam rem (cujus tamen definitam speciem habet) apprehendat; naturę architectus instrumentariæ caussę majorem concesserit perfectionem, quam ipsi caussæ principali, quum polydædala illa manus non commendari possit ab ullo opere, ad eam referri solito, nisi quatenus subservit in expressione, confecti actione[?], atque absolutione illius ipsi menti, manu imperanti, illiusque ductus moderanti. Denique, si Scepticorum effata valere debeant, artes, quarum ingens numerus vix ad digitos revocari potest, servient magis turbandae huic nostrae vitae, quam eidem perficiendae. At quis hoc in animum suum induxerit? Consequentia ex eo patet: quod omnibus artibus, quae praesupponunt in artifice definitam cognitionem objecti tum extrinseci, tum intrinseci (uti loquuntur) dubiae, fallacesque esse debeant, magisque servire excarnificandae menti, vitaeque quae ab e-adem ordinatur regiturque, quam perficiendae: Verbi caussa enim, quam voluptatem sutor, hominum pedibus muniendis adversus sexcentas iniurias vacans, percipiet ex suo labore & opere, si dubitare debeat, an illud circa quod occupatur corium, papyrus, arboris folium, aut quid simile alterius rei sit? Item, an quod absolvit opus, capiti magis, an pedi vestiendo servire aptum sit? Atqui sic tamen illius mens oberrare debet, & fluctuationum variarum aestibus iactari, si quam fidem Pyrrhonij mereantur.
units.tr: Besides the arguments already brought forward in this chapter, we add three more. The third is this: if we men could grasp nothing with certainty, we would be far inferior not only to beasts and dumb cattle but even to inanimate things. Who would believe that a most noble nature, ordered toward perfection, has been denied what has been granted even to the lowliest things? I say nothing of the tiniest birds, which, however far they wander from their nests, know without error how to return to them, distinguishing them from others. Nor do I mention the bees, which never go astray around their hives, or the ants, which know their little caves distinctly and precisely. Trees know definitely and uniformly how first to put forth leaves, then flowers, and finally to shape their fruits, so that no error arises in the whole process. If someone says that this knowledge is only metaphorical, I reply that it is nonetheless certain. I add that if certainty cannot be denied even to metaphorical knowledge, it must much less be denied to proper knowledge. Indeed, if certainty shows itself there, where no reasoning intelligence stands even nearby in the subject itself as director and orderer of the process, it must all the more be acknowledged where its reason is present as a near cause directing it. Fourthly, this too deserves consideration: if our intellect cannot attain its goal, and must be constantly frustrated in its end, it will be inferior to the hand, the bodily instrument granted to us for grasping and holding bodily things. For even children know that what they have once grasped firmly and surely with the hand, they also hold and keep firmly, and they do not doubt whether that grasp of a definite bodily thing is deceptive. They know that by that very grasp they are holding a stick rather than a slippery eel, and they do not know that the eel is held. The intellect is not unlike the hand: if it does not grasp what it seems to perceive through a definite species, and must be in doubt whether it grasps this thing rather than that one (though it has a definite species of it), then the architect of nature has granted the instrumental cause a greater perfection than the principal cause itself. For that many-skilled hand can be commended for no work usually ascribed to it, except insofar as it serves in expressing, completing and finishing the work for the mind itself, which commands the hand and guides its movements. Finally, if the sayings of the Sceptics were to hold, the arts, whose number is so great that they can hardly be counted on the fingers, would serve rather to disturb this our life than to perfect it. But who could bring himself to think this? The consequence is plain: all arts, which presuppose in the craftsman a definite knowledge of the object, both extrinsic and intrinsic (as they say), would have to be doubtful and deceptive, and would serve to torment the mind and the life ordered and governed by it, rather than to perfect it. For instance, what pleasure would a shoemaker, busy protecting men's feet against countless injuries, derive from his labour and his work, if he had to doubt whether the leather he is working on is leather, papyrus, a tree leaf, or something of that sort? Likewise, whether the finished work is fit to serve for covering the head rather than the foot? Yet on this view his mind would have to wander and be tossed about by the varying surges of fluctuation, if the Pyrrhonists deserve any credence.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM OCTAVUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER EIGHTEEN.

units.la: E Scriptura ostenditur Scepticorum absurditas: quæ ignorantiæ infesta cum sit, nos ad scientiam invitat.
units.tr: From Scripture the absurdity of the Sceptics is shown: since ignorance is hostile to it, it invites us to knowledge.

units.la: QUam vero absona non tantum, sed blasphema quoque sit sententia Scepticorum, omnem scientiam abolentium, præ cæteris Scripturæ filiis exploratum. Spiritus siquidem Sanctus non solum pios, eosque, ad quos velut filios loquitur, dehortatur ab ignorantia (2. Thess. 4. v. 13.) verum etiam eam Deus ipse exprobrat tum idololorum cultoribus, Esa. 44. v. 18.19. tum populo suo, Psal. 95.v.10. Ierem.4.v.22. quandoquidem hominem alienat à vita Dei, Eph.4.v.18. sic ut pœnam æterni exitij illi luituri sint, qui non noverint Deum, 2. Thess. 1.v.4. atque inde ipsa ignorantia ex stylo Spiritus sancti pro quo cunque peccato accipiatur, Heb.9.7. Sed, quomodo hæc omnia aliquis cum Dei iustitia conciliare poterit, siquidem in hominem, ut persuasum cuperent Sceptici, scientia cadere non potest? Quos homines si quis audiat, beatissimi censendi illi erunt, qui per affectatam ignorantiam ad compositum mentis statum, illiusque imperturbatam quietem pervenire possunt. Verum tantum abest, ut Scriptura ijs felicitatem spondeat, amplius ostendit, affectatam ignorantiam meritum mortis æternæ supplicium augere, Luc.12.v.47. Tam infesta vero Scepticorum pulliciei Scriptura est, ut non tantum detestetur ignorantiam, velut malorum maximum, sed amplius in cognitione, sive scientia, summam hominis felicitatem constituat: quare & ipse Christus Ioh.17.v.3. ad discipulos suos ait: Hæc est vita æterna, ut te cognoscant esse illum solum verum Deum, & quem misisti Icsum Christum. utque per fidem in Iesum Christum servantur, quotquot ad salutem ab æterno ordinati sunt, ita ad fidem hanc adeo necessario cognitio requiritur, ut nihil frequentius sit, quam in Scriptura cognitionem Christi, & fidem in eum tanquam synonyma usurpari, ut præter locum modo adductum, patet ex Esa.53.v.11. Philip. 3.v.8. & aliis pluribus locis. Sed, si quid Scepticis deferendum, necessario fides salvifica, cui tanquam effectus formalis adest. inseparabiliter, quod ad actum primum, certa persuasio (Gal.2. v.16,20. Rom.8. v.16, 37,38. Act. 15.v.11. 2.Cor. 4.v.13, 14. Heb. 10.22.) perpetuo vacillare ac fluctuare debebit. Quomodo enim aliter fieri poterit, quin ipsa fides fluctuet miserrime, si cognitio, quam præsupponit, dubia atque incerta sit? Norat Augustinus, qui proinde tam infestus quoque Academicis à prima ætate fuit. Inde hoc ejus verbum Enchir. cap. 20. Apud nos iustus ex fide vivit. At si tollatur assensio, & fides tollitur: quia sine assensione nihil creditur.
units.tr: How absurd, and indeed how blasphemous, the opinion of the Sceptics is, which abolishes all knowledge, is well known to be a matter of Scripture above all else. For the Holy Spirit not only dissuades the pious, and those to whom he speaks as to sons, from ignorance (1 Thess. 4:13), but God himself also reproaches it, both in the worshippers of idols (Isa. 44:18–19) and in his own people (Ps. 95:10; Jer. 4:22), since it estranges a man from the life of God (Eph. 4:18), so that those who do not know God will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction (2 Thess. 1:4). And hence ignorance itself, in the style of the Holy Spirit, is taken for any sin whatever (Heb. 9:7). But how could anyone reconcile all these things with the justice of God, if, as the Sceptics would have us believe, knowledge cannot fall to man? If anyone listens to these men, those will have to be judged most blessed who, through a deliberate ignorance, can attain a composed state of mind and its undisturbed quiet. Yet Scripture so far from promising them happiness, shows further that deliberate ignorance increases the punishment of eternal death (Luke 12:47). Scripture is so hostile to the vanity of the Sceptics that it not only detests ignorance as the greatest of evils, but further places the highest happiness of man in the knowing, or knowledge. Hence Christ himself says to his disciples: This is eternal life, that they know you to be the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). And just as all who are ordained to salvation from eternity are preserved through faith in Jesus Christ, so knowledge is so necessarily required for this faith that nothing is more frequent in Scripture than for the knowledge of Christ and faith in him to be used as synonyms, as is clear from Isa. 53:11, Phil. 3:8 and many other passages. But, if anything is to be conceded to the Sceptics, saving faith, which is present to it as its formal effect inseparably, must, as regards the first act, which is certain persuasion (Gal. 2:16, 20; Rom. 8:16, 37–38; Acts 15:11; 2 Cor. 4:13–14; Heb. 10:22), waver and fluctuate perpetually. For how could it happen otherwise than that faith itself should fluctuate most wretchedly, if the knowledge which it presupposes is doubtful and uncertain? Augustine knew this, and therefore he was from his earliest years as hostile to the Academics as he was. Hence his saying in the Enchiridion, chapter 20: With us the righteous lives by faith. But if assent is removed, faith is removed too, because nothing is believed without assent.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM NONUM
units.tr: CHAPTER NINETEEN

units.la: Respondetur breviter ad illa argumenta, quae pro Scepticis, quasi e Scriptura adferri videntur.
units.tr: A brief reply to those arguments which seem to be drawn from Scripture in support of the Sceptics.

units.la: DEin ex re est, paucis expendamus ea, quae cum applausu pro Scepticis, ignorantiam hominis felicitati accensentibus, adferri videntur. Duplicia vero sunt: Testimonia & rationes. quod ad testimonia, ea depromuntur e Scriptura, ad quam ut haeretici caeteroquin absurdissimi confugere solent, quo videantur non sine praetextu quodam pertinaciter errori patrocinari; ita in Scepticorum quoque gratiam quidam instituerunt eandem sollicitare, si forte pro deliriis ineptissimis aliquid in speciem plausibile ex ea adferri posset. Initio adducitur locus Iobi cap. 34. v. 24. & seqq. ubi sic Elihu loquitur: Memento quod ignores opus Dei, de quo cecinerunt viri. Omnes homines vident eum, unusquisque intuetur procul. Ecce Deus magnus vincens nostram scientiam. Quomodo locus hic multis difficilis itelligi debeat, maximopere controvertitur. Primum versum ex Hebraeo Iunius atque Tremellius sic reddiderunt: Recordare ut amplifices opus ejus, quod contemplati sunt mortales. Sed quocunque modo verba ex Ebraeo reddantur, neutiquam tamen ex hoc loco eruetur nihil ab homine cognosci posse. Vulgata versio si audiatur, opus aliquod Dei olim factum, & ut quibusdam placuit, diluvium, respicietur, quod a seculis aliquot celebraverint ij. Quae vero consequentia ab opere tam extraordinario, ad ea, quae cognitionis humanae proportionatum esse possunt obiectum. Literae ac veritati Ebraeae si inhaereatur, locus hic suadebit Deum glorificandum esse propter opera illa, quae quotidie oculis nostris subiiciuntur. Dato vero, plene ea non cognosci, an propterea in universum omnis cognitio atque scientia abolenda erit? Nec inferre illa cum ratione licet, propterea omnem cognitionem negandam atque abolendam esse, quod cum a Deo hic exulemus, eum per speculum solum atque eminus cognoscamus. Quamvis enim perfecte eum non queamus nosse, sic ut mens illius ideam habeat, quemadmodum jam antea fuit probatum, tamen ratio, argumento omnibus natura noto & obvio, eundem esse concipit. Quo respiciens Lactantius lib. I. Divin. Instit. cap. 3. dicit: Nemo est qui sapiat, rationemque secum putet, qui non unum Deum esse intelligat, qui & condiderit omnia, & eadem, qua condidit didit virtute, moderatur. Secundus Scripturæ locus, quo alij hic nituntur, occurrit Eccles.cap. I. v. 12. & seqq. ubi ita Salomon: Ego Ecclesiastes, quum essem rex super Israelem Ierusalem: Applicans animum meum ad disquirendum, & ad explorandum sapientiam de omni eo, quod fit sub cælis, hanc occupationem malam inveni. Unde inferunt scientiam non posse acquiri, cum ipsa occupatio circa eam acquirendam mala sit. Sed si subsequentem versiculum XIV. legissent, & eum cum his verbis comparassent, verecundiùs philosophati fuissent: siquidem mala occupatio ea dicitur, quæ molesta atque laboriosa est, quomodo & Christus dicit Matth. 6. 34. Sufficit diei malitia sua. Quæ autem hæc consequentia: cum molestia atque difficultate, rerum reconditarum cognitio acquiritur, ergo applaudendum Scepticis, nihil nos scire contendentibus? Imo eo ipso quod labore atque molestia scientia comparatur, aliquid scitur. Præclare Lactantius lib. 3. Div. Inst. cap. 6. Quis velit laborare, ne quicquam sciat? aut ejusmodi suscipere doctrinam, ut etiam communem scientiam perdat. Non valet consequentia ab iis quæ secundum quid dicuntur, ad eadem absolute spectata. Non simpliciter Salomon damnat investigationem scientiæ: sed eatenus quatenus non potest ne minimam quidem rem contortam corrigere, aut perditam repræsentare, nedum vitam cælestem procurare, prout abunde liquet ex subsequenti versu xv. Quæ enim ratio quod Salomon Scepticorum instar omnem scientiam laboraverit subvertere, quum ipsa Regina Scheba ex longinqua regione venerit, quo exploraret illius sapientiâ, 1. Reg. 10. Christo ipso hoc non improbante, Matt. 12. v. 42. atque pro eo commendando Spiritus Sanctus testetur, quod sapientia ipsius major fuerit, quam sapientia omnium Orientalium, & quam omnis sapientia Ægyptiorum: item elocutus sit ter mille sententias, fuerintque cantica ejus quinque supra mille: eloquutus etiam sit de plantis, à cedro, quæ est in Libano, usque ad hyssopum, quæ prodit è pariete: denique eloquutus sit de jumentis, & de volucribus, & de reptilibus, & de piscibus, 1. Reg. 4. v. 29. & seqq. Tertio adducitur ex eodem Salomonis libro v. 11. cap. 3. ubi secundum vulgatum Interpretem sic legitur: Cuncta fecit bona (Deus) in tempore suo, & mundum credidit disputationi eorum, ut non inveniat homo opus, quod operatus est Deus ab initio usque ad finem. Sed ut gravissime hic impegit vulgatus interpres, ita in originali textu longe alius sensus occurrit, quem sic Latinè Iunius & Tremellius expresserunt. Deus scil. unumquodque facit pulchrum suo tempore: etiam cum seculo, [seu quam diu seculum est] exponit animo illorum [excepto eo, quod homo non assequitur] opus quod
units.tr: It is worth our while to weigh briefly those passages which are brought forward, to general applause, on behalf of the Sceptics, who count human ignorance among the sources of happiness. These arguments are of two kinds: testimonies and reasoning. As for the testimonies, they are taken from Scripture. The most absurd heretics are wont to take refuge in Scripture, so that they may seem to defend their error stubbornly with some pretext. In the same way, some have undertaken to press Scripture into the service of the Sceptics too, in case something plausible could be drawn from it in support of their most foolish raving. First, the passage of Job 34, verse 24 and following, is cited, where Elihu speaks thus: Remember that you do not know the work of God, of which men have sung. All men behold it; each one looks upon it from afar. Behold, God is great, surpassing our knowledge. How this passage is to be understood is much disputed among many. Junius and Tremellius rendered the first verse from the Hebrew thus: Remember to magnify his work, which mortals have contemplated. But however the words are rendered from the Hebrew, nothing at all will be drawn from this passage to the effect that man can know nothing. If we follow the Vulgate, some work of God done in the past is meant, which some, as it has pleased them, take to be the Flood, and which people have celebrated for many ages. But what consequence follows from a work so extraordinary to those things which can be an object proportionate to human knowledge? If we keep to the letter and the Hebrew truth, this passage will urge that God is to be glorified for those works which are set before our eyes every day. But granted that these are not fully known, will all knowledge and science therefore be abolished altogether? Nor is it right to infer, with any reason, that all knowledge is to be denied and abolished because, while we are exiles from God here, we know him only through a mirror and from afar. For although we cannot know him perfectly, so that our mind has an idea of him, as was proved above, nevertheless reason conceives that he exists, from an argument that is known to all by nature and lies open to everyone. Looking to this, Lactantius, in Book 1 of the Divine Institutes, chapter 3, says: There is no one who is wise and thinks for himself who does not understand that there is one God, who both made all things and governs them by the same power by which he made them. The second passage of Scripture on which others here rely occurs in Ecclesiastes 1, verse 12 and following, where Solomon speaks thus: I, the Preacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem. I applied my heart to seek and to explore wisdom concerning all that is done under heaven; I found this task an evil one. From this they infer that knowledge cannot be acquired, since the very task of acquiring it is evil. But if they had read the following verse, 14, and compared it with these words, they would have philosophized more modestly. For an evil task is one that is burdensome and laborious, just as Christ says in Matthew 6:34: Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof. But what kind of consequence is this: because knowledge of hidden things is acquired with trouble and difficulty, therefore we should applaud the Sceptics, who maintain that we know nothing? Indeed, by the very fact that knowledge is gained with labour and effort, something is known. Lactantius rightly says in Book 3 of the Divine Institutes, chapter 6: Who would be willing to labour so as to know nothing? Or to undertake such a teaching that he even loses common knowledge? A consequence does not hold from things said in a qualified sense to the same things taken absolutely. Solomon does not simply condemn the search for knowledge, but only so far as man cannot even straighten one crooked thing or set right one that is lost, much less secure the heavenly life, as is abundantly clear from the following verse 15. For what reason is there to say that Solomon, like the Sceptics, laboured to overthrow all knowledge, when the Queen of Sheba herself came from a distant land to test his wisdom (1 Kings 10), Christ himself not disapproving this (Matthew 12:42), and when the Holy Spirit bears witness, in commending him, that his wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the East and all the wisdom of the Egyptians; that he uttered three thousand proverbs, and his songs were a thousand and five; that he spoke of plants, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that springs out of the wall; and finally that he spoke of beasts, and of birds, and of creeping things, and of fishes (1 Kings 4:29 and following). Thirdly, Ecclesiastes 3, verse 11, from the same book of Solomon, is cited, where according to the Vulgate translator it reads thus: God has made everything beautiful in its time, and has given the world into their debate, so that man cannot find the work which God has done from the beginning to the end. But just as the Vulgate translator has gone badly astray here, so the original text yields a quite different sense, which Junius and Tremellius expressed in Latin thus: God, that is, makes each thing beautiful in its time; even with eternity, [or as long as the age lasts] he sets forth in their minds [except that which man does not attain] the work which

units.la: Ex Vulgata; Iunius & Tremellius; scholion marginal references not legible. quod facit ipse à principio, ad finem usque. Ex quo loco bene expenso convenienter contrarium collegeris: Si enim Deus opera sua à principio ad finem usque à se facta exponit hominum animis, ut in iis se occupent, excepto tantum uno genere operum; ne hominis quoque mens plurima cognoscendo assequi potest. Quænam vero definite à Salomone hic excipiantur, quis dixerit? Ego in genere iis applicuero verba Apostoli Rom. 11. v. 33. & seqq. O profundas divitias tum sapientiæ tum cognitionis Dei! quam inscrutabilia sunt eius iudicia, eius viæ inpervestigabiles! quis enim cognovit mentem Domini? aut quis eius fuit à consilio? Quarto & postremo iterum idem Salomon sollicitatur, & quidem ex eodem libro cap. 8. v. 16. ubi sic secundum vulgatum Interpretem legitur: Et intellexi, quod omnium operum Dei nullam posse homo invenire rationem, eorum quæ fiunt sub Sole, & quanto plus laboraverit quærendo, tanto minus inveniat, etiam si dixerit sapiens se nosse, non poterit reperire. Sed & hæc aliquanto aliter in textu Originali leguntur, quem sic Latine expresserunt Iunius atque Tremellius: Animadverti totum opus Dei, non posse hominem assequi illud opus, quod fit sub sole, quamvis laboriose homo quærat non tamen assequuturum esse. Ad hoc Salomon non loquitur absolute de omnibus rebus creatis, adimendo homini earum cognitionem; sed tantum de administratione rerum mundanarum: cuius duo constituit genera, unum ab hominibus, cap. 8. usque ad verf. 15. alterum à Deo, subseqq. verf. utrumque vero ita varium incertumque esse demonstrat, ut de eo nihil certi per ullum hominem possit definiri. Quę vero cōsequentia: homo non potest assequi admirandam rationem divina gubernationis circa mundum & res mundanas, ergo pariter ex iudicio Pyrrhoniorum omnis scientia possessione excludendus est?
units.tr: From the Vulgate; Junius and Tremellius; the marginal references of the scholion are not legible. He himself does from the beginning to the end. From this passage, properly weighed, you may fittingly gather the contrary: for if God sets forth in men's minds the works he has made from the beginning to the end, so that they may occupy themselves with them, with the sole exception of one kind of work, then the mind of man too can attain to know a great deal. But who would name precisely what Solomon excepts here? I, for my part, will apply in general the words of the Apostle in Romans 11, verse 33 and following: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgements, and his ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? Fourthly and lastly, the same Solomon is again called upon, and indeed from the same book, chapter 8, verse 16, where according to the Vulgate translator it reads thus: And I understood that man cannot find any reason for all the works of God that are done under the sun, and the more he labours in seeking, the less he finds; even if the wise man says he knows, he will not be able to find it. But these words also read somewhat differently in the original text, which Junius and Tremellius expressed in Latin thus: I observed that the whole work of God is such that man cannot attain that work which is done under the sun; although man seeks laboriously, he will not attain it. On this point Solomon does not speak absolutely of all created things, denying man the knowledge of them, but only of the government of worldly affairs. He sets up two kinds of this: one by men, in chapter 8 up to verse 15, and the other by God, in the following verses. He shows that each is so varied and uncertain that nothing certain about it can be defined by any man. But what consequence is this: man cannot attain the admirable reason of the divine government of the world and worldly things; therefore, by the judgement of the Pyrrhonists, all knowledge must likewise be excluded from man's possession?

units.la: CAPUT VIGESIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWENTY.

units.la: Proponuntur sexdecim principia, velut totidem fontes solutorij, ex quibus non difficile est respondere ad omnia Scepticorum argumenta in contrarium adferri solita.
units.tr: Sixteen principles are set out, as it were so many sources of solution, from which it is not difficult to answer all the Sceptics' arguments usually brought against us.

units.la: EX lege Methodi, deinceps singula Scepticorum argumenta, primo libro per certas classes digesta examinanda forent, sed cum compendio hic studere queamus, suggerendo generales quosdam fontes solutorios, lectorem brevitatis studiosum morari nolumus: quę enim distincte hic videntur annotanda esse, ea non incommode libro quarto proponi poterunt: quando distincte de tribus Logicæ instrumentis, Definitione, Devisione, ac Syllogismo agendum erit. Inter fontes vero hii considerandos agmen ducat illud, quod perquam diserte dicitur à Lactantio lib. 3. Divini Inst. cap. 6. Alij, inquit, putaverunt, sciri posse omnia: hi sapientes utique non fuerunt. Alij nihil, ne hiquidem sapientes fuerunt. Illi quia plus homini dederunt: hi, quia minus. Utrisque in utramque partem modus defuit. Ubi ergo sapientia est, ut neque te omnia scire putes, quod Dei est: neque omnia nescire, quod pecudis. Est enim aliquid medium, quod sit hominis, id est, scientia cum ignoratione conjuncta, & temperata &c. per hunc quasi pontem transire sine cadendi periculo licet: nam sic illi omnes qui in alteram partem inclinaverunt, aut dextro, aut sinistro versum ceciderunt. II. Etiam illorum vera potest esse cognitio, quorum scientia est imperfecta: quamvis enim omnium eorum quæ scimus, non pariter habeamus scientiam omnibus numeris perfectam, sive scientiam caussalem, cognitionis tamen possessione mens non deturbanda. III. Posito hoc principio, libro proxime subsequente pluribus confirmando, omnem cognitionem provenire à sensibus, sive mediate scil. sive immediate, observandum est amplius quasdam res sensibus proximas, quasdam vero sic ab ijs remotas esse, ut vel nunquam per se sub eos cadant, vel tantum incidenter, & ex aliarum rerum consecutione: unde consequens ut intellectus eas res, quæ
units.tr: By the rule of method, each of the Sceptics' arguments would have to be examined in turn, first arranged into certain classes in the first book. But since we wish to be brief here, we do not want to delay the reader who values brevity by proposing some general sources of solution. For what needs to be noted distinctly here can conveniently be set out in the fourth book, where we shall have to treat distinctly of the three instruments of logic: definition, division and syllogism. Among the sources to be considered, let the first be the one stated very clearly by Lactantius in the third book of the Divine Institutes, chapter 6: Others, he says, have thought that everything can be known: these were certainly not wise. Others [thought] that nothing can be known; not even these were wise. The former because they gave man too much, the latter because they gave him too little. Both lacked measure in each direction. Where then is wisdom? It is that you neither think you know everything, which belongs to God, nor know nothing at all, which belongs to cattle. For there is something in between which belongs to man, namely knowledge joined with ignorance and tempered, and so on. One may cross over this, as it were a bridge, without danger of falling; for all those who have leaned toward the other side have fallen either to the right or to the left. II. Even of those things whose knowledge is imperfect, a true cognition can still be had. For although we do not have equally, in every respect, a perfect knowledge (or causal knowledge) of all the things we know, the mind should not for that reason be deprived of the possession of cognition. III. Once this principle is laid down, and confirmed at greater length in the book that immediately follows, namely that all cognition arises from the senses, whether mediately or immediately, it must be observed further that some things are close to the senses, while others are so remote from them that they either never fall under the senses in themselves, or only incidentally and through the consequence of other things. Hence it follows that the intellect has the things

units.la: II. Ibid.
units.tr: II. Ibid.

units.la: quæ sunt sensibus familiariores, magis quoque exploratas habeat, cæteras vero à sensibus remotiores minus secundum formalem suum conceptum. iv. Nec tamen valet pariter consequentia à perfectiori cognitione eorum, quæ pariter sub sensum cadunt, ad subversionem cognitionis illorum, quæ sensibus per se non objiciuntur. v. Hominum authoritas neutiquam censeri potest sciendi modus, quam cum ne quidem Dogmatici ipsi admiserint, frustra sunt Sceptici, quando passim [videatur solus Sextus Empiricus] authoritates humanas inter se committere laborant. vi. Quod dicit Lactantius l. d. observandum diligenter: Quaecunque doctrina est, scientia constet necesse est. Sumi vero debet nomen scientiæ late, siquidem omnis doctrina [quicquid alii contendant] tendit ad scientiam. Et verum est, quod subiicit Lactantius: Si non est (finis scil. doctrinæ scientia) quis tam stultus est, ut discendum id putet, in quo aut nihil discitur, aut omnino dediscitur? vii. Quod monet Galenus libel. de optimo docendi genere, hic omnino notare convenit: Si nihil est evidens intellectui, aut certum exsefe, perijt omne rerum iudicium. Contra si est quidem, velut oculus in corpore, sic intellectus in animo, non tamen omnibus pariter acutus: confentaneum est, ut quemadmodum qui cernit acutius adducat eum ad id, cui visus est hebetior: ita quibus in rebus intelligibilibus contigit intellectu clare perspicere id quod offertur, maxime acutientem ad eandem contemplationem. VIII. Clarum in plerisque est effectum respondere caussæ, dilucideque illud ostendit regressus: quem etiamsi mens ubique notare non queat, nihilominus tamen non frustratur cognitione. IX. Vt falsum est omnia in perenni motuet fluctuatione esse, ita nec quælibet agitatio mentis tum attentionem, tum perceptionem impedit. X. Pariter falsum est omnia sic confusa esse, ut neque á se invicem discerni, neque distincte percipi possint. XI. Non est difficile menti [quemadmodum falso Sceptici persuadere laborant] tum conjungere tum etiam separare notionem. XII. Alia est ratio judicii de affectu nostro, alia de rebus externis. XIII. Menti non solum perspicacia inest, per quam citra probationem multis rebus assentiatur, verum etiam fœcunditas per quam è præmissis conclusionem inferat: quod qua ratione fiat, libro quarto distinctius docebimus. XIV. Ratione cognitionis verae non necessarium est, ut ultimam perpetuo rei differentiam assequamur; cum ratione imperfectæ nostræ cognitionis sufficiat sæpe duntaxat genus à nobis apprehendi. XV. Falsum est [ut Sceptici voluerunt] innumerabilium enumerationem requiri ad inductionem. XVI. Quamvis affectus non sint stabiles, & homines sæpe mutentur, tamen illa mutatio (quicquid Scepticis quoque visum fuerii) non accidit sine prævia cognitione: quatenus enim modo hoc modo illud mens apprehendit, etiam affectus variant: hi siquidem á notitia pendent, atque ad eandem conformantur. Norat hoc Alcibiades, qui in quadam oratione apud Thucyd. lib. 4. sic inquit: Si quis mihi injuste iratus fuit, nunc cognita veritate mihi fuit placatus. Idem patet ex colloquio Solonis cum Thalete, cujus meminit Plutarchus in vita Solonis: cum enim iter eos agitaretur hæc quæstio, cœlibatus [Thales cœlebs erat] an coniugalis vita [maritus erat Solon] felicior esset, Thales ut pro suo statu triumpharet, subornavit quendam tabellarium afferentem falsum nuncium de morte filii Solonis. quo accepto Solon, ut pater liberorum suorum amans, in magno luctu fuit: quod cum animad verteret Thales, alium subornavit, qui veram famam spargeret de vita filii Solonis. qua accepta, Solon rursus ad lætitiam excitatus fuit: certo argumento, notitiam, ut certam menti, affectus quoque contrarios gignere.
units.tr: which are more familiar to the senses more thoroughly known, and the others, which are more remote from the senses, less so, according to their formal concept. IV. Nor does the inference hold equally from a more perfect cognition of those things which likewise fall under the senses to the overthrow of the cognition of those which are not objects of the senses in themselves. V. The authority of men can by no means be regarded as a mode of knowing; since not even the Dogmatists themselves have admitted it, the Sceptics labour in vain when they everywhere [see Sextus Empiricus alone] try to set human authorities against one another. VI. What Lactantius says in the place cited must be carefully observed: Whatever the teaching is, it must rest on knowledge. The word knowledge must be taken broadly, since every teaching [whatever others may contend] aims at knowledge. And what Lactantius adds is true: If (namely, knowledge is not the aim of teaching), who is so foolish as to think it worth learning that in which either nothing is learned or everything is unlearned? VII. What Galen warns in his little book on the best method of teaching ought to be noted here: If nothing is evident to the intellect, or certain in itself, all judgement of things has perished. On the contrary, if there is such, then just as the eye is in the body, so the intellect is in the mind, yet not equally sharp in all. It is fitting that, just as one who sees more sharply leads on the one whose sight is duller, so those to whom it has been granted to see clearly, by the intellect, in intelligible matters, what is presented, should especially sharpen those who contemplate the same thing. VIII. In most cases it is clear that the effect corresponds to its cause, and regression shows this plainly. Although the mind cannot note this everywhere, nonetheless it is not deprived of cognition. IX. Just as it is false that everything is in perpetual motion and flux, so no agitation of the mind hinders either attention or perception. X. It is equally false that everything is so confused that things cannot be distinguished from one another or perceived distinctly. XI. It is not difficult for the mind [although the Sceptics falsely labour to persuade us otherwise] both to join and to separate a notion. XII. The judgement about our own affect is one thing, the judgement about external things another. XIII. The mind has not only a keenness by which it assents to many things without proof, but also a fruitfulness by which it infers a conclusion from premises; how this happens we shall teach more distinctly in the fourth book. XIV. For true cognition it is not necessary that we always grasp the ultimate difference of a thing, since for our imperfect cognition it is often enough that we apprehend only the genus. XV. It is false [as the Sceptics have held] that an enumeration of innumerable instances is required for induction. XVI. Although affects are not stable, and men are often changed, that change (whatever the Sceptics may think) does not happen without prior cognition. For as the mind apprehends now this, now that, the affects also vary; these indeed depend on knowledge and are conformed to it. Alcibiades knew this, who in a certain speech in Thucydides, book 4, says: If someone was unjustly angry with me, now that the truth is known he has become reconciled to me. The same is evident from the conversation of Solon with Thales, which Plutarch mentions in the Life of Solon. For when they were debating on their journey the question whether the celibate life [Thales was unmarried] or the married life [Solon was a husband] is happier, Thales, so that he might triumph in favour of his own state, suborned a messenger to bring a false report of the death of Solon's son. On receiving it, Solon, being a father who loved his children, was in great grief. When Thales noticed this, he suborned another who spread a true report about the life of Solon's son. On hearing it, Solon was again roused to joy. This is a sure proof that knowledge, when it is certain to the mind, also produces contrary affects.

units.la: LIBER TERTIUS DE SCEPTICISMO.
units.tr: BOOK THREE, ON SCEPTICISM.

units.la: CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Antiquiores Scepticos, eosque, qui ante Pyrrhonem in Scepticorum sensu fuerunt, sensuum certitudinem atque iudicium in dubium vocasse ostenditur. In ea sententia Democritus, Heraclitus, aliique plures, qui hic enumerantur.
units.tr: It is shown that the older Sceptics, and those who held the Sceptical view before Pyrrho, called into doubt the certainty and judgement of the senses. Democritus, Heraclitus and several others, who are listed here, held this view.

units.la: SUperiori libro, cum ostenderimus non tantum aliquid esse, sed etiam illud quod est, suo modo cognosci posse, reliquum est ulterius progrediamur, modumque cognoscendi distincte expendamus atque definiamus. Occurrunt autem primo sensus, à quibus ut omnis cognitio procedit, ita cognitionem ijs competere in confesso est apud illos, qui sciunt sentiendi organa ad hoc data esse hominibus, ut eorum subsidio noxia à salutaribus distinguere possint. quod quanquam creditur non solum à vulgo hominum, sed plerisque etiam Philosophorum; in dubium tamen vocatum fuit ab ijs ipsis, qui ex antiquis Philosophis, Academicis atque Pyrrhoniis praeivere. Democritus enim, ut inde incipiamus, in lib. qui Canones inscribitur, dicit: Sententiae duae sunt: tenebricosa quidem haec omnia; visio, auditio, gustatio, tactio. Eadem sententia secundum quosdam, ut loquitur Tertullianus lib. 3. de Anima, cap. 17. Heraclti fuit. quamvis per errorem quidam pro Heraclito apud Tertullianum substituere voluerint Heraclidem. Chalcidius enim in Timæum citat hanc Heraclti sententiam circa sensationem: Heraclitus intimum motum, qui est intentio animi, sive animadversio, dicit porrigi per oculorum meatus, atque ita tangere tractareque visenda. At vero Heraclidem in eandem sententiam cum Empedocle copulat Plutarchus lib. 4. de placitis cap. 9. ubi tractat veri ne sensus sint: Empedocles, Heraclides per meatuum concinnitatem dicunt sensum fieri, cum quodvis sensile suo sensui accommodetur. Ex qua sententia sequitur similis acatalepsia, atque in sententia Academicorum, cum tamen neque diversa videatur hæc definitio sensationis, tributa Heraclidi à Plutarcho, ac illa, quam nuper citavit Chalcidius ex Heraclito. Nihil ergo muto in Tertulliano, quia expresse probatum est libro superiori derogasse fidem sensibus Heraclitum. Sed ut ad Empedoclem accedamus, qui Democrito æqualis fuit, eadem illius de sensibus sententia fuisse videtur: ut non tantum Sextus lib. adv. Mathem. ex versibus illius probat; verum ex parte quoque Philosophus innuit; lib. 3. de Anim. cap. 3. t, 150. ubi illum accenset ijs ex antiquis, qui idem docebant esse, sentire & intelligere; quod existimarent veritatis iudicatorium soli rationi acceptum esse referendum, nullo vero pacto sensibus. Frustra vero est Picus Mirandulanus, quando lib. 2. cap. 11. & lib. 6. cap. 4. de vanit. doct. Getium; Empedoclis patrocinium contra Peripateticae Philosophiae dictatorem suscipit. Horum exemplo Parmenides, non tantum perhibuit sensus minus idoneos esse ad percipiendum, ut iam ante fusius probatum est: verum falsum quoque esse dixit eorum iudiciu, teste Theodoret. lib. 2. de Graec. affect. curat. Nec aliud senserunt Xenophanes Colophonius, Zeno Milesius, Stilpo, & Megarici, qui omnes fidem sensibus ademerunt, secundum Euseb. lib. 14. de praep. Evangelica. Socratis quae sententia fuerit, ex Cice. lib. 4. Acad. Q. libro primo ostendimus: cujus exemplo Plato, qui amat sententiam suam instar praeceptoris premere, in Timaeo sensus astus vocat, quibus quasi jactetur, fluctuet ac absorbeatur animus; ut Chalcidius illud explicat. Ut haut mirandum sit, conditorem mediae Academiae Arcesilam, mysteria doctorum suorum propalasse, ac Platonicae Philosophiae mangones, vanosque ostentatores docuisse sensuum judicium falsi redarguere. vide Tertull. lib. de Anim. cap. 17. & Augustinum lib. contra Academicos. Similiter Pyrrho rho, cujus discipuli Sceptici primo dicti sunt, sensibus fidem nullam habendam esse docebat, teste Diog. Laërt. lib. 9. Sexto Empir. adv. Mathem. et Euseb. lib. 14. de Præpar. utque hujus brutæ insensibilitatis documentum ederet, medicamenta putria, [teste Laërt. l. d.] item sectiones, ac ustiones ulceri cuidam adhibitas, tanta constantia tulit, ut ne supercilia quidem contraxerit: sed hoc ad ostentationem & pompam tantum factum: quemadmodum & alterum illud, quod refert Laërt. ib. Cum navi aliquando veheretur, & socij tempestate acti animo dejectiores essent, ipse tranquillo animo porcellum in navi edentem ostendebat, addens sapientem hanc illius imitari securitatem. Sed si undabundum mare navim fregisset, quis dubitet eum, qui [ut refert Lucianus] dicebat forte tranquillitatem esse, tabulam quam apprehensurum fuisse. Quæ vero ejus de sensibus propria sententia fuerit, docet discipulus Timon: qui ita apud Laërt. l. d. in lib. de sensib. Quod [inquit] istud dulce sit, non pronuncio, quod autem videatur, assentior.
units.tr: In the previous book we showed that not only is something, but that what is can be known in its own way. What remains is to advance further, to examine carefully the mode of knowing, and to define it. Now the senses come first. All knowledge proceeds from them, and everyone who knows that the organs of sense were given to human beings for this purpose, so that with their help they can distinguish the harmful from the beneficial, admits that knowledge belongs to them. Although this is believed not only by the common people but by most philosophers too, it was called into doubt by those among the ancient philosophers who went before, the Academics and the Pyrrhonists. To begin with Democritus: in the book entitled Canons he says: "There are two kinds of judgement: indeed all these are obscure: sight, hearing, taste, touch." The same view, according to some, as Tertullian says in On the Soul, chapter 17, was held by Heraclitus, although some have wished, through error, to substitute Heraclides for Heraclitus in Tertullian. For Chalcidius, in his commentary on the Timaeus, cites this opinion of Heraclitus about sensation: "Heraclitus says that the inner motion, which is the attention of the mind or its awareness, extends through the passages of the eyes, and so touches and handles visible things." But Plutarch, in the fourth book of On the Opinions of the Philosophers, chapter 9, where he treats whether the senses are true, joins Heraclides to Empedocles in the same view: "Empedocles and Heraclides say that sensation happens through the fitting together of the passages, when each sensible object is adapted to its sense." From this view there follows a similar acatalepsy, in the manner of the Academics, although this definition of sensation, attributed to Heraclides by Plutarch, does not seem different from the one Chalcidius recently cited from Heraclitus. So I do not alter Tertullian, since it has been clearly shown in the previous book that Heraclitus took away trust from the senses. But to come to Empedocles, who was a contemporary of Democritus, his view on the senses seems to have been the same as Democritus's. Not only does Sextus, in Against the Mathematicians, prove this from his verses, but the philosopher [Aristotle] also hints at it in part, in On the Soul, book 3, chapter 3, text 150, where he counts him among the ancients who taught that to sense and to understand are the same, because they thought the judge of truth must be attributed solely to reason and in no way to the senses. Pico della Mirandola is wrong, when in book 2, chapter 11, and book 6, chapter 4, of On the Vanity of the Disciplines, he takes up the defence of Gaetius and of Empedocles against the master of Peripatetic philosophy. Following their example, Parmenides not only said that the senses are less fit for perceiving, as was already proved more fully earlier, but also said that their judgement is false, as Theodoret testifies in the second book of On the Cure of Greek Maladies. Xenophanes of Colophon, Zeno of Miletus, Stilpo and the Megarians did not think otherwise; all of them took away trust from the senses, according to Eusebius in the fourteenth book of Preparation for the Gospel. What Socrates's view was, we showed in the first book from Cicero's Academica, book 4. Following his example, Plato, who likes to press his own opinion as a teacher would, in the Timaeus calls the sensations "agitations," by which the mind is, as it were, tossed, unsettled and swallowed up, as Chalcidius explains it. So it is no wonder that Arcesilaus, the founder of the Middle Academy, disclosed the mysteries of his teachers, and taught the hucksters and empty boasters of Platonic philosophy to refute the judgement of the senses as false. See Tertullian, On the Soul, chapter 17, and Augustine's book Against the Academics. Likewise Pyrrho, whose disciples were first called Sceptics, taught that no trust at all should be placed in the senses, as Diogenes Laertius, book 9, Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians, and Eusebius, book 14 of Preparation, testify. To give proof of this brute insensibility, he endured rotten medicines (as Laertius relates), and likewise cuttings and burnings applied to a certain ulcer, with such constancy that he did not even raise his eyebrows. But this was done only for show and display. The same is true of the other story that Laertius tells in the same place: when he was once sailing on a ship, and his companions were dejected in spirit because of the storm, he himself, with a calm mind, pointed to a little pig eating on the ship, adding that the wise man should imitate this man's composure. But if the raging sea had broken the ship, who would doubt that he would have grabbed a plank, he who (as Lucian reports) said that calm was merely chance? What his own view of the senses was, his disciple Timon shows, who says in Laertius, in his book On the Senses, as follows: "What that sweetness is, I do not pronounce; what seems so, I assent to."

units.la: CAPUT SECUNDUM
units.tr: CHAPTER TWO

units.la: His Scepticorum delirijs quídam ex antiquis hæreticis, negantes sensibus fidem tribuendam, assensi sunt.
units.tr: Some of the ancient heretics, denying that faith is to be given to the senses, assented to these delusions of the Sceptics.

units.la: Scepticorum vestigijs institerunt, omnemque fidem sensibus derogarunt quidam ex antiquis hæreticis, nominatim Valentiniani, Gnostici, & Basilidiani, qui, ut Deum ignorantiæ tenebris involverent, miram quandam sensuum emissionem iactabant. Irenæus lib. 2. adv. Hæret. cap. 18. Quæ dicta sunt de sensuum emissione, similiter & adversus eos, qui à Basilide sunt, aptata sunt & adversus reliquos Gnosticos. Emissionem autem hanc primo sic sensibus aptabant, ut eorum iudicium per eam primum obscurarent, ac deinde ipsum Deum, quem ut corporeum concipiebant, ignorantiæ arguerent. Quemadmodum fusius eo loco Irenæus docet. Varij quidem ex antiquis hæreticis pertenderunt, Christi carnem non veram, sed imaginariam esse: adeoque Christum non habuisse verum corpus, sed solum in phantasmate & putative apparuisse, consequenter quoque passum esse, nominatim Saturninus & Basilides, Irenæus lib. 1. cap. 22. & 23. item Tertullianus de præscript. adv. hæret. cap. 46. Marcus & Colarbasus, Tertullianus ib. cap. 51. & denique Manichæi, teste Augustino libel. de Hæref. cap. 46. nullus tamen ex hisce omnibus, præter solum Marcionem, ad patrocinium huius dogmatis Scepticorum adhibuit tela, contenditque sensibus nullam deferendam fidem esse, & consequenter non curanda quoque ea argumenta à sensibus desumpta, quibus humanæ Christi naturæ veritas astrui videbatur. Eos unos notando Tertullianus lib. de Anima cap. 17. sic loquitur: Contingit nos illorum etiam quinque sensuum quæstio, quos in primis literis discimus, quoniam & hinc aliquid hæreticis procuratur. Visus est, & auditus, & odoratus, & gustus, & tactus. Horum fidem Academici durius damnant, secundum quosdam & Heraclitus, & Diocles, & Empedocles. Certe Plato in Timæo irrationalem pronunciat sensualitatem & opinioni complicitam. Itaque mendacium visui obijcitur, quod remos in aqua inflexos, vel infractos adseverat adversus conscientiam integritatis, quod turrem quadrangulam de longinquo rotundam persuadeat, quod æqualissimam porticum angustiorem in ultimo infamet, quod cœlum tanta sublimitate suspensum mari iungat. Perinde auditus fallaciæ reus, ut cum cœlestè murmur putamus, & plaustrum est: vel tonitru meditante, pro certo de plau-
units.tr: Some of the ancient heretics, namely the Valentinians, Gnostics and Basilidians, followed in the footsteps of the Sceptics and took away all trust in the senses. In order to wrap God in the shadows of ignorance, they boasted of a certain wondrous emission of the senses. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, book 2, chapter 18: What has been said about the emission of the senses applies in the same way against those who are from Basilides, and is adapted also against the remaining Gnostics. They first fitted this emission to the senses in such a way that by means of it they would first darken the senses' judgment, and then charge God himself, whom they conceived as corporeal, with ignorance, as Irenaeus teaches more fully in that place. Various of the ancient heretics maintained that the flesh of Christ was not true but imaginary, and that Christ therefore did not have a real body but appeared only in a phantasm and in appearance, and consequently also suffered only in appearance. Namely Saturninus and Basilides: Irenaeus, book 1, chapters 22 and 23; likewise Tertullian, On the Prescription against Heretics, chapter 46. Marcus and Colarbasus: Tertullian, ibid., chapter 51. And finally the Manichaeans, as witnessed by Augustine, the little book On Heresies, chapter 46. Yet none of all these, except Marcion alone, brought the weapons of the Sceptics to the defence of this doctrine, and contended that no trust is to be placed in the senses, and consequently that those arguments drawn from the senses, by which the reality of Christ's human nature seemed to be established, were not to be heeded either. Noting these alone, Tertullian speaks thus in his book On the Soul, chapter 17: The question of those five senses also concerns us, which we learn in our first letters, since something is also gained from them for the heretics. Sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. The Academics condemn their trustworthiness more harshly, and according to some also Heraclitus, Diocles and Empedocles. Certainly Plato in the Timaeus pronounces sensation irrational and bound up with opinion. Thus sight is charged with deceit, since it asserts that oars bent or broken in water, since it persuades, against the consciousness of integrity, that a square tower seen from afar is round, since it defames the most even portico as narrower at its far end, since it joins the sky, suspended at such a height, to the sea. Hearing is equally guilty of deception, when we think of heavenly thunder and it is a wagon; or when thunder is brewing, we are certain the sound comes from a wagon.

units.la: stro credimus sonitum. Sic & odoratus & gustus arguuntur, siquidem eadem unguenta eademque vina posteriori quoque usu depreciantur. Sic & tactus deprehenditur; siquidem eadem pavimenta manibus asperiora, pedibus leviora credundur, & in lavacris idem calidus lacus ferventissimus primo, de hinc temperatissimus renunciatur. Adeo, inquit, sic quoque fallimur sensibus, dum sententias vestimus. Hactenus Tertullianus: qui ob eandem caussam hosce Marcionitas, non solum Academicos vocat libello de carne Christi, sed, ipsum Marcionem quoque in vestibulo illius libelli sic exagitat: Sed & qui carnem Christi putativam introduxit, æque potuit nativitatis quoque phantasmata confingere, ut & conceptus, & prægnatus, & partus virginis, ut ipsius exinde infantis ordo apparens haberetur. Eosdem oculos, eosdemque sensus sefellissent, quos carnis opinio inlusit. Verum de his pluribus contra ipsos Marcionitas agendum erit alio loco.
units.tr: So too smell and taste are accused, since the same ointments and the same wines are later found to be disparaged by a later use. So too touch is caught out, since the same pavements are believed rougher to the hands and smoother to the feet, and in the baths the same pool is first announced as scalding hot and then as lukewarm. So, he says, we are deceived by the senses even as we clothe our opinions. Thus far Tertullian, who for the same reason calls these Marcionites not only Academics in his little book On the Flesh of Christ, but in the opening of that book attacks Marcion himself in this way: But also he who introduced a phantasm-flesh of Christ could equally have fabricated the phantoms of his birth too, such as the conception, the pregnancy and the birth of the virgin, so that from it the order of the infant himself would seem to appear. They would have deceived the same eyes and the same senses which the opinion of the flesh has deluded. But these matters, and more on them against the Marcionites themselves, will have to be dealt with in another place.

units.la: Caput Tertium.
units.tr: Chapter Three.

units.la: Cum Scepticis fidem sensibus abrogavit Petronius Arbiter, itemque Franciscus Picus Mirandulanus: ijs frustra accensi sunt Martyres.
units.tr: Petronius Arbiter abrogated faith in the senses along with the Sceptics, and so did Francesco Pico della Mirandola. Martyrs were vainly provoked by these men.

units.la: Quum ex re sit, constare quinam vere, quinam autem per calumniam Scepticismi insimulentur. simulentur, haut abs re nos facturos credo, si hoc etiam caput inpenderimus hujus rei examini. Ut ergo inde incipiamus, ad Scepticorum de sensuum fallaciis sententiam prope accedere videtur Petronius Arbiter, disertus quidem, sed nequam. Cujus hi versus noti: Fallunt nos oculi, vagique sensus Oppressa ratione mentiuntur. Nam turris prope quae quadrata surgit, Attritis procul angulis rotatur. Hyblaeum refugit satur liquorem, Et naris casiam frequenter odit. Hoc illo magis, aut minus placere Non posset, nisi lite destinata Pugnarent dubio tenore sensus.
units.tr: Since it matters which men are truly Sceptics and which are falsely accused of Scepticism through slander, I believe we shall not be acting beside the point if we devote this chapter also to examining the question. To begin, then, Petronius Arbiter seems to come close to the Sceptics' view on the deceptions of the senses. He was eloquent, but worthless. His lines are well known: The eyes deceive us, and the wandering senses lie when reason is overborne. The tower that rises square from a distance turns round, its corners worn away. The sated man flees the Hyblaean honey, and often the nose hates the cassia. Things could not please more or less than this, unless the senses, with their wavering judgment, fought over a disputed matter.

units.la: Ex recentioribus in eadem sententia fuit vir alias summus Franciscus Picus Mirandulanus lib. enim 4. de vanitate Doctrinae Gentium cap. 12. perstringit Aristotelicam Physiologiam, quod in sensu fundetur ac ex eo originem trahat. Cum, inquit, Aristotelis doctrina fundetur in sensu, idea facile convincitur incerta: quia non incertus modo ut plurimum, sed saepe numero fallax, & pluribus modis alijs, quam putaverat Aristoteles, & decipere potest & decipit. Nec multum ab ea recedunt varij recentiores, quiea quae constanti sensuum judicio per secula multa sunt explorata, in dubium vocare audent; quod unus aliquis, forte aut oculis suis animadvertere, aut auribus audire
units.tr: Among the more recent writers, Francesco Pico della Mirandola, a man otherwise most eminent, held the same view. In book 4 of his On the Vanity of the Teaching of the Gentiles, chapter 12, he attacks Aristotelian physiology because it rests on the senses and draws its origin from them. Since, he says, the teaching of Aristotle is founded on sense, that idea is easily shown to be uncertain: for the senses are not only for the most part unreliable, but often deceptive, and they can deceive, and do deceive, in many ways besides those Aristotle had supposed. Several recent writers do not differ much from him, and they dare to call into doubt what has been tested through many ages by the settled judgment of the senses, on the ground that a single person may not have been able to notice with his own eyes or hear with his own ears what one or other of the senses has so often perceived.

units.la: non potuerit, quod toties alteruter sensuum animadvertit. Verum quidem est, uti ipse Hippocrates in principe illo Aphorismo exclamat, experimentum periculosum esse; non tamen inde colligere licet, omnia experimenta suspecta habenda esse, quod sensibus ut plurimum multae fallaciae subesse confuerint. Gravius illi impingunt, & propius ad Scepticismum vergunt, qui sic circa sensus dispensant, ut velit eos duces agnoscere in regenda vita, neutiquam vero in inquirenda veritate. Quicquid enim tales praetexant, a Scepticismo excusari haut posse, patebit ex illis, quae postea distincte disputanda venient. Quidam ex atheis, Deique contemptoribus, jam olim Martyres Scepticismi quoque arguere, aut saltem suspectos reddere instituerunt, quod maxima tormenta haut secus pertulerint, quam si usum omnium sensuum amisissent. Ceterum verum quidem est, ex Dei singulari misericordia, maxima tyrannorum tormenta, quae alias intoleranda esse caro judicat, tolerabilia & mitia martyribus fuisse reddita, illudque non tantum ex sexcentis exemplis, quae suppeditant martyrologia, colligi potest, verum prae caeteris liquet ex insigni hoc documento, quod occurrit in Martyrologio Anglico Foxi Temporibus Marianis, anno scil. 1555. Thomas siquidem Hauxus Anglus ob intrepidam ororthodoxæ fidei confessionem, ad vivicomburium condemnatus, ab amico tepidiusculo, qui sub horam mortis in carcere eum invisebat, rogatus est, ut signum aliquod in medijs flammis ederet, quo certior fieret flammæ tormentum tolerabile esset. Sic autem inter eos convenit, ut si flammæ vis intolerabiliter esset cruciabilis, Thomas quietus staret; sin autem tolerabilis, quæ facile vinci posset, palmas junctas super verticem sublatas, ad cælum tolleret: Memor autem promissæ fidei constantissimus martyr, cum omnes eum jam jam expiraturum esse crederent, semiustas manus ardoreque æstuantes supra caput ad Deum viventem erexit, terque magno cum plausu concussit. Sed quis tamen ex hoc, similibusq; exemplis colligat tactu somniu esse, aut eos omni sensu fuisse destitutos, qui constantiæ, fidei, ac dilectionis vehementia tormenta omnia exstinxerunt? Prudentius quoque Peristephanon hymno 14. introduxit martyrem sic expostulantem cum carnifice: O non virile robur, ô molles manus! Unam labantis dissipare tamdiu Vos non potesse fabricam corpusculi! Vix jam cohæret, nec tamen penitus cadit, Vincens lacertos dexterarum inertium!
units.tr: It is true, as Hippocrates himself exclaims in his famous first aphorism, that experiment is dangerous. Yet it does not follow from this that all experiments must be regarded as suspect, merely because the senses are usually subject to many errors. Those men come much closer to Scepticism, and more dangerously, who so divide up the senses that they would have them recognised as guides in governing life, but by no means in inquiring after truth: they should be acknowledged as leaders in ordering life, but never in the search for truth. For whatever such men may pretend, it will be clear from what I shall discuss in detail later that they cannot be excused from Scepticism. Some atheists and despisers of God have long since tried to prove, or at least to make suspect, that the martyrs were also Sceptics, because they bore the greatest torments as if they had lost the use of all their senses. It is indeed true that by God's singular mercy the greatest torments of tyrants, which the flesh by its nature judges intolerable, have been made bearable and gentle for the martyrs. This can be gathered not only from the six hundred examples that the martyrologies supply, but most clearly from the notable document found in Foxe's English Martyrology, in the Marian persecution, in the year 1555. Thomas Hauxus, an Englishman, was condemned to be burned alive for his fearless confession of orthodox faith. A somewhat lukewarm friend, who visited him in prison in the last hour of his life, asked him to give some sign amid the flames, by which it could be known whether the torment of the fire was bearable. They agreed that if the fire's force were unbearably painful, Thomas would stand still; but if it were bearable and could easily be endured, he would raise his joined palms above his head towards heaven. The martyr, mindful of his promise, was most steadfast. When everyone believed he was about to die, he lifted his half-burned and glowing hands above his head towards the living God, and shook them three times with great applause. But who would conclude from this and similar examples that those who extinguished all torments by the vehemence of their constancy, faith and love were insensible or deprived of all feeling? Prudentius too, in hymn 14 of the Peristephanon, makes a martyr speak thus to the executioner: O unmanly strength, O soft hands! You have not been able for so long to shatter the one fragile frame of this little body! It now scarcely holds together, yet it does not fall entirely, conquering the arms of your idle right hands!

units.la: in eumque sensum multa præclara habet Basilius Serm. de Barlaam: Martyres siquidem perfusi Spiritus Sancti consolatione, quam anima sola percipit. corporis obliti fuerunt ejusque pelleci suavitate, atque ut Ascetici loquuntur, refrigerio, ferri, ignis, & equulei tormenta ne quidem senserunt. Hinc Theodorus Antiochenus adolescens, qui sub Juliano Apostata propter psalmorum cantum horrendis tormentis subjectus fuerat, optabat ijs reddi, quo iterum consolatione illa frui posset: affirmabatque tormenta voluptati potius quam dolori fuisse. Socrat. l. 3. Hist: Eccles. cap. 16. Theodor. lib. 3. Hist. Eccles. cap. 10. Dici etiam potest, Deum, qui suos non sinit tentari supra id quod possunt, 1. Cor. 10. quique in fornace Babylonica, Dan. 3. actum secundum ignis cohibuit, aut tormenta intoleranda alias, tolerabilia reddere, aut membra patientium stupore perfundere, quo minus corporeos dolores persentiscant. Quod & Diabolus Deo permittente facere posse videtur, 1. Reg. 18. v. 28. acciditque, ut plurimum exstasin immittat. Denique non sine ratione quis suspicetur, Iavanos quoq; Scepticis accenseri posse: uti enim testis est Bontius in Notis ad Garciam ab Orta, piper, quod omnium judicio calidum est, (potentiali calore in actum se exerente, simulac masticatum fuerit) frigidum esse pronunciant. Sed quis eos ob hoc circa piper iudicium ad Pyrrhoniorum tribum ablegare velit? Namque, aut respiciunt calidiora aromata & herbas, quibus ordinario uti solent: [calor autem & frigus, non tam absolute, quam relative æstimari debent] aut hoc innuerevolunt, calidum innatum à frequentiori piperis usu infirmari, atque intus propelli.
units.tr: Basil also has much that is excellent to this effect in his sermon on Barlaam. The martyrs, filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit, which the soul alone perceives, forgot their bodies and were enticed by its sweetness; and, as the ascetics say, by its refreshment, they did not even feel the tortures of iron, fire and the rack. Hence Theodore of Antioch, a young man who under Julian the Apostate had been subjected to dreadful torments for singing psalms, wished to be given them again, so that he might enjoy that consolation once more, and he affirmed that the torments had been a pleasure rather than a pain. Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 16; Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 10. It may also be said that God, who does not allow his people to be tempted beyond what they can bear (1 Cor. 10), and who in the Babylonian furnace (Dan. 3) restrained the fire's usual effect, can either make torments that would otherwise be intolerable bearable, or pour numbness over the limbs of the sufferers, so that they feel their bodily pains less. The devil too seems able to do this, with God's permission (1 Kings 18:28), and he usually brings on an ecstasy. Finally, one might not unreasonably suspect that the Javanese too may be counted among the Sceptics. For, as Bontius bears witness in his notes to Garcia ab Orta, they pronounce pepper cold, although by universal judgment it is hot (its potential heat coming into action as soon as it is chewed). But why should anyone wish to banish their judgment about pepper to the tribe of the Pyrrhonists? For either they are looking at hotter spices and herbs, which they are accustomed to use ordinarily (and heat and cold ought to be judged not so much absolutely as relatively), or they wish to suggest that the innate heat is weakened by the more frequent use of pepper and driven inward.

units.la: CAPUT QUARTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FOUR.

units.la: Protagoras, Epicuræi, ac Stoici nimium sensibus tribuerunt. Ad illos Tertullianus accessit.
units.tr: Protagoras, the Epicureans and the Stoics attributed too much to the senses. Tertullian joined them.

units.la: UT vero Sceptici nihil sensibus tribuere volunt, omnes eosdem in dubium vocando, atque de eorundem fide ambigendo; ita alij, jam olim nimium quantum iis instituerunt tribuere, atque in præjudicium mentis, cui soli primæ partes debentur, omnia ijsdem deferre. Inter hos familiam duxit Protagoras Democriti auditor. ita enim de illo Laërtius lib. ix. Dicebat nihil animam esse præter sensus, omniaque esse vera, sicut & Plato refert in Theæteto. Præ cæteris vero hæc fuit sententia Epicureorum: unde Augustinus lib. 8. de Civit. cap. 7. Epicurei posuerunt judicium veritatis in sensibus corporis, eorumque infidis & fallacibus regulis, omnia quæ dicuntur, metienda esse censuerunt. Hinc Seneca de ijsdem lib. 1. Nat. Qu. cap. 4. Solem quem toto Orbe terrarum majorem probat ratio, aciesque nostra sic contraxit, ut sapientes viri pedalem esse contendant. Et de Epicuro ipse Cicero lib. 2. Academ. Q. Epicurus, inquit, eo rem dimittit, ut si unus sensus semel in vita mentitus sit, nulli unquam sit credendum. Hanc opinionem amplexus quoque videtur Tertullianus lib. de Anima cap. 17. Quanquam vero Augustinus l. d. Stoicos Epicureis jungit, paulum tamen ab iis diversum senserunt. Neque enim omnem sensum quidem verum, sed eorum quae sentiuntur quaedam vera, quaedam vana esse crediderunt. Hinc Cic. in Acad. Q. de Zenone patre eorum loquens, dicit: Sed ad haec quae visa sunt, & quae sic accepta sensibus, assensionem adjungit animorum, quam esse vult in nobis positam & voluntariam. Visis non omnibus adjungebat fidem, sed iis solum quae propriam quandam haberent declarationem earum rerum, quae viderentur. assentitur Ciceroni Plutarchus lib. 4. de Placitis Philosophorum cap. 9. sic loquens: Stoici sensus non falls judicant, visorum alia vera esse, alia falsa. Epicurus utrisque veritatem ex aequo attribuit. Opinionum alias veras esse, alias falsas. Sensum uno tantum modo falli, cum suum de rebus mente cernendis interponit judicium. Phantasiam duobus, cum & sensilium sit, & intelligibilium. Nec alia mens est Tertulliano loco aliquoties citato, ubi distincte de Stoicis & Epicureis agens, haec inter alia habet: Moderatius Stoici non omnem sensum, nec semper, de mendacio onerant. Epicurei constantiter parem omnibus atque perpetuam defendunt veritatem, sed alia via. Non enim sensum mentiri, sed opinionem, sensum enim pati, non opinari, animam enim opinari. Abscederunt & opinionem à sensu, & sensum ab anima: & unde opinio, si non à sensu. Cum vero utraque extrema opinio à veritate recedat, medię locus videtur concedendus esse, cui quantum deferri debeat, deinceps subsequentibus capitibus explicatum ibimus.
units.tr: Just as the Sceptics wish to grant the senses no authority at all, calling all of them into doubt and questioning their trustworthiness, so others have long since granted them too much, and in prejudice to the mind, to which alone the first place is due, have handed everything over to them. Among these, Protagoras, a hearer of Democritus, led the way. For Laërtius, book 9, says this of him: He said that the soul is nothing but the senses, and that all things are true, as Plato also reports in the Theaetetus. Yet this opinion was held above all by the Epicureans; hence Augustine, De Civitate Dei, book 8, chapter 7: The Epicureans placed the judgment of truth in the senses of the body, and they thought that everything that is said must be measured by their faithless and deceptive rules. Hence Seneca, on the same men, Natural Questions, book 1, chapter 4: The sun, which reason proves to be larger than the whole earth, has so shrunk our sight that wise men contend it is a foot wide. And Cicero himself, of Epicurus, Academica, book 2: Epicurus, he says, puts the matter so that if a single sense has once in a lifetime deceived us, no sense should ever be trusted. Tertullian, De Anima, chapter 17, also seems to have embraced this opinion. Although Augustine, in the passage cited, joins the Stoics with the Epicureans, the Stoics in fact thought somewhat differently from them. For they did not believe that every sensation is true, but that some of what is perceived is true and some false. Hence Cicero, speaking of Zeno, their founder, in the Academica: But to these things that appear, and that are received in this way by the senses, he adds the assent of the mind, which he holds to lie within us and to be voluntary. He did not give belief to all appearances, but only to those which had a certain clear mark of the things that seemed to be. Plutarch agrees with Cicero, in book 4 of De Placitis Philosophorum, chapter 9, speaking thus: The Stoics hold that the senses do not judge falsely, but that some appearances are true and others false. Epicurus attributes truth equally to both. Some opinions are true and some false. The sense is deceived in only one way, when it adds its own judgment about the things to be discerned by the mind. Imagination is deceived in two ways, since it concerns both sensible and intelligible things. Tertullian, cited several times, has the same view. In discussing the Stoics and Epicureans separately, he says among other things: The Stoics, more moderately, do not charge every sense, nor always, with lying. The Epicureans consistently defend a truth that is equal and constant for all, but by another route. For it is not the sense that lies, but opinion; the sense only suffers, it is the soul that opines. They separate opinion from sense and sense from the soul; and whence would opinion come, if not from sense? But since each extreme opinion departs from the truth, a middle place seems to be granted, and how much trust should be given to it we shall explain in the following chapters.

units.la: CAPUT QUINTUM
units.tr: CAPUT QUINTUM

units.la: Distinctis assertionibus declaratur quantum fidei sensibus tribuendum sit.
units.tr: Through distinct assertions it is shown how much trust is to be placed in the senses.

units.la: OMnia, huc spectantia, ut quam commodissime proponi & explicari possint, primo, & quasi in antecessum, certis assertionibus explicabimus, quantum sensibus deferri debeat, ut deinceps distinctius cognosci queat, quomodo sensus errare contingat. Inter eas primos ordines hæc ducat: Sensus nunquam falli potest circa objectum suum, spectatum non tantum secundum rationem communem seu genericam objecti; verum etiam spectatum ad modum objecti cuique sensui proprii. Quælibet enim facultas ita est determinata ad objectum suum percipiendum, ut circa alterius facultatis objectum versari nequeat. Quomodo enim visus determinatus ad videndum colorem ac lucem, pro ijs apprehendere posset sonos aut sapores? aut auditus pro sono percipere odorem? Dixi ad hoc sensum circa senæbile per se proprium nunquam falli: quod verum est, nec exemplis auris tinnientis, aut linguæ amara omnia judicantis convellitur: cum enim auris tinniens sonos percipit, revera sonos percipit, sed intra auris tympanum inclusos, non extra editos: cum lingua amara omnia judicat, revera amaritudinem sapit, sed non ciborum, verum ipsi linguæ inhærentem, ipsamque inficientem; quod idem dicas de ijs, quorum oculus bile affusus omnia flavi coloris intuetur: non enim ex ijs similibusque exemplis patet, circa sonos, sapores, & colores sensum falli, sed circa sonorum, saporum, colorum subjecta: sonos siquidem vere ut sonos, sapores, ut sapores, colores ut colores singulos in sua specie percentit: sed in eo errat quod hæc accidentia aliis subjectis affixa judicet, quam nativis & suis, colorem v. g. bilis judicat inhærere subjectis, amarorem linguæ insidere putat cibis, sonos spirituum ac flatuum intra auris organum inclusorum, exterioribus corporibus affixos arbitratur: in quibus contingit a parte quasi sensus [postea enim hæc distinctius explicabimus] salsitas, non circaobjecta propria, & per se, sed circa eorum subjecta què per accidens tantum sentiuntur. Hinc secunda fit assertio: Sensus falli potest ex accidenti circa particularem objecti proprij rationem; quomodo sæpe visus cæruleum pro nigro, rubrum pro viridi apprehendit. Addimus ex accidenti, ob ea qnæ antea sunt dicta. Tertio, contingit falli quoque sensum non tantum in applicatione proprij objecti ad subjectum, uti dictum fuit, sed etiam in applicatione ad locum. Quarto, sensus quoque facile fallitur circa sensibile per accidens, ut circa substantias. Quinto & postremo, quicunque externus sensus errare potest, circa sensibile commune: ut cum visus procul judicat indicem horologij quiescere, qui tamen movetur, accipiendo sic unum genus communis sensibilis pro altero, quietem scil. pro motu. Omnes tamen hi errores, maxime circa propria sensibilia, evitari magnam partem possunt, si observentur conditiones, quæ tanquam requisita circa unumquemque sensum attendi atque rescribi solent. Vulgo tria hæc censentur, I. Organum recte constitutum. II. Medium aliena qualitate non affectum. III. Debita distantia inter objectum & organum. Ut vero liquidius atque distinctius omnia proponi queant: Notandum quod sensus sit vis animæ sentivæ, sensibilia sibilia objecta percipiens, ad quem præ cæteris requiruntur objectum sensile, species sensilis, organum & medium interveniens inter objectum & organum, sensio ipsa seu sensatio, ac modus cognoscendi. Quatuor priora sunt propter sensionem: ut enim ea commode fieri possit, quodque ex illis requisitis debitas conditiones habere debet: nihil enim aliud sensio sive sensatio est, quam perceptio rei sensibilis, cujus modus consistit partim in patiendo sive recipiendo, partim in agendo & judicando. Sic oculus, organum visus, accipit in se speciem sensibilem coloris, de qua dein specie recepta judicat anima, & ita fit sensatio hoc est visio. Ratione duplicis hujus modi, duplicia considerabimus requisita, primo quæ pertinent ad receptionem in ordine ad quinque sensus externos: dein ea quæ ratione animæ judicantis, authominissentientis, intervenire debent.
units.tr: To set out everything relevant to this as conveniently as possible, I will first, and as it were in advance, explain by certain assertions how far the senses should be trusted, so that we may then more distinctly understand how the senses come to err. Among these, the following should come first in order: the senses can never be deceived about their own object, when that object is considered not only according to its general or generic nature but also according to the manner in which it belongs to each particular sense. Every faculty is so determined to perceive its own object that it cannot be concerned with the object of another faculty. For how could sight, which is determined to see colour and light, apprehend sounds or flavours in their place? Or how could hearing perceive an odour as a sound? I said that a sense is never deceived about the sensible that is proper to it. This is true, and it is not overturned by the examples of the ringing ear or of the tongue that judges everything to be bitter. When the ringing ear perceives sounds, it really does perceive sounds, but sounds enclosed within the drum of the ear, not sounds emitted from outside. When the tongue that judges everything bitter tastes, it really does taste bitterness, but not the bitterness of the food; it is the bitterness inherent in the tongue itself and tainting it. The same may be said of those whose eye, suffused with bile, sees everything as yellow. For such examples and similar ones do not show that the sense is deceived about sounds, flavours and colours, but about the subjects of sounds, flavours and colours. Indeed, the sense perceives each sound truly as a sound, each flavour as a flavour, each colour as a colour within its own kind. Its error lies in judging that these accidents are attached to subjects other than their own natural ones.
