For example, it judges the colour to inhere in the subjects when it belongs to the bile, it thinks the bitterness of the tongue lodges in the food, and it supposes that the sounds of spirits and winds enclosed within the organ of the ear are attached to external bodies. In such cases there occurs, on the part of the sense as it were, a falsity (for we will explain these matters more distinctly later), not about the proper and essential objects but about those subjects which are perceived only accidentally. Hence the second assertion is this: the sense can be deceived accidentally about the particular nature of its proper object; thus sight often takes blue for black and red for green. We add "accidentally", for the reasons already given. Thirdly, the sense may also be deceived not only in applying its proper object to a subject, as has been said, but also in applying it to a place. Fourthly, the sense is also easily deceived about the sensible per accidens, such as about substances. Fifthly and lastly, any external sense can err about the common sensible: for example, when sight judges from a distance that the hand of a clock is at rest when it is in fact moving, taking one kind of common sensible for another, namely rest for motion. Yet all these errors, especially concerning the proper sensibles, can for the most part be avoided if the conditions are observed which are customarily noted and listed as requisites for each sense. These are commonly held to be three: I. a rightly constituted organ; II. a medium not affected by an alien quality; III. the due distance between the object and the organ. But so that everything may be set out more clearly and distinctly, it should be noted that sense is a power of the sentient soul, perceiving sensible objects. For it, beyond all else, the following are required: a sensible object, a sensible species, an organ, and a medium intervening between the object and the organ; the sensing itself, or sensation; and the mode of knowing. The first four are for the sake of sensation: so that it can be conveniently accomplished, and each of these requisites must have its due conditions. For sensation is nothing other than the perception of a sensible thing, whose mode consists partly in suffering or receiving and partly in acting and judging. Thus the eye, the organ of sight, receives into itself the sensible species of colour, and the soul then judges concerning the species received, and so sensation, that is vision, comes about. Because of this twofold mode, we will consider a twofold set of requisites: first those which pertain to reception with respect to the five external senses, and then those which must intervene on the part of the judging soul, the sentient man.

units.la: CAPUT SEXTUM
units.tr: CHAPTER SIX

units.la: De requisitis visus in perceptione occupati.
units.tr: On the requisites of sight in the act of perception.

units.la: Ut ergo ordine singulos sensus cum suis requisitis expendamus, eos dividimus in mediatos, & immediatos; illi medio indigent, suntque tres numero, inter quos jure merito visus nobilissimus habetur, cujusque octo requisita distinctè considerare convenit. I. Debita distantiâ
units.tr: So, to examine the individual senses in order along with their requisites, we divide them into mediate and immediate. The former need a medium. There are three of them, and among them sight is rightly considered the noblest. It is fitting to consider its eight requisites separately. I. There must be a due distance

units.la: { } distantia occurrere debet inter visus objectum, ejusque organum. Omne enim objectum certo spatio est circumscriptum, ultra quod videri non potest: unde ejus ratione certa quaedam distantia ad accuratum intuitum requiritur, quae justa ac debita esse censetur, cum in ea cerni possunt partes, quae totius comparationem proportionem sensibilem habent. Quare quotiescunque immoderata distantia rei visibilis ab oculo, & nulla intermedia corpora interjacent, notabiles deceptiones oboriuntur. Quales v.c. sunt hae: [1] Quando qui ab amne remotiores sunt, res ulteriores a citerioribus non distinguunt. [2] Cum visus judicat stellas errantes ac fixas aeque a nobis remotas esse. [3] Quotiescunque in horizontis ambitu coelum terrae connexum esse videtur. [4] Item cum arborum ac columnarum longo ordine dispositarum in anteriorem partem quae remotissimae distant, conjunctae esse videntur. [5] Coelum juxta horizontem longius a nobis distare videtur, quam juxta verticem, [6] Ignes noctu conspecti viciniores videntur, &c. ll. Ut vera sit visio, objectum debita magnitudine dilatatum esse debet, quaedam enim ob exiguitatem non videntur: ejusque rei causam visivae facultatis natura in se continet. Quia enim visio per pyramidem fit, cujus vertex centrum visus sit, basis vero res ipsa: ex angulorum verticalium amplitudine, rerum magnitudines colliguntur: quorum spatia si eo-usque attenuentur, ut sub sensum non cadant, ipsa visibilia, quæ illis angulis subtenduntur, omnino evanescunt: Hinc pictúrææ & sculpta signa, in quibus majores partes accurate sunt expressæ, minores vero ruditer effigiatæ [quia hæ procul non videntur] eminus elegantiam præsefe ferunt: cominus vero si videantur, sordent, quia minores partes, minus eleganter expressæ majorum gloriam obscurant. Minimi quoque pulviseuli & alia corpora atomica non cernuntur. III. Visibile debet debitum situm habere: cernitur autem in sola oppositione: cujus hæc ratio, quod rerum aspectabilium formæ rectis lineis semper protrudantur. Ratione disparis hujus situs (1) Templorum pavimenta ingredientibus faftigiata videntur. (2) Maris convexitas gibbi in morem protuberare cernitur. (3) Planæ superficies libella expensæ, sivisus altitudinem superant, alveolate apparent. IV. Quicquid videtur opacum esse debet & aliquo modo esse solidũ. Unde cum visibile cum diaphano vel cum medio similis est perspicuitaris haut discernitur. V. Visibile, ut videri queat, lumine irradiatum esse debet. non ideo tátum, quia lumen velut quædam colorum hypostasis, species ab objectis prodeuntes sustinet, atque ad oculum vehit: sed vel maxime, quod colorum formæ dignoscendi facultatem excitare non possunt, nisi cum lumine permisceatur. Porro quia hæc illustratio diversimodo fit, & varie lux recipitur, varij colores exoriuntur: imo, quidam etiam phantastici colores, apparentes vulgo dicti. Eos n. dari certū, contra quam non nemo ex recentioribus existimat: nulli vero certo ac proprio subjecto insunt, sed soli diaphano, neque sunt propagines alterius corporis colorati, sed phantastici aut apparetes (ita vocantur, quod præter lucem, nullā veritatem habeant) sunt existimandi VI. Medium quoque diaphanum, & uniforme inter corpus visibile & oculum intercedere debet: quod si impurius aut diversæraritatis fuerit, visus variè fallitur: quemadmodum quivis animadvertere potest, quando aër nebulosus, aut alio modo crassus est. VII. Ut visio certa sit, tempus & mora quædam requiruntur ad visibile considerandum. Quis enim simplici ac primo intuitu omnia dijudicare potest? ut vero sæpius ille instituatur, tempore opus est. VIII. Organum visorium debet esse per omnia sanum: ægritudines enim oculorum, visum vel debilitant vel dissipant. velut lippitudo, lachryma, oculi inflammatio, cava ejus ulcera, fenilis caligatio, suffusio, paralysis, mydriasis, &c. Hinc & humor citrinus, aut rubens talia visa arguit: si in pupilla humor crassus, perforata videntur: si niger, plena muscis. Si ponatur digitus supra angulum oculi, vel in angulo, res duplex videtur: si moveatur cum digito, res ipsæ moveri videntur, &c. Tam multi vero & varij, ob laboriosam & multiplicem naturæ fabricam, morbi oculis accidunt, ut, ne inter ipsos quidem medicos ve de numero eorum conveniat, quotidie adhuc novis incommodis in polydædalo hoc naturæ opere se prodentibus. Ob uberem hanc vitiorum segetem (quis ab omnibus vitijs immunem se esse dixerit?) omnes homines haut quaquam apti censeri possunt, qui visus adminiculo vacent contemplationibus fidelibus instrumentorum subsidium exigentibus, aut, alias talibus experimentis, in quibus ordinandis visui, atque propter eum oculis, primæ partes assignari debent. Quis enim existimet oculo vitiato melius hominem videre posse, quam lingua, cujus nervi obstructi sunt, posse sic sapores explorare, ut pariter eidem à mente convenienter dijudicentur? Circa sæculum decimum tertium à Christo nato, cum Optices scientia exuscitaretur per Vitellionem, Rogerium Baconem, & Joannem Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem, in usu esse coeperunt perspicilla, variaque vitra visui firmando
units.tr: A suitable distance must lie between the object of sight and its organ. For every object is bounded by a certain space, beyond which it cannot be seen. Hence a certain fixed distance is required for accurate sight, and it is judged to be just and due when the parts can be discerned that bear a perceptible proportion to the whole. Therefore, whenever the distance of the visible thing from the eye is excessive and no bodies intervene, notable deceptions arise. Examples are: (1) those who are farther from a river do not distinguish the objects beyond from those nearer; (2) sight judges the wandering and the fixed stars to be equally distant from us; (3) whenever the sky seems joined to the earth within the compass of the horizon; (4) likewise, the most distant of trees or columns arranged in a long row seem joined to those in front; (5) the sky seems farther from us near the horizon than near the zenith; (6) lights seen at night seem nearer, and so on. II. For sight to be true, the object must be enlarged to its due size, since some things are not seen because of their smallness; the nature of the visual faculty itself contains the reason for this. For since vision occurs through a pyramid whose apex is the centre of sight and whose base is the thing itself, the sizes of things are gathered from the amplitude of the visual angles. If these spaces are so reduced that they fall beneath sense, the visible things subtended by those angles vanish altogether. Hence paintings and carved statues, in which the larger parts are precisely expressed while the smaller are roughly fashioned [because these are not seen from afar], show elegance from a distance; but seen close at hand they look shabby, because the smaller parts, less elegantly expressed, obscure the glory of the larger. The smallest dust motes and other atomic bodies are also not discerned. III. The visible must have its proper position, and it is perceived only in opposition. The reason is that the shapes of visible things are always projected in straight lines. From this unequal position: (1) the floors of temples appear sloping to those who enter; (2) the convexity of the sea is seen to bulge like a hump; (3) plane surfaces examined with a level, if they exceed the height of sight, appear hollowed out. IV. Whatever is seen must be opaque and in some way solid. Hence a visible thing is not discerned when it is set against the transparent, or against a medium of similar clearness. V. The visible, in order to be seen, must be illuminated by light. This is not only because light, as a kind of substance of colours, carries the species that issue from objects and conveys them to the eye; it is chiefly because the forms of colours cannot awaken the power of discerning unless they are mixed with light. Moreover, since this illumination takes place in different ways and light is received in various fashions, various colours arise; indeed there are also certain phantastic colours, commonly called apparent. That these exist is certain, contrary to what some of the more recent writers think. They inhere in no certain and proper subject, but only in the transparent; they are not offshoots of another coloured body, but are to be regarded as phantastic or apparent (so called because, apart from the light, they have no reality). VI. A transparent medium, uniform and clear, must also lie between the visible body and the eye. If it is impure or of differing density, sight is variously deceived, as anyone can notice when the air is misty or otherwise thick. VII. For sight to be certain, some time and delay are required for considering the visible. For who can judge everything at a simple first glance? To make the examination more frequent, time is needed. VIII. The organ of sight must be sound in every respect, for diseases of the eyes either weaken or destroy vision: such as bleary eyes, watering, inflammation of the eye, its hollow ulcers, dimness of sight, cataract, paralysis, mydriasis, and so on. Hence a yellow or reddish humour also indicates such appearances: if the humour in the pupil is thick, things seem pierced through; if it is black, things seem full of flies. If a finger is placed above the corner of the eye, or at the corner, the thing seems double; if it is moved with the finger, the things themselves seem to move, and so on. So many and varied diseases befall the eyes, because of the laborious and manifold structure of nature, that even physicians do not agree on their number, as new troubles appear daily in this many-crafted work of nature. Because of this abundant crop of defects (who would say he is free from all defects?), not all men can be considered fit for those contemplations that depend on sight and need the aid of faithful instruments, or for other experiments in which sight, and for its sake the eyes, must be given first place. For who would think that a man with a defective eye can see better than a tongue whose nerves are obstructed can taste flavours so that they are rightly judged by the mind? About the thirteenth century after the birth of Christ, when the science of optics was revived through Vitellio, Roger Bacon and John, Archbishop of Canterbury, spectacles and various lenses for strengthening and aiding sight began to be in use.

units.la: Ex Greek mando atque juvando servientia : (falluntur gravissime qui existimant multis seculis ante, eadem recepta fuisse, quibus arguendis serviunt ea, quę habet Lipsius diligentissimus antiquitatis ruspator Cent. 3. Misc. Ep. 36.) sed cum ijs ipsis instrumentis sępe aut vitia quę subsint, aut non bene his illisve aptentur, itemque, ob refractionem variam, cum judicio adhiberi debeant, patet singulari cautela hic opus esse.
units.tr: (Those are gravely mistaken who think they were received many centuries earlier; the things that Lipsius, the most diligent searcher of antiquity, has in Cent. 3, Misc. Ep. 36, are used to refute that view.) But since defects may lie in the instruments themselves, or they are not well fitted to this or that eye, and since, because of their varied refraction, they must be applied with judgment, it is clear that singular caution is needed here.

units.la: CAPUT SEPTIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SEVEN.

units.la: Proponuntur requisita auditus & odoratus.
units.tr: The requirements of hearing and smell are set out.

units.la: PRæter visum, mediatorum quoq; sensuum rationem habent auditus, atque odoratus, de quibus hoc capite acturi sumus. Quantum ad auditum, illius sex sunt requisita. I. Sonus e-jusve species secundum debitam distantiam ad aures adferri debet: quod ubi non fit, sæpe pecudis vox pro humana, aut, bombardæ strepitus pro tonitru habetur. II. Medium per quod sonus defertur commotum non sit: liquet in aëre, qui ubi ventis agitatur, soni per eum difficulter aut commeant, aut turbati ad sensorium accedunt. Hinc noctu distinctius & expeditius, quam interdiu, auditus suo officio fungitur. rum grati odores vix à vulturio quo percipiuntur, si aër vicinus Vesuviani incendii excrementis imbutus sit. IV. Moderate sensorium afficere debent: nimia vehementia ac acrimonia si illud turbent aut lædant, commoda & sufficiens eorum non poterit dijudicatio instituí. V. Organum [quod existimamus præcipue mamillares processus esse ]ab omni vitio immune esse convenit: si coryza, aut tenuis serosaque pituita, aut etiam crassa, aliave materia osis cribrosi foraminula obstruxerit, aut nares fuerint obstipatæ, item si polypus molestias creet, olfactus officio suo fungi aut incommode, aut nulla ratione poterit.
units.tr: Besides sight, hearing and smell are the other senses that work through a medium, and this chapter deals with them. As for hearing, it has six requirements. (I) The sound, or its species, must be carried to the ears at the proper distance. When this does not happen, a beast's cry is often taken for a human voice, or the noise of a cannon for thunder. (II) The medium through which the sound travels must not be disturbed. This is plain in the case of air: when it is stirred by winds, sounds either pass through it with difficulty or reach the sense organ garbled. Hence at night hearing performs its task more clearly and readily than by day. (III) The sense organ must be free of obstruction, and the medium must not be too thick. Pleasant odours are scarcely perceived by the nose if the air nearby is laden with the fumes of the Vesuvian fire. (IV) The objects must affect the sense organ in moderation. If they are too violent or sharp, and disturb or injure it, a sound and sufficient judgement cannot be formed. (V) The organ, which we think is chiefly the mammillary processes, should be free from every defect. If a cold, thin and watery phlegm, or thick matter of some other kind, has blocked the small holes of the ethmoid bone, or the nostrils are stopped up, or a polyp causes trouble, then the sense of smell cannot perform its office, or performs it badly, or not at all.

units.la: CAPUT OCTAVUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER EIGHT.

units.la: De requisitis tactus, atque gustus.
units.tr: On the requirements of touch and taste.

units.la: POst sensus mediatos, considerandi secundum definitas suas conditiones sensus immediati, tactus & gustus. Tactus, cujus organum immediatum per totum corpus diffusum secundum doctissimos medicorum & Philosophorum membrana est, unicus est sensus, habetque pro objecto qualitates tactiles. Ut vero officio suo fungi possit, quatuor hæc requisita concurrere debent. I. Tangibile obiectum corporeum esse debet, vere enim Lucretius: Tangere, vel tangi, nisi corpus nulla potest res. Probaturque illud á Salvatore nostro Luc. cap. 54. v. 39. Tactus enim certius quam visus judicare potest, sitne res corporea an incorporea. II. Ubicunque est tactus, ibi debet esse membrana. Hinc quia per pilos, offa & ungues non est diffusa membrana, neque tactus diffusus est. III. Ut tangibiles qualitates secundum species percipi á membrana queant, illi proxime admotæ sint: subjecta earum rerum admoveri haut necessum. Uttamen qualitates earum intentionales ad tactus sensorium accedere possint, intra activitatis suæ sphæram collocatæ esse debent, illudque contingere si non per contactum, saltem per existentiam. IV. Organa tactus nulla ratione vitiata esse debent: quod fit á stupore aut formicatione. Alter immediatus sensus gustus est, quem quidam minus commode ad tactum referre, atque illius quasi speciem constituere instituerunt. Ejus requisita potissimum tria considerati solent. I. Mixtum esse debet, quod saporum [qui non tantum qua tales, sed etiam secundum species sensorium afficiunt] rationem habebit. Inde aëris puri puti, & aquæ limpidissimæ nullus percipitur sapor. II. Quamvis gustus externum medium non requirat, ut rei tamen sapor percipi possit, linguæ applicari debet. III. Instrumentum gustus, lingua nemᵖᵉ
units.tr: After the mediated senses, the immediate senses, touch and taste, must be considered according to their defined conditions. Touch, whose immediate organ is the membrane spread through the whole body, according to the most learned physicians and philosophers, is a single sense, and its object is tactile qualities. But for it to perform its office, four requirements must come together. (I) The object touched must be a corporeal body, for, as Lucretius truly says: Nothing can touch or be touched except a body. Our Saviour also proves this, Luke ch. 54 v. 39, for touch can judge more certainly than sight whether a thing is corporeal or incorporeal. (II) Wherever there is touch, there must be membrane. Hence, because the membrane is not spread through hair, bones or nails, touch is not spread there either. (III) So that tangible qualities can be perceived by the membrane according to their species, they must be brought close to it. The substances of those things need not be brought near. But so that their intentional qualities can reach the sense organ of touch, they must be placed within the sphere of its activity; and this happens if not by contact, at least by presence. (IV) The organs of touch must not be impaired in any way, as happens with numbness or pins and needles. The other immediate sense is taste, which some have inappropriately referred to touch and set up as a kind of species of it. Its requirements are usually considered as three. (I) The thing must be mixed, for it has the nature of a flavour, which affects the sense not only as flavour but also according to its species. Hence no flavour is perceived in pure air or in the clearest water. (II) Although taste does not require an external medium, the tongue must nonetheless be applied to the thing so that its flavour can be perceived. (III) The instrument of taste, namely the tongue, must be free of every defect, above all not be soaked in morbid humour. For the tongues of feverish people, swollen often with bilious humour, judge everything to be bitter.

units.la: nempe pe, omni vitio carere debet: præ cæteris morbido humore non esse imbuta. Febricitantium enim lingua quia bilioso sæpe humore turgida, ipsi omnia amara esse judicant.
units.tr: Namely, it must be free of every defect: above all, not be steeped in a morbid humour. For the tongue of feverish people, often swollen with bilious humour, judges everything to be bitter.

units.la: CAPUT NONUM. De requisitis sensuum considerandis à parte homi- nis, ut rationali anima præditi.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. On the requisites of the senses to be considered on the part of man, as endowed with a rational soul.

units.la: EΤ sic quidem patet, quæ requisita attendi debeant á parte facultatis sentientis, ad hoc ut sensuum iudicio ratio sua constet: deinceps ex ordine ipsum suppositum sentiens, sive homo [de eo enim hic solummodo quæstio est] considerari debet: qui quanquam iudicium sensitivum solummodo exercet ratione animæ ratiocinativæ, quatenus ea virtualiter est sentiens, hic tamen considerari debet, partim ratione suppositi, partim quoque animæ, & denique partim respectu inferiorum facultatum sensitivæ huic functioni subservientium. Quæ omnia uti patent, distincteque cognosci queant, breviter sequentes assertiones ordine proponimus. Primo, requiritur ut homo non sit intentus aliis rebus, sed ijs tantum, quæ sensui obiiciuntur. Contrarium si faciat, sæpe objecta sensibilia recte non percipiet: quod quivis in se animadvertere potest: alijs enim cogitationibus intentus, ne
units.tr: And thus indeed it is clear which requisites must be attended to on the part of the faculty that senses, so that the judgement of the senses may be sound. Next, in order, the sentient subject itself, or the man (for it is of him alone that the question is here), must be considered. Although he exercises sensitive judgement only by means of the rational soul, insofar as that soul is virtually sentient, he must nevertheless be considered here partly in respect of the subject, partly also of the soul, and finally partly with respect to the lower sensitive faculties that serve this function. Since all these things may be seen and distinctly known, we set out the following assertions briefly and in order. First, it is required that a man not be intent on other things, but only on those that are presented to the senses. If he does otherwise, he will often not perceive sensible objects correctly; anyone can notice this in himself, for when absorbed in other thoughts he will not even see familiar people passing before his most open eyes, or hear louder sounds. This happens for the most part to those in ecstasy. Second, the imagination must not be corrupted: for without mania or frenzy, even a slight fever disturbing it can present the senses with remarkable deceptions, as may be seen in...

units.la: quidem apertissimis oculis familiarissimos praetereuntes videbit, aut sonos vehementiores audiet. Accidit hoc ut plurimum ecstaticis. Secundo, phantasia non debet esse corrupta: ea enim citra maniam aut phrenesin levicula tantum febri turbata, sensibus miras fallacias exhibere potest, ut videre est apud Gal. I. de differ. Symptom. cap. 3. in Theopholo medico, qui cetera prudens, cum febricitaret, opinabatur prope lectulum tibicines, & cornicines assistere, & continuo auribus suis occinere: idque jam sanus accidisse sibi pertinaciter contendebat. Tertio mens sententis integra & sana per omnia esse debet: si phrenitis, aut corybantismus molestias creet, sensibus judicium vix deferri potest. Hic vero prae ceteris molestus, visui enim tollit somnum, & auribus indit vitium, quo sibi tinnitus & sonitus audire videantur. Quia Argivo illi mens laesa, exististimabat in theatro, ubi ne musca quidem hominum erat, se audire tragoedos: & ut Horat. ait in Ep. ad Florum: In vacuo laetus sessor, plausorque theatro.
units.tr: Second, the imagination must not be corrupted. For it, without mania or frenzy, but disturbed only by a slight fever, can present the senses with remarkable deceptions, as may be seen in Galen, On the Differences of Symptoms, chapter 3, concerning the physician Theophilus, who, otherwise prudent, when he had a fever, believed that flute-players and horn-players stood near his couch and continually played in his ears; and he stubbornly maintained that this had happened to him even after he was well. Third, the mind must be entire and sound in all respects: if phrenitis or corybantism causes disturbance, the senses can scarcely be trusted to judge. This is especially troublesome, for it takes sleep from the eyes and implants a fault in the ears, so that they seem to hear ringing and noises. That Argive, whose mind was impaired, thought that he was hearing tragic actors in a theatre where there was not even a fly of men; and, as Horace says in his Epistle to Florus: "Happy sitter and applauder in an empty theatre."

units.la: Egregie Tertullianus lib. de Anima cap. 17. Qui insaniunt, alios in alijs vident, ut Orestes matrem in furore, & Aiax Vlyssem in armento, & Athamas & Agave in filijs bestias. Quae posteriora illustrans Plutarchus libello de Superstitione dicit: Infortunatus fuit Tiresias, quod videre liberos & iniðinimicos non potuit. Infeliciores eo fuerunt Athamas & Agave, qui liberos videntes, cervos & leones esse putaverunt: ac nimirum Herculi furenti utilius erat praesentes filios neque cernere, neque sentire, quam carissimos ita ut hostes tractare. Agave siquidem filium Pentheum, Athamas Learchum, feras eos putantes, trucidaverunt; ut utriusque furorem illum fusius descripsit Euripides in Bacchis. Idem existimandum de Melancholia profundiori, quae proximus ad Maniam gradus esse solet. Cum vero sensus communis animalibus datus sit, ut omnium exteriorum sensuum objecta medijs sensibus exterioribus percipiat, diversorum sensuum objecta agnoscat ac dijudicet, moveatque phantasiam, eique species sensibiles offerat, quae dein sub intellectum cadunt, dicimus quarto, quod nulla ratione sensus communis aut turbatus aut laesus, aut etiam sopitus esse debeat: eoque in dormientibus sensus externi officio suo non funguntur, quia communis hic sensus quiescit. Quinto, animum sentientis nullo vehementiore affectu, praeceteris pavore, occupatum turbatumque esse convenit. Quia scilicet turbati & consternati erant discipuli, Christum quem videbant, spiritum esse censebant. Luc. 24. v. 37.
units.tr: Tertullian excellently says in his book On the Soul, chapter 17: Those who are insane see others in other things, as Orestes saw his mother in his frenzy, and Ajax saw Ulysses in a herd of cattle, and Athamas and Agave saw beasts in their sons. Illustrating the latter point, Plutarch in his little book On Superstition says: Tiresias was unfortunate because he could not see his children and enemies. Athamas and Agave were more unhappy than he, for seeing their children they thought them stags and lions; and indeed it was more useful for Hercules in his frenzy not to see or perceive his present sons than to treat his dearest as enemies. Agave indeed killed her son Pentheus, and Athamas Learchus, thinking them wild beasts; Euripides described the madness of both more fully in the Bacchae. The same must be held of deeper melancholy, which is usually the step nearest to mania. Since, however, the common sense is given to animals so that it may perceive the objects of all the external senses through the external senses as intermediaries, recognise and distinguish the objects of the different senses, move the imagination, and present to it sensible species, which then fall under the intellect, we say fourth that the common sense ought in no way to be disturbed, injured, or even lulled to sleep; for this reason, in sleepers the external senses do not perform their office, because this common sense is at rest. Fifth, it is fitting that the mind of the perceiver be occupied and disturbed by no more vehement emotion, above all by fear. For the disciples, being troubled and terrified, thought that Christ, whom they saw, was a spirit. Luke 24:37.

units.la: CAPUT
units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM
units.tr: CHAPTER TEN

units.la: Proponitur thesis adversus Scepticos, atque ex ipsa Scriptura ostenditur, sensibus, si debita requisita concurrant, fidem deferendam esse.
units.tr: A thesis is put forward against the Sceptics, and from Scripture itself it is shown that the senses, if the due requisites concur, are to be trusted.

units.la: OMnibus hisce praemissis, redimus ad thesin jam antea, & quasi in antecessum, propositam capite quinto hujus libri, dicimusque, tum contra Scepticos, tum semi-Scepticos, sensus iudicium, sivmnia illius requisita adsint, nullumque ulla ratione praepediatur, adhoc ex parte sententis cuncta bene se habeant, nulla ratione decipi posse circa proprium suum objectum. Quod adeo verum est, ut ipse Deus in Scriptura, ad sensuum judicium veluti certum atque infallibile, nos attendere velit. Luc. 24. v. 32. Christus dicit: Palpate & videte. & Iohan. ep. 1. c. 1. v. 1. Quod erat a principio, quod audivimus, quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod spectavimus & manus nostrae contrectarunt de sermone illo vitae, v. 3. id annuntiavimus vobis. Item in Evangelio ejusdem c. 1. v. 14. Spectavimus gloriam ejus ut unigeniti a Patre, Similiter Petrus ep. 2. c. 1. v. 16. Oculis nostris aspeximus illius majestatem. & v. 18. Hanc vocem audivimus e coelo delatam. Quare & Lucas Evangelio suo fidem facturus dicit se scribere narrationem earum rerum verum, quarumplena ei fides erat facta, quasque acceperit ab ijs, qui ab initio spectatores ipsi fuerant, & ministri sermonis, cap. I. v. 1. 2. Ut per omnia explodendi sint Libanius, Porphyrius, & Iulianus, qui historiam Evangelicam pro artificioso aliquo commento habuerunt. Non audiendi quoque Marcionitæ, qui ut cum ratione Christo phantasticum corpus affingerent, in castra Scepticorum transierunt. Eleganter Tertullian, lib. de Anima cap. VI. Non licet, non licet nobis, inquit, in dubium sensus istos devocare, ne & in Christo de fide illorum deliberetur, ne forte dicatur quod falso satanam prospectarit de coelo præcipitatum: aut falso vocem Patris audierit de ipso testificatam: aut deceptus sit cum Petri socrum tetigit: aut alium postea unguentem senserit spiritum, quod in sepulturam suam acceptavit: alium postea vini saporem, quod in sanguinis sui memoriam consecravit. Sic enim & Marcion phantasma eum maluit credere, totius corporis in eo dedignatus veritatem. Atqui ne in Apostolis quidem ejus ludificata natura est: fidelis fuit, & auditus, & visus in monte, fidelis & gustus vini illius, &c. Quia sensibus requisitis omnibus munitis fides habenda, ideo Deus in maximi momenti rebus ad eorum judicium provocat, & vidisse ac audivisse populum suum facta sua inculcat. Deut. 29. v. 2. 3. ita ipse per Moisen: Vos vidistis omnia, quæ fecit Iehova ante oculos vestros in terra Ægypti Parhoni, & omnibus servis ejus, totique regioni ejus. Probationes illas maximas, quas viderunt oculi tui, signa & prodigia illa maxima. Imois, qui solus est infallibilis, & solus sapiens, non dubitat hominem invitare ad contemplationem, & sensualem operum suorum experientiam, ut erudiatur, & sapere discat. Esajæ cap. 43. v. 26. Attollite in sublime oculos vestros, & videte quis creaverit ista, producens numero suo exercitus ipsorum. & Math. 6. v. 26. os veritatis Christus: Intuemini in volucres cœli: non enim serunt, neque metunt, neque cogunt in horrea. Nec præter rationem, uti enim docet Apostolus Rom. 1. v. 20. Ipsius invisibilia, jam inde à condito mundo, ex ijs, quæ fecit, mente perpensa videntur, æterna videlicet ejus tum potentia, tum divinitas, ad hoc ut sint inexcusabiles. Inde pij quique in subsidium vocatis sensibus, opera Dei contemplari solent, ut sapiant, atque admiranda Dei opera cognoscant. David de se ipso Psal. 8. v. 4. & 5. Quum inspicio cœlos tuos opus digitorum tuorum, lunam, & stellas, quas statuisti: quid est mortalis, quod memor sis ejus? aut filius hominis, quod visites eum. & iterum Psal. 107. v. 24. nomine omnium piorum dicit: Qui vident opera Iehova, & mirabilia ejus in profundo. Videre autem opera hæc Sceptici, & quicunque eos sequuntur, non possunt; unde, quamdiu sensuum suum judicium, de illo ambigendo, in dubium vocant, semetipsos eo thesauro, quo major cogitari non potest, spoliant. Denique certitudo resurrectionis Christi plane subvertitur, si sensibus sua non constabit ratio. Vt enim sub initium dixerant angeli Matth. 28. 6. resurrexit, non est hic. Videte locum. Ita per oculatos testes ejusdem veritatem probat Sp. Sanctus Act. 1. v. 9. 1. Cor. 15. v. 5. & seqq. quæ probatio sab-sit dicto blasphemia] ridicula erit censenda, si quid Scepticis deferendum hic fuerit.
units.tr: With all these things premised, we return to the thesis already proposed in the fifth chapter of this book, as it were in advance, and we say, against the Sceptics and the semi-Sceptics alike, that the judgment of the senses, if all its requisites are present and nothing is hindering it in any way, and if in that respect all things are in good order, cannot be deceived in any way about its own proper object. This is so true that God himself in Scripture wishes us to attend to the judgment of the senses as certain and infallible. Christ says in Luke 24:32: Handle me and see. And in 1 John 1:1: What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have gazed upon and our hands have handled, concerning that word of life; v. 3: this we proclaim to you. Likewise in the Gospel of the same writer, 1:14: We have beheld his glory, as of the only begotten of the Father. Similarly Peter, 2 Pet. 1:16: We have seen with our own eyes his majesty; and v. 18: We heard this voice brought from heaven. Hence Luke too, wishing to give assurance in his Gospel, says that he is writing a narrative of those things which are true, of which he had been fully assured, and which he received from those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses themselves and ministers of the word, Luke 1:1, 2. Thus Libanius, Porphyry and Julian, who regarded the Gospel history as some clever invention, must be utterly rejected. The Marcionites, too, are not to be heard, who, in order to attribute a phantom body to Christ with some reason, passed over into the camp of the Sceptics. Tertullian writes elegantly in his book On the Soul, chapter 6: "We are not permitted, we are not permitted," he says, "to call those senses into doubt, lest in Christ too their witness should be debated, lest perhaps it be said that he falsely saw Satan fall from heaven, or falsely heard the Father's voice bearing witness concerning him, or was deceived when he touched Peter's mother-in-law, or afterwards perceived another scent of ointment, which he accepted for his burial, or afterwards another taste of wine, which he consecrated in memory of his blood. For thus Marcion too preferred to believe in a phantom, disdaining the truth of the whole body in him. And yet even in his Apostles his nature was not mocked: they were faithful both in hearing and seeing on the mountain, faithful also in tasting that wine," and so on. Because, with all the requisite senses guarded, the senses are to be trusted, God in matters of the greatest moment appeals to their judgment, and impresses upon his people that they have seen and heard his deeds. Deut. 29:2, 3, thus speaks Moses: You have seen all the things that Jehovah did before your eyes in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh and to all his servants and to all his land; the great trials which your eyes have seen, those great signs and wonders. He, who alone is infallible and alone wise, does not hesitate to invite man to contemplate his works and to learn by sensible experience, that he may be instructed and learn to be wise. Isaiah 40:26 (cf. 43): Lift up your eyes on high and see who created these things, bringing out their host by number. And Christ, the mouth of truth, Matt. 6:26: Look at the birds of the heaven: for they neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns. Nor is this without reason, for as the Apostle teaches, Rom. 1:20: His invisible things, from the creation of the world onward, are seen by the mind when they are considered in the things he has made, namely his eternal power and also his divinity, so that they are without excuse. Hence all the godly are wont, calling in their senses for aid, to contemplate the works of God, that they may grow wise and come to know the wonderful works of God. David speaks of himself, Ps. 8:4, 5: When I look at your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars which you have set in place, what is man that you are mindful of him, or the son of man that you visit him? And again, Ps. 107:24, speaking in the name of all the pious: They see the works of Jehovah and his wonders in the deep. But the Sceptics, and all who follow them, cannot see these works; therefore, as long as they call into doubt the judgment of their senses by hesitating about it, they deprive themselves of that treasure than which none greater can be imagined. Finally, the certainty of Christ's resurrection is utterly overthrown if the reliability of the senses is not established. For, as the angels said at the beginning, Matt. 28:6: He is not here; see the place. So the Holy Spirit proves the truth of it by eyewitnesses, Acts 1:9; 1 Cor. 15:5 and following. That proof would be judged ridiculous, and bordering on blasphemy, if anything were to be yielded here to the Sceptics.

units.la: CAPUT UNDECIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Auctoritate omnis generis Scriptorum ostenditur, sensibus fidem adhibendam esse.
units.tr: It is shown by authority of every kind of writer that the senses must be trusted.

units.la: Svfficere posset divina authoritas, videreque possem minus necessaria agere, dum humanam authoritatem, cui alias haut multum tribuendum est, ad thesios antea propositæ confirmationem advoco: quoniam tamen ex re est, thesios certitudinem contra obloquentium impudentiam quocunque argumentorum genere tutari, non inconsultum videtur quorumcunque suffragia ad illius stabilimentum accersere. A Platone vero initium facere lubet, quod, uti antea patuit, alias sensuum judicio videatur
units.tr: Divine authority would be enough, and I could seem to be doing less than necessary, but since I am calling on human authority, which otherwise is not to be valued highly, to confirm the thesis proposed earlier, nonetheless, since it is worthwhile to defend the certainty of the thesis against the shamelessness of its objectors by every kind of argument, it does not seem unwise to summon the support of all sorts of witnesses to establish it. I am pleased to begin with Plato, who, as was shown before, seems elsewhere to have been more hostile to the judgment of the senses.

units.la: infestior fuisse. Ejus interpres optimus est Chalcidius, qui ita ex illius mente ad Timaeum: Visus enim juxta meam sententiam, causa est maximi commodi plerisque non otiose natis, atque institutis, ob id ipsum quod nunc agimus. Neque enim de universa re quispiam quaereret, nisi prius stellis, sole, caloque visis. At nunc diei noctisque insinuata nobis alterna vice, menses, annorumque obitus, & anfractus nati eorumque ipsorum dinumeratio. Et ex dinumeratione perfectus, & absolutus extitit numerus. Tum temporis recordatio, quae naturam universa rei quaeri docuit: curaINQUE investigationis iniecit mentibus, quasi quoddam seminarium Philosophiae pandens. Quo bono nihil majus unquam ad hominum genus a divina munificentia commeavit. Imo Plato ipse in Theeteto: Maxime enim Philosophis hoc usu venit, ut admirentur. Neque enim aliud praeter hoc est Philosophiae principium. Et qui eam Thaumantis, id est admirationis filiam esse tradidit, non absurde originem ejus explicuit. Quomodo vero quis admirari rem aliquam poterit, si eandem antea sensibus non perceperit? Clarius longe sensuum certitudinem atque veritatem [de ea postea distinctius acturi sumus] defendit Aristoteles, qui ita loquitur lib. 8. Phys. tex. 22. Invalitudo quaedam mentis est, repudiata sensuum auctoritate, ac constantia, rationem requirere. & lib. 3. de Gener. Anim. cap. 10. Sensui magis, quam ratiustandum est, rationi hactenus fidendum si qua demonstrantur, cum ijs consentiant, qua nobis sunt à sensu indita & impressa. Aristoteli astipulatur Galenus lib. 2. de Usu Partium cap. 3. in fine: Quicunque vult operum naturæ esse contemplator, eum proprijs oculis credere oportet, & aut ad nos accedere, aut cum aliquo eorum, qui nobiscum versati sunt, versari, aut ipsum per se diligenter exercerí anatomis manu obeundis. imo lib. 4. Simpl. cap. 18. pronunciat, sensuum evidentiam, quam longissime prævertere fidei rationis. & lib. 2. Simpl. cap.
units.tr: His best interpreter is Chalcidius, who, following his mind, says in the commentary on the Timaeus: For sight, in my view, is the cause of the greatest benefit to those who are born and trained for no idle purpose, and this is the very reason for what we are now doing. For no one would ask about the whole nature of things unless first he had seen the stars, the sun and heat. But now, since day and night have been made known to us in alternation, and months, the passing of years and their courses, and the counting of these, a number has come into being, perfect and complete from the counting. Then the memory of time, which taught men to inquire into the nature of all things, cast into their minds the care of investigation, as a kind of seedbed opening up philosophy. No greater gift has ever come to the human race from divine generosity than this. Indeed Plato himself says in the Theaetetus: For this experience comes especially to philosophers, to wonder. For there is no other beginning of philosophy than this. And he who said that she was the daughter of Thaumas, that is of wonder, did not explain her origin absurdly. But how can anyone wonder at something if he has not first perceived it by the senses? Aristotle defends the certainty and truth of the senses far more clearly, and he speaks thus in the eighth book of the Physics, text 22: It is a kind of weakness of mind to ask for a reason after rejecting the authority and steadiness of the senses. And in the third book of On the Generation of Animals, chapter 10: Trust the senses rather than reason; reason is to be trusted only so far as demonstrations agree with the things that are impressed upon us by sense. Galen agrees with Aristotle, in On the Use of the Parts, book 2, chapter 3, near the end: Whoever wishes to be an observer of the works of nature must believe his own eyes, and either come close to them himself, or associate with someone who has done so, or diligently practise anatomy himself with his own hands. Indeed in book 4 of the Simples, chapter 18, he pronounces: The evidence of the senses goes far beyond the trust placed in reason. And in book 2 of the Simples, chapter 1: Those who put reason before the senses are left without any first principle for proving things.

units.la: 1. Qui sensibus anteferunt rationem, omni ad demonstrandum principio destituuntur. Accedit his Lucret. lib. 4. sed ex mente Epicuri, sic canens:
units.tr: 1. Those who put reason before the senses are left without any first principle for proving things. Lucretius agrees with these, in the fourth book, but in the spirit of Epicurus, singing thus:

units.la: Quid referemus enim, quod nobis sensibus ipsis
units.tr: For what shall we say could be more certain

units.la: Certius esse queat, queis vera & falsa notamus
units.tr: than the senses themselves, by which we mark true and false,

units.la: Qui nisi sint veri, ratio quoque claudicet omnis.
units.tr: which, if they are not true, all reason too must limp.

units.la: & iterum eodem libro: convellere tota Fundamenta, quibus nixatur vita salusque. Non modo enim ratio ruat omnis, vita quoque ipsa Concidat extemplo, nisi credere sensibus ausis, Præcipitésque locos vitare & cætera quæ sint.
units.tr: And again in the same book: to overturn the whole foundations on which life and safety rest. For not only would all reason fall, but life itself would at once collapse, unless we dare to trust the senses and to avoid steep places and other such dangers.

units.la: Nec alius sensus est Marci Tullii Ciceronis, inter Romanos Philosophos summi, atque in controversijs contra Academicos exercitatissimi: sic enim pronunciat lib. 4. Academ. Quest. Sensuunt suum ita clara judicia & certa sunt, ut si optio naturæ nostræ detur, & ab ea Deus aliquid æquirat, contentane sit suis integris incorruptisque sensibus, an postulet melius aliquid? non videam quid quærat am-plius. & paulo post: Maxima est in sensibus veritas, si & sani sunt & valentes, & omnia removentur quæ obstant & impediunt. Nec male Rabbinorum doctissimus Maimonides in Ep. de Astrolog. Inprimis scitote, inquit, hæc tria tantum homini credenda esse, neque quicquam præterea. Primum id, cujus certam habet & evidentem probationem humana sua ratione & scientia investigatam, velut ratio numerandi, Geometria & revolutiones. Alterum id, quod homo deprehendit uno ex quinque sensibus. Tertium & postremum id, quod accepit à Prophetis pia memoria & à justis.
units.tr: Marcus Tullius Cicero, the greatest of the Roman philosophers and most practised in disputes against the Academics, holds the same view. For he pronounces thus in the fourth book of the Academica: The judgments of the senses are so clear and certain that, if nature gave us the choice, and God required something from it, whether we would be content with our senses whole and uncorrupted, or would ask for something better, I do not see what more one could seek. And a little later: The truth in the senses is greatest, if they are both sound and strong, and all things that hinder or obstruct them are removed. Nor did the most learned of the rabbis, Maimonides, speak badly, in his letter on astrology: First of all, know, he says, that only these three things are to be believed by man, and nothing beyond them. The first is that for which he has a certain and evident proof, investigated by his own human reason and knowledge, such as the art of counting, geometry and the revolutions of the heavens. The second is what a man perceives by one of the five senses. The third and last is what he has received by pious tradition from the Prophets and the righteous.

units.la: CAPUT DUODECIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWELVE.

units.la: Variis rationibus amplius adversus Scepticos evincitur, sensibus fidem adhibendam esse.
units.tr: Various further arguments show against the Sceptics that the senses must be trusted.

units.la: QUandoquidem vero Sceptici, eorumque fautores, non solum humanam authoritatem in dubium vocare solent; sed ipsi quoque Deo in Scriptura loquenti obloqui, alia argumenta conquirenda sunt, quibus eorum pertinacia expugnetur. Eoque per rationes ulterius contra eos sic progredimur. I. Si sensuum judicium cium perpetuo fallax, eique nulla fides adhibenda, næ frustra sensuum organis Deus & natura animalium nobilissimum hominem instruxerunt? Quæcunque enim in corpore inftrumenta inveniuntur, destinata sunt naturalibus certisque functionibus, non vero incertis atque fortuitis. Nec verum hoc tantum de inftrumentis inservientibus functionibus vitalibus & naturalibus, ut liquet ex corde, pulmone, &c. ventriculo, mesenterio, intestinis &c. sed etiam ex instrumentis, sive partibus functionibus animalibus inservientibus. Etenim si nervi ab officio motorij dicti, & musculi, dati sunt homini non tantum ut instrumenta essent quasi motus, sed veri certi & animalibus naturalis: oculus quoque, auris, nasus, lingua, & palatum, item partes membranose & nervosæ datæ sunt, non quasi atque incerto modo peragendis functionibus animalibus à sensibus externis elicitis, sed vere, certo, & infallibiliter. Si præpediantur ratione organi hæ ipsæ functiones, per accidens illud fieri putandum est. II. Nullo privilegio præ saxis & stipitibus homo gaudebit, si sensuum judicium per omnia sallax sit: nam sic otiosa quoque & fallax ipsa mens, quatenus supra sensus elevata, futura erit, siquidem in illius recessus nihil nisi per apertas sensuum fenestras intrat. Verum quippe
units.tr: Since the Sceptics, and those who favour them, are wont not only to call human authority into doubt but also to speak against God himself speaking in Scripture, other arguments must be sought by which their obstinacy may be overcome. So we proceed against them further by reasoning as follows. I. If the judgment of the senses is always deceptive and no trust is to be placed in it, then has God, and nature in animals, instructed man, the most noble of creatures, in vain with organs of sense? For whatever instruments are found in the body are designed for natural and certain functions, not for uncertain and chance ones. And this holds true not only of the instruments serving the vital and natural functions, as is plain from the heart, lungs, stomach, mesentery, intestines and so on, but also of the instruments, or parts, serving the animal functions. For if the nerves, called motor, and the muscles were given to man not merely as instruments of motion but as true, certain and natural to animals, then the eye, ear, nose, tongue and palate, likewise the membranous and nervous parts, were given not to carry out the animal functions, elicited by the external senses, in an uncertain manner, but truly, certainly and infallibly. If these same functions are hindered through some defect of an organ, that must be thought to happen by accident. II. Man will enjoy no privilege over stones and logs if the judgment of the senses is deceptive in all things. For then the mind too would be idle and deceptive, insofar as it is raised above the senses, since nothing enters its recesses except through the open windows of the senses. Indeed,

units.la: Illud Physicorum axioma; Nihil est in intellectu quod non prius fuerit in sensibus. At quomodo intellectus officio suo perfungi poterit, si mendaces species sensibiles ei suppeditentur? III. Si sensuum functionibus nulla fides deferenda, homo infelix jure meritoque est habendus, quia definita eorum organa accepit. Cui bono enim illa, quam ad miserum hominem excarnificandum: quando omnia quippe egit, ut eorum subsidio proprium ac definitum cujusque sensus objectum cognoscat, nihil egit: quia dum v. c. oculis intentis & attentis spectavit nigrum, nescit ex Scepticorum principiis hoc ne magis nigrum an album sit. IV. Se ipsos misere confundunt Sceptici, dum edunt, & instar aliorum hominum cibum capiunt. Neque enim hoc tantum faciunt ex consuetudine, sed quia persentiscunt divulsionem ventriculi ex membrorum fabrica. Si sensus illius divulsionis fallax, & in opinione consistit, possunt etenim non animad vertere ad eum, & avertere sinistram illam opinionem. Sed ut ut omnia agant, sensum eum agnoscere compelluntur, ac fateri eum subsequi appetentiam animalem, qua cibum expetunt. Destinatum vero & certum ijs sit, inedia mori, nihilominus nulla arte molesta illa sensione liberari peterunt: Quod facile tamen esset, si in nuda opinione consisteret. Contra aliorum sensuum certitudinem, quamvis pertinacia se munire possint, tactui tamen manus dare coguntur. Volentes nolentes enim fateri debent, aliter se affici quando dolores corporeos percipiunt, aliter vero quando voluptates. Volent vero dolores voluptates, & contra: fateri tamen cogentur aliam esse rationem dolorum, aliam voluptatum: clamet enim v. c. Scepticus quando manus ejus in igni ustulatur, se haud aliter affici ac si in balneo lavaretur & ungueretur: nihilominus quia ignis tormentum omni ratione aut declinare aut mitigare, quando sui juris est, laborat; fateri debet aliter se affici ab igni, aliter quando in balneo est. Atqui sic herbam porrigit. V. Si sensus omnes fallant, fallet quoque auditus, atque frustra erit Apostolus; quando ad Rom. 10. v. 17. docet fidem ex auditu esse. Nam quomodo aliquis fide amplecti poterit ea, quae a praecone Evangelij dicuntur, si auditus instar reliquorum sensuum fallax sit: cum nesciat an ad consolationem, an vero ad condemnationem secundum legem loquatur. VI. Si sensibus fides non adhibenda, frustra in judicio adducentur testes, nec privilegium oculatis testibus prae auritis deferendum erit. Et tamen ipse Deus voluit, ut aliquis morte quoque afficeretur ex sermone duorum aut trium testium, Deuter. 17. v. 6.
units.tr: That is the axiom of the natural philosophers: There is nothing in the intellect which was not first in the senses. But how will the intellect be able to perform its office if deceptive sensible images are supplied to it? III. If no trust is to be given to the functions of the senses, man is rightly and justly to be regarded as unfortunate, since he has received organs for them that are defined. For to what end are they, if they serve only to torture wretched man? When he has done everything to know, with their help, the proper and defined object of each sense, he has accomplished nothing; for while he looks intently and attentively with his eyes at something black, by the principles of the Sceptics he does not know whether it is black or white. IV. The Sceptics miserably confound themselves when they eat and take food like other men. For they do this not only from habit, but because they perceive the distension of the stomach from the structure of their limbs. If the sense of that distension is deceptive and consists in opinion, they could indeed fail to attend to it and turn away that mistaken opinion. But however they act, they are compelled to acknowledge that sense and to confess that it follows the animal appetite by which they seek food. Yet even if they were destined and certain to die of hunger, they could not by any tricky art free themselves from that troubling sensation, which nonetheless would be easy if it consisted in mere opinion. Against the certainty of the other senses, however obstinately they may fortify themselves, they are compelled to yield to touch. For whether they will or no, they must admit that they are affected one way when they perceive bodily pains, and another when they perceive pleasures. They may wish pains to be pleasures and the reverse; yet they will be compelled to confess that there is one kind of pain and another of pleasure. For example, let the Sceptic cry out when his hand is burned in the fire that he is affected no differently than if he were bathing and anointed; nevertheless, since he strives in every way to avoid or to lessen the torment of the fire when it is in his power, he must admit that he is affected by fire one way and in the bath another. And yet he holds out his hand [to be burned]. V. If all the senses deceive, hearing too will deceive, and the Apostle will be in vain, when he teaches in Rom. 10.17 that faith is from hearing. For how could anyone embrace by faith what is said by the herald of the Gospel, if hearing, like the other senses, is deceptive, since he would not know whether he is speaking for consolation or for condemnation according to the law? VI. If the senses are not to be trusted, witnesses will be brought in judgment in vain, and no privilege is to be granted to eyewitnesses over earwitnesses. And yet God himself willed that someone should be put to death on the word of two or three witnesses, Deut. 17.6.

units.la: VII. Patroni Scepticorum dogmatis se in mi- seriarum abyssum, aut verius tormentorum officinam pertinacia intoleranda præcipitant.
units.tr: VII. The patrons of the Sceptical dogma plunge themselves, through intolerable obstinacy, into an abyss of miseries, or rather into a workshop of torments.

units.la: Nesciunt enim an corpus scarabæi, an maris, an asini, an vero alterius animalis circumferant; sintne fusci, nigri, candidi, an virides; nasumne habeant aquilinum, porcinum, rhinocerotis, an simile elephantis proboscidi; quia oculis fidem abrogant. Incertum ijs an rudant, rugiant, latrent, hinniant, crocitent, an loquantur, quia fallacem clamant esse auditum. Ignorant v. c. sitne sal dulce, amarum, acidum, an salsum, quia mendacij arguunt gustum. Qua de causa etiam Iovis quod ferculum & porcorum lautitiæ eodem Icco apud illos censeri debent. In summa nulla differentia secundum eos inter lucem & tenebras, calorem & frigus, terram & cœlum, ignem & aquam, murem & elephantem, hominem & gallum gallinaceum, muscam & aquilam, ferrum & stramen, aurum & plumbum, lapillum vilem & margaritam, Rubiconem fluvium & vastum Oceanum, exiguam arcem ac montem Atlantem esse posse, quia sensuum judicio nihil defendum esse clamitant. Imo ipsa jura cognationis atque sanguinis confundunt. Si enim sensus sunt fallaces, parentes, sorores, & fratres ab aliis hominibus distinguere non poterunt. Et quia nullæ secundum eos rerum differentiæ, possunt contrariæ qualitates inter se amice conspirare, & contradictoria simul esse verissima. Quod absurdum omnem absurditatem superat. Pathetice proinde contra hos atque similes Tertul. l. d. Quid agis procacissime? totum vitæ statum evertis, omnem naturæ ordinem turbas, ipsius Dei providentiam excæcas, qui cunctis operibus suis intelligendis, recolendis, dispensandis, fruendisque fallaces & mendaces Dominos sensus præfecerit.
units.tr: For they do not know whether they are carrying about the body of a beetle, of a sea creature, of an ass, or of some other animal; whether it is dark, black, white, or green; whether they have an aquiline nose, a pig's snout, a rhinoceros's, or one like an elephant's trunk, since they deny faith to their eyes. It is uncertain to them whether animals bray, roar, bark, neigh, or caw, or whether they speak, since they cry out that hearing is deceptive. They do not know, for example, whether salt is sweet, bitter, sour, or salty, since they accuse taste of lying. For this reason, too, among them the dish of Jove and the delicacies of pigs must be counted in the same place. In short, according to them there is no difference between light and darkness, heat and cold, earth and heaven, fire and water, a mouse and an elephant, a man and a barnyard cock, a fly and an eagle, iron and straw, gold and lead, a worthless pebble and a pearl, the river Rubicon and the vast Ocean, a tiny fortress and Mount Atlas; they can be the same, since they cry out that nothing is to be defended by the judgement of the senses. Indeed, they confuse the very laws of kinship and blood. For if the senses are deceptive, they will be unable to distinguish parents, sisters, and brothers from other people. And since, on their view, there are no differences between things, contrary qualities can agree with one another in friendship, and contradictories can both be most true at once. This absurdity surpasses every absurdity. Tertullian, in the passage cited, therefore speaks movingly against these men and others like them: What are you doing, most shameless fellow? You overturn the whole state of life, you throw the whole order of nature into confusion, you blind the very providence of God, who has set deceitful and lying masters, the senses, over all his works, to understand, to attend to, to dispense, and to enjoy them.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM TERTIUM. In qua facultate proprie consistat fallacia: non tam sensus, quam intellectus fallitur.
units.tr: CHAPTER THIRTEEN. In which faculty error properly resides: it is not so much the senses that are deceived as the intellect.

units.la: PRiusquam expendere instituimus argumenta, quibus tum Sceptici, tum Semi-Sceptici sensuum certitudinem jam olim labefactare laborarunt; haut abs re erit aliquanto penitius expendere, propriene sensus fallaciarum argui debeant, an vero ipsa ratio sensuum moderatrix. Verum quidem est quod supra notavimus, sensibus consequenter fallaciam accidere posse; cæterum cum ea proveniat propter defectum alicujus requisiti, aliter fieri non poterit, quin caussa ignorata, sive defectu illo non explorato ab intellectu, à sensione fallaci ipsa pariter ratio circumveniatur: quæ caussa, sive defectus si exploratus fuerit, facile est, non tantum intellectui, sed etiam aliis sensibus, errantem sensionem restituere. Sic visus si cernat pomum cereum ita affabre factum ut verum mentiatur, illud verum pomum esse primo judicabit: sed mox errorem corriget ratio, si tactu, item odoratu, ac gustu idem pomum explorandum esse dictaverit. Recte Numenius lib. de Natur. homin. cap. 7. Quocirca interdum aspectus caeterorum sensuum testimonio indiget, cum id quod cernitur artificio ad fallendum factum fuerit, ut in pictura. Nam pingendi artis opus est, fallere aspectis non veris eminentijs & lacunis: si res ejusmodi natura est, ubi opus sit maxime tactum quidem adscisci; interdum tamen etiam gustatum, aut odoratum, ut in pomo cereo. Cum vero deceptio & error proprie accidant facultati interne dijudicanti proprie loquendo sensuum organa nonpossunt dici decipi, imo formaliter ipsi sensus non decipiuntur, sed fallitur ipsa anima dijudicans; quatenus enim speciem receptam ob defectum alicujus requisiti vitiosam, propter ignorantiam nescit distinguere, aut rite judicare, ipsa sensio sive sensualis cognitio objectorum sensibilium vitiosa aut fallax esse dicitur: ita ut error accidat ratione actionis ipsius sensionis. Si Epicurei hoc tantum voluerint non longe a scopo aberraverunt. Ipsi enim sensus quatenus patiuntur fallaciam laciam nequaquam redargui possunt: recipiunt enim perpetuo, quod talibus caussis existentibus recipere potuerunt. Idem sensus est Augustini lib. de vera Religione cap. 33. Corporea species, quia nullam voluntatem habet, non mentitur: si vero etiam non putetur esse quod non est, nec fallit. Sed ne ipsi quidem oculi fallunt, non enim renunciare possunt animo, nisi affectionem suam. Quod si non solum ipsi, sed etiam omnes corporis sensus its renunciant ut afficiuntur, quid ab eis amplius exigere debeamus, ignoro. Tolle itaque vanitates, & nulla erit vanitas. Si quis remum frangi in aqua opinatur, & cum aufertur, integrari, non malum habet internuncium, sed malus est judex. Nam ille pro sua natura non potuit aliter in aqua sentire, nec aliter debuit: si enim aliud est aer, aliud aqua, iustum est aliter in aere, aliter in aqua sentiatur. Quare oculus recte videt: perverse judicat, cui ad contemplandam summam pulchritudinem, non oculus factus est. Item lib. 3. adversus Academ. cap. 11. Dicat Epicureus quispiam, nihil habeo quod de sensibus conquerar, Injustum est enim ab eis exigere plus quam possunt: quicquid autem possunt videre oculi, verum vident: Ergone verum est quod de remo in aqua vident? Prorsus verum. Nam tauffa accedente, quare ita videretur, si demersus unda remus rectus appareret, magis oculos meos falsae renunciationis arguerem. Non enim viderent, quod talibus existentibus causis videndum fuisse. fuit &c. Amplius lib. 12. in Genef. cap. 25. sic loquitur: In omnibus, inquit, corporalibus visis, & aliorum sensuum contestatio, & maxime ipsius mentis atque rationis adhibetur; ut quod in hoc eorum genere verum est, inveniatur, quantum inveniri potest. Augustino per omnia astipulatur Anselmus dialogo de veritate cap. 6. Non mihi videtur hæc veritas, vel falsitas in sensibus esse, sed in opinione. Ipse namque sensus interior se fallit, non illi mentitur exterior. Quod aliquando facile cognoscitur, aliquando difficile. Cum enim puer timet sculptum draconem aperto ore, facile cognoscitur, quia hoc non facit visus, qui nihil puero renunciat, plusquam seniibus, sed puerilis sensus interior, qui nondum bene scit discernere inter rem & rei similitudinem. Tale enim est, cum similis est: aut cum audiens quis non hominis vocem, putat esse hominis vocem. Nam & hoc facit sensus interior. Et mox generatim: Cum multa alia nobis aliter videntur visus & alij sensus nuntiare, quam sint, non culpa sensuum est, qui renunciant quod possunt, quoniam ita posse acceperunt: sed judicio animæ imputandum est. quod non bene discernat quid possint illi, aut quid debeant. rursus sufficiat dicere, quia sensus quicquid renunciare videantur, sive ex sua natura hoc faciant, sive ex aliqua alia caussa, hoc faciant quod debent, & ideo rectitudinem & veritatem faciunt. Nec aliud videtur voluisse Philosophus, quando lib. 4. Metaph. cap. 2. pronunciat unius tujusque generis tum unum sensum, tum unam scientiam esse. Certe ipsum Ciceronem ab hac sententia alienum non esse, liquebit ex ijs, qu̅ alias adducenda erunt ex ipsius lib. 4. Academ. Quæst.
units.tr: Before we set out to weigh the arguments by which the Sceptics, and the Semi-Sceptics too, have long tried to shake the certainty of the senses, it will not be out of place to examine more closely whether the senses are properly charged with error, or whether reason itself is the governor of the senses. It is true, as we noted above, that error can follow from the senses; yet since it arises from the lack of some requisite, it cannot happen otherwise: unless the cause is known, or that defect is detected by the intellect, the reason is equally taken in by the faulty sensation. But if the cause or defect is detected, it is easy to restore the erring sensation, not only by the intellect but also by the other senses. Thus, if sight sees a wax apple so skilfully made that it counterfeits a real one, it will at first judge it to be a real apple; but reason will soon correct the error, if it directs that the same apple be tested by touch, and likewise by smell and taste. Numenius rightly says in his book On the Nature of Man, chapter 7: Hence sometimes the testimony of the other senses is needed for sight, when what is seen has been made by artifice to deceive, as in a painting. For the painter's art works to deceive the eye with false projections and hollows; and if the thing is of such a nature that touch in particular must be called in, sometimes taste or smell must be called in as well, as with the wax apple. But since deception and error properly belong to the inner faculty that judges, the organs of sense, strictly speaking, cannot be said to be deceived. Indeed the senses themselves are not formally deceived; it is the judging soul that is deceived. For insofar as it does not know how to distinguish, or to judge rightly, a received image that is faulty through the lack of some requisite, owing to ignorance, the sensation itself, that is, the sensory knowledge of sensible objects, is said to be faulty or deceptive, so that the error arises from the very act of sensing. If the Epicureans meant only this, they did not stray far from the mark. For the senses, insofar as they suffer deception, can by no means be refuted: they always receive what they could receive when such causes are present. This is also the view of Augustine in his book On True Religion, chapter 33: A bodily appearance, since it has no will, does not lie; and even if it is thought to be what it is not, it does not deceive. But the eyes themselves do not deceive either, for they cannot report to the mind anything but their own affection. And if not only the eyes but all the bodily senses report only how they are affected, I do not know what more we ought to demand of them. Remove, then, the vanities, and there will be no vanity. If someone thinks an oar is broken in water, and whole when it is taken out, the messenger is not at fault; the fault lies with the judge. For by its nature the sense could not perceive otherwise in water, nor ought it to have done so: if air is one thing and water another, it is right that things be perceived differently in air and in water. So the eye sees rightly; it is the judgment that is perverse, since the eye was not made to contemplate the highest beauty. Likewise in book 3 Against the Academics, chapter 11: Let some Epicurean say: I have no complaint about the senses. For it is unjust to demand more of them than they can do; and whatever the eyes can see, they see truly. Is it then true that they see an oar broken in water? Entirely true. For when the water is present, why should it appear thus? If the oar appeared straight when submerged in the wave, I would rather accuse my eyes of false report. For they would not see what they ought to have seen, given such causes. And so on. Again, in book 12 on Genesis, chapter 25, he speaks thus: In all bodily sights, the testimony of the other senses, and above all of the mind and reason itself, is called upon, so that what is true in this class of things may be found, as far as it can be found. Anselm agrees with Augustine in everything, in his dialogue On Truth, chapter 6: It seems to me that truth or falsity lies not in the senses but in opinion. For the inner sense itself deceives itself; the outer sense does not lie to it. This is sometimes easily recognized, sometimes with difficulty. When a boy fears a carved dragon with its mouth open, it is easily recognized, because it is not sight that does this (sight reports nothing to the boy more than to the old), but the boy's inner sense, which does not yet know well how to tell a thing from its likeness. For that is what happens when something is like another; or when someone hears a sound that is not a human voice and thinks it is a human voice. For the inner sense does this too. And soon he says in general terms: When many other things appear to us otherwise than they are, and sight and the other senses report them so, it is not the fault of the senses, which report what they can, since that is how they have received their power; the fault belongs to the judgment of the soul, which does not discern well what the senses can do or ought to do. Again, let it suffice to say that whatever the senses seem to report, whether they do so by their own nature or from some other cause, they do what they ought, and therefore they are right and true. Nor does the Philosopher seem to have meant otherwise, when in book 4 of the Metaphysics, chapter 2, he declares that for each kind of thing there is one sense and one science. Certainly it will be clear that Cicero himself is not at odds with this view, from the passages to be cited below from his fourth book of the Academica Quaestiones.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM QUARTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FOURTEEN.

units.la: Occurritur illi Scepticorum argumento, quod contra sensuum certitudinem à locorum di- stantijs adduxerunt.
units.tr: The Skeptics' argument, which they brought against the certainty of the senses from differences of distance between places, is answered.

units.la: HIs præmissis, expendere instituimus præcipua argumenta, quibus jam olim Sceptici sensuum certitudinem oppugnare instituerunt. Neque enim omnia ex re est excutere, cum quæ superersunt, ex ijs, quæ examinabimus, facile á quovis dilui queant. Initium autem facimus, ab argumento, quod á locorum differentijs petierunt. ac quidem sensibus nihil deferendum esse, inde collegerunt, quod una eademque res pro diversorum locorum ratione alia atque alia compareat: in quem sensum Sextus lib. 1. Pyrrh. Hypoth. adducit lucernæ lumen in Sole quidem obscurum, in tenebris autem splendidum: remum intra mare quidem fractum, extra autem rectum: & ovum in ave quidem molle, in aere autem durum: & lyncurium, in lynce quidem humidum humidum: in aëre autem durum, & coralium in mari quidem molle, in aëre autem durum. Vocem diversam in tuba, diversam in tibijs, diversam in fistulis inaëre simpliciter. Sed si quis consideraverit res ipsas, sive objecta sensibilia pro diversorum locorum ratione diversa esse, argumenti hujus imbecillitatem videbit. Etenim sensus per species sensibiles talia objecta sensibilia esse percipiunt, qualia a parte rei exstant, atque per species repræsentantur; diversimode autem sese habent pro diversorum locorum ratione, unde non possunt non diversimode quoque percipi, intellectu diversam illam rerum faciem pro diversorum locorum circumstantijs diversimode se habere debere, indicante & dijudicante: ampliusque monente plures sensus pro uno corrigendo in consilium adhibendos esse. Ne quid vero pertinax Scepticorum natio præteritum à nobis esse proclamet in palmario suo argumento, singula lubet excutere. Initium autem facimus á remo, eum siquidem potissimum crepare solent. Sed nihil tribuendum illi esse, præter Augustinum capite superiori ad partes vocatum, ostendit quoque Tertullianus lib. de Anima cap. 17. Nam ut in aqua remus inflexus, vel infractus appareat, aqua in causa est. Denique extra aquam integer visui remus. Temeritas autem substantiæ illius, quæ speculum ex lumine efficitur, prout ista icta seu mota est, ita & imaginem vibrans evertit lineam recti. Vt enim recte Optici docent, diversitas medij, rari vel densi facit, ut discipentur vel contrahantur lineæ, unde refractio apparet; atque omne agens uti per lineam rectam operatur, ita mutatione medij necessum est infringatur pauliper. Seneca 1. Nat. Quæst. 6. Omnia per aquam videntibus longe sunt majora. Litera quamvis minuta & obscura per vitreám pilam aqua plenam majores clarioresque cernuntur. Poma forte fiora quam sint videntur, si innatant vitro. Syamplior a per nubem aspicienti cernuntur, quia acies nostra in humido labitur, nec apprehendere quod vult fideliter potest. Quod manifestum si vas adimpleveris aqua, & in id conjeceris annulum. Nam cum in ipso fundo jaceat annulus, facies ejus in summo aquæ redditur. Quicquid videtur per humorem, longe amplius vero est. Idem ratione remorum quoque eleganter expressit Lucretius versibus sequentibus.
units.tr: Having set out these points, we propose to weigh the chief arguments with which the Skeptics long ago set about attacking the certainty of the senses. It is not necessary to examine everything, since whatever is left over can easily be refuted by anyone from the points we shall examine. We begin with the argument they drew from differences of place. From it they concluded that nothing should be trusted to the senses, because one and the same thing appears different according to the place it occupies. To this effect Sextus, in Book 1 of the Pyrrhonian Hypotyposes, adduces: the light of a lamp is dim in sunlight but bright in darkness; an oar is broken within the sea but straight outside it; an egg is soft in a bird but hard in the air; lyncurium is moist in a lynx but hard in the air; and coral is soft in the sea but hard in the air. Likewise the voice is one thing in a trumpet, another in pipes, and another in flutes, and simply different in the open air. But if anyone considers the things themselves, that is, the sensible objects, and sees that they differ according to the circumstances of different places, he will see the weakness of this argument. For the senses perceive, through sensible species, such sensible objects as they are in the thing itself and are represented through those species. Since these objects stand in different relations according to the circumstances of places, they cannot but be perceived differently. The intellect, judging and discerning, should understand that this diverse appearance of things stands in diverse relations to the circumstances of places, and it further advises that several senses should be called in to counsel to correct one. Lest the obstinate race of Skeptics proclaim that we have passed over anything in their favourite argument, let us examine each example separately. We begin with the oar, since they are especially fond of harping on it. But that nothing should be granted to it, beyond what Augustine, called to the stand in the preceding chapter, has granted, Tertullian also shows in his book On the Soul, chapter 17. For the reason the oar appears bent or broken in water is the water itself. Outside the water the oar appears whole to sight. The tenuity of that substance which, by its light, makes the mirror, as it is struck or moved, so, in vibrating, it distorts the image of the straight line. For as the opticians rightly teach, the difference of a medium, whether rare or dense, causes the lines to be spread apart or drawn together, whence refraction appears; and every agent, while it acts along a straight line, must by a change of medium be bent a little. Seneca, in Book 1 of the Natural Questions, chapter 6: Everything seen through water appears much larger. A letter, however small and faint, is seen larger and clearer through a glass globe full of water. Fruit floating in glass looks perhaps larger than it really is. A star is seen larger through a cloud, because our sight slips in the moisture and cannot faithfully grasp what it wants to. This is plain if you fill a vessel with water and drop a ring into it. For though the ring lies at the bottom, its image is presented at the surface of the water. Whatever is seen through moisture is in truth far larger. Lucretius expressed the same point about oars elegantly in the following verses.

units.la: Ac maris ignaris, in portu clauda videntur Navigia aplustris fractis obnitier undis. Nam quæcunque supra rorem salis edita pars est Remorum, recta est, & recta superne gubernat; Quæ demersa liquere obeunt, refracta videntur; Omnia converti, rursumque supina reverti Et reflexa prope in summo fluctuare liquere.
units.tr: And ships in harbour, seen by ignorant men of the sea, appear crippled, their sterns struggling against the broken waves. For whatever part of the oars rises above the spray of the salt water is straight, and it steers straight from above; but the parts that are sunk beneath and drown appear bent. All things seem turned about, and bent back upon themselves, and to float on the surface, bent and reflected.

units.la: Nec aliam ob caussam, quam propter hanc eandem numus in vase aqua pleno longe major videtur, ut frustra per omnia sit Zanches Scepticus genuinus, quando in libello, quo scepsin propugnare laboravit, contra sensuum & scientiae certitudinem inter alia hoc argumento, aut verius experimento nititur: Monetam, inquit, vasculo lato impone: humi resídere fac vas: à quo eo te se moveris, donec monetam non videas amplius. Tunc jube aquam impleri vas: videbis statim monetam, & majorem quam antea per aërem videri, cum per se opacum sit medium. Cur nunc major apparet moneta? Nescimus. Secundum Sexti experimentum haud melioris quoque monetae: namque lucernae lumen in Sole non comparet obscurum, in tenebris vero splendidum: sed impeditur, quo minus sese prodere possit, quatenus lux fortis debilem intercipit, & opprimit.
