Sol enim lucem vividam jaculans, stellarum luces, & lucernarum omnium opprimit, non destruendo, aut impediendo quo minus radient: sed quia fortiter sensum afficit atque cum quadam efficacia, debiles vero stellarum & lucernarum luces visum non afficiunt efficaciter. Similiter lux facula ingeniti igni apposita opprimitur. Alias subducta quasi solis luce, tum stellae, tum lucernae se conspiciendas praebent. Gnarum hoc ipsi Galeno erat lib. 10. de usu Partium magnis inquit, Solis defectibus stellae apparent, quod & suis temporibus accidisse Thucydides commemorat. Atque errandi hic obvenit sensibus? Mens caussam hujus rei si exploratam habuerit inter Solis lucem atque lucernarum lumen levi negotio divisionem facere poterit. Succedit ovum in ave quidem molle, in aëre autem durum. At quid Scepticum in sensuum prejudicium hoc juvare potest? In ave quandiu hæret ductile & molle est, ne sua duritie ei molestias creet, postea mox indurescít aëre exiguū illud humidū educente, duritiemque hac ratione procurante. Namque ut ovum in ave vere est molle & flaccidum, extra vero illud durum, ita fallaciæ argui non potest sensus, aut verius mens distincte dijudicans ea, quę à parte rei distincte sese habent. Volùerunt quidem nonnulli in dubium vocare an ovum in ave molle, extra vero illam durum sit; sed redarguit eos Sextus ante ad partes vocatus, astipulante ipsa experientia, à nobis sæpius circa varia singularia ova in consilium adhibita. Applauditque tum Sexto, tum experientiæ Aristoteles lib. 3. de Gen. Anim. cap. 2. ubi hæc observatione digna verba occurrunt: Patet primo membranam mollem id esse, quod postremo testa efficitur: perfecto enim ovo durum ac rigidum evadit ita modice, ut exeat adhuc molle. Dolorem enim moveret, nisi ita exiret. Egressum statim refrigeratum duratur: evapotato humore quam primum, qui exiguus est, relictaque portione terrena
units.tr: Nor is the coin in a vessel full of water seen much larger for any other reason than the same cause; so Zanches, the genuine Sceptic, labours in vain when, in the little book in which he tried to defend scepticism, he relies, among other things, against the certainty of the senses and of knowledge, on this argument, or rather experiment: Place a coin, he says, in a wide little vessel; set the vessel on the ground; move away from it until you no longer see the coin. Then have the vessel filled with water. You will see the coin at once, and larger than it was before through the air, although the medium is opaque in itself. Why does the coin now appear larger? We do not know. Sextus's second experiment, concerning the coin, is no better. For the light of a lamp does not appear dim in the sun, and bright in the dark; rather, it is hindered from showing itself, insofar as a strong light intercepts and overpowers a weak one. For the sun, darting its vivid light, overpowers the light of the stars and of all lamps, not by destroying them or preventing them from shining, but because it strongly affects the sense and with a certain force, whereas the faint lights of stars and lamps do not affect sight effectively. Likewise, a faint flame placed beside an innate fire is overpowered. Otherwise, when the light of the sun is withdrawn, as it were, both the stars and the lamps show themselves to be seen. Galen knew this well, in the tenth book of On the Use of the Parts: In the eclipses of the sun the stars appear, as Thucydides records that happened in his own times. Does error arise here for the senses? If the mind has understood the cause of this matter, it will be able to distinguish, with little effort, between the light of the sun and the light of lamps. Next comes the egg, which is soft in the bird but hard in the air. But what can this help the Sceptic's prejudice against the senses? While it remains in the bird, it is soft and pliable, so that its hardness may not cause it trouble; afterwards it soon hardens as the air draws out the little moisture and so brings about the hardness. For just as the egg is truly soft and flabby within the bird, and hard outside it, so the sense cannot be charged with deception, or rather, the mind distinguishing these things judges them as they truly stand in reality. Certain persons have indeed wished to call into doubt whether an egg is soft inside a bird and hard outside it; but Sextus, called to the cause before, refutes them, and experience supports him, which we have often called in as counsel about various individual eggs. Aristotle, in the third book of On the Generation of Animals, chapter 2, applauds both Sextus and experience, where these words worthy of observation occur: It is clear that first there is a soft membrane, which at the end is made into a shell: for when the egg is complete, it becomes hard and rigid only so far that it can still come out soft. For it would cause pain if it came out otherwise. Once it has come out, it is cooled and hardened at once, as the small amount of moisture evaporates and the earthy part is left behind.

units.la: Sic & Plinius lib. 10. Nat: Hist. cap. 52. Exeunt [ova scilicet] à rotundissima sui parte, dum pariuntur, molli putamine, sed protinus durescente, quibuscunque emergunt portionibus. Suadeturque idem hac etiam ratione, disjuncta ab ea, quam modo Philosophus adduxit: Quoniam non ubique æqualis ovorum rotunditas est, procurari hoc debet per compressionem mollioris testæ, dum ovum paritur: Cur enim rotunditas in ea parte: quæ primo exit, major esset, nisi ovum in fine comprimeretur, siveretque acutius? Quid quod acumen ovi in quo est ovi primordium, connectitur umbilico, aut ut loquuntur, grandinibus; à quibus pendere non potest nisi testa mollis adhuc sit. Cum vero acumen hoc ultimo exeat, certum est ab umbilico inter exeundum lemum separari. Vt non attendenda sit experientia Marsilij Cognati, qui lib. Var. Observ. c. 9. loquitur: Notavimus aliquando gallinas tam repete ta, & illa duro putamine exclusisse, ut qui vidisset, mo potuisset sibi persuadere, tam brevi momento nporis extra ventrem illius dura evasisse, manibus in gallinam tenuimus, cui repente ovum excidens rum idem persuasit. fregimus etiam in cujusdam tre ovum, eaque dissecta apparuerunt putaminis menta, omnino illius similia, quæ naturaliter rgunt. Quod postremum experimentum inquam præ cæteris contra Philosophum &
units.tr: So also Pliny, Natural History, book 10, chapter 52: The eggs come out from their most rounded part while they are being laid, in a soft shell, which however hardens at once in whatever parts they emerge. The same is suggested also by this reason, apart from the one the Philosopher has just cited: since the roundness of eggs is not everywhere equal, this must be brought about by the compression of the softer shell while the egg is laid. For why would the roundness in that part which comes out first be greater, unless the egg were compressed at its end and became more pointed? Moreover, the pointed end of the egg, in which lies the beginning of the egg, is connected with the umbilicus, or as they say, with the chalazae, on which it cannot depend unless the shell is still soft. But since this pointed end comes out last, it is certain that the yolk is separated from the umbilicus while it comes out. So the experience of Marsilio Cognato should not be disregarded, who says in Various Observations, chapter 9: We once observed hens that had laid, with a hard shell, so quickly that anyone who saw it could hardly persuade himself that the egg had become hard outside the belly in so short a moment. We held the hen in our hands, and the egg suddenly fell out, which likewise persuaded us. We also broke an egg of a certain hen, and when it was cut open, the membranes of the shell appeared, wholly similar to those which are naturally formed. This last experiment, I say, more than the others, seems to fight against the Philosopher and

units.la: Sextum militare videtur, nequaquam tamen illos ferit. Nam diligens ovorum ruspator, non poterit fragminailla videre sine ventris apertione. Atqui facto vulnere & hiatu erumpens aër durabit testam, quemadmodum & corallia sub mari mollia, mox ubi aër illa circumflare incipit, rigescunt. Quod nulli mirum videri debet, cum in ovo in utero perfecto proxima dispositio sit ad indurationem. Nec valet ejusdem ratio, quæ in sequentibus verbis l. d. occurrit; Cautius facisse natura videtur, ut intus obdurescerent; nam si mollia exirent, sæpissime perderentur. Ne hoc enim fiat, communis mater cavit, ovum muniendo, quamdiu in utero est, tunica viscida & tenaci, quæ in lapidis duritiem, simulac in aëra producitur, facili negotio concrescere possit. Sed ad Sextum: is deinceps adducit pro se corallium, quod in mari molle, & extra illud durum est. Haut magis vero illud juvare eum poterit, atque ovum: siquidem sensus pro diverso corallij statu, & loco, diversimode illud affectum esse secundum rei veritatem judicant. Quod vero Sextus hic de corallio præsupponit ut verum, consentientibus antiquis authoribus sine numero, in dubium vocare voluit quidam Gluckradt Med. Doctor in additamentis ad Tyrocinium Chymicum Beguini lib. 2.cap. 10. quemhic adducere lubet, ut argui queat. Ita ergo ergo ibi: Generosus Dominus Iohannes Baptista de Nicole, Eques Massilienfis, & Regis piscationis coralliorum, in regno Thunetano Praesectus, certo mihi confirmavit: quod cum anno M. D. LXXXV. mense Iulio, in mari Bizertino, regni illius Thunetani, piscationem instituisset: cupiditate naturae coralliorum investigandae inductus, juvenem, funibus sufficienter longis alligatum, & pondere viginti quinque librarum, in utraque manu, ad descensum tutiorem & commodiorem libratum, in mare istud centum perticas profundum, demiserit; ipsique in mandatis dederit, corallium evelleret, & inter evellendum, curiose attenteque observaret, an molle durumue esset.
units.tr: The Sceptic also seems to press this point, but it does not strike these examples at all. For no careful searcher of eggs could see those fragments without opening the belly of the egg. Yet when the wound is made and the hole opened, the air that rushes in hardens the shell, just as corals that are soft under the sea harden as soon as the air begins to play about them. That should surprise no one, since in an egg that is fully formed in the womb, the nearest disposition is towards hardening. Nor does the reason given in the following words, which he cites as Cautius facisse natura videtur, ut intus obdurescerent; nam si mollia exirent, sæpissime perderentur ("Nature seems to have acted more cautiously in making them harden inside, for if they came out soft they would very often be lost"), hold good. For to prevent this, the common mother took care to protect the egg, while it is in the womb, with a viscid and tenacious membrane, which can easily set into the hardness of stone as soon as it is brought out into the air. But to return to Sextus: he next adduces coral, which is soft in the sea and hard outside it. Yet this will help him no more than the egg does, since the senses, according to the truth of the matter, judge that it is affected in different ways according to the different state and place of the coral. As for what Sextus here takes for granted about coral, that it is true, the ancient authors agree without number; yet a certain Gluckradt, Doctor of Medicine, in his additions to Beguin's Tyrocinium Chymicum, book 2, chapter 10, wished to call it into doubt. I am pleased to cite him here so that he may be refuted. His words are these: Ita ergo ergo ibi: "Lord John Baptist de Nicole, a knight of Marseilles and prefect of the king's coral fishery in the kingdom of Tunis, assured me with certainty that in the year 1585, in July, when he had undertaken a fishery in the Bizerte sea of that kingdom of Tunis, moved by a desire to investigate the nature of coral, he let down into that sea, to a depth of one hundred poles, a young man tied with sufficiently long ropes and weighted with twenty-five pounds in each hand, so that he would descend more safely and conveniently; and he instructed him to pull up coral and, while pulling it, to observe carefully and attentively whether it was soft or hard."

units.la: Qui, ubi rursus ascendisset; utraque manu corallii ramum attulerit, constanterque observavit: illud non minus sub mari, quam supra illud, durum esse: & se, cum ad octo perticas, aut circiter, prope fundum maris adpulisset, magnam ibi frigoris vim sensisse Immo, quod ipsemet etiam, cum relationi istius fidem adeo non haberet, in mare, cum retia, quibus corallium piscari solent, extrahenda essent, antequam in ipsum aerem effferretur, ad profunditatem unius perticae, se immersisset, & corallium, retibus adhaerens, manu prehenderit, idque tum aeque durum, ac cum jam aeri externo esset positum, observarit. Idem etiam confirmavit D. de la Poetier, Nobilis Lugdunensis, qui anno CIO IOCXIII. ab ejusmodi piscatione, è Barbaria reversus est: Hæc ille. Sed quis, cui constat modo ratio, sublestis hisce experimentis, contra constantem fidem antiquorum, aliquid tribuere velit? Lubens concedo, corallium, simulac à stirpe sua revulsum est, lapidem referre, & hoc nobilem illum potuisse tactu experiri; sed quis inde dederit, quandiu petris adhæret, atque sub aquis crescit & augetur, molle esse non posse? Certissimum est & per experientiam constat, corallium fruticem esse, instar quercus durum, atq; etiam eo tempore quando in aqua degit, cortice lapidescente quasi tectum, mollem autem tum censeri quod non gaudeat tanta duritie, quanta postea illi accedit à succo lapidescente, quo constricto per avulsionem fruticis ipsius, lapidea durities per totam ligni, sic petrificati, substantiam sese prodit, durumque illud censetur, quód antea secundum quid mollius habebatur. Hanc esse corallij genuinam naturam, veramque historiam, alibi fusius ostendimus: quam si quis diligentius attenderit, videbit quantum tribuendum sit assoveratiōni hominis juvenis, qui cum existimaret cum multis, in gradu summo corallium sub aqua molle esse debere, durum esse
units.tr: When he had come up again, he brought up a branch of coral in each hand and observed steadily that it was no less hard under the sea than above it. He also said that when he had reached, at about eight poles, the bottom of the sea, he had felt a great force of cold there. Indeed, since he himself did not at all trust this report, when the nets with which coral is usually fished had to be drawn up, before it was brought into the open air, he plunged himself to a depth of one pole into the sea, and taking hold of coral that was caught in the nets with his hand, he observed that it was then just as hard as when it had already been placed in the external air. D. de la Poetier, a nobleman of Lyons, who returned from Barbary in the year 1613 from such a fishery, confirmed the same thing. Hæc ille. But who, knowing the reasoning, would wish to attribute anything to these flimsy experiments against the constant faith of the ancients? I gladly concede that coral, as soon as it is torn from its stock, resembles stone, and that the nobleman could have tested this by touch; but who would conclude from this that it cannot be soft while it adheres to rocks and grows and increases under the waters? It is most certain, and established by experience, that coral is a shrub, hard like an oak, and that even at the time when it lives in the water, covered as it were by a petrifying bark, it is then regarded as soft, not because it lacks that hardness which it afterwards acquires from the petrifying juice; and when that juice has constricted, on the tearing away of the shrub itself, the stony hardness displays itself through the whole substance of the wood thus petrified, and that is called hard which before was considered in some respects softer. We have shown elsewhere, at greater length, that this is the genuine nature and true history of coral. If anyone attends to this more carefully, he will see how much credence is to be given to the assertion of that young man, who, although he thought with many that coral under water at a great depth ought to be soft, pronounced it hard, because he found it less soft than he had believed.

units.la: . esse pronunciavit, quod minus quam crediderat, molle esse experiretur. Certe, uti lubens fateor, historiam naturalem, jam olim multis fabulis conspurcatam fuisse; ita tamen ab ea non recedo, nisi aut gravibus rationibus, aut certissimisque exceptione majoribus experimetis convictus, quae cum hic nulla occurrant, non possum recedere ab Ovidio, qui, astipulantibus Orpheo & Plinio ex antiquis, Cardano vero, Baccio, Boetio, Matthiolo, & Gansio ex recentioribus, jam olim lib. 4. Metamorph. sic cecinit:
units.tr: Certainly, as I gladly admit, natural history was long ago defiled by many fables; yet I do not depart from it unless I am convinced either by weighty reasons or by most certain experiments of greater weight than any exception; and since none of these occur here, I cannot depart from Ovid, who, with Orpheus and Pliny among the ancients, and Cardan, Bacci, Boethius, Matthiolus and Gesner among the more recent writers, long ago sang thus in book 4 of the Metamorphoses:

units.la: Sic & Coralium quo primum contigit auras
units.tr: Sic & Coralium quo primum contigit auras

units.la: Tempore, durescit, mollis fuit herba sub undis.
units.tr: In time it hardens; it was soft grass beneath the waves.

units.la: Ut ad Sextum autem redeamus, adducit is amplius lyncurium in lynce humidum, in aere autem durum. Sed hic licet nobis per omnia securis esse; siquidem hoc commentum, quo sensuum certitudinem subvertere laborat Sextus, jam olim ab ipso Plinio explosum fuit. Qui ita lib. 37. Nat. Hist. cap. 3. De Lyncurio, inquit, proxime dici cogit authorum pertinacia. Quippe etiamsi non electrum id esset, Lyncurium tamen gemmam esse contendunt. Fieri autem ex urina quidem Lyncis, sed egestum in terra protinus bestia operiente eam, quoniam invidet hominum usui. Esse autem, qualem in igneis succinis, colorem, scalpique. Nec folia tantum aut stramenta ad serapere, sed aeris etiam ac ferri laminas, quod Diocli Theophrastus credidit. Ego falsum id totum arbitror, nec visam in ævo nostro gemmam ullam ea appellatione, & quod de medicina simul proditur, calculos vesicæ eo puto elidi & morbo regio occurri, si ex vino bibatur, aut si portetur etiam. Superest postremum Sexti exemplum: Vox, dicit, diversa videtur in tuba, diversa in tibijs, diversa rursus in aëre simpliciter. Imo non videtur tantum diversa esse, sed revera quoque diversa est, ob diversam allisionem & repercussionem soni. Neutiquam vero hic erroris redargui debet auditus, aut potius ratio, diversimode sonos illos dijudicans, qui auditus sensorium diversimode feriunt. Ea quippe quæ à parte rei distincte se habent, distinguit: quod est judicij probe subacti, nec fallacis. Et ne quis hoc exemplo afficiatur; non quidem propter Scepticos qui Scripturam rejiciunt, sed propter eos, qui videri volunt aliquid adhuc illi deferre, adduco ipsum Apostolum Paulum, qui expresse 1. ad Corinth. 14. v. 7. & subseqq. tum auditum, tum ipsam quoque mentem ab errore vindicat: Atqui, inquit, anima expertia, quæ sonum edunt, tibia, & cithara, nisi distinctionem sonis dederint, quomodo cognoscetur, quod tibia canitur aut cithara? Etenim si incertum sonum tuba dederit, quis apparabitur ad bellum? Ita & vos nisi per linguam ediderit bene significantem sermonem, quomodo cognoscetur, quod dicitur, eritis enim in aërem loquentes.
units.tr: To return to Sextus, he adds that lyncurium is moist in the lynx but hard in the air. Here, however, we may be entirely at ease, since this invention, by which Sextus labours to overturn the certainty of the senses, was long ago refuted by Pliny himself. In book 37 of the Natural History, chapter 3, he writes: "The obstinacy of the authors compels me to speak of it next. For even if it is not amber, they maintain that lyncurium is a gem. It is made from the urine of the lynx, but the animal covers it with earth as soon as it is voided, because it begrudges it to human use. It has the colour of fiery amber and can be scraped. Not only leaves or straw cling to it, but also thin plates of bronze and iron, as Theophrastus believed on the authority of Diocles. I consider all of this false, and I have never seen in our age any gem by that name. As for what is also reported of its medicinal use, I think that it breaks up stones of the bladder and counters jaundice if it is drunk in wine, or even if it is merely carried." There remains Sextus's last example: "The voice, he says, seems different in a trumpet, different in pipes, and different again in the open air." Indeed it does not merely seem different; it really is different, owing to the different striking and reflection of the sound. Nor should the hearing, or rather the reason which judges between those sounds that strike the organ of hearing in different ways, be charged with error at all. For it distinguishes things that are distinct in their own nature, which is the mark of a judgement properly trained and not deceptive. And lest anyone be moved by this example, I bring forward the Apostle Paul himself, not on account of the Sceptics who reject Scripture, but on account of those who wish to seem still to defer something to it. In 1 Cor. 14, verses 7 and following, he expressly vindicates both the hearing and the mind itself from error: "But even lifeless things that give sound, such as the flute and the harp, unless they give a distinction to the sounds, how will it be known what is played on the flute or the harp? For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? So also you, unless through the tongue you utter speech that signifies well, how will it be known what is said? For you will be speaking into the air."

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM QUINTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FIFTEEN.

units.la: Respondetur ad Scepticorum tum experimenta, tum rationes à distantia petitas contra sensuum fidem.
units.tr: It is answered to the Sceptics' experiments, and to their arguments drawn from distance, against the trustworthiness of the senses.

units.la: Secundus modus, quo Sceptici certitudinem sensuum evertere laborarunt, pertinet ad distantiam. Quoniam enim ea, quae secundum aliam atque aliam distantiam sensibus obiiciuntur, alia atque alia comparent, videtur nulla certitudo deferenda esse sensui, qui ad definitam distantiam actum sensitivum exercet. Verba Sexti Empirici haec sunt: Eadem, inquit, porticus ab altero quidem ingressu intuenti videtur in acutum desinere: à media autem parte spectanti, undique aequalis. & idem navigium procul quidem intuentibus parvum videtur esse & exstare: prope autem magnum esse & moveri. Et eadem turris procul quidem videtur rotunda, prope autem quadrata. Eaedem objectiones jam olim notę fuerunt Tertulliano, qui & ijsdem occurrit lib. 3. de Anima, cap. 17. Ut turris eludat, intervalli conditio compellit in aperto; aequalitas enim circumfusi aëris pari luce vestiens angulos, obliterat lineas. Sic & uniformitas porticus acuitur in fine, dum acies in concluso stipato illic tenuatur, quo & extenditur. Ut vero omnia pateant, repetimus quod antea diximus, sensum sensui non esse imputanda illa, quæ objectis ratione sensationis minus proportionati accidunt. Notum sensum convenienter mediante specie objectum suum percipere non posse, nisi debita distantia inter illum & objectum intercedat, quæ si proportionata non fuerit, aut ratione excessus, aut defectus; sensatio perfecte non instituetur, non quidem quod fallax sit sensus, aut hallucinetur ratio; sed quod deficiat ea conditio, quæ à parte objecti requiritur. Recte Tertullianus loco dicto: Quod si caussa, inquit, fallunt sensus, & per sensus opiniones: jam nec in sensibus constituenda fallacia est, qui causas sequuntur, nec in opinionibus, quæ à sensibus diriguntur, sequentibus causas. Indispositio objecti, & deficiens in distantia ejusdem à sensorio proportio; non quidem ad modum causæ positivæ, sed defectivè consideranda, ex accidenti in errorem sensum trahunt, alias secutum omnis erroris, si distantia debita objecto acciderit, omniaque requisita, titulo causarum hic à Tertulliano condecorata, accesserint. Instat quidem Zanches contendendo distantiam illam esse imperceptibilem, ac consequenter sensui quam necessitatem errandi incumbere. Ita enim loquitur: Quæ longe sunt, obscura apparent, & parva: quæ prope nimis, aut non videntur, aut aliter quam sunt.Quid facies? Medium tenendum. Ubi medium illud? An ad duos passus aut quolibet alio certo numero? Qui longe a nobis est, etiamsi celerrime admodum currat, tamen lente admodum moveri videtur: praecipue si deorsum ex alto, aut contra inspicias. Quanquam vero, ut hic Scepticismi patronus contendit, definite atque in genere dici non potest, quanta distantia requiratur ratione cujusque sensus, cum organum pro individuorum ratione, non minus varium sit, atque varia est quantitas, item qualitas & motus ipsorum objectorum; nihilominus tamen ratione distantiae, agitur magis de communibus objectis sensibilibus, quae de propriis; atq; in actu exercito [uti loquuntur] eam adhibitam fuisse, inde constare potest; quod uni sensui plures succurrant, uniusque certitudo per consentiens alterius judicium probetur. Ut verbi causa, video in definita [ut mihi videtur] distantia nanum aliquem giganti astare, ac ratione visus judico hunc illo longiorem esse: caeterum accedit Scepticus, eadem mihi difficultates movens, quas antea Zanches proposuit, quibus ut initio moveor, ita postea eas negligo; propius enim ad utrumque illum accedendo, & utrumque palpando, disco plura in gigante occurrere quae palpare queam, quam in nano, utque desinam fluctuare, arripio perticam & utrumque mensurare incipio, per quem actum mensuranmensurandi, ut judicium visus mei respectu indefinite antea certum, definite certum redditur, ita fluctuare desino. Sic visum à tactu confirmari posse, gnarum erat Thomæ Apostolo, ad tempus Scepticismi profundo immerso; cujus infirmitati occurrendo benedictus noster Salvator, non tantum dicit Joh. 20. v. 27. Vide manus meas: sed amplius, Infer digitum tuum huc, & profer manum tuam, & immitte in latus meum. Quae movet Zanches, itemque que occurrunt in exemplis Sexti, ex censu sensibilium communium sunt, circa quę unum aliquem particularem sensum à ratione semotum falli posse, ultro jam antea ostendimus; usque sumus exemplo horologij, cujus indicem videri procul eum conspicientibus, quiescere, ibidem notavimus: ut non audiendus idem iterum sit, loco dicto sic proclamans: Quae sensim fiunt, sensum effugiunt; ut radij motus in horologio. Quomodo certo iudicabis? Ignoras. Magis ego. Enimvero certo judicare possum, quotiescunque circa sensibile commune ratione comite plures sensus adhibere licet. Quibus quia uti non possum in dimetiendo cælo & corporibus cælestibus, eorundem magnitudinem, locum, & distantiam definite à me cognoscci non posse, memor me hominem esse, lubens agnosco: ut non sit necessum me hoc discere ex Zanches, qui sic deinceps cornicatur:
units.tr: The second way in which the Sceptics have laboured to overturn the certainty of the senses concerns distance. For since things presented to the senses at different distances appear differently, it seems that no certainty should be granted to a sense that exercises its sensory act at a fixed distance. The words of Sextus Empiricus are these: "The same portico, seen by someone looking from one entrance, seems to end in a point; but seen from the middle, it is equal on every side. And the same ship seems small and motionless to those looking at it from far off, but large and moving when near. And the same tower seems round from afar, but square close up." These same objections were known long ago to Tertullian, who also meets them in book 3 of On the Soul, chapter 17: "The condition of the interval deceives the tower in the open; for the evenness of the surrounding air, clothing the angles with equal light, blots out the lines. So too the uniformity of the portico is sharpened at its end, while the sight is narrowed there in the enclosed space to which it also extends." To make everything plain, I repeat what I said before: those things which happen to objects not suited to the manner of sensation are not to be imputed to the sense. It is known that a sense cannot perceive its object properly through the intervening species unless a due distance lies between it and the object; if that distance is not proportionate, either by excess or by defect, the sensation is not carried out perfectly. This is not because the sense is deceptive or reason is hallucinating, but because the condition required on the part of the object is lacking. Tertullian rightly says in the passage cited: "But if causes deceive the senses, and through the senses our opinions, then deception is to be placed neither in the senses, which follow causes, nor in opinions, which are directed by the senses, which follow causes." The indisposition of the object, and the deficient proportion of its distance from the sensory organ, are not to be considered as a positive cause but in a deficient way; by accident they draw the sense into error. Otherwise, if the due distance had been present for the object and all the requisites had been present, there would be error of the kind for which Tertullian here gives the title of causes. Zanches indeed presses the point, contending that this distance is imperceptible, and consequently that a necessity of error lies upon the sense. For he speaks thus: "Things far away appear obscure and small; things too near either are not seen, or are seen otherwise than they are. What will you do? The mean must be held. But where is that mean? Two paces, or some other fixed number? He who is far from us, even if he runs very fast, seems to move very slowly, especially if you look at him from above or from below." Yet although, as this patron of Scepticism contends, it cannot be stated definitely and in general how great a distance is required for each sense, since the organ varies among individuals no less than the quantity, quality and motion of the objects themselves vary, nevertheless with regard to distance it is more a matter of common sensible objects than of proper ones; and that the distance was adopted in the exercised act [as they say] can be established from this: that several senses come to the aid of one, and the certainty of one is proved by the agreeing judgement of another. For example, I see at a fixed distance [as it seems to me] a certain dwarf standing beside a giant, and by sight I judge him to be shorter than the other. But the Sceptic adds, raising in me the same difficulties that Zanches proposed earlier; and as I am at first moved by them, so afterwards I disregard them. For by going nearer to each of them and touching both, I learn that more can be touched in the giant than in the dwarf; and that I may stop wavering, I take a pole and begin to measure each. By this act of measuring, my visual judgement, which before was certain only indefinitely, is made definitely certain, and so I stop wavering. That sight can be confirmed by touch was known to the Apostle Thomas, who had sunk deep into a time of Scepticism; and our blessed Saviour, meeting his weakness, says not only Joh. 20. v. 27: "See my hands," but further: "Put your finger here, and reach out your hand, and put it into my side." What Zanches raises, and what occurs in the examples of Sextus, belongs to the class of common sensibles. Concerning these, we have already shown above that a particular sense, apart from reason, can be deceived; and we noted in the same place the example of the clock, whose hand, seen from afar by those looking at it, seems to be at rest. So that Zanches should not be heard again, proclaiming in the passage cited: "Things that happen gradually escape the sense, as the motion of the hand on a clock does. How will you judge with certainty? You do not know. I know even less." Indeed, I can judge with certainty whenever several senses can be brought to bear on a common sensible together with reason. Since I cannot use them in measuring the heavens and the heavenly bodies, and so cannot know their size, place and distance definitely, I gladly acknowledge, mindful that I am a man; there is no need for me to learn this from Zanches, who then croaks on as follows:

units.la: Nec vero hoc parum scire refert. Hinc enim emergit perpetua dubitatio de magnitudine stellarum: ut de distantia, de celeritate, de loco o taceam: quae omnia inde videntur pendere. Scientiae definiti sunt limites, uti fusius postea ostendemus: Sim liber quoque sensationis. Ut omnia definite ijs apprehendere non possum, ita tamen certus sum ad aliqua certo exploranda me ab his ducibus deduci posse. Quum vero Tertullianus laboraverit causas proponere, ob quas accidat, ut visus ob minus proportionatam distantiam communia sensuum objecta distincte percipere non queat, aliquanto distinctius singula expendemus. Adducit autem Sextus primo porticum, quae ab altero quidem ingressu intuenti videatur in acutum desinere, a media autem parte undique aequalis. Significare quippe vult, quod dicit Seneca lib. 1. N. Q. 3. Columnarum intervalla porticus longiores jungunt, & quod Chalcidius in Timaeum: Ex obliquo visa porticus in exile deficit. Quod accidit quando paulatim omnia in unum punctum coeunt, & ut Lucretius canit:
units.tr: Nor indeed is it a small matter to know this. From it there arises a constant doubt about the size of the stars, not to mention their distance, speed and place, all of which seem to depend on it. The limits of the sciences are defined, as we shall show more fully later. I am also a free judge of sensation. Just as I cannot grasp all things definitely by these guides, so I am nonetheless certain that I can be led by them to explore some things with certainty. Since Tertullian has tried to set out the causes on account of which it happens that sight, because of a distance not sufficiently proportionate, cannot perceive the common objects of the senses distinctly, we shall weigh the individual points somewhat more distinctly. Sextus first adduces the portico, which seen from one entrance seems to end in a point, but from the middle is equal on every side. He clearly means what Seneca says in book 1 of the Natural Questions, chapter 3: "The portico's longer intervals join the columns," and what Chalcidius says on the Timaeus: "Seen obliquely, the portico tapers away into a thin point." This happens when all things gradually come together into a single point, as Lucretius sings:

units.la: Tecta solo junguntur, & omnia dextera laevis, Donec in obscurum coni ducantur acumen.
units.tr: "The roofs join with the ground, and everything on the right and left, until they are drawn together into the obscure point of a cone."

units.la: Cujus rei hanc rationem reddunt Optici, fusius eam demonstrantes, quod in porticibus pavimenta, columnae & latera in illud horizontis punctum secundum visum feruntur, in quod radius opticus planis illis parallelus, atque horizonti æquilibris terminatur. Secundo proponit navim, quæ cum celerrime moveatur, eminus tamen conspecta videatur quiescere. Cujus rei hæc est ratio, quod quo mobile longius ab aspectu est remotum, eo etiam tardius moveri videatur. Uti Opticorum hoc effatum probat Aguilonius lib. 4. Opt. prop. 143. Tertio jactat turrim quadratam, quæ eminus rotunda videatur. Rationem commodam jam ante ex Tertulliano audivimus: in longiori enim distantia, tenues angulorum extremitates extra conspectum deferuntur, reliquo corpore manente conspicuo. Convenienter Lucret. lib. 4. Quadratasque procul turres cum cernimus urbis, Propterea fit, uti videantur sæpe rotundæ, Angulus obtusus quia longe cernitur omnis, Sive etiam potius non cernitur, ac perit ejus Plaga, nec ad nostras acies allabitur ictus; Aëra per multum quia dum simulachra feruntur, Cogit hebescere eum crebris offensibus aër: Hunc ubi suffugit sensum simul angulus omnis, Fit, quasi ut ad tornum saxorum structa tuantur, Non tamen ut coram quæ sunt, verèque rotunda, Sed quasi adumbratim paullum simulata videntur.
units.tr: The opticians give this reason for it, demonstrating it more fully: in porticoes the paving, the columns and the sides are carried, as regards sight, to that point of the horizon at which the optical ray, parallel to those planes and level with the horizon, terminates. Second, he presents a ship which, though it moves very swiftly, seems at rest when seen from afar. The reason for this is that the farther a moving thing is removed from sight, the slower it appears to move. Aguilonius, in book 4 of the Optics, proposition 143, proves this maxim of the opticians. Third, he brings up a square tower which from afar looks round. We have already heard a convenient reason from Tertullian: at a greater distance the slender extremities of the corners are carried beyond sight, while the rest of the body remains visible. Lucretius agrees in book 4: "When we see the square towers of a city from afar, they often seem round for this reason: every obtuse angle is seen from far off, or rather is not seen at all, and its blow perishes and does not reach our eyes; for as the images travel through much air, the air by its frequent collisions makes the angle blunt. When every angle has thus escaped the sense, the buildings seem as if they were turned on a lathe, yet not as they really are, truly round, but as if they were shown slightly shaded in outline."

units.la: Quæ si quis distincte expendat atque consideret, reliquorum, quæ ab aliis adduci hic solent, convenienter rationem reddere poterit. Quamvis quotquot ingenui, in multis hic ignorantiam suam lubentes fatentur. Quis enim omnia hic sibi explorata esse dicere audet? Ut in multis cespitamus, & vix homines sumus, ita hic quoque. Quis enim V. C. dicere audit, sibi definite exploratum esse, cur stellae fixae scintillent, non vero erratice. Scio a multis multa hic excogitata fuisse: at si omnes sententiae quoque sub examen vocentur, (quod alibi a nobis fiet) in quaque plurimum desiderari deprehendetur.
units.tr: If someone weighs and considers these things carefully, he will be able to give a sound account of the remaining points that are usually brought forward here by others. Indeed, all honest men readily confess their ignorance on many of these matters. For who would dare to say that everything here is fully explored for himself? As we stumble over many things and are scarcely men, so it is here too. For who, most learned sir, has ever heard anyone say that he has definitely established why the fixed stars twinkle, but the wandering ones do not? I know that many explanations have been devised here by many people; but if all these opinions too are brought under examination (which we shall do elsewhere), each will be found to lack a great deal.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM SEXTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SIXTEEN.

units.la: Obviam itur illis Scepticorum argumentis, quae, pro labefactanda sensuum fide, petierunt a diverso situ.
units.tr: We meet those Sceptical arguments which they drew from a different position, in order to undermine trust in the senses.

units.la: DEinceps Sceptici, uti fidem facit Empiricus, argumentari contra sensus solent, a situ quoniam enim pro diverso situ res aliae atq; aliae comparent, concluserunt sensus fallaces, nihilque eorum judicio tribuendum esse. Exempla haec adfert Sextus: Eadem imago, refupinata quidem, laevis esse, si autem aliquantum propendeat, aliquid prominens & aliquid retrusum habere videtur. Sed & columbarum cervices, prout diverse inflectuntur, diversum habere videntur colorem. Zanches autem, qui eodem utitur argumento, sequentia: In coloribus, inquit, quantum interfit situs, ostendit Iris, vitrum aqua plenum, columba variegata, serica tela ex diversis contexta coloribus, vicinitas corporis splendentis alterius coloris (ut etiam, si plano perpendiculariter imponas aueam, argenteamve laminam: multoque magis si deorsum inclines:) quae omnia huc atque illuc mota varium admodum referunt colorem. Quae jam praecedenti capite in genere dicta fuerunt, hic repetita cupimus. Omnia haec non arguunt aliquam in sensibus inconstantiam aut fallaciam, sed aut diversam objectorum affectionem, ob quam non potest non sensus aliter atque aliter judicare: aut deficientiam quorundam requisitorum, quibus non concurrentibus, sensus quoque accingi non deberet ad exercendum suum judicium. Quod resupinata laevia, & iterum si aliquantum promineant, quid retrusum habere videntur, accidit propter distantiam aequo majorem, ob quam uti non potest recte judicari ex qua parte lumen proveniat, ita quoque exigua illa prominentia quid extra imaginem esse videtur, cum tamen revera nihil sit extra illam. Nec collum columbinum, solaribus radiis expositum, quod teste Martiano Capella Arcesilam in sua haesitatione confirmavit, contrarium ostendit; nam haut magis fallaciarum arguere potest visum, atque panni serici ex diversi colorIs filamentis contexti, quos illi suscenturiat Zanches.
units.tr: Next, the Sceptics, as Empiricus makes clear, are accustomed to argue against the senses from position. Since different things appear different depending on the position from which they are viewed, they have concluded that the senses are deceptive and that nothing should be attributed to their judgment. Sextus gives these examples: The same image, if seen lying on its back, looks smooth; but if it leans forward a little, it seems to have something projecting and something receding. And the necks of doves, as they are bent in different ways, seem to have different colour. Zanchius, who uses the same argument, says the following: In colours, he says, how much position matters is shown by the rainbow, a glass full of water, a variegated dove, silk cloth woven from threads of different colours, the proximity of a body shining with another colour (as also, if you place a bronze or silver plate perpendicular to a flat surface, much more so if you tilt it downwards): all of which, moved here and there, present a very varied colour. These things were already said in general in the previous chapter, and we wish them repeated here. All these things do not show any inconstancy or deceitfulness in the senses, but either a different affection of the objects, on account of which the sense cannot but judge differently and differently, or the lack of certain requisites, without which the sense ought not even to be brought to exercise its judgment. As for smooth things seen lying on their backs, and again, if they project a little, seeming to have something receding: this happens because the distance is too great, so that one cannot rightly judge from which side the light comes. Likewise that slight projection seems to be something outside the image, when in reality there is nothing outside it. Nor does the dove's neck, exposed to the rays of the sun, which according to Martianus Capella confirmed Arcesilaus in his suspension of judgment, show the contrary. For it can no more argue deceit of sight than the silk cloth woven from threads of different colour, which Zanchius puts forward.

units.la: Multi præter Scepticos hæc exempla adducunt, ut probent præter veros colores, alios apparentes dari. Cæterum minus apposite: inculari folummodo hic debet diuersus situs oculorum, qui ut modo directo ad has pennas columbarum, aut filamenta pannorum feruntur; modo vero ad alias aut alia, existimant videntes pro diuerso luminis illapsu, quem fingunt, diuersos sibi apparere colores. Uti enim plumarum villi, & pannorum flocci non uno eodemque colore tincti sunt; ita quoque pro diuerso aspectu, modo ad hos, modo ad illos colores directo, varii apparent. Applicari huc potest illud Ciceronis lib. 4. Acad. Qu. Itaque, inquit, & lumen mutari sæpe volumus, & situs earum rerum, quas intuemur, & intervalla aut contrahimus, aut diducimus, multaque alia facimus, usque eo dum aspectus fidem faciat sui judicij. Iris quoque Scepticos juvare non potest: uti enim certum est illius colores phantasticos tantum esse, [insunt quippe soli corpori diaphano, nec ab ullo corpore simili colore imbuto proveniunt] ita tales a mente, cui subservit hic visus, judicantur, quales apparent; uti accidit quoque circa halones, parelios, itemque vitrum, cujus meminit Zanches. Si Scepticici cum ratione hoc argumentum urgere velint, ante probent, apparentes hosce colores aliter sese habere a parte iridis in qua apparent, atque arque à visu apparere in ea judicantur. Ipsi hi colores quoniam à parte rei sic sese habent, non potest visus ministrans intellectui, eidem alios colores quam apparentes exhibere.
units.tr: Many besides the Sceptics adduce these examples, to prove that besides true colours there are other apparent ones. But this is less to the point. Only the differing position of the eyes should be noted here: when they are directed now straight at these dove feathers or threads of cloth, and now at other parts or other things, people who see them think that different colours appear to them because of the different incidence of light which they imagine. For just as the down of feathers and the flock of cloths are not dyed with one and the same colour, so too, according to the different view, directed now at these colours, now at those, they appear various. What Cicero says in book 4 of the Academica can be applied here: Thus, he says, we often want to change both the light and the position of the things we look at, and we either draw them closer or move them apart, and do many other things, until the sight gives confidence in its own judgment. The rainbow also cannot help the Sceptics. For just as it is certain that its colours are merely appearances [for they are present only in the transparent body, and do not come from any body imbued with a similar colour], so such colours are judged by the mind, to which this sense serves, as they appear. The same happens with halos, parhelia, and likewise the glass which Zanchius mentions. If the Sceptics wish to press this argument with reason, let them first prove that these apparent colours are otherwise in the part of the rainbow where they appear than they are judged to appear by sight. Since these colours are in the thing itself just as they are, sight, ministering to the intellect, cannot present to it colours other than the apparent ones.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM SEPTIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SEVENTEEN.

units.la: Respondetur ijs experimentis, atque rationibus quas Sceptici contra sensuum certitudinem petierunt ab ijs, quae conjuncta sunt cum objectis sensibilibus.
units.tr: An answer is given to those experiments and arguments which the Sceptics have brought against the certainty of the senses, drawn from the things that are joined with sensible objects.

units.la: VLterius progrediuntur Sceptici, contendunt though sensibus omnem fidem abrogandam esse, quod nunquam objectum suum per se solum percipiant, sed semper cum alio permixtum. Ita enim Empiricus: Sextus modus est ex admistionibus. ex que inferimus, quum nullum subjectum sub sensus nostros ipsum per se cadat, sed cum aliquo: qualis quidem sit permissio, & ex externo, & ex eo quocunque cernitur, posse nos fortasse dicere: quale autem sit externum subjectum pure & sincere, nequaquam dicere posse. Tribui quid posset huic rationi, si aut cuique sensui definitum non foret objectum, aut permixtio haec neque à natura, neque à ratione corrigeretur: Unusquisque sensus fertur ad proprium suum objectum, ad quod definite percipiendum uti solum animali concessum est. sus est; ita reliqua omnia, quæ cum specie ejusdem exhibentur, ex accidenti tantummodo percipit; quatenus scilicet mens in homine, aut phanthasia in muta-pecude, per speciem sensibilem objecti sensui proprio oblatam, simul aliud quid, occurrens in eo, cujus species offertur, percipit. Ita verbi caussa feli objicitur tantum externa species albedinis, á lacte promanans; cæterum avide accurrit ad illud, non quod feratur ad albedinem, sed ad lac dulce. quod cum specie illa alba conjunctum esse, monet phanthasia quæ pariter speciem dulcedinis reconditam habet in memoria, cum ejusmodi albedine conjunctæ; simulque oblectationis perceptę, ex largiori usu rei hujus albæ simul atq; dulcis. Idem judicium de aliis omnibus serendum, quæ à quocunque sensu simul ex accidenti percipiuntur. Conglobat quidem Sextus multa exempla, sed nullum eorum stringit, aut ad rem facit. I. Aromata, inquit, in balneo ac sole odore suo vehementius pungunt, quam in aëre frigido. Sed, an proinde fallitur odoratus? Quoniam calor tum Solis, tum balnei, fumosas illas exhalationes, in quibus consistit odor (licet per speciem illis respondentem percipiatur) educit, easque frigus, vi resolvendi destitutum, educere non potest, inde res odoratæ in locis calidioribus fragantiorem exhalant odorem, quam in frigidioribus; non ipso loco, uti fingit Sextus, cum specie odorifera organo odoratus se offerente, sed qualitatibus activis, que in eo notari possunt, diversimode in res odoratas agentibus. Tamdiu autem calor odorem in rebus odoriferis excitare, atque intendere potest, quam in ijs humidum pingue, per calorem diffolubile, superest. Experientia siquidem constat, aromata exarefacta penitus, omnique humido destituta, inodora plane esse.
units.tr: The Sceptics go further and contend that all trust must be taken away from the senses, because they never perceive their object by itself alone, but always mixed with something else. Thus Empiricus: The sixth mode is from admixtures. From this we infer that, since no subject falls under our senses by itself, but always with something else, we can perhaps say what the external appearance is, both from the external object and from that by which it is seen, but we cannot at all say what the external subject is in its purity and sincerity. This argument might carry some weight if either no object were assigned to each sense, or if this mixture were corrected neither by nature nor by reason. Each sense is directed to its own proper object, which the animal alone is granted to perceive definitely. All the other things that are presented together with the species of that object it perceives only incidentally, namely, insofar as the mind in man, or the imagination in a dumb beast, through the sensible species of the object offered to the proper sense, at the same time perceives something else that meets it in that which the species presents. For example, the mere outward appearance of whiteness, flowing from milk, is presented to a cat. Yet it eagerly runs to the milk, not because it is carried toward whiteness, but toward the sweet milk. The imagination, which also keeps stored in memory the species of sweetness joined with such whiteness, reminds it that the two are conjoined; and at the same time there is a perception of pleasure from the more frequent use of this thing which is at once white and sweet. The same judgment is to be made about all other things which are perceived incidentally at the same time by any sense. Sextus indeed heaps up many examples, but he grasps none of them, nor do they bear on the matter. (1) Aromatic substances, he says, in the bath and in the sun sting more sharply with their odour than in the cold air. But is the sense of smell therefore deceived? Since the heat of both the sun and the bath draws out those smoky exhalations in which the odour consists (though it is perceived through the species corresponding to them), and since cold, which lacks the power of dissolving, cannot draw them out, scented things give off a stronger odour in warmer places than in colder ones. This happens not because of the place itself, as Sextus pretends, with the odoriferous species presenting itself to the organ of smell, but because the active qualities noted in them act in different ways upon the scented things. Heat can stir up and intensify the odour in odoriferous things only as long as a moist, oily substance, dissoluble by heat, remains in them. Indeed, experience shows that aromatic substances which have been thoroughly dried and deprived of all moisture are altogether odourless.

units.la: II. Pergit Sextus aliud exemplum adferendo: Oculi, inquit, nostri in se ipsis habent, & tunicas & humiditates. Visibilia ergo quia absque his cernere non possumus, non percipiuntur exacte & pure. cum admistione enim percipimus. Sed cogitare deberet Sextus, haec pertinere ad fabricam, atque structuram oculi, qui habet rationem organi visorii vitiosi, si hae ipsae partes ad fabricam illius pertinentes aut sint viriatae, aut distractae, aut etiam ab extraneo corpore qualitatibus extraneis peregrinisque prędito, prępeditae ad edendas suas functiones. Si sive tunicae, sive humores quoq; ideo, quādoquidem in oculo tanquam ad eundem pertinentes notantur, impedimento forent exercitio functionis visivae, cum applausu recipi posset hoc ipsum argumentum: sed cum sint oculi requisita, atque ad illius fabricam spe ētent, non possunt, si omnia circa illa legitime se habeant, visioni ullum aut impedimentum, aut etiam eidem per se fallaciam procurare. nec valet instantia Empirici sic deinceps loquentis: Ac propterea icteritis quidem omnia pallida videntur esse, hypospghagma autem habentibus, sanguinea. Quam vero iniquum est, velle sensationem probam & perfectam exigere ab organo vitioso? Si enim oculus ictérici non foret imbutus per morbum extraneo hoc humore, equidem sufficeret aeque suo officio peragendo atq; oculus nullo morbido humore inquinatus. Sed deveniendo ad ictericos, quos arquatos & veternosos antiquitas vocavit, perhibet quidem Sextus ijs omnia videri flava sive pallida: atque astipulatur ei Lucret. lib. 4. Lurida praeterea fiunt quaecunque tuentur Arquati.
units.tr: (2) Sextus goes on, bringing forward another example: Our eyes, he says, have in themselves both coats and humours. Therefore visible things, since we cannot see them without these, are not perceived exactly and purely, for we perceive them with an admixture. But Sextus ought to consider that these things pertain to the make-up and structure of the eye, which has the character of a defective visual organ, if these very parts belonging to its structure are either diseased, or displaced, or hindered in performing their functions by a foreign body endowed with foreign and alien qualities. If the coats or the humours, being noted in the eye as belonging to it, were an impediment to the exercise of the visual function, this argument might be received with applause. But since they are requisites of the eye and belong to its structure, they cannot, if all things concerning them are rightly disposed, either hinder vision or cause deception in it of themselves. Nor does the instance of Empiricus, speaking thus next, hold: And for this reason, indeed, all things look pale to the jaundiced, but reddish to those who have hyposphagma. But how unfair it is to demand a sound and perfect sensation from a diseased organ! For if the eye of a jaundiced person were not tainted by this foreign humour through disease, it would surely suffice for performing its office as well as an eye not polluted by any morbid humour. But coming to the jaundiced, whom antiquity called arquati and veternosi, Sextus does indeed assert that everything looks yellow or pale to them, and Lucretius agrees with him in book 4: Moreover, whatever the arquati look upon becomes sallow.

units.la: idem perhibente Cassio Medico Probl. 26. item Galen. lib. 1. de caus. Sympt. cap. 2. & lib. de Ocul. aff. part. 4. cap. 6. at uti recte observatum est abHieronymo Mercuriale lib. 6. Var. Lect. cap. 12. nihil tale circa hunc ipsum morbum observatum est ab Hippocrate, Celso, Caelio Aureliano, atque Avicenna diligentissime licet omnia symptomata huc pertinentia persequenta: nec tale quid, qui hoc morbo laborant, unquam circa semet ipsos notarunt. quid quod ratio quoque idem non patiatur. Nam si hoc ictericis ictericis accideret, humor albugineus flava bile tinctus esse deberet: quod tamen accidere non potest. quamvis enim in illis bilis per totum universum corpus diffusa sit, illa tamen latitat duntaxat in venis qua majoribus, qua minoribus: atqui, neque in humore albugineo, neque in illa parte corneæ, eidem proxima, ullæ inveniuntur venæ; aut si quæ occurrant, sunt admodum exiles atque perbreves. Interim subinde, licet rarius, per venas illas angustas extraneum aliquem humorem apparenter diffundi, propter constitutionem corporis morbidam, negari non potest.
units.tr: The same is asserted by Cassius the physician, Probl. 26; likewise by Galen, book 1 On the Causes of Symptoms, chapter 2, and book On the Affections of the Eye, part 4, chapter 6. But, as Girolamo Mercuriale rightly observed, Lib. 6, Var. Lect., chapter 12, nothing of this kind has been observed concerning this very disease by Hippocrates, Celsus, Caelius Aurelianus, or Avicenna, although they pursued all the symptoms pertaining to it most diligently; nor have those who suffer from this disease ever noticed any such thing in themselves. What is more, reason also does not allow it. For if this happened to the jaundiced, the albuginous humour would have to be tinged with yellow bile; yet this cannot happen. For although in them the bile is diffused through the whole body, it lies hidden only in the veins, both the larger and the smaller. But no veins are found in the albuginous humour, nor in that part of the cornea which is nearest to it; or if any do occur, they are very thin and extremely short. Meanwhile, it cannot be denied that from time to time, though more rarely, some foreign humour may apparently diffuse itself through those narrow veins, on account of the morbid constitution of the body.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM OCTAVUM:
units.tr: CHAPTER EIGHTEEN:

units.la: Solvuntur ea argumenta, quæ à Sexto contra sensuum certitudinē petita sunt, á diversis quantitatibus & subjectorum sensibilium constitutionibus.
units.tr: The arguments that Sextus draws against the certainty of the senses, from different quantities and from the different constitutions of sensible objects, are answered.

units.la: PErgunt ulterius Sceptici, atque ut sensibus omnis fides abrogetur, argumentantur à variis quantitatibus, & diversis constitutionibus subjectorum sensibilium. Per exempla, more suo, argumentum hoc deducit & illustrat Sextus sic loquens: Ramenta cornu caprini apparent quidem alba simpliciter & sine compositione ea inuenintuentibus : composita autem in ipsius cornu essentia, nigra apparent cernentibus. Itidem & argenti ramenta si seorsum fuerint, nigra apparent: at cum toto, tanquam alba sub sensum cadunt. Quin & Tænarei lapidis partes quidem albæ videntur, quum lęvigatæ fuerint ac cum toto, flavæ. Similiter & arenæ separatæ aliæ ab aliis asperæ apparent: at in acervum compositę, molles à sensu percipiuntur. Præterea elleborum, si tenerum & lanuginosum quis ipsum edat, suffocationem affert: sin autem crassum, non item. Insuper & vinum si moderate bibatur, corroborat nos: si largius quam par est, sumatur, corpus frangit & dissolvit. Sic etiam cibus pro quantitate diversam facultatem profert, sæpe enim largior cibus sumptus corpus purgat per cruditatem & cholericas passiones. Hactenus Sextus. Sed nec huic argumento pro exarmandis sensibus plus ponderis inest quam reliquis, quę jam antea examinavimus. Quoniam res modo aliter atque aliter se habent, non possunt non quoque sub alia atque alia specie, obječtis sensibilibus adæquari solita, sub sensum cadere: Non debet quidem á quantitate [ut multis perperam persuasum fuit] tanquam caussa sufficienti peti ratio omnium eorum, quæ circa corpora naturalia animadvertuntur; interim tamen sub diversa quantitate (quæ est obiectum sensibile commune) deprehendi solent diversæ quoque qualitates: quæ si varient, cur non sensus quoque propter apprehensionem diversam ratione sui judicii varient? Verum ut à Sexto hic exhibetur farrago mera, exemplaque, quæ coacervantur, non cohærent; operæ pretium fuerit singula distincte considerasse. Atque quæ initio adferuntur de ramentis cornuum caprinorum, adeo inepta & diluta sunt, ut responsionem vix merearentur: cum cornibus caprinis, cervina cornua, & pariter dentes elephantini [quos perperam quidam inter cornua referre instituerunt] comparari possent: omnia enim ut intus candent, ita ratione exterioris superficiei nigredinem præ se ferunt: nec magis fallaciarum arguicirca hæc visus potest, distinctos quando colores notat, quam quando aliter iudicat sese habere juglandem nucem ratione exterioris corticis, quum viret, atque secundum respectum interioris corticis, sive medullæ, quæ exquisitum candorem præ ferre deprehenditur. Quod de argenti ramentis, diverso colore à massa argentea tinctis porro dicitur, ejusdem censeri debet farinæ cum præcedenti exemplo: argentum siquidem (ut observatum est ab omnibus rei Metallicæ scriptoribus) quo tempore è terræ visceribus primum eruitur, varium colorem, atque ut plurimum nigrum sive terreum præ se fert, nec candorem exquisitum acquirit, nisi aliquoties lotum, in catino coctum, eaque ratione expurgatum ac quasi à sordibus suis defæcatum fuerit: quod si aliunde non constaret, vel ex Scripturæ testimonio verum esse deprehenderetur, quæ quando aliquid ratione puritatis cum argento comparat, non simpliciter argenti meminit, sed aut argenti purgati in catino lectissimo terræ: & defæcati septies, ut Pf. 12. v. 7. aut, argenti conflati & sic probati, Pf. 66. verf. 10. aut, fusorii vasis, in quo quasi idem metallum defæcetur, Prov. 17. 3. & ut argentum, purgatum quoque, facili negotio (vel mulierculis illud notum est) quascunque sordes contrahit, ita ramentis & grumis eædem adhærent, adeo ut propterea nigram & terream faciem, eamque admodum diversam à candore argenteo, præ se ferre videatur. Circa argentum, hoc ut plausibilius notarentur, quod cum ipsum candidum sit, corpori tamen lineas nigras imprimat, uti post Plinium lib. 33. Nat. Hist. cap. 6. notavit Isidorus lib. 16. Orig. cap. 18. sed ne sic quidem sensibus quid deceptet: ut enim visus non fallitur, quando argentum iudicat esse candidum, ita neque fallitur, quando lineas illas judicat esse nigras, quatenus argentum admodum molle impressionem facit secundum fecundum ductilem mollitiem suæ substantiæ. Postea accedit Sextus ad Tænarium lapidem, [ credo innuit marmor Tœnarium ] cujus partes lœvigatæ albæ videantur, in toto autem consistentes nigræ sint. Sed, quid ab hoc qualicunque experimento derogatur certitudini sensuum? flavum lapidem, si politus fuerit, ratione repercussi, quod illapsum est, luminis, album videri quis miretur? Quæcunque tersa & lævigata corpora, ut recte docent atque demonstrant Optici, [videatur præ aliis Aguilonius lib. 4. Optic. Theorem. 149.] sive ab ea parte qua obscuritatem præ se ferunt, sive à qua parte illapsum lumen remittunt, sic sæpe afficiuntur, ut translucida quoque appareant. Pergit Sextus ad arenas, quarum singulæ seorsum consideratæ asperæ videantur, complures vero numero in acervum aggestæ molles appareant. Per mollitiem existimo intelligit ejusmodi arenarum dispositionem, secundum quam ipsæ immunes quasi ab aspera scabritie lævigatæ appareant visui: qui dum sic judicat, nequicquam fallitur, quum apprehendat illud, quod per adæquatam objecto sensibili speciem exhibetur: atque visum hic neutiquam falli, inde mihi manifestum, quod tactus, in consilium si adhibeatur, intellectui idem dijudicandum offerat, quod per expressam & convenientem
units.tr: The Sceptics go on further, and to strip all trust from the senses they argue from the varying quantities and the different constitutions of sensible objects. Sextus, in his usual manner, draws out and illustrates this argument with examples, speaking thus: "Filings of goat's horn appear white and unmixed to those who look at them alone, but when the substance of the horn is put together they appear black to those who see them. Likewise, filings of silver, if taken apart, appear black; but when they are with the whole mass, they fall under the senses as white. Indeed, the parts of the Taenarian stone appear white when they are polished, but yellow when they are with the whole. Similarly, sands separated from one another appear rough, but when heaped into a pile they are perceived by the sense as soft. Moreover, if someone eats hellebore tender and downy it brings on suffocation, but if it is thick it does not. Further, wine if drunk in moderation strengthens us, but if taken more than is fitting it breaks and dissolves the body. So too food produces a different power according to its quantity, for a larger meal often purges the body through indigestion and bilious passions." Thus far Sextus. But this argument has no more weight for disarming the senses than the others we have already examined. Since things sometimes stand one way and sometimes another, they cannot but fall under the senses under one or another appearance, corresponding to the sensible objects as they usually do. Indeed, the reason for all the things observed in natural bodies ought not to be sought from quantity as a sufficient cause, as many have wrongly been persuaded; yet under different quantities (which is a common sensible object) different qualities are commonly detected as well. If these vary, why should the senses not also vary in their judgment, on account of their different apprehension? But since Sextus here presents a mere hodgepodge, and the examples he heaps together do not cohere, it will be worth while to consider each one separately. And what is first brought forward about filings of goat's horn is so silly and feeble that it hardly deserves a reply. For stag's horns, and likewise elephant's teeth [which some have wrongly undertaken to count among horns], could be compared with goat's horn: all of them shine white within, yet show blackness on their outer surface. Nor can sight be shown to be more deceived here in noting distinct colours than when it judges, in respect of the outer husk, that a walnut is green, but in respect of the inner shell or pith, which is found to display exquisite whiteness, judges otherwise. What is said next about filings of silver, tinged with a colour different from the silver mass, must be counted of the same meal as the preceding example. For silver (as all writers on metallurgy have observed) at the time it is first dug from the bowels of the earth bears a varied colour, most often black or earthy, and does not acquire its exquisite whiteness unless it has been washed several times, heated in a basin, and in this way cleansed and, as it were, purged of its dregs. If this were not otherwise established, it would be shown to be true from the testimony of Scripture, which, when it compares something with silver for purity, does not mention silver simply, but either silver purified in a most choice vessel of earth and refined seven times, as in Ps. 12.7; or silver melted and so tried, Ps. 66.10; or a founder's vessel, in which the same metal is, as it were, purified, Prov. 17.3. And just as silver, even when purified, with ease (as even women know) contracts whatever dirt, so the filings and clots cling to it in the same way, so that for that reason it seems to present a black and earthy face, quite different from silvery whiteness. Concerning silver, this is noted to make the point more plausible: that although it is itself white, it nevertheless leaves black lines on the body, as Isidorus noted after Pliny, Natural History book 33, chapter 6, and Isidore, Origins book 16, chapter 18. But even so the senses are not deceived about anything: for as sight is not deceived when it judges silver to be white, so neither is it deceived when it judges those lines to be black, insofar as silver, being very soft, makes an impression according to the pliable softness of its substance.

units.la: speciem visus exhibuit. De elleboro deinceps agit Sextus, quod tenerum & lanuginosum suffocationem adferat, crassum non item: quod an ita se habeat, non deprehendo, unum Empiricum si excipias, a quoquam antiquo Scriptore memoriae traditum fuisse. At dato, hoc verum esse, an proinde quicquam decedit sensitivi judicii certitudini? hoc solum colligere licet, elleborum novellum, & adultum inveteratumque distinctis gaudere facultatibus, easque, ut diversimode se habent, diversimode quoque tum hominem afficere, tum sensibus quoque percipi. Quod postea subjicit de vino responsionem non meretur: illud ut hominis valetudini conservandae & restaurandae servit, si moderate sumatur, ita eandem laedit atque affligit, si in eo sumendo modus non fuerit observatus: sed, an propterea convenit sensus sua certitudine multare, eosque fallaciarum arguere? neutiquam. quia vinum, diversimode, pro diversa quantitate sumptum vires suas exerit, convenit distinctum pariter esse sensuum judicium. Eadem cibi ratio, a quo ad proslituendos sensus quando argumentatur postremo Sextus, tantundem facit, ac si vellet probare, ideo ventriculum hominis non sufficere digestioni cibi, quoniam una vice tantundem digerere non potest, quam sumere atque digerere solet Elephas.
units.tr: Sextus next deals with hellebore, that the tender and downy kind causes suffocation, the coarse kind does not. Whether this is so I do not discover, since, apart from one Empiric, no ancient writer has handed it down to memory. But even granting that this is true, does anything thereby detract from the certainty of sensitive judgement? All we can gather from this is that young hellebore and mature, aged hellebore have different powers, and that, as they are variously constituted, they affect a man in different ways and are perceived by the senses in different ways. What he adds afterwards about wine does not deserve a reply: wine serves to preserve and restore a man's health if it is taken in moderation, and in the same way it harms and afflicts him if due measure is not observed in taking it. But does it follow that the senses ought for that reason to be deprived of their certainty and convicted of deception? Not at all. Because wine, taken in different amounts, exerts its powers differently, it is fitting that the sensory judgement likewise be distinct. The same reasoning applies to food, with which Sextus, arguing last of all to overthrow the senses, does just as much as if he wished to prove that the human stomach is not sufficient for digesting food because it cannot digest at one time as much as an elephant is accustomed to take in and digest.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM NONUM
units.tr: CHAPTER NINETEEN

units.la: Quid existimandum sit de ludibriis diaboli, i- temque præstigiis, à quibus ordinario Scep- ticismi patroni argumentari solent.
units.tr: What is to be thought of the mockeries and illusions of the devil, by which the ordinary champions of Scepticism usually argue.

units.la: Amplius Sceptici ad evertendam sensuum certitudinem argumentari solent à ludibriis diabolicis, præstigiis, multiplicibusque circa sensationem defectibus, extraordinario accidere solitis. Contingunt vero hi defectus, sæpe arte diaboli, cui permittit aliquando Deus sensibus, prę ceteris visui, ludos facere. Hinc orta magia præstigiatrix. ut vero diabolus incautos præstigiis suis circumveniat, non tantum ratione organi & medii visorii, verum etiam objecti, visum impedire & fallere solet. Ex parte organi fallacias struit; cum aut mutat situm organi, aut humores agitat, ut res aliter ac sunt videantur; aut denique impedit sensationem, crassiore aliquo humore obstruendo viam, ne spiritus ad organum perveniant. Ex parte vero medii idem agit, quando impedit ne species ad oculum deferantur: aut cum medium imbuit aliqua qualitate, qua species per medium transeuntes sic modificantur, ut objectum non quale est, repræsentent. Aut si medium circa ipsum objectum incrasset: aut si. moto aëre medio, simul species moveat: aut denique quando species varie conformat & multiplicat, quod nonnunquam contingit ex parte instrumenti per quod videtur. Ex parte objecti oculis illudit: cum aut subito ex elementis, potissimum aëre, objectum format & spectatoribus offert, aut ostensas subito occultat, & alias loco earum supponit, aut objectum varie collocat, separat, ac conglutinat, aut postremo perspectivæ subsidio efficit, ut res, propter diversam collocationem, aliæ quam sunt, videantur. Secundum hos fallaciarum modos (qui plures sæpe conjunguntur) diabolum per sacerdotes suos coram Pharaone serpentes exhibuisse opinantur Iosephus, author quæstionum apud Iustinum Martyrem quæst. 26. Tertull. lib. de Anima cap. 57. Hieronym. ad Algasiam, Gregor. Nyssenus in vita Moysis, Sedulius lib. 4. Carmin. elink. Quæ sententia cum prę altera, quæ statuit veros serpentes à diabolo fuisse producios, paucioribus difficultatibus sit obnoxia, nobis cum Cl. D. Riveto ad 7. Exod. cap. aridet. Sic enim alias fallere quoque solet: ut cum v. c. facit ut hominės lupi, aut onocephali videantur, quod accidit aliquando in convivio quodam, teste Guil. Parif. p. ult. de univerf. cap. 22. Simili arte effecit, ut Claudiæ Zonam, navis, quæ vehebat matrem Idæam, sequi videretur, de quo Tertull. in Apolog. cap. 22. & Auguft. lib. 10. de civit. DEI cap. 16. Talibus quoque ludibriis, cooperante diabolo, admirandum se reddidit Simon Magus, teste Anastafio Nicęno q. 23. in Script. nec aliis pręstigiis celebris diaboli cliens Apollonius Thianæus credulum popellum circumvenit: quem frustra Cl. Gabriel Naudæus nupero tractatu magorum numero eximere, & clarissimis philosophis accensere laborat. Contrarium etenim ex Philostrato, & responso Eusebii Cæsarensis ad Hieroclem liquet. Eadem ludificatione Zedechias Iudęus, teste Trithem. in Chron. Hirsgav. tempore Ludovici Pii, hominem in aëre jactabat, in membra discerpebat, & ea recolleċta jungebat; currum etiam onustum fœno cum equis & agitatore coram toto populo absorbebat. Ejusdem notæ est fallacia Alberti Magni, cujus meminit Iohannes de Beka in Chron. Trajeċt. Nec tantum diaboli, sed boni etiam angeli visum turbant, concitando tum ejus sensorium, tum alterando medium aëra. Exemplum occurrit Genef. 19. v. 11. Neque enim e cœcitate putandum est percussos fuisse Sodomitas, sed potius aŏrafia: quæ qualis sit, docet August. lib. 22. de civit. Dei. cap. 19. Author Apocryphus libri Sapientiæ cap. 19. v. 16. de Sodomitis dicit eos circumamictos fuisse tenebris: quasi solum medium fuerit vitiatum, cum & organum & obiectum visus omnia sua requisita non videantur habuisse. Alias ipse Deus immediate, non utendo aut bono aut malo angelo, sensui, maxime visui, errandi occasionem praebere solet. Exempla occurrunt Num. 22. v. 31. 2. Reg. 6. v, Ioan. 20. v. 15. Luc. 24. v. 16. Quare vero à discipulis & Magdalena non fuerit agnitus Christus, scrupulosius inquirant eloquiorum divinorum interpretes. Quia Scriptura expresse de discipulis dicit retentos fuisse eorum oculos, malumus cum Augusti. lib. 3. de cons. Evang. & Hieron. ep. ad Pammach. dicere, prae ceteris mutationem fuisse in oculis spectantium, non vero aeque in ipso Christo, qui visus obiectum erat. Sed quamvis haec ita se habeant, neutiquam tamen hinc inferre licet omni tempore haec impedimenta a diabolo sensibus exhiberi. Quod quidam enim dicunt fieri posse ut ludibria a diabolo perpetuo exhibeantur, impietate non caret. Neque enim hostis generis humani dictator est, absolutumque imperium in hoc mundo habet. Catena divinae omnipotentiae constrictus ne quidem porcos vexare potest, nisi ei, cui volens nolens que subesse compellitur, antea placuerit. Math. 8. vocatur quidem ab Apostolo Eph. 2. v.2. princeps aëris. At hoc non favet Scepticis, ut non nemo putat. Haut magis enim inde sequitur, diabolum pro arbitrio, & quidem ordinario, aëra medium visus & auditus turbare ad fallendos homines posse, quam absolutum in mundum imperium obtinere: quia ab Apostolo scilicet in eadem epistola cap. 6. v. 12. dominus mundi adpellatur, hoc est, ut Tertul. lib. contra Marcionem vertit, mundi tenens. Quod expendens Augustin. in Ps. 54. dicit: Ne forte cum dixisset Mundi, intelligeres daemones esse rectores caeli & terrae: mundi dixit, tenebrarum harum: mundi dixit amatorum mundi: mundi dixit, impiorum & iniquorum: mundi dixit, de quo in Euangelio dicit: Et mundus eum non cognovit. Sic ergo & aëris principes sunt secundum quid, quia Deo permittente in eo aliquando varia meteora miscent & concitant. Iob. 1. v. 12. 16. 19. Apoc. 7. v. 1. Deo interim subservientes. Nam Iehova est, qui concitat nimbos Zach. 10. v. 1. Denique quod ad praestigias, eae sunt de raro contingentibus, nec semper diabolus iis ludere potest. Ad hoc ex duobus signis quae semper concurrunt, haut difficulter earum essectus internosci possunt. Nam [1.] tales essectus non oriuntur a motu locali, & superant naturalium causarum applicatarum activitatem. 2. Omnis praestigiosa machinatio statim evanescit, & nunquam diu perdurat. Recte Jamblichus de Mysterijs: Que fascinati imaginamur, praeter imaginamenta nullam habent actionis & essentia veritatem. Ejusmodi namque finis est magica artis, non facere simpliciter, sed usque ad apparentiam imaginamenta porrigere, quorum mox nec vola (quod dicitur) nec vestigium apparet. Duas vero has notas conjungere, non separare convenit.
units.tr: Furthermore, to overturn the certainty of the senses, the Sceptics usually argue from diabolical mockeries, illusions, and the many defects in perception that occur out of the ordinary. These defects happen often by the art of the devil, to whom God sometimes allows the power to play tricks on the senses, above all on sight. Hence arose the magic of illusion. But so that the devil may deceive the unwary with his illusions, he usually prevents and deceives sight not only through the organ and the medium of vision, but also through the object. He contrives deceptions through the organ, when he either alters the position of the organ, or stirs the humours so that things appear otherwise than they are, or finally hinders perception by blocking the way with some thick humour, so that the spirits cannot reach the organ. He does the same through the medium when he prevents the species from being carried to the eye, or when he imbues the medium with some quality by which the species passing through it are so modified that they represent the object not as it is. Or if he thickened the medium around the object itself; or if, by moving the air of the medium, he moves the species at the same time; or finally when he shapes and multiplies the species in various ways, which sometimes happens through the instrument by which one sees. He mocks the eyes through the object: when he either suddenly forms the object out of the elements, chiefly air, and presents it to the onlookers, or suddenly hides what was displayed and puts something else in its place, or arranges, separates, and joins the object in various ways, or finally, with the help of perspective, makes things appear different from what they are because of their different arrangement. According to these modes of deception (which are often combined in many ways), they think the devil, through his priests, displayed serpents before Pharaoh: Josephus; the author of the Questions attributed to Justin Martyr, Quest. 26; Tertullian, On the Soul, ch. 57; Jerome, To Algasia; Gregory of Nyssa, In the Life of Moses; Sedulius, Carmina, book 4. Since this opinion, which holds that the serpents were real and produced by the devil, is exposed to fewer difficulties than the other, it pleases us, with the most illustrious D. Rivet, on Exodus 7. For the devil is accustomed to deceive in other ways too, as when he makes men appear as wolves or onocentaurs, which happened once at a banquet, as William of Paris, last page of On the Universe, ch. 22, attests. By a similar art he caused Claudia's girdle to seem to follow the ship which carried the Idaean Mother, as Tertullian, Apology, ch. 22, and Augustine, City of God, book 10, ch. 16, report.
