Simon Magus, too, made himself admired by such mockeries, with the devil's cooperation, as Anastasius of Nicaea, Questions on Scripture, q. 23, attests; nor did Apollonius of Tyana, the famous client of the devil, deceive the credulous crowd with other illusions: whom the distinguished Gabriel Naudé labours in vain, in a recent treatise, to remove from the number of magicians and to count among the most celebrated philosophers. For the contrary is clear from Philostratus and from Eusebius of Caesarea's reply to Hierocles. By the same trickery the Jew Zedechias, as Trithemius, in the Hirsau Chronicle, attests, in the time of Louis the Pious, threw a man into the air, tore him limb from limb, and then gathered the pieces and joined them together; he also swallowed up, in front of the whole people, a chariot loaded with hay, together with the horses and the driver. Of the same kind is the illusion of Albert the Magnus, which John of Beka mentions in his Chronicle of Utrecht. Nor do only devils disturb sight, but also good angels, by stirring up the sensorium and altering the medium of the air. An example occurs in Genesis 19:11. For it should not be thought that the Sodomites were struck with blindness, but rather with aorasia, whose nature Augustine, City of God, book 22, ch. 19, explains. The apocryphal author of the book of Wisdom, ch. 19:16, says of the Sodomites that they were wrapped in darkness, as if only the medium had been impaired, when neither the organ nor the object of sight appear to have lacked any of their requisites. At other times God himself, acting immediately, without using either a good or a bad angel, is accustomed to offer the senses, above all sight, an occasion of error. Examples occur in Numbers 22:31; 2 Kings 6; John 20:15; Luke 24:16. Why Christ was not recognised by the disciples and by Magdalene, the interpreters of the divine oracles inquire more carefully. Since Scripture expressly says of the disciples that their eyes were held, we prefer, with Augustine, Harmony of the Gospels, book 3, and Jerome, letter to Pammachius, to say that the change was chiefly in the eyes of the onlookers, and not equally in Christ himself, who was the object of sight. But although these things stand thus, it does not follow at all from this that these impediments are presented to the senses by the devil at all times. For those who say that the devil can perpetually produce illusions lack no impiety. Indeed, the enemy of the human race is not the ruler of the world and does not hold absolute power in it. Bound by the chain of divine omnipotence, he cannot even trouble the pigs, unless it has first pleased Him to whom he is compelled to be subject, willing or unwilling. In Matthew 8 he is indeed called, by the Apostle, Ephesians 2:2, the prince of the air. But this does not favour the Sceptics, as someone thinks. For it does not follow any more from this that the devil can, at his own discretion, and indeed ordinarily, disturb the air, the medium of sight and hearing, in order to deceive men, than that he holds absolute dominion over the world: since, in the same epistle, by the Apostle, ch. 6:12, he is called lord of the world, that is, as Tertullian renders it in his book against Marcion, holder of the world. Augustine, weighing this in Psalm 54, says: Lest perhaps, when he had said "of the world," you should understand the demons to be the rulers of heaven and earth, he said "of the world" of these darknesses: he said "of the world" of the lovers of the world: he said "of the world" of the impious and the wicked: he said "of the world" of whom the Gospel says: "and the world did not know him." So then the princes of the air are such only in a certain respect, because, with God permitting, they sometimes stir up and mix various meteors in it, Job 1:12, 16, 19; Revelation 7:1, while serving God all the while. For it is Jehovah who stirs up the storms, Zechariah 10:1. Finally, as for illusions, they concern things that rarely happen, and the devil cannot always play such tricks. For this, their effects can be distinguished without much difficulty by two signs which always occur together. For (1) such effects do not arise from local motion, and they exceed the activity of the natural causes applied; (2) every illusory contrivance vanishes at once and never lasts long. Jamblichus rightly says in On the Mysteries: What the enchanted imagine has no reality of action or essence beyond the imaginings. For this is the aim of the magic art: not simply to make, but to extend the imaginings as far as an appearance, of which soon neither wing (as they say) nor trace appears. It is fitting to join these two marks, not to separate them.

units.la: CAPUT VIGESIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWENTY.

units.la: Dum sensuum judicio vacat homo vigilans, non debet, aut cum somniante, aut melancholico aliquo componi.
units.tr: While a waking man is free to judge by his senses, he ought not to be compared either with a dreamer or with some melancholic.

units.la: AMplius Sceptici, ut sensibus plane fidem abrogent, eosque omni certitudine atque fide exuant, adducunt tum homines fanaticos, tum etiam dormientes, quibus inter somniandum mirabilia saepe ludibria exhibentur, ijsdem tanta quoque pertinacia adhaerendo, ut jurare non solum audeant, sed paratissimi quoque sint, quecunque potius tormenta perpeti, quam deponere hanc opinionem, sibi non esse exhibitas tales species rerum sensibilium, quales nullus mortalium unquam in ullare animadvertere potuit. In exemplis ne haeream, quilibet in se descendere poterit, atque expendere qualia in somnio viderit, simulque excutere deliria hominum melancholicorum, quorum admirandæ, imo ridiculæ quoque historiæ apud medicos occurrunt. Ut respondeam vero, atque huic dubio satisfaciam, velim lectorem meminisse, me jam antea, quum agerem de sensatione hominis in communi, præsuppositum fuisse, ratione judicii mentem non debere vacillare, sed sanam atque integram esse. quod si hic iterum notetur, dico, ante omnia distingui oportere inter ipsas species sensitivas dormientibus & melancholicis exhibitas, & objectum extrinsecum per species illas repræsentatum: quod ad species phantasiæ repræsentatas, ut ut monstrosæ & confusæ quoque fuerint, nullum omnino dubium est, quin quales videntur, atque per conjunctionem comparationemque variarum specierum sensibilium (memoriæ custodiæ commissarum) efformantur, vere atque realiter phantasiæ, simulque menti ad easdem species se convertenti, exhibeantur; ut non mirum sit, melancholicis, reliquisque, quibus ratio vacillat, nulla ratione opinionem hanc eximi posse, quin tales species ijs sint exhibitæ, quæ quibusdam risum movent, aliis vero stuporem incutiunt. Ideo vero, sive somniantes sive melancholicos contingit falli circa has ipsas species, quod cum tantum coaluerint ex iis speciebus, quas intus apud se reconditas habent, pariter existiment iis respondere certa quædam objecta; quod accidit propter vitiosam ratiocinationem, quatenus hi ipsi non attendunt ipsam phantasticam facultatem, sufficere productioni novarum quarundum specierum sensibilium, ex ijs ipsis quas jam antea admisit: quibus novis speciebus si formaliter non inveniatur respondere ullum objectum sive extra somniantem, sive extra eum, cui atra bilis molestias exhibet, nequicquam tamen decedit illis imaginibus, quas alteruter horum intus penes se reconditas habet.
units.tr: Furthermore, in order to strip the senses of all trust and deprive them of all certainty and credit, the Sceptics bring forward both fanatics and sleepers. To sleepers, astonishing delusions are often shown in their dreams, and they cling to these so stubbornly that they not only dare to swear, but are most ready to endure any torment rather than give up the opinion that such appearances of sensible things were not shown to them, appearances that no mortal has ever been able to perceive while awake. Not to dwell on examples, anyone may look into himself and consider what he has seen in a dream, and at the same time examine the delusions of melancholic men, whose wonderful, indeed ridiculous, histories are found in the writings of physicians. To answer and satisfy this doubt, I would have the reader recall that I assumed earlier, when I treated of sensation in man in general, that reason should not waver in judgement but should be sound and whole. If this is objected again here, I say that one must first distinguish between the sensory species presented to sleepers and melancholics, and the external object that those species represent. As for the phantasy-species represented, however monstrous and confused they may be, there is no doubt at all that they truly and really appear to the imagination as they seem, and that they are formed through the conjoining and comparing of various sensory species (committed to the keeping of memory), and are presented both to the imagination and to the mind turning itself toward those same species. So it is no wonder that melancholics and others whose reason wavers cannot by any means be freed from this opinion, since such species are presented to them as move some to laughter and strike others with dread. And the reason why sleepers or melancholics are deceived about these very species is this: since they have been built up entirely out of the species they keep stored within themselves, they likewise suppose that certain objects correspond to them. This comes from faulty reasoning, in that they do not notice that the phantastic faculty is sufficient to produce new sensory species out of those it has already admitted. If no object formally corresponds to these new species, whether outside the dreamer or outside the man whom black bile troubles, nevertheless they do not depart from those images which each of these men keeps stored within himself.

units.la: Præterea haut raro qua somniantibus, qua melancholicis à spirituum animalium aut crassitie, aut confusione accidit turbari imagines, speciesque sensibiles; quæ ut hoc in casu non possunt aliter se habere atque se habent, ita per confusionem se aliosque decipit, quisquis non attendit ad impedimentum suæ imaginationi obortum: ut enim is, qui suffusione oculorum laborat, gnarusque est hujus impedimenti, non potest ad suam visionem tanquam accuratam provocare; ita neque somnians, neque melancholicus & febricitans, contendere aut potest aut debet, á parte rei, extra se mox occurrere illa omnia, quorum vitiosas species circumfert. in hunc sensum convenienter Themistius ad Aristotelis libellum de Insomnio cap.
units.tr: Moreover, it happens not rarely, both to dreamers and to melancholics, that the images and sensory species are disturbed by the thickness or confusion of the animal spirits. As in this case they cannot be otherwise than they are, so whoever does not attend to the impediment that has arisen in his imagination deceives both himself and others. Just as one who suffers from a cloudiness of the eyes, and knows of this impediment, cannot appeal to his own vision as accurate, so neither the dreamer, nor the melancholic, nor the feverish man can or should maintain, as a matter of fact, that all those things whose faulty species he carries about will at once meet him outside himself. Themistius speaks to this effect in agreement, in his commentary on Aristotle's little book On Sleep, chapter

units.la: 4.. loquitur: Ex iis, inquit, omnibus illud quoque constat eandem rationem, qua morbo quodam aliqui in vigilia falluntur, facere uti in somno quoque decipi soleamus. Vt enim spiritus quidam in ægrotis ad caput viam molitus crassamento suo visibile spiritum vehementer conturbat, committitque ut omnia quæ tuentur gemina videantur, & ut lineamnta albarii operis immanium belluarum speciem referant (nam simulachra delineaturarum sine materia intra oculos recepta, & cum spiritu visuali male habito & lacessito confusa, formas illas animalium truces repræsentant) ita & in somno illo idem spiritus caussa est erroris. Sed & valentes quoque atque adeo scientes [nempe quatenus intellectus ad impedimenta objecta non attendit] interdum falli contingit, ut si res nimio tractu remota & longiuscule dissita sit, aut si qua oculi motiuncula obstupescant: nam & pedalis sol spectantibus, & terra moveri & commeare navigantibus videtur. Quod si hoc verum in scientibus & valentibus est, quanto in ægro verius sit, & adhuc in dormiente propensius? Hæc ille. Injurii vero non in hominem sensibus & ratione à Deo instructum, verum in ipsum quoque Deum sunt, quotquot persuasum cupiunt, hominem vigilantem quoque, parum aut nihil à dormiente & somniante distare, jubentque. jubentque eum non minus vigilantem & videntem,quam somniantem suspectare illas imagines quæ subsidio sensuum exhibentur. Non inficias iverim, forte hos ipsos, qui talia argumentorum præsidia pro Sceptics excogitaverunt, (quum perpetuo animo fluctuent, nec ulli rei toto animi conatu assentiantur, præterquam quando inanes sperant applausus) difficulter distinguere posse inter semetipsos, qua vigilantes, qua somniantes: Interim cui placuerit ad ea attendere, quę superioribus hujus libri capitibus propositimus, pariterque comprobavimus, ei non poterunt non omnia pro hoc discrimine quam explorata esse. Somniantes ut sensus ligatos habent, ita eorundem pariter phantasia mirum quam confusa atq; turbata est, rationeq; talis impedimenti, illas imagines quæ obversantur, & circa quas hærent, subsidio aliorum sensuum examinare non instituunt; minime vero tactum pro eorundem confirmatione præsidioque adhibent, aut, si magis casu quam consilio hoc facere instituerint, ilico, velut exstimulante tanto monitore, non minus somnus quam somnium propelluntur, atque vanitas imaginum, fallacissima quæque menti exhibentium, quantoocyus deprehenditur: quomodo constat noctambulos, secundum exhibitas imagines mirabilia sæpe expedientes, excitari, simulque rationi, sensuique à ratione directo magis respondent, simulatque alicubi forte, aut pedem, aut aliud aliquod corporis membrum alliserint, validiorique concussione admoniti fuerint de fallacia imaginum, à quibus paulò ante ad inusitata impellebantur. Secundum quod principium progrediendo, convenienter dicere possum, certum mihi esse, me non somniare, aut ut in somnio functiones meas exercere, quia imagines secundum quas progredior, non solum ipsi objecto, quod repræsentare videntur, applicare possum, verum etiam si suspectem unum aliquem singularem sensum, plures, duce ratione, pro examine & confirmatione eorum, quæ ab hoc unico sensu per species exhibita videntur, tuto examino.
units.tr: 4.. speaks: From these things, he says, it is also clear that the same cause by which some are deceived when awake by a certain disease is the cause by which we are accustomed to be deceived in sleep as well. For just as a certain spirit in the sick, having made its way to the head, greatly disturbs the visual spirit with its thickness, and causes everything they look at to appear double, and the outlines of a whitewashed work to resemble the shapes of monstrous beasts (for the images of the drawings, received without matter within the eyes and confused with the visual spirit that is ill-disposed and irritated, represent those savage forms of animals), so in sleep the same spirit is the cause of the error. But it also sometimes happens that even healthy and indeed learned people are deceived [namely, insofar as the intellect does not attend to the obstacles], as when the object is very far away and set at too great a distance, or when some small movement of the eye is dulled; for the sun, which is a foot wide, appears so to onlookers, and the earth seems to move and to glide along to those who sail. But if this is true of the learned and healthy, how much truer is it of the sick, and still more inclined to be so of the sleeper? That is his view. Yet those who wish to be persuaded of this do wrong not only to man, who is furnished by God with senses and reason, but to God himself, when they declare that a waking man differs little or not at all from a sleeper or dreamer. They bid him, while awake and seeing, to be no less suspicious of those images which are presented with the help of the senses than a dreamer is. I will not deny that perhaps these very men, who have devised such arguments as props for the Sceptics (since they are always wavering in mind and do not assent with their whole heart to any matter, except when they vainly hope for applause), may find it hard to distinguish between themselves, whether they are waking or dreaming. Meanwhile, anyone who has been pleased to attend to what we set out in the earlier chapters of this book, and likewise proved, will find that all these things are sufficiently established for this distinction. Sleepers have their senses bound, and in the same way their phantasy is wonderfully confused and disturbed; and because of such impairment they do not set about testing, by the help of their other senses, the images that present themselves and to which they cling. They by no means use touch to confirm and support them; or if they happen by chance rather than by design to do so, then at once, as though stirred by so great a warner, both sleep and dream are driven off, and the vanity of the images, which present the most deceptive things to the mind, is quickly detected. Thus it is evident that sleepwalkers, who often carry out extraordinary acts in accordance with the images presented to them, are woken, and at once respond more to reason and to the senses directed by reason, as soon as they happen to strike a foot or some other part of the body somewhere, and, being admonished by a sharper jolt, recognise the falsehood of the images by which a little before they were driven to unusual actions. Proceeding on this principle, I can rightly say that I am certain I am not dreaming, nor exercising my functions as in a dream, because the images by which I proceed can not only be applied to the very object they seem to represent, but also, if I suspect any single sense, I can safely test them with several senses, guided by reason, for the examination and confirmation of what seems to be shown through the species by that one sense alone.

units.la: Mirum vero, eos, qui non solum alieni à Scepticismo videri cupiunt, sed amplius censeri inter Christianos, tantam difficultatem invenire, ut possint se vigilantes à semet tum dormientibus tum somniantibus distinguere, cum tamen Scriptura tam dilucide actus illos, ratione earum quoque personarum, quibus acciderunt, non uno in loco distinguat. Noachus, qui vino inebriatus in profundiorem somnum inciderat, expresse evigilasse dicitur Gen. 9. vers. 24. & cognovisse illud, quod filius suus Cham fecerat similiter de Iacobo testatur Spiritus sanctus Gen. 28. vers 16. quod evigilaverit è somnio suo: atque de Simpsone pariter quod expergefactus fuerit è somno suo, Iud. 16. 20. que omnia admodum inconvenienter, atque præter veritatem proponerentur, si vigilans à dormiente aut somniante non distaret. Pari ratione deliria melancholicorum, phreneticorum, hominumque similium detegi possunt: quamvis enim ipsi hæreant atque fluctuent in examine imaginum, quæ sibi obversantur, atque circa quas subsistunt sæpe nimis quam pertinaciter. alii tamen, quibus ipsi suas imagines ac simulacra explicant, quantum iisdem deferri mereatur deprehendunt, simulac easdem objectis, quæ pariter præsentia cogitant melancholi, similesque secundum ea, quæ jam antea proposita fuerunt, applicare instituunt. Imo subsidio tactus, qui fallaciis præ aliis sensibus minus obnoxius existit, ipsi melancholici, atque qui iis similes sunt, deprehendunt sæpe fallacias circa imagines phantasticas, nimis prepropere à se objectis exæquari, si non cum iisdem confundi solitar. Objiciunt vulgo nonnulli adversus ea, quæ jam dicta sunt, atque è præcedentibus, si cum iisdem comparentur, clarius patere possunt, eos, quibus vigilantibus quoque, sive pes, sive brachium gangræna aut sphacelo correptum, præcisum fuerit, quod postquam pro vitæ conservatione ex consilio prudentis medici, iisquoque membris multati fuerint, nihilominus conquerantur de majori quodam dolore, tanquam inhærente membris, quæ jam à reliquo corporis trunco separata sunt. Sed, quibus hoc argumentum velut Achilles est, cogitare deberent hos ipsos, quos testimonium contra veritatem dicere compellunt, post ablationem membrorum suorum, non conqueri solere de dolore aliquo ex suo sensu subjectivè inhærente ipsis illis membris quæ ablata sunt, sed de dolore, quem maximum persentiscunt in loco admodum propinquo iis membris, quæ ob præcavendum majus incommodum actu separata esse sciunt. Nec causa hujus rei est obscura: quod spiritus post sectionem institutam, tam copiose ad extremitatem truncorum artuum deferri consueverint, ut propter divulsionem distractionemque, quam vehementiori hoc illapsu procurant, haud aliter se affici, & in equuleo molesti atq; dolorifici morbi exerceri existiment, atque cum similis ex sua sententia sensatio in affecto membro deprehenderetur.
units.tr: It is strange, however, that those who wish not only to appear alien to Scepticism, but to be counted among Christians, find it so difficult to distinguish themselves, when awake, from those who are asleep or dreaming, since Scripture in more than one place distinguishes these states so clearly, with regard also to the persons to whom they happened. Noah, who had fallen into a deeper sleep after being overcome with wine, is expressly said to have awoken and to have known what his son Ham had done (Gen. 9. vers. 24). The Holy Spirit likewise testifies of Jacob that he awoke from his sleep (Gen. 28. vers. 16), and of Samson, equally, that he was awakened from his sleep (Judg. 16. 20). All these things would be set forth most inappropriately and contrary to truth if a waking man did not differ from a sleeper or dreamer. By the same reasoning, the delusions of melancholics, the frenzied, and men of similar sort can be exposed. For although they themselves hesitate and waver in examining the images that present themselves to them, and cling to them often more stubbornly than is right, others, to whom they describe their images and phantoms, discover how much credit they deserve, as soon as they begin to apply these images to objects which the melancholic likewise thinks present, and to similar ones, according to what has been set out above. Indeed, with the help of touch, which is less liable to deception than the other senses, the melancholics themselves, and those like them, often discover deceptions about phantastic images, which they had too hastily equated with objects, or at least were accustomed to confuse with them. Some commonly object against what has been said, and it can be seen more clearly from the preceding if these are compared with it, that persons who, while awake, have had a foot or arm seized by gangrene or sphacelus and cut off, afterwards, even though for the preservation of life, on the advice of a prudent physician, they have been deprived of those limbs, still complain of a greater pain, as though it inhered in the limbs that have already been separated from the rest of the trunk. But those for whom this argument is their Achilles' heel should consider that those very men whom they compel to bear witness against the truth, after the amputation of their limbs, are not accustomed to complain of a pain inhering subjectively in those amputated limbs by their sense, but of a pain which they feel most strongly in a place very near those limbs, which they know have been removed in order to prevent a greater harm. Nor is the cause of this thing obscure: after the incision has been made, the spirits are usually conveyed so copiously to the extremity of the severed limbs that, because of the tearing and stretching which this more violent influx produces, they believe they are affected in no other way, and are tormented by painful and troublesome disease as on the rack. And so, according to their opinion, a similar sensation is perceived in the affected limb.

units.la: CAPUT VIGESIMUM PRIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE.

units.la: Quamvis ratio superior sensusfit, non tamen ei omnia, abrogatis sensibus, deferri debent.
units.tr: Although the higher reason is the judge of the senses, nevertheless not everything is to be handed over to it once the senses have been set aside.

units.la: ULterius nobis progrediendum, & despiciendum est, an etiam Philosophi sit sensus in consilium adhibere, & non potius illorum usus relinqui debeat vulgo, quod circa corticem duntaxat herere, & ad interiora rerum penetralia progredi non solet. Affirmativa assertio haut paucis hoc seculo placet, qui tamen à Scepticis atque Academicis longissime remoti videri cupiunt. Non diffitendum vero, sensus circa externa accidentia tantum haerere, atque propria eorundem obiecta esse nudas qualitates, & quidem singulares, nullatenus vero illos aut ipsas substantias, sive naturas substantiales, aut universalia quoque, circa quae tamen sola scientiae omnes versantur, posse per se percipere. Interim tamen Sapiens iis se multare non debet, atque in gratiam substantiarum & universalium abdicare sensus sive in totum, sive saltem suspectare eorundem certitudinem, quatenus eadem hactenus a nobis considerata fuit: nam ut non permittimus ratione hominis sensui suam certitudinem, nisi arbitrante ipsa mente de illis requisitis, quae circa sensationem omnem à mente ipsa expendenda esse diximus: ita quoque in his naturalibus (de supernaturali speculatione postea) non concedendū ulla ratione menti, ut aliquid pronunciet, quod sensuum judicio ab ipso intellectu directe deprehenditur contrarium esse. Fateor equidem ad multa pertingere rationem, ad quæ nullus sensus accedere potest, interim tamen reluctantibus sensibus hæc penetralia ratio ipsa subire non debet. Imo, quo subeat talia profunda, quicquid aliis hic videatur, indiget subsidio sensuum tanquam ductorum. Verum quippe illud Philosophi lib. 3. de Anima cap. 7. Nunquam sine phantasmate [in naturalibus scil.] intelligit anima. & iterum cap. 8. Quando intellectus speculatur, necesse est una cum phantasmate speculari. Qualia vero hæc ipsa phantasmata sint postea addit: Nam phantasmata velut sensibilia sunt; præterquam quod sint sine materia. Quod verissimum esse, contra dissentientes probo ab exemplo rerum mathematicarum, à quibus tamen, ut postea liquebit, illi ipsi ordinario argumentari solent. Quæ enim ratio, quod qui à nativitate cæcus ac surdus est, Geometriam addiscere non queat, cum tamen sufficiat aliis disciplinis addiscendis, imo ipsi quoque Arithmeticæ, ac Musicæ? nulla alia, quam quia figuras Geometricas, quas nunquam sensibus percepit, animo quoque repræsentare non potest. Præclare Themistius ad lib. 3. de Anima cap. 53. Omnia, dicit, pendent à materia sensili. Cujus rei firmissimum argumentum est, quod qui inde ab ortu cæcus surdusque fuerit, non potest Geometriam condiscere, quia circulum, triangulum, quadrantale animo concipere aut præsentire compos non est, sed fervidum, algidum, dulce, amarum, odorolentum, obolidum, atque hæc quoque ideo quia sentiuntur. Intellectu quoque unitatis & binarii, postremo numeri omnis de sensibilibus venit. Quamobrem quoties hoc genuere rum speculatur meditaturque animus, necessario sibi visa quædam & similitudines confingit, ad quæ, dum cogitat, subinde se convertit. Imo ipsi sensus ut præcedunt intellectum, ita serviunt confirmationi eorum, quæ intellectus ratiocinando secundum sensus quasi collegisse videtur. Quod liquebit, si unum aut alterum exemplum subduxerimus iis, qui in præjudicium seusuum pro rationis sive intellectus prærogativa digladiantur. Ut sensuum ergo fallaciam arguant, eosque eo nomine proscribant, adducere solent Lunam, quam visus lucidam esse existimat, quum tamen ex sensu suo sit opaca, & altera quædam terra suos montes, valles, mare, fluvios, & insulas habens. quod si admittamus, queram, an non hanc ipsam Lunę faciem duce visu intellectus exploraverit? nisi enim oculus adjutus fuisset telescopii subsidio, illa, quæ a quovis in Luna animadverti non possunt, neutiquam notata forent, nec posset intellectus ex iis concludere Lunam opacam pariter esse: tubus siquidem, ut & conspicilia omnia, quod in organo visorio desideratur, emendant. Sed cum viri maximi, atque inter eos Claramontius, tubi alias admirandi, atque in Batavia primitus inventi, certitudinem suspectare, nec sine omni ratione coeperint; quomodo intellectus poterit reddi certus ratione observationum per hunc tubum circa corpora cælestia institutarum, nisi in iis, quæ palpari atque pluribus sensibus explorari possunt, similem ejusdem aut æqualis tubi certitudinem exploraverit. Iterum iidem existimant, sensus imbecillitatem ex eo argui, quod cum famem quidem percipiat, ad ejus tamen causam accedere non queat. Sed neque ratio, nisi in subsidium venirent sensus, eam ipsam causam investigare posset: quis enim judicaret eam oriri inde, quod in ventriculo membranoso fibrarum & nervorum contractio fiat, nisi ipso visu certò exploratum foret, hanc ventriculi fabricam atque constitutionem esse. Denique, ut finiam, quæ sententia petulanti hoc seculo majori cum applausu recepta fuit, atque ea, cujus author censetur Harvæus esse, de circulatione scilicet sanguinis? in qua explicanda, atque omnigenis rationibus confirmanda, diligentius qua medici, qua philosophi quotidie occupantur? at ea ipsa tamen, quæ multorum judicio venerabilem antiquitatem & philosophiam sensualem (ita multis loqui placet) prosltituit, à sensualibus observationibus incepit. Illique, qui maxime probabiliter pro eadem stare videntur, rationibus suis fulcrum solidissimum accedere existimant, si rationem explicationis (de ea non convenit) experimentis sensualibus afferre queant: sic, ut mirari lubeat, cur quidam, qui hanc tamen & similes novitias sententias quam maxime admirantur, adeo abjecte de sensuum usu in Philosophia arbitrentur. Intellectiva facultas superior est sensitiva, atque ad hominis perfectionem pertinet, quod sensuum moderatricem rationem habeat: interim ratio in rebus sensibilibus non debet sibi arrogare dictatoriam potestatem, ut aliquid de iis ipsis pronunciare, sensibus neque favent ibus, neque qua ratione ipsum intellectum juvantibus. Est quædam perfectio (postea pluribus hac de re acturi sumus) mentem à sensibus posse abducere; sed hæc ipsa abductio non requiritur circa sensibilia, de quibus si pro suo arbitrio sepositis sensibus intellectui hariolari liceat, quascunque Chimæras atque Centauros impune proponere poterit.
units.tr: We must go further and consider whether the philosopher too ought to take the senses into counsel, and whether their use should not rather be left to the common people, who usually cling only to the bark of things and do not penetrate to their inner sanctuaries. The affirmative view pleases not a few in this age, who nonetheless want to appear far removed from the Sceptics and Academics. It must be admitted that the senses cling only to external accidents, that their proper objects are bare qualities, and indeed particular ones, and that they can in no way perceive by themselves either substances or substantial natures, or universals, though all the sciences are concerned with these alone. Still, the wise man should not deprive himself of the senses, nor renounce them altogether for the sake of substances and universals, nor even become suspicious of their certainty, so far as we have considered it up to now. For just as we do not allow the senses their certainty by human reasoning, except when the mind itself weighs the requirements which we said must be assessed by the mind in every sensation, so too in these natural matters (we will speak of supernatural speculation later) the mind must on no account be permitted to pronounce anything which the intellect itself directly perceives to be contrary to the judgement of the senses. I grant indeed that reason reaches many things to which no sense can attain; yet, while the senses resist, reason ought not to enter these sanctuaries. Indeed, whatever others may think here, reason needs the help of the senses as guides in order to penetrate such depths. For the saying of the Philosopher is true, in De Anima book 3, chapter 7: The soul never understands [in natural matters, that is] without a phantasm. And again, chapter 8: When the intellect contemplates, it must contemplate together with a phantasm. He then adds what these phantasms themselves are like: For phantasms are as it were sensibles, except that they are without matter. That this is most true I prove against the dissenters from the example of mathematical things, from which, as will later become clear, they themselves ordinarily argue. For what reason is there that a man blind and deaf from birth cannot learn geometry, although he is able to learn other disciplines, and even arithmetic and music? There is no other reason than that he cannot represent to his mind the geometrical figures which he has never perceived by the senses. Themistius rightly says on De Anima book 3, chapter 5: Everything, he says, depends on sensible matter. The firmest proof of this is that one who has been blind and deaf from birth cannot learn geometry, because he is not able to conceive or grasp in his mind a circle, a triangle, or a quadrant; but he can grasp the hot, the cold, the sweet, the bitter, the odorous, and the tasteless, and these also because they are sensed. Even the concept of unity and of two, and indeed of every number, comes from sensible things. Therefore, whenever the mind contemplates and meditates on these kinds of things, it necessarily forms certain images and likenesses to itself, to which it keeps turning while it thinks. Indeed, just as the senses precede the intellect, so they also serve to confirm those things which the intellect seems to have gathered, by reasoning, from the senses. This will become clear if we take one or two examples from those who wrangle for the pre-eminence of reason or intellect to the prejudice of the senses. To prove the senses deceptive, and so to banish them on that ground, they usually cite the Moon, which sight judges to be bright, although by its own sense it is dark, and is another earth having its own mountains, valleys, seas, rivers and islands. But if we grant this, I ask whether the intellect itself would have explored this very face of the Moon guided by sight? For unless the eye had been aided by the help of the telescope, those things which cannot be observed on the Moon by anyone would never have been noticed, nor could the intellect have concluded from them that the Moon is likewise dark: for the tube, like all spectacles, corrects what is lacking in the organ of vision. But since very great men, and among them Claramontius, have begun to doubt the certainty of the tube, admirable in other respects and first invented in Batavia, not without good reason, how could the intellect be made certain, by reason of observations of the heavenly bodies made through this tube, unless it had first tested the same or an equal certainty of the tube in things which can be touched and examined by several senses? Again, the same men think that the weakness of the senses is shown by the fact that, although they perceive hunger, they cannot reach its cause. But reason itself could not investigate that cause unless the senses came to its aid: for who would judge that it arises from a contraction of fibres and nerves in the membranous stomach, unless it had been surely established by sight that this is the structure and constitution of the stomach? Finally, to end, what opinion has been received with greater applause in this petulant age, the one whose author is thought to be Harvey, namely that concerning the circulation of the blood? Physicians and philosophers busy themselves every day, more diligently, both in explaining it and in confirming it by every kind of argument. Yet this very doctrine, which in the judgement of many has prostituted venerable antiquity and sensual philosophy (as some like to put it), began from sensible observations. And those who seem most plausibly to stand for it think that their arguments gain the firmest support if they can bring forward an explanation of it (on which there is no agreement) by sensible experiments. So it is a wonder that some who so greatly admire this and similar new opinions think so meanly of the use of the senses in philosophy. The intellectual faculty is superior to the sensitive, and it belongs to human perfection that reason should govern the senses. Yet reason, in matters that are sensible, must not claim for itself a dictatorial power to pronounce anything about them while the senses are neither favourable nor helpful to the intellect in any way. There is a certain perfection (we shall speak of this at greater length later) of being able to lead the mind away from the senses; but this withdrawal is not required in the case of sensible things, for if the intellect were allowed, with the senses set aside at its own pleasure, to conjecture about them, it could propose with impunity whatever Chimaeras and Centaurs it liked.

units.la: CAPUT VIGESIMUM SECUNDUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWENTY-SECOND.

units.la: Quid existimandum sit de abstractione men- tis à sensibus, cujus indicantur pericula.
units.tr: What is to be thought of the abstraction of the mind from the senses, and the dangers it brings.

units.la: PRogrediendo in hac doctrina, despiciendum deinceps, quid existimandum sit de mentis abstractione: multi siquidem quo menti ad submotionem sensuum prærogativam procurent, contendunt eam à sensibilibus & singulari-bus omnibus abstrahendam esse, quod eo modo abstracta sibique relicta ante se quasi habeat ideas, [uti loquuntur] veritatis atq; certitudinis, quas tepositis sensibus si intueatur, tum demum liquidas veritates, de quibus ambigere non liceat, sibi propositas intueri possit. Multa jactari quidem audio de hac abstractione, sed lubens fateor, me videre non posse, quomodo mens tali modo abstracta sublevetur in cognitione rerum naturalium. nam quamvis negare non liceat, quin mens abstrahi possit, ac quedam eidem perfectio per hanc ipsam abstractionem accedat, interim tamen abstracta à sensibus, sistitur in contemplatione aut sui, aut eorum quæ eidem ad modum communium notionum
units.tr: Proceeding in this teaching, we must next consider what is to be thought about the abstraction of the mind. Many people, in order to give the mind precedence in setting aside the senses, contend that it must be abstracted from all sensible and particular things. In that abstracted state, they say, the mind has left to itself, as it were, certain ideas of truth and certainty, [as they put it], and if it looks at these with the senses set aside, it can then at last behold clear truths before it, about which it is not permitted to doubt. I hear many claims made about this abstraction, but I frankly confess that I cannot see how a mind abstracted in this way is raised up to knowledge of natural things. For although it cannot be denied that the mind can be abstracted, and that a certain perfection comes to it through this very abstraction, nevertheless, once abstracted from the senses, it stops in contemplation either of itself or of those things which inhere in it in the manner of common notions

units.la: notionum de rebus immaterialibus inhærent, quæ qualia sint, deinceps distinctè infra hoc libro expendemus. Nec aliter fieri potest, nam eo ipso quod per abstractionem mens sese subducit à rebus corporeis, sublevari debet ad ea, quæ incorporea sunt, quæ à mente percepta eam pariter non deducere ad cognitionem rerum corporearum, deinceps liquebit. Egregie Augustinus lib. 12. de Trinit. cap. 15. Credendum est, inquit, mentis intellectualis ita conditam naturam esse, ut rebus intelligibilibus, naturali ordine disponente conditore, subjuncta, sic ipsa videat in quadam luce sui generis incorporea; quemadmodum oculus carnis videt quae in hac corporea luce circumadjacet; cujus lucis capax eique congruens est creatu. at quis incorporea hæc definite explicet? inter ea ut primo loco occurrit Deus, ita quatenus per hanc abstractionem cognoscendo attingatur deinceps explicabimus. hoc loco duo solum monemus: primo non omnes capaces esse hujus abstractionis, quod fateri coguntur illi ipsi, qui eandem maxime urgent. multorum mens sensibus nimium quam addicta, imbecillior est, quâ ut avelli ab iis queat, quibus ordinario adhærere solet. Quibus si quis author esse præsumpserit, ut mentem sublevent, atque à sensibilibus & corporeis rebus abstrahant, non solum iis difficultatem maximam procurabit
units.tr: notions of immaterial things. What these are we shall examine distinctly later in this book. Nor can it happen otherwise. For by the very fact that through abstraction the mind withdraws itself from corporeal things, it must be raised up to those things which are incorporeal. That these things, once perceived by the mind, do not likewise lead it to knowledge of corporeal things will become clear later. Augustine writes admirably in book 12 of On the Trinity, chapter 15: It must be believed that the nature of the intellectual mind is so constituted that, subjected to intelligible things by the ordering of nature by the Creator, it sees itself in a certain incorporeal light of its own kind, just as the eye of the flesh sees the things that lie around it in this corporeal light; and the creature is capable of this light and fitted to it. But who explains these incorporeal things definitely? Among them, God first comes to mind; how far he is attained by knowing through this abstraction, we shall explain later. In this place we note only two things. First, not all are capable of this abstraction, which those very men who press it most are forced to admit. The mind of many is too strongly given over to the senses and too weak to be torn away from those things to which it ordinarily clings. If anyone presumes to be the author for them, to lift up their minds and abstract them from sensible and corporeal things, he will not only create the greatest difficulty for them

units.la: verum viam quoque muniet ad carceres phreneticorum. Dum enim in hoc toti sunt, ut à sensibus, & sensibilibus omnibus divortium faciant, contingit admodum turbari spiritus, & ab iis cerebrum ; quod species phantasticæ ægre patientes hanc separationem, in spiritibus quibus deferuntur, maximam, eamque tumultuariam commotionem agitationemque procurent. verum quidem, mens nostra est inorganica, nec dependet ratione suarum operationum aut à corpore, aut illius temperie, interim tamen quandiu anima in corpore, tanquam in ergastulo delitescit, indiget subsidio sensuum tum internorum, tum externorum, intelligendoque phantasmata contemplatur; quorum diuturnior atque intensior contemplatio ut lassitudinem & fatigationem intelligenti adfert; [quocunque meditante hoc testante] ita in separatione hac exstatica multis tanta cerebri & spirituum qui in eo sunt agitatio contingit, ut primo in vertiginem, dein delirium, ac postremo quoque in phrenesin incidant: quod si per exempla probandum esset, varii ex ordine eorum ipsorum, qui præ cæteris novam hanc methodum amplexi fuerunt, adduci possent. Alterum incommodum, quod circa hanc abstractionem noto, est illud, quod ex Dei indultu diabolus sæpe sese consueverit immiscere cogitationibus eorum, qui huic abstractioni propemodum contra suam naturam plus æquo indulgent, eosque specie falsi miserandum in modum circumvenire. De Plotino Philosopho Platonico incomparabili ita in vita illius Porphyrius: Simul secum erat, & cum aliis, intentionemque mentis ad se conversa nunquam intermittebat, nisi forsan cum dormiret. Quamvis & sommum ab eo procul excusserit tum cibi parcitas, tum assidua quaedam conversio ipsius ad mentem. Hunc ipsum tamen sacris quoque magicis operatum fuisse ignorare nos non finit idem Porphyrius, narrat quippe eum daemonem familiarem habuisse, ad quem divinum semper suae mentis oculum sublimius erigeret. Præter Plotinum alij quoque Academici, speciatim Porphyrius, Olympius, Amelius, Jamblichus, reliqui que qui circa tempus Diocletiani Imp. vixerunt, toti in eo esse solent, ut mentem suam altius erigerent, eamque à rebus sensibilibus atque terrenis averterent: sed dum hoc agunt, omnesque suae mentis nervos intendunt, ne quid præter ipsam mentem à sensibus & rebus sensibilibus viduatam contemplentur, magicarum rerum cupiditate depravati sunt, quemadmodum testatur August. Epist. 56. rationem idem adfert lib. 10. Confess. cap. 42. quando ita loquitur: Multi conantes ad te redire, ne-que que per se ipsos valentes, sicut audio, tentaverunt hæc, & inciderunt in desiderium curiosarum visionum, & digni habiti sunt illusionibus. Elati enim te quærebant doctrinæ fastu, exercentes potius quam tundentes pectora, & adduxerunt sibi per similitudinem, cordis sui conspirantes & socias superbę suę potes-tates aëris hujus; a quibus per potentias magicas deciperentur, quærentes mediatorem per quem purgarentur, & non erat. Hæc tile. Quamvis dici in communi possit, diabolum ibi maxime suis præstigiis fallaciisque ludere posse, ubi offendit mentem ob indispositionem phantasiæ confusam turbatamque. Per hanc occasionem existimaverjm quoque Socratem incidisse in familiaritatem cum dæmone. Transformat quidem hunc ipsum in Deum Apulejus in peculiari libello, quem scripsit de Deo Socratis, sed arguit eum, ac quidem jure merito Augustinus lib. 8. de Civit. Dei cap. 14. Hæc si ita sunt, inquit, qua licet apud alios quoque reperiantur, Apulejus tamen Madaurensis, de hac re sola unum scripsit librum. cujus titulum esse voluit, de Deo Socratis, ubi disserit & exponit, ex quo genere numinum numen sibi Socrates habebat adjunctum, & amicitia quadam conciliatum, a quo perhibetur solitus admoneri, ut desisteret ab agendo, quando id quod agere volebat. prospere non fuerat eventurum. Dicit enim apertissime & copiosissime asserit, non illum Deum fuisse, sed Daemonem, diligenti disputatione pertractans istam Platonis, de deorum sublimitate, hominum humilitate, & daemonum meditate sententiam. Mirum vero quam maxime, Apuleium, reclamantibus ipsis antiquis Philosophis, hunc Socratis daemonem instituisse condecorare titulo Dei, quum ipse Socrates toties apud Platonem eum daemonem vocet, nec alio elogio eundem cohonestent Xenophon & Cicero. Ne jam dicam Plutarchum peculiare opusculum scripsisse de daemonio Socratis, atque Maximum Tyrium Platonicum Philosophum geminam apodixin de eodem. Falluntur autem gravissime, & parum quin Atheismum suum prodant, quicunque existimant, sive Socratis ecstasin, sive cujuscunque Philosophi abdicationem a sensibus, mentalemque asensum comparari posse cum raptu Pauli Apostoli, eaque Ecstasi, quae contigit prophetis Deique hominibus supernaturali modo, atque secundum rationem Deo soli notam, saltem ignotam iis ipsis, quibus contigit: ut ingenue ratione sui fatetur ipse Apostolus Paulus poster. Epist. ad Corinth. cap. xii. verf. 3. adeo ut frustra omnino sint illi, qui praetexentes Pauli exemplum, contendunt omnibus modis hoc agendum esse, ut mens a sensibus abduci separarique queat, cum Paulus ipse haut quaquam cognoverit qua ratione hæc ecstasis, mentalisque raptus contigerit, sic enim expresse ipse: An in corpore, an extra corpus acciderit, nescio: Deus novit. quæ ergo vesania, velle modum definire circa ea, quæ ne quidem intelligendo, licet in se peragantur, homo potest percipere.
units.tr: but also pave the way to the cells of the mad. For while they are wholly intent on divorcing themselves from the senses and from all sensible things, it happens that the spirits, and with them the brain, are greatly disturbed. Phantasms, which bear this separation badly, cause a very great and tumultuous commotion and agitation in the spirits by which they are carried. It is true that our mind is inorganic, and that in the manner of its operations it depends neither on the body nor on its temperament. Nevertheless, as long as the soul lies hidden in the body as in a workhouse, it needs the aid of the senses, both internal and external, and in understanding it contemplates phantasms. Their longer and more intense contemplation brings weariness and fatigue to the understanding; [as anyone meditating on this can attest]. So in this ecstatic separation, many suffer such agitation of the brain and of the spirits within it that they fall first into dizziness, then delirium, and finally frenzy. If this had to be proved by examples, various men could be cited from the very ranks of those who embraced this new method above all others. The second inconvenience I note about this abstraction is this: by God's permission the devil is often accustomed to insinuate himself into the thoughts of those who indulge in this abstraction beyond measure, almost against their nature, and to deceive them in a pitiable way under the appearance of falsehood. Concerning Plotinus, the incomparable Platonic philosopher, Porphyry says thus in his Life of him: He was always with himself and with others, and never let up the intention of his mind turned towards itself, except perhaps when he slept. Even sleep was driven far from him, both by the scantiness of his food and by his constant turning of himself to the mind. Yet that same Porphyry does not allow us to be ignorant that this man also practised magic rites: for he relates that he had a familiar demon, to whom he was always raising higher the divine eye of his mind. Besides Plotinus, other Academics too, especially Porphyry, Olympius, Amelius, Iamblichus, and the rest who lived around the time of the emperor Diocletian, are wholly intent on raising their minds higher and turning them away from sensible and earthly things. But while they do this, and strain every nerve of their mind so that they contemplate nothing except the mind itself, stripped of the senses and sensible things, they have been corrupted by a lust for magical things, as Augustine testifies in Letter 56. The same Augustine gives the reason in Confessions book 10, chapter 42, where he speaks thus: "Many, trying to return to you, and not able of themselves, as I hear, have attempted these things, and have fallen into a desire for curious visions, and were deemed worthy of illusions. For, lifted up by the pride of learning, they sought you, exercising rather than beating their breasts; and they drew to themselves, by likeness, the powers of this air, conspiring with their heart and allies of their proud power; by whom they were deceived through magic powers, seeking a mediator through whom they might be purified, and there was none. Thus far. Although it can be said in general that the devil can most of all play with his tricks and deceptions where he finds the mind confused and disturbed by an indisposition of the imagination, on this occasion I think Socrates also fell into familiarity with a demon. Apuleius indeed transforms this very thing into a god, in a special little book he wrote On the God of Socrates; but Augustine rightly refutes him, in City of God book 8, chapter 14: If these things are so, he says, although they may be found among others too, Apuleius of Madaura has written one book on this matter alone, whose title he wanted to be On the God of Socrates, where he discusses and sets out from which class of divinities Socrates had a divinity attached to him and joined by a certain friendship, by whom he is said to have been accustomed to be warned to desist from acting when what he wished to do would not turn out well. For he says very plainly and copiously asserts that he was not a god but a demon, treating with careful argument that opinion of Plato about the sublimity of the gods, the lowliness of men and the intermediate nature of demons. Truly it is most wonderful that Apuleius, though the ancient philosophers themselves protested, undertook to adorn this demon of Socrates with the title of God, since Socrates himself so often calls him a demon in Plato, and Xenophon and Cicero honour him with no other epithet. Not to mention that Plutarch wrote a special little work On the Demon of Socrates, and Maximus of Tyre, a Platonic philosopher, a twofold demonstration on the same subject. But those are gravely mistaken, and come close to betraying their atheism, who think that either the ecstasy of Socrates, or the withdrawal of any philosopher from the senses and his mental assent, can be compared with the rapture of the apostle Paul, and with that ecstasy which befell the prophets and the men of God in a supernatural way, according to a manner known to God alone, or at least unknown to those to whom it happened, as the apostle Paul himself frankly confesses in his second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 12, verse 3. So those are altogether in vain who, pretending Paul's example, contend that this must be done by every means, so that the mind may be drawn away and separated from the senses, when Paul himself did not at all know by what manner this ecstasy and mental rapture came about; for he himself says expressly: Whether it happened in the body or out of the body, I do not know: God knows. What madness, then, to want to define a method for things which a man cannot perceive even by understanding, though they are carried out within himself.

units.la: CAPUT VIGESIMUM TERTIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWENTY-THIRD.

units.la: An homo abducendo se à sensibus possit devenire ad liquidam veri cognitionem secundum Platonicorum principia: quam periculosa sit subvectio hæc Platonica, docetur.
units.tr: Whether a man, by withdrawing himself from the senses, can attain to clear knowledge of the truth according to the principles of the Platonists; and how dangerous this Platonic ascent is.

units.la: NE quid intactum relinquamus, omniaq; ad sensuum quoque abductionem pertinentia, nobis quam explorata sint, deinceps proxime expendere convenit quæstionem jam olim inter eos, qui Platonis sectatores videri volebant, quam maxime controversam. Quæsitum autem fuit, an quando mens à corpore se abducit, per illam abductionem perveniat ad liquidam veritatis cognitionem. Existimare sic quidem videtur Socrates, paulo siquidem ante cicutæ haustum, postquam multum diuque cum Phædone disputasset, in celebratissimo illo Dialogo hunc in modum proloquitur: Cæterum, inquit, demonstratum est revera, siquando optamus aliquid pure intelligere, recedere à corpore debere, atque ipso animo res ipsas considerare. Atque tunc, ut apparet, compotes ejus, quod affectamus, cujusve amatores profitemur nos, scilicet sapientiæ fieri, cum videlicet mortui fuerimus, dum autem vivemus, nequaquam, nempe si nihil cum corpore discerni potest, è duobus alterum esse, aut nullo modo posse scientiam consequi, aut post mortem. Tunc enim animus per seipsum erit seorsum à corpore, prius vero nequaquam. Atque dum vivimus, ita proxime ad scientiam accedemus, si quam minime cum corpore commercium habuerimus, neque quicquam cum illo communicaverimus, nisi quantum summa cogat necessitas. Sed ab ejus contagione cavebimus, quoad Deus ipse nos solvat, atque ita puri & à corporis insania liberati, cum talibus erimus, cognoscam usque per nos ipsos sincerum quodvis, id est, ipsum verum. Hactenus Socrates. Cui se similes exhibere complures quidem hoc seculo laborant, existimantque, dissimulato licet Socratis & Platonis nomine, facile sibi esse mentem supra sensus & corpus evehere; cum interea ad animum non revocent, quæ & quanta incommoda hanc ipsam abstractionem secundum Platonica principia comitentur. Nam primo in eodem dialogo ipse Socrates author est sub persona Simmiæ, si in hac vita per abstractionem mentalem non possit acquiri veritas, ut eo in casu confugiatur ad monitorem aliquem externum, sive Genium. sic quippe Collocutor Simmias inquit: Oportet circa hæc alterutrum efficere, aut discere, vel invenire quemadmodum se habeant; aut si hæc fieri nequeant, optimam atque tutissimam humanarum rationum eligere, qua quis tanquam rate vehatur, atque ita procellas hujus vitæ pertranseat, si nequeat firmiori quodam vehiculo, vel divino aliquo verbo tutius ac minori cum periculo tranare. Hæc ille. mentio quidem fit divini verbi, verum per illud neutiquam intelligi potest illud quod à Prophetis & Apostolis est consignatum ad salutem filiorum Dei, verum sive Genius sive Dæmonium Socratis, toties ab eo ipso jactatum; si non Oraculum quoque in variis Græciæ vicinarumque regionum locis per diabolum edi solitum. Jam olim circumlatus fuit liber Magicus, Arbatel dictus, in quo propemodum eadem, cum ijs quæ antea ex Socratis quasi mente proposita fuerunt, occurrunt. atque quam hæc ratio abstrahendi mentem viam, ad Magiam muniat, superiori capite, adductis ipsorum Platonicorum Philosophorum exemplis ostendimus. Secundo, ex mente Socratis, difficulter per abstractionem mentis in hac vita deveniri potest ad veritatis arcem; sed exspectanda mors est, ultima illa rerum linea, à qua demum menti hæc felicitas obtingit, ut liquido quascunque veritates, atque ipsas res in proprijs suis ideis intueri queat: adeo, ut illi, qui Socratis æmuli haberi cupiunt, frustra admodum sint, quando per hanc abstractionem existimant se in hac vita alijs servituros, disciplinasque superiores perfecturos esse. Tertio, quicquid sive in hac vita, sive ab excessu ecstaticus Philosophus ut verum apprehendet, nititur ridiculo Platonis commento de reminiscentia, sive absurdissima illa opinione, qua statuit omnem nostram cognitionem nihil aliud esse quam quandam reminiscentiam. Ex Socrate enim, si scisciteris quomodo aliquis Philosophus evadere possit, respondebit in Phædro: Si postquam anima prior corpore, & proinde ad reminiscendum disposita, in veritatis campo supercælesti comitata fuerit Deum, (id est mundi circuitum) aliquid ex ijs, quæ vera sunt inspexerit, plurimaque viderit; postea lege Adrastiæ irrepat in genituram futuri Philosophi, aut pulchritudinis cupidi, etc. sic tamen ut postea nihil novi acquiratur, sed tantum in memoriam omnia ea quę jam antea visa atque explorata sunt, recurrant. qua opinione, ad quam explicandam Oedipo conjectore opus est, quum nihil sit absurdius, mirandum omnino est, quosdam ex recentioribus pro se qua Platonem, qua ipsum Socratem in hac abstractione mentali uti fingunt præ aliis exercitatum, audere adducere. nisi forte ex sententia eorum, pariter statui debeat, mentem cælitus devolutam atque per abstractionem à sensibus abductam, solummodo recolere memoriam eorum, quæ antequam corpori (loquor ex Platonis mente) tanquam ergastulo inclusa foret, in suis ideis intuita erat. Quarto, ut abstractio hæc Socratica, sive Platonis ecstasis, potissimum respectum habuit ad ea, quæ post mortem occurrunt, ita videtur quoque vergere ad supernaturalem quam felicitatem: caeterum in ea explicanda, uterque, nempe Socrates & Plato, tam absurdi sunt, ut eorum commenta parum distent ab ijs, quæ Indorum barbarissimi post hanc vitam sibi eventura fingunt. Sub finem Dialogi, qui Phædrus inscribitur, occurrit hoc Socratis votum: O amice Pan, & omnes qui hunc locum incolitis, Dij, date mihi ut pulcher intus efficiar; & quæcunque extrinsecus habeo, intrinsecus sint amica: divitem autem sapientem solum existimem. Tantum vero mihi sit auri, quantum nec ducere, nec ferre queat aliud, quam vir temperans. Si Euclio revivisceret, aliud votum Plutonis genibus non affigeret. In eodem Dialogo fingit undecim Deorum ordines, quos anima subvecta adIntelligentiarum locum cognoscat. Inter alia vero, sequentia ibi occurrunt verba: Animæ, quæ immortales vocantur, cum (alijs evectæ) ad summum pervenerint, extra progressæ in cæli dorso consistunt. Ibi constitutas circumferentia ipsa circumfert, atque illa intuentur, quæ sunt extra cælum. Sed qui & qualis est ille locus supercælestium? sine colore, figura, tactuque. Essentia vero existens animæ gubernatore solo intellectu contemplante utitur, circa quam verè scientiæ genus hunc habet locum. Itaque Dei dianœa mente & scientia immaculata se vertens: Omnis etiam animæ cogitatio, quæ suscepta est convenientem sibi conditionem, intuita per tempus Tò On, amore fruitur & contemplata ea, quæ sunt vera, nutritur & gaudet, donec circulo in idem redeat circumferentia, etc. Hæc eo loco Socrates. At quam absona hæc animæ abstractæ contemplatio? Deum vocat mundum, qui circulo fertur. In convexa illius parte dicit existere veras ideas, quas anima subvecta contempletur & cognoscat, donec redire domum cogatur, etc. Postea negat eodem reverti eam, nisi elapsis decies mille annis, donec aliæ recrescant, etc. Summa bona acquiri ait per furorem amatorium, quem etiam divinam alienationem vocat. Denique asserit omnem animam hominis intuitam esse, quę vera sint, alias non venisse in hoc animal, etc. ne jam dicam in Timęo homines assignare Planetis certis, quos quisque sequatur, & cum eis lustret Ideas mundi intellectualis, etc. In Gorgia, Deos suos, mundum, stellas, & reliqua temperantia & justitia ornat, quæ virtutes si in homine sint, faciant, ut homo Dijs sit cognatus & amicus, indeque felix.Quę omnia si diligenter expensa fuissent ab ijs, qui pro mentis subvectione, ejusdemque abstractione à corpore, tanquam pro aris & focis digladiantur, haut quaquam absonæ sententiæ laborassent procurare applausum aut à Socratis exemplo, aut etiam è principijs Philosophiæ Platonicæ.
units.tr: LEST we leave anything untouched, and so that we may next weigh carefully how well established all the matters are that pertain to the withdrawal of the senses, we should consider the question, long since the most hotly disputed among those who wished to be seen as followers of Plato: whether, when the mind withdraws itself from the body, it thereby arrives at clear knowledge of the truth. Socrates seems indeed to think so. Shortly before drinking the hemlock, after he had disputed at length with Phaedo, he speaks in this manner in that most celebrated Dialogue: "Moreover," he says, "it has in fact been shown that whenever we desire to understand something purely, we must withdraw from the body and consider the things themselves with the mind alone. Then, it seems, we shall possess what we aim at and profess ourselves lovers of, namely wisdom, when we have died, but not while we live. For if nothing can be discerned along with the body, one of two things follows: either wisdom cannot be obtained in any way, or only after death. For then the soul will be by itself, apart from the body, but never before. And while we live, we shall come nearest to knowledge if we have as little intercourse as possible with the body, and share nothing with it except what the greatest necessity compels. We must guard against its contagion until God himself releases us; and so, pure and freed from the madness of the body, we shall be with such as ourselves, and shall know through ourselves whatever is pure, that is, the truth itself." Thus far Socrates. Many in this age labour to resemble him, and they think that, even though the name of Socrates and Plato is kept out of sight, it is easy for them to raise the mind above the senses and the body. Meanwhile they do not call to mind what great inconveniences accompany this very abstraction according to Platonic principles. For first, in the same dialogue Socrates himself, in the person of Simmias, says that if truth cannot be acquired in this life by mental abstraction, one should in that case take refuge in some external guide, or Genius. Simmias, his interlocutor, says as follows: "One must either bring about one of two things concerning these matters: learn or discover how they stand; or, if this cannot be done, choose the best and safest of human reasons, on which one may be carried as on a raft, and so pass through the storms of this life, unless one can cross more safely and with less danger on some firmer vehicle, or by some divine word." Thus he. Mention is indeed made of a divine word; but by it cannot in any way be understood that which was sealed by the Prophets and Apostles for the salvation of the sons of God, but rather the Genius or Daemon of Socrates, so often vaunted by himself, if not also the oracle which was customarily given through the devil in various places in Greece and the neighbouring regions. Long ago a magical book called Arbatel was circulated, in which almost the same things occur as those previously set forth as if from the mind of Socrates. How this way of abstracting the mind paves the road to magic, we have shown in the previous chapter, by citing the examples of the Platonic philosophers themselves. Secondly, according to the mind of Socrates, one can with difficulty arrive in this life, by abstraction of the mind, at the citadel of truth; rather, death must be awaited, that last boundary of things, from which at last this happiness falls to the mind, so that it can clearly behold whatever truths, and the things themselves, in their own ideas. Thus those who wish to be thought the rivals of Socrates are quite vain when they suppose that by this abstraction they will in this life serve others and bring the higher disciplines to perfection. Thirdly, whatever the ecstatic philosopher grasps as true, whether in this life or after departure, rests on Plato's ridiculous fiction of reminiscence, or on that absurdest opinion by which he holds that all our knowledge is nothing other than a certain recollection. For if you ask Socrates in the Phaedrus how a philosopher may come to be, he will answer: if the soul, having previously been with the body, and therefore disposed to recollect, has followed God (that is, the circuit of the world) in the supercelestial field of truth, and has beheld some of the things that are true and seen very many, and afterwards slips by the law of Adrastia into the birth of a future philosopher, or of one who desires beauty, and so on; yet in such a way that afterwards nothing new is acquired, but only all those things which were previously seen and examined return to memory. Since this opinion needs an Oedipus to interpret it, and since nothing is more absurd, it is truly astonishing that some of the more recent writers dare to adduce, in their own defence, either Plato or Socrates himself, whom they pretend to have been more practised than others in this mental abstraction. Unless perhaps, according to their view, it should likewise be held that the mind, sent down from heaven and drawn away from the senses by abstraction, merely recalls to memory those things which, before it was enclosed in the body (I speak in Plato's mind) as in a prison, it had beheld in their ideas. Fourthly, just as this Socratic abstraction, or Platonic ecstasy, has regard chiefly to those things that happen after death, so it seems also to tend towards a supernatural happiness. Yet in explaining this both Socrates and Plato are so absurd that their fictions differ little from those which the most barbarous Indians imagine will befall them after this life. Near the end of the dialogue entitled Phaedrus occurs this vow of Socrates: "O dear Pan, and all you gods who dwell in this place, grant that I may become beautiful within, and that the things I have outwardly may be friendly to what is within; and may I regard the wise man alone as rich. And may I have as much gold as only a temperate man could carry or bear." If Euclio were to come back to life, he would not fasten any other vow to the knees of Pluto. In the same dialogue he imagines eleven orders of gods, to which the soul, carried up, comes to know the place of the Intelligences. Among other things, the following words occur there: "Souls which are called immortal, when they have been carried up (with the others) and reached the summit, go out and stand on the back of heaven. There, once they have been placed, the revolution itself carries them round, and they behold the things that are outside heaven. But what and of what kind is that place of the supercelestial beings? It is without colour, shape or touch. The existing essence, which is the soul's governor, employs only the intellect as contemplator, and about it the kind of true knowledge has its place. Thus the divine mind, turning itself in pure knowledge and understanding: and every thought of the soul also, which has received a fitting condition, beholds [τὸ ὄν] for a time, enjoys love, and, contemplating those things which are true, is nourished and rejoices, until the revolution returns to the same circle," and so on. Thus Socrates in that passage. But how discordant is this contemplation of the abstracted soul! He calls the world that which is carried in a circle. On the convex part of it he says that the true ideas exist, which the soul carried up contemplates and knows, until it is forced to return home, and so on. Afterwards he denies that it returns to the same place unless ten thousand years have elapsed, until others grow up, and so on. He says that the highest goods are acquired through amorous frenzy, which he also calls divine alienation. Finally he asserts that every soul of man has beheld the things that are true, otherwise it would not have come into this animal, and so on. Not to mention that in the Timaeus he assigns men to certain planets, each to follow, and with them to survey the Ideas of the intellectual world, and so on. In the Gorgias he adorns his gods, the world, the stars and the rest, with temperance and justice; and if these virtues are in a man, they make him kin and friend of the gods, and thereby happy. All these things, if they had been carefully weighed by those who fight for the elevation of the mind and its abstraction from the body as if for their altars and hearths, would never have laboured to win applause for an opinion so far from absurd, either from the example of Socrates or from the principles of the Platonic philosophy.

units.la: CAPUT VIGESIMUM QUARTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWENTY-FOURTH.

units.la: An Deus, & angeli possint cognosci per se, ac citra comparationem cum ente corporeo?
units.tr: Whether God and the angels can be known through themselves, and apart from comparison with corporeal being.

units.la: QUod jam antea visi fuimus promittere, hoc capite expendere debemus, an Intellectus scil. apprehendens ens incorporeum, illud
units.tr: What we have already promised to take up, we must consider in this chapter: namely, whether the intellect, when it apprehends incorporeal being, can apprehend that being without any help from corporeal being.

units.la: apprehendere queat citra ullum subsidium entis corporei. jam antea examinavimus ideam Deo quasi respondentem, quam multi menti insculptam esse fingunt: & quid de ea censendum sit, libere edisseruimus; hoc loco examinabimus primo rationem concipiendi hoc ipsum ens, & deinde rationem concipiendi angelos, sive intelligentias. Et, quantum quidem ad conceptionem Dei, initio diligenter notandum est, quamvis dicant vulgo Philosophi, conceptum objectivum, sive rem ipsam conceptam adæquari conceptui formali, sive modo concipiendi, quatenus scil. conceptus formalis sic debet esse adæquatus conceptui objectivo, ut cum ei adæquetur, alteri pariter adæquari non possit, neutiquam tamen ratio conceptus objectivi æstimari debet, ex ratione conceptus formalis: hic enim ut respectum habet ad eum ipsum qui concipit, ita inter rationem concipiendi eidem propriam, ipsamque rem conceptam, sæpe nulla proportio intercedit, ipseque qui concipit, quo conceptum habeat definitum, sæpenumero compellitur per species inadæquatas sibi repræsentare rem ipsam conceptam; quam licet adæquate propriaque specie non apprehendat, nihilominus tamen is ipse conceptus inadæquatus nulli alteri rei applicari potest, adeo, ut etiam tum verus censeri debeat, quando imperfectus est, atque hic non pugnent inter se hęc duo: Cognitio incompleta, & eadem vera. Quo jacto fundamento, deinceps dico, nullam creaturam, nedum hominem angelis longe imperfectiorem, adæquato conceptu Deum, sive ens infinitum apprehendere posse. Ut enim nulla omnino proportio datur, aut cogitari potest inter ens finitum & inter ens infinitum; (cum hoc nulla ratione sit mensurabile, nedum mensuratum; præclare quippe Augustin. lib. 4. de Gen. ad liter cap. 3. Deus sine mensura, mensura est, cui æquatur quod de illa est, nec aliunde est.) ita neque ens finitum aut formare aut admittere potest conceptum, plene atque sufficienter repræsentantem illum, qui solus infinitus est. Innuit hoc Paulus 1 Cor. 13. v. 12. quando testatur nos per speculum duntaxat atque per ænigma cernere. qua loquendi formula hoc significatur, nostram cognitionem quam de Deo habemus, tenebricosam, modisque infinitis impersectam esse. quamvis enim hic ipse conceptus non possit applicari ulli alij enti, quam enti infinito simpliciter, sive Deo; neutiquam tamen formaliter ipsi Deo, ut infinito, talis conceptus respondet. Si enim Deo qua tali responderet, Deus pariter, qui infinitus est, ad modum mensurati cognosceretur: aliter enim fieri non posset quin intellectus qui finitus est, deberet esse mensura Dei infiniti proportionatusque cognoscendo Deo. At quam absonum sit hoc etiam cogitare, ex ijs, quæ jam antea notata sunt, liquet. Eoque, ut noster conceptus, & modus loquendi, quem eidem aptamus, inadęquatus est, sic non potest aliter Deo denotando servire, nisi quatenus ab eo ipso ut imperfecto, & à modo explicandi tanquam Deo improprio, submoveatur omne illud, quod imperfectionem implicat, per quam submotiunem tamen, licet cognoscatur quid Deus non sit, neutiquam tamen pariter cognosci potest, quid ipse sit. Præclare August. lib. 5. de Trinitate cap. 1. Quo intellectu, inquit, Deum capit homo, qui ipsum intellectum suum, quo eum vult capere, nondum capit? Si autem hunc jam capit, attendat diligenter, nihil esse eo in sua natura melius, & videat, utrum ibi videat ulla lineamenta formarum, nitores colorum, spatiosam granditatem, partium distantiam, molis distensionem, aliquas per locorum intervalla motiones, vel quid ejusmodi. Nihil certe istorum invenimus in illo, quo in natura nostra nihil melius invenimus, id est, in intellectu nostro, quo sapientiam capimus, quantum capaces sumus. Quod ergo non invenimus in meliore nostro, non debemus in illo quærequærere, quod longe melius est meliore nostro. Ut sic intelligamus, Deum si possumus, quantum possumus, sine qualitate bonum, sine quantitate magnum, sine indigentia creatorem, sine situ præsentem, sine habitu omnia continentem, sine loco ubique totum, sine tempore sempiternum, sine ulla mutabilitate mutabilia facientem, nihilque patientem. Quisquis Deum ita cogitat, etsi nondum potest omnino invenire, quid sit, pie tamen cavet quantum potest, aliquid de eo sentire, quod non sit. Hastenus Augustinus. Hinc Gregorius Nazianzenus Orat. 2. de Theolog. sententiam Platonis in Timæo improbat quod dixerit, Deum intellectu percipere difficile esse, eloquii autem impossibile. Ego vero (inquit) ita potius dicendum censeo: Dei naturam nullis quidem verbis explicari posse: animo autem atque intellectu comprehendi minus posse. Ideo quoque Scholastici non inconvenienter docuerunt Deum a nobis cognoscendum solummodo proponi partim per viam eminentiæ, partim per viam negationis: quatenus attributa ea, uti loquuntur, quæ censentur absoluta atque positiva, nobis quadantenus repræsentamus & exhibemus per viam eminentiæ, consideranto eminenter atque secundum infinitam perfectionem ea in ente infinito, quæ in ente finito,
units.tr: We have already examined the idea which many pretend is impressed on the mind as corresponding to God, and we have set out freely what should be thought of it. In this place we will examine first the manner of conceiving this very being, and then the manner of conceiving angels, or intelligences. And as regards the conception of God, it must first be carefully noted that although the philosophers commonly say that the objective concept, or the thing itself as conceived, is adequate to the formal concept, or mode of conceiving, in the sense that the formal concept must be so adequate to the objective concept that, being adequate to it, it cannot likewise be adequate to another, nevertheless the nature of the objective concept must by no means be judged from the nature of the formal concept. For the formal concept, insofar as it has regard to the one who conceives, often has no proportion between the manner of conceiving proper to that person and the thing conceived itself; and the one who conceives, in order to have a defined concept, is often compelled to represent the thing conceived to himself through inadequate species. Although he does not grasp it adequately and through its own proper species, nevertheless that inadequate concept can be applied to no other thing, so that it must be counted true even when it is imperfect; and these two do not conflict: an incomplete knowledge, and yet the same knowledge true. On this foundation laid, I say next that no creature, much less man, who is far more imperfect than the angels, can grasp God, or infinite being, by an adequate concept. For just as no proportion at all is given, or can be thought, between finite being and infinite being (since the latter is in no way measurable, much less measured; Augustine says admirably in book 4 of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, ch. 3: "God without measure is the measure to which what is of Him is equal, and it is from nowhere else."), so neither can finite being form or admit a concept that fully and sufficiently represents Him who alone is infinite. Paul hints at this in 1 Cor. 13:12, when he testifies that we see only through a mirror and in a riddle. By this form of speech is signified that our knowledge of God is dim and imperfect in infinite ways. For although this very concept cannot be applied to any other being than the simply infinite being, that is God, nevertheless such a concept by no means corresponds formally to God himself as infinite. For if it corresponded to God as such, God, who is infinite, would likewise be known in the manner of a measured thing; for otherwise it could not happen that the intellect, which is finite, would have to be the measure of the infinite God and proportionate to knowing God. But how absurd it is even to think this is clear from what has been noted before. And so, just as our concept, and the mode of speaking that we fit to it, is inadequate, so it cannot serve to denote God except insofar as everything that implies imperfection is removed from God as imperfect, and the mode of explaining is removed as improper to God. Through this removal, although one knows what God is not, one cannot in the same way know what he himself is. Augustine, On the Trinity, book 5, ch. 1, admirably: "By what understanding, he says, does a man grasp God, when he does not yet grasp his own understanding by which he wishes to grasp him? But if he now grasps this, let him attend carefully that nothing in its nature is better than it, and let him see whether he finds there any outlines of forms, brightness of colours, spacious greatness, distance of parts, extension of mass, any motions through intervals of place, or anything of that kind. Certainly we find none of these in that which, in our nature, is nothing better, that is, in our understanding, by which we grasp wisdom so far as we are able. What therefore we do not find in our better part we ought not to seek in that which is far better than our better part. So let us understand God, if we can, as far as we can: good without quality, great without quantity, creator without need, present without position, containing all things without possession, whole everywhere without place, everlasting without time, making changeable things without any change, and suffering nothing. Whoever thinks of God in this way, even if he cannot yet wholly discover what he is, nevertheless devoutly takes care, as far as he can, not to think anything of him that is not." So far Augustine.
