Hence Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 2 On Theology, disapproves of Plato's saying in the Timaeus that to perceive God by the intellect is difficult, and to speak of him is impossible. "I rather think," he says, "that it should be said thus: the nature of God cannot indeed be explained by any words, and it can be comprehended by the mind and intellect even less." So too the Scholastics not unfittingly taught that God is to be known by us only as set before us, partly by the way of eminence and partly by the way of negation: insofar as those attributes which are called absolute and positive, as they say, we represent and set forth to ourselves in some measure by the way of eminence, considering that those things which occur in a finite being, especially in angels, occur only formally, and are to be considered as occurring eminently and according to infinite perfection in the infinite being;

units.la: maxime in angelis, formaliter duntaxat occurrunt: attributa vero ea, quae negativa vocantur, apprehendimus per viam negationis, quatenus omnes imperfectiones separamus ab eo, qui solus infinitus atque perfectissimus est. Licet fatendum sit, nos à Deo omnes imperfectiones, prę imbecillitate intellectus nostri separare non posse, multo minus apprehendere eminenter omnes perfectiones in eo, cum ne quidem easdem formaliter in ipsis creaturis, quemadmodum libro sequenti docebimus, cognoscere queamus. Nec contrarium colligi potest, quemadmodum obiter jam antea innuimus, ex Dei cognitione naturali insita: admissa quippe ea, {uti omnino, præeunte ipso Apostolo Paulo, admitti debet) non tamen inde sequetur, quemadmodum jam antea patuit, nobis insitam esse talem ideam, quæ examussim Deo respondeat, eique adæquata sit: quum etiam per ipsam Scripturam, quæ longe perfectiori modo nos Deum cognoscere docet, quam è lumine naturæ cognosci potest, non queamus eum adæquate, & comprehensive ad suam essentiam cognoscere, licet subjectivé atque secundum statum æternę felicitatis perfecte cognoscatur ab electis; usque adeo ut secundum Apostolum 1. Cor. 15. v. 28. eorum respectu in regno gloriæ, sit omnia in omnibus. Quæ cum ita sint, liquet quomodo ad concipiendum ens incorporeum & infinitum non possit mens nostra, quæ finita omnino est, pervenire, nisi per ens corporeum: sive enim per viam eminentiæ progrediatur, ab hoc debet incipere; sive per viam negationis, ab ente corporeo abstrahit quicquid est imperfectionis, adhoc ut remaneat aliqua perfectio, ab hallucinante intellectu modo eminenti Deo tribuenda. Nec audiendi sint, qui volunt vice entis corporei proponi à mente angelum, sive spiritum finitum, atque ab eo eandem procedere tum per viam negationis, tum per viam eminentiæ. Nam quamvis verum sit, Angelos expertes esse compositionis Physicæ, adhoc incorporeos, atque in Scriptura, speciatim Eph. 6. & Hebr. 1. vocari spiritus; neutiquam tamen mens nostra, propria atque adæquata specie, naturam hanc angelicam apprehendere, sibique repræsentare potest: nam si hoc posset, per definitam illam speciem, citra submotionem ullius corporeitatis, posset pariter sibi sic exhibere naturam illam angelicam, ut comparando cum ea suam animam [consequenter per propriam quoque speciem apprehensibilem] definite indicare posset differentiam intercedentem inter essentiam angelicam, atque hanc suam animam. At nullus hactenus, ex omnibus, qua Theologis, qua Philosophis Christianis, eo audacię accessit, ut sibi arrogaverit definitam hujus differentiæ explicationem. Eoque cum neque angelos, neque animas nostras incorporeas cognoscere possimus, nisi à rebus corporeis abstractione facta, patet ad ipsorum quoque angelorum & animarum nostrarum conceptum formandum nos indigere subsidio rerum corporearum: nisi enim res corporeas antea perspectashabuerimus, neutiquam ab ijs abstractionem facere poterimus.
units.tr: especially in angels, occur only formally. The attributes called negative, however, we grasp by the way of negation, insofar as we separate all imperfections from him who alone is infinite and most perfect. It must be granted that, because of the weakness of our intellect, we cannot separate all imperfections from God, much less grasp eminently all perfections in him, since we cannot even know the same perfections formally in the creatures themselves, as we will show in the following book. Nor can the contrary be inferred, as we hinted in passing before, from the innate natural knowledge of God. For although that knowledge is admitted (as it must be admitted, the Apostle Paul himself leading the way), it does not follow from it, as has already been made clear, that such an idea is innate in us as corresponds exactly to God and is adequate to him. For even through Scripture itself, which teaches us to know God in a far more perfect way than can be known from the light of nature, we cannot know him adequately and comprehensively in his essence, although he is known perfectly by the elect, subjectively and according to the state of eternal happiness; so much so that, according to the Apostle in 1 Cor. 15:28, with respect to them, in the kingdom of glory, God may be all in all. Since these things are so, it is clear how our mind, which is wholly finite, cannot arrive at conceiving incorporeal and infinite being except through corporeal being. For whether it proceeds by the way of eminence, it must begin from this; or by the way of negation, it abstracts from corporeal being whatever is imperfect, so that some perfection remains, to be attributed to God in an eminent manner by a deceived intellect. Nor should those be heard who want the mind to put an angel, or a finite spirit, in place of corporeal being, and to proceed from it in the same way both by negation and by eminence. For although it is true that angels are free of physical composition, and in Scripture, especially Eph. 6 and Heb. 1, are called spirits, nevertheless our mind cannot apprehend and represent to itself this angelic nature by its own and adequate species. For if it could, through that defined species, without removing any corporeity, it could likewise present that angelic nature to itself in such a way that, by comparing it with its own soul [consequently also through the soul's own apprehensible species], it could definitely indicate the difference lying between the angelic essence and this soul of ours. But no one so far, of all the theologians and Christian philosophers, has had the audacity to claim for himself a definite explanation of this difference. And so, since we can know neither angels nor our incorporeal souls except by making abstraction from corporeal things, it is plain that for forming the concept even of the angels themselves and of our souls we need the help of corporeal things: for unless we had first perceived corporeal things, we could by no means make abstraction from them.

units.la: CAPUT VIGESIMUM QUINTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWENTY-FIFTH.

units.la: Ex Ioanne Sarisberiensi ostenditur, quam irreceptisint Sceptici, cum quibus hactenus disputatum est.
units.tr: From John of Salisbury it is shown how poorly the Sceptics with whom we have so far disputed have been received.

units.la: ASserta non minus scientiæ certitudine, quam ipsorum sensuum, certis tamen requisitis astrictorum, adversus Sceptico; priusquam librumhunc finio, unum illud amplius monere debeo, illos Philosophiæ mangones, non minus in Deum Omnipotentem hominis creatorem, quam in ipsum hominem, animal illud admirandum, atque ab angelis secundum injurios esse. Dum enim certi quid ab homine cognosci negant, eundemque parum quin omnibus sensibus multent, quid aliud faciunt, quam ut infra omnes belluas illum collocent, cui ab ipso Deo, authore atque conservatore universi, potestas dominica in omnes belluas concessa est. Quod cum elegantér admodum ostensum fuerit a Joannes Sarefberiensi, Curialium nugarum censore, operæ pretium factursus videor, si ejusdem verba hic exhibuero. Sic vero is ipse loquitur lib. 7. de Nugis Curialium cap. 2. Cum in eo homo cæteris animalibus præstet, quod ratione viget & intelligentia (nam in sensibus, qui licet animæ sint, corporis esse dicuntur, facile superatur, neque lynci valeat æquari perspicacia oculorum: sus auditu prævalet, vultur aut canis odoratu, gustu simia, aranea tactu.) Cum inquam, discernendi & intelligendi viribus homo præcedat, quis præstantiorem bestijs, aut potius quis non inferiorem & ut ita dicam quis brutiorem non credat hominem, cui ratio non discernit, intellectus non sapit; cum & bruta ad quandam rationis imaginem quodammodo videantur assurgere. Nam & canis suos discernit affectus, beneficiorum memor est, familiaritatem cum homine ab experientia rerum & usu contrahit, & amicitiæ præ cæteris, quasi fidem familiaribus exhibens, rationis & intellectus quodam nobilitatur ingenio. Sed & injuriarum memoria camelo tenaciter residet, & Rhinoceros, qui & unicornis est, virginis integritatem sic agnoscit, ut duntaxat illius fere amplexibus capiatur. Odorem pantherə cætera sequuntur animalia; &, quod mirabilius est, pisces in gurgitibus ad speciem auri conveniunt, unde & sævientis luxuriæ Imperator Nero, aureis, ut dicitur, retibus piscabatur. Quid multa?
units.tr: Assertions held with no less certainty than that of the senses themselves, but bound by fixed requirements, must be maintained against the Sceptics. Before I finish this book, I must give one more warning: those hawkers of philosophy are no less unjust to Almighty God, the creator of man, than they are to man himself, that admirable animal, and they are even unjust to him when compared with the angels. For while they deny that anything certain can be known by man, and nearly fine him for all his senses, what else do they do but place him below all beasts, though God himself, the author and preserver of the universe, granted him dominion over all beasts? This has been shown very elegantly by John of Salisbury, the censor of courtly trifles, and I think it will be worth the effort if I set out his very words here. He speaks thus in book 7, On the Trifles of Courtiers, chapter 2: "Since man excels the other animals in that he is strong in reason and understanding (for in the senses, which though they belong to the soul are said to belong to the body, he is easily surpassed, and the sharpness of the lynx's eyes cannot be matched: the pig excels in hearing, the vulture or the dog in smell, the ape in taste, the spider in touch), since, I say, man surpasses them in the powers of discernment and understanding, who would not think man either superior to the beasts, or rather inferior and, if I may say so, more brutish than they, when reason does not discern and intellect has no wisdom; especially since beasts also seem in a certain way to rise to some image of reason. For the dog too discerns its affections, is mindful of benefits, gains familiarity with man through experience and use, and, showing faithfulness to its intimates above all others in friendship, is in a way ennobled by a kind of reason and intelligence. But the camel also retains the memory of injuries tenaciously, and the rhinoceros, which is also the unicorn, recognises a virgin's chastity so that it is almost only by her embraces that it is taken. Other animals follow the scent of the panther; and, what is more wonderful, fish gather in the whirlpools at the sight of gold, whence the Emperor Nero, raging in his lust, is said to have fished with golden nets. Why say more?"

units.la: Torva leæna lupum sequitur, lupus ipse capellam, Florentem cithisum sequitur lasciva capella.
units.tr: The fierce lioness follows the wolf, the wolf itself follows the goat, the wanton goat follows the flowering cytisus.

units.la: Et in hunc modū voluptate sua trahuntur plurima: quod (ut credo) evenire non posset, si de affectibus suis dubitarent. Qui ergo ad singula nescij sunt, qua temeritate, vel impudentia, philosophandi professionem arripiunt? Nam sicut ab eo, quod notum est, notio, sic & ratio ab eo, quod ratum est, id est, certum & firmum, grammatice denominatur: & profecto inanis est ratio hominis, cui nihil persuaderi potest, quin semper & in omnibus opinionum lubrico vacillet. Quid enim ei philosophia confert, qui semper fluctuat opinionibus; & qui in ostendenda felicitatis via rationis lumen extinguit, & quasi oculum eruit, ut cautius & rectius pergat viator, cui oftentura est viam? Nonne & plurimum obest illi, qui excæcatur? Quid potius sequetur, qui tanta contrarietate distrahitur? Sane ad patriam nemo pervenit, nisi qui unam sequitur via; & qui omni verbo aurem accommodat nunquam quietus erit. Nonne similior est lethargico, aut insipienti, sive insano, quam Philosopho, qui cum somnij meminerit, an dormierit dubitat, & cum cibo satiatus est, an jejunus sit, nescit, & nullius eorum quę egit, vel in proximo scientiam habet? Deinde, quanam via in Philosophiæ investigatione proficiet, cui ratio nihil persuadeat, quod teneat, aut sequatur, sed est ad omnia semper incertus? Huc usque Saresberiensis: Simulque hac gemma hunc tertium librum obsigno.
units.tr: And in this way very many are drawn along by their pleasures, which (I believe) could not happen if they doubted their affections. Who, then, ignorant of each particular thing, takes up the profession of philosophy with such rashness or impudence? For just as notion is named grammatically from what is known (notum), so reason (ratio) is named from what is ratum, that is, certain and firm. And surely the reason of a man who can be persuaded of nothing, but always wavers in the slipperiness of opinions, is empty. For what does philosophy confer on one who is always tossed about by opinions; and who, in showing the way to happiness, extinguishes the light of reason and, as it were, tears out the eye, so that the traveller to whom the way is to be shown may go more cautiously and rightly? Does this not greatly harm the one who is blinded? What will follow for one who is pulled apart by such contrariety? Surely no one reaches home unless he follows a single road; and he who lends his ear to every word will never be at rest. Is he not more like a lethargic, foolish, or insane person than a philosopher, who, when he remembers a dream, doubts whether he has slept, and when sated with food does not know whether he is fasting, and has no knowledge even of the things he has just done? Furthermore, by what road will he make progress in the investigation of philosophy, for whom reason persuades nothing that he may hold or follow, but who is always uncertain about everything? Thus far Saresberiensis. And with this jewel I seal this third book.

units.la: LIBER QUARTUS DE SCEPTICISMO.
units.tr: THE FOURTH BOOK ON SCEPTICISM.

units.la: Caput Primum.
units.tr: Chapter One.

units.la: Quomodo dispositus is esse debeat, & quibus præsidiis instructus, quem una, aut plures disciplinæ perficient.
units.tr: How a person ought to be disposed, and with what safeguards equipped, whom one or more disciplines are to perfect.

units.la: QUum superiori libro sufficienter videamur egisse de sensuum certitudine, illorumq; judicio, quo omnia, quæ adversus Scepticos disputanda restant, pertractare atque edisce rere queamus, hoc libro singulas disciplinas ordine considerabimus, ac quaenam in ijs certitudo occurrat, contra Scepticos, aliosque earum adversarios, quam fieri poterit brevissime, expendemus. Priusquam vero quamque disciplinam sigillatim atque distincte aggredimur, operae pretium fuerit ostendere, quomodo dispositus is esse debeat, ac quibus adminiculis instructus, qui ad disciplinas animum non solum applicabit, verum in ijs quoque sic versabitur, ut in ijs censeri queat non peregrinus. nam, quod haut quaquam dissimulari debet, jam olim Academici & Sceptici aestimantes ipsas disciplinas ex earum cultoribus, instituerunt non solum eas ut imperfectas arguere, verum etiam ijsdem convitium dicere, nullam aliam ob causam, quam quod viderent multos, qui tamen quantiuis pretij viderique uolebant, in ijs admodum infeliciter versari & parum quin ipsas quoque illas disciplinas prostituere. Qualium ut quecamus securi esse, & ne postea nobis objiciantur, operae pretium fuerit, breviter expendere non solum ea,quae requirunrur in eo, quem paedia perficiet, verum etiam examinare penitiusque trutinare ea media, quibus idem ille instructus esse debet.
units.tr: Since in the previous book we seem to have dealt sufficiently with the certainty of the senses and their judgment, by which we may be able to treat and master everything that remains to be argued against the Sceptics, in this book we shall consider the individual disciplines in order, and weigh, as briefly as possible, what certainty is found in each of them against the Sceptics and their other opponents. Before we approach each discipline one by one and distinctly, it will be worth the effort to show how a person ought to be disposed, and with what aids equipped, who will not only apply his mind to the disciplines but will so engage with them that he may be counted among them as no stranger. For, as must by no means be concealed, the Academics and Sceptics of old, judging the disciplines themselves by their practitioners, set out not only to disparage them as imperfect but even to revile them, for no other reason than that they saw many who, though they wished to be thought of great worth, were very unsuccessful in them, and who almost prostituted the disciplines themselves. So that we may be safe from such charges and they may not be thrown at us afterwards, it will be worth the effort to consider briefly not only the qualities required in the one whom the disciplines are to perfect, but also to examine and weigh more thoroughly the means by which that same person ought to be equipped.

units.la: Initio ergo in eo, qui a disciplina aliqua,quam didicerit, commendari debebit, debet esse naturalis aliqua ingenij vis & perspicacia, quam non tam studio, labore, & assiduitate aliquis sibi comparaverit, quam ab ipsa natura eandem acceperit. Inde Averroës adversus Algaz: ad internoscenda ea, quę verè apud Philosophum natura nota sunt, & ea quæ ab incunte ætate teneris animis instillata putantur ut nota natura, virum requirit perfectæ, ut interpres loquitur, naturalitatis. Et Aristoteles non uno in loco antiquis Philosophis objicit ἀρρῶσίαν τῆς διανοίας[?]. Quum vero facultati intellectivę, qua homo tanquam animal ratione præditum est, conveniant hæc tria, apprehensio, inventio, & dijudicatio, ratione harum trium quasi virtutum, cum, de quo loquimur, expeditum & absolutum pariter esse convenit. Et quantum ad apprehensionem, quæ à Latinis vocatur docilitas, & ab Arnobio eleganter lib. 5. adv. Gentes vivacitas ingenij, eaab inventione, sive à secunda virtute, quæ proprie dicitur subtilitas, nonnihil est distincta: nam docilitatis propria functio est, facilis perceptio eorum quæ ab alio proponuntur sive viva voce, sive scriptis: subtilitatis vero operatio, est excogitatio sive inventio eorum, quæ rei conveniunt. Unde subtiles eos vulgo censere solemus, qui valent inventione. non semper vero concurrunt hæ duæ facultates ingenij: multi siquidem occurrunt, qui facillime quidem discunt aliena, sed nihil interim ex suo promptuario depromere possunt: quanquam vero multi hoc evenire existimant ratione differentis temperiei, non censuerim tamen illius solius habendam rationem esse. Hoc ingenij acumen, proprie si consideretur, facultas naturalis est, & tamen plurimum adjuvatur exercitatione, arteque Logica, cui convenienter plane succenturiantur quoque disciplinæ Mathematicæ: neque enim præter ratio- nem dixit jam olim Plotinus, artes Mathematicas proponendas esse ad mentem acuendam, cum constet hunc potissimum ob finem à Pythagoreis & Academicis Mathemata exulta & celebrata esse. Sed neque ingenij vivacitas, neque subtilitas hic sufficiunt: sed requiritur quoque speciatim, & quidem potissimum, judicium: cum acumen ingenij frequentissime noxium fuerit deprehensum, si judicio non regeretur. Quomodo homines solertissimos videmus in absurdissima errata incidisse propter judicij defectum. quæ enim beneficio acuminis excogitantur, non raro sunt infirma & sutilia, imo incerta, quæ si quis haberi velit ra- ta & velut Apollinis responsa, aliter fieri non poterit, quin in errores graves & periculos os incidat. Propterea ea quæ docentur a præceptoribus, non semper talia sunt, ut debeant optima censeri. Nam recte docentium rara valde copia est: & qui non eo profectus suos promoverit, ut de præceptore suo recte judicare sciat, non est quod magnam gloriam ex literis sibi polliceatur. Existimat quidem Fabius Quintilianus lib. 6. Orat. Instit. cap. 6 judicium ex asse naturæ attribendum esse, atque arte neutiquam adjuvari posse; cæterum præferri merentur eorum sententia, qui arte logica potissimum illud juvari posse existimant. Quæ sententia veteribus quoque sedit, qui non dubitarunt Logicam proinde Criticam vocare, uti constat ex eodem Quintil. lib. 5. Orat. Instit. cap. ult. & Boëthio lib. 1. Comm. in Topica Ciceronis. Certe Alexander Aphrodisæus Quintiliano longe major, in princ. Comment. in libros prior. Analyt. Aristotelis, Logicam ad dogmatum inventionem, & dijudicationem summopere utilem esse statuit. Præ cæteris vero tum ad hanc tum ad secundam quoque facultatem plurimum adjumenti adferunt præcepta Apodictica. Nam ut author est Eustratius, illa eundem fere usum discentibus & docentibus adferunt, quem architectis regula & perpendiculum: nec præter rationem plurimis in locis ab Aristotele, illiusq; interpretibus Græcis notantur antiqui philosophi, quod ignari essent demonstrationum. Et Galenus in eandem sententiam, hoc unum ait esse initium pravorum dogmatum, nihil de demonstrationibus prius esse contemplatum, sed una res inquirere, & tanquam scires quid sit demonstratio, tentare demonstrationes afferre. Unde alibi idem quoque notat eorum arrogantiam, qui sine arte analytica scientias aggrediuntur, multaque incommoda commemorat, quæ necessum est incurrant, qui sine hoc lumine philosophantur: nam neque nota inquit, assumunt, neque ignota demonstrant: sed veluti legislatores, id quod placet, constituunt: denique progressu orationis, instar Eurypi cujusdam, summam inconstantiam præ se ferunt. Ut ex iis, quæ dicta sunt, liquet, quomodo dispositus is debeat, quem disciplina aliqua absolvet, ita proxime despiciendum, quibusnam subsidiis idem ille instructus esse debeat. Sunt vero subsidia illa duplicia, quædam extrinseca ei ipsi, qui perficietur, quædam intrinseca. Inter extrinseca primo loco occurrit Deus Opt. Max. quem conciliandum in partes à discente esse ipsis Academicis fuit gnarum, statuentibus æquo cognitionem nostram à Deo procedere, atque illuminationem à Sole. Lumen mentium, (sunt verba Augustini lib. 8. de C. D. cap. 7.) esse dixerunt Platonici ad discenda omnia euntem ipsum Deum, à quo facta sunt omnia. Idem Augustinus eod. lib. cap. 10. ex Platonicorum sententia Deum appellat causam constituendæ universitatis, lucem percipiendæ veritatis, & fontem bene(?)dæ felicitatis. Pariter Nazianzenus Orat. in sacra lumina, prolixus est in explicanda hac Platonis sententia, licet ex eo ipso, nec non Socratis dissertationibus apud eum, nobis jam antea constiterit, hunc ipsum Deum obscurum satis esse, nec de eo liquere habeatne boni an mali Genij rationem. Alexander Aphrodiseus, aliique è familia Aristotelis, inhærentes ex parte pricipiis Platonicis, partes has vindicarunt intellectui agenti. Sed missis obscurioribus quaPlatonis, qua Aristotelis dogmatibus, cogitandum hic illud Synesij ep. 139. Deo præsente, quicquid est difficile, facile fit. & illud Ciceronis lib. 2. de N. D. Nemo virmagnus sine aliquo afflatu divino unquam fuit. potissimum vero meditanda ipsa Spiritus Sancti sententia, annotata ab Apostolo Jacobo cap. 1. Epist. Cath. verf. 17. Omnis donatio bona, & omne integrum donum est superne, descendens à Patre luminum. quod vero idem docet eodem capite verf.5 .hic quam maxime etiam cogitandum: Si cui vestrum deest sapientia, petito à Deo, qui dat eam omnibus benigne, nec exprobrat, & dabitur ei. quomodo an-notapretibus Græcis notantur antiqui philosophi, quod ignari essent demonstrationum. Et Galenus in eandem sententiam, hoc unum ait esse initium pravorum dogmatum, nihil de demonstrationibus prius esse contemplatum, sed una res inquirere, & tanquam scires quid sit demonstratio, tentare demonstrationes adferre. Unde alibi idem quoque notat eorum arrogantiam, qui sine arte analytica scientias aggrediuntur, multaque incommoda commemorat, quæ necessum est incurrant, qui sine hoc lumine philosophantur: nam neque nota, inquit, assumunt, neque ignota demonstrant: sed veluti legislatores, id quod placet, constituunt: denique progressu orationis, instar Eurypi cujusdam, summam inconstantiam præ se ferunt. Ut ex iis, quæ dicta sunt, liquet, quomodo dispositus is debeat, quem disciplina aliqua absolvet, ita proxime despiciendum, quibusnam subsidijs idem ille instructus esse debeat. Sunt vero subsidia illa duplicia, quædam extrinseca ei ipsi, qui perficietur, quædam intrinseca. Inter extrinseca primo loco occurrit Deus Opt. Max. quem conciliandum in partes à discente esse ipsis Academicis fuit gnarum, statuentibus æquo cognitionem nostram à Deo procedere, atq; illuminationem à Sole. Lumen mentium, (sunt verba Augustini lib. 8. de C. D. cap. 7.) esse dixerunt Platonici ad discenda omnia eundem ipsum Deum, à quo facta sunt omnia. Idem Augustinus eod. lib. cap. 10. ex Platonicorum sententia Deum appellat causam constituendæ universitatis, lucem percipiendæ veritatis, & fontem beatitudinis felicitatis. Pariter Nazianzenus Orat. in sacra lumina, prolixus est in explicanda hac Platonis sententia, licet ex eo ipso, nec non Socratis dissertationibus apud eum, nobis jam antea constiterit, hunc ipsum Deum obscurum satis esse, nec de eo liquere habeatne bonian mali Genij rationem. Alexander Aphrodisæus, alijque è familia Aristotelis, inhærentes ex parte prıcipiis Platonicis, partes has vindicarunt intellectui agenti. Sed missis obscurioribus quaPlatonis, qua Aristotelis dogmatibus, cogitandum hic illud Synesij ep. 139. Deo præsente, quicquid est difficile, facile fit. & illud Ciceronis lib. 2. de N. D. Nemo vir magnus sine aliquo afflatu divino unquam fuit. potissimum vero meditanda ipsa Spiritus Sancti sententia, annotata ab Apostolo Jacobo cap. 1. Epist. Cath. verf. 17. Omnis donatio bona, & omne integrum donum est superne, descendens à Patre luminum. quod vero idem docet eodem capite verf. 5. hic quam maxime etiam cogitandum: Si cui vestrum deest sapientia, petito à Deo, qui dat eam omnibus benigne, nec exprobrat, & dabitur ei. quomodo an-notanotatum est, Hermannum Contractum, Comitem Heingensem, filium Volfardi Comitis, & Cænobij S. Galli Monachum, quum membrorum usu a prima ætate multatus esset, precibus solis, omnigenam, & supra seculum illud diffusissimam eruditionem sibi impetrasse; itemque Albertum Magnum, cum alias hebetioris ingenij esset, devota oratione percipiendi vim attecutum fuisse. Sed, qui futurus hic Deo supplex, quod illud, quod petit, ab eo impetrare queat, castas manus tollere debet, mentemque suam defæcare ab omni vitij contagione. Hoc antiquis Philosophis, à Christiana licet veritate remotis exploratum fuit quum futuro Philosopho docerent necessarias esse quasdam virtutes expurgatrices (sic loquuntur) de quibus præ alijs consulendi sunt Plotinus, Proclus Comm. in Timæum, Maximus Tyrius, Macrobius, alijque. Huc referendum, quod Ammonius & Simplicius inter conditiones, quas requirunt in Philosophiæ Aristotelicæ consulto, primo reponunt ut hi justus, & temperans. Post Deum inter externa subsidia atque media collocari debent præceptores viva voce docentes, quos quia multi jam olim aut neglexerunt, aut contemptim habuerunt, in profundum Scepticismi inciderunt. Et tamen quotquot ex antiquis Philosophis celebriolebriores frugisque bonæ fuerunt, præceptores honorarunt, atque in pretio summo habuerunt. Sic Democritus apud Clen entem Alexandr. lib. 1. Strom. & apud Eusb.[?] lib. 7. de Præp. Evang. cap. 2. gloriatur se octuaginta annos à patria exulasse, quo celebratissimos orbis Doctores audiret, atque uberiores sapientiæ & eruditionis opes sibi compararet. Diogenes Laërtius, Jamblichus, & Porphyrius Malchus in vita Pythagoræ scribunt, eum relicta patria Ægyptum petiisse, sacerdotum adyta ingressum, apud Chaldæos cum Magis conversatum, cunctisque Barbaris & Græcis mysterijs initiatum fuisse: deinde in Creta cum Epimenide in Idæum antrum descendisse. Cle-mens Alexandr. lib. 1. Stromat. quod & sequitur Theodoretus Serm. 1. addit eum circumcisum fuisse, quo admitti posset ad adyta Ægyptiorum, atque addiscere mysticam eorum Philosophiam. De peregrinatione Platonis Apulejus in lib. de Dogmate Platonis sic loquitur: Postquam Socrates homines reliquit, Plato ad Pythagoræ disciplinam se contulit, & quod Pythagoreorum ingenium adjutum aliis disciplinis sentiebat ad Theodorum Syenem, ut Geometriam disceret est prosectus, & Astrologiam ad usque Ægyptum ivit petitum, ut inde Prophetarum ritus addisceret, & ad Italiam iterum venit, & Pythagoreos sectatus est. I-dem dem de Platone testatur Diogenes Laërtius, & ante Diogenem Cic. lib. 5. de Finib. Similiter Xenocratem, Theophrastum, Zenonem, Cleanthem, Chrysippum, Carneadem, Posidonium, aliòsque Philosophos quam plurimos, diicendi studio in longinquas regiones se contulisse, ut celebratæ sapientiæ viros audirent, testatur Theodoretus Serm. 1. ad Græcos, & ante Theodoretum Hieronymus in Epist. ad Paul. Antiqui quoque Romani sapientiæ acquirendæ gratia aut in Græciam & quidem Athenas, aut in Asiam, aut denique Rhodum se conferebant, ut ab illis viris doctissimis, qui in illis locis degebant atque docebant, sapientiæ thesauris locupletarentur. Ita Cicero Rhodi audivit Apollonium Molonem, & in Asia Apollonium Alabandensem. Pariter Julius Cæsar apud Rhodios operam dedit Moloni, Tiberius Theodoro Gadareno, Augustus Apollodoro. quin etiam soliti fuerunt viros doctos ex Asia & Græcia Romam deducere, quos in ædibus privatis audirent: quemadmodum hoc liquet ex Plutarcho inLucullo & Cicerone. Imo ipse Cicero lib. 1. de N. D. testatur, donum suam eruditissimis viris floruisse, inter quos recenset Diodotum, Philonem, Antiochum, & Posidonium. Nec minus præceptores, eorumque necessitatem probant atque commendant antiqui Patres Ex quorum mente sic Hieronym. in Epist. ad Rusticum: Nulla ars (inquit) absque magistro discitur. Idem in Epitaphio Paulæ ad Eustochium: propter assiduitatem [inquit] & crebras postulationes ejus præstiti, ut docerem quod didiceram, non à me ipso, id est, à præsumptione pessimo præceptore, sed ab Illustribus Ecclesiæ viris. Accedit totius orbis consensus. Nam in omnibus Christiani orbis partibus, imo etiam apud ipsos Mahumetanos erectæ sunt scholæ & Academiæ, in quibus eruditionis candidati sub præceptorum disciplina proficere possint. Quales vero præceptores eligendi sint, quum ab aliis prolixe sit tractatum hoc argumentum, supervacuum est expendere. Ut ipsum, pium, doctum atque fidelem esse convenit, ita discipulus quam primum se eidem in disciplinam dedit, pariter fidem habere debet; neque enim frustra ab Aristotele in Elenchis dictum fuit, oportere discentem credere: quod probatur quoque Galeno in lib. de Docendi ratione adversus Phavorinum: nec præter rationem in Schola Pythagoræ ad tempus receptum fuit illud: Ipse dixit. Ratio vero cur fides dictis præceptoris adhibenda sit, hæc est, quia si discipulus non admittat principia docentis, neutiquam ad conclusiones, quæ ex illis principiis educuntur, progredi possit.
units.tr: At the outset, then, the person who is to be commended for any discipline he has learned must have some natural power and sharpness of mind, which he has acquired not so much by study, labour and diligence as received from nature itself. Hence Averroës, against Algazel: to distinguish those things that are truly known by nature in the Philosopher, and those that are thought to be known by nature because they have been instilled in tender minds from early childhood, requires a man of perfect "naturalness," as the translator puts it. And Aristotle, in more than one place, reproaches the ancient philosophers with [ἀρρῶσίαν τῆς διανοίας] infirmity of mind. Since three things belong to the intellectual faculty, by which man as a rational animal is endowed, namely apprehension, invention and judgement, it is fitting that the person we are speaking of should be equally ready and complete in respect of these three, as if they were three virtues. As to apprehension, which the Latins call docility, and which Arnobius elegantly calls liveliness of wit (Adv. Gentes, bk. 5), it differs somewhat from invention, or from the second virtue, which is properly called subtlety. For the proper function of docility is the easy grasping of what is put forward by another, whether by the living voice or in writing; the work of subtlety, however, is the devising or invention of what fits the matter in hand. So we commonly call subtle those who excel in invention. These two faculties of wit do not always go together. Many are met with who learn other people's teaching most readily, yet can bring nothing forth from their own store. Although many think this happens because of a difference of temperament, I would not judge that this alone should be taken into account. This keenness of wit, properly considered, is a natural faculty, and yet it is greatly helped by exercise and by the art of logic, to which the mathematical disciplines are also fittingly added as auxiliaries. For Plotinus long ago said, not without reason, that the mathematical arts are to be set before us for sharpening the mind, since it is plain that the Pythagoreans and the Academics cultivated and celebrated mathematics chiefly for this end. But neither liveliness nor subtlety of wit is sufficient here; judgement in particular is also required, since the keenness of wit is very often found to be harmful if it is not governed by judgement. We see how the most clever men have fallen into most absurd errors through lack of judgement. For what is devised by the help of keenness is often weak and flimsy, indeed uncertain, and if anyone wishes it to be held as settled and as the oracles of Apollo, he cannot avoid falling into grave and dangerous errors. Therefore what is taught by teachers is not always of such a kind that it ought to be counted the best. For truly good teachers are very rare, and whoever has not advanced so far as to know how to judge his teacher rightly should not promise himself great glory from his letters. Indeed Fabius Quintilian (Institutio Oratoria, bk. 6, ch. 6) thinks that judgement is to be attributed wholly to nature and can in no way be helped by art; yet the opinion of those is to be preferred who think that it can be helped chiefly by the art of logic. This view also pleased the ancients, who did not hesitate to call logic accordingly criticism, as appears from the same Quintilian (Institutio Oratoria, bk. 5, last ch.) and from Boethius (Commentary on Cicero's Topics, bk. 1). Certainly Alexander of Aphrodisias, far greater than Quintilian, in the opening of his commentary on the Prior Analytics of Aristotle, holds that logic is very greatly useful for the invention and judgement of doctrines. Above all, the precepts of demonstration contribute much help both to this faculty and to the second. For, as Eustratius records, they bring to learners and teachers almost the same use as the rule and the plumb-line to architects. And not without reason, in many places, Aristotle and his Greek interpreters remark that the ancient philosophers were ignorant of demonstrations. Galen too, to the same effect, says that this one thing is the beginning of bad doctrines: to have contemplated nothing about demonstrations beforehand, but to seek out one thing after another, and, as if one knew what demonstration is, to attempt to bring forward demonstrations. Hence elsewhere he also notes the arrogance of those who approach the sciences without the analytic art, and he recounts the many inconveniences that must befall those who philosophise without this light: for, he says, they take for granted things that are not known, and do not demonstrate things that are unknown; but like lawgivers they lay down what pleases them; and finally, in the course of their discourse, like a certain Euripus, they display the greatest inconstancy. As is clear from what has been said, it follows that we should next consider how the person whom some discipline is to complete ought to be disposed, and with what aids he ought to be equipped. These aids are twofold: some external to the one who is to be perfected, some internal. Among the external, first of all comes God, Best and Greatest, whom the learner must, as the Academics themselves knew, win to his side, since they held that our knowledge proceeds equally from God, and illumination from the Sun. The light of minds, (these are the words of Augustine, City of God, bk. 8, ch. 7) the Platonists said, is God himself, going forth to teach all things, by whom all things were made. The same Augustine, in the same book, ch. 10, following the opinion of the Platonists, calls God the cause of the constitution of the universe, the light for perceiving truth, and the fountain of blessed happiness. Likewise Gregory Nazianzen, in his oration On the Holy Lights, is lengthy in explaining this opinion of Plato; although it has already been established for us, from that very passage and also from the discourses of Socrates in Plato, that this God is obscure enough, and that it is not clear whether he has the nature of a good or of an evil genius. Alexander of Aphrodisias and others of the school of Aristotle, partly adhering to Platonic principles, claimed these functions for the agent intellect. But setting aside the more obscure doctrines, whether of Plato or of Aristotle, we should here think on that saying of Synesius (Letter 139): With God present, whatever is difficult becomes easy; and on that of Cicero (De Natura Deorum, bk. 2): No great man has ever been without some divine inspiration. Above all we should meditate on the very judgement of the Holy Spirit, noted by the Apostle James in the first chapter of his Catholic Epistle, verse 17: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights. What the same teaches in the same chapter, verse 5, we should also consider most of all here: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it will be given to him. As it has been noted, Hermann Contractus, Count of Heing, son of Count Volfard and a monk of the abbey of St Gall, though deprived of the use of his limbs from his earliest age, obtained for himself by prayer alone a learning of every kind, spread far beyond his age; and likewise Albert the Great, though otherwise of a duller wit, is said to have attained the power of understanding through devout prayer. But he who is to be a suppliant to God, if he is to obtain from him what he asks, ought to lift up chaste hands and cleanse his mind from every contagion of vice. The ancient philosophers, though remote from Christian truth, knew this, when they taught that certain purifying virtues (so they call them) are necessary for the future philosopher; on this point the reader should consult above all Plotinus, Proclus (Commentary on the Timaeus), Maximus of Tyre, Macrobius and others. To this belongs what Ammonius and Simplicius put first among the conditions they require in one who is to study the philosophy of Aristotle: that he be just and temperate. After God, among the external aids and means, teachers who teach by the living voice ought to be placed; many, because they neglected them or held them in contempt, have long since fallen into the depths of Scepticism. Yet all the most famous and most worthy of the ancient philosophers honoured their teachers and held them in the highest esteem. Thus Democritus, in Clement of Alexandria (Stromata, bk. 1) and in Eusebius (Preparation for the Gospel, bk. 7, ch. 2), boasts that he spent eighty years away from his native land, so that he might hear the most celebrated teachers of the world and acquire for himself richer stores of wisdom and learning. Diogenes Laertius, Iamblichus and Porphyry the Malchus, in their lives of Pythagoras, write that he left his homeland and sought Egypt, entered the shrines of the priests, lived among the Chaldeans with the Magi, and was initiated into all the mysteries of the barbarians and the Greeks; then in Crete he went down with Epimenides into the Idaean cave. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata, bk. 1), whom Theodoret follows (Sermon 1), adds that he was circumcised so that he might be admitted to the shrines of the Egyptians and learn their mystical philosophy. Concerning Plato's travels, Apuleius in his book On the Doctrine of Plato speaks thus: After Socrates left men, Plato turned himself to the discipline of Pythagoras; and, feeling that the talent of the Pythagoreans was aided by other disciplines, he went to Theodorus of Cyrene to learn geometry, and went as far as Egypt to seek astronomy, so that from there he might learn the rites of the prophets; and he came again to Italy and followed the Pythagoreans. Diogenes Laertius testifies the same of Plato, and before Diogenes, Cicero (De Finibus, bk. 5). Likewise Theodoret (Sermon 1 to the Greeks), and before Theodoret Jerome (Letter to Paulinus), testify that Xenocrates, Theophrastus, Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus, Carneades, Posidonius and very many other philosophers betook themselves to distant regions out of zeal for learning, in order to hear men of renowned wisdom. The ancient Romans too, for the sake of acquiring wisdom, used to betake themselves either to Greece, and indeed to Athens, or to Asia, or finally to Rhodes, so that they might be enriched with the treasures of wisdom by those most learned men who dwelt and taught in those places. So Cicero heard Apollonius Molon at Rhodes, and Apollonius of Alabanda in Asia. Likewise Julius Caesar at Rhodes gave his attention to Molon, Tiberius to Theodorus of Gadara, Augustus to Apollodorus. Indeed they were also accustomed to bring learned men from Asia and Greece to Rome, to hear them in their private houses, as is clear from Plutarch in his life of Lucullus and from Cicero. Indeed Cicero himself, in De Natura Deorum, bk. 1, testifies that his own house flourished with most learned men, among whom he names Diodotus, Philo, Antiochus and Posidonius. The ancient Fathers no less prove and commend teachers and the necessity of them. From their mind, thus Jerome in his letter to Rusticus: No art, he says, is learned without a teacher. The same in the Epitaph of Paula to Eustochium: On account of her constant and frequent requests, I undertook, he says, to teach what I had learned, not from myself, that is, from presumption, the worst of teachers, but from the illustrious men of the Church. To this is added the consensus of the whole world. For in every part of the Christian world, and even among the Mahumetans themselves, schools and academies have been set up, in which candidates for learning can make progress under the discipline of teachers. But what sort of teachers ought to be chosen, since this subject has been treated at length by others, it is superfluous to examine here. As the teacher ought to be pious, learned and faithful, so the pupil, as soon as he has given himself to his discipline, ought likewise to have faith in him; for it was not in vain that Aristotle said in the Sophistical Refutations that the learner must believe, which is also proved by Galen in his book On the Method of Teaching, against Favorinus; nor without reason was that saying received for a time in the school of Pythagoras: He himself said it. The reason why faith must be given to the words of the teacher is this: if the pupil does not accept the principles of the one teaching, he can by no means advance to the conclusions that are drawn from those principles.

units.la: T 5 Nec proinde aut discipulum servum pecus esse voluemus, aut obloquimur nobis ipsis hoc capite, quando partes judicandi de præceptis præceptorum discipulo vindicavimus: siquidem tum demum ad judicandum sese componere debet, quando ex principiis ipsas conclusiones cognovit, nec imitari temerarios illos adolescentes, qui damnare suorum præceptorum placita incipiunt, quando nondum quid doceant explorarunt, multo minus eorundem conclusiones ex principiis proprijs elicere sciunt. Præter præceptorem vivum atque animatum, ei qui serio proficiet, necessarium quoque sunt præceptores inanimati sive muti, quos libros vocare solemus. Quos quisquis contemnit, nae oftendit se [illegible, ~3 letters] dire ad politissimam atque utilissimam virorum doctorum impellectilem. Quam portentosum Aristotelis fuerit ingenium, ne quidem æmuli ipsius unquam id dubium vocarunt, is ipse vero vehementer illud non solum aluit, verumetiam locupletavit voluminum ubertate, quam instructus Magni Alexandri epibus sibi comparavit. Imo tantam libris tribuit, ut teste Laërtio, vel tribus talentis Speusippi libros coëmerit, atque in lectione adeo assiduus erat, ut propterea magnoftes ab ipso Platone vocatus fuerit. Nec præter rationem, ut e- nim ad Hieronymum scribit Damasus: [videt cur Epist. 122. Hieronymi) Hoc veluti quotidiano cibo alitur, & pinguescit oratio. Et tamen librorum accuratus est habendus delectus, nec tam multa sunt legenda, quam multum: ut enim recte dicebat Aristippus apud Diogenem Laërtium: Sicut non qui plurima comedunt recte valent, ita non qui plurima, sed, quae utilia legunt, eruditi atque sapientes habendi sunt. Et tantum quidem de externis praesidijs, quibus instructus esse debet discipulus: praeter haec vero, itemque internas animi dotes jam antea distincte consideratas, quilibet, qui in disciplinis cum ratione versabitur, nec in ijs, ut dicitur, oleum & operam ludet, quam diligenter attendere debet ad experientiam observationesque tum proprias, tum aliorum fide dignorum: quarum cum nonnulli ex antiquis Philosophis parum quam securi essent, jure merito vapulárunt, atque ab Aristotele aliisque reprehensi fuerunt. Nec tamen in omni scientiarum genere aeque necessaria est experientia. In Mathematicis disciplinis certe exigua quaedam animadversiunicula videtur sufficere: at in Physicis longe major, multoque accuratior jure desideratur. Inde pueri Mathematici fieri possunt, Physici tamen non possunt.
units.tr: T 5 Nor, for that reason, do we wish the student to be a slave or a sheep, nor do we contradict ourselves in this chapter, when we have granted the student the right to judge the teachers' precepts. For he should set himself to judge only once he has come to know the conclusions from their principles, and he should not imitate those reckless young men who begin to condemn their teachers' opinions before they have investigated what those teachers teach, much less know how to draw the conclusions from principles of their own. Besides the living and breathing teacher, the one who is going to make serious progress also needs silent, lifeless teachers, which we are accustomed to call books. Whoever despises these shows that he [illegible] unfit for the most refined and most useful faculty of learned men. No one, not even his rivals, has ever doubted how prodigious Aristotle's genius was, yet he himself not only nourished it greatly but also enriched it with an abundance of volumes, which he acquired with the wealth that Alexander the Great had given him. Indeed, he devoted so much money to books that, according to Laërtius, he bought the books of Speusippus for three talents, and he was so constantly engaged in reading that he was called "the Intellect" by Plato himself. Nor without reason, for Damasus writes to Jerome: "Speech is nourished and grows fat on this as on daily food" [see Jerome, Epist. 122]. Still, the selection of books must be made with care, and one must not read so many as much as read much; for, as Aristippus rightly said in Diogenes Laërtius: "Just as those who eat the most are not thereby healthiest, so those who read the most are not thereby learned and wise, but those who read what is useful." And so much for the external aids with which a student ought to be equipped. Beyond these, and likewise the inner endowments of mind already considered separately above, anyone who engages in the disciplines with reason, and does not, as they say, waste oil and labour on them, must attend carefully to experience and observation, both his own and those of trustworthy others. Some of the ancient philosophers were rather careless about these, and they were rightly and deservedly whipped and were rebuked by Aristotle and others. Yet experience is not equally necessary in every branch of learning. In the mathematical disciplines a small observation seems certainly enough, but in physics a much greater and far more exact observation is rightly required. Hence boys can become mathematicians, but they cannot become physicists.

units.la: CAPUT SECUNDUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWO.

units.la: Ad quam disciplinam quisquis se applicare debeat: quidam propensi sunt ad omnes disciplinas, alij ad aliquas duntaxat.
units.tr: To which discipline each person should apply himself: some are inclined to all disciplines, others only to certain ones.

units.la: NOn sine ratione ab Aristotele lib. 5 Polit. cap.12. dictum fuit, aliquos inveniri, quos bonos fieri & eruditi fit impossibile. Quantum enim ad eos quos disciplina perficiet, atque ab eruditione commendabuntur, nisi in iis fuerit propensa quædam facultas ad has illasve disciplinas cognoscendas, frustra iisdem se consecrabunt, neque feliciter, quicquid quoque egerint, progredi poterunt: unde Galenus in lib. de optimo docendi genere, in discente requirit non solum quandam propensionem ad disciplinas, à quibus perficietur, verum etiam amatoriam quandam insaniam. Eadem est sententia Senecæ Epist. 108. & Cardani lib. 2. de Sapientia, ubi refert Ægyptiorum hunc morem fuisse, ut pueros suos circumducerent per civitatem, cum arti cuiquam eos addicere vellent, quo eligerent illam artem, quæ pro aliis iisdem magis placeret. Nec præter rationem: nam ubi est propensio ad discendum, ibi est oblectatio, ubi vero est oblectatio, exiguo tempore plurimum proficitur. Deinde propropensio ad disciplinas percipiendas efficitut discens in suis studiis constantiam praestet: atque sicut absque constantia in studiis nihil assequi possumus, ita ubi constantia cum methodo conjuncta fuerit, certissima eruditionis spes affulget. Accedit, quod viri, qui navarunt operam disciplinis, ad quas naturalem propensionem habebant, eruditissimi & excellentissimi evaserint, ut veteres referunt de Euclide atque Archimede, qui cum se Mathematicis disciplinis addixissent, sine exemplo maximi evaserint. Refertur de Baldo eminentissimo legum Interprete, eum prima aetate Medicinae operatum fuisse, sed in ea nihil laude dignum praestare potuisse: itaque defeIrta medicina ad Iurisprudentiam se contulisse, ad quam cum mctus videretur, intra paucos annos ita in ea profecit, ut Iurisconsultorum Coryphaeus haberetur. Meminit Lucianus de se, cum sculpturae traditus esset, vapulasse ob tabulam fractam: inde somnio monitum ad literas se contulisse, ad quas cum esset propensus, brevissimo temporis spatio plurimum profecit. Testatur etiam Galenus parentem suum Niconem admonitum in somnio fuisse, ut se Medicinae consecraret, ad quam cum non tam factus, quam natus foret, brevissimo temporis spatio medicus excellentissimus evasit. Duplex vero censeri illud potest, ad quod intellectus cognoscendum fertur: vel enim universaliter se se habet, vel particulariter. quæ distinctio originem trahit ex ingenio, quod vel ita ordinatum est, ut indefinite feratur ad omnia complectenda, quæ modo cognoscibilia sint, vel duntaxat ad unam aliquam disciplinam, aut disciplinæ partem. Prioris ordinis ingenium respondet illi descriptioni, quæ occurrit apud Platonem lib. 3. de Repub. illudque notatum fuit in Asinio Pollione, qui proinde omnium horarum homo dictus est. ut refert Quint. nec aliud ingenium Origenis fuit, qui & feliciter omnes disciplinas percepit, & Alexandriæ laboriose docuit, ut testis est Eusebius in Hist. Eccles. & Epiphanius quando de Origenistis agit: atque ad hunc ordinem retulero quoque Aristotelem, Erathosthenem, Francisc​um Picum Mirandulæ Comitem, Julium Cæsarem Scaligerum, & fortassis quoque Hermodorum. quem cum civitate sua expellerent Ephesij, proclamarunt: Nemo de nobis unus excellat: sed si quis extiterit, alio in loco, & apud alios sit. Particularis ingenij propensio nascitur ex particulari quodam instinctu, atque, si ita loqui fas sit, impetu: qui ut pro diversarum per sonarum ratione diversus est, sic quæritur utra præferri debeat, universalis an particularis propensio. Et quidem, quod aliquis miretur, Alexander Aphrodifiensis in Commenc. ad lib. 8. Topic. universalem illam propensinem particulari postponit. Qui enim, inquit, ad omnem scientiam aeque parati sunt, & ad percipiendum faciles, non sunt proprie ingeniosi, quia in se non habent facultatem judicandi, sive primam boni ingenij notam: ut enim apud Galenum medicamenta polychresta nihil eximij in definito aliquo morbo praestare possunt, quamvis in pluribus legitime adhibeantur, ita neque haec ipsa ingenia; & quidem ideo, ut recte notavit Alexander, quod cum ijs parum judicij consueverint esse conjunctum: & tamen (ut iam antea quoque patuit) judicium plane necessarium est, ne in varios errores incidamus: quod certe videtur Origeni, viro alias summo accidisse, qui propter judicii defectum non solum in errores, sed & haereses incidit. Interim ego duplicem hic adhibuero distinctionem. Nam primo lata differentia intercedit inter ingenia heroica, & inter ea ingenia, quae ad modulum ordinarium sunt composita, nec quae illis forte cum ratione concedi possunt, pariter quoque his attribuere fas est. Cum aquilis in nubibus componi non meretur integer ille avium grex, qui circa volitrem noctuam animadverti soler. Deinde distingui quoque debet inter amorem erga disciplinas, atque perceptionem earum. Nam quamvis aliquis omnes scientias desiderare queat, atque, ad eas addiscendas pleno animi desiderio atque affectu ferri, eas omnes tamen non potest capescere, quia unius studium quoque, in hac vitæ brevitate, quę aliud agendo magnam partem elabitur, à perfecta alterius inquisitione non solum nos avertit, verum plane quoque abducit.
units.tr: Aristotle was not without reason when he said, in the fifth book of the Politics, chapter 12, that there are some people who cannot possibly become good and learned. For as for those whom a discipline will perfect and recommend for learning, unless there is a certain natural aptitude in them for knowing these or those disciplines, they will devote themselves to them in vain, and whatever they undertake, they will not be able to make progress. Hence Galen, in his book on the best method of teaching, requires in the learner not only a certain inclination toward the disciplines by which he will be perfected, but also a kind of passionate madness. Seneca, Letter 108, and Cardano, in the second book of On Wisdom, hold the same view, where Cardano reports that it was the custom of the Egyptians to lead their boys about the city when they wished to apprentice them to some craft, so that they might choose the craft that pleased them more than the others. Nor is this unreasonable: where there is an inclination to learn, there is delight, and where there is delight, much progress is made in a short time. Moreover, the inclination toward perceiving the disciplines brings it about that the learner shows constancy in his studies; and just as without constancy we can achieve nothing in our studies, so when constancy is joined with method, a most certain hope of learning shines forth. In addition, men who have devoted their effort to the disciplines for which they had a natural inclination have turned out most learned and most excellent, as the ancients report of Euclid and Archimedes, who, when they had devoted themselves to mathematical disciplines, became greatest beyond all example. It is related of Baldus, the most eminent interpreter of the laws, that in his early years he worked at medicine but could achieve nothing worthy of praise in it; so, medicine having been abandoned, he turned to jurisprudence, for which he seemed fit, and within a few years he advanced in it so far that he was regarded as the leader of the jurists. Lucian mentions of himself that, when he had been apprenticed to sculpture, he was beaten for a broken tablet; then, warned by a dream, he turned to letters, for which he had an aptitude, and in a very short time he made great progress. Galen also testifies that his father Nicon was warned in a dream to dedicate himself to medicine, and that, being born for it rather than made for it, he became a most excellent physician in a very short time. Now, the inclination of the intellect toward knowing something can be considered twofold: it either relates to everything universally, or to particular things. This distinction arises from the nature of the mind, which is either so ordered that it is directed indefinitely toward embracing all things that are knowable, or only toward one discipline or part of a discipline. The first kind of mind corresponds to that description which occurs in Plato, Republic, book 3; and it was noted of Asinius Pollio, who was therefore called a man for all hours, as Quintilian reports. Origen's mind was no different, for he both mastered all disciplines successfully and taught laboriously at Alexandria, as Eusebius attests in his Ecclesiastical History, and Epiphanius when he treats of the Origenists. To this order I would also assign Aristotle, Eratosthenes, Francis Pico, Count of Mirandola, Julius Caesar Scaliger, and perhaps also Hermodorus, whom the Ephesians, when they expelled him from their city, proclaimed: "Let no one among us excel; but if anyone does, let him be elsewhere and among others." The inclination of a particular mind arises from a particular impulse and, if I may so speak, a kind of momentum; and as this varies according to the nature of the different subjects, so the question is which should be preferred, the universal or the particular inclination. Indeed, what might surprise someone, Alexander of Aphrodisias, in his commentary on the eighth book of the Topics, places that universal inclination below the particular one. "For those," he says, "who are equally prepared for every science and quick to grasp it, are not properly gifted, because they do not possess in themselves the faculty of judgment, which is the first mark of a good mind." For just as, according to Galen, polychrest remedies can achieve nothing remarkable against some definite disease, although they are rightly applied in many cases, so too are these minds. And this is so, as Alexander rightly observed, because little judgment is usually joined with them; yet judgment, as has already been shown above, is entirely necessary, lest we fall into various errors. This seems to have happened to Origen, otherwise a man of the highest rank, who, through lack of judgment, fell not only into errors but also into heresies. Meanwhile, I shall here introduce a twofold distinction. For, first, a wide difference lies between heroic minds and those minds that are constituted on the ordinary scale; nor is it right to attribute to these what may perhaps reasonably be granted to those. The whole flock of birds that is observed flying about the owl does not deserve to be compared with eagles among the clouds. Second, a distinction must also be made between love of the disciplines and the perception of them. For although someone may desire all sciences, and be carried with full mental desire and feeling to learn them all, he cannot nevertheless grasp them all; because the study of even one thing, in this brief life, which is largely lost in doing other things, not only turns us away from the complete investigation of another, but also plainly leads us away from it.

units.la: CAPUT TERTIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER THREE.

units.la: Quam periculosum, imo arduum discenti sit, pravis opinionibus mentem habere imbutam atque præoccupatam.
units.tr: How dangerous, indeed how hard, it is for a learner to have his mind steeped and preoccupied with false opinions.

units.la: VT hactenus duobus præcedentibus capitibus breviter ostendimus, quomodo dispositus esse debeat, & quibusnam præsidiis instructus, qui cum fructu in disciplinis sic occupabitur, ut à Scepticismo ei nihil periculi immineat; ita deinceps circa scopulos quosdam convenienter occupabimur: nisi enim eos velut angues evitaverit, atque ab iis quam scrupulose ibi caverit, neutiquam devenire poterit ad illum ipsum scopum, in quem tamen respicere & collineare debet. Atque initio quidem nihil pædiæ æque adversatur, quam primis annis aut audivisse quædam falsa, aut ad ea ab aliis proposita mente convertisse; sive id per legislatorem fiat ex præscripto instituto patriarumlegum, sive etiam per doctores male institutos & consequenter male instituentes, atque adventitiam mentis suæ scabiem improvidæ juventuti affricantes. Quod enim alibi ab Aristotele dictum, verissimum est: Quæ audita sunt transeunt in mores. Unde jam olim notatum fuit ab Ammonio, Aristotelis interprete quantivis pretii, eos, qui innutriti erant institutis sive Ægyptiis, sive Pythagoricis, sive aliis ridiculis, multa ridicula, puerilia, atque inepta adeo pertinaciter defendisse, ut neutiquam voluerint quacunque ratione eadem sibi eripi. Quamquam vero jam antea, in antecessum quasi, ostendimus, omnia in quacunque disciplina esse æstimanda ratione demonstrationis, hi tamen qui tam erroneis persuasionibus occupati sunt, omnem demonstrationis doctrinam censere duntaxat instituunt secundum præconceptas hasce opiniones, quas citra demonstrationes illas tamen atquein consulto, moti quasi solius legislatoris authoritate, admiserunt: quum tamen ut plurimum alia vox legislatoris, alia demonstratoris esse consueverit, atque apud Galenum non uno loco velut V è diametro opponantur, demonstrare, atque legislatorum more aliquid assumere. Evidentissima huius impedimenti documenta, ne alia iam proponam, inveniuntur apud Averroem, & Algazelem; Mauritanicam de Deo, rebusque divinis superstitionem & Philosophiam saepissime confundentes, atque pro principiis indemonstrabilibus ea sumentes, quae quam maxime demonstratione indigebant. Huic vero incommodo, sane quam noxio, atque prae caeteris adversanti serio profectui, haut difficulter occurri poterit, si tum praeceptor, tum ipse discipulus suo defunctus fuerit officio. Et quidem praeceptor quando disciplinam aliquam docere incipit, eamque suo discipulo proponere, distincte non minus quam scrupulose proponat, quisnam in quaque disciplina debeat esse rationum modus quodnam definitionum genus admittendum, itemque qualis debeat esse auditor. Qua in re si officio suo rite ordineque defungatur praeceptor, discipulus ex illius praescriptione quam scrupulose se gerere debet, atque unamquamque disciplinam non ad adulterinam, sed ad propriam regulam atque amussim componere. Quod si egerit, verbi causa, in Physica aut arte Medica non flagitabit demonstrationes Mathematicas: nec in Mathematicis acquiescet demon-
units.tr: As in the two preceding chapters we have briefly shown how a student should be disposed, and what safeguards he should be equipped with, if he is to occupy himself profitably in the disciplines without any danger from Scepticism, so now we shall deal in due order with certain rocks. For unless he avoids them as he would snakes, and takes the most scrupulous care to keep clear of them, he will by no means be able to reach that very goal at which he must nonetheless look and aim. And at the outset, nothing is so hostile to learning as to have heard certain falsehoods in one's early years, or to have turned one's mind to them as proposed by others. This happens either through the lawgiver, by the prescribed institution of the ancestral laws, or through teachers who are themselves badly taught and therefore teach badly, rubbing the foreign scab of their own minds into heedless youth. For what Aristotle says elsewhere is most true: What has been heard passes into habits. Hence Ammonius, the interpreter of Aristotle and a man of no small worth, long ago observed that those who had been brought up in the institutions of the Egyptians, or of the Pythagoreans, or of other absurd sects, defended many absurd, childish and foolish things so stubbornly that they would by no means allow them to be taken away by any reasoning. Although we have already shown beforehand, as it were in advance, that everything in any discipline must be judged by the standard of demonstration, those who are occupied with such erroneous persuasions set out to judge all the doctrine of demonstration only according to these preconceived opinions, which they admitted without those demonstrations, indeed deliberately, moved as it were by the sole authority of the lawgiver. Yet for the most part the voice of the lawgiver is usually one thing and the voice of the demonstrator another, and in Galen, in more than one place, they are set over against each other as directly opposed: to demonstrate, and to assume something in the manner of lawgivers. The most evident proofs of this impediment, not to mention others now, are found in Averroes and Algazel, who very often confuse Moorish superstition concerning God and divine things with philosophy, and take as indemonstrable principles those very things which most of all needed demonstration. This inconvenience, which is quite harmful and above all hostile to serious progress, can be met without difficulty, if both the teacher and the pupil himself discharge their duty. Indeed, when a teacher begins to teach some discipline and to set it before his pupil, he should set out clearly and no less scrupulously what manner of reasoning ought to be used in each discipline, what kind of definitions must be admitted, and likewise what sort of hearer he ought to be. If the teacher discharges this duty properly and in order, the pupil must follow his instruction most scrupulously, and fit each discipline to its own rule and measure, not to a counterfeit one. If he does so, for example, he will not demand mathematical demonstrations in physics or the medical art, nor in mathematics will he be satisfied with demonstrations

units.la: strationibus rationibus aut Politicis, aut Rhetoricis: idem neque orthodoxam & syncerissimam Theologiam sine ullo distinctionis lumine tractabit Philosophice, nec vice versa Philosophiam Theologice: sed quamque disciplinam proprio suo metietur modulo, observansque justitiæ sic suum cuique assignabit, ut tamen nullam inter cognatas licet disciplinas patiatur confusionem. Placuit mihi semper & placebit illud Hieronymi: Quid mihi loqueris de Philosophia, dum versor in Theologia? & iterum, Quid mihi loqueris de Theologia, dum versor in Philosophia?
units.tr: drawn from political or rhetorical reasons. Likewise he will not treat orthodox and most sincere theology philosophically, without any light of distinction, nor, conversely, treat philosophy theologically. Rather he will measure each discipline by its own proper standard, and, observing justice, will so assign to each its own, yet without allowing any confusion between disciplines that are related. I have always liked, and always shall like, that saying of Jerome: Why do you speak to me of philosophy, when I am engaged in theology? and again, Why do you speak to me of theology, when I am engaged in philosophy?

units.la: CAPUT QUARTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FOUR.

units.la: An is, qui cum fructu in disciplina aliqua occupabitur, antea se multare debeat omnium, quæ novit, cognitione, quam veritatem aliquam in ea ipsa sufficienter apprehendere queat?
units.tr: Must one who is to occupy himself profitably in some discipline first strip himself of all his knowledge, before he can sufficiently grasp some truth in that very discipline?

units.la: QUam grave sit mentem præoccupatam habere erroneis opinionibus, & quantum præjudicium veritati creent præjudicia, abunde ex superiori capite liquet: sed ut ex re est ea deponete, atque ijsdem mens liberari debet, ita quæritur, an pariter reliqua omnia mens abjicere debeat, priusquam sese accingat ad veritatis investigationem. Sic enim quidam existimant, moti maxime hac similitudine, quod quemadmodum is, qui speciosas aedes & solidas structuras exstruere vult, caducas & depressiores antea evertit atque funditus demolitur; neque earum, aut saltem partis inconcinnae vicinia operis elegantia turbetur: pariter sapientiae & solidae eruditionis candidatus antea omnes, quas in mente invenit, opiniones abjicere debeat, quam ab ulla re intelligibili, per speciem exhibita, mentem suam perfici patiatur. Sed, ut non potest satis commendari morosa eorum diligentia, qui omni conatu atque studio hoc agunt, ut erroneas, si quas imbiberunt, sententias effurcillent, ac praejudicia veritati gravia atque prejudiciosa exuant; ita cum hac inutili saburra pariter exonerare non convenit primas veritates, sententiasque ab omni falsi contagione liberas. Nam ut pauca verba commodato accipiam a viro quodam variis scriptis editis celeberrimo: Vt humores quidem omnes abjici, nisi cum vita profusione non possunt, ita neque opiniones omnes quae in mente sunt. nisi cum totius memoriae jactura. Hinc ne existimes me nolle praejudicia ulla esse evertenda; eam habeo hac in re delectum, quem in purgatione humorum. Vt enim satis simus felices, si humores pravos excernere potuerimus, si non etiam laudabileis, probosque ejecerimus; ita felices nimium simus, si habitis quibusdam sanis, verisque opinionibus; intemeratis, ac salvis illis, deponere potuerimus, quas insanas, noxias, incertas, falsitatis suspectas habemus. Nam quicquid viri alias eximij atque ingeniosi hic praetexant, hoc fieri non posse citra abolitione ipsius mentis, atque facultatis intellectivae insignem laesionem, sequentes rationes docent. 1. Quum tantum cognoscamus, quantum recordamur, omnisque nostra scientia aestimetur ratione eorum, quę in memoriae sacrario habemus recondita, ut omnibus, quae scimus, liberetur mens, omnium debebimus oblivisci. Sed multa tam profunde in memoriae penu sunt recondita, ut difficile, si non impossibile sit, eadem effurcillare. quivis circa res tristes atque nihili experiri potest, quas deprehendimus etiam tum sui speciem menti exhibere, quando haec ipsa omni molimine sese componit ad eas propellendas. notum, Simonidem, qui primus artem memorandi condidisse perhibetur, non potuisse in gratiam Themistoclis tradere artem oblivionis, nec hunc ipsum, ut ut omnia ageret, quivisse exuere memoriam eorum, quae in adolescentia perperam egerat. 11. Si viri egregij audiendi fuerint, aliquis Messala Corvinus aut quis ei similis, qui per morbum, aliumve casum omnium rerum oblivione mulctatus est, maxime dispositus erit ad quascunque disciplinas cognoscendas: siquidem ut in eo non superfunt ullius rei simulacra, ita nulla quoque praejudicia occurrunt, quibus in acquirenda rerum cognitione impediri queat. Nullus tamen, cui modo mens integra, tale subjectum tanquam maxime idoneum disciplinis consecrare voluerit. III. Plurima inveniuntur quorum memoriam deponere neq; utile neque pium est. Quis enim velit exuere cognitionem de Deo, a nativitate ita profunde menti humane insculptam, ut quamvis sepius obscuretur, (quemadmodum fit ab ijs, de quibus loquitur Apostolus Rom. I. 21.) nullatenus tamen penitus obliterari ulla ratione queat. Imo quis existimet obliterari posse aut debere omnes primas veritates, omnibus hominibus, qui modo terminos intelligere possunt, aeque exploratas. Si liceat homini, eas omnes, tanquam praejudicia sibi gravia & velut taburam aliquā inutilem abjicere, non solum miserandum in modum circumagetur & fluctuabit, verum etiam ambigere diu debebit circa honesta & turpia, atque ut in ijs nullum invenire poterit discrimen, sic eodem redibit, quomodo vitam suam instituat. IV. Nec hoc leve, aut praeterreundum incommodum, quod hac ratione præpediatur omnis ulterior profectus. Nam si omnia debeant abjici, prima quoque principia, & certitudo eorum erit abjicienda: sed quid fiet, quando intellectus hoc ipsum lumen in se extinxit; sane nisi forinsecus aliquis aut Genius, aut mens assistens accesserit, ipse intellectus manebit similis sacculo Catulliano, qui aranearum plenus erat. Omnis quippe cognitio ut procedit e prioribus, tanquam principijs, ita tandem devenitur ad prima quedam principia, in se a priori indemonstrabilia, quæ ut ab intellectu cognoscuntur, simul ac termini modo ab eo apprehenduntur; ita non potest intellectus pariter primas hasce veritates dimittere ac deponere: eas enim si abjiciat, nihil omnino invenit & apprehendit, aut a quo possit incipere, aut ad quod tanquam primam regulam & amussim omnia a semet examinentur. Nec contrarium suadere potest ratio a simili desumpta: ut enim similia non sunt eadem, & argumenta ex hoc cognatorum loco petita magis serviunt illustrandæ, quam astruendæ indubitatæ & immutabili veritati; ita convenienter ad hanc similitudinem alicubi sic respondet vir quidam eximius: Nulla hic similitudo. Nemo enim tam est stultus, ut si lapidem, aut tignum aliquid vitij contraxisse videat, e vestigio totam domum sibi evertendam putet, id enim si faciendum est, est, integra tandem urbes evertenda erunt, cum nulla sit domus in qua non indies aliquid labis deprehendatur: ita nec omnes continuo opiniones ex animo ejiciendae, etiam vera, quia ijs admissas aliquas falsas deprehendimus.
units.tr: How grave it is to have the mind preoccupied with erroneous opinions, and how great a hindrance to truth prejudices create, is clear enough from the previous chapter. But as those opinions should be put away, and the mind freed from them, the question is whether the mind must likewise cast off all the rest before it girds itself to investigate the truth. Some hold this view, moved chiefly by the following comparison: just as one who wishes to build a splendid house and solid structures first overthrows and tears down utterly the flimsy and sunken parts, lest the elegance of the work be disturbed by the neighbourhood of any crooked part, so the candidate for wisdom and solid learning ought first to reject all the opinions he finds in his mind, before he allows his mind to be perfected by any intelligible thing presented to it in an image. But just as the painstaking diligence of those cannot be sufficiently commended who make every effort and exert every zeal to pull out whatever erroneous opinions they have imbibed, and to strip off the prejudices that are heavy and harmful to truth, so it is not right to unload along with this useless ballast the first truths and opinions, which are free from all contagion of falsehood. For, to borrow a few words from a certain man, most celebrated for his various published writings: Just as all humours cannot be cast out except with the loss of life, so neither can all the opinions that are in the mind be cast out except with the loss of the whole memory. Hence, do not think that I am unwilling for any prejudices to be overthrown; in this matter I have the same selection as in the purging of humours. For just as we shall be fortunate enough if we have been able to expel the bad humours, if we have not also thrown out the good and wholesome ones, so we shall be far too fortunate if, while keeping intact and unharmed certain sound and true opinions, we have been able to put aside those which we hold to be insane, harmful, uncertain and suspect of falsehood. For whatever distinguished and ingenious men may pretend here, the following reasons show that this cannot be done without the abolition of the mind itself and a notable injury to the faculty of understanding. 1. Since we know only as much as we remember, and all our knowledge is valued by reason of what we have stored away in the sanctuary of memory, if the mind is to be freed from all that we know, we must forget everything. But many things are so deeply stored in the storehouse of memory that it is difficult, if not impossible, to dislodge them. Anyone can test this with regard to sad and worthless matters, which we notice still present their image to the mind even when the mind itself applies all its effort to drive them away. It is known that Simonides, who is said to have first devised the art of memory, could not, to please Themistocles, hand over the art of forgetting; nor could Themistocles himself, however much he tried, strip off the memory of what he had foolishly done in youth. 2. If distinguished men are to be heard, then some Messala Corvinus, or someone like him, who has been deprived of the memory of all things by illness or some other accident, will be most suited to learn any discipline whatever; for in him no images of anything remain, and so no prejudices arise that could hinder him in acquiring knowledge of things. Yet no one who has a sound mind would wish to consecrate such a subject as most fit for the disciplines. 3. There are very many things whose memory it is neither useful nor pious to lay aside. For who would wish to strip himself of the knowledge of God, so deeply engraved in the human mind from birth that, although it is often obscured (as happens with those of whom the Apostle speaks in Rom. 1.21), it can nevertheless by no means be utterly obliterated? Indeed, who would think that all first truths, which are equally certain to all men who can understand the terms, can or ought to be obliterated? If a man were permitted to cast all these off as heavy prejudices and as some useless ballast, he would not only be tossed about and wander in a wretched manner, but would also be long in doubt about honourable and shameful things, and, since he could find no distinction between them, he would return to the same place as to how he should conduct his life. 4. Nor is this a slight or negligible inconvenience, that by this method every further progress is hindered. For if all things must be cast off, the first principles and their certainty must be cast off too. But what will happen when the understanding has extinguished that very light within itself? Unless some genius or mind from outside comes to assist, the understanding itself will remain like the Catullian purse, which was full of spiders. For just as all knowledge proceeds from earlier things as from principles, so at last we arrive at certain first principles, which are indemonstrable in themselves and a priori; these are known by the understanding as soon as the terms are grasped, and so the understanding cannot likewise dismiss and put aside these first truths. For if it rejects them, it finds and grasps nothing at all from which it could begin, or by which as a first rule and measure all things may be examined by itself. Nor can reasoning drawn from a similar case persuade otherwise: for just as similar things are not the same, and arguments taken from this kinship serve rather to illustrate than to establish an indubitable and unchangeable truth, so, in answer to this comparison, a certain eminent man replies somewhere as follows: There is no similarity here. For no one is so foolish that, when he sees a stone or a beam has contracted some defect, he thinks at once that his whole house must be pulled down. For if that were to be done, whole cities would have to be overthrown, since there is no house in which some flaw is not detected day by day. So neither must all opinions be expelled at once from the mind, even true ones, because we detect some false ones admitted among them.

units.la: CAPUT QUINTUM.
