units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Agnoscendam esse Grammaticam, à Scepticis jam olim controversam atque in dubium vocatam. Occurritur breviter eorum rationibus per quasdam generales responsiones.
units.tr: Grammar must be acknowledged, though the Sceptics once disputed it and called it into doubt. Their arguments are briefly met by some general replies.

units.la: GEneralibus hisce pertractatis, deinceps nobis accedendum ad speciales disciplinas, circa quarum divisionem ut nolumus morosi atque scrupulosi esse, ita initium faciemus à Grammatica, quam Scepticorum gens, quantum in se, evertere laboravit. Atque dum hoc agimus insistemus pariter vestigijs Sexti Empirici, qui in lib. adverf. Mathemat. ex ordine omnes disciplinas examinaturus, initium facit à Grammatica pro se investibulo cap. 3. hanc adferendo rationem: Quandoquidem, ex sapientis Epicuri sententia, neque quarere neque dubitare licet absque anticipata notione, bene erit si ante omnia consideremus quid sit Grammatica, &c. simulque se accingit ad evertendam Grammaticam, sic tamen ut eam distinguat à Grammatistica, quam admittit ut publice utilem. Est vero Grammatistica legendi atque scribendi ars. nec sine ratione. ut enim ipse eo loco dicit, medetur oblivioni. in quem sensum quoque Lactantius lib. 3. cap. 14. Discenda ista communes litteras propter usum legendi, quia in tanta rerum varietate, nec discI audiendo possunt omnia, nec memoria contineri. Sed seposita Grammatistica, ut ad ipsam Grammaticam accedamus, eam Empiricus l. d. cap. 3. ex Dionysio Thrace describit, quod sit experientia maxima ex parte eorum, quae dicuntur apud poëtas & scriptores. revera autem nihil aliud est, quam ars bene loquendi: in hoc distincta à Rhetorica, quod quemadmodum haec agit de sermonis ornatu, illa agat de sermonis puritate. Cui licet admodum infestus sit Sextus, tamen eam admittendam esse ex paucis his rationibus liquet. 1. Si nulla ars bene loquendi foret, sermo qua talis homini naturalis esse deberet; sed disciplinae eum esse contra Platonem sufficienter ostendit Aristoteles in libel. de Interpret. cap. 1. astipulante ratione multiplici, cui plus tribuere convenit, quam soli authoritati. Sed quaecunque per disciplinam aliquam adquiruntur, & quorum ars datur, ea gradus perfectionis admittere posse consentaneum est. Ergo aut Grammatica non erit agnoscenda ars, aut etiam ad suum finem pervenire poterit. II. Grammaticae, ut arti bene loquendi, si nihil tribuere conveniat, puer balbutiens & voces sine constructione ulla producens, dici poterit perfecte loqui: nec refert, quod usus secundum constructiones eundem pariter bene perfecteque loqui doceat, quum Grammatica secundum usum & communissimum & castigatissimum nos loqui doceat: sic ut non inconvenienter Dionysius Thrax dixerit eandem quandam experientiam esse, probante hoc ipso (quemadmodum jam patuit) Sexto. III. Grammaticae si nihil tribuendum foret, nulli aut solecismi aut barbarismi in ulla lingua notari possent, & vulgus æque censeretur perfecte loqui, atque illi qui in aliqua gente politiores sunt, & si non per artem, saltem per experientiam [ad quam artem se componere modo dictum est] suum idioma quotidianum polierunt. At quis hoc dixerit? IV. Ipsi quoque Sceptici, qui, ut ex Sexto liquet, peculiares loquendi formulas frequentare & in usu habere solent, frustra de iis observandis, & aliis inculcandis laborarent; si non daretur ars quaedam bene loquendi. Quamvis enim dicere possint quamq; disciplinam ptoprios peculiaresque suos terminos habere, atque definitionem significationum iis competentium, ab eadem pendere: Tamen neque illi loquendi termini, neque axiomata certis terminis constantia & comprehésa, commodum in ulla disciplina sensum admittere possunt, nisi antea Grammaticæ præceptis, quod ad inflexionem terminorum & constructionem eorundem, satisfactum fuerit. v. Si audiendi forent hac in parte Sceptici, atque eliminanda esset Grammatica, pariter Orthographia, quæ Grammaticæ pars, exterminari deberet, & consequenter ea proscripta, eodem redirét, quibuscunque literis aliquis in scribendo, certisque vocibus per literas exprimendis, uteretur. At quis sanæ mentis hoc unquam statuerit? vi. Denique, si non admittenda foret Grammatica, neque idioma alicujus populi, pro ratione certarum ætatum modo perfectius modo imperfectius censeri posset: siquidem Grammatica, attendendo eam ætatem, qua idioma alicujus gentis præ cæteris cultum tersumque fuit, illius ratione sua præcepta ordinare proponereque solet. Pauca hæc argumenta, si quis mentis exactiori trutina expendere diligentius instituerit, videre poterit, quam incommode, si non pariter per injuriam, Grammatica à Scepticis proscripta fuerit. Multa quidem argumenta conglobat Sextus, quo evertat disciplinam, pro qua hæc pauca duntaxat adduximus, interim haut difficile erit iis omnibus occurrere, ex paucis, quae sequuntur, classibus respondebimus.
units.tr: Having dealt with these general matters, we must now come to the particular disciplines. We will not be fussy or scrupulous about their division, and we shall begin with grammar, which the sect of the Sceptics has laboured, so far as it could, to overthrow. In doing so we shall follow the footsteps of Sextus Empiricus, who, in his book against the mathematicians, intending to examine all the disciplines in order, begins with grammar. In chapter 3 he prefaces it with this argument: Since, according to the opinion of the wise Epicurus, one may neither inquire nor doubt without a prior notion, it will be well if before all else we consider what grammar is, etc. At the same time he sets himself to overthrow grammar, but he distinguishes it from grammatistic, which he admits as publicly useful. Grammatistic is the art of reading and writing, and not without reason, for, as he himself says in that place, it cures forgetfulness. Lactantius also has the same sense in book 3, chapter 14: These common letters are to be learned for the sake of the use of reading, because in such a variety of things all cannot be learned by hearing nor held in the memory. But setting grammatistic aside, so that we may come to grammar itself, Empiricus, in the same chapter 3, describes it after Dionysius Thrax as experience, for the most part, of the things that are said by poets and writers. In truth, it is nothing other than the art of speaking well. In this it differs from rhetoric: as rhetoric deals with the ornament of speech, grammar deals with its correctness. Although Sextus is very hostile to it, it is clear from the following few arguments that it must be admitted. 1. If there were no art of speaking well, speech as such ought to be natural to man. But Aristotle, in the book On Interpretation, chapter 1, sufficiently shows, against Plato, that speech is a matter of training, and reason, which supports this in many ways, deserves more weight than authority alone. Yet whatever is acquired through some discipline, and whose art is given, may reasonably be admitted to have degrees of perfection. Therefore either grammar must not be acknowledged as an art, or it can attain its end. 2. If nothing is to be attributed to grammar as the art of speaking well, a stammering child who utters words without any construction could be said to speak perfectly. Nor does it matter that usage, following constructions, teaches us to speak equally well and perfectly, since grammar teaches us to speak according to the most common and most refined usage. So Dionysius Thrax was not wrong to say that grammar is a kind of experience, and this very point is proved by Sextus himself, as has already been shown. 3. If nothing were to be attributed to grammar, no solecisms or barbarisms could be noted in any language, and the common people would be judged to speak as perfectly as those who are more polished in some nation, even if they had polished their daily idiom not by art but by experience (to which art, as has just been said, one must conform). But who would say this? 4. The Sceptics themselves, who, as is clear from Sextus, are accustomed to use and maintain peculiar forms of speech, would labour in vain to observe these and to impress them on others, if there were no certain art of speaking well. For although they may say that every discipline has its own peculiar terms, and that the definition of the meanings belonging to them depends on that discipline, nevertheless neither those terms of speech nor axioms consisting of fixed and comprehended terms can suitably admit any sense in any discipline, unless first the precepts of grammar have been satisfied regarding the inflection of the terms and their construction. 5. If the Sceptics were to be heard in this matter, and grammar were to be eliminated, then orthography, which is a part of grammar, would likewise have to be banished. Consequently, once it was proscribed, it would come to the same thing whatever letters anyone used in writing and whatever fixed sounds he expressed by letters. But who of sound mind would ever lay this down? 6. Finally, if grammar were not admitted, the idiom of any people could not be judged more or less perfect according to the standards of certain ages. For grammar, attending to that age in which the idiom of a given nation was cultivated and refined beyond the rest, is accustomed to set out its precepts according to that standard. If anyone were to weigh these few arguments more carefully on the more exact scales of the mind, he would be able to see how unfairly, if not also unjustly, grammar has been proscribed by the Sceptics. Sextus indeed gathers many arguments by which he overthrows the discipline, of which we have adduced only these few. Meanwhile it will not be difficult to meet them all, and we shall reply to them from the few classes that follow.

units.la: I. Methodus qua disciplina aliqua traditur, censeri debet ex natura ipsius, nec omnes disciplinae aeque exacte ad leges methodi castigatissime castigari possunt: sufficit Grammaticam Methodicam eatenus censeri, quatenus ea, circa quae occupatur, suo modo methodice proponit.
units.tr: I. The method by which a discipline is taught ought to be judged from its nature, and not all disciplines can be corrected with equal exactness by the rules of the most refined method. It is enough that grammar be counted methodical so far as the things with which it is occupied are set out methodically in their own way.

units.la: II. Literae circa quae, ut simplicissima vocum principia occupatur Grammatica, elementa vocantur, quia vox omnis generatur ex iis primo, inque ea postremo resolvitur, ut loquitur Plato in Cratylo: nec cavillationes Sexti, circa hanc ipsam denominationem literarum, pili faciendae sunt.
units.tr: II. The letters with which grammar is occupied, as the simplest principles of words, are called elements, because every voice is first generated from them and finally resolved into them, as Plato says in the Cratylus. Nor are Sextus's quibbles about this very name of the letters worth a hair.

units.la: III. Vocum quantitates non tam esse censendas secundum liquidas rationes, ut Sextus contendit, quam potius secundum usum & rationem pronunciandi, cuique genti proprium certissimum est, & firmari potest ipsius Scripturae authoritate, notantis Ephraimitarum Sibboleth, pro Schibboleth, Iud. 12. 6. originem duxisse non ab inconstantia praeceptorum Grammaticorum, aut ignorantia eorundem, sed blęsa Ephraimitarum lingua.
units.tr: III. The quantities of words are to be judged not so much by the clear reasons that Sextus contends for, as by the usage and manner of pronunciation that is most certainly proper to each people. This can be confirmed by the authority of Scripture itself, which notes that the Ephraimites' Sibboleth, for Shibboleth, Judges 12:6, arose not from inconsistency of the grammarians' precepts, nor from their ignorance, but from the lisping of the Ephraimites' tongue.

units.la: IV. Nec propter hęc eadem, incerta redditur ipsa ars Grammatica, cum cuiusque linguae propria serviat, nec unius linguae Grammatica, ex Grammatica alterius censeri queat nisi quatenus aut inter illas linguas quædam affinitas intercedit, aut utriusque Grammaticæ secundum tractationis modum consentiunt. v. Genuinæ notæ Grammaticus nunquam rationi præusu prærogativam concedit; sed ita omnia sua præcepta ordinat, ut nunquam à consuetudine inter plures, eosque politiores recepta, aberret. vi. Ejusdem consuetudinis Grammatica est observans, ratione quantitatis syllabarum, quam non ordinat secundum suum arbitrium; sed secundum praxin meliorum & castigatiorum poëtarum, qui ipsi ad usum quoque præ cæteris attenderunt. vii. Quemadmodum queque disciplina terminos technologicos habet, sibi proprios, suaeque naturæ convenientes, ita quoque Grammatica: quæ quando octo orationis partes proprijs quibusdam terminis distinguit, vult illas easdem partes esse classes vocum, non solum ratione significationis distinctarum, verum etiam terminatione, inflexioneque differentium. viii. Nec refert quosdam Grammaticos aut non commode has ipsas partes orationis definivisse, aut etiam quadantenus confudisse: quum sufficiat esse classes doctrinæ gratia satis convenienter disparatas: nec conveniens sit aut errata Grammaticorum ipsi Grammaticæ imputare, aut consequens sit propterea nullam distinctionem nem intercedere inter Orationis partes, quod de paucis quibusdam vocibus controvertatur, ad quamnam orationis partem referri debeant.
units.tr: IV. Nor, for these same reasons, is the art of grammar itself rendered uncertain, since each language has its own grammar, and the grammar of one language cannot be judged by that of another, except so far as some affinity exists between those languages, or the grammars agree in their manner of treatment. V. A genuine grammarian never grants priority to reason over usage, but so orders all his precepts that he never strays from the custom received among many, and more refined, speakers. VI. Grammar observes the same custom in respect of the quantity of syllables. It does not order these according to its own judgement, but according to the practice of the better and more correct poets, who themselves paid more attention to usage than others did. VII. As every discipline has technical terms proper to itself and suited to its nature, so too has grammar. When it distinguishes the eight parts of speech by certain proper terms, it means these same parts to be classes of words that differ not only in their meaning but also in their ending and inflection. VIII. It makes no difference that some grammarians have either defined these parts of speech unsuitably or even somewhat confused them. For it is enough that they be classes sufficiently and conveniently distinguished for the sake of teaching. Nor is it fitting either to impute the errors of grammarians to grammar itself, or to conclude from the fact that some few words are disputed as to which part of speech they should be referred to, that there is no distinction at all between the parts of speech.

units.la: ix. Anomalia in partibus orationis frequens, nequaquam evertit analogiam. Ut enim similitudinem inter homines intercedentem neutiquam quidam monstrosi partus evertunt; ita neque putandum est, propterea in sermone nullam analogiam occurrere, quod eadem in aliquibus deficiat: sed potius, multo magis agnoscenda est, quod in multo pluribus sese prodat.
units.tr: IX. An anomaly frequent among the parts of speech by no means overturns analogy. For just as certain monstrous births do not destroy the likeness that exists among men, so it should not be thought that no analogy occurs in speech because it fails in some instances. Rather, analogy should be acknowledged all the more, since it shows itself in far more instances.

units.la: x. Haut satis graphice vero personam ScepticI tuetur Sextus lib. i. adverf. Mathem. cap. 10. quando pro anomalia atque analogia in utramque partem disputat; quum potius, si lineis suis inhaerere voluisset, unam per alteram evertere debuisset.
units.tr: x. Sextus, in book 1 of Adversus Mathematicos, chapter 10, does not portray the persona of the Sceptic vividly enough when he argues for anomaly and against analogy in turn. If he had wished to keep to his own lines, he should rather have overthrown the one by means of the other.

units.la: xi. Quę in vocibus analogia notatur, non authoritate unius alicujus authoris [ut perperam contendit Sextus I. d.] uti debet; sed consuetudine, non tam doctorum, quam potius vulgi, [quod tamen Grammatica, ut antea quoque patuit, secundum diversas aetates modo cultius, modo fordidius in loquendo observat] quoniam rationem in loquendo semper sequi praesumitur: unde etiam secundum Flaccum in Arte, penes illud arbitrium est, & vis, & norma loquendi. adeo ut tum sapiens quoque eidem cedere debeat, quando in loquendo rationi penitus obloqui videtur. xii. Grammatica de orthographia non agit ex suo arbitratu, aut secundum solam rationem, sed rationem usui copulat, nunquam patiendo ut illa huic etiam hac in parte adversetur. A quibusdam Grammaticis secus si factum fuerit, haut quaquam fas est ipsi arti hoc imputare. xiii. Frustra valde est Sextus lib. i. adv. Mathem. cap. 10. quando existimat ideo artem Grammaticam aboleri, quod consuetudo & usus, quae artem inducunt, non opus habeant arte. siquidem primo Grammatica hanc consuetudinem, quae variat, quantum in se ad ipsas rationis & artis lineas perpetuo non solum exigere, verum etiam castigare praesumit. Deinde illius subsidio peregrinis, qui usum alicujus linguae habere non possunt, per compendium consulitur: quorum sermo quoniam semper ad artis lineas est exactus, saepe admirationi ipsis indigenis est, quorum idioma laplu temporis vitiari atque a rationis artisque lineis declinare solet. Unde & accidit, ut, qui ex Grammatica linguam aliquam didicerunt, corrigere eos ipsos possint, quibus alias ea ipsa lingua vernacula esse solet. Contra quam ipse Sextus existimat, qui loco dicto sic oquitur: Nam aliter quoque licet ostendere, quod ad Graece loquendum non opus habemus Grammatica.
units.tr: xi. The analogy noted in words should not be governed by the authority of any single author [as Sextus wrongly contends, in the passage cited above], but by usage: not so much the usage of the learned as that of the common people. [Grammar nevertheless observes this usage, as was shown earlier, now more refined and now more vulgar in speaking according to the different ages.] For reason is always presumed to be followed in speaking. Hence, according to Horace in the Art of Poetry, the judgement, the power and the norm of speaking rest with usage. So much so that even the wise man must yield to it, when he seems entirely to oppose reason in speaking. xii. Grammar does not treat orthography at its own pleasure, or by reason alone, but joins reason to usage, never allowing the one to oppose the other in this respect. If some grammarians have done otherwise, it is by no means right to impute this to the art itself. xiii. Sextus, in book 1 against the mathematicians, chapter 10, is quite wrong when he thinks grammar should be abolished because custom and usage, which bring about the art, have no need of art. For, first, grammar always presumes to demand, and indeed to correct, by the very lines of reason and art, this custom which, as far as it is in itself, varies. Next, by its aid, foreigners who cannot have command of a language's usage are instructed in a short way; their speech, since it has always been held to the lines of art, is often a marvel even to the natives themselves, whose idiom is wont to be corrupted with the passage of time and to depart from the lines of reason and art. Hence it also happens that those who have learned a language from grammar can correct the very people for whom that language is otherwise usually the mother tongue. Sextus himself thinks the contrary, who in the passage cited says: For we can show in another way too that we have no need of grammar for speaking Greek.

units.la: Nam in iis, qui conferuntur sermonibus, aut in aliquibus dictionibus offendentur multi, aut non offendentur. &, si offendantur quidem, non statim corrigent. quo fit ut ex iis, quae in usu vitae versantur, habeamus Graecum sermonem, non autem à Grammaticis. Sin autem non agre ferunt, ex iis, quae dicuntur, assentiuntur tanquam apertis & rectè habentibus: & nos in eis perfistimus. Quod dilemma nullo negotio ex superioribus dilui potest. Nam vulgus, quod secundum consuetudinem saepe corrupte loquitur, ut errores in loquendo patienter valde ab alio, imo à se ipso, committi fert; ita neque errantes, etiam si vellet, castigare potest. xiv. Atque hinc patet, quam bene cohaereant ea, quae habet Sextus loco dicto: Si optime, inquit, loqui dicimus Thracice, eum qui loquitur Thracice ut qui consueverit, & maxime Romane, qui Romane consuevit: sequetur etiam eum loqui recte Graece, qui Graece loqui consuevit, si sequamur usum ac consuetudinem, non autem praeceptionem. Fallitur quippe gravissime Scepticismi patronus, quando in quaque lingua, eum maxime culte & terse loqui existimat, qui praeceteris convenienter consuetudini loquitur. Hoc enim si valeret, nullum privilegium competeret iis qui diserti in suo idiomate censentur, praeterim tunicato popello, eloquentiaeque candidatus aeque tuto imitari potest, hunc posset hunc, atque illos: ad hoc ratio non constitisset aut Ciceroni; aut Valerio Maximo circa iudicium de Platone. Sic enim de eo Tullius lib. de Clar. Orat. Quis uberior in dicendo, Platone? Iovem sic, ut ajunt Pqilosophi; si Graece loquatur; loqui. Valerius vero lib. 8. cap. 7. de eodem: Omnium mortalium sapientissimus habitus, eo quidem usque; ut si ipse Iupiter cælo descendisset; nec elegantiore nec beatiore facundia usurus videretur. Falsus iterum fuisset Cicero, quando modo Xenophontis serinonem melle dulciorem, modo molle illius orationis genus, & denique Musas quasi voce ejusdem locutas celebrat, in Orat. & in Bruto. Denique minime ratio constitisset Fabio Quintiliano, quando lib. 10 cap. 1. hoc elogium de disertissimo Romuli nepotum proponit: Apud posteros id consecutus, ut Cicero jam non hominis, sed eloquentiae nomen habeatur. xv. Falsus pariter idem Sextus est, quando in loquendo præsentis perpetuo consuetudinis haberi vult rationem: ut enim hoc facile concessierim (quemadmodum ex antecedentibus jam liquet) si ipse loquendi usus ad rationis amussim sit exactus; ita declinante eo à ratione, quantum fieri potest, resistendum, & non cedendum, nisi jam prævalido ipso usu contra rationem: quo tamen in casu alia ratio locutionis, alia vero scriptionis est. quamvis enim in loquendo utendum perpetuo sit verbis præsentibus, inter scribendum tamen præterita ad optimam consuetudinem duce Grammatica convenientissime adhibentur. Quomodo V. C. plurimi ex scriptoribus Latinis labente cum Romano imperio ipsa lingua, quam scrupulose tamen sibi caverunt à seculi nævis, & in hoc toti fuerunt, ut uterentur castigatioris ævi locutione.
units.tr: For among those who converse, many will take offence at some expressions, or others will not. And even if they do take offence, they will not immediately correct them. So it comes about that we have the Greek language from those things which belong to the practice of life, and not from the grammarians. But if they do not take it ill, they assent to what is said as open and correctly expressed, and we persist in them. This dilemma can easily be dissolved from what was said above. For the common people, who speak corruptly according to custom, bear with great patience the errors in speech committed by others, indeed by themselves, and so they cannot correct the erring, even if they wished to. xiv. And from this it is plain how well those things hold together which Sextus has in the passage cited: "If," he says, "we say that the best speaking is in the Thracian manner, then he who speaks Thracian as he has been accustomed, and most of all he who has been accustomed to speak Roman in the Roman manner, will also be said to speak Greek correctly, if he speaks Greek, provided we follow usage and custom and not precept." The advocate of scepticism is gravely mistaken when he thinks that in every language he speaks most refinedly and elegantly who speaks most in agreement with common custom. For if this held, no privilege would belong to those who are judged eloquent in their own idiom; especially since the tunic-wearing rabble, and the candidate for eloquence, can imitate this one or that one equally safely. Reason would not have held for Cicero or Valerius Maximus in their judgement about Plato. For Tully says of him in his book On Famous Orators: Who was more copious in speaking than Plato? Jove himself, as the philosophers say, would seem to speak if he spoke Greek. Valerius, in book 8, chapter 7, says of the same man: He was regarded as the wisest of all mortals, to such an extent that if Jupiter himself had come down from heaven, he would not seem likely to use a more elegant or more fortunate eloquence. Cicero would have been mistaken again, when in the Orator and in the Brutus he praises the speech of Xenophon sweeter than honey, now the soft kind of his oratory, and finally the Muses as if they had spoken with his voice. Lastly, reason would not have held for Fabius Quintilian, when in book 10, chapter 1, he puts forward this eulogy of the most eloquent of Romulus's descendants: He has attained among posterity that Cicero is now held not the name of a man, but of eloquence.

units.la: CAPUT SEXTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SIX.

units.la: De arte historica, ejusque certitudine, ad- versus Sextum Empiricum.
units.tr: On the historical art and its certainty, against Sextus Empiricus.

units.la: POst Grammaticam impugnare instituit artem historicam Sextus Empiricus lib. adverf. Mathemat. cap. 12. præsupponitque ex sententia Asclepiadis, Dionysij Halicarnassensis & Taurisci, Cratetis auditoris, ipsam artem historicam ad Grammaticam pertinere, ex quorum mente ut quam plurima adducit, varias insuper proponendo Grammaticæ divisiones subdivisionesque, sic concludit historicam nullatenus artem censeri posse, aut ei assignari aliquam methodum, quod tota Grammatica subsidio tractationis methodicæ destituatur, atque partis eadem debeat esse ratio, quę totius: ne quid dicam de specialibus argumentis, quibus deinceps per speciales classes responsorias haut difficulter occurri poterit. Antequam Historiæ certitudinem asserere & vindicare instituimus, omnino distinguere convenit inter historicam quatenus est ars quædam præcepta tradens, resgestas ex rei veritate ordine atque methodice explicandi, atque eandem quatenus usui Grammaticorum servit, quorum eruditio cum non censeretur esse persecta, nisi quatenus se extenderet quoque ad explicationem verarum atque falsarum historiarum, factum est ut historica, quæ alias est ars distincta, cœperit succenturiari ipsi Grammaticæ. Quod cognoscere est vel ex ipsis Sexti Empirici verbis, quibus cum ex Asclepiadis libro de arte Grammatica retulisset, triplicem esse historiam, circa quam Grammaticæ occupetur; veram, falsam, & quasi veram: de vera ita scribit: vera autem tres rursus sunt partes. Nam alia quidem versatur in describendis personis deorum & heroum, & virorum illustrium: alia autem in locis & temporibus: alia in actionibus. Falsæ speciem esse dicit genealogias Deorum, quasi vero exemplum facit comœdias & mimos. Mox veræ ita concludit: Atque quod Grammaticæ quidem partem velint esse historicam, ex his est perspicuum. Esse vero artem historicam admittendam, contra quam Scepticorum filiis placuit, & post eos quoque Iacobo Zabarellae Philosopho eximio in libris, quos de Natura Logicae scripsit, probant pauca sequentia argumenta. I. In qua scriptione pro diversa tractandi ratione aliquis vere aut laudem aut vituperium referre potest, circa eam ars quaedam agnosci debet, quae sequestrato vituperio, alicui solam laudem procuret. Sed hoc de scriptione historica agnosci debet. Major propositio adeo certa est, ut de illa nemo ambigere possit. Ne de minore dubitare possunt, quicunque unquam defaecato judicio, diversos, qua antiquos, qua recentiores historicos inter se conferre instituerunt, noruntque quae differentia intercedat inter Pontificum Maximorum rudes inconditosque annales, & historias qua Graecas, qua Latinas, à summis scriptoribus stylo elegantissimo adornatas. II. Circa quam scriptionem Methodus arbitraria, à prudentia maxime commendabilis, observatur, circa eandem pariter versari quedam ars debet, ostendens quomodo ejusmodi methodo sua ratio constare ubique debeat. Quid vero certius, quam ejusmodi methodum, (gnarum iis est, qui in historicorum lectione non sunt peregrini) circa historias, diversa ratione tractari solitas, diversimode ex prudentiae præscripto scripto applicari. III. Cujus scriptionis partes secundum artis regulas dirigi ordinarique possunt, ea ipsa secundum se tota pariter ab arte ordinari poterit. Atqui quaeque partes historicae scriptionis ad speciales artis regulas examinari possunt. Ergo. Antecedanea propositio adeo certa est, ut neutiquam fas sit de eadem ambigere. Quum enim ipsa ars sit systema quoddam, ex singulis particulis integrum corpus conflari certum est. pariter veritati consentanea est Assumptio: quis enim adeo hospes, qui nesciat in descriptione historica alicujus rei, particularis quam maxime, sedulo attendendum esse, ne illud quod prius gestum est, tanquam posterius referatur, aut vice versa. Atqui universa Methodi, sive Ordinis ratio in hoc consistit, ut conservetur differentia inter prius atque posterius. IV. Si datur memoria artificialis, pariter quaedam ars historica agnosci debet. Sequele ratio inde elucet, quod historiae subsidio non solum hominum mortalium memoriae, immortalitati quasi consecrentur; sed quam maxime ab interitu ea vindicentur, quae alias vix ultra unius viri aetatem durare posse videntur. Adversarijs argumentis haut difficulter quis occurret, si modo sequentia diligenter attenderit. I. Adversus Zabarellam, Aristotelis, Philosophi licet sum-
units.tr: After Grammar, Sextus Empiricus sets out to attack the historical art in book 12 of his Against the Mathematicians. He takes it for granted, following Asclepiades, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Tauriscus, a pupil of Crates, that the historical art belongs to Grammar. Citing many of their views and adding various divisions and subdivisions of Grammar, he concludes that history cannot be regarded as an art at all, nor can any method be assigned to it, since the whole of Grammar lacks the support of methodical treatment, and a part must have the same nature as the whole. I say nothing here of the special arguments, to which replies can be made without difficulty through particular counter-classes. Before we undertake to assert and vindicate the certainty of history, we must carefully distinguish between history as an art that teaches how to set out deeds in order and methodically, according to the truth of the matter, and history as it serves the grammarians. Since their learning was not thought complete unless it extended also to the explanation of true and false histories, it came about that history, which is otherwise a distinct art, began to be attached as a subordinate to Grammar itself. We can see this from Sextus Empiricus' own words. After reporting from the book on the art of Grammar by Asclepiades that there are three kinds of history with which Grammar is concerned, true, false and quasi-true, he writes of the true kind: The true history, moreover, has three parts. One deals with describing the persons of gods, heroes and illustrious men; another with places and times; another with actions. He says that the false kind is the genealogies of the gods, and he gives comedies and mimes as examples. Then, on the true kind, he concludes: And from this it is clear that they wish history to be part of Grammar. That history is to be admitted as an art, contrary to what the sons of the Sceptics thought, is proved, after them, by Jacob Zabarella, an eminent philosopher, in his books on the nature of logic, by the few following arguments. I. In any writing, one may rightly praise or blame the manner of treatment; so there must be some art concerned with it, which, setting aside blame, secures praise for something alone. But this must be recognised in historical writing. The major premise is so certain that no one can doubt it. Nor can those doubt the minor, who, with a sound judgement, have ever undertaken to compare historians with one another, ancient and modern, and who know what difference lies between the rough and unpolished annals of the High Priests and the histories, Greek and Latin, adorned in the most elegant style by the greatest writers. II. In such writing an arbitrary method is observed, which is especially to be commended by prudence. Some art must likewise be concerned with this, showing how such a method ought everywhere to be constituted. What is more certain than this, that such a method (as is known to those who are not strangers to the reading of historians) is applied in different ways to histories, which are commonly treated in different ways, according to the rule of prudence? III. Whatever parts of historical writing can be directed and ordered according to the rules of an art, the whole of it, considered in itself, can likewise be ordered by an art. But the parts of historical writing can each be examined by the special rules of the art. Therefore, etc. The major premise is so certain that it is by no means right to doubt it. For since the art is a certain system, it is certain that a whole body is made up of its individual parts. The minor is likewise consistent with the truth; for who is so ignorant as not to know that in the historical description of any matter, even a particular one, great care must be taken that what happened first is not recounted as later, or the reverse? Yet the whole principle of method, or order, consists in this, that the difference between prior and posterior is preserved. IV. If there is an artificial memory, a historical art must likewise be recognised. The consequence follows from this, that by the aid of history not only the memories of mortal men are, as it were, consecrated to immortality, but those things are especially rescued from perishing which otherwise seem scarcely able to last beyond the life of a single man. The arguments of the opponents can easily be met, if only one attends carefully to the following points. I. Against Zabarella: although Aristotle, the Philosopher, is to be greatly esteemed and is rather too much devoted to the authority of that great man, nevertheless disciplines are to be considered according to their own nature, and are not to be valued in vain by the sense of one man alone. I grant willingly that Aristotle did not treat history as an art; but does it follow that history therefore ceases to be what it is, or departs in any way from its genuine nature?

units.la: {*} Mark at the foot of the page, not legible as a word. summi, authoritati plus æquo addictum, nonrandum, disciplinas, secundum propriam suam idolem considerandas, nequicquam æstimandas esse ex unius illius sensu. Do lubens, Aristotelem historicam non tractasse ut artem; sed, an proinde definit esse quod est, aut quicquam decedit genuinæ ejusdem naturæ. II. Neque verum, omnes Grammaticæ partes methodice tradi, neque universas & singulas methodice tractandas esse. Distinctione hic omnino opus: vel enim partes Grammaticæ occupantur circa præcepta, vel circa exegesin. Illæ astrictæ sunt legibus methodi, non pariter hæ. III. Neutiquam sequitur, propterea Grammaticæ officium esse docere, quomodo scribenda sit historia, quia ipsa docet quomodo historici sint explicandi. Alias omnes illas disciplinas Grammatica ordinare deberet, quibus servit pro explicandis illis conceptibus, quos alijs explicare laborant. At quam absonum hoc? IV. Dato, quosdam jam olim sine Methodi lege historiam scripsisse, non tamen inde sequitur, negandam esse artem historicam: nam & vulgus suum sermonem non exigit ad Methodi leges, & tamen (ut ex superiori capite patet) agnoscenda Grammatica, a qua idem ille sermo ordinetur. VI. Distinguere omnino convenit inter ipsam historiam ut scriptam & plene tractatam, artemque ipsam secundum quam scribi tractariq; debet. Ipsa historia non est ars, qua talis, nec tamen propterea historica, jam antea quoque distincta ab ipsa historia, ars esse definit. VII. Verum quidem est illud Philosophi lib. 1. Post. Analyt. cap. 3. Impossibile est infinita animo percurrere: nec tamen propterea valet Sexti ratiocinium, quo colligit nullam esse agnoscendam artem historicam, quod ipsa historia occupetur circa singularia, quae infinita sunt: siquidem hic distinguere omnino convenit inter singularia seorsum atque distincte, & quasi ab aliis abstracte, considerata, & eadem universim, seu simul scripta. Valeret Empirici argumentum, si historia omnia singularia conjunctim, sive ut universa, sibi tractanda proponeret, sic enim spectata singularia si non sunt infinita, saltem considerantur quasi infinita: sed ex pluribus singularibus quaedam seligit, unum plurave sibi proponendo, quae consideret, suoque modo pertractet. VIII. Quamvis agnoscere omnino conveniat historiam Mythologicam, non tamen propterea evanescit ars historica, historiam in veri consideratione occupatam ordinans. nam ut definit ens reale esse illud, quod est; propterea quod ens ratione ab intellectu secundum similitudinem entis realis effigietur ac concipiatur: ita neque historiae in vera
units.tr: {*} Mark at the foot of the page, not legible as a word. Though he is the highest authority, too much given over to authority, it must be noted that disciplines are to be considered according to their own nature, and are in vain to be judged by the opinion of that one man. I gladly grant that Aristotle did not treat history as an art; but does it therefore cease to be what it is, or lose anything of its genuine nature? II. Nor is it true that all parts of grammar are taught methodically, or that all of them, both singly and together, must be treated methodically. A distinction is wholly needed here: for the parts of grammar are concerned either with precepts or with exegesis. The former are bound by the laws of method; the latter are not equally bound. III. It by no means follows that, because it is the office of grammar to teach how history is to be written, it is therefore grammar's office to teach how historians are to be explained. Otherwise grammar would have to order all those disciplines which it serves in explaining those concepts that others labour to explain. But how absurd is this? IV. Granted that some men long ago wrote history without the law of method, it does not follow that the art of history must be denied. For the common people also do not subject their speech to the rules of method, and yet (as is clear from the preceding chapter) grammar must be recognised, by which that same speech is ordered. VI. It is wholly right to distinguish between history itself as written and fully treated, and the art according to which it ought to be written and treated. History itself is not an art as such; nor, for that reason, does the art of history, already distinguished before from history itself, cease to be an art. VII. True is that saying of the Philosopher, Posterior Analytics book 1, chapter 3: "It is impossible to run through infinite things with the mind." Yet for that reason Sextus' argument does not hold, by which he concludes that no art of history is to be recognised because history is occupied with singulars, which are infinite. For here it is wholly necessary to distinguish between singulars considered separately and distinctly, as it were abstracted from others, and the same considered universally or written together. The Empiricist's argument would hold if history proposed to itself all singulars conjunctly, or to treat them as a whole; for so regarded, the singulars, if not infinite, are at least considered as if infinite. But history selects some out of many singulars, proposing to itself one or several to consider and treat in its own way. VIII. Although it is wholly right to acknowledge mythological history, the art of history, which orders history occupied with the consideration of truth, does not on that account vanish. For just as real being is defined as that which is what it is, because a being of reason is shaped and conceived by the intellect according to the likeness of real being, so the worth of history occupied with the true

units.la: {X 4} vera narratione occupatæ pretium diminuitur ex eo, quod ad informandum commodius intellectum, quædam narrentur ut re vera gesta, quibus tamen nihil aliud veri subest, quam quod ab ipso intellectu iisdem inesse fingitur.
units.tr: ...the value of a history occupied with true narration is diminished by the fact that, in order to shape the understanding more conveniently, certain things are narrated as though they were actually done, though nothing of truth underlies them beyond what the understanding itself imagines to be present in them.

units.la: IX. Nec obstat, quo minus ipsa historia Mythologica, secundum lineamenta artis historicæ ordinetur: nam, si ens rationis à mente factum secundum ens reale, spectatumque ad similitudinem ejusdem, tractatur eodem modo ut ens reale: cur non pari ratione historia Mythologica eodem modo tractari potest, atque historia genuina & proprie sic dicta? X. Dato, ut ex antecedentibus liquet, historiam occupari circa singularia, non obstat tamen, quo minus ea ipsa ab arte, quæ est habitus intellectualis practicus, ordinari queat. Nam tractatio, quæ circa singularia instituitur, æque subjecta est Methodi legibus, atque ea ipsa quæ universalia concernit.
units.tr: IX. Nor does it stand in the way that mythological history should not be arranged according to the outlines of the historical art. For if a being of reason, made by the mind, is treated in the same way as a real being, and is regarded as resembling one, why could mythological history not be treated in the same way as genuine history, properly so called? X. Granted, as is clear from what has been said above, that history is concerned with singulars, this nevertheless does not prevent those very singulars from being ordered by art, which is a practical intellectual habit. For the treatment that is set up concerning singulars is no less subject to the laws of method than that which concerns universals.

units.la: Nec contrarium suadet Philosophus lib. 1. Phys. tex. 49: quo loco quando dicit rationem esse universalium, sensum vero singularium; accipiendum hoc est secundum sensum oppositum: quasi dicere vellet Philosophus, sensus est singularium, ita ut non sit universalium: quæ universalia sic ab intellectu solo cognoscuntur, ut pariter idem ille intellectus cognoscat singularia. Nam cum intellectus cognoscat universale per abstractionem a singulari, quomodo idem intellectus universale cognoscere poterit, nisi pariter cognoscendo ipsum singulare, a quo abstrahitur. Denique non obstat quoque quod vulgo dicitur singularia ab arte remota esse, ac proinde non posse admitti artem aliquam historicam, propterea quod historia solis singularibus inhæreat atque immoretur: nam quantum ad vulgatum axioma, ut illud procedit theoretice, sic neutiquam ratione praxios, sive secundum usum artis admitti potest. Ars historica non magis hoc quam illud singulare respiciens, præcepta tradit cujuscunque historiæ tractationi servientia, quæ tamen præcepta in exercitio ipsius artis sic applicantur uni alicui materiæ singulari, ut pariter alij neque applicentur, neque applicari queant.
units.tr: Nor does the Philosopher persuade otherwise in Physics book 1, text 49, where he says that reason is of universals and sense of singulars. That statement must be understood in the opposite sense: as if the Philosopher meant that sense is of singulars in such a way that it is not of universals, these universals being known by the intellect alone in such a way that the same intellect likewise knows singulars. For since the intellect knows the universal by abstraction from the singular, how could the same intellect know the universal unless it also knew the singular itself, from which it is abstracted? Finally, what is commonly said, that singulars are removed from art, and therefore that no historical art can be admitted because history clings to and dwells only on singulars, does not stand in the way either: for as far as the common axiom goes, it may hold in theory, but it cannot be admitted in terms of practice, that is, according to the use of the art. The historical art, looking no more to this singular than to that, hands down precepts serving the treatment of any history whatever; yet in the exercise of the art these precepts are so applied to one particular matter that they are not applied, and cannot be applied, to others as well.

units.la: CAPUT SEPTIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SEVEN.

units.la: Quantum poësi sit tribuendum: ubi simul occurrit tur Sexti Empirici aliorumque argumentis adversus eam.
units.tr: How much weight is to be given to poetry; where at the same time the arguments of Sextus Empiricus and others against it are met.

units.la: POst artem historicam dein expendere convenit Poeticam, quam ut ad Grammaticam tanquam furculum ad suum ramum, refert Sextus; ita non inconvenienter proximum hoe caput eidem consecraverimus. Quamvis vero Pyrrho, Sceptica familiae ductor, fatente ipso Sexto Empirico, in tanto pretio habuerit Homerum, ut eum non solum legerit, verum etiam non exiguam sapientiae suę partem eidem acceptam referre debuerit; excusare tamen quaestitis quibusdam coloribus hoc studet idem Sextus, ac capite tertio decimo adversus Mathematicos in eo totus est, ut non solum artem Poëticam, incertam eam reddendo, quasi enervet, verum etiam ipsi Poësi, quicquid etiam exi stimationis eidem superesse apud alios posset, contemptum, si non invidiam quoq; procurret. Poëtis, praeter hunc Sceptices doctorem, maledixerunt plures, speciatim Plato in Phędro, & lib. 2. de Rep. ubi ne quidem locum ijsdem in sua Republ. relinquit: cujus vestigijs ex antiquis Ecclesiae Doctoribus instituerunt Hieronymus Epist. ad Damasum, & Augustinus lib. 2. de Civit. Dei cap. 14. ac lib. 18. cap. 14. Omnibus ut occurri posset, atque ut tam poësis, quam ipsa ars Poëtica in suo statu sint: convenienter admodum Poësin adumbrasse mihi videtur Maximus Tyrius Orat. 29. cum eam vocaret Philosophiam, tempore vetustam, consonantiam metricam, eamque argumento fabulosam. nam quamvis poëta numeros suos aptare quoque queat veræ narrationi; eidem tamen proprium est, veris, non solum ad ornatum, verum etiam ut melius persuadeat, fabulas & figmenta adjicere, haud aliter atque pictores, quo colores, emortuos alias, exuscitent, imaginibus castigatissimis umbras obducere consueverunt. Ut vero distincta est historia ab historica; quemadmodum ex superiori capite liquet: sic pariter distinguere convenit inter poësin, & artem eandem dirigentem. Laborat quidem Sextus hanc omni certitudine exuere, at æque feliciter hoc agit, atque circa artem historicam laboravit, uti liquebit deinceps ex illis solutionum fontibus, quos tum illius, tum aliorum argumentis opponemus. Esse vero admittendam artem poëticam, (de qua præter ipsum Aristotelem & Horatium ex antiquis, post Hieronymum Vidam opus judiciosissimum pretijque quantivis Julius Cæsar Scaliger scripsit) præter alia, quæ adduci hic possent, argumenta; abunde suadent duæ subsequentes rationes.
units.tr: After the art of history, it is right next to weigh up Poetics, which Sextus compares to a little branch on its bough, to Grammar; so it is not inappropriate that we devote this next chapter to it. Although Pyrrho, the founder of the Sceptical school, held Homer in such high esteem, as Sextus Empiricus himself admits, that he not only read him but also owed no small part of his wisdom to him, Sextus nevertheless labours to excuse this with some far-fetched colours. In the thirteenth chapter of his work against the Mathematicians, he is wholly intent on weakening the art of poetry, as if by making it uncertain, and on bringing contempt, if not even envy, upon poetry itself, whatever esteem it might still enjoy among others. Besides this teacher of Scepticism, several have spoken ill of poets: Plato especially, in the Phaedrus and in book 2 of the Republic, where he leaves them not even a place in his commonwealth. Following his footsteps, among the ancient Doctors of the Church, Jerome in his letter to Damasus, and Augustine in book 2 of The City of God, chapter 14, and in book 18, chapter 14, have done the same. So that all these objections may be met, and so that both poetry and the art of poetry itself may stand in their proper condition, Maximus of Tyre seems to me to have sketched poetry quite fittingly in Oration 29, when he called it philosophy, ancient in time, metrical in harmony, and fabulous in subject matter. For although a poet can also fit his metre to a true narrative, it is nevertheless characteristic of him to add fables and fictions, not only for ornament but also to persuade more effectively, just as painters, to bring back colours that would otherwise be dead, are accustomed to spread shadows over their most polished images. But just as history is distinct from the historical art, as is clear from the previous chapter, so likewise we must distinguish between poetry and the art that directs it. Sextus labours to strip this art of all certainty, but he succeeds in this as well as he laboured over the art of history, as will become clear later from those sources of solutions which we shall set against his arguments and those of others. That the art of poetry must be admitted (on which, besides Aristotle and Horace among the ancients, Vida after Jerome wrote a most judicious work, and Julius Caesar Scaliger one of priceless worth) is abundantly shown, apart from other arguments that could be brought forward here, by the two following reasons.

units.la: 1. Quod secundum certas regulas, aut diligentius aut negligentius observatas, modo majorem modo minorem laudem meretur, illud ab arte certa dirigatur, necessum est. Sed rerum hoc de poësi esse, nullus omnino est, qui imbigere queat. Si Scepticus dicat nunquam ic ullum poema ad artis regulas componi posfe, quin fexcenta occurrant, quæ in eodem argui queant: tantum evicerit, aut non occurrere ullum hominem, qui omnes artis numeros præingenij sui imbecillitate explere potuerit, aut arti, agnoscendę quatenus hactenus à cultoribus suis tradita fuit, multa adhuc deesse, quæ ad complementum ejusdem ulterius desiderari possint. II. Disciplina omnium antiquissima, & ab omnibus nationibus exculta, cum singulari & admirando effectu,non potest plane vana, & omni certitudine destitu-ta censeri. At verum hoc de poetica arte, Consequentiæ ratio evidentissima est. Quis enim illud quod ab immemoriali ævo, non politioribus solum gentibus, sed ipsis quoque barbaris nationibus placuit, & non solum placuit, verum etiam apud cujuscunque ordinis homines singularem ad persuadendum vim habuit, ausit arguere, tanquam inutile non solum studij genus, sed omni quoque certitudine destitutum. At poësin singularem ab antiquitate commendationem mereri, quis est qui ignoret? Nam, ut hoc loco mittam, quod Tatianus Syrus, vir quidem doctissimus, sed parum in rebus divinis constans, scribit in eo libro, quo ostendit Græcos artes & disciplinas à Barbaris inventas colendo perfectiores reddidisse: illud certissimum, longe ante solutam orationem Poëticam ex-cam exeam extitisse, excultamque fuisse. Cujus rei evidentissimum illud est argumentum, quod qui primi solutam orationem invenere, Cadmus scil. Milesius, & Argivus Acusilaus, non multo ante illa tempora floruerint, quibus Xerxes in Græciam descendisse fertur, ut præter Flavium Josephum, & Eusebium, testis est Eustathius in Homerum: ante quos longe ante claruerant Orpheus, Musæus, Linus, Homerus, aliique. Quod dico, calculo suo probant quatuor omnii exceptione majores testes. Ex quibus primus Strabo lib. 1. Geograph. sic loquitur: Primo omnium poëticus apparatus in medium prodijt, approbationemque meruit: post eum imitantes, mensura dissoluta, reliquis poëticis conservatis, sua conscripserunt Cadmus, Pherecydes, atque Hecataeus: deinde posteriores subinde aliquid tale subtrahentes, orationem ad hanc, qua nunc usurpatur, formam deduxerunt, veluti de sublimi quodam statu: perinde ac si quis diceret, Comœdiam esse à tragœdia procreatam, hujus sublimitate depressa usque ad eam formam, quæ nunc prorsæ vocatur orationi similis. Iam quod veteres vocabulo canendi pro voce dicendi usi sunt, hoc ipsum testatum facit, fontem & principium orationis artificiosæ atque rhetoricæ fuisse poëticam. Secundus testis est Maximus Tyrius, qui ita Dissert. 29. Sicut, inquit, antiqua illa victusque simplici facilius arti locum relinquebant, quae postea secuta sunt varietate medicina opus habuerunt corpora: ita & animi olim simplicitas aut, ut hi homines dicerent, ruditas, Philosophiam requirebat Musicam, magisque lenem: quasi fabularum eos jucunditate, non aliter quam alumnos suos nutricula, duceret ac tractaret. Mox processu temporis una cum aetate facta acutior, veterique illa simplicitate discussa, diffidens penitus ac vafra, in fabulas inquirere coepit, nec amplius obscuritatem illam ferre. Tertio loco commemorandus Lactantius, cujus non solum haec verba sunt lib. 7. Divin. Instit. cap. 22. Poëtae sunt multo antiquiores quam historici, & Oratores, & cetera scriptorum genera: verum etiam in eodem opere lib. 5. cap. 5. sic loquitur: Nunc reddenda est disputatio proposita, quae aut ipsa summa virtus, aut fons est ipsa virtutis: quam non modo Philosophi quaesierunt, sed & poëtae quoque, qui & priores multo fuerunt, & ante natum Philosophiae nomen pro sapientibus habebantur. His quarto loco jungendus Isidorus ex lib. 1. Originum: Praeterea, inquit, sciendum tam apud Graecos, quam apud Latinos longe antiquiorem fuisse curam carminum, quam prosa. Omnia enim prius versibus condebantur, prosa autem studium sero viguit. Primus apud Graecos Pharecides Syrus soluta oratione scripsit, apud Romanos autem Appius Caecus adversus Pyrrhum solutam orationem primus exeruit. At quorsum intestimonijs cumulandis occupor, concernentibus poëtas Græcos, eorumque ratione, prærogativam præ omnibus scriptoribus ejusdem gentis? quum antiquissimus scriptorum omnium Moses, eiusque [secundum accuratiores Chronologos] coætaneus Jobus, metro quoque inter scribendum usi fuerint. Et quidem de Mose sic Josephus lib. 2. Antiq. Judaic. cap. ult. Et Moses oden in Deum (encomiumque ac gratiarum actionem in Deum continentem, puta Canticum quod occurrit Exod. cap. 15.) hexametro versu composuit. ac lib. 4. cap. ult. de eodem: Deinde poëma hexametrum ijs reciavit: quod in sacro libro reliquit. relpicit vero illud, quod legitur Deuter. cap. 32. Item Euseb. lib. 11. de Præpar. Evang. cap. 3. Sunt etiam apud Ebræos poëmata metrica, ut magna Mosis Ode, & Davidis Psalmus centesimus decimus octavus. De Jobo sic Hieronymus tom. 3. epist. ad Paulinum: Prosa incipit: versu labitur: pedestri sermone finitur. De utroque vero qua Mose, qua Jobo, Isidorus lib. 1. Origin. cap. 18. occasione carminis heroici: Omnibus inquit, quoque metris prius est. Hoc primum Moses in cantico Deuteronomij, longe ante Pherecydem & Homerum cecinisse probatur. Unde & apparet antiquius fuisse apud Hebræos studium carminum, quam apud Gentiles. Siquidem & Iob, Mosi temporibus adæquatus, hexametro versu, dactylo spondaoque decurrit. Sed cum antiquissimi hi Scriptores sacri, inter scribendum, à Spiritu Sancto [qui illis dux in omnem veritatem fuit] directi agitatique fuerint; quis dubitet, [quicquid Sceptizis videatur] poësin, quæ ipsum Spiritum Sanctum authorem agnoscit, tanquam utile Dei donum agnoscere? Cujus pretium dein commendat quoque unanimis omnium gentium consensus, remotissimis Afris, & Americanis gentibus plerisque, ab omni licet cultu literisque, nedum humanioribus disciplinis, alienissimis, modulata oratione majorum suorum res præclare gestas decantantibus. Ogganniant licet Sceptici; sola poësios efficacia abunde eos arguit: de qua cum ex re sit consulere Platonicum Philosophum sui nominis, Maximum Tyrium scil. in dissertatione jam antea ad suffragium vocata, plura huc pertinentia non adfero. Hoc unum notetur, ex præscripto ipsius Platonis ibi loqui & Philosophari Tyrium: ille enim expresse in Phædro, Musicæ [quæ nihil aliud quam prisca illa poësis, ac proinde perfectissima eloquentia est] ac Gymnasticæ, si modo recte exerceantur, atqs pulcherrima, qualem ipse describit, moderatione temperentur, non solum uniuscujusque nostrum, sed totius reip. salutem attribuit. Nec tanti ea sunt, quæ in contrarium adferuntur à Sexto: ad quæ diluenda, praeter ea, quae jam antea superiori libro in genere, & praecedentibus hujus libri capitibus in specie notata sunt, [convenienter enim hic applicari possunt] sequentia notentur. I. Ignorantia Grammaticorum multoties prodita circa interpretationem poetarum, nequicquam aut arti poeticae, aut ipsius poësios existimationi detrahere potest: haut magis atque Scepticae Philosophiae pretium ex eo minuitur, quod pauci admodum terminos, & modum procedendi eidem peculiarem intelligant. II. Dissensus poëtarum [ ad quem tamen antea in genere responsum fuit] praeter rationem à Sexto in praejudicium ipsius artis urgetur: cum opinionum varietas diversos solum circa homines ratione alicujus disciplinae prosectus arguat, neutiquam vero sublestae notae ipsam disciplinam esse prodat. III. Ut cuique poetae sua competit libertas, sic perpetuo respicere convenit scopum, ob quem hoc illudve sinxerit; quem si quis in quovis poëta distinctius exploret, variae contradictiones tolli poterunt, liquebitque saepe apparentias contradictionum apud imperitos verarum contradictionum loco censeri. IV. Frustra vero est Sextus, quando poësi detractum cupit propterea, quod poëtae, quicquid lubitum fuerit, canant. nam ut ipsi fallí possint instar pictorum, qui sym-metrias
units.tr: 1. Whatever deserves greater or lesser praise according as it is observed more or less carefully according to fixed rules must necessarily be directed by a certain art. That this holds for poetry, no one at all can doubt. If the Sceptic says that no poem can ever be composed according to the rules of the art without countless faults being found in it, he will prove only one of two things: either that no man has ever existed who, through the weakness of his own talent, could fulfil all the requirements of the art, or that the art, as far as it has so far been handed down by its practitioners, still lacks much that could be desired in order to complete it. 2. The most ancient of all disciplines, cultivated by all nations with singular and admirable effect, cannot be judged altogether vain and destitute of all certainty. And the reasoning of the consequence in the case of the poetic art is most evident. For who would dare to argue that what has pleased from time immemorial, not only the more civilised peoples but even the barbarian nations, and not only pleased but also had a singular power to persuade men of every rank, is a useless kind of study, destitute of all certainty? That poetry has deserved singular commendation from antiquity, who does not know? For, to pass over here what Tatian the Syrian, a most learned man but not very sound in divine matters, writes in the book in which he shows that the Greeks made the arts and disciplines, which they had received from the barbarians, more perfect by cultivating them, it is most certain that poetry existed and was cultivated long before prose oratory was first produced. The clearest proof of this is that those who first invented prose, namely Cadmus of Miletus and Acusilaus of Argos, flourished not long before the times in which Xerxes is said to have invaded Greece, as Eustathius attests in his commentary on Homer, besides Flavius Josephus and Eusebius. Long before them had flourished Orpheus, Musaeus, Linus, Homer, and others. Four witnesses, all beyond exception and greater than the rest, confirm what I say. The first is Strabo, who speaks thus in book 1 of his Geography: First of all, the poetic apparatus came forward and won approval; after it, those who imitated it, having dissolved the metre but keeping the other poetic features, wrote their own works: Cadmus, Pherecydes, and Hecataeus. Then later writers, gradually taking away something of this kind, brought speech down to that form which is now used, as if from some lofty condition; just as if one were to say that comedy was born from tragedy, and that, its loftiness being lowered, it was brought down to that form which is now called prose, similar to ordinary speech. Moreover, that the ancients used the word for singing in place of the word for speaking itself shows that poetry was the source and beginning of artful and rhetorical discourse. The second witness is Maximus of Tyre, who says in Dissertation 29: Just as in those ancient times, when life was simple, bodies, which had less need of medicine, more easily gave place to the art [of medicine], but later, through the variety of things that followed, came to need it, so too the minds of men once required philosophy in the form of music, and that a gentler one: as if the Muse led them by the pleasantness of tales, just as a nurse leads and tends her charges. Later, as time went on and with age they became sharper, and that old simplicity was dispelled, they became wholly distrustful and cunning, began to inquire into fables, and could no longer bear that obscurity. The third witness to be mentioned is Lactantius, whose words are not only these, in book 7 of the Divine Institutes, chapter 22: The poets are much older than the historians and orators and other kinds of writers. In the same work, book 5, chapter 5, he also speaks thus: Now the proposed discussion must be undertaken, which is either the highest virtue itself or the source of virtue itself; this was sought not only by the philosophers but also by the poets, who were much earlier, and who were held to be wise before the name of philosophy was born. To these, in fourth place, Isidore should be joined, from book 1 of the Origins: Moreover, it must be known that among the Greeks as among the Latins, care for songs was far older than care for prose. For everything was first composed in verse, while the study of prose flourished late. Among the Greeks, Pherecydes of Syros first wrote in prose; among the Romans, Appius Caecus first brought forth prose against Pyrrhus. But why do I busy myself with heaping up testimonies concerning the Greek poets and their reasoning, and their precedence over all the writers of that people? Since the most ancient of all writers, Moses, and his contemporary Job (according to the more accurate chronologers) also used metre in their writing. And indeed Josephus says of Moses in book 2 of the Jewish Antiquities, at the end of the chapter: And Moses composed an ode to God (containing a song of praise and thanksgiving to God, namely the canticle which occurs in Exodus chapter 15) in hexameter verse. And in book 4, at the end of the chapter, about the same man: Then he recited to them a hexameter poem, which he left in the sacred book. He refers to what is read in Deuteronomy chapter 32. Likewise Eusebius, in book 11 of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 3: There are also metrical poems among the Hebrews, such as the great Ode of Moses and the hundred and eighteenth Psalm of David. Of Job, Jerome says thus in volume 3, in his letter to Paulinus: It begins in prose, glides into verse, and ends in plain speech. And Isidore, in book 1 of the Origins, chapter 18, speaking of both Moses and Job on the occasion of heroic verse: It comes first in all metres, says he. It is proved that Moses first sang this in the Song of Deuteronomy, long before Pherecydes and Homer. Whence it also appears that the study of songs was older among the Hebrews than among the Gentiles. Indeed Job, who was contemporary with the times of Moses, runs on in hexameter verse, in dactyls and spondees. But since these most ancient sacred writers, in writing, were guided and moved by the Holy Spirit [who was their leader into all truth], who would doubt (whatever the Sceptics may think) that poetry, which acknowledges the Holy Spirit himself as its author, must be recognised as a useful gift of God? Its worth is then further commended by the unanimous consent of all nations, including the most remote Africans and most of the American peoples, who, though quite alien to all culture and letters, let alone the humanities, sing in measured speech of the famous deeds of their ancestors. The Sceptics may sneer, but the efficacy of poetry alone abundantly refutes them. Since it is appropriate to consult the Platonic philosopher who bears his name on this matter, namely Maximus of Tyre in the dissertation already cited as a witness, I will not adduce more that bears on it. Let this one point be noted: the Tyrian there speaks and philosophises in accordance with Plato's own prescription. For Plato expressly says in the Phaedrus that music (which is nothing other than that ancient poetry, and therefore the most perfect eloquence), and gymnastic, if they are rightly practised and tempered by that most beautiful moderation which he himself describes, bring salvation not only to each one of us but to the whole commonwealth. Nor are the things Sextus brings forward to the contrary of such weight. In order to refute them, besides what has already been noted in the previous book in general and in the preceding chapters of this book in particular (for they can conveniently be applied here), the following should be observed. (I) The ignorance of the grammarians, shown many times in their interpretation of the poets, can in no way detract from the poetic art, nor from the esteem of poetry itself; no more is the worth of Sceptical philosophy diminished because very few understand its particular terms and method of proceeding. (II) The disagreement of the poets (to which, however, an answer has already been given in general) is pressed by Sextus to the prejudice of the art itself. But a variety of opinions only shows that men differ in their judgements about the reasoning of some discipline; it by no means reveals that the discipline itself bears a mark of weakness. (III) As each poet has his own freedom, so we must always look to the aim for which he invented this or that. If one examines this aim more carefully in any poet, many apparent contradictions can be removed, and it will often be clear that what appears to the unskilled to be a contradiction is really no contradiction at all. (IV) Sextus is wrong when he wants poetry to be disparaged on the ground that poets sing whatever they please. For just as painters who do not know how to observe and measure the symmetries and shadows in their pictures

units.la: . metrias atque umbras in suis tabulis convenienter observare atque dimetiri non sciunt, pras artis imperitia: ita poëta artis suae peritus nullam materiam tractat, quam quę oblectando aliquid quod honestum persuadeat. V. Qui versus Fescenninos scribunt quamvis poëtae boni i censeri queant, non pariter tamen habendi sunt boni viri, quod per lascivos suos versus bonos mores corrumpere studeant. Utque nihil arti Medicae per quosdam Medicos aut philtra parantes, aut venenata pocula miscentes, decedit; ita neque per hos artis Poeticae mangones quicquam detrahi poterit pretio atque existimationi artis qua utilissimae, qua jucundissimae.
units.tr: ...metrias and shadows in their paintings, since they do not know how to observe and measure them properly, through lack of skill in their art. So a poet who is skilled in his art handles no subject except one which, by delighting, persuades something honourable. Those who write Fescennine verses may be counted good poets, yet they are not equally to be regarded as good men, because by their lewd verses they strive to corrupt good morals. And just as nothing is taken away from the art of medicine when some quacks prepare love potions or mix poisoned cups, so nothing can be taken away from the price and reputation of the art of poetry, which is at once most useful and most pleasant, through these hack-peddlers of the poetic art.

units.la: V. Furor poëticus, [de quo sic Plato in Phaedro: Quisquis sine furore fores poeticas pepulit, persuasit, quod arte sola poëta possit evadere; is conatus fuit irritus, & item poësis ejus evanescit] nihil aliud est quam ingenij sublimioris felicitas: qua cum pollere magis poëta debeat, quam arte instructus esse, furorem [qui nihil aliud quam naturae instinctus est] viri sapientes jam olim in poëta desiderarunt. Verum quippe perpetuo de poëtis illud Tullij Orat. pro Arch. poëta: Etiam illud adjungo saepius ad laudem, atque virtutem, naturam sine doctrina, quam sine natura valuisse doctrinam. VI. Nec tamen aliquid decedit arti poeticae ex eo, quod primas obtineat natura, ac plus deferendum sit felicitati ingenij, quam institutioni, sive praeceptis. namque cogitandum perpetim illud Horatij,ex arte Poetica:
units.tr: V. Furor poëticus, [de quo sic Plato in Phaedro: Whoever knocks at the doors of poetry without madness, persuaded that he can become a poet by art alone, has attempted in vain; and his poetry too fades away.] is nothing other than the happy gift of a higher genius. Since a poet ought to excel in this more than be equipped with art, wise men have long since demanded this frenzy [which is nothing other than an impulse of nature] in a poet. Indeed Tully says constantly about poets, in the speech for Archias the poet: I add also this, which is often said in praise and in virtue: that nature without learning has counted for more than learning without nature. VI. Yet nothing is taken away from the art of poetry by the fact that nature holds the first place, and that the happy gift of genius must be given more weight than training or precepts. For we must constantly bear in mind that line of Horace from the Art of Poetry:

units.la: Natura fieret laudabile carmen, an arte, Quaesitum est. Ego nec studium sine divite vena, Nec rude quid possit video ingenium: alterius sic Altera poscit opem res, & conjurat amice.
units.tr: Whether a poem becomes praiseworthy by nature or by art has been asked. I see that study without a rich vein, and talent without cultivation, are of no use; each thing demands the help of the other, and they join together in friendship.

units.la: Quamvis enim haut praeter rationem Bacchus apud Aristophanem in Ranis foecundum poëtam requirat, qui e proprio suo thesauro quidvis proferre queat; interim si huic venae ubertati moderatrix ars accesserit, tum intra terminos se continebit, tum etiam ordinate perpetuo fluet, non vero impetuose ruet. Atque ut haec dicta sufficiunt, pro vindicanda arte poetica; ita nequicquam derogari potest existimationi ipsius poësios, sive per Platonis, sive per Hieronymi authoritates. nam quantum ad Platonem, non ipsam poësin censet eliminandam esse, sed loco jam antea citato, sive lib. 2. de Rep. contendit quosdam duntaxat poëtas expellendos esse propter flagitia & scelera quae Dijs affingunt. quomodo Socrates lib. 10. de Repub. postquam multa in poëtas dixit, tandem justa sententia litem dirimit, pronunciando secundum bonos poëtas, quos retinendos existimat, quod carmina illorum tum fortitudinem tum castitatem animo ingenerare queant. Nam haud omnibus in universum poëtis bellum indictum fuisse à Platone, ex ejusdem Cratylo patet, ubi philosophos sophistasque irridens, consulit ut poëtæ adeantur, virtutisque ab ijsdem ratio exposcatur. Quid, quod Plato familiarissimus fuit Euripidi Tragico, quem ab eo quoque in scribendo adjutum fuisse perhibetur: cumque Antimachus occupatus in recitandis suis poëmatibus ab omnibus auditoribus deserteretur, unus illi instar omnium fuit: ne jam dicam Homerum, quem præter alios poëtas toties ad suffragium vocat, in Jone, hoc ab eodem elogio condecorari, quod sit optimus & divinus poëta. Quod ad Hieronymum, fateor quidem poëtas, aut verius eorum fabulas ab eo vocari dæmonum pabulum, verum haud alio sensu, quam quatenus eorum figmenta, eaque, quæ ab ijsdem fabulosè dicta & scripta sunt, tanquam veræ de Deo divinisque rebus sententiæ apprehenduntur: alias quid fiet Justino Martyri, Eusebio, Origeni, Athanagoræ, Clementi Alexandrino, atque Lactantio, qui quando cum Gentilibus disputant, passim poëtas ad suffragia vocant; maxime quid fiet Chrysostomo, qui perhibetur Aristophanem perpetuo pulvino suo suppositum habuisse, atque ex Attico illo scurra divinæ eloquentiæ theatrum erexisse.
units.tr: Not unreasonably, Bacchus in Aristophanes' Frogs seeks a fertile poet who can bring forth whatever he likes from his own store; yet if a controlling art is added to this abundance of talent, then it will keep itself within bounds and flow on in an orderly way, not rush along in headlong haste. And as these remarks are enough to vindicate the art of poetry, so the esteem of poetry itself cannot be disparaged by the authority of Plato or of Jerome. For as far as Plato is concerned, he does not judge poetry itself to be banished, but, in the passage cited earlier, or in book 2 of the Republic, he maintains only that certain poets should be expelled on account of the shameful deeds and crimes they ascribe to the gods. Thus Socrates, in book 10 of the Republic, after saying much against the poets, at last settles the dispute with a just verdict, pronouncing in favour of the good poets, whom he thinks should be retained, because their songs can instil both courage and chastity in the mind. For that Plato did not declare war on all poets without exception is clear from his Cratylus, where, ridiculing the philosophers and sophists, he advises that the poets be approached and an account of virtue be demanded from them. What of the fact that Plato was very close to the tragic poet Euripides, who is said to have been helped by him in his writing? And when Antimachus, busy reciting his poems, was deserted by all his hearers, Plato alone was worth all of them to him. Not to mention Homer, whom he summons so often as a witness, beyond the other poets, and whom in the Ion he honours with this praise, that he is the best and divine poet. As for Jerome, I admit that he calls poets, or rather their fables, food for demons, but in no other sense than insofar as their fictions, and the things said and written fabulously by them, are taken as true opinions about God and divine matters. Otherwise, what will become of Justin Martyr, Eusebius, Origen, Athenagoras, Clement of Alexandria and Lactantius, who, when they dispute with the Gentiles, everywhere summon the poets as witnesses? Above all, what will become of Chrysostom, who is said to have kept Aristophanes constantly under his pillow and to have built a theatre of divine eloquence out of that Attic buffoon?

units.la: CAPUT OCTAVUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER EIGHT.

units.la: Rhetorica existimatio vindicatur adversus vari- as Sexti Empirici objectiones.
units.tr: The rhetorical judgment is defended against the various objections of Sextus Empiricus.

units.la: A Poetica dein Sextus nos deducit ad Rhetoricam, cui non minus infestus est, atque aliis disciplinis, quas adversus ejusdem cavillationes hactenus asseruimus: &, ut liqueat, quam hoc eidem seriùm sit, cap. 14. adversus Mathematicos, quam plurimas proponit rationes, quibus non solum disciplinæ hujus existimationem laborat deterere, sed eandem penitus quoque subvertere. Ut ordine progrediamur, atque omnia huc pertinentia, distinctè proponere liceat, initio despiciendum quid per Rhetoricam conveniat intelligere. Quam laborarint jam olim viri summi circa ejusdem definitiones, verumque finem, illi solùm ignorare possunt, qui à cultura humanitatis per omnia alieni sunt. nolo vero aliorum, sive antiquorum, sive recentiorum definitiones aut proponere, aut propositas examinare: pro mistituti præsentis ratione Rhetorica agnosci debet facultas, quæ subsidio peculiaris aut loquendi aut scribendi modi, ordinati secundum certum animi affectum, tum artificis, tum auditoris, auditori illud laborat persuadere, quod artificci dicen-
units.tr: Next Sextus leads us from poetry to rhetoric, which he attacks no less than the other disciplines that we have defended so far against his sneers. To show how seriously he takes this, see chapter 14 of Against the Mathematicians, where he sets out very many arguments meant not only to weaken the reputation of this discipline but to overturn it completely. To proceed in order, and to set out clearly everything relevant here, we should first consider what is to be understood by rhetoric. How much the greatest men have struggled over its definitions and its true end can be unknown only to those who are wholly strangers to the cultivation of humanity. I do not wish either to propose or to examine the definitions of others, ancient or modern. For the purpose of the present work, rhetoric must be recognized as the faculty which, by the aid of a particular manner of speaking or writing, arranged according to a certain disposition of mind in both the artist and the hearer, labours to persuade the hearer of what the speaker, already equipped with the resources of speech, has already been persuaded of, or at least ought to be.

units.la: Y ci dicendi præsidijs instructo jam antea persuasum est, aut saltem persuasum esse debet. De sufficientia hujus definitionis nihil dico, quum ex subsequentibus liquere possit, eam convenientem esse. Quo vero certitudo hujus ipsius artis liquido demonstrari queat, præmonstrandum, non illam solum orationem censendam esse exactam ad Rhetoricæ leges, quæ dicendi præceptis, vulgo à Rhetorum filijs tradi solitis, respondet; sed, eam quoque quæ licet non respondeat ordinarijs præceptis, sufficiat tamen secundum regulas ordinarias ei, qui eo modo dicit idoneè ad persuadendum. quod existimandum non solum de Demade, qui ex nauta orator erat factus, teste Suida: unde Cicero in Oratore dixit, eum nauticos sales in forum transtulisse: verum etiam de oratione Abigaelis 1.Sam.cap. 25. cujus artificium, & structuram ad persuadendum ordinatam non semel sum miratus; itemque de oratione, qua ad eundem Davidem utebatur cata illa mulier, quam pro reductione Absalonis subornarat Joabus, quemadmodum liquet ex lib. 2. Sam. cap. 14. quod enim Plinius lib. 6. epist. dicit: Video multos parvo ingenio, literis nullis, ut bene agerent, agendo consecutos: hoc ita accipiendum est, per illam diuturnionem consuetudinem, secundum quam in agendo illi, de quibus loquitur, occupati fuerunt, habitum aliquem ingenitum suisse, qui cum ordinatus sit ad operationem aliquam, quis alio nomine quam artis, eumdem cohonestet? ut enim primi quique in quocunque genere artifices, non per disciplinam aliquam, (neque enim invenerunt praeceptores ante se] sed per crebros actus, paulatim magis atque magis castigatos, sibi habitum, artemque comparaverunt; ita secula praecedentia nonsolum aquilas tulerunt, sed omni tempore invenire potuerunt tam felicia ingenia, quae per se idem praestarent, quod primi artium inventores felicitér praestiterunt. Hisce praemissis, paucae quae sequuntur rationes, sufficient pro asserenda arte Rhetorica. I. Si datur Grammatica, agnoscenda quoque est Rhetorica. Sed Grammaticam dari jam antea liquidis, isque indubitaris argumentis probatum fuit.
