Ratio consequentiæ est haec: Quoniam si secundum artis regulas quotidianus sermo ordinari potest, quo quotidie utimur, multo magis probabile est secundum artis regulas eum sermonem ordinari posse, quo subinde duntaxat, atq; in concionibus, ad hoc illudque persuadendum utimur. quae enim extraordinario fiunt, multo magis ab arte dirigi ordinarique debent, quam ea quae quotidiana sunt? Vix ars aliqua requiritur, secundum quam homo suas vestes induat, disciplina tamen opus est, &, per disciplinam acquiri solita arte, ad hoc ut tales formet literas & lineas, quarum subsidio alijs mentis suæ conceptus interpretari atque explicare queat. II. Per quod, tanquam possessionem propriam, studio & labore acquisitam unus homo ab altero vere distinguitur, illud agnoscendum dari tanquam principium vere distinguens, nec refragari quis potest, aut ambigere, quin illud ipsum detur. At per Rhetoricam, artemque dicendi unus homo ab altero distinguitur. Ergo. De majoris propositionis veritate, si diligenter expendatur, nullus ambigere potest. De minori vero sic Cassiodorus lib. 1. Var. ep. in Præf. Loqui nobis communiter datum est: ornatus est, qui discernit indoctos. & prolixius Isocrates in Panegyr. In alijs, inquit, actionibus eæ sunt fortunæ perturbationes, ut læpenumero & prudentes votorum inopes fiant: & stolidi successus prosperos habeant: Orationis autem præclaræ artificiosæque facultas & stupidis negata, & prudentis animi munus peculiare est: atque etiam ei, qui vel eruditi vel indocti perhibentur, hac re inter se potissimum differunt: & ab ineunte ætate liberaliter educati, nec ex fortitudine, nec ex opibus, nec alijs id genus bonis agnoscuntur, sed ex oratione potissimum perspiciuntur: eaque institutionis cujusque nostrum signum est certissimum & evidentissimum. Hæc ille. III. Quicquid singularem vim & efficaciam habet ad movendos hominum animos, eosque, incitandos ad honesti studium, aut aliud quid præclari tentandum: Illud agnosci debet tanquam disciplina utilis societati humanæ; cui dum agnoscitur inservire, consequens pariter est eandem dari. Atqui hoc verum est de facultate oratoria, consideranda secundum eas limitationes atque differentias, quas initio proposuimus. Major propositio me quidem in dubium vocari potest. Pro minoris autem confirmatione, quæ non rationes, experimenta, & testimonia adferri possent? Ex testium nubibus suffecerit unus Tullius Romanorum oratorum princeps, de quo sic Plin. lib. 7. Nat. hist. cap. 30. Te dicente, legem agrariam, hoc est, alimenta sua, abdicaverunt tribus: te suadente, Roscio Theatralis autores legis ignoverunt, notatasque de discrimine sedes æquo animo tulerunt: te orante, proscriptorum liberos, honores petere puduit: tuum Catilina fugit ingenium: tuum M. Antonium proscripsit. Salve primus omnium parens patriæ appellate, Latiarumque literarum parens; atque (ut dictator Cæsar, hostis quondam tuus, de te scripsit) omnium triumphorum lauream adepte majorem: quantoplus est ingenij Romani terminos in tantum promo-visse.
units.tr: ...equipped with the resources of speech, has already been persuaded, or at least ought to be. I say nothing of the sufficiency of this definition, since it will be clear from what follows that it is adequate. But to show clearly that this art is certain, it must first be noted that we should count as exact to the laws of rhetoric not only that speech which answers to the precepts of speaking commonly handed down by the teachers of rhetoric, but also that speech which, though it does not answer to the ordinary precepts, is nonetheless sufficient, according to the ordinary rules, for the one who speaks in that way to persuade effectively. This must be thought true not only of Demades, who was made an orator from a sailor, as Suidas testifies, whence Cicero said in the Orator that he had carried nautical wit into the forum; but also of the speech of Abigail in 1 Samuel chapter 25, whose skill and structure, arranged for persuasion, I have more than once admired; and likewise of the speech which that wise woman, whom Joab had instructed for the recall of Absalom, made to the same David, as is clear from 2 Samuel chapter 14. As for what Pliny says in book 6 of his Letters, I see many with little talent and no learning who by acting have attained to acting well, this must be understood thus: through that long-continued habit by which those of whom he speaks were occupied in practice, some innate habit was formed, which, being ordered to some operation, by what other name than art could one honour it? For just as the first artisans in any field did not acquire their skill through any discipline (for they had no teachers before them) but through repeated acts, gradually refined more and more, and so procured for themselves a habit and an art, so the preceding ages not only bore eagles but at all times could produce such gifted minds as would achieve by themselves what the first inventors of the arts achieved successfully. With these things premised, the few reasons that follow will suffice for asserting the art of rhetoric. I. If grammar exists, rhetoric too must be acknowledged. But that grammar exists has already been proved by clear and indubitable arguments. The reasoning of the consequence is this: if everyday speech, which we use every day, can be arranged according to the rules of art, it is much more probable that that speech which we use only occasionally, and in sermons, to persuade this or that, can be arranged according to the rules of art. For should not things done on extraordinary occasions be directed and ordered by art much more than things that are everyday? Hardly any art is required for a man to put on his clothes, yet a discipline is needed, and an art acquired through discipline, so that he may form such letters and lines by whose aid he can interpret and explain the conceptions of his mind to others. II. That by which one man is truly distinguished from another, as a property acquired by study and labour, must be acknowledged as a principle that truly distinguishes, and no one can deny or doubt that it exists. But one man is distinguished from another through rhetoric and the art of speaking. Therefore (it exists). The truth of the major premise, if it is carefully weighed, no one can doubt. As for the minor, Cassiodorus says thus in the preface to book 1 of his Variae: To speak has been given to us in common; it is eloquence that sets apart the unlearned. And Isocrates says more at length in the Panegyricus: In other activities, he says, the turns of fortune are such that often the prudent are left without their wishes, and the foolish have prosperous outcomes. But the faculty of excellent and skilful speech is denied to the dull and is the peculiar gift of a prudent mind. Moreover, those who are reckoned learned or unlearned differ chiefly in this, and those who from early youth have been liberally educated are recognized not by courage, nor by wealth, nor by goods of that kind, but are seen chiefly through their speech; and this is the most certain and most evident sign of each one's upbringing. So he. III. Whatever has a singular power and efficacy for moving men's minds, and for stirring them to the pursuit of honour or to attempting some other noble thing, must be acknowledged as a discipline useful to human society; and since it is acknowledged to serve that society, it follows that it exists. And indeed this is true of the oratorical faculty, considered according to those limitations and distinctions which we set out at the beginning. The major premise may perhaps be called in doubt by me, but for the confirmation of the minor, what experiences and testimonies, not merely reasons, could be adduced? From a cloud of witnesses let it suffice to take Tully alone, the prince of Roman orators, of whom Pliny says thus in book 7 of his Natural History, chapter 30: When you spoke, the tribes gave up the agrarian law, that is, their own food supply; when you urged it, the authors of the Theatrical law pardoned Roscius and bore with equanimity the seats marked out by distinction; when you pleaded, the children of the proscribed were ashamed to seek office; Catiline fled from your talent; Mark Antony proscribed you. Hail, first of all called father of the country, and father of Latin letters; and (as Caesar the dictator, once your enemy, wrote of you) you gained a greater laurel than all the triumphs; how much more it is to have extended the bounds of Roman talent than of empire.

units.la: Y 5 — vi∫∫e 2 visse, quam Imperij. IV. Cujus artis præceptu inter scribendum usi fuerunt ipsi Spiritus Sancti amanuenses Prophetę & Apostoli; illa ipsa ars agnosci debet tanquam utilis: & eo ipso, dum talis agnoscitur, patet eam dari. nam quod non datur, ne quidem utile esse potest. Major iterum in confessio erit, si non apud Scepticos, quos parum curare convenit, saltem apud Scripturæ filios, quorum major habenda ratio. Ne singulos Prophetas & Apostolos, quod fieri posset, sollicitem, aliquos solum speciminis gratia adducam, incipiendo à Mose, de quo non solum Stephanus in sua concione Act. 7. v. 22. testatur, quod fuerit potens dictis & factis: Sed cui Longinus in libello de sublimi charactere dicendi, hoc etiam elogium perhibet: Judæorum ille Legislator non fuit vir de trivio, qui numinis virtutem pro dignitate cognovit, & verbis explicavit. Quid de Isaja dicam, qui jure merito à Chrysostomo Hom. 8. in Genes. Propheta vocalissimus, & Hom. 40. in 1. ad Corinth. magniloquentissimus vocatur. Jeremiæ quoque artificium Rhetoricum plane subduci nequit, amplector siquidem de eo testimonium Hieronymi in procem. lib. 6. Comm. in eum: quantum, inquit, in verbis simplex videtur & facilis, tantum in majestate sensuum profundissimus est. De aliis Veteris testamenti Scriptoribus ne dicam, ex ijs, qui pertinent ad N. T. solum Petrum & Paulum Apostolos adduxisse suffecerit. Quod ad illum, quanta vis eloquentiae ejusdem, qui primis concionibus tot millia Hierosolymis, non tam loquendo, quam fulminando perculit, atque prostravit, ut legere est Act. 2. & 4. quam insignis vero in hoc majestas atque nobertas, qui Lystris (vide Act. 14.) ob eloquentiam habitus est alter Mercurius, qui antistes ac Deus eloquentiae civibus illius urbis colebatur? quem totius orbis terrarum disertissimum appellat Joannes Chrysostomus Serm. in 12. Apost. & cujus copiam & facultatem dicendi, Hieronym. Apol. adverf. Rufin. & ep. ad Algaf. itemque Augustinus lib. 4. de doctr. Christ. cap. 6, ipsi judices optimi, demirantur ac venerantur? Quantum ad argumenta adversaria, quam vis prolixus admodum sit Sextus in ijs deducendis, laboretque non tam rationum pondere, quam verborum copia disciplinam utilissimam, illiusque cultores obruere, haud difficulter tamen quis se expedire poterit, si praeter illa, quae praecedentibus capitibus jam notata sunt [nam & illa convenienter hic applicantur] subsequentia ad modum fontium observentur. I. Damus lubentes, naturam vim maximam adferre ad dicendum, ut L. Crassus recte disserit apud Cicer. lib. 1. de Orat. nihilominus non sequitur quod inferre vult Sextus, & cum eo multi alij, nempe otiosam plane esse artem oratoriam: utrumque enim per se indigens alterum alterius auxilio veget, ut commodem pauca à Sallust. in princ. Catilinar. Posse vero ratione huius hypothesios, ea, quæ natura recte fiunt, in artis præcepta redigi, clare ostendit Cicero lib. 2. de Orat. Etenim, inquit, cum plerumque temere, & nulla ratione, causas in foro dicant; nonnulli autem propter exercitationem, aut propter consuetudinem aliquam, callidius id faciant: non est dubium, quin si quis animadvertit, quid sit, quare alij melius, quam alii dicant; is, si non plane artem, at quasi artem quandam invenerit. quod argumentum, fusius superioribus capitibus deductum declaratumque, adeo firmum est, ut neutiquam de eo ulla ratione ambigere liceat. II. Quamvis ratione eloquentiæ nihil posset sine exercitatione, ac vice versa exercitatio plurimum polleat sine arte: non putandum, tamen propterea solam, ut quibusdam post Sextum persuasum est, sufficere exercitationem: ut jure summo eo nomine Syrianus Hermogenis interpres reprehendat Euagoram Sophistam. longe rectius calculum collocat Crassus apud Ciceronem lib. 1. de Orat. cum dicit: In quo fallit eos, quod audierunt; dicendo homines, ut dicant, efficere solere. Verum etiam illud dicitur, perverse dicere homines perverse dicendo facillime consequi. III. Etiam atque etiam cogitandum, Rhetoricam esse facultatem: est vero facultatum haec indoles, ut non semper finem suum consequantur. Eoque frustra omnino sunt, quicunque non expendentes ad quam disciplinarum classem pertineat Rhetorica, ei rationem sic constare volunt, ut nunquam suo fine excidat. Hoc eidem proprium est tanquam facultati. Nec propterea quicquam ejusdem existimationi decedit. Si enim fidem faciente Aristotele lib. 2. de Auscult. Phys. cap. 8. tex. 82. ipsa natura quoque fine suo aliquando excidat, quis miretur, artem, quae naturam imitatur, & proinde eadem inferior est, pariter aliquando fine suo excidere, atque ad eundem devenire non posse? IV. Hoc si notetur, liquebit perquam convenienter finem Rhetoricae constitui persuasionem, ettamsi aliquando fine suo orator excidat, atque illud persuadere non queat, quod cum maxime tamen persuasum cupit: Modo ex lege artis, ut persuadere posset omnia egerit orator, nihilque omiserit ad persuasionem pertinens, ratio ei constabit, atque ars salva futura. Eleganter Seneca lib. 7. de Benef. cap. 13. Quaedam, inquit, ejus conditionis sunt, ut effectum praestare debeant: quibusdam pro effectis est omnia attentasse, ut efficerent. Si omnia fecit, ut sanaret, peregit medicus partes suas. Etiam, damnato reo, oratori constat eloquentiæ officium, si omni arte usus est. v. Quod alia quoq; persuadeant, aurum, scil. forma, & similia: aut, ut Sextus urget, senes Troiani conspeƈta Helenæ facie statuis omnibus emendationi sententiam mutaverint, ac Phryne meretrix (præter Sextum hoc referunt Plutarchus in vitis Orat. Quintil. lib. 2. cap. 15. & Athen. lib. 13. Dipnos.) capitis periculo liberata sit, non tam Hyperidis actione, quanquam mirabili, quam conspectu corporis speciosissimi, quod diducta tunica nudaverat; nequicquam ad rem facit, aut ulla ratione officere potest: neque enim hæc tam persuadent, quam judicem objecta sui specie fallunt, impelluntque ad illud, quod orator solus concinna oratione, sufficientiq; argumentorum robore suffulta persuadere ex lege artis contendit. Quis enim Helenam & Phrynem tam movisse judices, quam potius eosdé effascinasse dicat: haut magis sane dici possunt persuasisse, atq;auro, quod judices corrumpit, atque à justitiæ tramite abducit, vis persuadendi ex rei veritate tribui potest. Is enim proprie persuadet, qui subsidio tum rationis, tum orationis rei alicujus fidem astruit. VI. Ratio quoque non constat Sexto
units.tr: Y 5 — "...visse, quam Imperij" [probably a running head, garbled in the scan; sense: to have lived rather than to have ruled]. IV. The inspired amanuenses of the Holy Spirit, the Prophets and Apostles, used the precepts of this art when they wrote. This same art must be acknowledged as useful, and by the very fact that it is recognised as useful, it is shown to exist. For what does not exist cannot even be useful. Again, the case will be stronger if we address not the Sceptics, whom it is fitting to care little about, but at least the sons of Scripture, whose judgement deserves the greater weight. Lest I trouble myself with each of the Prophets and Apostles, which could be done, I will cite only a few by way of example, beginning with Moses. Of him Stephen not only testifies in his sermon (Acts 7:22) that he was mighty in words and deeds; Longinus, in his book on the sublime style of speaking, also pays him this tribute: that Legislator of the Jews was no common man, who grasped the power of the divinity as it deserved and expressed it in words. What shall I say of Isaiah, whom Chrysostom rightly calls the most eloquent of the Prophets (Homily 8 on Genesis) and most lofty in speech (Homily 40 on 1 Corinthians)? Nor can the rhetorical craft of Jeremiah be wholly removed; I accept the testimony of Jerome in the preface to his sixth book of commentary on him: however simple and easy he seems in words, so much is he deepest in the majesty of his meanings. Of the other writers of the Old Testament I say nothing; of those who belong to the New, it will suffice to have named the Apostles Peter and Paul. As for Peter, how great was the power of his eloquence, who in his first sermons struck down and overthrew so many thousands at Jerusalem, not so much by speaking as by thundering, as may be read in Acts 2 and 4! And how remarkable the majesty and nobility of Paul, who at Lystra (see Acts 14) was held, on account of his eloquence, to be another Mercury, and was worshipped by the citizens of that town as the priest and god of eloquence! Him John Chrysostom calls the most eloquent man in the whole world (Sermon on the Twelve Apostles); and his abundance and skill in speaking are admired and revered by Jerome (Apology against Rufinus and letter to Algasia), and likewise by Augustine (On Christian Doctrine, book 4, ch. 6), the best of judges. As for the arguments of the adversaries: although Sextus is very long-winded in setting them out, and labours to overwhelm this most useful discipline and its practitioners less by the weight of his reasons than by a flood of words, one may nevertheless without difficulty extricate oneself, if, besides those points already noted in the preceding chapters (for these also apply here appropriately), the following are observed in the manner of sources. I. We gladly grant that nature brings great power to speaking, as L. Crassus rightly argues in Cicero (De Oratore, book 1). Nevertheless, what Sextus wishes to infer, and with him many others, does not follow: namely, that the art of oratory is wholly idle. For each, being in itself in need, is strengthened by the help of the other, as Sallust briefly observes at the beginning of the Catiline. That those things which are done rightly by nature can be reduced to precepts of art, on this hypothesis, Cicero clearly shows (De Oratore, book 2): For, he says, since most men plead cases in court rashly and without reason, and some, through practice or some habit, do so more skilfully, there is no doubt that if someone notices why some speak better than others, he will have found, if not a full art, at least something like an art. This argument, set out more fully in the preceding chapters, is so firm that there can be no reasonable doubt about it. II. Although nothing can be done in eloquence without practice, and conversely practice is very powerful without art, we must not think that practice alone suffices, as some have been persuaded after Sextus. Syrianus, the interpreter of Hermogenes, therefore rightly reproves the sophist Euagoras on this account. Crassus places the balance far more correctly in Cicero (De Oratore, book 1), when he says: Here they are deceived by what they have heard: that by speaking men usually make themselves able to speak. But it is also said that men who speak badly, by speaking badly, very easily attain the same. III. We must think again and again that rhetoric is a faculty, and it is the nature of faculties that they do not always attain their end. Therefore those are wholly mistaken who, without considering to which class of disciplines rhetoric belongs, want its account to be such that it never falls from its end. This is proper to it as to any faculty, and its reputation suffers no loss on that account. For if, as Aristotle asserts (Physics, book 2, ch. 8), nature itself sometimes falls short of its end, who would wonder that an art which imitates nature, and is therefore inferior to it, should likewise sometimes fall short of its end and be unable to reach it? IV. If this is noted, it will be quite clear that it is most fitting to define the end of rhetoric as persuasion, even though the orator sometimes falls short of his end and fails to persuade what he most wishes to persuade. Provided that, following the rule of the art, the orator has done everything so that he might persuade, and has omitted nothing pertaining to persuasion, his account will stand and the art will remain intact. Seneca elegantly says (On Benefits, book 7, ch. 13): Some things are of such a kind that they ought to produce the effect; for others, it is enough to have tried everything to produce it. If the physician has done everything to heal, he has performed his duty. Even when the accused is condemned, the orator keeps the office of eloquence, if he has used every art. V. As for the claim that other things also persuade, such as gold, namely beauty and the like, or, as Sextus presses, that the elders of Troy, on seeing the face of Helen, changed their opinion and voted for her restoration, and that the courtesan Phryne was freed from a capital charge (Sextus reports this, and so do Plutarch in the Lives of the Orators, Quintilian book 2 ch. 15, and Athenaeus book 13 of the Deipnosophists), not by the speech of Hyperides, however admirable, but by the sight of her very beautiful body, which she had uncovered by drawing aside her tunic: all this has nothing to do with the matter, nor can it in any way hurt it. For these things do not so much persuade as deceive the judge by presenting their outward show, and drive him to that which the orator alone, by a well-turned speech supported by the strength of sound arguments, sets out to persuade according to the rule of the art. For who would say that Helen and Phryne moved the judges, rather than that they bewitched them? Persuasion can no more be said to have been effected by gold, which corrupts judges and leads them from the path of justice, than the power of persuading can be attributed to the truth of the matter. For he properly persuades who establishes the credibility of a thing by the aid both of reason and of speech. VI. Nor does the reasoning of Sextus the Empiricist hold good when he infers that rhetoric is not an art because it is occupied with falsehood, for instance by defending adultery or murder, which ought not to be undertaken but punished according to the laws. For just as the sophists, who abuse the art of disputation, can in no way detract from dialectic, so neither do the hack-advocates of the art of oratory, who lend their services to base causes and aim to be able to argue against anyone, diminish the value of that most noble art.

units.la: Empirico, quando colligit, Rhetoricam propterea non esse artem, quod circa falsum occupetur, puta patrocinium adulterii, aut homicidii, quod suscipiendum non esset, sed secundum leges puniendum. Vt enim Sophistæ, qui arte differendi abutuntur, neutiquam derogare possunt Dialecticæ: ita neque oratoriæ artis mangones, qui turpibus causis patrocinium suum commodant, & hoc agunt, ut disputando omnibus adversari possint, ne quicquam imminuunt pretium artis nobilissimæ.
units.tr: Sextus the Empiricist, when he gathers that rhetoric is not an art because it is concerned with falsehood, for instance the defence of adultery or murder which ought not to be undertaken but punished according to the laws, is no use. For just as the sophists, who abuse the art of disputation, can in no way detract from dialectic, so neither do the hack-advocates of the art of oratory, who lend their services to base causes and aim to be able to argue against anyone, diminish the value of that most noble art.

units.la: Sexto, qui Platonis in Gorgia & Critolai testimonio præ cæteris nituntur opponi fas est Quintilianum lib. 2. Orat. Instit. cap. 15. sic loquentem: Quidam Rhetoricen, neque vim, neque scientiam, neque artem, putaverunt. Athenæus fallendi artem. Plerique autem, dum pauca ex Gorgia Platonis à prioribus imperite excepta, legere contenti, neque hoc tantum, neque alia ejus volumina evolvunt, in maximum errorem inciderunt: creduntque eum esse in hac opinione, ut Rhetoricen, non artem, sed peritiam quandam gratiæ ac voluptatis existimet: & alio loco civilitatis particulæ simulachrum, & quartam partem adulationis: quod duas partes civilitatis corpori assignet, medicinam, & quam interpretantur exercitatricem: duas animo, legalem, atque justitiam: adulationem autem medicinæ, vocet coquorum artificium: & exercitatricis, mangonum, qui colorem fuco, & verum robur inani sagina mentiantur: legalis, cavillatricem: justitiæ, Rhetoricea. Quæ omnia sunt quidem scripta in hoc libro, dictaque à Socrate; cujus sub persona videtur Plato significare quid sentiat: sed alij sunt ejus sermones ad coarguendos qui contra disputant, compositi, quos Elenctticos vocant: alii ad præcipiendum, qui dogmatici appellantur. Socrates autem, seu Plato, eam quidem, quæ tunc exercebatur, Rhetoricen, talem putavit. etc. Sed in illud hominum genus, quod facultate dicendi male utebatur, invectus est. Nam & Socrates inhonestam sibi credidit orationem, quam ei Lysias reo composuerat: & tum maxime scribere litigatoribus, quæ illi pro se ipsi dicerent, erat moris, atque ita juri, quo non licebat pro altero agere, fraus adhibebatur. Doctores quoque ejus artis parum idonei, Platoni videbantur, qui Rhetoricen à justitia separarent, & veris credibilia præferrent: nam id quoque dicit in Phædro. Hæc Fabius. VII. Interim, quicquid aut Sexto, aut, aliis quoque Scepticismi patronis visum fuerit, Rhetorica non desinet esse facultas; sic ut proprium eidem maneat de themate aliquo in utramque partem
units.tr: Against Sextus one may fairly set those whom he relies on most, Plato in the Gorgias and the testimony of Critolaus, as Quintilian says in book 2 of the Institutes of Oratory, chapter 15, speaking thus: Some have thought rhetoric to be neither a power, nor a science, nor an art, but, as Athenaeus says, the art of deceiving. Most people, however, content with reading a few passages of Plato's Gorgias which earlier readers had carelessly excerpted, and not unrolling this or his other books, have fallen into the greatest error. They believe that he held the opinion that rhetoric is not an art but a certain skill in gratification and pleasure; and in another place that it is the image of a part of politics and the fourth part of flattery; because he assigns to the body of politics two parts, medicine and what they call gymnastics, and to the soul two, legislation and justice; and he calls the flattery of medicine the craft of cooks, and that of gymnastics the craft of hucksters, who disguise colour with paint and true strength with empty fat; that of legislation, sophistry; and that of justice, rhetoric. All these things are indeed written in this book and spoken by Socrates, under whose persona Plato seems to indicate what he himself thinks; but there are other discourses of his composed to refute those who argue against him, which they call elenctic, and others for teaching, which are called dogmatic. Socrates, or Plato, certainly thought rhetoric, as it was then practised, to be such. And so on. But he attacked that class of men who used the faculty of speaking badly. For Socrates also believed it dishonourable to make the speech which Lysias had composed for him as a defendant; and at that time it was customary to write for litigants what they were to say on their own behalf, and so fraud was practised against the law, which did not permit one to plead for another. Teachers of that art, too, who separated rhetoric from justice and preferred the plausible to the true, seemed unsuitable to Plato; for he says this also in the Phaedrus. Thus Fabius.

units.la: probabiliter differere: quod uti Rhetoricæ secundum suam naturam consideratæ perpetuo convenit; ita nihilominus orator rhetoricæ præsidio instructus distinguere debet inter illud, quod per artem licet, atque inter illud, quod à justitia, cujus perpetim studiosus esse debet, permittitur. V. C. Adulterio, aut homicidio per fraudem ab homine malæ notæ perpetrato, ab eo, qui dicendi præsidijs instructus est, facile quid prætexi potest; cum nullum occurrat flagitium, cui non aptari queat color: nec tamen propterea mox illius, qui ut réus insimulatur, patrocinium quilibet orator suscipere debet: sed distinguere perpetuo inter illud, quod sibi licet ut oratori, atque id quod ab eodem, ut viro bono exigitur. Atque inde fortasse [quamvis alij sequitus interpretentur) atque in deteriorem partem rapiant, jam olim Æschines oratorem definivit, quod sit vir bonus dicendi peritus. VIII. Nec propterea Rhetoricæ pretium deteritur, quod qui orator ad unguem factus censendus, omnium rerum peritus esse debeat. quamvis enim Crassus apud Ciceronem lib. 1. de Orat. sic loquatur: Is erit Orator, mea sententia, hoc tam gravi dignus nomine, qui, quacunque res inciderit, quæ sit dictione explicanda, prudenter, & copiose, & ornate, & memoriter dicat, cum quadam & actionis dignitate.
units.tr: to probably argue both sides: this suits rhetoric consistently when it is considered according to its own nature; nevertheless the orator, equipped with the resources of rhetoric, ought to distinguish between what is permitted by the art and what is permitted by justice, which he must always diligently observe. For example, adultery or murder committed by fraud by a man of bad reputation can easily be given some pretext by one who is trained in the resources of speaking, since no crime occurs for which some colour cannot be found; yet on that account no orator should at once undertake the defence of one who is accused as a criminal. Rather, he must always distinguish between what is allowed to him as an orator and what is required of him as a good man. And from this, perhaps (though others interpret it otherwise and turn it to a worse sense), Aeschines long ago defined the orator as "a good man skilled in speaking." VIII. Nor is the worth of rhetoric diminished by the fact that the one who is to be judged a perfect orator ought to be skilled in all things. For although Crassus in Cicero, On the Orator, book 1, speaks thus: "In my opinion, he will be an orator worthy of this weighty name who, whatever matter comes up that must be explained in speech, speaks prudently, copiously, elegantly and from memory, with a certain dignity of delivery."

units.la: Z neque enim oratori distincta omnium rerum cognitione opus est; sed sufficit ut sic universalem omnium notitiam habeat, ut tamen plenius accuratiusque cognoscat ea, de quibus crebrius dicere solet. IX. Quod Sophistarum filij, ut de Corace illiusque discipulo ostendit Sextus, captiosis dilemmatibus, similibusque strophis Sophisticis veritatem implicare consueverint, ad rem non facit: nec propterea quicquam arti nobilissimae decedit; haut magis, atque si quis contenderet, ideo exemplo Turcarum ubique locorum vites amputandas esse, quod multi in vino sumendo modum servare nesciant. X. Liberalior aequo Sextus est, quando sic loquitur: Artes quidem non expellunt civitates, ut quae sciant eas vitae valde utiles esse: quomodo nec Oeconomicos expellimus ab aedibus, nec bubulcos a grege. Omnes autem dicendi artem, tanquam infestissimum hostem ubique persequuntur, & undique ejicium.Sed quos populos adducit Scepticismi patronus? Cretenses, & Lacedaemonios: quibus jungere posset Romanos, qui aliquando pari ratione Carneadem, & Diogenem Stoicum, ab Athenien\-sibus missos legatos speciali Senatusconsulto urbe sua ejecerunt, ne juventutem, eam artem dicendi docendo, corrumperent, quemadmodum discere est ex Cicer. lib. 2. & 3. de Orat. Sueton. de Clar. Orat. & A. Gellio lib. 15. Noct. Att. cap. II. similiter præter Romanos, aliquis pro Sexto, modernos Musulmanos sive Turcos, qui toto suo imperio artem dicendi proscripserunt, tanquam subsidiarias copias adduxerit. Sed, ut pro Romanis abunde respondet Ovidius, lib. 3. Fast. sic canens:
units.tr: For the orator does not need a distinct knowledge of all things; it is enough that he have such a general acquaintance with everything that he knows more fully and accurately those things about which he is accustomed to speak more often. IX. That the sons of the Sophists, as Sextus shows concerning Corax and his pupil, were accustomed to entangle the truth with captious dilemmas and similar sophistical twists, does not bear on the matter; nor does this detract anything from that most noble art, no more than if someone were to contend that, because many people do not know how to keep moderation in drinking wine, vines should be cut down everywhere, after the example of the Turks. X. Sextus is more generous than is fair when he speaks thus: "Cities do not expel the arts, since they know them to be very useful to life: just as we do not expel household managers from the house, nor herdsmen from the flock. But they pursue the art of speaking everywhere as a most hostile enemy, and cast it out on every side." But what peoples does the advocate of Scepticism bring forward? The Cretans and the Spartans. To these one could add the Romans, who once by a special decree of the Senate expelled from their city the envoys sent from Athens, Carneades and the Stoic Diogenes, lest they corrupt the youth by teaching them that art of speaking; as may be learned from Cicero, On the Orator, books 2 and 3, Suetonius, On Famous Orators, and Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 15, chapter 11. Similarly, besides the Romans, someone on Sextus' behalf might adduce the modern Muslims or Turks, who have banished the art of speaking throughout their whole empire, as auxiliary troops. But, as Ovid answers well on behalf of the Romans, singing thus in Fasti, book 3:

units.la: Nondum tradiderat victas victoribus artesGræcia, facundum sed male forte genus. Qui bene pugnabat Romanam noverat artem, Mittere qui poterat pila disertus erat.
units.tr: "Greece had not yet handed over the arts to her conquerors, a clever race but unfortunately ineffective. He who fought well knew the Roman art; he who could throw the javelin was eloquent."

units.la: Significare volens, quo tempore Quiritium verba adhuc olerent allium, eos non æstimasse eloquentiam, quam tamen subsequentibus seculis in summo pretio habuerunt: Ita de Cretensibus atque Lacedæmonijs dici primo potest: (quorum meminit quoque Plato lib. 1. de Legibus) cum rebus agendis præ cæteris intenti essent, minus humaniores disciplinas, speciatim artem oratoriam, æstimasse. Secundo, cum eloquentiæ studium proprium esset Atheniensibus, reliquos Græciæ populos minori pretio hoc ipsum censuisse, ne se æquales redderent ijs, quos oderant. Nam ut Cicero in Bruto loquitur, ubi de oratoria facultate scribit: Hoc autem studium, inquit, non erat commune Græciæ, sed proprium Athenarum. Quis enim aut Argivum oratorem, aut Corinthium, aut Thebanum scit suisse temporibus istis? Nisi quod de Epaminonda, docto hominie suspicari licet. Lacedæmonium vero usque adhoc tempus audivi fuisse neminem. Tertio ipsi illi rigidi Lacedæmonij, quorum Laconicam brevitatem tantopere prædicat Sextus, postea ab ea ipsa desciverunt. Quo pertinet illud Epaminondæ. Nam quum Spartani multa & magna crimina Thebanis impingerent, & prolixe ea commemorarent: Ita, inquit, Epaminondas, docuerunt vos Thebani longa oratione uti & breviloquentiæ finem imponere, ut scribit Plutarchus de Philautia.
units.tr: He means to say that at the time when the words of the Quirites still smelt of garlic, they did not value eloquence, which nevertheless in the following centuries they held in the highest esteem. So it can be said first of the Cretans and the Lacedaemonians (whom Plato also mentions, book 1 of the Laws) that, being more intent than others on affairs of action, they esteemed the more humane disciplines, and especially the art of oratory, less. Secondly, since the study of eloquence was peculiar to the Athenians, the remaining peoples of Greece thought little of it, lest they make themselves equal to those whom they hated. For as Cicero says in the Brutus, where he writes of the oratorical faculty: "This study," he says, "was not common to Greece, but peculiar to Athens. For who knows that there was an orator of the Argives, or the Corinthians, or the Thebans in those times? Except that one may suspect it of Epaminondas, a learned man. And I have heard that there was no Spartan orator up to this time." Thirdly, those very stern Lacedaemonians, whose Laconic brevity Sextus praises so highly, afterwards themselves departed from it. To this belongs the saying of Epaminondas. For when the Spartans brought many great charges against the Thebans and recounted them at length, "Thus," said Epaminondas, "the Thebans have taught you to use long speeches and to put an end to brevity," as Plutarch writes in On Self-Love.

units.la: Caput Nonum. De Geometria, tantopere à Sexto vexata toto libro tertio adversus Mathematicos, cujus o- mnes rationes per generales classes responsori- ās examinantur.
units.tr: Chapter 9. On Geometry, which Sextus attacks so vigorously throughout the whole third book against the Mathematicians, where all of his arguments are examined under general classes of answers.

units.la: POst assertam Rhetoricam sive dicendi artem deinceps progredimur ad asserendam pariterque vindicandam Geometriam, cui sic infestus est Sextus, ut eidem subvertendæ integrum librum, tertium scil. quem adversus Mathematicos scripsit, consecraverit. Possemus secundum alterius methodi lineamenta progredi, sed quod initio dixerimus, nos insistere velle vestigijs ipsius Sexti, ab ijs non recedemus.
units.tr: After asserting rhetoric, or the art of speaking, we now go on to assert and likewise defend geometry, against which Sextus is so hostile that he devoted an entire book, namely the third of his work against the mathematicians, to overthrowing it. We could proceed along the lines of a different method, but, as we said at the beginning, we wish to follow the footsteps of Sextus himself, and we will not depart from them.

units.la: Quod Geometrię vero bellum indixerit, ei commune est cum Cynicis, qui cum soli Philosophię Practicæ intenti essent, præter alias disciplinas ad Encyclopædiam pertinentes, speciatim Geometriam sollicitarunt, eidem labetastandæ intenti, ut videre est apud Laërt.lib.6. quomodo & Epicurus non minus universæ Mathesi, quam peculiariter Geometriæ existimationem deterere voluit, monendo Polyenum sectatorem suum, ut hanc ipsam disciplinam, quam laboriose didicerat, dedisceret, sicut testatur Plutarchus in Opusc. quomodo secundum Epicurum beate sit vivendum. Ne quis miretur Lucianum in Hermotimo, ubi omnes sectas sollicitat, Geometriam ideo admirandam vocare, quod ex falsis principijs admodum admirandas si non pertentosas, conclusiones colligar. Quo omnia distinctè explicari queant, initio prænotamus, scientiam nobilissimam pariter atq; certissimam, non esse æstimandam ratione nominis, quod prima fronte adeo angustos ejusdem fines arguere videtur, ut ipse Plato in Epinomide vocabulum ridiculum esse censeat: quum disciplina hæc què à terræ dimensione cœpit, servire possit omnibus illis mensurandis, quibus modo mensuræ ratio applicari potest. Deinde, notandum, eandem, inse ac secundum propriam naturam consideratam, esse disciplinam
units.tr: In declaring war on geometry he shares a position with the Cynics, who, though intent on practical philosophy alone, harassed other disciplines belonging to the encyclopedia, and geometry in particular, intent on undermining it, as may be seen in Diogenes Laertius, book 6. Epicurus too wished to lower the esteem of all mathematics, and of geometry in particular, advising his follower Polyaenus to unlearn this very discipline which he had laboriously learned, as Plutarch attests in his work on how one should live happily according to Epicurus. Let no one be surprised that Lucian, in the Hermotimus, where he stirs up all the sects, calls geometry admirable on the ground that it draws admirable, if not wearisome, conclusions from false principles. So that everything may be explained distinctly, we note at the outset that this most noble and at the same time most certain science is not to be judged by its name, which at first sight seems to point to such narrow limits that Plato himself in the Epinomis thought the word ridiculous, since this discipline, which began with the measurement of land, can serve all those things which can be measured wherever the principle of measure can be applied. Next, it should be noted that the same discipline, considered in itself and according to its own nature, is

units.la: Theoreticam, quæ ut docet rei mensurabilis affectiones mente considerare, sic ipsam mensuram certis schematibus non minus illustrat, quam demonstrat. Nec aliter Practica censeri potest, quam quatenus instrumentum certum adhibet, applicando illud certæ rei quantæ. Quibus præmissis, pro Geometria asserenda subsequentes rationes noto. I. Quæ disciplina ex certis indubitatisque principiis, certo atque infallibiliter varias continuæ quantitatis proprietates atque proportiones demonstrat, illa disciplina certa censeri debet. Atqui hoc verum est de Geometria. Ergo. De majoris propositionis infallibili certitudine nullus omnino vel ambigere potest. Minor inde vero probatur, quæcunque in hac disciplina traduntur, non solum procedant ex certis indubitatisque principiis, quæ, termini modo noti fuerint, ab omnibus citra difficultatem ullam probantur; verum etiam omnes conclusiones ad illa prima principia revocari possint, atque per eadem certo infallibiliterque probari. Adeo, ut non sine ratione dictum fuerit à Seneca lib. I. Nat. Q. cap. 4. Rationes quæ non persuadent, sed cogunt, à Geometris adferuntur. II. Quæ scientia aliis disciplinis inserviendo, non solum singulari illis est subsidio, verum etiam ijsdem certitudinem majorem procurat, illa in se certa esse debet. Sed hoc verum de Geometria. Ergo. De majori propositione nullus iterum ambigere potest: cum circa eam locum habeat vulgatum illud axioma, quod convenienter hic applicatur: Per quod unumquodque tale est, illud magis tale est. Ne aga m distincte de minori propositione, quam probatam infra exhibebo, cum de Physica agam, circa eam varias quaestiones proponendo: hoc certum in genere est, eos, qui in Geometria probe exercitati sunt, ad quascunque disciplinas percipiendas prae aliis magis esse idoneos. Quod adeo verum est, ut ipse Ariftoteles diffiteri non potuerit, cujus hoc verbum notum ex lib. 10. Ethic. cap. 5. Geometrae fiunt, singulaque certius assequuntur, qui Geometria delectantur: atque si Xenocrates de Mathematicis disciplinis in genere consideratis, teste Plutarcho de virt. mor. dicere potuerit easdem ansas philosophiae esse, eminenti quadam ratione Geometriae hoc applicari potest. Convenienter Alcinous de doctrina Platonis cap. 7. Mathematicorum, inquit, consideratio, quoddam ad divinorum contemplationem est quasi praeludium. Arithmetica quippe & Geometria, quaeque eas colunt, ad illius quod revera est, pervenire desiderant cognitionem. III. Quae disciplina a vulgo non solum, sed a pueris quoque, propter certitudinem suam, citra prolixum difficultatem apprehendi potest, eam certam esse necessum est. Sed talis Geometria. Quanquam pro minore propositione aliquam multa dici possent, hæc pauca tamen instar omnium erunt, atque sufficient. Non temerario consilio, sed matura deliberatione institutum atque receptum, utPlato suæ Academiæ hoc præscriberet: Nullus, qui Geometriæ imperitus, ingrediatur. namque Geometria pueris convenientissima disciplina est, non solum pro præparandis eorum ingeniis ad sublimiores disciplinas, quæ, ut vel ex solo Aristotele constare potest, exemplis Geometricis illustrari solent, verum etiam eorundem captui admodum est conveniens; quod solius rationis subsidio, citra usum & experientiam [qua pueri neutiquam sunt instructi] ea omnia, quæ in Geometria proponuntur, convenienter non minus apprehendantur, quam etiam dijudicentur. Nam Geometrica principia adeo certa & evidentia sunt, tantaque ijs inest ratione consequentiæ, quę in consectarijs animad vertitur, certitudo, ut ipsi quoque pueri, simul ac modo ratione uti incipiunt, neque circa antecedentia, neque consequentia ulla ratione ambigere queant. Quod vero ab omni ætate, etiam prima, sive à pueris ut certum apprehenditur, de eo neutiquam licet ambigere, quicquid Sceptici quoque clament, qui abun-de ostendunt se infra pueros censendos, isque posteriores esse, quando hanc rationem in dubium vocare præsumunt. Argumentis adversarijs facili negotio quis occurret ex subsequentibus principijs responsorijs. 1. Falsus est omnino Sextus, quando præsupponit omnia à priori demonstrari posse: dantur quædam primę veritates, quæ, simulac termini modo noti fuerint, ab omnibus citra fluctuationem aliquam apprehenduntur: quæ uti sunt primæ veritates, ita ante eas ne quidem apprehendi possunt priora quædam principia, è quibus demonstrentur: alias eo, quod primo primum est, aliquid prius daretur. Interim eorundem à posteriori institui potest probatio, quæ licet habeat sese instar demonstrationis, neutiquam tamen demonstratio proprie sic dicta, sive demonstratio formalis vocari potest. 11. Ut in Geometria ad modum principiorum demonstrabilium distincte considerantur definitiones sive suppositiones, petitiones, sive postulata, & axiomata: Ita omnium tanta est certitudo atque evidentia, ut auditis modo terminis, à quovis apprehendi queant. Nec censeri possunt, ut perperam persuadere laborat Empiricus, suppositiones mere ratiocinativæ, quarum veritas pendeat à solo intellectu. Taliter enim si affectę forent, non essent suppositiones universales, sed mera entia rationis, ijsque contingeret quod omnibus entibus rationis, atque pro diverso hujus, illiusve concipientis conceptu diversimode se haberent. Sed experientia docet, omnis ordinis homines, adeoque ipsos quoque pueros, [ut jam antea oftensum fuit] cognitismodo terminis, assensu suo comprobare has ipsas primas veritates Geometricas. Certo argumento, non posse hypotheses aliquas, contradictorias ijs hypothesibus [quæ proprie agnoscuntur esse Geometricę] aut cum veritate ab aliquo assumi, aut etiam tanquam hypotheses Geometricas agnosci: quamvis enim alias contingenter ex falsis præmissis, velut hypothesibus, vi dispositionis vera consueverit colligi conclusio; nequaquam tamen hoc fieri potest in Geometria, scientia longe certissima, cujus omnes qua hypotheses, qua conclusiones convenit esse verissimas & certissimas. III. Quamvis non solum Geometria, sed universa quoque Mathesis quantitatem non consideret, quatenus est in rebus sensibilibus, sed eandem mente à materia singulari & sensibili abstractam; neutiquam tamen inde sequitur, hanc ipsam quantitatem abstractam, esse aut figmentum, aut mendacium: ut enim nulla ratione potest, quicquid erronibus quibusdam videatur, aut quantitas sine materia, aut materia sine quantitate subsistere, sic hæc abstractio nihil statuit extra materiam; sed illud duntaxat sine materia considerat, quod materiæ actualiter, atque uti loquuntur, à parte rei inhæret. Notum vulgatum Philosophorum axioma: Abstrahentium non est inendatium; quatenus scil. à mente secundum rationem abstractionis, ea, quæ abstracta sunt, spectantur. IV. Tantum abest ut ratio abstractionis, qua abstractionis fallat; ejusdem subsidio clarius atque distinctius ea ipsa quæ sunt Mathematicæ considerationis, perspicere possumus. Si enim in ratione materiæ, atque cum ea considerarentur, ob ejusdem ruditatem imperfectionemque, ea neutiquam cognoscerentur. Ut uno enim exemplo duntaxat ex tam multis alijs, quæ adferre hic liceret, utamur; Secundum ipsum Philosophum lib. I. de Anima cont. 13. consideratur linea recta sphæram æneam in puncto tangere: quod non nisi ratione abstractionis, aut considerari, aut concipi potest: cum in rerum natura nulla occurrat linea, quæ sphæram duntaxat in puncto tangat: ut enim Geometris objiciebat Protagoras, & ipse Scepticus insignis (ut liquet ex lib. primo] sphæra semper aliqua parte suæ superficiei subjectam lineam contingit. At quod corporis oculis nulla ratione yideri potest, illud Mathematicus sive Geometra per abstractionem non difficulter mentis oculis cernit. v. Non audiendus denique Sextus, quando omnes adhibet machinas, ut labefactet Geometricas definitiones: secure illæ sunt, & omnes Sexti objectiones circa illas sua sponte evanescunt, si considerentur secundum abstractionem Geometriæ propriam, secundum quam ut punctum, linea, atque superficies definiri solent, sic non valet consequentia ab ijs confideratis Mathematice, ad eorundem confiderationem Physicam, aut realem inexistentiam in rebus corporeis.
units.tr: theoretical, for just as it teaches us to consider in the mind the properties of a measurable thing, so it illustrates and demonstrates measure itself by certain figures no less than it proves it. Nor can it be regarded as practical except insofar as it employs a fixed instrument, applying it to a definite quantity of a thing. With these premises laid down, I offer the following arguments in support of geometry. I. Whatever discipline demonstrates with certainty and infallibility the various properties and proportions of continuous quantity from certain and indubitable principles must be considered a certain discipline. But this is true of geometry. Therefore... The major premise, once its terms are understood, cannot be doubted by anyone at all. The minor is proved as follows: whatever is handed down in this discipline not only proceeds from certain and indubitable principles, which are accepted by everyone without any difficulty once the terms are known, but also all its conclusions can be traced back to those first principles and proved by them with certainty and infallibility. So much so that Seneca, in Natural Questions, book 1, chapter 4, did not speak without reason when he said: Rationes quae non persuadent, sed cogunt, a Geometris afferuntur. [The arguments that geometers bring forward do not persuade, but compel.] II. A science which, by serving the other disciplines, not only gives them singular help but also procures for them greater certainty, must itself be certain. But this is true of geometry. Therefore... Again, no one can doubt the major premise, since the common axiom applies here appropriately: whatever makes a thing such, makes it more such. I will not discuss the minor premise in detail here, since I will prove it below when I treat physics, raising various questions about it. This is certainly true in general: those who are well practiced in geometry are more fit than others to grasp any disciplines whatever. This is so true that Aristotle himself could not deny it; his well-known saying from Ethics book 10, chapter 5, is: Geometers are made, and those who delight in geometry grasp each thing more certainly. And if Xenocrates, as Plutarch reports in the work on moral virtue, could say that mathematical disciplines considered in general are handles of philosophy, this can be applied to geometry in a pre-eminent way. Similarly Alcinous, in the teaching of Plato, chapter 7: The consideration of the mathematicians, he says, is in a certain way a prelude to the contemplation of divine things. For arithmetic and geometry, and those who cultivate them, desire to attain knowledge of what truly is. III. A discipline which can be grasped, because of its certainty, not only by the common people but even by boys, without lengthy difficulty, must necessarily be certain. But geometry is such. Although many things could be said in support of the minor premise, these few will stand in for all and will suffice. Plato did not establish, by rash counsel but after mature deliberation, the rule that his Academy should have: Let no one ignorant of geometry enter. For geometry is the most suitable discipline for boys, not only for preparing their minds for the higher disciplines, which, as can be gathered from Aristotle alone, are usually illustrated by geometrical examples, but also because it is thoroughly suited to their capacity. By the help of reason alone, without use and experience (which boys by no means possess), all the things proposed in geometry are grasped and judged no less readily. For the principles of geometry are so certain and evident, and there is such a certainty in the logical sequence which is observed in the corollaries, that boys themselves, as soon as they begin to use reason, cannot doubt either the premises or the conclusions in any way. That which is apprehended as certain at every age, even the earliest, or by boys, cannot in any way be doubted, whatever the Sceptics may cry out, who plainly show themselves to be below boys, and younger, when they presume to call this reasoning into doubt. Anyone can easily meet the adversaries' arguments with the following responses. 1. Sextus is wholly mistaken when he presupposes that everything can be demonstrated from a prior principle. There are certain first truths which, as soon as their terms are known, are apprehended by all without any wavering. Just as they are first truths, so before them there cannot even be apprehended any prior principles from which they might be demonstrated; otherwise something would exist prior to what is first. Meanwhile, a proof of these truths can be set up from what is posterior, which, although it has the appearance of a demonstration, can by no means be called a demonstration properly so called, or a formal demonstration. II. Just as in geometry, definitions or suppositions, petitions or postulates, and axioms are distinctly considered as the principles of demonstration, so their certainty and evidence are so great that, as soon as the terms are heard, anyone can grasp them. Nor can they be regarded, as Empiricus labours to persuade us, as mere suppositions of reasoning whose truth depends solely on the intellect. For if they were of this kind, they would not be universal suppositions but mere beings of reason, and it would follow that they would be related differently to each being of reason, according to the differing concept of this or that person conceiving them. But experience teaches that men of every rank, and so even boys, [as has already been shown] by merely grasping the terms, confirm these very first geometrical truths by their assent. This is a sure argument that no hypotheses contradictory to those which are properly acknowledged as geometrical can be assumed by anyone with truth, or even acknowledged as geometrical hypotheses. For although a conclusion true by the arrangement of the premises is sometimes drawn, by chance, from false premises as hypotheses, this cannot in any way happen in geometry, a science by far the most certain, in which all the hypotheses as well as the conclusions ought to be most true and most certain. III. Although not only geometry but all mathematics does not consider quantity insofar as it exists in sensible things, but considers it by the mind as abstracted from singular and sensible matter, it does not follow at all that this abstracted quantity is either a fiction or a falsehood. For just as, whatever some erroneous people may think, quantity cannot subsist without matter, nor matter without quantity, so this abstraction establishes nothing outside matter; it considers apart from matter only what actually inheres in matter, as they say, in reality. The common axiom of the philosophers is well known: There is no error in those who abstract, insofar as, namely, the things that are abstracted are viewed by the mind according to the reason of abstraction. IV. So far is the reason of abstraction from deceiving that, by its help, we can perceive more clearly and distinctly the very things that belong to mathematical consideration. For if they were considered in the light of matter, and together with it, they would by no means be known, because of its crudeness and imperfection. To use one example only, out of the many others which could be cited here: according to the Philosopher himself, in On the Soul, book 1, a straight line is considered to touch a bronze sphere at a point, which can be considered or conceived only by reason of abstraction, since in the nature of things there occurs no line which touches a sphere at a point only. For, as Protagoras objected to the geometers, and as the notable Sceptic himself (as is clear from book 1) says, a sphere always touches the line lying beneath it with some part of its surface. But what cannot be seen by the eyes of the body in any way, the mathematician or geometer discerns without difficulty by abstraction with the eyes of the mind. V. Finally, Sextus is not to be heeded when he brings up all his machinery to overthrow the geometrical definitions. They are secure, and all Sextus's objections to them vanish of their own accord if they are considered according to the proper abstraction of geometry, by which points, lines and surfaces are usually defined. The inference from these things, considered mathematically, to their physical consideration or to their real existence in corporeal things, does not hold.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TEN.

units.la: De Arithmetica, cujus certitudo adversus Sex- tum asseritur & vindicatur.
units.tr: On Arithmetic, whose certainty is asserted and vindicated against Sextus.

units.la: ARithmeticæ quoque infestus Sextus, laborat eandem post Geometriam (sed conatu parum fausto) submovere: priusquam rationes proponam, ex quibus aliquis cavillationibus ejusdem verius, quam argumentis occurrere possit, ipsa primitus Arithmetica asserenda atque in statu suo collocanda venit. Versatur autem circa numerum, quatenus numerum, sive, ut Plato in Philebo loquitur, circa numerum mentalem, cui apud eundem Platonem opponitur is numerus, qui secundum eum quasi sub manibus positus esse dicitur: inter quos duos numeros hoc interest, quod secundum abstractionem Mathematicam Arithmeticæ quoque communem, prior à materie omni sit abstractus, posterior vero cum eadem concretus. Et ut Geometriam jam antea duplicem consideravimus; sic, duplex quoque agnoscí debet Arithmetica: Theorica, & practica. Theorica explicat proprietates numerorum à rebus numeratis abstractorum, quas per propria quoque principia demonstrat, quam respiciens Plato ita loquitur in Theæteto: Arithmeticus qui est, perfecte omnium numerorum scientia in anima ipsi inest. Practica quam Plato in Gorgia logisticam vocat, præcipue occupatur circa numeros concretos, seu denominatos ab ijs rebus, quæ numerantur. Differentiam expressit idem Plato in Philebo. Vulgi arithmetica, inquit, unitates inæquales numerorum numerat, ut duo minima, duo maxima; Philosophi vero nunquam eos sequuntur, etc. & dial. 7. de repubi. Arithmetica, inquit, animam valde sursum ducit, & de ipsis numeris disserere cogit, nullo modo admittens, si quis numeros corpora, quæ videri aut tangi possunt, habentes, ipsi proponens disputet. Quibus præmissis, millis, ut contra quascunque cavillationes Scepticorum, disciplinam nobilissimam asseramus, omnibusque constet, Arithmeticam ut habitualem esse admittendam, præsupponimus verum esse, quod luculenter probat Aristoteles in Problem. sect. 30. qu. 5. nempe facultatem numerandi æque homini propriam esse, & profluere à ratione, qua pollet, atq; eidem proprium est ridere. Obquam caussam ut olim dixit Pythagoras (testis est Jamblichus) hominem ideo prudentissimum esse, quod numerare sciat, ita non inconvenienter Socrates apud Platonem in libris de Republ. sic disserit: Quid vero, ait, numquamne animadvertisti, qui natura arithmetici sunt, eos ad omnes artes percipiendas perspicaces & acutos esse? ac si tardi & hebetes in hoc studio erudiantur & exerceantur, si alio non adjuventur, attamen, confessione omnium, promptiores & acutiores fieri? Cum enim habitus definiti sint ad perficiendas ratiocinativas facultates indifferenter se habentes, ad hoc ut convenienti modo ordinatæ suos actus perseste atque citra errorem ullum edant; aliter fieri non potest, quin aut mentis emotæ esse, aut communi sensu carere isipse censeatur, qui neque secundum ductum luminis naturæ numerare potest, neque etiam perficitur ab habitu, solito alias perficere illud ipsum, quod naturale est. Unde, teste Suida, jure summo imputatum fuit insaniæ, quod Amphistides numerare non sciret: æque enim hoc nom ne risum debebat ijs, qui aliorum infirmitate ad oblectamentum abutuntur, atque cum dubitaret, uter è parentibus se peperisset, aut, cum testaretur, se sponsam suam non devirginaturum, ne à matre ejusdem objurgaretur. Quibus præmissis sic I. pro Arithmetica argumentor: Quæ facultas est homini propria, nec ab habitu superveniente aliter perficitur, quam quatenus patitur insitum rationi lumen, illa ipsa facultas, ut directa ab habitu, ordinato perpetuo secundum insitum illud lumen, convenienti sua certitudine gaudere debet. Sed talis est Arithmetica. Consequentiæ ratio in hoc consistit: quod cum insitum rationis lumen in talibus sit invariabiliter certum, non possit non quoque scientia, secundum illud lumen pro ulteriori ejusdem perfectione progrediens, pariter certa esse. quandoquidem non licet ei ulla ratione recedere à lineis hujus certitudinis. II. Cujus scientiæ invariabilem certitudinem sensibiliter omnes homines, in subjectis cujuscunque generis quotidie experiuntur, ea ipsa scientia debet esse certa. Sed hoc verum est de Arithmetica. Quæcunque enim Arithmetica præcepta, applicata sive nummis, sive ponderi, sive mensurae, sive quibuscunque alijs rebus ut quantis, tum secundum additionem, tum subtractionem, tum multiplicationem, tum divisionem, eodem modo, atque aeque invariabilitet perpetuo sese habere deprehenduntur: certo atque indubitato argumento, non posse illius disciplinae praecepta tanquam incerta suspectari, quorum certitudo toties palpabiliter ab alijs deprehenditur. III. Inter Christianos sic etiam argumentari licet: Si Deus explicationem numerorum in maximis mysterijs, ijs, qui a sapientia commendari volunt, commendat: nae debet quaedam esse certitudo illius disciplinae, quae circa numeros versatur. Sed hanc numerorum explicationem in Scriptura Deus commendat. Ergo. Pro minori propositione, alia ne adferam, sufficere potest numerus bestiae Apocalypticae, quem mandat inquiri ipse Deus Apoc. 13. & 15. Ratio vero consequentiae est haec: Quod Deus, qui est verax & infallibilis, non circa incerta, sed certa [notae enim hujus est ipsius verbum, & omnia, quae in eodem occurrunt] hominem & rulpatorem mysteriorum verbi sui occupari velit. Loco fontium solutoriorum, praeter ea, quae jam antea ex praecedentibus notavi, atque hoc loco convenienter admodum applicari possunt, sequentia breviter notentur: Primo.Contendum rendunt nonnulli, in speciem quasi pro Scepticis, hominem ratione præditum secundum naturam suam, pariter per rationem atq; convenienter naturæ suæ aptum esse ad nummerandum, & proinde non opus esse arte, si natura sufficiat: quod equidem ego ipse quoque concederem, si per naturam homo æque aptus foret ad bene numerandum, omnesque circa numerum difficultates expediundas, atque ad numerandum simpliciter. At quisnam hoc ipsum dixerit, quum quotidie videamus homines simpliciores, & Arithmeticæ artificialis imperitos ratione tum additionum tum subtractionum, ne quidem practicæ Arithmeticæ regulas admittere, nisi quatenus earum certitudo sive calculis, sive creta palpabiliter ob oculos quasi ponitur & delineatur. Indubitato argumento, admittendam esse Arithmeticam aliquam habitualem, supra naturalem: nam si illa æque naturalis foret, non opus esset deductione; atque eandem simul certam esse inde constat, quod nullus non, post popularem demonstrationem eidem assensum suum commodét, circa quem antea tamen, cum ex artis regulis procederetur, difficiliorem se præbebat.
units.tr: Sextus, who is also hostile to arithmetic, labours to overthrow it after geometry, though with little success. Before I set out the reasons by which one may meet his sophistries (more truly than his arguments), arithmetic itself must first be asserted and set in its proper position. It is concerned with number as number, or, as Plato speaks in the Philebus, with mental number. Plato opposes to this the number which, he says, is as it were placed under the hands. Between these two numbers there is this difference: according to the mathematical abstraction common also to arithmetic, the former is abstracted from all matter, while the latter is joined with matter. And just as we have already considered geometry as twofold, so arithmetic must also be recognised as twofold: theoretical and practical. Theoretical arithmetic explains the properties of numbers abstracted from the things numbered, and it demonstrates these by its own principles. Plato, having this in view, says in the Theaetetus: The arithmetician, who is such, has within his soul a perfect knowledge of all numbers. Practical arithmetic, which Plato in the Gorgias calls logistic, is chiefly occupied with concrete numbers, or numbers named after the things that are counted. Plato himself stated the difference in the Philebus: The arithmetic of the crowd, he says, counts unequal units of numbers, such as two smallest and two largest; but philosophers never follow them, and so on. And in the seventh book of the Republic: Arithmetic, he says, draws the soul powerfully upward, and compels it to discourse about numbers themselves, by no means admitting if anyone, when disputing, proposes to it numbers that have bodies which can be seen or touched. With these points laid down, I do not need to defend this most noble discipline against every sceptical cavil. Since it is agreed by all that arithmetic must be admitted as a habit, I presuppose the truth of what Aristotle clearly proves in the Problems, section 30, question 5: that the faculty of counting is as proper to man as laughter, and that it flows from the reason which he possesses. For this reason, as Pythagoras once said (Iamblichus is witness), man is most wise because he knows how to count. Thus Socrates, in Plato's books on the Republic, reasonably argues as follows: But, he says, have you never noticed that those who are by nature arithmeticians are keen and sharp in grasping all the arts? And even if the slow and dull are trained and exercised in this study, though they are not helped in anything else, yet, by the agreement of all, they become quicker and sharper? For since habits are defined as those which dispose the reasoning faculties to perform their acts in a fitting manner, perfectly and without any error, it cannot be otherwise: whoever cannot count according to the guidance of the light of nature, and is not perfected by the habit which elsewhere perfects that very natural faculty, must be judged either out of his mind or lacking common sense. Hence, as Suidas reports, it was rightly counted as the height of folly that Amphistides did not know how to count. For this deserved laughter no less than from those who mock the weakness of others for their amusement; and no less than when he doubted which of his parents had begotten him, or when he swore that he would not deflower his betrothed, lest he be scolded by her mother. With these points laid down, I argue thus for arithmetic. First: a faculty which is proper to man, and which is perfected by a habit added to it only insofar as it admits the light implanted in reason, must, as that faculty is directed by a habit ordered constantly according to that implanted light, enjoy a certainty suited to it. But arithmetic is such. The reason for the consequence is this: since the implanted light of reason is invariably certain in such matters, the science which advances towards its further perfection according to that light must likewise be certain, since it is in no way permitted to depart from the lines of this certainty. Second: that science whose invariable certainty all men experience every day, in subjects of every kind, must itself be certain. But this is true of arithmetic. For whatever rules of arithmetic are applied to coins, to weight, to measure, or to any other quantities, whether by addition, subtraction, multiplication or division, are found always to behave in the same way, invariably and equally. This is a sure and undoubted argument that the precepts of that discipline cannot be suspected as uncertain, since their certainty is so often plainly confirmed by others. Third: Christians may also argue thus: if God commends the explanation of numbers in the greatest mysteries to those who wish to be commended for wisdom, then there must be some certainty in that discipline which is concerned with numbers. But God commends this explanation of numbers in Scripture. Therefore... As for the minor premise, to bring forward no others, the number of the beast in the Apocalypse may suffice, which God himself commands to be sought out, Rev. 13 and 15. The reason for the consequence is this: God, who is true and infallible, wishes man, the interpreter of the mysteries of his word, to be occupied not with uncertain things but with certain ones [for this is the character of his word, and all things that occur in it]. Apart from the solutions already noted from what precedes, which can very suitably be applied here, the following may be briefly noted. First: some maintain, in appearance on behalf of the Sceptics, that man, endowed with reason according to his nature, is likewise by reason and in agreement with his nature fitted to count, and therefore that there is no need of art if nature is sufficient. I myself would grant this, if man were by nature equally fit to count well, to resolve all difficulties concerning number, and simply to count. But who would say this, since we see every day that simpler people, unskilled in artificial arithmetic, do not accept the rules even of practical arithmetic for addition or subtraction, unless their certainty is set before the eyes, as it were, and drawn out plainly with counters or chalk? This is an undoubted argument that some habitual arithmetic, above nature, must be admitted. For if it were equally natural, there would be no need of deduction; and that it is certain at the same time is clear from the fact that everyone, after a popular demonstration, gives his assent to it, when before, while proceeding by the rules of the art, he had been more reluctant.

units.la: Secundo differentiæ artificiales, quæ circa Arithmeticam contingunt, cum rationabiles omnino sint, nequaquam arguunt ipsius artiincertitudinem, verum ejusdem amplitudinem atque divitias, quatenus unus atque idem calculus variis modis subduci poterit: cum enim omnes illi modi sint rationi consentanei, atque certo probari queant, non est, quod Scepticus hic secum ambigat, quaerendo cui modo potius accedere debeat. Tertio non est quod Scepticum ulla ratione turbent compendia, quae in hac arte varia contingunt: siquidem operandi modorum, qui compendiosissimi quoque videntur, tum certa datur demonstratio, tum etiam hi ipsi modi per alios, ampliores, & in vulgus magis notos, demonstrari convenienter possunt. Quarto. Quanquam, accurate loquendo, & numeri voce praesumpta, unitas non possit censeri numerus; [ut voluit quoque Aristoteles lib. 3. Metaphys. Cont. 16. & lib. 10. Metaph. cont. 90. & 91.] interim tamen, quicquid cornicetur Sextus, per multiplicem sui in se complexionem atque uniformem connexionem apta est numerum constituere: quatenus haec natura est entium aggregativorum, ut per hanc sui connexionem, illud secundum formam aggregationis fiant, quod, seorsum si consideretur, per se fieri non possunt. Nam ratio formalis aggregationis, uti loquuntur, consistit in conjunctione & accumulatione omnium eorum, ex quibus aggregatum aliquod, seu ens aggregativum constituitur. Quinto. Unitas, in numero alteri unitati aut accedit, aut subtrahitur, quatenus partes materiales entis aggregati, sive numeri, aut plures, aut pauciores sumuntur. Eoque, quando tollitur unitas v. c. à denario, neque à denario qua denario, neque à singulis unitatibus abstrahitur unitas, sed, à decem unitatibus per aggregationem mentalem ad actum numeri denarij accumulatis, una unitas tollitur, qua sublata tanquam parte materiæ, quæ restant unitates, novam formam aggregativam recipiunt à mente, sic ut in se quoque habeant novam materiæ rationem. quum vero mens non inveniat totidem, quot antea unitates, non potest quoque æqualem apud se collectionem facere, cum non sint quoque totidem partes materiales aggregabiles: quæ vero ratio subtractionis, eadem additionis est. Pariter ex hisce duabus [loqui sic fas sit] Arithmeticæ affectionibus, haud difficile est de reliquis judicare.
units.tr: Second, the artificial differences which occur in arithmetic, since they are wholly reasonable, do not in any way show its uncertainty, but rather its breadth and riches, insofar as one and the same calculation can be worked out in various ways. For since all those methods agree with reason and can be proved with certainty, there is no reason for the Sceptic to doubt in his own mind which method he ought rather to adopt. Third, there is no reason why the shortcuts which occur in this art should trouble the Sceptic in any way. For a sure demonstration is given even of the methods of operation that seem most compendious, and these same methods can also be suitably demonstrated through others that are fuller and better known to the common people. Fourth: although, speaking strictly and taking the word "number" in its proper sense, unity cannot be counted as a number [as Aristotle also held, in the third book of the Metaphysics, comment 16, and in the tenth book, comments 90 and 91], nevertheless, whatever Sextus may chatter, by its manifold self-combination and uniform connection it is fit to constitute a number. For this is the nature of aggregative entities: through this connection of themselves, they become, according to the form of aggregation, something which, if considered separately, they could not become by themselves. For the formal reason of aggregation, as they call it, consists in the conjunction and accumulation of all those things from which some aggregate, or aggregative being, is constituted. Fifth: a unit, within a number, is either added to another unit or subtracted from it, insofar as more or fewer of the material parts of the aggregate being, or number, are taken. Therefore, when a unit is taken away, for example, from ten, the unit is not abstracted either from the ten as ten or from the single units; rather, one unit is removed from the ten units gathered by mental aggregation into the act of the number ten. When that unit is removed, as a part of the matter, the remaining units receive from the mind a new aggregative form, so that they also have in themselves a new relation of matter. But since the mind does not find as many units as before, it cannot likewise make an equal collection in itself, since there are not equally many material parts that can be aggregated. The reasoning for subtraction is the same for addition. In the same way, from these two affections of arithmetic [if I may speak thus], it is not difficult to judge the rest.

units.la: CAPUT UNDECIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER ELEVEN.

units.la: De Astronomia, quæ adversus suos adversarios disseritur.
units.tr: On Astronomy, which is argued against its adversaries.

units.la: QUandoquidem jam antea declaravimus, nobis propositum esse Sexti Empirici vestigijs am ipsam clementius à Sexto fuisse exceptam, atque alias discipulinas. ut enim ex vestibulo lib. quinti ejusdem liquet, existimat eversis à se quasi Arithmetica & Geometria, evertisse pariter ipsam Astronomiam, quod haec sint duae illæ alæ, quibus Plato jubebat nos in cælum evolare. Atque, ut hoc agere incipiamus, initio notamus, complures, & quidem extra Scepticorum sectam, in eahæresi fuisse, cælum comprehendi non posse, & consequenter quoque non posse aliquam scientiam dari; atque Astronomiam, si quæ jactetur, esse relegandam ad illas disciplinas, quæ vulgo Stochastica vocari solent, uti libro sexto uberius expendimus. Ne de Socrate enim loquar, cujus hoc verbum notum est: Quæ supra nos, nihil ad nos: quum Anaxagoras [at quantus vir!] diceret se natum esse, ut dissereret de rebus cælestibus: publicus ille Græciæ sannio Diogenes [testis est Laërtius] cum risu ex eo quæsivit: Quando de cælo venisti? quasi ille humanæ cognitionis sphæram excedere laboraret, qui præsumpserat de cælo, isque, quę ad cælum pertinent, aliquid cognitione dignum proponere. Imo Platonis Ebræi, sive Philonis Judæi, lib. de somnijs à Deo immissis, verba sunt: Incomprehensibilem naturam cælum habet, nec ulla illius certa ad nos dimanat notitia. Ab eo non dissentiri sentia Lactantius lib. 3. Divin. Inst. cap. 3. sic scribens: Caelum ipsum qua magnitudine, qua materia constet, utrum quietum sit an mobile, an incredibili celeritate volvatur. quanta sit terra crassitudo, aut quibus fundamentis librata & suspensa sit. Hæc [inquam] disputando & conjecturis velle comprehendere, tale est profecto, quale si differere velimus, qualem arbitremur cujusquam remotissimæ generis urbem, quam nunquam vidimus, cujusque nihil aliud, quam nomen audivimus. Imo, quod quis miretur, Tycho Brahe Atlas ille Danicus, non dubitat in quadam Epistola ad Rhotmannum suum sic loqui: Nemo mortalium de ipsissima cæli materia [si modo è materia aliqua proprie constare dici potest] certi quid in medium proferre potest. Est enim cælum abstractum quid, & immateriali simile, nostrum captum fugiens, quod sane potius quid non sit, quam quid sit, percipitur. Quo vero disciplinæ Astronomicæ suum pretium constare queat, priusquam definitas rationes adferimus pro eadem afferenda, ex re est in antecessum quædam notemus, quæ subsequentibus lucem fænerentur. I. Astronomia non est pura puta disciplina Mathematica, sed, uti loquuntur, mixta: siquidem cum Physica coalescit, non solum ab ea accipiendo subjectum, quod consideret; verum etiam supponendo ut vera, ea, quæ in Physica tanquam legitima principia proponuntur. Quo traxerim illud, quod habet Strabo lib. 2. Geogr. Astronomus principia mutuatur à Physico. II. Nec tamen simpliciter omne corpus naturale considerat Astronomus, sed solummodo cæleste, in eo spectando tum motum, sive revera, sive apparenter (neque enim de hoc convenit) tantum convenientem corporibus cælestibus, III. Distincta quoque disciplina à Physiologia censeri debet: siquidem modus considerationis, sive, uti loquuntur, formalis ratio materiale subjectum distinguit. nam Physica versatur quidem circa cælum, sed quatenus corpus naturale est: Astronomia vero illud ipsum considerat secundum rationem motus, quem ut convenienter explicare queat, in subsidium potissimum adhibet Geometriam; [sic tamen ut eidem Arithmetica subserviat) usque adeo, ut vocari recte possit Geometria in corporibus cælestibus occupata. IV. Est vero disciplina difficillima, adeo ut non sine ratione apocryphus author libri Sapientiæ cap. 9. vers. 15. & seqq. dixerit: Corpus, quod corrumpitur, aggravat animam, & terrena habitatio deprimit sensum multa cogitant m. Et difficile existimamus, quæ in terra sunt: & quæ in prospectu sunt, invenimus cum labore: quæ autem in cælis sunt quis investigabit? Sensum autem tuum quis sciet, nisi indideris sapientiam, & miseris Spiritum Sanctum tuum de altissimis. Unde multis eisdem opus est subsidijs, & aliis inferioribus discipulis, quo mutuatitio hoc praesidio instructaqueat ad scopum suum pervenire. V. Non potest vero ad suum scopum pervenire, nisi quinque disciplinarum subsidio. Nempe: Historiae, Physicae, Opticae, Geometriae, & Arithmeticae.
