Atque primo historia quidem opus est, propter observationes de longitudine & breve vitae dierum, variam animi formam pro diversis populis variari solitam, item eclipses, imo propter sexcenta alia, quae longum foret hic commemorare: secundo requiritur quoque Physica, quandoquidem hypotheses Astronomicae, licet sese habere posse tamen duntaxat objective à parte intellectus, & ad modum entium rationis, non tamen plane debent esse contrariae naturae ipsius caeli, corporumque caelestium. Tertio, ob multiplices refractiones, quae inter observandum sese offerunt, necessario quoque Optica in partes venire debet. Sed quarto prae-ceteris praesentaneam operam confert Geometria per praeclaram, &, supra quam dici potest ingeniosam doctrinam triangulorum qua planorum, qua sphaericorum. Cui quinto loco accedent Arithmetica, per logisticen ultimam manum disciplinae, hac ratione perficiendae, imponit. VI. Multum diuque quidem inter Astronomos jam olim disputatum suit, an admitti debeant hypotheses in disciplina hac nobilissima, quibusdam plane eas eliminantibus, aliis ex parte duntaxat, nonnullis vero pro ijsdem haud aliter atque pro aris & focis digladiantibus: Cui conflictui ne nos immiscea-mus [neque enim necessum est] dicimus: Quod quemadmodum olim apud antiquissimos Ægyptios & Græcos siderum scientia tradita atque tractata fuit absque ullis hypothesibus; sic possibile quoque esse eandem absque his adminiculis intellectus nostri proponere: nihilominus utiliter atque convenienter nostro modo apprehendendi, ea, quæ circa motum corporum cælestium alias non nisi difficillime à mente apprehenduntur, per hypotheses explicari: quæ tamen non nisi hypotheses censeri debent: ut enim apud Logicos, conditionalis propositio, qua talis nihil in esse ponit: ita neque per hypotheses Astronomicas, à mente excogitatas, ullæ reales affectiones ipsis corporibus cælestibus accedunt. quod si aptetur orbibus Excentricis & Epicyclis, liquebit, quomodo quid à nobis tanquam anomalum & irregulare concipi possit, quod tamen tale non sit à parte rei. Hisce præmissis, duabus duntaxat rationibus contra Scepticos assertum ibimus Astronomiæ veritatem. Primo: Ad quorum cognitionem per certa & vera media pervenire licet, eorum etiam scientia haberi potest. Atqui ad cognitionem corporum cælestium & motus eorundem perveniri potest per certa atque proportionata media. Ergo. Major propositio est certa: ut enim media ex fine æstimantur, ita vicissim finis e suis medijs:quę si convenientia & proportionata fuerint, atque simul concurrant, ipse finis attingi potest. Quod valet maxime in intelligentibus entibus, quæ proprie propter finem agunt: quando enim cognoscunt suum finem tanquam bonum, sibique convenientem, pariterque cognitionem mediorum ut facilium atque proportionatorum habent, creduntur, quando propter finem agunt,sisem quoq; illum posse attingere. Minor vero propositio patet ex ijs, quæ jam antea notata sunt, de disciplinis subsidiarijs, quarum præsidio astronomica scientia tum acquiritur, tum etiam perficitur: quibus enim subsidijs unaquæque disciplina inventa est, ab ijs quoque ulterius perfici potest: imo actu quoque perficitur. Iis quinque disciplinis, de quibus jam tantea egimus, ab alijs annumeratur Mechanica, occupata in confectione eorum instrumentorum, quibus Astronomi inter observandum uti solent. Sed cum illa instrumenta secundum leges Geometriæ & Arithmeticæ, si non Opticæ quoq; cę quoqste ordinari debeant, non fuit necessum seorsum mentionem Mechanicæ facere. Secundo. Ad quorum contemplationem, imo penitiorem cognitionem Deus in Scriptura omnes invitat, ea cognosci posse, eorumque scientiam dari, certum est: Sed ad corporum cęlestium cognitionem hominem Deus inScriptura invitat. Ergo. De majoris propositionis veritate nullus omnino dubitare potest. Minor vero ex infinitis propemodum Scripturę textibus confirmari potest: ex quibus ut quosdam delibemus, & tamen ordine progrediamur. I. Astra tanquam illustrissima omnipotentiæ, sapientiæ, & bonitatis Dei testimonia augustissimis Elogijs condecorantur. Psal. 148. v. 3. Laudate Iehovam Sol & Luna, laudate eum omnes stellæ lucis. Amos. 5. v. 8. Quærite opificem Pleiadum & Orionis. Job. 9. v. 9. Qui facit Arcturum, Orionem, & Pleiadas, ac penetralium Austri sidera. Psal. 33. v. 6. Verbo Iehovæ cæli facti sunt, & Spiritu oris ejus totus exercitus eorum. Ps. 19. v. 2. Cæli enarrant gloriam Dei fortis, & opus manuum ejus indicat expansum eorum. II. Inde Deus sæpe ad demonstrandam, sanctis promissionum suarum infallibilem certitudinem, ad astra, eorumque motus, velut ad certissima symbola provocat. Abrahamo, quem Josephus testatur fuisse Astronomum & à Chaldæis Mathematum studia didicisse, ut de certitudine multi plicandi sui seminis confirmaretur, atque suspe contra spem crederet, stellarum multitudinem monstrat, Genef. 15 Josepho regiam majestatem, qua patrem & fratres tempore famiservaturus sit, delineat insomnijs, non modo per manipulos, verum etiam per devotam adorationem Solis, Lunæ, & undecim stellarum, Genef. 37 Hiskiæ Regi vitam prorogaturus ad annos xv. Solem velut quod sacramentum proponit, per loca peracta reducem, ipso & Propheta coram, in horologio Achaz spectantibus, Ef. 38. Magis præconem, qui eos ad filium suum unigenitum incarnatum & natum invitaret, inter astra collocat, Matth. 2. Toti mundo Deum naturæ pro salute humani generis crucifixum mori, phænomeno cælesti inusitatæ Eclipsis patefieri voluit, Luc. 23. Et, ut supernaturales apparentiæ commendant naturales, ita illæ non cognoscerentur, nisi hæ prius cognitæ forent. Ejusdem generis est, quod Deus exardescentem suam iram denunciaturus, atque tristia temporum fata descripturus, eadem comparat tristibus astrorum apparentijs. Ita legere est Esajæ cap. 13.v.10. Stella cælorum & sidera eorum non facient ut luceat lux sua: Sol tenebricosus erit ab exortu suo, & Luna splendidam non edet lucem suam. & iterum apud eundem Prophetam cap. 14. v. 12. Quomodo, decidisti de calis Lucifer, nate Aurora? succisus es usque in terram? Quid quód benedictus mundi Salvator Christus comparetur cum Sole, apud Malach. cap. 4. v. 2. in illustri illo vaticinio: Exorietur vobis, ō timentes nomini mei, Sol justitiæ. Quæ illustria Prophetarum testimonia nullo modo intelligi possent, si nulla certitudo foret scientiæ fideræ. Nec aliter in N. T. Spiritus sanctus loquitur. Alia ne proferam, quid notius quam post Danielem cap. 12. futuri seculi gloriam splendore Solis, Lunæ, atque differentium lumine stellarum describi? Exempla alia ne adferam, videri possunt, 1 Cor. 15. & Matth. 13. III. Sed hoc maxime notandum, quod ipse Deus nos invitat, imo vocat, ad contemplandum cælum, & omnia, quæ in illo sunt. Sic legere est Es. 40. v. 26. Attollite in sublime oculos vestros, & videte quis creaverit ista, producens numero suo exercitum ipsorum. At si plane vana foret scientia Astronomica, eique nulla certitudo inesset, frustra non solum homo invitaretur ad contemplandam quasi rem, quā percipere non poterit: verum etiam (venia dicto concedatur!) Deus homini quasi ludos acere videretur, cælum & exercitum cælestem non solum proponendo tanquam exemplar omnipotentiæ divinæ, verum etiam res gravissimæ. gravissimas cum ijsdem comparando: neque enim ulla ratione intelligi potest comparatio, ut ut concinna, quę inter res ignotas, imo ab homine non comprehensibiles, instituitur. Quod gnarum quam maxime fuit magno illi Prophetę Christo Jesu, qui, quo tempore in hoc mundo versabatur, simplices erudiendo, uti sepe multis parabolis ac similitudinibus usus fuit; ita easdem fere desumpsit à rebus obvijs & quotidiánis, quod illi, cum quibus ei negotium erat, easdem quam accurate intelligerent, ac penitissime exploratas haberent.Præter ea, quæ in antecessum jam notavi, ampliùs tria subsequentia ad modum fontium sedulo notentur. I. Non ideo Astronomia definit esse scientia, quod omnia pertinentia ad cælum atque corpora cœlestia non habeat perspecta, sed aliqua duntaxat: quum certum sit, non tam extensive, quam intensivè, atque ratione formalitatis, quamvis ratione nostri se non extendentis ad omnia, quæ ad obječtum pertinent, scientiam æstimandam esse. Observatione digna sunt verba Zabarellæ lib. de Nat. Cæli, cap. 1. Etsi, inquit, ita abscondita nobis est natura cœlestis corporis, ut ipse quoque summus Aristoteles, sola conditionum sublunarium negatione, eam declinare potis fuerit: Attamen ea est ejus præstantia, & nobilitas, ut vel rudis & imperfecta secta ejus cognitio expetibilior sit, quam exquisita & perfecta aliarum rerum ignobilium. II. Dato, diversas hypotheses inter Astronomos esse receptas, atque sæpe circa illas usque ad rixas ab earundem patronis contendi; non tamen inde quicquam decedit certitudini ipsius disciplinæ, in se atque secundum suam naturam consideratæ: quamvis enim certum sit, has præ illis hypothesibus magis consentaneas esse Physicæ veritati, non tamen præcise ratione hujus veritatis æstimari debent: quum possint esse habere ad modum entium rationis, atque hypothesium notionalium. Unde videmus v. c. æque per Ptolemaicas, atque per Pythagoreas, sive Copernicanas hypotheses, subsidio tabularum secundum suas hypotheses conditarum, prædici posse Eclipses utriusque sideris, reliquaq; phænomena statò tempore in cælo recurrentia, atque notari solita. III. Ut jam antea distinximus Astronomiam ab Astrologia, sive disciplina Genethliaca, aut judiciaria, ita hanc ex illa neutiquam æstimare licet.
units.tr: Since we have already declared that our purpose is to follow in the footsteps of Sextus Empiricus, we note that astronomy itself was treated by Sextus more mildly than the other disciplines. For, as is clear from the opening of his fifth book, he thinks that by overthrowing arithmetic and geometry, as it were, he has likewise overthrown astronomy, since these are the two wings by which Plato bade us fly up to heaven. To begin this task, we first note that many men, and indeed some outside the sect of the Sceptics, have held that heaven cannot be comprehended, and consequently that no science of it can be had; and that astronomy, if it is said to be a science, must be relegated to those disciplines which are commonly called stochastic, as we have examined more fully in the sixth book. For, not to speak of Socrates, whose saying is well known, What is above us is nothing to us: when Anaxagoras (what a great man he was!) said that he was born to discourse about heavenly things, that public buffoon of Greece, Diogenes (Laertius is the witness), asked him with a laugh, When did you come down from heaven? as if he who had presumed to speak of heaven were striving to exceed the sphere of human knowledge, and who proposed something worthy of knowledge about the things that pertain to heaven. Indeed, the words of the Hebrew Plato, or rather of the Jewish Philo, in his book On Dreams Sent by God, are these: Heaven has an incomprehensible nature, and no certain knowledge of it flows down to us. Lactantius, writing in book 3 of the Divine Institutes, chapter 3, does not dissent from him, saying: What heaven itself is made of, in respect of size and matter; whether it is at rest or moving; whether it turns with incredible speed; how great the thickness of the earth is, or on what foundations it is poised and suspended: to wish to grasp these things [I say] by disputation and conjecture is truly like wanting to describe some city in the most distant land, which we have never seen and of which we have heard nothing but the name. Nay, what may surprise one, Tycho Brahe, that Danish Atlas, does not hesitate to speak thus in a certain letter to his friend Rothmann: No mortal can bring forward anything certain about the very matter of heaven [if indeed it can properly be said to consist of any matter]. For heaven is something abstract and like the immaterial, escaping our grasp, and it is perceived to be rather what it is not than what it is. But before we bring forward definite reasons for the worth of astronomy, so that it may be seen what worth this discipline can claim, it is fitting to note in advance some points which will shed light on what follows. I. Astronomy is not a purely mathematical discipline, but, as they say, a mixed one: for it is joined with physics, not only taking from it the subject which it considers, but also supposing as true those things which physics sets forth as legitimate principles. To this belongs what Strabo says in book 2 of his Geography: The astronomer borrows his principles from the physicist. II. Yet the astronomer does not consider every natural body simply, but only the heavenly bodies, and in them he regards only motion, whether real or apparent (for on this point there is no agreement), insofar as it belongs to the heavenly bodies. III. It must also be counted a discipline distinct from physiology: for the mode of consideration, or, as they say, the formal aspect, distinguishes the discipline from the material subject. For physics is indeed concerned with heaven, but insofar as it is a natural body; astronomy, however, considers that same heaven according to the aspect of motion, and to explain this properly it chiefly calls in the aid of geometry [yet in such a way that arithmetic serves it too], so much so that astronomy may rightly be called geometry occupied with the heavenly bodies. IV. Yet it is a most difficult discipline, so that not without reason the apocryphal author of the Book of Wisdom, chapter 9, verses 15 and following, said: The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things. And we find it hard to conjecture what is on earth, and what is before us we find with labour: but who shall search out what is in the heavens? And who shall know your counsel, unless you give wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from on high? Hence this science needs many aids and other lesser disciplines, so that, being equipped with this borrowed help, it may reach its goal. V. Nor can it reach its goal without the help of five disciplines, namely: history, physics, optics, geometry, and arithmetic. First, indeed, history is needed, on account of observations of longitude, and of the length of days and years, and of the varying forms of the mind which have customarily varied among different peoples; likewise eclipses; indeed, on account of countless other things which it would be long to mention here. Second, physics is also required, since astronomical hypotheses, although they may be such as can exist only objectively, on the side of the intellect, and in the manner of beings of reason, nevertheless ought not to be altogether contrary to the nature of the heavens and the heavenly bodies themselves. Third, because of the manifold refractions which present themselves during observation, optics too must necessarily come into play. But fourth, above all, geometry provides the immediate work, through the excellent and, beyond what can be said, ingenious doctrine of triangles, both plane and spherical. To this, in the fifth place, arithmetic is added, which by the final operation of calculation puts the finishing touch on the discipline, to be brought to completion in this way. VI. Among the astronomers of old there has been much and long dispute whether hypotheses ought to be admitted in this most noble discipline: some altogether rejecting them, others only in part, and some fighting over them as fiercely as for altars and hearths. We will not mix ourselves into this conflict (for it is not necessary), but we say this: just as of old among the most ancient Egyptians and Greeks the science of the stars was handed down and treated without any hypotheses, so it is possible for us also to set out the same science without these aids of the intellect; yet, in our manner of apprehending, it is useful and fitting that those things concerning the motion of the heavenly bodies, which otherwise can be grasped by the mind only with the greatest difficulty, be explained through hypotheses; which nevertheless ought to be counted only as hypotheses. For just as among the logicians a conditional proposition, as such, posits nothing in being, so neither by astronomical hypotheses devised by the mind do any real affections attach to the heavenly bodies themselves. And if this is applied to eccentric orbs and epicycles, it will be clear how something may be conceived by us as anomalous and irregular, which yet is not such in reality. With these things premised, we shall advance the truth of astronomy against the Sceptics by two reasons only. First: that of which knowledge can be reached by certain and true means, of that a science too can be had. But the knowledge of the heavenly bodies and of their motions can be reached by certain and proportionate means. Therefore. The major premise is certain: for as the means are judged from the end, so conversely the end from its means; and if these are fitting and proportionate, and concur together, the end itself can be attained. This holds especially for intelligent beings, which properly act for the sake of an end: for when they know their end as good and suited to themselves, and likewise have the knowledge of the means as easy and proportionate, they are believed, when they act for the sake of the end, to be able also to attain it. The minor premise is evident from what has already been noted about the auxiliary disciplines, by whose aid astronomical science is both acquired and perfected: for by the same aids by which each discipline was discovered, it can also be further perfected; indeed, it is actually perfected by them. To these five disciplines, which we have already treated above, others add mechanics, occupied with the making of those instruments which astronomers customarily use in observing. But since those instruments must be arranged according to the laws of geometry and arithmetic, and also of optics, there was no need to mention mechanics separately. Second. That to the contemplation, and indeed to the deeper knowledge, of which God in Scripture invites all men, those things can be known and a science of them can be had, is certain: but to the knowledge of the heavenly bodies God in Scripture invites man. Therefore. No one at all can doubt the truth of the major premise. The minor premise can be confirmed from almost countless texts of Scripture, of which, to pluck a few and yet proceed in order: I. The stars, as most illustrious testimonies of the omnipotence, wisdom and goodness of God, are adorned with most august praises. Psalm 148, verse 3: Praise Jehovah, sun and moon; praise him, all you stars of light. Amos 5, verse 8: Seek him who made the Pleiades and Orion. Job 9, verse 9: Who made Arcturus, Orion and the Pleiades, and the stars of the chambers of the south. Psalm 33, verse 6: By the word of Jehovah the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth. Psalm 19, verse 2: The heavens declare the glory of God the strong, and the firmament shows the work of his hands. II. Hence God often, to demonstrate to the saints the infallible certainty of his promises, appeals to the stars and their motions as to most certain signs. To Abraham, whom Josephus testifies was an astronomer and learned mathematics from the Chaldeans, in order that the certainty of the multiplication of his seed might be confirmed and that he might believe against hope, he shows the multitude of the stars, Genesis 15. To Joseph, by dreams, he portrays the royal majesty by which he would preserve his father and brothers in time of famine, not only through the sheaves but also through the devout adoration of the sun, moon and eleven stars, Genesis 37. To King Hezekiah, about to grant him a prolonging of life for fifteen years, he sets forth the sun, as it were a sacrament, returning by the places already traversed, in the presence of the prophet himself, before those looking on at the dial of Ahaz, Isaiah 38. He places among the stars the herald who was to invite them to his only-begotten Son, incarnate and born, Matthew 2. That God of nature, crucified for the salvation of the human race, should die for the whole world, he willed to be made manifest by an unusual celestial phenomenon, an eclipse, Luke 23. And as supernatural appearances commend natural ones, so the former would not be known unless the latter were known first. Of the same kind is what God, about to declare his burning wrath and to describe the sad fates of the times, compares to the sad appearances of the stars. Thus it is to be read in Isaiah, chapter 13, verse 10: The stars of heaven and their constellations will not give forth their light: the sun will be dark from its rising, and the moon will not send out its bright light. And again in the same prophet, chapter 14, verse 12: How have you fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the dawn? Have you been cut down to the earth? What of the fact that Christ, the blessed Saviour of the world, is compared with the sun in that famous prophecy in Malachi, chapter 4, verse 2: The Sun of righteousness shall rise for you who fear my name. These illustrious testimonies of the prophets could in no way be understood, if there were no certainty of sidereal science. Nor does the Holy Spirit speak otherwise in the New Testament. To say nothing of other examples, what is better known than that, after Daniel chapter 12, the glory of the future age is described by the splendour of the sun, the moon, and the differing light of the stars? As for other examples, they may be seen in 1 Corinthians 15 and Matthew 13. III. But this above all must be noted: that God himself invites us, indeed calls us, to contemplate the heavens and all that is in them. Thus it is to be read in Isaiah 40, verse 26: Lift up your eyes on high and see who created these things, bringing out their host by number. But if astronomical science were altogether vain, and had no certainty in it, then not only would man be invited in vain to contemplate what is, as it were, a thing he cannot perceive; but also (let the remark be pardoned!) God would seem to make sport of man, proposing the heavens and the heavenly host not only as an example of divine omnipotence, but also comparing the most weighty matters with them: for no comparison, however apt, drawn between things unknown, indeed not comprehensible by man, can be understood in any way. This was very well known to that great Prophet, Christ Jesus, who, while he dwelt in this world, in teaching simple people, as often with many parables and similitudes, so took almost all of these from common and everyday things, because those with whom he had to do would understand them most accurately and have them most thoroughly explored. Besides what I have already noted in advance, the following three points are to be carefully marked as sources. I. Astronomy is not called a science because it has perfect knowledge of all things pertaining to heaven and the heavenly bodies, but only of some: since it is certain that a science is to be judged not so much extensively as intensively, and by its formal aspect, even though, on our side, it does not extend to all the things that belong to its object. Worthy of note are the words of Zabarella in his book On the Nature of the Heavens, chapter 1: Although, he says, the nature of the heavenly body is so hidden from us, that even the highest Aristotle himself was able to approach it only by denying the conditions of things beneath the moon: yet its excellence and nobility are such that even a slight and imperfect knowledge of it is more desirable than the exact and perfect knowledge of other, lesser things. II. Granted that diverse hypotheses have been received among the astronomers, and that often, over them, their patrons have contended even to quarrels; nothing thereby detracts from the certainty of the discipline itself, considered in itself and according to its own nature: for although it is certain that these hypotheses are more consonant with physical truth than those, yet they ought not to be judged precisely by reason of this truth, since they can exist only in the manner of beings of reason and notional hypotheses. Hence we see, for example, that eclipses of either heavenly body, and the other phenomena that recur and are customarily noted in the heavens at fixed times, can be predicted equally by the Ptolemaic hypotheses as by the Pythagorean or Copernican ones, with the help of tables constructed according to their respective hypotheses. III. As we have already distinguished astronomy from astrology, that is, the genethliacal or judicial discipline, so astronomy must in no way be judged by that.

units.la: CAPUT DUODECIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWELVE.

units.la: Asseritur Musica, pariterque vindicatur à Sexti Empirici objectionibus.
units.tr: Music is affirmed, and likewise defended against the objections of Sextus Empiricus.

units.la: ASTrologia, non inconvenienter à Sexto prostituta, uti à nobis fuit deposita; ita capitè superiori videmur convenienter Astronomiam, cæterum ab Astrologia distinctam, asseruisse adversus suos ofores: quâ asserta cum redeamus ad lineas ab ipso Sexto ductas & præformatas, proxime Musicam, disciplinam antiquam, atque jam olim à maximis viris excultam, considerate simulque in gradu, quem jàm obtinet, tutari debemus. Non summinus vero Musicam late, ut sæpe fit, & quatenus complectitur universum disciplinarum orbem; sed strictè, quatenus est icientia considerans sonos, omniaque, quæ ad illos pertinent; sic tamen ut non simpliciter ipsi hi soni considerentur, sed quatenus, ut Græci Magistri loquuntur, Rhythmorum rationem habent, hoc est, illi ipsi soni auritum rationisque judicio numerantur & mensurantur. Sic, ut non inconvenienter ipsa Musica vocari queat, Arithmetica sonans, sive Arithmetica in sonis occupata; quo sensu quoque vera propriaque subalternationé ipsi Arithmeticæ subalternata censeri solet. Iam olim duplicem hanc ipsam Musicam constituerunt Canonicam, atque Mathematicam. Canonica quę subnixa putabatur sensuum judicio, non quidem à Canone, instrumento sic dicto, nomen habet; verum à rectitudine, quod ratioid quod rectum est, inveniat utendo canonibus. Mathematica autem eatenus hæc ipsa Musica censebatur, quatenus non tam sensuum judiciumι, quam rectitudinem rationis speculationisque pro fundamento habebat. Amplius, tres Musicę partes solent constitui: Harmonica, Rhythmica, & Metrica. Harmonica in sonis expendit acutum & grave: rhythmica, celeritatem & tarditatem: metrica, longitudinem & brevitatem. Prima occupatur circa melodiam, altera circa rhythmum, & tertia circa metrum atque poëmata. Quibus præmissis, pro asserenda Musica tanquam scientia, primitus utor communi argumento, quod jam antea ratione aliarum quoque disciplinarum adhibui, sic argumentando: Quæ apta sunt per consuetudinem quadantenus fieri, in subjecto capaci disciplinæ per artem supervenientem corrigi, perfectiusque fieri possunt. Sed per consuetudinem quadantenus sumus Musici. Ergo. Circa Majorem propositionem, jam antea ex parte consideratam atque probatam, ne plura dicam, suffecerit adduxisse duntaxat, authoritatem Philosophi lib. 1. Rhetor, cap. 1, sic loquentis: Vulgo igitur alij quidem hæc temere præstant, alij autem propter consuetudinem, ex habitu. Quando igitur utroque modo id evenit, constat, fieri posse, ut hæc ad certam viam rationemque redigantur. Quid e-
units.tr: Astrology, which Sextus has not unfittingly lumped together with astronomy, has been set aside as we set it aside. In the previous chapter we seem to have rightly defended astronomy, as distinct from astrology, against its opponents. With that defence made, let us return to the lines drawn and laid out by Sextus himself. Next we must consider music, an ancient discipline already cultivated long ago by the greatest men, and we must maintain it in the position it now holds. I do not take music broadly, as is often done, as embracing the whole circle of the disciplines. I take it strictly, as a science that considers sounds and everything that pertains to them. Yet sounds are not considered simply in themselves, but insofar as, as the Greek masters put it, they have the character of rhythm; that is, those very sounds are numbered and measured by the judgement of the ear and of reason. So music may not unfittingly be called sounding arithmetic, or arithmetic occupied with sounds. In this sense it is also commonly regarded as a true and proper subalternate science, subordinated to arithmetic. Long ago this music was divided into two kinds, canonical and mathematical. Canonical music, which was thought to rest on the judgement of the senses, takes its name not from the canon, the so-called instrument, but from rectitude, because it finds what is right by using rules. Mathematical music was judged to be music insofar as it took as its foundation not so much the judgement of the senses as the rectitude of reason and speculation. Further, three parts of music are usually set out: harmonic, rhythmic and metric. Harmonic weighs the high and the low in sounds; rhythmic, speed and slowness; metric, length and shortness. The first is concerned with melody, the second with rhythm, and the third with metre and poems. With these things premised, in order to assert music as a science, I first use a common argument, which I have already used before in the case of other disciplines, arguing thus: what can to some extent be done by habit can, in a subject capable of it, be corrected and made more perfect by an art that supervenes. But we are, to some extent, musicians by habit. Therefore... As for the major premise, which I have already considered in part and proved, I will not say more here. It will suffice to adduce only the authority of the Philosopher, in the first book of the Rhetoric, chapter 1, speaking thus: Commonly, then, some people do these things rashly, and others from habit. When both happen in both ways, it is clear that these things can be reduced to a certain path and method. What the

units.la: B b enim enim sit caussa, cur & qui consuetudine, & qui cassu id faciunt, id quod volunt consequantur, videri ac perspici potest. Id autem jam omnes artis opus esse fateantur. Quo respiciens Quintilianus lib. 2. Orat. Inst. dixit: Qua in re alius se inartificialiter, alius artificialiter gerat, in ea esse artem fatendum. Minor vero propositio adeo certa, ut de eadem ambigere non liceat. II. Quum ipsa Scriptura testetur, quosdam Musicæ peritos fuisse, illiusque artis peritia censos æs- timatosque fuisse, haut quaquam dubitare licet, an Musica artis rationem habeat. Ut enim abstractum est forma concreti, ita illud in ipso concreto, si hoc existat, existere creditur. De Minore vero dubitare haut quaquam licet. alia in Scriptura testimonia ne adferam 1. Samuel. cap. 16. Saul à Spiritu melancholico correptus, jubet pro se quæri aliquem scientem pulsare citharam, & postquam famuli Saulis diligentiam in quærendo adhibuissent, tandem invenerunt, Davidem filium Iischai Beth-lechemitæ, cui & hoc testimonium perhibetur, quod sciverit citharam pulsare. III. Quum Scriptura ipsa probet differentiam Musicæ artificialis, qua talis, eam ipsam hactenus probandam, nec omnis certitudinis suspectandam esse, certum est. Consequentiæ ratio apud eos ipsos, qui Scripturæ quicquam modo tribuunt, adeo certa est, ut neutiquam hic dubitare liceat. Assumptio manifesto probatur ex ijs, quae habet Apostolus 1. Cor. 14. v. 7. 8. Anima expertia, quae sonum edunt, & tibia, & cithara, nisi distinctionem sonis dederint, quomodo cognoscetur quod tibia canitur, aut cithara? Etenim si incertum sonum tuba dederit, quis apparabitur ad bellum? Si enim instrumentis Musicis, secundum ipsum Apostoli judicium, aliquid tribuendum est, quatenus diversimode tractantur; nae ipsi arti quoque, secundum quam haec instrumenta usurpantur, aliquid deferri debet. Siquidem secundum differentias jam propositas tractari non possunt, nisi quatenus ipsa ars artifici prescribit rationem, secundum quam diversimode tractari tum possunt, tum debent. IV. Nec hoc argumentum insuper habere convenit: Si ipse Spiritus Sanctus filios insuper Dei, electosque commendat, quod invenerint instrumenta Musica: pariter censendum per ipsum Sp. sanctum omnis veritatis authorem commendari quoque ipsam artem Musicam. Consequentie ratio cera: nam quorsum distincte commendarentur instrumenta Musica, nisi ars eorum directrix adesset? ut enim ipsa sunt artis opus, ita nemo ijsdem, ratione finis, ad quem definita sunt, uti frui poterit, nisi pariter supponat ars Musica, sufficiens ordinationi convenienconvenienti usu, tum proprij, tum debiti ipsis instrumentis Musicis? Deveniendo ad antecedens, illud ratione filiorum Scripturæ in Spiritus sancti monumentis liquido proponitur. Ne longius enim abeamus, an non ratione certorum instrumentorum, laudatur David, non minus prophetica authoritate, quam regia dignitate insignis, quod ad celebrandum Iehovam, quædam instrumenta Musica contulerit. 2. Chron. 7. & 5. juncto Amos. 6. v. 3. unde etiam hæc ipsa instrumenta, usui tam sacro destinata, exprese vocantur instrumenta Davidis, 2. Chro. 29. v. 26. & instrumenta Musica Davidis, Nehem. 12. v. 36. Sed sepositæ Scriptura, & argumentis ex Scriptura desumptis, quæ nequaquam universalia aut censeri possunt aut cupimus, contra Scepticos pro vindicanda Musica hoc argumentum maximi momenti esse censemus: Quicquid ab omnibus gentibus, ut ut barbaris, ad modum artis exercetur, illud communi quasi omnium hominum suffragio artis rationem habere putandum est. Sed hoc verum de Musica. Major propositio adeo certa est, ut antea cognoverimus ipsum Sextum Empiricum argumentantem pro evertenda arte Rhetorica, ex eo, quod multæ gentes, aut, ut ipse falso persuasum cupiebat, plerque eidem bellum indixerint, eamque excludere meditatæ fuerint. Quæ consequentia pro evertenda disciplina utilissima, si ex mente quasi Sceptici valere debuerit; omnino multo magis æquum est, ut communis ferme gentium consensus conspiret pro asserenda disciplina maximi usus in universa hominum societate. Minor propositio æque certa, si non certior: ne enim discurram per gentes maxime barbaras, an non ipsi Brasiliani, velut alteri Aborigenes, & inter eos Anthropophagi definita sua tripudia habent, institui solita ad modulum qua instrumentorum Musicorum, qua vocis assę, in se quidem incondite, ceterum ex utentium sensuum vere artificiosæ? Pro fontibus solutorijs sequentes obiectiones serviant. 1. Frustra est Sextus Empiricus, quando ex primis suis principiis laborat evertere Musicam; negando tum esse vocem, tum esse animam, quę actum sentiendi edere possit: quamvis enim haut in proclivi sit dicere, quænam definite qua soni, qua vocis ipsius ratio sit: non tamen inde colligere licet, vocem nihil esse; quum animadvertamus ipsas pecudes à sonis tum inarticulatis, quos ipsi edunt, tum etiam ab ipsis nostris vocibus diversimode affici. quod sane non contingeret, si vox purum putum nihil esset. Nec minus frustra est idem Sextus, quando sic arguit: Si nceft aanima, nec non sunt sensus, ij enim sunt ejus partes, nam eo ipso, quod Scepticus laborat omnia ratiocinando evertere, agnoscere debet se animam habere à corpore distinctam: dato enim revera falsa esse omnia, quae sensibus percipit, atque actu eum circa omnes res corporeas decipi: nihilominus tamen certum ei manet, aut se decipi circa res illas, aut circa illas dubitare, aut saltem se exist imare aut decipi, aut dubitare; sed haec perceptio sive perceptionis, sive dubitationis; sive etiam quasi deceptionis, aut dubitationis, est actus animae. Si ergo animam, & quidem ratiocinativam volens nolens quasi admittere debet Scepticus, ut ex antecedentibus jam patet, adest dux & rector sensuum, qui eos exorbitantes corrigere ordinem redigere queat. II. Aeque frustra est Sextus, quando ex eo evertere laborat Musicam, quod nulli sint rhythmi; quos probat rejiciendos esse inde, quod nullum sit tempus, nec ulla realitas ipsi tempori attribui queat: Rhythmus vero sit compositio quaedam ex pedibus. Pes autem id sit, quod constat ex elevatione & positura. Elevatio autem & positura considerentur in quantitate temporum, quorum aliqua tempora contineat positura, aliqua elevatio: quae omnia necessum sit subverti & concidere negato tempore. quod ipsum ideo negat concedendum, quod constet ex illis quae esse esse non possunt. Sed cum mensura temporis à parte rei sit, Deusque Opt. Max. duo luminaria in cœli expanso collocaverit, ut mensurando tempori servirent; ipsumque tempus proprie atque accurate loquendo [loqui sic fas sit] nihil aliud sit quam partes motus numerabiles, maxime secundum motum primi mobilis, uti loquuntur, quod [licet quilibet motus continuus habeat suum tempus] adhiberi solet tanquam mensura aliorum motuum, utpote notissima, brevissima, ac maxime uniformis; neutiquam ens rationis censeri potest. nec obstat hic Aristoteles qui lib.4.Phys.t, 131. dicit, quod si non daretur intellectus habilis ad numerandum, non fore numerum, ac proinde quoque non fore tempus: siquidem hoc intelligi debet de tempore, prout eodem, actu atque reipsa utimur, tanquam externa mensura motus & quietis, neutiquam vero de ipsa temporis essentia, quæ est numnerabilitas ab intellectu independens. Nec tempori perit sua realitas, quod illius partes separatim non existant: siquidem est ex ordine eorum entium, quæ successiva, sive fluentia vocantur: quorum hæc ratio est, quod non existant cum omnibus suis partibus simul, sed quod eorum partes in iugi sive perpetua successione sint, sic ut qnędam præcedant, aliæ sequantur. III. Quod quidam inveniantur, quos non afficiat Musica, arti nequicquam derogare potest: cum hi, velut qui Timones, hominum simulacra potius, quam homines censeri debeant. Quanta enim cognatio inter hominis naturam, atque cantum intercedat, graphice admodum ostendit Chrysostomus, cujus proinde quoque verba ex homil. in Psal. 41. hic repræsento: Nostra certe natura usque adeo delectatur canticis, & carminibus, & tantam cum eis habet necessitudinem & convenientiam; ut vel infantes ab uberibus pendentes, si fleant, & afflictantur, ea ratione sopiantur. Nutrices quidem certe, quæ eos gestant in ulnis, sæpe abeuntes & redeuntes, & quædam puerilia eis carmina decantantes, supercilia eorum ita sopiunt. Quocirca viatores meridie agentes jugalia animalia, hoc faciunt canentes, itineris molestiam illis consolantes. Nec solum viatores; sed etiam agricolæ uvas in torculari calcantes, vindemiantes, & vites colentes, & quodcunque aliud opus facientes, sæpe cantant. Nautæ etiam remos impellentes, hoc faciunt. Iam vero mulieres texentes, & confusa stamina radio discernentes; sæpe quidem & per se singulæ, sæpe autem etiam omnes concorditer unam quandam melodiam concinunt. Hoc autem faciunt & mulieres, & viatores, & agricolæ, & nautæ, qui ex opere faciendo suscipitur, laborem cantu consolari volentes; eo, quod anima, si carmen & canticum audierit, molesta & difficilia sit facilius toleratura. Huc usque Chrysostomus.
units.tr: For For what is the cause why both those who act by custom and those who act by chance attain what they want can be seen and understood. Yet all men admit this is a matter of art. Quintilian, in the second book of the Institutio Oratoria, had this in view when he said: "In whatever matter one man acts without art and another with art, we must admit that art is present in that matter." The minor premise is so certain that it is not permissible to doubt it. II. Since Scripture itself witnesses that some were skilled in music and were esteemed and valued for their skill in that art, we may by no means doubt whether music has the nature of an art. For just as the abstract is the form of the concrete, so the abstract is believed to exist in the concrete when the concrete exists. Nor may we doubt the minor premise at all. Not to cite other testimonies of Scripture: in 1 Samuel 16, Saul, seized by a melancholy spirit, orders that someone who knows how to play the harp be sought for him. After Saul's servants had applied diligence in the search, at last they found David, son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, to whom this testimony is also given, that he knew how to play the harp. III. Since Scripture itself proves the difference between artistic music, as such, it is certain that this must be proved so far, and must not be suspected of any certainty. The force of the inference is so certain even among those who ascribe anything at all to Scripture that it is not permissible to doubt it here. The assumption is plainly proved from what the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 14:7–8: "Even things without life that give sound, whether flute or harp, unless they give a distinction in the sounds, how will it be known what is played on the flute or the harp? For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle?" For if, by the Apostle's own judgement, something must be ascribed to musical instruments, insofar as they are handled in different ways, then something must also be granted to the art itself, according to which these instruments are used. For they cannot be handled according to the differences just stated, except insofar as the art itself prescribes the rule according to which they can and must be handled in different ways. IV. Nor is it proper to dismiss this argument: if the Holy Spirit himself commends to the sons of God and the elect that they have found musical instruments, then likewise it must be judged that the Holy Spirit, the author of all truth, commends also the art of music itself. The force of the inference is plain: for why would musical instruments be distinctly commended, unless their directing art were present? For just as they are the work of art, so no one, with regard to the end for which they are designed, will be able to use and enjoy them unless the art of music likewise supplies a suitable use, both proper and due, for the musical instruments themselves. Coming to the antecedent, it is clearly set forth in the records of the Holy Spirit by the testimony of Scripture. For, not to go too far afield, is not David praised, distinguished no less by prophetic authority than by royal dignity, because he provided certain musical instruments for celebrating Jehovah? See 2 Chronicles 7 and 5, joined with Amos 6:3, whence these very instruments, destined for so sacred a use, are expressly called the instruments of David (2 Chronicles 29:26) and the musical instruments of David (Nehemiah 12:36). But, setting aside Scripture and arguments drawn from Scripture, which cannot be regarded or desired as universal, we think this argument, against the Sceptics, to be of the greatest weight in vindicating music: whatever is practised according to the manner of an art by all nations, however barbarous, must be thought to have the nature of an art by the common, as it were, suffrage of all men. But this is true of music. The major premise is so certain that we have already seen Sextus Empiricus himself arguing for the overthrow of the art of rhetoric from the fact that many nations, or, as he wrongly wished to be persuaded, most of them, had declared war on it and had planned to exclude it. If this inference ought to hold, as it were in the mind of a Sceptic, for overturning a most useful discipline, then it is altogether much more fair that the common consent of nearly all nations should agree in asserting a discipline of the greatest use in the whole society of men. The minor premise is no less certain, if not more certain: for not to run through the most barbarous nations, do not the Brazilians themselves, like another set of aborigines, and among them the cannibals, have their set dances, customarily arranged to a measure, either of musical instruments or of voice, crude in themselves but truly artful in the sense of those who use them? In support of the solution, let the following objections serve. 1. Sextus Empiricus labours in vain when from his first principles he tries to overthrow music, denying both that there is voice and that there is a soul able to produce the act of sensing. For although it is not easy to say what the precise nature of sound, or of voice itself, is, yet it does not follow from this that voice is nothing; since we observe that the beasts themselves are affected in different ways by the inarticulate sounds which they make, and also by our own voices. This would certainly not happen if voice were pure nothing. Nor is the same Sextus any less in vain when he argues thus: "If there is no soul, neither are there senses, for these are its parts." For by the very fact that the Sceptic labours to overturn everything by reasoning, he must acknowledge that he has a soul distinct from the body. For even granting that everything which he perceives by the senses is in truth false, and that he is in fact deceived about all bodily things, nevertheless it remains certain to him either that he is deceived about those things, or that he doubts about them, or at least that he thinks himself either deceived or in doubt; but this perception, whether of perception or of doubt, or also of what is as it were deception or doubt, is an act of the soul. If therefore the Sceptic, willy-nilly, must admit a soul, and indeed a rational soul, as is now clear from what has gone before, there is present a leader and ruler of the senses, who can correct them when they go astray and bring them back into order. II. Sextus is equally in vain when he tries to overturn music from the fact that there are no rhythms, which he proves must be rejected because there is no time, and no reality can be attributed to time itself: "Rhythm is a certain composition of feet. A foot, however, is that which consists of elevation and position. Elevation and position are considered in the quantity of times, of which some times are contained in position, some in elevation; all of which must be overturned and collapse if time is denied. Time itself is denied to be granted only because it consists of things which cannot be." But since the measure of time is in the nature of things, and the best and greatest God has placed two lights in the expanse of heaven so that they might serve to measure time, and since time itself, properly and strictly speaking ([if it is permitted to speak so]), is nothing other than the countable parts of motion, chiefly according to the motion of the first mover, as they say, which [though every continuous motion has its own time] is customarily employed as the measure of other motions, as being most well known, most brief, and most uniform, it cannot by any means be regarded as a being of reason. Nor does Aristotle, who says in the fourth book of the Physics, chapter 14 (219b), that if there were no intellect able to count, there would be no number, and consequently no time, stand in the way: for this must be understood of time insofar as we actually and in fact use it as the external measure of motion and rest, and by no means of the very essence of time, which is countability independent of the intellect. Nor does time lose its reality because its parts do not exist separately: for it belongs to the order of those beings which are called successive or flowing, whose nature is that they do not exist all at once with all their parts, but that their parts are in a continual or perpetual succession, so that some precede and others follow. III. The fact that some are found whom music does not move cannot in vain detract from the art: since such people, like Timon, ought to be regarded as the images of men rather than men. How great a kinship lies between human nature and song, Chrysostom shows vividly; so I here present his words from the homily on Psalm 41: "Our nature certainly delights so much in songs and poems, and has such kinship and affinity with them, that even infants hanging from the breast, if they cry and are distressed, are lulled to sleep by this means. Nurses, who carry them in their arms, often, as they go and come, sing some childish songs to them, and so lull their eyelids to sleep. For this reason travellers at noon, driving yoked animals, do this, singing and consoling the animals in the weariness of the journey. Nor only travellers, but also farmers treading grapes in the wine-press, gathering the vintage, tending the vines, and doing whatever other work, often sing. Sailors too do this as they drive their oars. Moreover, women weaving and separating the tangled threads with the spindle, often indeed each by herself, often too all together in harmony, sing one melody. And women, travellers, farmers, and sailors do this, all of them wishing to console with song the labour undertaken in doing their work; because the soul, if it has heard a poem and a song, will bear what is troublesome and difficult more easily." Thus far Chrysostom.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM TERTIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER THIRTEEN.

units.la: Logicæ sive Dialecticæ certitudo & existima- tio afferuntur; simulque propositis variis classibus responsoriis Sexti argumentis occurritur.
units.tr: The certainty and the worth of logic or dialectic are set out, and at the same time the various arguments of Sextus are met by a series of replies.

units.la: NEà lineis abeamus, quæ nobis præeunte Sexto ductæ sunt, & quibus, ordinis ratione habita, diximus nos insistere velle; proxime agere debemus de Logica sive Dialectica, cui sic infestus est Sextus, ut prolixe admodum occupetur in colligendis omnis generis argumentis, sufficientibus quasi ad deturbandam de gradu suo disciplinam nobilissimam: quamvis interim lib. 1. adversus Logicos, eam antiquam & a priscis Philosophis excultam esse fateatur. Ne vero occupemur circa nomen, quod alias molestias facessere solet, & de quo multa scrupulose quæruntur, adductis variis qua Aristotelis, qua Platonis locis; Logicam & Dialecticam pro una eademque disciplina censebimus, atque à nobis agnoscetur talis sive ars sive scientia [de genere proprio & adæquato nolumus hic multum laborare] quæ suggerendo certa instrumenta, sic per ea operationes intellectus nostri dirigit, ne cespitent in rerum cognitioue: ipsa quidem nullius distinctæ rei cognitionem proponit, cæterum quomodo omnia distincte & citra errorem ullum cognoscere queamus, ostendit, & quod caput est, ut sciamus nos quid scire operam dat. Unde non incommode Plato lib. 2. de Rep. dicit: Dialectica est, quæ mentis oculum barbarico luto obrutum, sursum vehit, ne ignorantia cæno mersus jaceat. hanc ut præ cæteris excoluerunt Stoici, ita negligentius Epicurus cum suis sectatoribus. Unde sic Hieronymus adversus Rufinum: Et quoniam Stoici dialecticam sibi vindicant, & tu hujus scientiæ deliramenta contemnis, in hac parte Epicureus es, nec quaris quomodo, sed quid loquaris. Stoici vero eandem voluerunt præ omnibus aliis disciplinis addisci, & tractari. quo cum faciat eximius omnino locus Arriani lib. 1. Disssert. Epicteti cap. 18. non pigebit eum in vestibulo hujus capitis integrum exhibere. Ita igitur ille: Nobis proponitur Logica, quemadmodum ante dimensionem frumentorum proponimus cognitionem mensuræ. Quod si ergo prius exploratum de modio non habuerimus, aut si libra cognita prius non fuerit, quæ aut cujusmodi sit, qui mensurare aut ponderare poterimus? Itaque in Logica arte etiam examen est aliarum rationum, quo reliquas nimirum addiscimus. Huic si operam non dederimus, exquisiteque eam non cognoverimus, num poterit fieri, ut res ullas alias accurate cognoscamus? At quomodo fieri istud potest? Certe potest: Etenim modius lignum est; & nullo fructu gratum: veruntamen nihilominus mensurat frumenta. Sic Logica præcepta fructum exhibent nullum, ex quibus nunc consider-abimus. Quod si istud etiam quispiam dederit, contenti sane erimus, nempe hæc esse quibus discernantur & dijudicentur reliqua, & ut sic loquar, mensurantia & ordinantia. Hactenus ille. Atque initio quidem adversus Scepticos hoc argumentum valere debet plurimum: Secundum quod ipse Scepricus censetur, & secundum quod semetipsum quoque censet, atque ab aliis distinctus haberi vult Philosophus, illud dari neutiquam vel ipse Scepticus negare potest: Atqui secundum solam facultatem ratiocinativam censeri potest Scepticus, imo semetipsum quoque censet: Ergo Scepticus volens nolens hanc ipsam facultatem, sive Dialecticam agnoscere debet. De consequentia nullus mortalium unquam, nedum ipse Scepticus unquam dubitaverit. Minor æque certa est. nam in quo consistit prima Pyrrhonismi, sive Scepticæ Philosophiæ ratio? in quo, nisi in hoc, quod omnium aliorum Philosophorum dogmata possit evertere: at quomodo ea ipsa evertit? solius dialecticæ præsidio: per hanc quippe ut aliorum dogmata inter se comparare scit; ita ejusdem quoque subsidio ad eadem subvertenda contendit. Quomodo vero Pyrrhonico ratiocinio, quod Scepticismi cultor certum esse contendit, hic sua ratio constiterit? Si contendat Scepticus nihil in Dialectica esse certi, necessum pariter est, fateatur nullas illationes Scepticorum adversus Dogmaticos esse certas, & consequenter, se, cum omnibus suis sociis insignem nugatorem esse, & indignum vel hominis titulo. Secundo si quemcunque hominem, Scepticum quoque, quotidiana experientia doceat, quod si rationem, qua ut homo gaudet, sæpius atque diligentius intenderit, posset ea ipsa in similibus felicius uti: nec agnosci quoque ars debet, quæ dirigat ipsam rationem eo modo, ne in suo ratiocinio fallatur: Atqui verum prius: Ergo. Connexio ut præcedentibus capitibus, in similibus argumentis accurate fuit examinata & expensa; ita non minus per experientiam ars producitur, quam ea ipsa possibilitatem artis manifesto manifesto ratiocinio arguit: quandoquidem experientia multiplex & ordinata nihil aliud quam ars est: quæ ars ad naturam collata, eam ipsam perficit; juxta illud, quod Aristoteles habet lib. 7. Polit. cap. 17. Omnis ars & doctrina natura defectum supplere vult. Minor propositio pariter evidens est, quandoquidem nullus, qui modo homo, invenitur, qui non hoc ipsum in semetipso experiri queat. Tertio non potest ulla cuicunque disciplinæ certitudo tribui, nisi ratio sciat dijudicare sua ratiocinia, noritque; se bene actus rationis edere. Sed, quænam disciplina hæc docet præter Dialecticam? de qua sic cum ratione Augustinus lib. de Ordine: Quando ergo ratio ad fabricanda transfiret, nisi sua ipsius machinamenta distingueret, notaret, dignosceret, proderetque ipsam disciplinam disciplinarum, quam Dialecticam vocant? hæc docet docere, hæc docet discere. Quicunque ergo Dialecticam admittere nolunt, eamque exuunt omni sua certitudine, quid aliud faciunt, quam ut negent menti constare posse de suo ratiocinio. Quarto sic argumentari licet: Si nulla aut datur Logica habitualis, aut si ea fallax & incerta est; Nulla quoque dabitur Logica naturalis. Sed falsum consequens, Ergo etiam antecedens. Logicam naturalem nemo negare potest; nam si eam negare liceat, pariter
units.tr: Let us now leave the lines that Sextus led us along and that we said we wished to follow in order. Next we must treat of Logic, or Dialectic, which Sextus so attacks that he spends a long time gathering arguments of every kind, enough, as it were, to dislodge this most noble discipline from its rank, although in book 1 Against the Logicians he admits that it is ancient and was cultivated by the early philosophers. But lest we be occupied with the name, which usually causes other troubles and about which many scrupulous questions are raised, citing various passages of both Aristotle and Plato, we shall regard Logic and Dialectic as one and the same discipline. We shall recognise as such an art or science [we do not wish to labour here over its proper and adequate genus] which, by supplying certain instruments, directs the operations of our intellect so that they do not stumble in the knowledge of things. It does not itself propose the knowledge of any particular thing, but it shows how we can know all things distinctly and without any error, and, what is the chief point, that we know what we are doing. Hence Plato in book 2 of the Republic not inappropriately says: Dialectic is that which lifts the eye of the mind, buried in barbarian mud, upward, lest it lie sunk in the mire of ignorance. The Stoics cultivated this discipline above all others, whereas Epicurus and his followers were more negligent of it. Hence Jerome against Rufinus: And since the Stoics claim dialectic for themselves, and you despise the follies of this science, in this respect you are an Epicurean, and you ask not how but what you speak. The Stoics wished this discipline to be learned and practised before all others. An outstanding passage of Arrian, book 1 of the Discourses of Epictetus, chapter 18, bears on this, and I shall not hesitate to set out the whole of it at the threshold of this chapter. Thus he: Logic is set before us just as, before measuring grain, we set before ourselves the knowledge of the measure. If therefore we have not first examined the bushel, or if the balance has not first been known, what it is and of what kind, how shall we be able to measure or weigh? So in the art of Logic there is also an examination of other reasons, by which we learn the rest. If we have not devoted effort to this and have not known it exactly, can it happen that we know any other things accurately? But how can that happen? Surely it can: for the bushel is wood and pleasing by no fruit, yet nevertheless it measures grain. So the precepts of Logic yield no fruit, and we shall now consider them in that light. But if someone will also grant this, we shall be content indeed, namely that these are the things by which the rest are discerned and judged and, so to speak, measured and ordered. Thus far he. And at the outset this argument ought to count for a great deal against the Sceptics. The Sceptic himself is reckoned, and reckons himself, a philosopher distinct from others, and wishes to be so held. That this is so the Sceptic himself can by no means deny. But the Sceptic can be reckoned so only by the faculty of reasoning alone, and indeed he reckons himself so. Therefore the Sceptic, willy-nilly, must acknowledge this very faculty, that is, Dialectic. No mortal has ever doubted the consequence, much less the Sceptic himself. The minor is equally certain. For in what does the first ground of Pyrrhonism, or of the Sceptical philosophy, consist? In nothing but this, that it can overturn the doctrines of all other philosophers. But how does it overturn them? Solely by the aid of dialectic. For just as it knows how to compare the doctrines of others with one another, so it strives by the same aid to subvert them. But how will this reasoning of the Sceptic, which the cultivator of Scepticism insists is certain, hold good by Pyrrhonian reasoning? If the Sceptic should contend that there is nothing certain in Dialectic, he must equally admit that no inferences of the Sceptics against the Dogmatists are certain, and consequently that he, with all his fellows, is a notable trifler, unworthy even of the name of man. Secondly, daily experience teaches any man, even a Sceptic, that if he were to direct the reason which as a man he enjoys more often and more diligently, he could use it more successfully in similar matters. Nor, indeed, ought that art to be unacknowledged which directs reason itself so that it is not deceived in its reasoning. But the former is true; therefore so is the latter. As in the preceding chapters the connection was carefully examined and weighed in similar arguments, so art is produced no less through experience, which itself manifestly proves by sound reasoning the possibility of art. For experience, when manifold and ordered, is nothing other than art, and art, when brought to nature, perfects it, according to that saying which Aristotle has in book 7 of the Politics, chapter 17: Every art and doctrine wishes to supply the defect of nature. The minor premise is equally evident, since there is no one who, being a man at all, cannot experience this in himself. Thirdly, no certainty can be granted to any discipline unless reason knows how to judge its own reasonings, and knows that it can perform the acts of reason well. But what discipline teaches this besides Dialectic? Of it Augustine rightly says in his book On Order: When therefore reason should pass over to constructing things, unless it were to distinguish, note and recognise its own machinery, and to put forward the discipline of disciplines which they call Dialectic? This teaches teaching, this teaches learning. Therefore whoever are unwilling to admit Dialectic, and strip it of all its certainty, do nothing else than deny that the mind can be assured about its own reasoning. Fourthly, the argument may be put thus: if either there is no habitual Logic, or if it is deceptive and uncertain, then there will be no natural Logic either. But the consequent is false; therefore the antecedent too. No one can deny natural Logic; for if that could be denied, it would equally be lawful to deny that man is a rational animal. But natural Logic is overthrown by the very fact that artificial Logic is overthrown.

units.la: Text is in roman with italic passages as printed. ter negare licebit hominem esse animal ratione praeditum. Sed Logica naturalis evertitur eo ipso, dum evertitur Logica artificialis. ut enim Logica naturalis nihil aliud est, quam naturalis potentia, ratione utendi, quae respectu actuum, quos edit, indifferenter sese habere potest, ita perfici potest per habitum, actus ea ratione determinantem, ut ab omni omnino errore sint immunes. Habitus vero hic, dum tali potentiae accidit atque supervenit, non potest no quoq; certus esse, quadoquidem neque naturali potetiae adversatur, neq; eam falli ratione actuum suorum patitur. quod tum contingit quando ipse supervenit habitus, sua praecepta ordinans, secundum illud, quod in potentia naturali respectu actuum, quos edit, rectum est, eoque modo illud, quod obliquum atque vitiosum est, castigans. Quod speciatim in Logica, quae potentiae ratiocinativae medicina est, notare convenit: nam omnia praecepta, quae artificialis Logica proponit, ad Logicam naturalem velut normam exigi debent: sic, ut non possit non, haec ipsa Logica omnium suorum praeceptorum respectu eatenus esse certa, quatenus ad talem normam est exacta. Nec tamen haec ipsa norma, per se sola sufficere potest, quoniam non potest se semper commode applicare: quod cum procuretur à Logica artificiali, liquet quomodo naturalis & artificialis Logica inter se conspirent. Quinto, nec hoc argumentum insuper habendum: Si nulla datur Logica artificialis, hoc modo Logicæ naturali perficiendæ serviens, quælibet ratiocinatio erit admittenda, & quidlibet ex quolibet colligi poterit. Sed quisnam hoc dixerit? ne ipse quidem Scepticus, qui vult ratiocinio suo constare rationem, quod existimet se convenientissime per illud Dogmaticorum scita subvertere. Consequentia autem certa. Simili argumento alicubi adversus Erasistratum utitur Galenus, dicendo: Si quidlibet ex quolibet colligi potest, hæc quoque argumentatio admitti poterit: Nix est alba: Corvus est niger: Ergo Erasistratus est fatuus. Pro fontibus solutoriis subsequentia notentur. I. Neutiquam existimandum est, Dialecticam adeo petulantem esse, ut eidem omnia pro arbitrio liceant, speciatim veritatem quamcunque incrustare, quemadmodum cum Scepticis non uni hoc seculo persuasum est. II. Ut Dialecticus à Sophista distinctus debet manere, ita neque Dialectica in abstracto confiderata confundenda est cum eadem in concreto: Illa vero propterea errare non potest, quod rationem perpetuo habeat naturalis Logicæ, quod in ea sanum est, ac post lapsum integrum permansit, sibi vindicando, atque fecundum illud tanquam regulam omnia sua præcepta dirigendo. Atque inde, ut exemplum adferam, quarta figura, quam male Arabes quidam Galeno affingere instituerunt; eam ob caussam quoque rejicitur, quod adversetur progressui difcurfivo, ad quem naturalis Logica nos ducit. II. Vt jam antea in genere, pariterque in specie notavimus, abusum nequicquam derogare usui; ita fpeciatim hic observandum, Sophistarum varias altercationes, atque pruriginem de quocunque themate præsidio doctrinæ Topicæ disputandi in utramque partem, neutiquam præjudicium creare genuinæ Logicæ, de qua cum ratione sic Cicero, licet ab Academicis haut longe remotus, lib. 5. Tufc. Q. Per omnes partes sapientiæ manat & funditur, qua quum definit, genera dispertit, sequentia adjungit, perfecta concludit, vera & falsa dijudicat, differendi ratio & scientia. Ex qua cum summa utilitas existit ad res ponderandas, tum maxime ingenua delectatio, & digna sapiente. nec inconvenienter Hieronymus in Ezech. Vere quicquid in seculo perversorum dogmatum est, quicquid ad terrenam scientiam pertinet & putatur esse robustum, hoc dialectica arte subvertitur, & instar incendij in cineres favillasque dissolvitur, ut probetur esse nihili, quod putabatur esse fortissimum. Alia
units.tr: …for as natural Logic is nothing other than the natural power of using reason, which can stand indifferently with respect to the acts it puts forth, so it can be perfected by a habit that determines those acts by reason, so that they are wholly free from every error. This habit, when it attaches to and supervenes upon such a power, cannot itself be uncertain, since it neither opposes the natural power nor suffers it to be deceived in respect of its acts. This happens when the habit supervenes, ordering its precepts according to what is right in the natural power with respect to the acts it puts forth, and thereby correcting what is crooked and faulty. This is especially to be noted in Logic, which is the medicine of the reasoning power: for all the precepts that artificial Logic propounds must be brought to natural Logic as to a standard, so that this Logic cannot but be certain in respect of all its precepts, in so far as they are exact according to such a standard. Yet this standard alone cannot suffice, since it cannot always apply itself conveniently; and since this is provided for by artificial Logic, it is plain how natural and artificial Logic agree with each other. Fifthly, nor should this argument be disregarded: if there is no artificial Logic serving to perfect natural Logic in this way, then any reasoning whatever must be admitted, and anything whatever can be inferred from anything. But who would say this? Not even the Sceptic himself, who wishes his own reasoning to rest on reason, since he thinks he can most conveniently overturn the Dogmatists' tenets by it. And the consequence is certain. Galen uses a similar argument somewhere against Erasistratus, saying: If anything can be inferred from anything, this argument too may be admitted: Snow is white; the raven is black; therefore Erasistratus is a fool. As solutions to these arguments, the following should be noted. I. It is by no means to be thought that Dialectic is so wanton that everything is permitted to it at will, and especially that it may besmirch any truth whatever, as has been held by more than one of the Sceptics in this century. II. As the dialectician must remain distinct from the Sophist, so Dialectic considered in the abstract must not be confused with the same considered in the concrete. The former cannot err, precisely because it constantly keeps to the natural Logic, claiming for itself whatever in that Logic is sound and remained whole after the fall, and directing all its precepts by it as a rule. And hence, to give an example, the fourth figure, which certain Arabs wrongly tried to attribute to Galen, is rejected also for this reason, that it hinders the discursive progress to which natural Logic leads us. II. As we have already noted above in general, and likewise in particular, that abuse cannot take away from use, so here it must be specially observed that the various wranglings of the Sophists, and the itch to dispute on any theme in either direction with the aid of the doctrine of Topics, by no means prejudice genuine Logic. Of this Cicero rightly says, though he was by no means far removed from the Academics, in book 5 of the Tusculan Disputations: It flows and spreads through all parts of wisdom; when it defines, divides genera, adds consequences, concludes what is perfect, and judges the true and the false, it is the method and science of reasoning. From it there arises the greatest utility for weighing matters, and especially a noble delight, worthy of the wise. Nor is Jerome inappropriate on Ezekiel: Truly whatever there is of perverse doctrines in this age, whatever pertains to earthly learning and is thought to be strong, is overthrown by the art of dialectic, and dissolves like a fire into ashes and sparks, so that what was thought the most powerful is proved to be nothing. Another

units.la: III. Alia ratio Logicæ, alia reliquarum disci- plinarum est.
units.tr: III. Logic has a different method from the other disciplines.

units.la: Quum enim Logica tradat rationem atque modum alias scientiás addiscendi, reliquæ vero scientiæ hunc ipsum modum præsupponant, eodemque utantur: Logica sic aliisdisciplinis inservit, ut pariter quoque ipsa, pro præceptorum suorum traditione, convenientique explicatione, suis propriis instrumentis, scil. definitione, divisione, reliquisque utatur. quomodo V. C. faber ferrarius non solum malleum conficit, ut inserviat fabro lignario; sed etiam ut ipse eodem uti queat in cudendo ferro.
units.tr: For while Logic teaches the method and manner of learning other sciences, the other sciences presuppose this same method and make use of it. So Logic serves the other disciplines in such a way that it also, in handing down its own precepts and explaining them properly, uses its own instruments, namely definition, division and the rest. This is like a smith who makes not only a hammer for the carpenter but also one that he himself can use in beating iron.

units.la: IV. Falsum est, antiquos Philosophos, antequam per Aristotelem ultima Logicæ manus impositá fuisset, omnino rudes fuisse Logicæ. Nam ut ipsi præditi fuerunt Logica naturali, ita diuturno usu eandem adeo exasciarunt, sibique ratione aliarum disciplinarum expeditam reddiderunt, ut tantundem fere subsidii ab eahabuerint, atque si artis præsidio instructi fuissent.
units.tr: IV. It is false that the ancient philosophers, before Aristotle had put the finishing touch to Logic, were wholly unskilled in it. For just as they were endowed with natural logic, so by long practice they polished it and made it ready for use in the light of other disciplines, so that they derived almost as much help from it as if they had been equipped with the aid of an art.

units.la: Præterea etiamsi extra alias disciplinas prisci sapientes non didicerint Logicam, didicerunt eam atque meditati fuerunt, in ipsis illis disciplinis, circa quas versabantur.
units.tr: Moreover, even if the ancient sages did not learn logic apart from other disciplines, they did learn it and practised it within those very disciplines with which they were occupied.

units.la: V. Logica quoniam de omnibus rebus commode differere debet, atq; mentem expedire omnibus salebris, in quas incurrit & incidit; non debet æstimari, ut à multis perperam hic factum, ratione aut certi alicujus argumenti, aut etiam ratione solius doctrinæ Topicæ, prout ea jam olim Sophistis ad hoc servire solet, ut possent de quocunque Themate in utramque partem ad vulgi maxime applausum disserere. nec procedere potest consequentia ab indigniori parte alicujus disciplinæ ad abusum expedita, ad totam disciplinam, omniaque quæ ad eandem pertinent.Quia nemo potest dici scire, nisi pariter sciat se scire, possitque ea, quæ videtur scire examinare, atque ad sua principia revocare, Logica cum primis necessaria est. quum enim aliarum disciplinarum subsidio hoc illudve scianus, per solam Logicam, quicquid scimus, examinare possumus. VI. Quamvis quidam e medio vulgo videantur non incommode definire, dividere, & argumentari, citra artis Logicæ præsidium; non tamen propterea ullum præjudicium creatur huic ipsi arti: siquidem ut vulgi hæc industria se duntaxat probat in paucis & facilibus quibusdam argumentis, neutiquam vero in omni materiæ genere; sic hi ipsi casu magis, quam consilio hoscæ actus edunt. quoniam sic eosdem edunt, ut non sciant se bene eos edere. neutiquam vero eosdem examinare possunt: cum ad hoc uti examinentur, requiratur Logica artificialis. VII. Logica quidem naturalis, quæ ipsa ratio est, pertinet ad hominis essentiam, neutiquam tamen per hanc naturalem potentiam æque facile homini est, actus Logicos edere, ac avi volare: quoniam plurimum interest inter hominis statum integrum atque corruptum. IIX. Lubens do, Logicam vulgo non commendare æque suos cultores, atque reliquę discipl næ eos, à quibus diligentius excoluntur. Quod mihi videtur accidere ob tres subsequentes rationes: 1. Quoniam ea ipsa est ex genere earum facultatum & artium, quæ ab omnibus exercentur, nec alios denominant, quam qui insigni ratione earum excoluerint. 2. Ordinario peritia Logica perinde quasi solet à disciplina cui applicatur: familiare siquidem vulgo est, habilitatem differendi tribuere illi arti, quam quis profitetur. 3. Pari ratione ordinario fere, artifex magis consuevit appellari à facultate obsequente & exequete, quam à facultate docete.
units.tr: V. Since logic ought to be able to speak fittingly about all things and to free the mind from all the difficulties into which it runs and falls, it should not be judged (as many have wrongly done) by some particular certain argument, or even by the Topical doctrine alone, which the Sophists were already accustomed to use for this purpose, so that they could argue on any theme on either side, chiefly to win the applause of the crowd. Nor can an inference proceed from the less worthy part of some discipline, turned to abuse, to the whole discipline and everything that pertains to it. Because no one can be said to know unless he likewise knows that he knows, and can examine what he seems to know and trace it back to its principles, logic is above all necessary. For when we know this or that with the help of other disciplines, we can examine whatever we know only through logic alone. VI. Although some men of the common sort seem to define, divide and argue not inappropriately without the aid of the art of logic, no prejudice is thereby created against this art itself. For just as the industry of the common people proves itself only in a few easy arguments and by no means in every kind of matter, so these men act more by chance than by design. They produce such acts without knowing that they produce them well, and they can by no means examine them, since for that examination artificial logic is required. VII. Natural logic, which is itself reason, belongs to the essence of man; yet by this natural power it is by no means as easy for man to perform logical acts as it is for a bird to fly, since there is the greatest difference between the state of man in integrity and his state in corruption. VIII. I willingly grant that logic does not commend its practitioners to the common people as much as other disciplines commend those by whom they are more diligently cultivated. This seems to me to happen for three reasons: (1) because logic belongs to the class of faculties and arts that everyone exercises, and they name no one except those who have cultivated them with distinguished skill; (2) as a rule, skill in logic is attributed to the discipline to which it is applied, for it is customary for the common people to ascribe the ability to reason to whatever art a man professes; (3) by the same reasoning, a craftsman is usually named from the faculty that serves and executes rather than from the faculty that teaches.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM QUARTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FOURTEEN.

units.la: De definitione, atque divisione: quæ duo instrumenta Logicæ serio afftruuntur, & à Sexti objectionibus vindicantur.
units.tr: On definition and division: two instruments of Logic that are seriously put forward, and defended against the objections of Sextus.

units.la: QUum Sceptici, eorumque antesignanus Sextus Empiricus, non solum Logicæ in universum
units.tr: Since the Sceptics, and their champion Sextus Empiricus, have declared war not only on Logic considered in general,

units.la: C c 2 universum consideratæ bellum indixerint, sed etiam singulis instrumentis Logicis, haud abs re fuerit, breviter expendere ea, quæ, pro exarmando quasi unoquoque instrumento Logico, adscrre solent. Hoc quidem capite acturi sumus de Definitione, & Divisione, in subsequentibus de reliquis. Atque ut agamus hic de Definitione, cum teste Themistio ad lib. 1. Post. Analyt. bellum quoque indixerat Speusippus, prænotamus ex Damasceno in Diaiect. cap. 8. vocem hanc à Mathematicis ad Logicos traductam. Sic enim ibi loquitur: Dicitur definitio à Metaphora finium, seu terminini positionum terræ. Quemadmodum enim finis seu termini positio separat proprium uniuscujusque, sic & definitio seu terminus naturam uniuscujusque separat ab alterius natura. neque enim insolens esse Logicę à Mathesi, ob analogiam, mutuo vocabula accipere, evincunt nomina syllogismi, figuræ, terminorum, etc. Hæc ipsa vero Definitio, si Platonem in Theæteto audiamus, est illud per quod accipimus differentiam, per quam res aliqua ab omnibus aliis differt. Secundum Ciceronem in Topicis, referente Boëthio in libel. de Definitione, est oratio, qua id, quod definit, explicat quid sit. quæ definitionis explicatio non multum differt ab ea, quam Arist. lib. 1. Top. cap. 4 & lib. 2. Poster. tex. 44. habet, quæque vulgo in Scholis est recepta: Est oratio explicans quod quid est ipsius rei. à quo quod quid est uti formarunt Metaphysici & Scholastici suam quidditatem, quę quasi sit illa explicatio, quæ per definitionem stricte sic dictam procuratur; ita hæc ipsa quidditas æque diversimode considerari potest, quam ipsa definitio diversimode se habet. Nam præterquam quod ipsum vulgus, consultum circa explicationem alicujus thematis simplicis, secundum ea, quæ de illo nosse videtur, illud explicare consueverit; Oratores, adhibito verborum exquisito lenocinio, pro ratione suorum auditorum, prolixius quasi definiendo illud explicant, quod iis, quorum favorem atque applausum præ cæteris ambiunt, quam exploratissimum esse expetunt: Poëtæ, cum pariter delectare desiderent, varia quasi emblemata fabularum, comparationum, similiumque adhibent, ut eandem explicationem pro suo instituto exhibere possint: Alii, qua ab oratoribus, qua à poëtis recedentes, ut applausum impetrent, sibique opinionem singularis ingenii atque industriæ acquirant, explicaturi rei alicujus naturam, studio obscuritatem captare solent, atque omnem suam industriam circa ænigmata occupare, quæ nihil aliud sunt, quam obscuræ quædam explicationes thematum quorundam simplicium per talia adjuncta, caussas, effectu-sque propositæ, quę cum minus, circa res notiﬁsimas quoque, considerari consueverint, earundem ratione quæ obvia, atque quotidiana sunt, iis ipsis, qui quotidie circa talia occupantur, non minus obscura evadunt, atque illa, quæ aut in penitiori Africa, aut in media India occultantur: Logici, imo quotquot Logicorum præceptis in quacunque etiam disciplina utuntur, propter ea, quę speciatim à Logica circa rationem definitionis præscribi solent, aliquanto morosiores in definiendo sunt, suasque definitiones astringunt quibusdam regulis, quarum alteri, in definiendo quoque occupati, securiores sunt, quod his propositum sit ex lege artis definitum explicare, illi vero hoc duntaxat agant, ut queant aliquam rem exhibere sub talibus signis, per quæ, sive proximè, sive remotè, devenire aliquis possit, ad illud ipsum, quod definiti rationem habet.
