Atque, cum Logici præ aliis definitiones suas regulis astringere consueverint, factum, ut soli censeantur definiendi rationem tradere, quum tamen soli ad regulas eadem examinent, quę ab aliis ex regularum præscriptis minus curari solent. Inde factum non solum, ut omnes definitiones æstimentur ex præscripto Logicorum regularum, sed etiam ipsi Sceptici, dum instituerunt definitiones oppugnare, quasi soli Logici in definiendo occupARentur, crediderunt sese subversuros in universum Definitionem, si quid modo notassent aut in norma Logica, aut in ipsis definitionibus ad eandem exactis. Vt vero definitionibus, secundum antiquam Logicam institutis, sua ratio constet, [de his quippe hoc loco, occasione Logicæ, incidit quæstio] operæ pretium fuerit in antecessum sequentia notasse. I. Vti per definitiones Logico modo institutas intenditur definitio explicatio, sic hæc explicario duntaxat, ut Scholastici loquuntur, quidditativa est: quum per eam ipsum definitum non explicetur plene atque sufficienter secundum omnia illa, quæ circa illud cognosci possunt, sed solum ostendatur, ad quamnam entium classem referri debeat. Injuria quippe fit, sive Philosophis in communi, sive distincte quoque Peripateticis, quando mens eorum sic explicatur, quasi ijdem definiendo intenderint per qualemcunque definito applicatam, definitionem exhibere plenam & distinctam (atque, ut in Scholis loquuntur, formalem) ejusdem rationem. II. Quum definitio solum sit indicina rei, distinctiva maxime, utque per eam convenientissime definitum ab aliis ejusdem ordinis distinguatur, existimandum est, hanc ipsam definitionem non egredi egredi sphæram cognitionis nostræ, sed instituiper ea n, quæ nobis cum maxime familiaria sunt. Adeo ut sæpe definitio, ob imbecillitatem intellectus nostri, nobis ipsum definitum non exhibeat secundum se suamque naturam, sed secundum illud solum, quod nobis datum est cognoscere. III. Quandoquidem conceptus rei Physicus distinctus est à conceptu Logico, non incommode definitio distinguitur in Physicam & Logicam; atq; ut illa attendit principia rem aliquam realiter sive constituentia, sive producentia; sic hæc in omni, quod definit, considerat genus, tanquam materiale & commune quid, itemque differentiá partem velut formalem: quamvis ob ignorantiam propriæ adæquataeq; differentiæ, sæpe pro adumbranda qualicunque differentia, Logica definitio cum Physica confundatur; quod in definitionibus caussalibus manifestum est. IV. Atque hinc accidit, ut, ratione habita compositionis Logicæ, quædam perfecte, ne quidem secundum leges Logicas, atque seposita nostra de iisdem ignorantia, definiri queant. Nam quod ad ea, quæ vocant transcendentia, itemque summa genera, cum aut supra se aliud tanquam genus non habeant, aut univoca censeri non queant, non gaudent quoque conceptu quasi composito, includente rationem generis ac differentiæ. Præterea individua non admittunt perfectam definitionem, & quidem duplici nomine: vel enim, ut individua Physica, tali ratione sunt affecta, ut in perpetua mutatione existant, cumque habeant proprietates mutabiles, atque sibi soli convenientes, sub definitione communi, qua talia, comprehendi non possunt: vel, ut in Deo Opt. Max. [individuo illo sine exemplo] tanta occurrit simplicitas, ut ne quidem compositio Logica ex genere & differentia locum habere queat. Quicquid enim alii existimant, Deus ut ens perfectissimum, atque a partibus componentibus plane independens, neutiquam dici potest ex genere atque differentia compositus esse. Interim hæc ipsa, quæ perfectam omnibus numeris definitionem non admittunt, dici possunt in suo genere perfecte definiri posse.
units.tr: but also on the individual instruments of Logic, it will not be out of place to examine briefly those things which they usually bring forward to disarm, as it were, each single Logical instrument. In this chapter we shall deal with Definition and Division, and in the following chapters with the rest. To deal with Definition here: Speusippus also declared war on it, as Themistius testifies in his commentary on the first book of the Posterior Analytics. We note first from Damascene in the Dialectic, chapter 8, that this word was transferred from the mathematicians to the logicians. For he speaks thus there: Definition is named from the metaphor of the boundaries or the placing of the limits of land. For just as the placing of a limit or boundary separates what is proper to each thing, so a definition or term separates the nature of each thing from the nature of another. Nor is it unusual for Logic, by analogy, to borrow words from Mathematics; the names syllogism, figure, terms, and so on, make this plain. This definition itself, if we listen to Plato in the Theaetetus, is that through which we grasp the difference by which a thing differs from all others. According to Cicero in the Topics, as reported by Boethius in his little book on Definition, it is a speech which explains what the thing defined is. This explanation of definition does not differ much from that which Aristotle gives in Topics book 1, chapter 4, and Posterior Analytics book 2, text 44, and which is commonly received in the Schools: It is a speech explaining what the thing itself is. From this phrase quod quid est, the Metaphysicians and Scholastics formed their quidditas, which is, as it were, that explanation procured through definition strictly so called. Thus this very quidditas can be considered in as many different ways as definition itself is variously related. For, apart from the fact that common people, when asked to explain some simple subject, usually explain it according to what they seem to know about it; orators, using an exquisite embellishment of words and suiting their hearers, explain it at greater length, as if defining it, because they wish it to be made most clear to those whose favour and applause they seek above all others; poets, since they likewise desire to delight, employ various emblems, as it were, of fables, comparisons and the like, so that they may present the same explanation according to their purpose; others, departing from the orators or from the poets, wishing to win applause and to gain for themselves a reputation for singular talent and diligence, when they are about to explain the nature of some thing, are accustomed to seek obscurity deliberately, and to spend all their effort on riddles. These are nothing other than certain obscure explanations of simple subjects through such adjuncts, causes and proposed effects. Since such things are usually considered with less care even when they are very well known, the things that are obvious and everyday become no less obscure, in their account, to those very people who are daily occupied with such matters, than those things which are hidden in the innermost parts of Africa or in the middle of India. The Logicians, indeed all who use the precepts of Logic in any discipline, because of what Logic specifically prescribes concerning the nature of definition, are somewhat more scrupulous in defining, and they bind their definitions with certain rules. Others, though also occupied with defining, are less concerned with these, since for the former the purpose is to explain the defined thing according to the law of the art, whereas the latter aim only at presenting some thing under such signs that one may arrive, either proximately or remotely, at that which has the nature of the defined. And since the Logicians are accustomed to bind their definitions by rules more than others, it has come about that they alone are thought to teach the nature of definition, although they alone examine these same things by the rules, which others are less accustomed to heed in accordance with the prescriptions of the rules. Hence it has come about not only that all definitions are judged by the prescriptions of the logical rules, but also that the Sceptics themselves, when they set about attacking definitions, believed that only the Logicians were occupied in defining, and so thought they would overturn Definition in general if they could note anything either in the Logical norm or in the definitions themselves conformed to it. But so that definitions framed according to the ancient Logic may have their rationale established (for this question has arisen here, occasioned by Logic), it will be worth while to note the following in advance. I. Just as the explanation intended by a definition framed in the Logical manner is quidditative, as the Scholastics say, since through it the defined thing is not explained fully and sufficiently according to all the things that can be known about it, but is only shown to what class of beings it ought to be referred, so too it is wrong, whether to Philosophers in general or to the Peripatetics in particular, when their mind is interpreted as if by a definition applied to whatever is defined they intended to present a full and distinct account of it (and, as they say in the Schools, a formal account). II. Since a definition is only an indication of a thing, and chiefly distinctive, so that through it the defined thing is most conveniently distinguished from others of the same order, it must be held that this definition does not go beyond the sphere of our knowledge, but is framed from those things which are most familiar to us. So that often a definition, because of the weakness of our understanding, does not present the defined thing to us according to itself and its nature, but only according to what we are able to know. III. Since the physical concept of a thing is distinct from the logical concept, a definition is not inappropriately divided into the Physical and the Logical. Just as the former attends to the principles that really either constitute or produce a thing, so the latter considers in whatever is defined the genus as a material and common element, and the difference as, as it were, its formal part. Although, because of our ignorance of the proper and adequate difference, the Logical definition is often confused with the Physical, as it sometimes shadows forth some kind of difference, which is clear in causal definitions. IV. And from this it happens that, given the composition required by Logic, some things cannot be defined perfectly, not even according to the Logical laws, quite apart from our ignorance of them. For as regards those things which they call transcendentals, and likewise the highest genera, since they either have nothing higher as genus or cannot be considered univocal, they do not enjoy a concept that is, as it were, composite, including the reason of genus and difference. Moreover, individuals do not admit a perfect definition, and that for a twofold reason: either, as physical individuals, they are so constituted that they exist in perpetual change, and since they have changeable properties which belong to them alone, they cannot be comprehended under a common definition as such; or, as in God Most Good and Greatest (that individual without example), such simplicity occurs that not even a logical composition of genus and difference can have a place. For whatever others think, God, as the most perfect being and entirely independent of component parts, can by no means be said to be composed of genus and difference. Yet these very things which do not admit a definition perfect in every respect can be said to be perfectly definable in their own kind.

units.la: V. Ne quis enim fallatur, definitionis ex Aristotelis maxime principiis eadem ratio est, quæ doctrinæ de prædicamentis: utraque enim proponitur secundum certas hypotheses, maxime Definitio: unde Aristoteles quoque lib. 7. Top. cap 5. expresse solas substantias per se definitionem admittere statuit: frustraque est Francisc. Patritius, quando par. 2. lib. 4. Peripat. Disputi. ignorantiæ Aristotelis interpretes arguit, quod hic de quacunque essentia essentia tia essentia dixit, ad solam substantiam restringi cupiant; quum Philosophus, ut cuivis textum inspicienti patere potest, manifesto substantiam cum accidente comparet. His præmissis [non sine fructu aliquo, ut speramus] proponimus subsequentes rationes. I. Si nullus est è vulgo, qui non quotidie secundum ea, quæ de hac illave re cognoscit, definitiones contexat: næ Philosophus quoque definire potest ea, quæ novit, secundum illas leges, quas sibi ipsi in definiendo præscribere voluerit. Antecedens uti certum est, sic pariter consequentia procedit: nam si procedat definitio, quam aliquis è vulgo conexit, secundum ea quæ de definito cognoscit, atque secundum eas leges, quas sibi ipsi in definiendo præscribit, cur non pariter admitti tanquam legitima debeat illa ipsa definitio, quam pari ratione Philosophus adornat? II. Ipse Scepticus (testis sit unus Sextus Empyricus in Pyrrh. Hypoth.) quo ab aliis intelligi queat, atque finem suum assequatur, suo modo definitiones adornat: quæ ratio ergo, cur non idem liceat Dogmaticis, quod adeo licentiose sibi Scepticus arrogat? III. Si tum quidditates rerum cognoscibiles sunt, tum easdem actu cognoscimus, admitti pariter definitio debet, modum proponens, secundum quem mens sibi per definitionem præponat hasce ipsas quidditates, explicatas oratione convenienti. Ratio consequentiae manifesta est. De quidditatibus vero ut cognoscibilibus ne multum disceptemus, sufficit hac vice per eas intelligere tales mentis conceptus, secundum quos thema aliquod simplex ratione distinctae notionis nobis repraesentamus. Vt enim jam antea patuit, definitionum omnium non una eademque ratio est: nec necessum est, pro praesenti instituto omnes definitiones sint essentiales. IV.
units.tr: V. For lest anyone be deceived, the rationale of definition according to the principles of Aristotle is the same as that of the doctrine of the predicaments; for both are set forth according to certain hypotheses, and especially Definition. Hence Aristotle also, in Topics book 7, chapter 5, expressly lays down that only substances admit definition in their own right. Francis Patritius is therefore mistaken when, in part 2 of book 4 of the Peripatetic Disputations, he accuses the interpreters of Aristotle of ignorance, because they wish to restrict to substance alone what he said of any essence; since the Philosopher, as anyone reading the text can see, manifestly compares substance with accident. With these things premised (not without some profit, as we hope), we put forward the following arguments. I. If there is no one among the common people who does not every day compose definitions according to what he knows about this or that thing, then the Philosopher too can define the things he knows, according to those rules which he has chosen to prescribe for himself in defining. The antecedent is certain, and the consequence likewise follows: for if the definition which someone from the common people composes proceeds according to what he knows of the defined thing and according to the rules which he prescribes for himself in defining, why should that same definition, which the Philosopher frames by the same method, not equally be admitted as legitimate? II. The Sceptic himself (Sextus Empiricus alone is witness, in the Outlines of Pyrrhonism) adapts definitions in his own way, so that he may be understood by others and attain his end. What reason, then, is there why the Dogmatists should not be allowed the same, when the Sceptic so licentiously claims it for himself? III. If quidditates of things are knowable, and if we actually know the same, then a definition must likewise be admitted, setting out the manner according to which the mind presents these quidditates to itself through definition, explained in fitting words. The consequence is plain. As for whether quidditates are knowable, let us not dispute much; for the present it is enough to understand by them those mental concepts according to which we represent to ourselves some simple subject by means of a distinct notion. For, as has already been made clear, there is not one and the same rationale of all definitions, and it is not necessary for the present purpose that all definitions be essential. IV.

units.la: Cum omnes homines, ut recte innuit Aristoteles lib. 1. Metaph. cap. 1. natura scire desiderent, naturali quoque appetitu, quem non convenit esse frustra, feruntur ad definiendum. Si enim scire est rem per causam cognoscere: nae ante omnia, cujusque rei, cujus scientia habetur, explorata debet esse distincta quidditas: nisi enim antea exploratum fuerit quid esse illius, cujus per demonstrationem scientia acquiritur, non potest quoque ipsa demonstratio, postea distincte consideranda, contexi & adornari. V. Quandoquidem, uti jam antea patuit ex Sexto, Sceptici argumentari quoque solent ab universali consensu, nos pariter eodem modo hic progredi possumus, sic argumentando: Si illi ipsi, qui Scepticismi fundamenta jecerunt, aut definiendi leges invenerunt, aut definitionibus prae ceteris usi fuerunt; pariter ex Sceptici mente plurimum tribuendum Definitionis doctrinæ, nec fas est ipse eidem sit infestus. Consequentia ratione Sceptici indubitato certa ac firma est. nec de antecedente dubitare licet, vel propter Aristotelis testimonium: qui lib. 1. de Part. Anim. cap. 1. adducta authoritate Democriti, eum jam tum circa definiendum intentum fuisse testatur. quomodo & constat Socratem, atq; Academicos omnes plurimū tribuisse definitionibus, easque in frequenti usu habuisse. Quamvis ex iis, quæ jam antea notata fuerunt, haut difficile sit argumentis, quæ in contrarium adducuntur, occurrere, næ qua tamen difficultas alicui superfit, sequentia, ad modum fontium, proponimus. I. Verum quidem, à Philosophis, antiquis quoque, augustis admodum elogiis condecorari Definitiones, neutiquam tamen ulli ex illis in mentem venit, sic definitionem pro rei explicatione admittere, ut exististimarent eum qui rei alicujus definitionem exploratam haberet, pariter perspecta habere omnia illa, quæ circa rem illam [ex definitione sua cognitam] cognoscì possent. II. Aggregativa rei definitio, secundum quam ratione thematis simplicis sive definiti, per loca tamen topica, omnia de themate illo cognoscibilia colliguntur, atque dein analytice quasi per partes iterum examinantur, non potest
units.tr: Since all men, as Aristotle rightly observes (Metaph. 1, ch. 1), desire to know by nature, they are also drawn by a natural appetite, which cannot be meant to be in vain, toward defining. For if to know is to know a thing through its cause, then before anything else the distinct quiddity of whatever thing is to be known must be established. Unless it has first been ascertained what it is that is acquired through demonstration, the demonstration itself cannot be framed and put together for later distinct consideration. V. As was already shown above from Sextus, the Sceptics also habitually argue from universal consent, and we may proceed in the same way here, arguing thus: If those very men who laid the foundations of Scepticism either discovered the laws of definition or made more use of definitions than others, then, by the Sceptics' own judgment, the doctrine of definition must be given very great weight, and it is not right for anyone to be hostile to it. The consequence is certain and firm by the Sceptics' own reasoning, and there is no room to doubt the antecedent, either on the strength of Aristotle's testimony, who in the first book of On the Parts of Animals, ch. 1, cites the authority of Democritus and testifies that he was already concerned with defining. It is also clear that Socrates and all the Academics attached great importance to definitions and kept them in frequent use. Although, from what has already been noted, it is not difficult to meet the arguments brought against this, nevertheless, so that no difficulty remains for anyone, we set out the following points, like springs. I. It is true that the ancient philosophers too honoured definitions with very high praise, but none of them ever thought of admitting a definition as an explanation of a thing in such a way as to suppose that whoever had a settled definition of some thing also had a complete grasp of all those things which could be known about that thing [as known from its definition]. II. A definition that is an aggregate of the thing, in which, by the topical places, all the knowable things about the simple theme or definiendum are gathered together and then examined again, as it were, piece by piece, analytically,

units.la: poterit potest censeri definitio proprie dicta, hæc enim brevis debet esse, atque exacta solum ad eas leges, secundum quas definitio est explicativa quidditatis, uti loquuntur. III. Quandoquidem definitio duntaxat declarat ad quamnam entium classem definitum referri debeat, non necessium est, ut omnia, de genere & differentia definitionis cognoscibilia, in ipsa definitione concerventur; quandoquidem dum constat quodnam definiti genus sit, pariter quoq; constat sub quonam genere summo, & remotiori contineatur. nam quicquid est ut species, illud præsupponit superius, cui substat. IV. Quum instrumenta Logica, ea, quæ distincte sunt comprehensa, conjungant, atque conjuncta dijudicent; frustra omnino Sextus est, quando exinde definitionem frustraneam vult esse, quod in ea proponantur illa, quæ jam antea cognoscuntur. Nam quamvis definiturus V.C.hominem, præcognoscere debet quodnam sit genus hominis, & quænam differentia: quando tamen hæc duo in ipsa definitione conjungit, tam patet quomodo pro explicando definito genus cum differentia cohæreat, quā etiam per conjunctionem eorum innotescit, ad quodnam ens homo cum definitione ab omnibus aliis distinguente pertineat. V. Frustra idem Sextus est, quando definitiones ex definitionibus dijudicari dicitur, quum nihil queat dijudicativum esse sui, atque distinguere conveniat inter leges sive regulas definitionis, & definitionem ad illas regulas exactam. Illa definitio aliis est perfectior, quę legibus magis respondet, unaque altera censetur esse perfectior mediantibus legibus, ad quas pariter exiguntur. V. Quum dictum sit, definitiones instituì aliter à vulgo, aliter vero ab iis, qui definitum secundum penitiorem de eo cognitionem explicant per definitionem Logicis regulis respondentem, [quisquis enim definit, pro definiti explicatione, ea quę novit, adfert] neutiquam servire expugnandæ definitioni possunt ea, quę à Sexto proponuntur loco dicto, ubi sic loquitur: Ecquis vero ridiculum esse debet, dicere definitionem aut ad comprehendendum, aut ad docendum, aut ad manifestandum conducere, quum nos tanta obscuritate involvant? Exempli gratia [libet enim paulisper iocari] Si quis ab aliquo scisci-tari velit an occurrerit ei homo insidens equo, & canem secum ducens, interroget hoc modo: O animal rationale, mortale, intellectus & scientiæ capax, occurritne tibi animal risibile, latis unguibus, scientiæ politicæ capax, habens conglobationes, firmatas super animali mortali, hinniendi facultatem habente: quod si cum secum ducit animal latrativum? Quomodo non fit hic risu excipiendus, qui hominem in re tam nota cogit obmutescere? Haëtenus Sextus. Nam ex hoc Sexti ratiocinio non licet colligere, has definitiones fuisse inconvenientes, sed solum obscuras ei, cui proponebantur, quod neque terminos intelligeret, neque perciperet conceptus generis & differentiae pro explicandis definitis ibidem propositos: pari ratione viris doctissimis aenigmata videntur, atque numeris Platonicis obscuriora ea, quae à variis artificibus, secundum artis suę terminos, ad modum definitionum proponuntur: quoniam non minus artificiales conceptus, quam terminos artificibus usitatos ignorant. Hunc ipsum enim viatorem Sexti, si quis propositis definitionibus popularibus aggressus fuisset, commodum ab eo responsum consequi potuisset. Neque enim haesisset in suo responso, si quis hunc in modum ex eo quaesivisset: An non obvium habuisti hominem senem cana barba praeditum, insidentem equo albo, quem canis niger comitabatur? Nam inconveniens est Sexti interrogatio, eoque nomine ut insufficiens rejicienda, quod cumappelletur ad viatoris sensus, neutiquam proponi iis possit quaestio thetica, sed hypothetica: dicte vero Sexti definitiones in quaestione Pyrrhonica cumulatae directae erant non ad individui viduæ sensibus per suas qualitates perceptibile, sed ad species solo intellectu comprehensibiles. Et hæc quidem dicta sufficiant pro Definitione. Converto me deinceps ad Divisionem, de qua idem Sextus agit lib. 2. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. 17. & duobus sequentibus. Expugnare vero laborat tum divisionem nominis, sive distinctionem, tum divisionem proprie sic dictam. Quantum quidem ad distinctiones, quamvis iis infestus sit Sextus eo nomine, quod vocum significationes ab arbitratu humano dependeant, eæ ipsæ tamen propterea admitti debent, nec insuper haberi possunt, quod nulla lingua tam locuples sit, quin deficiat in explicandis conceptibus per propria definitaque vocabula; unde ut metaphoras atque tropos non sola elegantiæ ratio, sed ex parte quoque necessitas invenit, ita una eademque vox servire cæpit pluribus explicandis conceptibus, quod pro horum multitudine æque multa non potuerint inveniri vocabula. Verum quidem est, illi qui in Scholis docent, quod omnia subtilius pressiusque enucleare consueverint, atque interiora quasi rerum viscera exenterare, magnam sibi arrogarunt libertatem, multaque vocabula, antiquis plane ignota, præsenti nota signarunt; interim næ hæc quidem conceptibus defæcatis explicandis sufficere potuerunt. Vnde necessarium necessum fuit vocibus alias receptis, tales aptare significationes [ pro Scholæ quasi usu ] quæ apud eos, qui extra Scholam consistunt, plane ignotæ sunt. Quid æquius ergo, quam quoties circa res ipsas, earumque considerationem difficultas aliqua oboritur, ante omnia voces, quarum multiplex significatio, difficultates multiplices parere potest, penitius expendere, evolutisque significationibus pluribus ac separatis, eam ex pluribus amplecti, secundum quam res ipsa convenienter concipi explicarique potest. nam hactenus valet sapiens illud Epicteti monitum, qui dicere solet: Principium doctrinæ est consideratio nominum. Ad considerationem hanc pertinet quoque Etymologia; sed cum ea ut plurimum aut sit incerta, aut perparum conferat ad considerationem ipsius rei, exi-stimandum est magni nominis Stoicum, eundemque virum sapientissimum, potissimum respexisse homonymias vocabulorum; distinctionum subsidio pro explicatione rerum ipsarum evolvendas. Siquidem distinctio nihil aliud est, quam explicatio multiplicis sensus, quem voces in aliqua propositione, pro usu sive communi sive doctrinali, admittere possunt. quod tum secundum rationem præxios convenienter fit, quando primo multiplex ille sensus explicando proponitur, ac dein discretionem adhibet iudicium, uno pluribusve sensibus rejectis unum aliquem velut convenientem admittendo. nec tamen quis ut petulans hic tolerandus, nec etiam distinctionum subtilitas, veritas (quæ per eas explicari debet) involvenda est, uti olim [haut præter veritatem] iis, quia Scoto nomen ferunt, objectum fuit. Voces ipsæ varias quidem, easque remotiores quoque significationes admiserunt, pro vario atque multiplici nostro concipiendi modo: interim tamen hic tria extrema sunt præcavenda, de quibus quoniam multi minus solliciti fuerunt, omnes distinctiones suspectas reddiderunt. I. Conceptus noster non debet sic ab ipsa re, circa quam instituitur, aberrare, ut in ea nullum fundamentum inveniat, sed perpetuo rei ipsi consentaneus esse: sive, ut in Scholis loquuntur, distinctio formalis respondere debet distinctioni objectivæ. 2. Non debet aliquis suos conceptus objicere vocibus, haut solitis ex usu, aut communi, aut doctrinalibus novis & particularibus conceptibus explicandis servire. frustra quippe is est, qui, ut adversarii oculis pulverem [hoc tamen sæpe fit] objiciat, plane ipsius assertioni, aut argumento, pro suo concipiendi modo multiplicem sensum, per distinctionem quasi explicandum, affingit. Distinctiones primario propter voces, secundario propter conceptus mentis adhiberi debent. quamvis enim mens nostra, quæ uno intuitu omnia lustrare non potest, multiplicibus distinctionibus indigeat, ut per eas res explicet; hæ tamen conceptuum diversitates, proprie non sunt distinctiones, sed partiales explicationes rerum, uno simplicique conceptu à nobis haud explicabilium: quum distinctiones ipsas voces concernant, pro multiplici conceptu ex usu multiplicem significationem admittentes. A distinctione seu divisione nominis, transimus ad divisionem ipsam proprie sic dictam, seu divisionem rei: quam pariter Sextus Nititur evertere lib. 2. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. 19. & 20, sed præter rationem. Quod enim ad divisionem totius quantitativi, cum instituatur per partes aut magnitudine aut numero differentes, sufficientia ejusdem inde liquet, quod illæ ipsæ partes per divisionem separatæ, si simul sumantur, atque iterum uniantur, constituendo toti, sic antea in partes diviso, sufficiant. Atque hæc divisio, quæ vulgo peculiari nomine partitio vocari solet, tam evidens atque certa est, uti ipsi quoque rustici, aliique à cultu alieni, existiment se convenienter eam instituere posse: ne dicam, ab Arithmeticis ac Geometriæ consultis, ejusdem veritatem atque certitudinem dilucide demonstrari.
units.tr: cannot be considered a definition properly so called. For a true definition ought to be brief and exact only according to those laws by which a definition is explanatory of the quiddity, as they say. III. Since a definition merely declares to which class of beings the defined thing should be referred, it is not necessary that everything knowable about the genus and difference of the definition be packed into the definition itself; for once it is clear what the genus of the defined thing is, it is equally clear under what highest and more remote genus it is contained, since whatever is a species presupposes the higher thing under which it stands. IV. Since the tools of logic join together what has been distinctly comprehended, and judge what has been joined, Sextus is quite wrong when he infers from this that a definition is useless because it sets forth things already known. For although one who is about to define man, the Venerable Man, must know beforehand what the genus of man is and what the difference is, yet when he joins these two in the definition itself, it is quite plain how the genus coheres with the difference to explain the defined thing, and through their conjunction it becomes known to what being man belongs, together with a definition that distinguishes him from all others. V. Sextus is equally wrong when he says that definitions are judged by definitions, since nothing can judge itself, and it is fitting to distinguish between the laws or rules of definition and a definition that is exact according to those rules. That definition is more perfect which corresponds more closely to the laws, and one definition is judged more perfect than another by means of the laws to which both are equally required to conform. V. Since it has been said that definitions are made in one way by the common people, and in another by those who explain the defined thing according to a deeper knowledge of it, through a definition that corresponds to the rules of logic (for whoever defines, in explaining the defined thing, brings forward what he knows), the passage of Sextus cited in that place cannot serve to overthrow definition at all, where he speaks thus: "Who indeed ought to think it ridiculous to say that definition is useful for comprehending, teaching, or making things manifest, when they involve us in such obscurity? For example [for let us jest a little]: if someone wishes to ask another whether he has met a man sitting on a horse and leading a dog with him, and asks him in this way: O rational, mortal animal, capable of understanding and knowledge, has there met you an animal capable of laughter, broad-nailed, capable of political science, having convolutions set upon a mortal animal and having the faculty of neighing; and if he leads with him a barking animal? Who would not be laughed at here, when he forces a man to be silent about so familiar a matter?" Thus far Sextus. For from this reasoning of Sextus it does not follow that these definitions were unsuitable, but only that they were obscure to the one to whom they were proposed, since he did not understand the terms, nor did he grasp the concepts of genus and difference which were set forth there for explaining the defined things. By the same token, to very learned men, riddles seem, and things more obscure than Platonic numbers, which are put forward in the manner of definitions by various craftsmen according to the terms of their craft; for those learned men are ignorant of concepts no less artificial than the terms the craftsmen use. Indeed, if someone had approached this very traveller of Sextus with popular definitions, he could easily have received a suitable answer from him. He would not have hesitated in his reply if someone had asked him in this way: "Did you not meet an old man with a white beard, sitting on a white horse, accompanied by a black dog?" For Sextus's question is inappropriate, and to be rejected as insufficient on that account, since, as it is addressed to the traveller's senses, it cannot be put to them as a thetic question but must be hypothetical; the definitions of Sextus, however, heaped up in a Pyrrhonian question, were directed not to the individual as perceptible to the senses through its qualities, but to species comprehensible by the intellect alone. Let these points suffice concerning definition. I turn next to division, of which the same Sextus treats in the second book of the Outlines of Pyrrhonism, ch. 17, and the two following chapters. He labours to overthrow both the division of a name, or distinction, and division properly so called. As regards distinctions, although Sextus is hostile to them on the ground that the meanings of words depend on human choice, they must nevertheless be admitted for that very reason, and they cannot be disregarded on the ground that no language is so rich that it fails to explain concepts through proper and defined words. Hence, just as necessity as well as the reasons of elegance has invented metaphors and tropes, so one and the same word has begun to serve for explaining several concepts, since words could not be found in equal number to the multitude of these concepts. It is true that those who teach in the Schools, because they are accustomed to unfold everything more subtly and closely, and to disembowel, as it were, the inner viscera of things, have claimed for themselves a great liberty, and have marked with present meanings many words entirely unknown to the ancients; yet these words could hardly suffice for explaining concepts that have been refined. Hence it was necessary to fit to words otherwise received such meanings [as are, so to speak, in the usage of the School] as are entirely unknown to those who live outside the School. What is fairer, then, than that whenever some difficulty arises concerning the things themselves and their consideration, one should first weigh carefully those words whose manifold meaning can produce manifold difficulties, and, when the several meanings have been unfolded and separated, embrace from among many that one by which the thing itself can be conceived and explained fittingly? For so far holds the wise admonition of Epictetus, who used to say: "The beginning of learning is the consideration of names." To this consideration belongs also etymology; but since this is for the most part either uncertain or contributes very little to the consideration of the thing itself, we must judge that the Stoic of great name, and that most wise man, chiefly had in view the homonymies of words, to be unfolded with the help of distinctions for the explanation of the things themselves. For distinction is nothing other than the explanation of the manifold sense which words in some proposition can admit, according to common or doctrinal usage. This is done properly, with the reason of the thing as guide, when that manifold sense is first set forth in explanation, and then judgment applies discernment, rejecting one or more senses and admitting one as, so to speak, fitting. Yet no one should be tolerated as wantonly petulant in this, nor should the veracity that distinctions are meant to explain be hidden beneath the subtlety of distinctions, as once happened, not without truth, to those who bear the name of Scotus. Words themselves have admitted various meanings, and even more remote ones, according to our varied and manifold way of conceiving; nevertheless, there are three extremes to be guarded against here, and since many have been careless of them, they have made all distinctions suspect. I. Our concept must not stray so far from the thing about which one is working that it finds no foundation in it, but must always be consonant with the thing itself; or, as they say in the Schools, a formal distinction ought to correspond to an objective distinction. 2. No one should throw his own concepts at words that are not customarily used in common or learned speech, to serve as new and particular concepts requiring explanation. He is wrong indeed who, to throw dust in his adversary's eyes (though this often happens), attaches to his own assertion or argument a manifold sense, as it were to be explained by distinction, according to his own way of conceiving. Distinctions ought to be used primarily on account of words, and secondarily on account of the concepts of the mind. For although our mind, which cannot survey everything at one glance, needs many distinctions in order to explain things through them, these diversities of concepts are not properly distinctions but partial explanations of things which we cannot explain by one simple concept; whereas distinctions concern the words themselves, admitting, according to usage, a manifold meaning for a manifold concept. From the distinction or division of a name we pass to division properly so called, or division of the thing, which Sextus likewise labours to overturn in the second book of the Outlines of Pyrrhonism, chs. 19 and 20, but without reason. As for the division of a quantitative whole, since it is made through parts differing in magnitude or number, its sufficiency is clear from this: that those very parts, separated by the division, if they are taken together and joined again, make up the whole that was previously divided into parts. And this division, which is commonly called by the special name partition, is so evident and certain that even rustics and others unversed in learning think they can carry it out properly; not to mention that its truth and certainty are clearly demonstrated by mathematicians and geometers.

units.la: D d quamvis secúdum disjunctas artes hæc ipsa partitio, [ evincit Anatomia, nobilissimum partitionis genus instituens]ob membrorum disjuncta, inpeculiaria nomina, sæpe imperfecte duntaxat institui queat. Frustra vero admodum Sextus est, quando adversus certitudinem ejusdem l. d. ab exemplo quasi, sic cornicatur: Quum aliquis decadem in unum, & duo, & tria, & quatuor dividi ait, non dividitur in hæc decas. Nam simulatque ejus prima pars sublata est, [ut per concessionem hoc nunc demus] verbi gratia, unitas: sunt novem, & omnino aliud quiddam quam denarius. Aliorum ergo ablatio & divisio non jam fit à decade, sed ab aliquibus alijs, quæ, prout fit unaquæque ablatio, variantur. Iam ergo videamus qui possibile sit, totum dividere in ea, quæ dicuntur esse ejus partes. Nam si dividitur totum in partes, solent partes contineri in toto ante divisionem: at non continentur. Verbi gratia, [ut in decade rursum orationem nostram figamus] decadis partem dicunt omnino esse novem. (dividitur igitur in unum & novem) sed & octo similiter: (dividitur enim in octo & duo) & septem similiter, & sex, & quinque, & quatuor, & tria, & duo, & unum. Si igitur hæc omnia in decade continentur, & composita cum ea, quinquaginta quinque siunt, nimirum in decem continentur tur quinquaginta quinque, quod absurdum. Ergo ne continentur quidem in Decade ea, quæ dicuntur esse ejus partes, nec decas in ea dividi potest, ut totum in partes, quæ nullo modo in ipsa conspiciuntur. Huc usque Sextus.
units.tr: Although this same partition, according to the separate arts, can often be carried out only imperfectly because the parts of a body have their own separate names (anatomy, the noblest kind of partition, makes this plain), Sextus is quite wrong when, as if by way of example, he chatters against the certainty of the same division: he chatters thus. When someone says that a decad is divided into one, and two, and three, and four, it is not divided into these. For as soon as its first part is removed, granting for the sake of argument that it is the unit, nine remain, and something altogether different from a denarius. The removal and division of the other parts, therefore, is no longer made from the decad, but from some other things, which change with each removal. Let us now see how it is possible to divide the whole into what are said to be its parts. For if the whole is divided into parts, the parts are usually contained in the whole before the division; but these are not contained in it. For example, to fix our discussion again on the decad, they say that a part of the decad is nine (so it is divided into one and nine), and likewise eight (for it is divided into eight and two), and likewise seven, six, five, four, three, two and one. If then all these are contained in the decad, and when added to it make fifty-five, then fifty-five would be contained in ten, which is absurd. Therefore the things said to be its parts are not even contained in the decad, and the decad cannot be divided into them as a whole into parts, since they appear in no way in it. Thus far Sextus.

units.la: At ratiocinium ejusdem plane absurdum est: siquidem ut numerus coalescit ex multis unitatibus pro definiti numeri constitutione coëuntibus, sic quæque unitas in eo occurrens non debet considerari ratione numeri constituti, atque unitate una, aut pluribus ademptis, diversimode se habentis, sed tanquam unitas: nec divisio, quæ numero obtingit, per unius, aut plurium unitatum subductionem, relinquit numerum post subductas unitates reliquum, qui sit sui pars, sed qui potius sit numerus distinctus. nam V. C. à decade, sublata unitate, numerus novenarius, qui superest, non est amplius pars denarij numeri, sed numerus distinctus, quod non ignorabat quoque Aristoteles cum lib. 8. Metaph. cap. 3. sic scriberet: Si quid eorum, ex quibus numerus constat, ab eo ablatum, aut additum fuerit, non idem jam numerus, sed diversus existit, etiamsi minimum auferas. Et hæc dicta sufficiant pro vindicanda partitione. quod ad divisionem generis in species, sive totius potentialis, ut ea censetur vulgo divisio propriissime dicta, sic Sextus pariter eidem infestus est. at præter rationem. Nam quamvis difficillimum sit genus aliquod dividere, ad illius divisionem adhibendo omnia differentiarum propriarum genera, nec ea quoque explorata habeamus; operam tamen dare debemus, ut adhibitis pluribus differentijs, diversi licet ordinis, concurrentibus tamen ad componendam aliquam speciem, eandem speciem determinemus. Nam quod initio contra Sextum notandum, genus qua genus potentia duntaxat tum suas differentias tum species complectitur; cumque dividitur per differentias in suas species, ulterius actuatur, suaeque speciei tanquam composito inest ad modum materiæ, vice formalis principij cum materia illa concurrente differentia. nec tamen genus in specie occurrit secundum suam formalitatem, sic enim species generi deberet esse æqualis; sed solummodo secundum materiam, sive eam naturam quæ genus dicitur, quæ ad speciem comparata, ejus duntaxat pars est, quemadmodum & species duntaxat pars est individui. utque genus respectu speciei pars ejus essentialis est, ita essentia speciei sic in quoque individuo est, ut unoquoque individuum speciei pariter superaddat multas differentias accidentarias. Quod si notasset Sextus, distinxisset inter hæc duo: Homo ambulat, & Dion ambulat: ut enim ambulare non pertinet ad essentialia hominis praedicata, sic qua Dion, qua Theon pariter homines sunt, & participiant omnia hominis praedicata, simulque perpetuo manebunt homines, animalia rationalia, risibilia, potentia loquendi praedita, &c. etiamsi Dion forte ambulet, & Theon sedeat. Amplius frustra Sextus est, quando fingit genus merum noema, sive, ut vulgo in Scholis loquuntur, notionem secundam esse. nam distinguere convenit inter generis materiale, & ejusdem formale, sive naturam inexistentem speciebus & per species singularibus, eandemque abstractam ab utrisque. Verum quidem, qua genus, qua speciem non habere propriam existentiam, ea enim singularium tantum est; interim tamen singularibus reipsa natura inest; quae convenienter pro diverso respectu, & generis & speciei nomen ferre potest. Sed missō Sexto, redeo ad divisionem generis, atque ut convenienter eadem instituatur; haec duo amplius notanda.
units.tr: But his reasoning is plainly absurd. For just as a number is formed from many units coming together to constitute a definite number, so each unit occurring in it ought not be considered in relation to the constituted number, as differently disposed by the subtraction of one unit or several, but simply as a unit. Nor does the division that befalls a number, by subtracting one or more units, leave the number that remains after the units are subtracted as a part of itself; it leaves rather a distinct number. For, to take an example, when one is taken from ten, the remaining nine is no longer a part of the number ten but a distinct number. Aristotle did not fail to know this either, when in book 8 of the Metaphysics, chapter 3, he wrote: If anything of those things from which a number consists is taken away from it or added to it, it is no longer the same number but a different one, even if you take away the smallest thing. Let these points suffice for vindicating partition. As for the division of a genus into its species, or of a potential whole, which is commonly called division in the strictest sense, Sextus is equally hostile to it, and again without reason. For although it is very difficult to divide any genus, since we would have to apply all the kinds of proper differences, and we do not yet have these explored, we must nevertheless make the effort: applying several differences, of different orders though they be, which concur to make up some species, we determine that same species. For what must be noted at the outset against Sextus is this: the genus, as genus, contains its differences and species only potentially. When it is divided by differences into its species, it is further actualized and is present in its species as in a composite, after the manner of matter, with the differentia, which concurs with that matter, taking the place of the formal principle. Yet the genus does not occur in the species according to its formality, for then the species would have to be equal to the genus; it occurs only according to its matter, or that nature which is called the genus, which, compared with the species, is merely a part of it, just as the species is merely a part of the individual. And as the genus is an essential part of the species with respect to it, so the essence of the species is in each individual in such a way that each individual likewise adds many accidental differences to the species. If Sextus had noticed this, he would have distinguished between these two: Man walks and Dion walks. For as walking does not belong to the essential predicates of man, so Dion and Theon are equally men, whether considered as Dion or as Theon, and both share all the predicates of man, and will always remain men, rational, risible animals endowed with the power of speech, and so on, even if Dion happens to walk and Theon to sit. Furthermore, Sextus is wrong again when he pretends that the genus is a mere noema, or, as they commonly say in the schools, a second notion. For it is right to distinguish between the material of the genus and its formal aspect, that is, the nature existing in the species and in the singulars through the species, and abstracted from both. It is true that the genus as genus, and the species as species, do not have their own existence, for that belongs only to singulars; yet the nature itself really inheres in the singulars, and can rightly bear the name of genus or of species according to the different respect. But setting Sextus aside, I return to the division of a genus; and so that it may be carried out properly, two things need further attention.

units.la: I. Non temere prosiliendum ab uno differentiarum genere ad aliud. II. Nec temere dividendum per remotiores differentias. Ut vero duplici ratione genus, tanquam totum potentiale dividi potest, nempe aut per differentias, aut in species; ita illa dividendi ratio naturae, haec autem nostrae imbecillitati convenientior est. Hæc quidem pro divisione sufficere possent, nisi quædam se offerret difficultas: quam cum quidam occasione doctrinæ Peripateticæ in prejudicium divisionis arripuerint, omnino hic expediunda est; quoniam enim Peripateticorum constans sententia est, divisione nihil probare, inde inferunt illius doctrinam planè inutilem censendam esse. Quod ut distinctius explicari ac intelligi queat, haud abs re fuerit cuncta paulo altius accersivisse. Ergo notari debet hic non convenisse Aristoteli cum Platone; nam cum hic in Philebo dividendi peritiam donum Dei vocasset, & in Phædro instrumentum præcipuum veritatis indagandæ; adeo ut non solum addat, amare se divisiones, sed, si quem invenirat dividendi & componendi, pra alijs peritum, eundem se, ut Dei vestigia secuturum esse; Aristoteles non obscure lib. 1. Prior. Anal. cap. 32. eo nomine eum arguere instituit, addendo; divisionem esse syllogismum invalidum, supponere enim id, quod probandum erat, & hoc ignorasse aut eos, qui eadem usi sint, imo divisione seu dividendo aliquid probare velle, nihil aliud esse, quam principium petere. Idem inculcat lib. 2. Poster. Anal. cap. 5. ubi ita loquitur: Nulla est vis necessario concludendi in divisionibus, sed si qua est in iis inutilitas, in eo est quod aliquo modo ad explicandam & illustrandam rem valet. Atque hæc etiam ratio est, cur in Organo ex professo non agatur de divisione, cum ibi duntaxat tractetur argumentatio. Atque hæc Aristotelis sententia veritati est consentanea: nam quisquis aut distinguit, aut proprie dividit, rem quidem illustrat atque ob oculos ponit, aut ea quæ multiplicem sensum admittere possunt, distinguendo; aut ea per species & partes explicando, quę ut habent rationem totius, ita uno conceptu à nobis commode apprehendi non possunt: sed dum hoc fit, nihil probatur, sed apprehenditur quid ut manifestum, quod ut manifestius aut nobis aut aliis fiat, sive distinctio, sive divisio adhibetur. Sed etiamsi hæc ita se habeant, non tamen cum Scepticis ipsam divisionem explodere, ejusve certitudinem negare convenit: Logica enim intellectus operationibus plene suffic enterque debet succurrere, nec illius doctrina exhauritur (ut ab his, cum quibus congredimur, præsupponitur) sola tractatione de argumentatione.
units.tr: I. One should not leap rashly from one kind of difference to another. II. Nor should one divide rashly by remote differences. For just as a genus, as a potential whole, can be divided in two ways, namely either by differences or into species, so the former method of division is more suited to nature, and the latter to our weakness. These points might suffice for division, were it not for a difficulty that some have seized upon, on the occasion of Peripatetic doctrine, to the prejudice of division. Since the constant opinion of the Peripatetics is that nothing is proved by division, they infer that this doctrine must be judged entirely useless. So that this can be explained and understood more clearly, it will not be out of place to go back somewhat further. Here it must be noted that Aristotle did not agree with Plato. For while Plato in the Philebus called skill in division a gift of God, and in the Phaedrus the principal instrument for investigating truth, so that he not only adds that he loves divisions, but also that if he found anyone skilled above others in dividing and combining, he would follow him as the footsteps of God, Aristotle, in book 1 of the Prior Analytics, chapter 31, sets out to argue against him on this ground, adding that division is an invalid syllogism, for it assumes what was to be proved; and that those who used it were ignorant of this, indeed that wanting to prove something by division or by dividing is nothing other than begging the question. He repeats the same in book 2 of the Posterior Analytics, chapter 5, where he speaks thus: There is no force of necessary conclusion in divisions; but if there is any usefulness in them, it lies in the fact that they help in some way to explain and illustrate the matter. This is also the reason why division is not treated professedly in the Organon, since there only argumentation is discussed. And this opinion of Aristotle agrees with the truth. For whoever either distinguishes or properly divides does indeed illustrate a thing and set it before the eyes: either by distinguishing things that can admit of several senses, or by explaining, through species and parts, things which, since they have the character of a whole, cannot be conveniently grasped by us in a single concept. But while this is done, nothing is proved; rather something that is already manifest is apprehended, and distinction or division is employed so that it may become more manifest to us or to others. Yet even if these things are so, one should not, with the Sceptics, reject division itself or deny its certainty. For logic ought fully and sufficiently to assist the operations of the intellect, and its doctrine is not exhausted (as is presupposed by those with whom we contend) by the treatment of argumentation alone.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM QUINTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FIFTEEN.

units.la: Vindicantur Syllogismus & inductio, à Sexti, aliorumque objectionibus.
units.tr: Syllogism and induction are vindicated against the objections of Sextus and others.

units.la: POst definitionem ac divisionem, inter instrumenta Logica per Scepticos controversa, occurrit Syllogismus, de quo, ut & de Inductione, quæ vulgo eidem censetur opposita esse, hoc præsenti capite tractationem instituemus. Quantum quidem ad Syllogismum, (quem hic magis ratione formæ quam materiæ consideramus) ei præter Sextum l. d. cap. 14. jam olim infestus quoque fuit Cresconius Grammaticus, (videatur August. lib. 1. adv. Crel. cap. 14.) objecit siquidem Augustino Dialecticæ peritiam, propterea quod inter disputandum syllogismis uteretur: ne dicamus de quibusdam recentioribus erronibus Dialecticæ in universum adversantibus, de quibus erit agendi locus libro proximo. Quo vero ratione syllogismi omnia liquida sint, eumque vindicare queamus; quicquid aliis videatur, syllogismis sive argumentationibus sua constare debet ratio, & quisquis ijs bellum indicit, tantundem facit, atque si vellet hominem ratione, à qua sola commendari meretur, exuere. Cæterum priusquam argumentationis certitudinem astruere incipimus, in antececsum quædam [alias idem fecimus] fas est pręmittere. Ergo primo notandum, Syllogismum, sive argumentationem [hæc duoeodem à nobis loco habentur] nobis ad hoc inservire, ut intellectus nostri imbecillitas hac ratione emendetur, ac progrediendo ab uno ad alterum ea cognoscamus, quę una simpliciqtie notione comprehendere non possumus. hæc enim solius Dei perfectio est, quod uno simpliciq; intellectionis actu cuncta comprehendere queat, nec ratione sui yllogismo indigeat, quamvis sæpe eodem utatur, quo imbecillitati nostræ succurrat; quomodo parentes quoque sese dimittentes ad modulum suorum infantum, cum ijsdem balbutire, ac verba tertiata quartaqaue formare solent. Secundo progressus Syllogisticus, qui ratione formæ secundum certas figuras modosque instituitur, non est arbitrarius, aut solius artis opus; sed æque certus atque progressus Geometricus & Arithmeticus: nititur siquidem non solum regulis artis, sed cum maxime regulis naturalis consequentiæ: qua cum destituatur ex parte quarta figura, illegitima censetur; quamvis alias respondeat atque exacta sit ad regulas artificialis consequentiæ. Nec hoc verum solum est de prima figura, quæ examussim respondet iss regulis, quæ vulgo vocantur canrur de omni & nullo: verum etiam de secunda tertiaque figura. Imo etiam de syllogismis expositorijs, & compositis omnibus, ut ostendi hic posset, nisi alibi à nobis ex professo praestitum foret. Tertio argumentationem à Logica plene proponi existimandum; ita ut per eam succurratur omnibus illis defectibus atque erratis, quę in tertia mentis operatione oboriri solent. Vnde non inconvenienter à quibusdam iam olim statuta fuit duplex: Critica sive iudicatrix, & Topica sive inventrix; sic ut prior iudicij vitijs medicinam faciat, posterior vero ingenium torpidum excitet. Illa quadruplex rursum agnoscenda: Analytica prior falsitatem abigens; Analytica posterior dubium & incertitudinem fugans; Sophistica fallacias detegens; & Methodica confusionem omnem praecavens. Si omnes Logici ex aequo suo officio hic non suerint defuncti, nequaquam ipsi artiimputari debet. Nam errata artificum nefas est ipsi arti imputare, quum plurimum intersit inter artem in concreto & in abstracto consideratam. Hisce praemissis ad ipsius argumentationis sive Syllogismi in genere considerati confirmationem me accingo. Et quidem initio, qui Scripturae filij agnosci volunt, sic argumentantur: Quod instrumentum Logicum pro astruenda veritate adhibuit Paulus Aposto-lus lus: [quem in omnem veritatem deduxit Sp. Sanctus] illud tanquam legitimum pro astruenda veritate instrumentum agnosci debet: Sed illud ipsum Syllogismus seu Argumentatio est. Ergo. Major propositio adeo certa est, ut de eadem ambigere non liceat. Minor vero, ut ex multis sublimis hujus Apostoli locis probari posset, sic instar omnium potest esse illud, quod legitur ad Rom. 3. vers. 28. agens enim ibi Apostolus de hominis justificatione, quando primariam quaestionem concludendo decidit, ita inter alia expresse dicit: Ratiocinando igitur concludimus, [hoc est, ex antecedentibus, & ex illis, quae proposuimus, inferimus] hominem justificari ex fide. Praeterea elenchus nihil aliud est, quam Syllogismus cum contradictione conclusionis, ut eum definit Aristoteles lib. 1. Elench. Sophist. cap. 1. sive, est talis syllogismus quo alteri contradicitur: Apostolus vero in Epistola ad Titum, instruens Episcopum, cap. 1. verf. 9. vult eum idoneum esse ad hoc ut possit contradicentes redarguere. Qui Elenchus non potest sane institui ab eo, qui Syllogisticae doctrinae, & consequenter Logicę ignarus est. At omisso Paulo, ita deinceps pro vindicando Syllogismo argumentamur: Ad quod omnes homines naturae instinctu feruntur, illud certitudinem aliquam habere bere, & artis subsidio absolvi posse, certum est. At ad construendos syllogismos omnes omnino homines naturæ instinctu feruntur. Ergo. Major propositio extra omnem dubij aleam collocata, atque in præcedentibus aliquoties asserta fuit. Minor pariter certissima est, siquidem animad vertere licet ipsos idiotas, atque homines ab omni literarum cultu remotos, sæpissime syllogismos, maxime in Barbara contexere; nec solum in perfectissimo modo perfectissimæ figuræ, verum etiam in secunda, tertiaque figura. Quotiescunque enim alter alteri obloquitur, negationis suæ certa allata ratione, toties ferme in secunda figura argumentatur: quomodo in tertia figura sub manum syllogismus nascitur, quando aut aliquis suam assertionem ab exemplo confirmare vult, aut alterius propositionem pariter ab exemplo evertere. Ignoratur quidem inter vulgus, quid sit syllogismus; sed sapientes, qui ad cuiusque discursus attendunt, vident imperitiores quoque haud aliter inter discurrendum satisfacere legibus consequentiæ, ac si Logicis magistris per meliorem ætatis suæ partem operam dedissent. Ut vero ars naturam præsupponit, & non ad eversionem, sed ad perfectionem illius tendit; sic pariter Logica artificialis, quando occupatur in doctrina de Syllogismo, præsupponit naturalis consequentiæ certitudinem, omniaque, quę de Syllogismo proponit præcepta, sic consentanea debent esse regulis naturalis consequentiæ, ut si ijs non responderint, falsa & erronea haberi debeant. Hoc unum argumentum quod instar omnium esse queat, eidem alia non superaddo. Quo adversarijs rationibus, speciose adduci solitis plene satisfiat, initio ad quos Scripturæ textus, quibus multi hic abuti consueverunt, respondere convenit. Prior occurrit ad Rom. cap. 1. verf. 21. vbi Apostolus de Gentilibus testatur, quod vani facti sint in suis ratiocinationibus. Sed eo loco non arguitur simpliciter & absolute actus mentis discursivus, sive ratiocinatio; sed ejusdem abusus. siquidem hic ipse Apostolus disputasse legitur ex Scripturis cum Iudæis, Act. 17. verf. 2. & conflictatus esse cum ipsis Stoicis, ib. verf. 18. qui tamen soli Logicam censebantur possidere. Multo minus adversatur alter locus 2. Cor. 10. verf. 4. quando enim Paulus dicit: Arma militiæ nostræ non sunt carnalia, sed divinitus valida ad destructionem munitionum: ratiocinationes evertendo, omnemque sublimitatem: nequaquam quid prejudicatum vult aut legitimo ratiocinio, aut syllogistico discursui, siquidem proximis verbis innuit, quasnam ratiocinationes Christi doctrina & fi-
units.tr: After definition and division, the instruments of logic that the Sceptics dispute, we come to the syllogism. In this chapter we will treat it, and induction too, which is commonly regarded as opposed to it. As for the syllogism, which here we consider more with regard to its form than its matter: besides Sextus, in the place cited above, Cresconius the Grammarian long ago also attacked it (see Augustine, book 1 against Cresconius, chap. 14). He charged Augustine with knowledge of dialectic because he used syllogisms in debate. I say nothing of certain more recent men who are wholly hostile to dialectic, of whom there will be occasion to speak in the next book. But in order that all things about syllogism be clear, and that we may vindicate it, whatever others may think, the reasoning of syllogisms or arguments must stand on its own, and whoever declares war on them does the same as if he wished to strip a man of reason, the only thing by which he deserves to be commended. Moreover, before we begin to establish the certainty of argument, it is permissible to set out some preliminary points (we have done the same elsewhere). So, first, it should be noted that the syllogism, or argument (these two we here regard as the same), serves us for this purpose: that the weakness of our understanding may be remedied by this method, and by advancing from one thing to another we may know those things which we cannot grasp in one simple notion. For it is the perfection of God alone that he can comprehend all things in a single simple act of understanding, and needs no syllogism for his own sake, although he often uses it to help our weakness, just as parents, when they lower themselves to the level of their infants, are accustomed to stammer with them and to form words in threes and fours. Second, the syllogistic progression, which is set up according to certain figures and moods with regard to form, is not arbitrary, nor the work of art alone. It is as certain as the progression of geometry and arithmetic. For it rests not only on the rules of art but above all on the rules of natural consequence. Since it lacks these in the fourth figure, that figure is judged illegitimate, although in other respects it corresponds to the rules of artificial consequence and is exact. Nor is this true only of the first figure, which corresponds exactly to those rules commonly called the canons of de omni and de nullo, but also of the second and third figures. Indeed the same holds of expository syllogisms and all compound ones, as could be shown here, were it not already done by us professedly elsewhere. Third, it must be thought that logic fully sets forth argument, so that by it all those defects and errors that usually arise in the third operation of the mind are remedied. Hence it was long ago not unfittingly laid down by some that there are two kinds: critical, or judging, and topical, or inventive, so that the former provides a remedy for the faults of judgment, and the latter rouses a sluggish mind. The former is again to be recognised as fourfold: prior analytics, which drives away falsity; posterior analytics, which flees doubt and uncertainty; sophistical, which detects fallacies; and methodical, which guards against all confusion. If not all logicians have discharged their duty in this matter, the fault must in no way be imputed to the art itself. For it is wrong to impute the errors of practitioners to the art itself, since there is a great difference between art considered in the concrete and in the abstract. With these things premised, I now set myself to confirm the argument, or syllogism, considered in general. And indeed, at the outset, those who wish to be recognised as sons of Scripture argue thus: The logical instrument that the Apostle Paul used to establish truth [whom the Holy Spirit led into all truth] must be acknowledged as a lawful instrument for establishing truth. But the syllogism or argument is that very instrument. Therefore... The major premise is so certain that it is not permissible to doubt it. The minor, which could be proved from many passages of this sublime Apostle, can, as a representative of all, be that which is read at Rom. 3, verse 28. For there the Apostle, treating of the justification of man, when he decides the main question by concluding, says among other things expressly: Therefore we conclude by reasoning [that is, from the antecedents, and from those things which we have set forth, we infer] that a man is justified by faith. Besides, elenchus is nothing other than a syllogism with the contradiction of the conclusion, as Aristotle defines it in book 1 of the Sophistical Elenchi, chap. 1; or it is such a syllogism by which one is contradicted. The Apostle, moreover, in his Epistle to Titus, instructing the bishop, chap. 1, verse 9, wants him to be fit to be able to refute those who contradict. Certainly such elenchus cannot be conducted by one who is ignorant of syllogistic doctrine and consequently of logic. But, setting Paul aside, we argue thus in defence of the syllogism: That to which all men are carried by natural instinct, and which has some certainty and can be perfected with the help of art, is certain. But all men without exception are carried by natural instinct to construct syllogisms. Therefore... The major premise, placed beyond all doubt, has been asserted several times above. The minor is equally certain, since one may observe that even simple people, and men far removed from all cultivation of letters, very often construct syllogisms, especially in Barbara, and not only in the most perfect mood of the most perfect figure, but also in the second and third figures. For whenever one person contradicts another, after giving a sure reason for his denial, he almost always argues in the second figure. In the same way a syllogism arises at hand in the third figure, when someone wishes to confirm his assertion by an example, or equally to overturn another's proposition by an example. Among the common people, indeed, what a syllogism is goes unknown; but wise men, who attend to the reasoning of each person, see that even the less educated, in their discourse, satisfy the laws of consequence no differently than if they had spent the better part of their life under logical teachers. But just as art presupposes nature, and tends not to its overthrow but to its perfection, so too artificial logic, when it occupies itself with the doctrine of the syllogism, presupposes the certainty of natural consequence, and all the precepts it sets forth concerning the syllogism must so agree with the rules of natural consequence that, if they do not correspond to them, they must be held false and erroneous. I will not add other arguments to this one, which can stand in place of all. So that the objections of adversaries, commonly brought forward with plausible show, may be fully met, it is fitting first to answer the passages of Scripture which many have been accustomed to misuse here. The first presents itself at Rom. 1, verse 21, where the Apostle testifies of the Gentiles that they became vain in their reasonings. But in that place there is not simply and absolutely argued the discursive act of the mind, or reasoning, but its abuse. For this same Apostle is read to have disputed with the Jews from the Scriptures, Acts 17, verse 2, and to have contended with the Stoics themselves, ib. verse 18, who nevertheless were alone thought to possess logic. Much less does the other passage, 2 Cor. 10, verse 4, oppose it. For when Paul says: The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds, casting down reasonings and every high thing, he by no means prejudges either lawful reasoning or syllogistic discourse, since in the immediately following words he indicates what reasonings the doctrine of Christ and fi-

units.la: des dis perferre non queant, quando dicit talem sublimitatem complanandam, quae sese extollit adversus cognitionem Dei. Pro reliquorum dubiorum solutione, proxime sequentia notentur.
units.tr: ...which they cannot bear, since he says that such loftiness, which raises itself against the knowledge of God, must be levelled. For the solution of the remaining doubts, the following points should be noted.

units.la: I. Syllogismus non solum servit eruendae veritati, quatenus ea illius subsidio ex certis principiis deducitur, sed cum maxime eidem asserendae atque confirmandae, imo dijudicandae quoque: quatenus non potest non veritas illa esse certa atque liquida, quae syllogismo inclusa aequaliter sese habet.
units.tr: I. The syllogism serves not only to draw out truth, insofar as truth is deduced from certain principles with its help, but it serves much more to assert and confirm it, and indeed to judge it. For that truth which is contained in a syllogism and stands equally firm cannot fail to be certain and clear.

units.la: II. Doctrina de Syllogismo haut magis aut circulum prodit, aut incertitudinis argui potest, quod per alium syllogismum haberi non queat, atque definitio ipsius definitionis: siquidem instrumenta Logica reflexe considerari quoq; debent, atque sic aliis applicariae inservire, ut etiam sibi inserviant. Praeterea multum interest inter syllogismum in communi, sive, ut in Scholis loquuntur, in actu signato consideratum, eundemque ut particularem, spectatumque in actu exercito. Doctrina de Syllogismo in communi astruitur & confirmatur per syllogismum particularem.
units.tr: II. The doctrine of the syllogism neither produces a circle nor can it be charged with uncertainty because it cannot be established through another syllogism, and because it is not defined by a definition of itself. Logical instruments must also be considered reflexively, so that they serve to be applied to other things and also serve themselves. Moreover, there is a great difference between the syllogism considered in general, or, as the schools put it, in the explicit act, and the same syllogism considered as particular, that is, viewed in its exercised act. The doctrine of the syllogism in general is established and confirmed by a particular syllogism.

units.la: III. Falsus est Sextus, quando existimat in Syllogismo, secundum regulas de omni & nullo quasi progrediente, committi circulum, quod conclusio, particularior quasi, quae infertur, serviat probationi propositionis universalioris: siquidem propositio universalis tam diu talis censetur, quam adversus illam non possit dari instantia alicujus exempli contrarij, legitimeque ab omni ad aliquid tam diu proceditur; quam de illo aliquo certum fit illud sub omni contineri. Eoque, quamvis hæc propositio neque fit de omni neque necessaria, Omnis verus Philosophus habet multos æmulos, nihilominus Enthymematice quoque inferre licet; Socrates habuit multos æmulos: quoniam de Socrate certum est, eum contineri sub veris illis Philosophis, quorum hæc fors fuit. IV. In illatione difjunctiva, affumptum verum censetur, non ratione majoris, quam qua talem recte Sextus dubiam esse censet; sed quoniam quod enunciatur, cum eo, de quo enunciatur, confentit. Ut V. C. cum dico: Aut dies est, aut nox: hactenus mihi quidem dubium est, fitne dies vel nox; sed quando fubfumo, Cum sol est ortus est dies, Ergo, Cum sol est ortus non est nox, amplius dubitare non licet, quin fugatis tenebris, per exortum Solis dies illuxerit. Et hæc quidem pro Syllogismo dicta sufficiant, converto deinceps me ad Inductionem, quæ Syllogifmo censetur opposita. quamvis alij, sed præter rationem laborarint ostendere, hæc duo sciendi instrumenta cognata esse. nam ut ille progreditur ab universalioribus ad magis particularia; ita hæc ordine inverso procedit, non quidem à singularibus ad universalia; (uti multi perperam tradere instituerunt) sed à minus universalibus ad magis universalia. Cumque singularia sensibus percipiantur, atque universalia qua talia soli intellectui, seu rationi objiciantur, neutiquam insuper habegeneral ri debet, quod habet Aristoteles lib. 1. Topic. cap. 13. ubi recte censet, inductionem quidem verisimiliorem & apertiorem esse, sensuumque judicio familiariorem & notiorem, ac vulgo usitatiorem; at syllogismum magis urgere, & ad eos, qui contradicunt, refellendos potentiorem esse. Ut vero hoc argumentandi genere, testè Aristot. lib. 1. & lib. 5. Metaph. Socrates frequenter uti solet; sic, in tribus potissimum casibus illius usus esse solet. 1. Epagogæ sive Inductiones in inveniendis scientiis utramque paginam faciunt, atque cum primis attendi debent. Quemadmodum enim omnis cognitio (ut jam antea à nobis declaratum fuit) à sensu initium suum trahit, sic prima quoque scientiarum primordia per Inductionem constituuntur. Iique, qui in scientiis fundandis occupantur, aut jam olim occupati fuerunt, inductive progredi debuerunt. II. Inductionibus locus est, quotiescunque in dubium vocantur primæ veritates, atque principia per se alias indemonstrabilia. Cum enim ex prioribus demonstrari non queant, veritas & certitudo eorum probantur per inductionem, atque adductis quibusdam singularibus, in quibus ejusmodi principiorum veritas elucescit, eorundem pariter certitudo ob oculos poni censetur.
units.tr: III. Sextus is wrong when he thinks that, in a syllogism following the rules of "of all" and "of none," a circle is committed, because the conclusion, being in a sense more particular, which is drawn, serves to prove the more universal premise. For a universal proposition is taken to be such for as long as no instance of a contrary example can be brought against it, and one proceeds legitimately from the all to some particular for as long as it is certain of that particular that it falls under the all. Hence, although this proposition, Every true philosopher has many rivals, is neither said of all nor necessary, one may nevertheless infer by enthymeme: Socrates had many rivals, since it is certain of Socrates that he is contained among those true philosophers whose lot this perhaps was. IV. In a disjunctive inference, the assumed premise is taken to be true, not on the ground of the major premise, which Sextus rightly considers doubtful as such, but because what is stated agrees with that of which it is stated. For instance, when I say: Either it is day or it is night: so far, indeed, it is doubtful to me whether it is day or night; but when I subsume, When the sun has risen, it is day, therefore, When the sun has risen, it is not night, it is no longer lawful to doubt that, the darkness having been dispelled, day has dawned through the rising of the sun. And let these things suffice as said about the syllogism. I now turn to induction, which is held to be opposed to the syllogism, although others have laboured, but without reason, to show that these two instruments of knowing are related. For while the one proceeds from the more universal to the more particular, this one proceeds in the reverse order, not indeed from singulars to universals (as many have wrongly undertaken to teach), but from less universal things to more universal ones. And since singulars are perceived by the senses, while universals as such are presented only to the intellect or reason, it must by no means be disregarded what Aristotle says in Topics book 1, chapter 13, where he rightly holds that induction is indeed more probable and clearer, more familiar and better known to the judgement of the senses, and more commonly used; but the syllogism presses harder and is more powerful in refuting those who contradict. Moreover, just as Socrates, as Aristotle attests in Metaphysics books 1 and 5, was accustomed to use this kind of argument frequently, so its use is usually found in three main cases. 1. Epagogai, or inductions, in discovering the sciences, serve both sides and must be attended to above all. For just as all knowledge (as we have already declared above) takes its beginning from the senses, so too the first beginnings of the sciences are established through induction. And those who are occupied in founding the sciences, or who were occupied in this long ago, have had to proceed inductively. II. There is room for induction whenever first truths and principles which are otherwise indemonstrable in themselves are called into doubt. For since they cannot be demonstrated from prior things, their truth and certainty are proved by induction, and, by adducing certain singulars in which the truth of such principles shines forth, their certainty is likewise held to be set before our eyes.

units.la: III. Servit quoque Inductio populari judicio, atque comprobationi popularium eorum, quae Syllogismo inclusa ex vulgi judicio minus evidentem probationem nancisci censentur. Sic Socrates, qui, si Aristoteli credimus lib. 13. Metaph. cap. 4. Inductionem invenerit, apud Platonem in Protagora, probaturus virtutem esse scientiam, Inductione utitur, ostendendo variis exemplis prolatis, quae ibi occurrunt ac legi possunt, optimos illos esse, qui earum rerum, quas tractant, peritissimi sint. Pro quocunque autem usu Inductio adhibeatur, fas est, pro colligenda & inferenda Conclusione universaliori, enumerare omnia minus universalia. quod cum ratione singularium, quae ad digitos revocari non possunt, vix fieri quoque posse videatur, sufficit modo aliqua enumerare, & addere reliquorum eandem esse rationem. quae enumeratio, licet minus in speciem sufficiens, nihilominus subsistit tam diu, quam non possit vel unum aliquod individuum adferri, cujus dispar ratio fit. quod si cogitasset Sextus Empiricus, haud quaquam lib. 2. Pyrrh. Hypoth. cap. 15. sic scripsisset: Inductionis modum facile rejici posse existimo, quoniam enim volunt per eam probare universale ex particularibus, aut omnia percurrentes particularia hoc facient, aut aliqua. Sed si quidem aliqua percurrent, non erit firma inductio, quum fieri possit ut aliqua ex praetermissis particularibus in inductione, contraria reperiantur universali. Sin omnia percurrere instituerint, aggredientur impossibilia, quum infinita sint particularia, nullisque terminis circumscripta. Haec ille.
