Pariter frustra illi sunt, qui in inductione notantes circulum, existimant idem per idem probari. quamvis enim singularia simul sumpta realiter idem sint cum universali, ratione tamen ab eodem distinguuntur. Non insolens vero ut aliquid probetur per illud, a quo non re, sed ratione solum differt. Sic genus potest probare speciem a qua ratione solum differt, itemque definitum probare potest definitionem, ac vicissim haec illud.
units.tr: III. Induction also serves popular judgement, and the confirmation of those popular views which, contained in a syllogism, are thought to have less evident proof from the judgement of the common people. Thus Socrates, who, if we believe Aristotle in Metaphysics book 13, chapter 4, invented induction, uses it in Plato's Protagoras, when he is about to prove that virtue is knowledge, by setting forth various examples which occur and can be read there, showing that those are the best who are most skilled in the things they handle. Whatever use induction is put to, it is lawful, in order to gather and infer a more universal conclusion, to enumerate all the less universal instances. Since, on account of the singulars, which cannot be counted on the fingers, this seems scarcely possible to do, it is enough merely to enumerate some and to add that the rest are of the same kind. Such an enumeration, although less sufficient in form, nevertheless holds good for as long as not even one single individual can be brought forward whose case is different. If Sextus Empiricus had considered this, he would certainly not have written in Outlines of Pyrrhonism book 2, chapter 15: "I think the mode of induction can easily be rejected, since, if they wish to prove the universal from particulars through it, they will either run through all the particulars or some. But if they run through some, the induction will not be firm, since it can happen that some contrary instance to the universal is found among the particulars passed over in the induction. But if they undertake to run through all, they will attempt impossibilities, since the particulars are infinite and bounded by no limits." Haec ille. Equally vain are those who, noting a circle in induction, think that the same is proved by the same. For although singulars taken together are really the same as the universal, they are nevertheless distinguished from it in reason. It is not unusual for something to be proved by that from which it differs only in reason and not in fact. Thus a genus can prove a species from which it differs only in reason, and likewise a thing defined can prove the definition, and conversely the definition the thing defined.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM SEPTIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SEVENTEEN.

units.la: Asseritur Demonstratio, nobilissimum sciendi instrumentum adversus Sextum, aliosque pariter agitur de Demonstrationibus Mathematicis, Theologicis, & ad Impossibile.
units.tr: The demonstration is asserted, the noblest instrument of knowing against Sextus; and there is also discussion of mathematical, theological, and reductio ad impossibile demonstrations.

units.la: DEvenimus ad Demonstrationem, quam ut convenienter adversus Sextum, reliquosque, qui eidem infesti sunt, tutari queamus, ante omnia ipsum nomen, ne cui propter ambiguitatem imponat, distinguere convenit. Atque initio quidem notamus dari Demonstrationes quasdam proprie sic dictas, consideratas, velut nobilissima sciendi instrumenta, ab Aristotele in libris Posteriorum Analyticorum, praeter quas agnoscere convenit alias secundario duntaxat tales, quas, distinctionis gratia, hic iterum triplices facimus: Mathematicas, Theologicas, & secundum impossibile. Fateor à multis has triplices Demonstrationes cum alteris confundi: at perperam. sicut ex iis, quae deinceps dicenda erunt, liquebit. Nec hoc ignotum antiquis Scepticis, qui ut infestissimi fuerunt Demonstrationibus, sic, sub nomine earundem, illas duntaxat intellexere, quas tam scrupulose vero vulgo ad demonstrationem propter quid, sive ad Demonstrationem proprie sic dictam, quatenus sunt ex prioribus & notioribus, quae in Mathematicis (quod veriores caussae non adsint) eodem loco censentur, ac si essent verae rei caussae. Idcirco principia Mathematica (Ammonius ea tantum statuit esse effata] convenienter ab Aristotele lib. 1. Eth. Eudem. cap. 6. similitudine principia vocantur. Ideo vero certae censentur demonstrationes huius ordinis, quoniam Mathesios propositiones adeo notae ac perspicuae sunt, ut vel sensibus ipsis patereant, usque adeo, ut non possimus non, terminis modo cognitis, ijsdem firmissime assentiri, ut docebat jam olim Simplicius ad lib. 1. de Anima, cap. 11. Atque hinc ipse Proclus ad lib. 1. Euclidis haut gravate concedit, Mathesin non gaudere demonstrationibus perfectissimis, quod omnia fere mathematica theoremata, plurimis modis, multisque diagrammatis ostendi queant. Quae si veras & proprie dictas caussas haberent, unius effecti tantum unica, vera, eaque propria caussa esset. Effata vero illa, quorum ex Ammonio facta fuit mentio, priora & notiora habentur, quoniam sunt maxime communia, simplicissima, firmissime credita, nulla probatione indigentia, & conclusionem necessario demonstrantia: quare
units.tr: We come to demonstration. So that we may defend it properly against Sextus and the others who are hostile to it, it is fitting first of all to distinguish the very name, lest anyone impose on it because of its ambiguity. At the outset we note that there are certain demonstrations properly so called, considered by Aristotle in the books of the Posterior Analytics as the noblest instruments of knowing. Besides these, it is fitting to recognise others that are such only in a secondary sense, which for the sake of distinction we here divide again into three kinds: mathematical, theological, and that from the impossible. I admit that these three kinds of demonstration are often confused with the others, but wrongly, as will be clear from what follows. Nor was this unknown to the ancient Sceptics, who, as they were most hostile to demonstrations, understood by that name only those which the common run of people so carelessly take to be demonstration of the reason why (demonstratio propter quid), or demonstration properly so called, insofar as they proceed from prior and better-known premises. In mathematics these are counted in the same place as if they were true causes of the thing, since truer causes are not present. Hence Ammonius held that mathematical principles are only sayings, and Aristotle, in the first book of the Eudemian Ethics, chapter 6, fittingly calls them principles by similitude. Such demonstrations are considered certain because the propositions of mathematics are so well known and clear that they are evident even to the senses, so much so that, once the terms are known, we cannot help assenting to them most firmly. Simplicius taught this long ago in his commentary on the first book of On the Soul, chapter 11. From this Proclus, in his commentary on the first book of Euclid, readily concedes that mathematics does not enjoy the most perfect demonstrations, since almost all mathematical theorems can be shown in many ways and by many diagrams. If these had true and properly so called causes, each effect would have only one true and proper cause. But those sayings mentioned by Ammonius are held to be prior and better known, since they are most common, most simple, firmly believed, in need of no proof, and necessarily demonstrate the conclusion. For this reason, in mathematics they are counted in almost the same place (where truer causes do not occur) as if they were the true causes of the thing. So much for mathematical demonstrations. Theological demonstrations follow. These too are demonstrations only improperly so called. But when they are referred here to theology, it is fitting to understand by this only revealed theology. Since all its conclusions must be resolved into the revealed Word of God, as the Apostle says in Romans 10:17, as their sole principle, everything it draws from this storehouse must be held to have the same authority that belongs to God himself, who is truth itself (John 14:3) and cannot lie (Titus 1:3). These conclusions, referred to their principle, cannot be regarded as demonstrations of the kind we shall consider later according to Aristotle. For they have the character not of a cause flowing into its effect, but of testimony. Nevertheless, the certainty of theological principles, which have been divinely revealed, is greater than that of philosophical principles, which, because of the corrupt nature of man, are covered in much darkness and depraved by various errors, so that often those things are held to be principles which are not principles. Therefore demonstrations in theology are more certain than in philosophy itself. These are not to be considered philosophically, or according to what Aristotle proposes in the Posterior Analytics, but only according to the reason of God himself, whose word possesses the same authority that must be attributed to him, that is, the highest. Clement of Alexandria, in the second book of the Stromata, when he disputes against the Gentiles who thought that the theology of the Christians lacked demonstrations, says among other things, not inappropriately: That alone is the true demonstration among you which is supplied from the divine Scriptures. From this it may be inferred that theological demonstrations, however certain, carry weight only with one who is persuaded of the divine and consequently infallible authority of holy Scripture. For all theological demonstrations, insofar as they are resolved into Scripture itself, are in the same way referred through Scripture to God himself, the author of the Scriptures,

units.la: E e 4 quare eodem fere loco censentur in Mathematicis [ubi veriores caussæ non occurrunt] ac si essent veræ rei caussæ. Et tantum quidem de Demonstrationibus Mathematicis: succedunt Theologicæ. Quæ & ipsæ sunt demonstrationes improprie ita dicte: ut vero hic referuntur ad Theologiam, sic per hanc intelligere convenit solam Theologiam revelatam: cujus conclusiones omnes quoniam debent resolvi in revelatum Dei verbum [juxta illa, quæ habet Apostolus ad Rom. 10. vers. 17] tanquam unicum earum principium, pariter omnia, quę depromit ex hoc narthecio, tantæ censeri debent authoritatis, quanta ipsi Deo, qui est ipsa veritas, Ioh. 14. vers. 3, & mentiri non potest, Tit. 1. v. 3. competit. Conclusiones quidem hæ ad suum principium relatæ, non possunt censeri tales demonstrationes, quales secundum Aristotelem deinceps considerabimus; neque enim caussæ in suum effectum influentis, sed testimonij, rationem habent: interim quanto major est certitudo principiorum Theologicorum, quæ divinitus revelata sunt, quam principiorum Philosophicorum, quę propter corruptam hominis naturam multa caligine contecta sunt, & variis erroribus depravata, sic, ut sæpe pro principiis habeantur ea, quę principia non sunt; tanto certiores dantur demonstrationes in Theologia, quam in ipla Philosophia, non considerandę quidem Philosophice, aut secundum ea, quæ in posterioribus Analyticis proponit Aristoteles, sed duntaxat secundum rationem ipsius Dei, cujus verbo eadem authoritas, quæ ei ipsi deferri debet, hoc est summa. Non inconvenienter Clemens Alexandrinus lib. 2. Strom. quando disputat contra Gentiles, qui censebant Theologiam Christianorum destitutam esse demonstrationibus, inter alia dicit: Ea sola apud vos est vera demonstratio, quæ ex divinis suppeditatur Scripturis: unde inferre licet, Demonstrationes Theologicas, quantumvis certas, pondus non habere, nisi apud eum, qui persuasus est de divina, & consequenter infallibili authoritate sacræ Scripturæ. omnes siquidem demonstrationes Theologicæ, ut resolvuntur in ipsam Scripturam, sic per Scripturam referuntur ad ipsum Deum, Scripturarum authorem,
units.tr: for which reason they are counted in Mathematics (where truer causes do not occur) almost in the same place as if they were the true causes of the thing. So much for mathematical demonstrations; theological ones follow. These too are demonstrations only improperly so called. But when they are referred here to theology, it is fitting to understand by this only revealed theology, whose conclusions, since they must all be resolved into the revealed Word of God (according to what the Apostle says in Romans 10:17) as their sole principle, must be held to have as much authority as belongs to God himself, who is truth and cannot lie (John 14:3; Titus 1:3). Such conclusions, referred to their principle, cannot be counted as demonstrations of the kind we shall later consider according to Aristotle, for they have the character not of a cause flowing into its effect but of testimony. Yet the more certain the principles of theology, which have been divinely revealed, are than the principles of philosophy, which are covered in much darkness through the corrupt nature of man and depraved by various errors, so that often things are held to be principles which are not principles, the more certain are the demonstrations in theology than in philosophy itself. These are to be considered not philosophically, nor according to what Aristotle proposes in the Posterior Analytics, but only according to the reason of God himself, whose word carries the same authority that is due to him, which is the highest. Clement of Alexandria, in the second book of the Stromata, not inappropriately, when he disputes against the Gentiles who thought that Christian theology lacked demonstrations, says among other things: That alone is the true demonstration among you which is supplied from the divine Scriptures. Hence it may be inferred that theological demonstrations, however certain, have weight only with one who is persuaded of the divine and consequently infallible authority of holy Scripture. For all theological demonstrations, insofar as they are resolved into Scripture itself, are likewise referred through Scripture to God himself, the author of the Scriptures,

units.la: 2. Tim. 3. 16. 2. Pet. 1. 20. 21. adeo ut omnes illi, [de his aliquid monemus lib. prox.] qui, sive directe, sive indirecte authoritatem sacrarum literarum labefactare instituunt, quantum in se ipsam Theologiam suis demonstrationibus, hoc est, sua certitudine [quæ ipsius gloria] exuere laborent. Succedit demonstratio ab impossibili (alias dicta deductio ad impossibile) quæ pariter pertinet ad modos demonstrationis improprie sic dictos, hoc vero commune habet cum duobus præcedentibus modis, quod pariter procedat ex communissimo principio, quod hoc est: Non potest simul esse & non esse. Fateor, quosdam non infimi subsellij Philosophos, hanc quasi Demonstrationem consuevisse vocare demonstrationem à priori: sed cum non instituatur per caussam tanquàm medium, sed duntaxat per medium extrinsecum, sive, incomparabilitatem contradictoriorum, potius ad demonstrationes secundario sic dictas refertur. Interim propter axioma, cujus jam facta fuit mentio, & cui innititur, non minus certa est, atque quaelibet demonstratio à priori. Quod quis vero miretur, emersit homo fanaticus hoc seculo, qui certitudinem atque indubitatam veritatem hujus demonstrationis ausus fuit convellere. Intelligo Valentinum Weigelium, sive illam omnium hæresium sententiam: cujus hoc offatum est, in Scholagratia, ut loquitur, duo contradictoria simul vera esse posse. Quod portentiosum dogma si valere debeat, Deus non solum erit mutabilis, atque seipsum negabit, verum etiam inter veritatem & mendacium nullum intercedet discrimen, confundetur omnis historiæ certitudo, nec ulli dogmati constabit sua certitudo, aut ullus propter ullum errorem poterit argui; imo falsus fuerit ipse Apostolus Paulus, quando 2. Cor. 1. verf. 19. sic scribit: Dei filius Iesus Christus, qui inter vos, per nos prædicatus est, &c. non fuit etiam & non, sed etiam fuit in ipso. Tam absurda vero hæc Weigelij assertio, ut non sine ratione jam olim dixerit Avicenna lib. 1. Metaphys. de iis, qui receptæ huic veritati obloqui præsumerent, verberandos esse hos tales aut igni exponendos tam diu, donec agnoscant, non esse idem verberari & non verberari, comburi & non comburi. Ut non sit necessum expendere rationes, quibus male-sanus homo absono suo effato studet patrocinari, quamvis & hoc accurate factum sit, à Rever. D. Iohanne Crocio in Examine Theol. Weigel. Hoc unum solum addo, Weigelium hic præcursores non tam antiquos hæreticos habuisse, quam quosdam ex Rabbinorum gente. Scribit quippe R. Salomo Jarchi commentans in locum Deuter. 17. 11. Iuxta legem, quam docuerint te, & juxta judicium, quod dixerint tibi facies, etc. etiamsi dixerint Rabbini de manu dextra, quod sinistra sit, & de manu sinistra, quod dextra sit, credendum in eo Iudæo esse. Idem docere R. Bechai, & R. Mosche Ben Nachman, author est Celeberrimus Buxtorfius in Synag. Judaica cap. 1.
units.tr: (2 Tim. 3. 16; 2 Pet. 1. 20. 21), so that all those who, whether directly or indirectly, set about weakening the authority of the sacred letters, labour to strip theology itself of its demonstrations, that is, of its certainty, which is its glory, so far as lies in them. [We shall say something about these matters in the next book.] A demonstration from the impossible follows (otherwise called reduction to the impossible). This also belongs to the modes of demonstration improperly so called. It has in common with the two preceding modes that it proceeds from the most universal principle, which is this: It cannot be that the same thing both is and is not. I admit that certain philosophers of no low rank have been accustomed to call this a demonstration as it were from the prior, but since it is not carried out through a cause as the middle term, but only through an extrinsic middle term, namely the incompatibility of contradictories, it is rather referred to demonstrations that are so called only in a secondary sense. Nevertheless, on account of the axiom already mentioned, on which it rests, it is no less certain than any demonstration from the prior. What someone may wonder at is that in this century a fanatic has arisen who dared to overthrow the certainty and indubitable truth of this demonstration. I mean Valentin Weigel, or rather that opinion of all heresies, whose saying, as he puts it in the Scholagratia, is this: two contradictories can be true at the same time. If this monstrous dogma were to hold, God would not only be mutable and would deny himself, but there would also be no distinction between truth and falsehood; the certainty of all history would be confounded, no doctrine would have its certainty assured, and no doctrine could be refuted on account of any error. Indeed the Apostle Paul would have spoken falsely when he writes thus in 2 Cor. 1. 19: The Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, etc., was not Yes and No, but Yes was in him. Yet this assertion of Weigel is so absurd that Avicenna, in the first book of the Metaphysics, rightly said long ago of those who presumed to speak against this accepted truth that such people should be beaten or exposed to fire until they acknowledge that it is not the same to be beaten and not to be beaten, to be burned and not to be burned. There is no need to weigh the reasons by which this ill-tempered man, with his absurd saying, labours to defend himself, although this too has been done carefully by the Reverend Dr. John Crocius in his Examination of Weigel's Theology. I add only this: Weigel had as forerunners here not so much ancient heretics as certain men of the race of the rabbis. For R. Solomon Jarchi, commenting on Deut. 17. 11, writes: According to the law which they teach you, and according to the judgment which they tell you, you shall do, etc. Even if the rabbis say that the right hand is the left, and the left hand is the right, you must believe them in that. That R. Bechai and R. Moses ben Nachman taught the same is attested by the most celebrated Buxtorf in the Synagoga Judaica, chapter 1.

units.la: Idem refert Lutherus ex Purchteto, libello de Schemhamphorasch. Quid quod passim in Talmude, ut idem Buxtorfius annotat, id inculcatur, si duo Rabbini inter se contendant & pugnent, ac sermones contradicentes proferant, non minus credendum esse, utrumque doctrinam suam a Mose accepisse; imo, quod blasphemum est, utramque sententiam verbum Dei viventis esse. Tantum quidem de Demonstrationibus secundario talibus: succedunt Demonstrationes proprie sic dictae, quibus praeter Scepticos, quorum in capitis vestibulo facta mentio, quam infestus quoque fuit vir alias summus Petrus Ramus, cujus haec occurrunt verba in principio lib. 9. Schol. Dial. Sic enim Aristoteles Syllogismum illum [de Demonstratione loquitur] velut unicum omnis artis ac scientiae artificem & magistrum dicere videtur, & certe duorum Posteriorum primo toto, nihil nisi Demonstrationis nomen audit, secundo etiam late celebratur. Quod si ita sit, ut esse tota Analysis accurate retexta judicat, certe Philosophus in Philosophiam monstrum horrendum induxit, ut artium & scientiarum firmandarum artem fingeret, cujus in artibus & scientiis exemplum nunquam animadvertisset, immo cum per naturam nullum esse possit, &c. Post Ramum idem egit Franciscus Patritius vir alias subtilis, qui in suis Discussionibus Peripateticis sic evertere laborat Demonstrationem, ut sarcastice magis, quam solide in Aristotelem insurgat. Sed, ut ad rem ipsam deveniamus, cum hic acturi simus de Demonstratione, quatenus ea ab Aristotele tradita est, per illam intelligimus Demonstrationem per excellentiam sic dictam, sive demonstrationem propter quid, inter quam & syllogismum Demonstrativum, quidam perperam distinguere instituerunt, contendentes admittendam quidem esse demonstrationem, neutiquam vero se pariter admittere posse Demonstrativum syllogismum, quod antequam hic contexatur, jam inventa debeat esse causla, & consequenter otiosus sit Syllogismus, utpote per quem non inveniatur causla, sed causla jam inventa exhibeatur. Quum syllogismus demonstrativus, ut & ipsa demonstratio, inter que duo antiqui Philosophi distinguere non solent, per connexionem suarum propositionum ostendat causlam adaequatam esse passioni propriae, que de subjecto suo per medium, quod habet rationem causlae immediatae, demonstratur. Quibus praemissis, ut ratio stet nobilissimo huic sciendi instrumento, pariter in antecessum notamus, nunquam, ne quidem per somnium, sive Aristoteli, sive illius interpreti in mentem venisse, docere, omnium omnino demonstrationem dari posse, quum se, quum corum proponi hic solent (quo liber excreſcat in aliquam molem, quam ſcrupuloſe praecavere laboro) ſtudio prætereo: Atque duo ſolum argumenta, ſolide evincentia has ipſas demonſtrationes admittendas eſſe, propono. I. Si datur ſcientia, eaque agnoſci debet, par quoq; eſt agnoſcere & admittere Demonſtra-tionem. Conſequentia inde patet, quod ſecundum doctrinam Ariſtotelis, ſcientia demonſtrationis ſit effectus, unde & vulgo ipſa Demonſtratio ab hoc effectu deſcribi ſolet, quod ſit Syllogiſmus ſcientiam pariêns: conſequentiæ certitudinem ipſi Sceptici jam olim exploratam habuerunt, dum occupati in evertenda ſcientiæ certitudine, exiſtimarunt eandem collapſuram eſſe, ſi demonſtrationem evertissent, unde eaſdem quoque machinas adverſus Demonſtrationem & ſcientiam dirigere ſolent. Quod ad minorem propoſitionem, ea certa eſt ex ijs, quæ jam antea pro ſcientiæ vindicatione dicta fuerunt: quare ijdem quoque sontes, qui notati fuerunt pro aſserenda ſcientia, hic convenienter pariter applicantur & uſurpantur. II. Quum certa & omnibus numeris abſoluta demonſtrationum exempla occurrant, inſtructa ſcil. omnibus requiſitis, quæ hypothetice in ſuis Demonſtrationibus Ariſtoteles requirit, nullatenus ambigere licet, quin Demonstratio tanquam nobilissimum sciendi instrumentum admitti debeat. Nam post Sextum, Ramus atque Patricius non tam exagitare instituerunt certitudinem ipsarum Demonstrationum, quatenus ex principijs Aristotelis procedunt, quam potius earundem impossibilitatem evincere; pariterque persuadere, Philosophum tale sciendi Instrumentum formasse ac scrupulose adornasse, quod nullum usum habeat, quum nulli rei applicari queat. Exempla hic nulla proponimus, quod nullum vel compendium Logicæ, systematice traditæ occurat, in quo non plena manu, quam plurima exhibeantur. Messem uberrimam quisquis desiderat, adeat Goclenium part. 3. Probl. Logic. probl. 72. Quæ duo argumenta cum hic queant instar omnium esse, sic nobis hactenus nihil aliud restat, quam ut proponamus quosdam fontes solutorios, omnium eorum, quæ dubia sunt, solutioni inservientes. Atque ex Clemente quidem Alexand. lib. 8. Strom. primo: Dico euim, qui demonstrat, oportere hac duo observare in omnibus, nempe ut veras quidem assumat propositiones, eis autem consequentem inferat illationem. 2. Huic eidem instituto, nostro serviunt ea, quæ Clemens loco eodem habet: Aut enim omnia egent demonstratione. aut etiam quædam ex ijs sunt credibilia. Sed si prius quidem verum est: uniuscujusque demonstrationis petentes demonstrationem, procedemus in infinitum, & sic evertetur demonstratio: sin autem secundum ea ipsa quae exsefsunt credibilia, erunt principia demonstrationum. Eoque, ut non datur progressus in infinitum, falsus per omnia Sextus est cum reliqua Scepticorum pullicie, quando nihil in Demonstratione tanquam primum, & quidem certo definitum agnoscendo, contendit in infinitum progressum posse institui. 3. Syllogismus ratione materiae & in specie velut demonstrativus consideratus, secundum modum considerandi communem sive generalem animadverti debet, atque, uti loquuntur, in actu signato, adeo ut differentia quae eidem ut Syllogismo aut Metaphysico, aut Physico, &c. accidit, aliter non debeat censeri, quam secundum applicationem, aut ratione actus exerciti. Qua considerandi ratione admissa, neutiquam, uti falso contendit Ramus, multiplicantur species aut demonstrativi syllogismi, aut syllogismi generaliter ratione materiae considerati. 4. Ratione habita requisitorum demonstrativi syllogismi, atque sejunctis, uti jam antea patuit, demonstrationibus qua Mathematicis, qua Theologicis, sive demonstrationibus secundario sic dictis, amplius notandum circa eadem requisita dispensari sic posse.
units.tr: The same is reported by Luther from Purchtetus, in his little book on the Schemhamphorasch. And what of the fact that, as Buxtorf again notes, it is everywhere insisted upon in the Talmud that if two rabbis dispute and fight with each other and put forward contradictory statements, one must no less believe that each has received his doctrine from Moses; indeed, what is blasphemous, each opinion is the word of the living God. So much for demonstrations of the secondary kind. There follow demonstrations properly so called, against which, besides the Sceptics (whose mention was made at the beginning of the chapter), the otherwise eminent Peter Ramus was also hostile. His words occur at the beginning of book 9 of the Scholae Dialecticae: For thus Aristotle seems to speak of that syllogism [of demonstration] as the sole craftsman and master of every art and science; and certainly in the whole first of the Posterior Analytics he hears nothing but the name of demonstration, and in the second it is also widely celebrated. If this is so, as the whole analysis, carefully unravelled, judges it to be, then certainly the Philosopher has introduced a horrible monster into philosophy, in devising an art of establishing the arts and sciences, of which he had never noticed an example in the arts and sciences; indeed, since by nature there can be none, etc. After Ramus, Francis Patrizi, a man otherwise subtle, did the same. In his Peripatetic Discussions he labours to overthrow demonstration in such a way that he attacks Aristotle more sarcastically than solidly. But, to come to the matter itself: since we are here to treat of demonstration insofar as it was handed down by Aristotle, by this we understand demonstration in the pre-eminent sense, or demonstration of the why (demonstratio propter quid). Some have wrongly tried to distinguish between this and the demonstrative syllogism, contending that demonstration is indeed to be admitted, but that the demonstrative syllogism cannot equally be admitted, because the cause must already have been found before the syllogism is woven together, and consequently the syllogism is idle, since through it the cause is not found but a cause already found is displayed. Yet the demonstrative syllogism, like demonstration itself (and the ancient philosophers were not accustomed to distinguish between these two), shows through the connection of its propositions that the cause is adequate to the proper passion, which is demonstrated of its subject through the middle term that has the character of an immediate cause. With these premises laid down, and so that the argument may stand firm for this most noble instrument of knowing, we also note in advance that it never, not even in a dream, came into the mind of Aristotle or of his interpreter to teach that a demonstration can be given of absolutely everything. I deliberately pass over the usual objections raised here (lest the book swell into some bulk, which I am scrupulously careful to avoid), and I propose only two arguments that solidly prove these very demonstrations must be admitted. I. If there is science, and it must be recognised, then it is equally necessary to recognise and admit demonstration. The consequence is plain, because according to Aristotle's doctrine science is the effect of demonstration, whence demonstration itself is commonly described by this effect as a syllogism producing science. The Sceptics themselves long ago grasped the certainty of this consequence: occupied in overturning the certainty of science, they judged that it would collapse too if they overturned demonstration, and so they are accustomed to aim the same engines against demonstration and science. As for the minor premise, it is certain from what has been said before in defence of science; therefore the same grounds that were noted for asserting science are here applied and used in the same way. II. Since certain examples of demonstrations, complete in every respect, occur, namely ones furnished with all the requisites that Aristotle hypothetically demands in his demonstrations, there is no room to doubt that demonstration must be admitted as the most noble instrument of knowing. For after Sextus, Ramus and Patrizi did not so much set out to harass the certainty of the demonstrations themselves, insofar as they proceed from Aristotle's principles, as to prove their impossibility; and likewise to persuade us that the Philosopher formed and scrupulously fashioned such an instrument of knowing as has no use, since it can be applied to no thing. I propose no examples here, since no systematically handed-down summary of Logic lacks them, one in which very many are set out with a full hand. Whoever desires a most abundant harvest, let him go to Goclenius, part 3 of the Problems of Logic, problem 72. Since these two arguments can here stand in for all, there remains for us only to propose certain sources of solution, serving the resolution of all the things that are doubtful. From Clement of Alexandria, Stromata book 8, first: For I say that he who demonstrates ought to observe these two things in all cases: namely, that he takes up true premises and infers a consequent conclusion from them. 2. To this same purpose serves what Clement has in the same place: For either all things need demonstration, or some of them are credible in themselves. But if the first is true, then, seeking the demonstration of each demonstration, we shall proceed to infinity, and thus demonstration will be overthrown; but if, according to those things which are credible in themselves, there will be principles of demonstrations. And so, since there is no progress to infinity, Sextus is wholly wrong, along with the rest of the Sceptic rabble, when, not acknowledging anything in demonstration as first and certainly defined, he contends that a progress to infinity can be instituted. 3. A syllogism considered as demonstrative, with respect to matter and in its species, ought to be regarded according to the common or general mode of considering and, as they say, in the signate act, so that the difference which attaches to it as a metaphysical or physical syllogism, and so on, ought not to be counted otherwise than according to its application or with respect to the act exercised. With this mode of considering admitted, the species of the demonstrative syllogism, or of the syllogism considered generally with respect to matter, are by no means multiplied, as Ramus falsely contends. 4. Having regard to the requisites of the demonstrative syllogism, and setting aside, as has already appeared, demonstrations both mathematical and theological (or demonstrations so called in a secondary sense), it should be further noted that these same requisites may be dispensed with in such a way

units.la: Ff posse, ut demonstrationes non solum locum habeant in disciplinis Theoreticis, sed ex parte quoque in disciplinis practicis. Quamvis enim practicę disciplinę non versentur circa res necessarias, sed contingentes, nihilominus tamen quadantenus præcepta earum necessaria sunt. 5. Demonstrationes quæ attendi debent in Demonstrativo Syllogismo, potissimum atque principaliter, majorem propositionem concernunt, ea enim vera, necessaria, immediata atque prima esse debet: quod propriam causam cum affectione copulet: minor propositio si duntaxat vera & necessaria fuerit, sufficit. Quod cum doceant ipsi Peripatetici, & inter eos Zabarella lib. 2. de proposit. necess. cap. 17. oppido frustra Ramus est, quando hoc nomine Aristotelis doctrinam sugillare instituit. 6. Quamvis propria affectionum causa à nobis sæpe ignoretur, non tamen semper & in omnibus eandem ignorari evincunt exempla plurimarum, earumque omnibus numeris absolutarum demonstrationum, quæ in mundo sunt, & apud quosvis Logicos notari possunt.
units.tr: that demonstrations have a place not only in theoretical disciplines but in part also in practical ones. For although the practical disciplines are not concerned with necessary things but with contingent ones, nevertheless their precepts are in some measure necessary. 5. The demonstrations that must be attended to in the demonstrative syllogism concern chiefly and principally the major premise; for this must be true, necessary, immediate and first, and must join the proper cause with the affection. The minor premise is sufficient if it is merely true and necessary. Since the Peripatetics themselves teach this, and among them Zabarella (book 2 On Necessary Propositions, chapter 17), Ramus is quite vainly attacking Aristotle's doctrine under this name. 6. Although the proper cause of affections is often unknown to us, the examples of very many demonstrations, complete in every respect, which exist in the world and can be noted among any logicians, show that it is not always and in all cases the same cause that is unknown.

units.la: 7. Laborat quidem demonstratio difficultate, & quadam obscuritate, sed, ea ipsi doctrinæ affricari non potest, cum vitium artificis atque discentis nihil omnino arti detrahat, & quod per accidens est, nihil deroget ei, quod per se est. 8. Plaudit sibi quidem admodum Ramus, quasi ostenderit Syllogismum demonstrativum non concludere quæstionem cur sit, sed quod sit: verum expendere debuisset illum syllogismum, sic non denominari à conclusione, sed à præmissis, quę semper adæquatam atque propriam affectionis caussam exhibent: deinde quæstio cur sit, est in præmissis solis materialiter & actualiter, in conclusione vero duntaxat potentialiter. 9. Haut fas est confundere quæstionem cur sit, cum responsione ad eam. Verum quidem, ipsam quæstionem qua talem, syllogismo includi non posse, interim tamen ipsa responsio syllogismo comprehendi potest, ut quęstioni satisfiat. Quemadmodum hoc patet ex omnibus demonstrativorum syllogismorum exemplis. 10. Quod censetur in Demonstrativo syllogismo demonstrari per caussam, pro diverso respectu tum proprij adjuncti, tum etiam proprij effecti rationem habet. Proprium siquidem adjunctum, aut propria passio est respectu minoris extremi sive subjecti quæstionis, cui inest, aut saltem accidit, & de quo demonstratur: proprium vero effectum ratione medij termini, qui ejusdem caussa est. 11. Distinguere convenit inter necessitatem syllogismo in communi convenientem ratione formæ, seu dispositionis, [cujus in ipsa Syllogismi definitione fit mentio ] & inter necessitatem propriam, eidem competentem ratione materiæ sive consequentis. Omnis syllogismus comparatus cum regulis de forma syllogismi, si ijsdem respondeat, necessarius quidem est necessitate consequentiæ; non vero pariter necessarius necessitate absoluta, sive materiæ, sive consequentis, cum quidam syllogismus constet ex materia necessario vera, quidam vero ex materia contingenter solum vera, sive probabili. 12. Quamvis nec circulus proprie sic dictus, nec circularis argumentatio, ulla ratione admitti queat, quod in ea occurrat manifesta contradictio, dum secundum eundem respectum unum atque idem prioris atque posterioris rationem habet; nihilominus tamen regressus, qui & ipse non raro circuli nomen ferre solet, (& distinctionis gratia vocari difformis seu multiformis, quum vitiosus uniformis sit) neutiquam improbari meretur: constat siquidem duobus syllogismis diversimode se habentibus, unus quippe progreditur à notioribus secundum nos, alter à notioribus secundum se: hic vero regressus convenienter institutus, cumprimis servit veritati atque certitudini syllogismi Demonstrativi. Atque sic hactenus hoc capite egimus de quadruplici demonstratione; utque demonstrationes proprie dictæ, item Mathematicæ, atque ad impossibile, serviunt omnibus in universum hominibus, & apud omnes, quibus modo ratio constat, fidem inveniunt; ita Theologicæ particulares sunt atque solummodo usum inveniunt apud Scripturæ filios, quandoquidem generant certitudinem, oriundam non tam ex veritatis, quam probant, profundiori penetratione, quam potius ex veracitatis & revelationis divinæ indubitata agnitione.
units.tr: 7. Demonstration indeed labours under difficulty and a certain obscurity, but this cannot be attributed to the doctrine itself, since the fault of the craftsman or the learner takes nothing at all from the art, and what is incidental does not detract from what is essential. 8. Ramus indeed plumes himself greatly, as if he had shown that the demonstrative syllogism concludes not the question why it is but that it is. But he ought to have weighed that such a syllogism is named not from its conclusion but from its premises, which always exhibit the adequate and proper cause of the affection. Moreover, the question why it is lies in the premises alone, materially and actually, but in the conclusion only potentially. 9. It is not right to confuse the question why it is with the answer to it. It is true that the question itself, as such, cannot be included in a syllogism; yet the answer can be comprehended in a syllogism, so that the question is satisfied. This is plain from all the examples of demonstrative syllogisms. 10. What is held in a demonstrative syllogism to be demonstrated through its cause has, according to the different respect, the character both of a proper adjunct and of a proper effect. For the proper adjunct is, or is a proper passion, with respect to the minor extreme or subject of the question, in which it inheres, or at least belongs, and of which it is demonstrated; the proper effect, on the other hand, is with respect to the middle term, which is the cause of it. 11. It is fitting to distinguish between the necessity that belongs in common to the syllogism in respect of its form or arrangement [of which mention is made in the very definition of the syllogism], and the proper necessity that belongs to it in respect of its matter or conclusion. Every syllogism, compared with the rules of the form of syllogism, if it answers to them, is indeed necessary with the necessity of consequence; but it is not likewise necessary with absolute necessity, whether of matter or of conclusion, since some syllogisms consist of matter that is necessarily true, and some of matter that is only contingently or probably true. 12. Although neither a circle properly so called nor circular argumentation can in any way be admitted, because in it a manifest contradiction occurs, since according to the same respect one and the same thing has the character both of prior and of posterior, nevertheless regress, which itself not rarely bears the name of circle (and, for the sake of distinction, is called difform or multiform, since the vicious kind is uniform), by no means deserves to be condemned. For it consists of two syllogisms that stand in different relations: one proceeds from things more known to us, the other from things more known in themselves. This regress, rightly instituted, serves above all the truth and certainty of the demonstrative syllogism. And so far in this chapter we have treated of the fourfold demonstration. Just as demonstrations properly so called, and likewise mathematical and ad impossibile demonstrations, serve all men in general and find credit with all who possess reason, so theological demonstrations are particular and find use only among the sons of Scripture, since they generate a certainty arising not so much from a deeper penetration into the truth that they prove as from the indubitable recognition of divine veracity and revelation.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM OCTAVUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER EIGHTEEN.

units.la: De subsidio, quod Mathematica disciplinæ Physicæ præstant: itemque de differentia, quæ intercedit inter hypotheses reales verequePhysicas, & inter hypotheses ratiocinativas, seu notionales.
units.tr: On the help that the mathematical disciplines give to physics, and on the difference between real, true physical hypotheses and reasoned or notional hypotheses.

units.la: FIlum tractationis nos deduxit ad Physiologiam, sive rerum naturalium scientiam, cui præter Scepticos, ut initio quoque notavimus, quidam usque adeo sunt infesti, ut propterea non dubitaverint hanc ipsam scientiam accensere ijs disciplinis, quæ vulgo Conjecturales vocantur: alij vero vice versa docent aperte, hominem, subsidio maxime Mathesios, eo usque progredi posse in cognitione rerum rum nanuralium, ut non existimem Salomonem, cujus eximiam circa res naturales cognitionem ipse Spiritus Sanctus in Scriptura commendat, ulterius unquam pervenille. utrumque extremum præcavere debebimus, &, ut queamus, ante omnia expendere convenit, quæ affinitas inter Mathefin disciplinam certissimam, atque inter Physiologiam intercedit, qua occasione expendere poterimus differentiam, quæ inter hypotheses Physicas occurrit, quas omnes cum quidam eodem loco habeant, non solum ipsi, ignorantes licet, in errorum præcipitium inciderunt, sed alios quoque eodem secum traxerunt. Atque initio quidem notamus, nullos ne quidem admitti posse ad rerum naturalium penetralia, nedum ut feliciter eadem recludant, qui vel Geometriæ, (ne de alijs Mathefios partibus jam dicam) imperiti fuerint. siquidem Mathematicarum disciplinarum in Physiologia usus longe maximus est. Adeo ut nesciam, quid in mentem venerit quibusdam, qui soli Peripatetici censeri volunt, dum persuasum voluerunt Philosophanti, speciatim futuro Physico, inutilem esse cognitionem Mathefios. Cum ratio-ne eos notat Galilæus de Galilæis, in suo Dialogo de Systemate mundi, pag. 390. sic loquens: Cogniti mihi & auditi fuere summi Philoso-phi phi Peripatetici, qui discipulos suos dehortati sunt a studio Mathematicarum disciplinarum, utpote quae reddant intellectum cavillationibus inhiantem, & ad bene philosophandum inhabilem. Quod institutum è diametro instituto Platonis adversatur, qui non admisit ad Philosophiam, nisi Geometriae exactissime gnaros. & post paulo, de Geometria loquens, addit: Nec enim ars ulla est ad detegendas talium Peripateticorum fallacias accommodatior. At frustra vir summus est, quando eodem loco cum his suae Philosophiae mangonibus ipsum Aristotelem componit. Ut ipse enim Platonis fuit discipulus, & consequenter in sacris Mathematicis probe subactus, sic passim, non solum Mathematicis utitur exemplis, sed variis in locis quoque ipsi Philosophiae Naturali lucem a Mathesi procurare nititur. Imo ipse varia quoque scripsit ad Mathesin pertinentia, quae per injuriam temporum non superstant. Ptolomaeus Opticam Aristotelis habuit, eamque copiosam fuisse testatur. Simplicius in Categoriis Geometricos atque Mechanicos ejusdem Philosophi libros laudat. Mechanica illius adhuc extant, atque in admiratione sunt. Attribuitur ei quoque liber de lineis individuis sed salso, cum satis in lectione appareat, esse interpretis cujusdam, nec admodum eruditi. Nihilominus hujus argumenti librum scripsisse viderur videtur adversus Anaxagoram. At Aristotelis erga Mathesin affectum præcipue Astrologica demonstrant. Seculo illo Astrologia apud Græcos adhuc jacebat, hypotheses quas Eudoxus primus invenerat, cum Callippo Aristoteles correxit, ut illius Commentatores ad libros de Cælo perhibuerunt. Et certe Aristoteles lib. xii. Metaph. hęsitans circa numerum sphærarum cælestium, & ad Astrologos tanquam iudices idoneos recurrens, non agnovit alias hypotheses, quam Eudoxi & Callippi, suasque de orbibus concentricis: nec tamen sibi satisfecit. Itaque studuit ad primum Mathematicæ Philosophiæ fontem recurrere. Alexander tum Asiā universam ferme tenebat, & Callisthenes pro Aristotele datus Alexandro, monitus est, ut si Babylon caperetur, Astrologia Babyloniorum à Chaldæis exquireretur, atque in Græciam mitteretur. Hæc enim optima Orientis spolia à Philosopho expetita sunt, & certe etiam Babylonicæ illæ, de quibus jam dixi, observationes annorum 1903. ad Aristotelem à Callisthene missæ memorantur. Ex quibus omnibus cum manifesto appareat nefas esse componere ipsum Aristotelem, cum male-Majis quibusdam illius sectatoribus, sic pariter hinc liquet secundum ipsum quoque Aristotelem, Mathematicas disciplinas futuro Philosopho losophi, speciatim Physico, non utiles solum, verum necessarias esse. Nec tamen exis�timandum (ut video quibusdam hoc seculo persuasum esse) omnia Physicae mysteria subsidio Mathematicarum disciplinarum erui & explicari posse. exploratum hoc erat ipsi Galilaeo de Galilaeis, qui, in libro jam antea citato, respectu quarundam rerum ad naturalem Philosophiam pertinentium, pag. 225. sic loquitur: In scientia Naturali, non est, ut Mathematicam requiramus evidentiam exquisitam. quod ut distincte liqueat, ex re fuerit attendere ad Mathesios objectum, & consyderare quatenus circa illud cognoscendum occupetur. Non putem ergo apud ullum, qui modo disciplinarum Philosophicarum distinctionem exploratam habet, dubium censeri posse, quin Mathematicae disciplinae circa solam quantitatem, velut suum objectum occupentur: quam quantitatem sive quis a substantia corporea distinxerit, sive existimaverit eandem esse cum substantia quanta, perinde est atque eodem redit; modo hoc, quod Methodi lex urget, pariter admittatur, nullam disciplinam per suum adaequatum objectum definitam, objecti ejusdem terminos excedere posse, hoc enim si admittatur, disciplinae ut distinctae considerari non poterunt, sed omnes inter se confuse erunt. Quo jacto fundamento, liquet quantum subsidij Physiologia à Mathematicis disciplinis expectare debeat. Nam cum ipsa occupetnr circa subjectum materiale, & extensum, quod ratione suæ extensionis & partium quantitativarum in loco est, debitumque situm habet; quotiescunque sive de quantitate, aut partibus quantitativis, aut ijs, quę inde oriuntur, quæstio est, nullum dubium, quin maximum subsidium conferre queant disciplinæ Mathematicæ: quod potissimum in corporibus cælestibus videre est, quorum natura explicari non potest, nisi quis instructus sit subsidio duarum alarum Platonicarum, Arithmeticæ scil. & Geometriæ. Præterea quando affectio quædam, Physica potissimum, aut oritur à materia quanta, aut cum ea arctissimam cognationem colit, aliter fieri non ipoteft, quin ad explicationem ejusdem conferant subsidium illæ disciplinæ, quæ circa quantitatis penitiorem explicationem occupantur, ut patet circa figuram corporum naturalium, itemque motum gravium & levium, nec non circa explicationem motus tanquam recti, & circularis, &c. Ad hoc, quotiescunque res quædam variat aut per distantiam majorem minoremve, aut pro ratione corporum diversæ quantitatis, in quæ incurrit, aliter quoque fieri non potest, quin in partes vocari debeat ipsa illa Disciplina, quae differentias tum quantitatis, tum ea ipsa, quae a quantitate originem ducunt, explicare poteft: cujus rei exemplum occurrit circa visionem, quare ad eam bene explicandam opus est Optica; disciplina ex Geometria originem suam trahente. Ulterius, qui Mathesios usum per Philosophiam naturalem extendunt, neutiquam legitime inter disciplinas oppositive se habentes sciunt distinguere, atque in multas difficultates incidunt. Dum enim Physicam ex sola Mathesi, neglectis aliis principiis cognoscendi, Physicae peculiaribus, laborant perficere, non solum inaudita, si non periculosa, cudunt dogmata; verum etiam saepe in tam absurdas incidunt sententias, ut risum debeant omnibus, quibus mica modo judicij superest, licet non diffitear, eosdem applausum consequi abijs, quos authoritas tam eximiorum Mathematicorum, quum ipsi in pulvere erudito plane sint hospites, excecavit. Alios ne in hoc Theatrum adducam, instar omnium fuerit Johannes Keplerus, Mathematicus Caesareus, scriptisque celeberrimus, de quo jure summo hoc dici potest: Ubi Mathematicus, nemo eodem melior & subtilior, ubi vero Physicus, nemo eodem pejor atque ineptior, ut saepissime doleam, si non ingemiscam, virum tam eximium, divinam illam Mathesin nugamentis suis Physicis adeo sæde commaculasse. Quid absurdius enim vel febricitans anus in somnio videat, quam quod terra ingens animal sit, quæ per montium crateres & caminos, ceu os aut nares, ventos exspiret? & hoc tamen expresse docet lib. 4. Harmonicæ cap. 7. ubi serio quoque probare nititur, quod terra cum cælo sympathiam colat, & naturali instinctu sidera posituram cognoscat. Similiter in scripto de Motibus Martis sol. 173. contendit Solem magnum magnetem, seu magneticum corpus esse, supra proprium centrum diurno motu circumactum, quod secundum speciem quandam diffusam, omnes reliquas Planetarum sphæras commoveat, & in orbem agitet. Nec sic Keplerus solum, per Mathesin imprudenter & infeliciter Physicæ applicatam, in errorum præcipitium ruit; sed cum eo multi quoque alij, quorum indicem alio in scripto, si Deo placuerit vitam prorogare, exhibebo. Sed, quid si res Physicæ, secundum Methodum Mathematicam tractentur, an non Physiologiæ eadem procurabitur certitudo, quæ in Mathematicis disciplinis notatur? Sic sane videtur multis viris egregijs, qui convertentes se à contemplationibus Mathematicis, in quibus meliorem ætatis partem consumpserant, ad
units.tr: The thread of our discussion has brought us to physiology, or the science of natural things. Besides the Sceptics, as we noted at the start, some people are so hostile to it that they have not hesitated to count this very science among those disciplines commonly called conjectural. Others, on the contrary, openly teach that a person, chiefly with the help of mathematics, can advance so far in knowledge of natural things that I do not think Solomon, whose outstanding knowledge of natural things the Holy Spirit himself commends in Scripture, ever got any further. We must avoid both extremes, and to do so we must first of all consider what affinity there is between mathematics, the most certain of disciplines, and physiology. From this we will be able to work out the difference that arises among physical hypotheses. Although some people, ignorant as they are, have put them all in the same class, not only have they fallen headlong into error themselves, but they have also dragged others along with them. We note at the outset that no one who is ignorant of geometry (not to mention other parts of mathematics) can be admitted to the inner secrets of nature, let alone unlock them successfully, since the use of mathematical disciplines in physiology is by far the greatest. So I do not know what came into the minds of certain people, who wish to be considered Peripatetics alone, when they persuaded a would-be philosopher, especially a future natural philosopher, that knowledge of mathematics is useless. Galileo Galilei rightly rebukes them in his Dialogue on the System of the World, p. 390, where he says: I have known and heard of the highest Peripatetic philosophers, who dissuaded their disciples from the study of the mathematical disciplines, as things that make the intellect greedy for quibbles and unfit for philosophizing well. This practice is diametrically opposed to the practice of Plato, who admitted to philosophy none but those thoroughly versed in geometry. And a little later, speaking of geometry, he adds: Nor is there any art better suited to uncovering the fallacies of such Peripatetics. But that great man is wrong when he puts Aristotle himself in the same class as these hacks of his philosophy. Aristotle was a pupil of Plato, and so was thoroughly trained in the sacred mathematics. Accordingly, he not only uses mathematical examples everywhere, but in various places he also strives to bring light from mathematics to natural philosophy itself. Indeed, he himself wrote various works bearing on mathematics, which have not survived the injuries of time. Ptolemy had Aristotle's Optics and testifies that it was extensive. Simplicius, in his commentary on the Categories, praises the geometrical and mechanical books of the same philosopher. His Mechanics still survives and is greatly admired. A book On Indivisible Lines is also attributed to him, but it is clearly the work of some interpreter, and not a very learned one, as is apparent enough on reading it. Nevertheless, he seems to have written a book on this subject against Anaxagoras. Aristotle's affection for mathematics is shown above all by his astronomy. In that century astronomy still lay neglected among the Greeks. Aristotle corrected the hypotheses that Eudoxus had first devised, together with those of Callippus, as his commentators on the books On the Heavens report. And certainly Aristotle, in book 12 of the Metaphysics, hesitating over the number of celestial spheres and turning to astronomers as competent judges, recognized no hypotheses other than those of Eudoxus and Callippus and his own about concentric orbs, and yet he was not satisfied with them. So he set himself to return to the first source of mathematical philosophy. Alexander by then held almost all of Asia, and Callisthenes, who had been given to Alexander in place of Aristotle, was advised that if Babylon were taken, the astronomy of the Babylonians should be sought from the Chaldeans and sent to Greece. For these were the finest spoils of the East that the Philosopher desired, and certainly the Babylonian observations of which I have just spoken, covering 1903 years, are recorded as having been sent to Aristotle by Callisthenes. From all these things it is plainly clear that it is wrong to put Aristotle himself together with certain malicious followers of his. Likewise it is clear, on Aristotle's own view, that the mathematical disciplines are not only useful but necessary for a future philosopher, especially a natural philosopher. Yet we must not suppose (as I see some people in this century have been persuaded) that all the mysteries of physics can be drawn out and explained with the help of the mathematical disciplines. Galileo Galilei himself was well aware of this, for in the book cited above he says, with respect to certain things pertaining to natural philosophy, p. 225: In natural science we do not require the exact evidence of mathematics. To make this clear, it will be worth attending to the object of mathematics and considering how far it is concerned with knowing that object. I think no one who has a clear grasp of the distinction among the philosophical disciplines can doubt that the mathematical disciplines are concerned only with quantity as their object. Whether one distinguishes this quantity from corporeal substance, or thinks it is the same as quantified substance, comes to the same thing, provided that what the law of method requires is equally admitted, namely that no discipline, defined by its proper object, can go beyond the limits of that object. For if this were admitted, the disciplines could not be considered as distinct, but would all be confused with one another. Once this foundation is laid, it is plain how much help physiology ought to expect from the mathematical disciplines. For since physiology is concerned with a material and extended subject, which, by reason of its extension and quantitative parts, is in place and has its due situation, then whenever the question concerns quantity, or quantitative parts, or what arises from them, there is no doubt that the mathematical disciplines can contribute the greatest help. This can be seen above all in celestial bodies, whose nature cannot be explained unless one is equipped with the help of the two Platonic wings, namely arithmetic and geometry. Moreover, when some affection, especially a physical one, either arises from quantified matter or keeps a very close kinship with it, it cannot happen otherwise than that those disciplines which are occupied with a deeper explanation of quantity contribute help towards explaining it. This is evident in the shape of natural bodies, and likewise in the motion of heavy and light bodies, and also in the explanation of motion as straight and as circular, and so on. Again, whenever a thing varies either with a greater or lesser distance, or according to the proportion of the bodies of different quantity into which it falls, it likewise cannot happen otherwise than that the discipline which can explain these differences, both of quantity and of those things that derive their origin from quantity, must be called in. An example of this occurs in vision, for to explain it properly one needs optics, a discipline that takes its origin from geometry. Furthermore, those who extend the use of mathematics through natural philosophy do not know how to distinguish legitimately between disciplines that stand in opposition to one another, and they fall into many difficulties. For while they labour to perfect physics from mathematics alone, neglecting the other principles of knowing that belong peculiarly to physics, they not only coin unheard-of, if not dangerous, doctrines, but they often also fall into such absurd opinions that they must be laughed at by everyone who has even a little judgement left. I do not deny, however, that such men win applause from those whom the authority of such eminent mathematicians blinds, since these men are complete strangers to learned study. To say nothing of others in this theatre, let John Kepler, the imperial mathematician and very famous writer, stand for all. Of him it may be said with the greatest justice: where he is a mathematician, no one is better or subtler; where he is a physicist, no one is worse or more inept. So I often grieve, if I do not groan, that a man so outstanding should have so foully stained that divine mathematics with his physical trifles. For what more absurd thing could even a feverish old woman see in a dream than that the earth is a huge animal, which breathes out winds through the craters and chimneys of mountains as through a mouth or nostrils? Yet he expressly teaches this in book 4 of the Harmonice, chapter 7, where he also seriously tries to prove that the earth has a sympathy with the heavens and by natural instinct knows the positions of the stars. Similarly, in his writing on the motions of Mars, p. 173, he contends that the sun is a great magnet, or magnetic body, turning on its own centre by a diurnal motion, which by a certain diffused kind of influence moves and drives all the remaining spheres of the planets around. Nor is Kepler the only one to fall headlong into error, through mathematics unwisely and unhappily applied to physics; many others have done the same, and I shall list them in another writing, if God is pleased to prolong my life. But what if the things of physics are treated according to the mathematical method: would not the same certainty be obtained for physiology as is observed in the mathematical disciplines? That is certainly how it seems to many eminent men who, turning from mathematical contemplations, on which they had spent the better part of their lives, to natural philosophy, are judged by many to have deserved well of it, and to have explained many secrets of nature with success. But, in order to set out my view freely, and yet in keeping with the rule of the arguments I put forward, I gladly grant that the one who is so practised and trained in mathematical demonstrations...

units.la: Naturalem Philosophiam, censentur multorum judicio haut male de ea meriti esse, multaque naturæ arcana quam feliciter explicuisse. Sed, ut libere, & tamen ex præscripto adferendarum rationum mentem meam proponam, do lubens, eum, qui in Mathematicis demonstrationibus quam exercitatus & subactus est, lumen magnum in Physicis habere, nec infelicem Demonstratorem fore, si modo ex lege prudentiæ distinguenda convenienter distinguere queat. Agnoscit hoc ipse Galenus, qui de se ipso non uno in loco lubens fatetur, quod cum scholas Peripateticorum & Stoicorum omnes sui temporis percurrisset, ac præcepta ipsa admirando cum ardore perpendisset, non potuisse tamen cognoscere quid demonstratio esset, imo subdubitasse an ea quoque daretur; usque dum ad Geometricas disciplinas rediens, quas puer mediocriter antea imbiberat, ex ista partim varietate & incertitudine, partim obscuritate præceptorum velut atra nebula qua, in Pyrrhoniam propemodum foveam præcipitatus fuerat, earundem disciplinarum subsidio felicissime sese explicaret. Quid quod ipse Aristoteles (ut ijs notum, qui in illius lectione peregrini non sunt) omnibus suis disputationibus lumen, non aliunde; quam a Geometria fænerari instituit? Sexcenta ex eo ipso loca proferre possem, & alibi proferam, ubi demonstrationum Geometricarum subsidio res quam abstrusas protulit, atque illustravit. Alio ne abeam, fidem facere possunt soli libri Posteriorum Analyticorum, generis hujus exemplis ubique scatentes, & ubi nominatim etiam has disciplinas ratione evidentiæ omnibus aliis præfert. Interim tamen [ut jam antea obiter innui] cautela, & quidem scrupulosa hic opus est. Nam Philosophus, & Galenus, non instituunt in disciplinis à Mathesi diversis Demonstrationes secundum Mathematicam Methodum, nisi ubi principia occurrunt tam certa, quæ non cedunt principiis Mathematicis. Mathematica vero principia [ut jam antea quoque dictum] universaliter sese habent, atque apud omnes æqualiter valent, nullo, qui modo terminos intelligit, de ijs principijs, eorumque veritate, ulla omnino ratione ambigente. Sed in Physicis, quę afsumuntur principia, & secundum Mathematicæ demonstrationis Methodum cum suis conclusionibus ordinantur, sæpe aut dubia, aut incerta, aut saltem notionales duntaxat hypotheses sunt, assumptæ magis à Demonstrante, quam à parte rei in ipsis rebus naturalibus occurrentes. Quod cum multi [quod deploro quam maxime] hoc seculo circa perficiendam Physicam mirum quam novaturientes, non observarint, decepti antea, alios secum in errorum praecipitium abripuerunt. Nam si quis non eam, quam requiro, prudentiam hic adhibuerit, ratio Demonstrationum Mathematicarum, ut ut per longum usum & experientiam familiaris fuerit, [ triduani quippe Mathematici, atque qui sacra Mathematica, primoribus solum labris delibarunt, ne quidem accingere se debent ad volvendum hoc saxum ] pro invenienda veritate impedimento magis, quam subsidio futura est. Nam quod bene notandum, ea ratio est progressuum Mathematicorum, ut ex suppositione vere in se falsa, ac tantum propter falsorum, imo impossibilium hypothetice assumptorum, cognationem cum principijs veris, vera atque certissima [ sed antea ignorata ) conclusio inveniri atque astrui queat. Ita divina illa Algebra ex nihilo [ quod alias naturae viribus adversatur] aliquid producit, dum ex numeris minoribus nihilo, ex se falsis & impossibilibus devenit ad abstrusissimarum rerum solutionem. Item Mathesios subsidio, e tot concentricis, eccentricis, epicyclis, qui etsi in rerum natura non sint, nec in spatio solido [ loquor ex mente fautorum horum orbium ) vel concipi queant, motuum nihilominus caelestium rationes ones vere & infallibiliter demonstratur. II. Ea est Demonstrationum Mathematicarum ratio, ut sæpe ex pluribus, ijsque diversis, si non contrarijs quoque principijs, institui possint. - Sic V. C. ne longius abeam, primum & decantatum illud Euclidis problema : Super data recta linea terminata triangulum æquilaterum constituere: Demonstratur non solum per hoc pronunciatum, sive effatum : Quæ eidem æqualia sunt, inter se quoque sunt æqualia: verum etiam per definitionem circuli, quæ hæc apud eundem Euclidem: Circulus est figura plana sub una linea comprehensa, quæ peripheria appellatur, ad quam ab uno puncto eorum, quæ intra figuram sunt posita, cadentes omnes rectæ lineæ inter se sunt æquales. Quę cum ita sint, quis non videt, haut quaquam tuto res Physicas, ex ratione Demonstrationum Mathematicarum, ijsdem applicatarum, censeri atque æstimari posse. Quando enim res Physicæ, sive naturales revocantur ad sua principia, præsupponitur illa ipsa principia æque realia esse debere, quam res naturales in se reales sunt, atque à parte rei sese habent. Sed reales eas esse, neutiquam evincere potest ratio Mathematicæ Demonstrationis, ijsdem aptatæ ac quasi convenientis. Falluntur quippe gravissime, si non imprudentiam summam probant, qui existimant, mox illas Physicas Demonstrationes paria facere cum Demonstrationibus Mathematicis, in omnibus suis requisitis ac partibus, & ad unguem quasi censeri debere exactas, in quibus dispositio Demonstrationum Mathematicarum elucet: nam si quaedam Demonstrationes quam maxime Mathematicę, uti jam antea evictum fuit, procedere possunt ex principijs non solum varijs & diversis, sed etiam manifesto falsis; Enimvero, quis non suspectet ipsa illa principia Physica, ut falsa & supposititia, pro quibus hoc solum dici potest, quod ex illis elici possint conclusiones veræ, cum suis præmissis ordinatæ atque dispositę secundum rationem quòrtnidum, qui applausum ambiunt ab his suis demonstrationibus Physicis, Mathematicis quasi æquivalentibus: Si hoc enim valere deberet pro asserenda veritate principiorum, ex quibus progrediuntur; multo magis in ipsa Mathesi idè valeret atque quęcunque illius principia ut vera & certa deberent censeri propter solam dispositionem. Miror, viros egregios, qui existimant, se dubiam reddidisse palmam Philosophis antiquis, legitime ab ijsdem partam ; atque tot persecula inculpate possessam, ad animum non revocare, quod ex diversis, si non pugnantibus principijs, secundum Mathematicę demonstrationis leges cum suis conclusionibus utrobique æque legitime comparatis, eædem conclusiones educi, atque æque convenienter colligi queant. Dispositio Demonstrativa Mathematica, atque evidentia progressus à principiis ad conclusionem, si valere hic debeant, atque inde evinci veritas principiorum assumptorum, possem ego ex decuplis principiis æque evidenter easdem conclusiones elicere. sed quis, cui modo mens sana, collegerit omnia illa principia, quæ ad conclusiones educendas æqualiter atque pari ratione ordinata sunt, æque à parte rei agnoscenda, atque pro realibus habenda esse? Longe ne abeam, an non illi, qui Ptolemaicis adhærent hypothesibus, ratione hypothesium è diametro, ut loquuntur, pugnant cum ijs qui Copernicum ducem sectantur? Et tamen utrique æque certo, nec non æq; infallibiliter, ex hypothesibus licet diversissimis, atque à se remotissimis, Eclipses, & reliqua phænomena cælestia prædicere possunt. Et, ut aliud proponam exemplum, quis ita hospes in Historia Physica, qui ignoret sententiis adversariis circa principia metallorum certari? Aristoteles cum ex duplici exhalatione metalla non absurde confeceret, sic tamen totam hanc materiam deseruit, ut ipse, quæ viri modestia est, fateatur se com-
units.tr: Natural philosophy has, by the judgment of many, been handled not badly, and they are thought to have explained many secrets of nature happily. But, to set out my own view freely, and yet in accordance with the rule for presenting arguments, I gladly grant that one who is trained and practised in mathematical demonstrations has a great light in physics, and will not be an unhappy demonstrator, provided he can make the proper distinctions according to the rule of prudence. Galen himself acknowledges this. He often and willingly confesses of himself that, after running through all the schools of the Peripatetics and Stoics of his time and weighing their precepts with admiring zeal, he could not nevertheless grasp what demonstration was, and even doubted whether it existed at all. Only when he returned to the geometrical disciplines, which he had moderately absorbed as a boy, was he most fortunately extricated, with the help of those disciplines, from the dark cloud, as it were, of the variety and uncertainty of the one set of precepts and the obscurity of the other, into which he had nearly fallen headlong into a Pyrrhonian pit. And what of Aristotle himself (as those know who are not strangers to reading him) who began to borrow light for all his disputations from nothing but geometry? I could cite countless passages from him on this point, and will cite them elsewhere, where with the help of geometrical demonstrations he has brought forward and illustrated matters that are quite obscure. Not to go elsewhere, the books of the Posterior Analytics alone can bear witness, teeming everywhere with examples of this kind, and where he even expressly places these disciplines above all others in respect of the evidence they give. Meanwhile, however, as I hinted earlier in passing, caution is needed here, and indeed scrupulous caution. For the Philosopher and Galen do not set up demonstrations in disciplines distinct from mathematics according to the mathematical method, except where principles occur that are as certain as they are and do not yield to mathematical principles. Now mathematical principles, as I have also said before, hold universally and are equally valid among all, and no one who understands the terms can have any doubt at all about those principles or their truth. But in physics, the principles that are assumed and arranged with their conclusions according to the method of mathematical demonstration are often doubtful, or uncertain, or at least mere notional hypotheses, assumed more by the demonstrator than found in the things of nature as they actually are. Since many in this age, (which I deplore above all), eager to perfect physics in a wonderfully novel way, have not observed this, having been deceived earlier they have dragged others with them into the precipice of error. For if anyone does not apply the prudence I require here, the method of mathematical demonstrations, however familiar it may be to him through long use and experience, will be an obstacle rather than an aid in finding the truth. [Mathematicians of three days, and those who have only tasted the sacred mathematics with the tips of their lips, ought not even to gird themselves to roll this stone.] For it must be well noted that the procedure of the mathematicians is such that from a supposition which is in itself false, and only through the kinship of falsehoods, indeed of impossibilities hypothetically assumed, with true principles, a true and most certain conclusion (previously unknown) can be discovered and established. Thus that divine Algebra produces something out of nothing (which is contrary to the powers of nature), while from smaller numbers, from nothing and from things false and impossible in themselves, it arrives at the solution of the most abstruse matters. Likewise, with the help of mathematics, the reasons of the heavenly motions are nevertheless truly and infallibly demonstrated from so many concentric, eccentric and epicycles, which, although they do not exist in the nature of things, nor can be conceived in solid space (I speak in the mind of the advocates of these orbs). II. Such is the way of mathematical demonstrations that often they can be set up from several, and those diverse, if not even contrary, principles. Thus, to pass over more distant matters, the first and much-sung problem of Euclid: On a given finite straight line to construct an equilateral triangle, is demonstrated not only by this axiom or saying: Things equal to the same thing are also equal to one another, but also by the definition of the circle, which in the same Euclid reads: A circle is a plane figure contained by one line, which is called the circumference, to which all straight lines falling from one point among those lying within the figure are equal to one another. These things being so, who does not see that physical matters cannot by any means safely be judged and estimated by the method of mathematical demonstrations applied to them? For when physical or natural things are traced back to their principles, it is presupposed that those principles must be as real as the natural things are real in themselves and stand as they are in fact. But that they are real, the reasoning of a mathematical demonstration, fitted and as it were accommodated to them, can by no means prove. Those are gravely mistaken, and show great imprudence, who think that these physical demonstrations are at once equal to mathematical demonstrations in all their requisites and parts, and ought to be judged exact to a nicety, in which the arrangement of mathematical demonstrations shines forth. For if certain demonstrations most purely mathematical can, as has been proved above, proceed from principles not only various and diverse but even manifestly false, then who would not suspect those very physical principles as false and supposititious, for which it can only be said that true conclusions may be drawn from them, arranged and ordered with their premises according to the reasoning of certain men who seek applause from these physical demonstrations, which are as it were equivalent to mathematical ones. For if this were to hold as proof of the truth of the principles from which they proceed, it would hold much more in mathematics itself, so that whatever principles it has would have to be judged true and certain on the strength of the arrangement alone. I marvel that distinguished men, who think they have rendered doubtful the palm rightly won by the ancient philosophers and possessed blamelessly for so many centuries, do not call to mind that from diverse, if not conflicting, principles, the same conclusions can be drawn and as conveniently inferred, the conclusions being equally lawfully derived on both sides according to the laws of mathematical demonstration. If the demonstrative arrangement and the evident progress from principles to conclusion ought to count for anything here, and from it the truth of the assumed principles is to be proved, I could from ten times as many principles draw out the same conclusions just as evidently. But who, having a sound mind, would gather that all those principles, which are arranged equally and in the same way to educe the conclusions, are to be acknowledged equally as things of fact and held as real? To go no further, do not those who cling to the Ptolemaic hypotheses stand, by reason of their hypotheses, as they say, diametrically opposed to those who follow Copernicus as leader? And yet both alike, with equal certainty and no less infallibly, can foretell eclipses and the other heavenly phenomena from hypotheses that are very diverse and remote from each other. And, to propose another example, who is so much a stranger to the history of physics as not to know that the opposing opinions contend about the principles of metals? When Aristotle, from a double exhalation, not absurdly made up metals, yet he so left this whole matter that he himself, with the modesty proper to a man, confesses that he had spoken only in common, or universally, about metals and metallic things, or, as people commonly say, mineral things, and left the more exact knowledge to those who would treat these matters more closely and expressly. Albertus Magnus, not so much to correct as to amend the master's opinion, devised an unctuous ...

units.la: muniter tantum, sive universaliter,de metallis & metallicis, sive uti vulgo loquuntur, rebus mineralibus, locutum esse, exactiorem vero cognitionem ijs reliquisse, qui de hisce presslius &expressius acturi essent. Magistri opinionem ut non tam castigaret, quam emendaret Albertus Magnus, excogitavit unctuosam seu viscosam humiditatem intremabilem, quae tantopere arrisit Cæsalpino, ut illius serium patrocinium suscepit adversus Georgium Agricola: qui, prae omnibus aliis, interiorum terrae penetralium rupator accuratus & diligens, pro unctuosa Alberti materia, substituit aqueam substantiam pauco terreo commissam. Ab his omnibus recedentes Chymici, pro suis illustribus decantatis principiis, nempe, Sale, Sulphure, & Mercurio, tanquam pro aris atque focis digliadiantur. Quis non videt, quatuor has discrepantes sententias multum a se distare, & quamvis plus uno verum esse non queat, quaeque tamen sententia suos, eosque quam plurimos habet patronos, qui ex iis, qui arripuerunt principia, videntur quam convenienter omnia dubia explicare posse, atque tales conclusiones colligere, quae cum suis principiis collatae provocare queant quascunque Mathematicorum Demonstrationes. His duobus exemplis, sexcenta alia superaddere liceret, nisi duo illa, quæ propósita sunt, instar omnium esse possent. Eoque existimem rationé naturalis scientiæ convenienter admodum Aristotelem censuisse, quando sub finem lib.
units.tr: only in a general way, or universally, about metals and metallic things, or, as people commonly put it, mineral things; and that he left the more exact knowledge of these matters to those who would treat them more closely and explicitly. Albertus Magnus, rather than correcting the Master's opinion, tried to amend it, and devised an oily or viscous humidity that does not melt, which so pleased Cesalpinus that he took up its earnest defence against Georgius Agricola. Agricola, above all others a careful and diligent explorer of the inner recesses of the earth, substituted for Albert's oily matter a watery substance mixed with a little earth. Departing from all these, the Chemists, for their famous principles, namely Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury, fight as if for altars and hearths. Who does not see that these four conflicting opinions differ greatly from one another, and that although no more than one can be true, each of them has its patrons, and very many of them? These patrons, starting from the principles they have adopted, seem able to explain all doubtful matters very neatly, and to draw such conclusions that, when compared with their principles, they could challenge any demonstrations of the mathematicians. I could add six hundred other examples to these two, were not these two that I have set out enough to stand for all of them. For this reason I think Aristotle judged quite fittingly, in accordance with the reasoning of natural science, when at the end of the book cited below he speaks thus:
