units.la: 1. Metaphys. sic loquitur: Mathematicorum accurata docendi ratio non in omnibus postulanda est, sed in iis, quæ materiam non habent. Quo fit, ut is modus naturalis non sit. Fortasse enim omnis natura materiam habet. Interim mirum, quam præconcepta hæc opinio, in Physicis non esse admittendas Demonstrationes, nisi Mathematice persectas, multos transversos abripuerit, qui reliquos Philosophos naturales, velut umbras volitantes contemnunt. Sed, ita accidit quoque ipsius Aristotelis ætate. Clara sunt ejus verba, quæ occurrunt loco jam dicto: Quidam nisi Mathematicorum more quis doceat, neminem dicentem admittunt. Quod cum à Platone, ejusque sectatoribus circa Physicam frequentari cœpisset, certe ut inconveniens eodem libro cap. 2. à Philosopho arguitur, quod Physica amplius attendere debeat ad caussam efficientem, & caussam finalem, quarum tamen Mathematici nullam rationem habent. Hac occasione, non inconvenienter notaverimus, in Physica duplices hypotheses occurrere posse: Reales, & Notionales. Per reales eas intelligimus, quarum demonstratio Physice cercertata & evidens sive à priori, sive à posteriori dari potest. queque si à priori certo probari non queant, à posteriori tamen, sive quod sint, tam evidenter cognoscuntur, ut ipsi quoque sensus veritatem eorundem comprobent, atque evincant. Nec refert, sintne illa principia incomplexa, an complexa; modo sint vera atque certa. V. C. tale est hoc principium: Non datur vacuum. De quo dubitari neutiquam posse, patet ex innumeris experimentis, liquido evincentibus naturam extremo conatu à vacuo abhorrere. Sed saepe haec ipsa principia valde temerario abrepta, & citra analysin atque examen à posteriori, neglectis illis cognoscendi principiis, quae Physicę eripienda non esse postea liquebit, valde non solum plausibilia videntur, sed etiam certa putantur, quod ratione dispositionis, & ratiocinativae magis convenientiae, quam Physicae & realis, per ea explicari possint, si non omnia, saltem plurimain natura arcana. Quot non diversas sententias, de primis & universalissimis principiis constitutivis corporum naturalium, in vestibulo librorum Physicorum & Metaphysicorum, enumeravit Aristoteles, quibus triplo plures, eaque absurdissimas adjicere liceret? Sed nullam mihi dabis tam absonam ex omnibus, quę non exi-stimet per dispositionem convenientem, si non Mathematicam, atq; in partes tanquam domina ratione veniente, subsidio suorum principiorum, saepissime sine ullo omnino judicio assumptorum, plurima naturae arcana explicare, atque profundos naturae recessus explicare posse? Certo atque indubitato argumento, plurima ex his principiis, tanquam primo primis, quum pariter subsistere, imo ne conciliari quidem possint, suspectari debere, & consequenter in Physiologia scrupulose inter ea distinguendum esse, quumplurimum interfit, inter hypotheses reales Physicae proprias peculiaresque, & inter hypotheses notionales, quae objective duntaxat a parte intellectus. Quemadmodum enim Logica docet, quod ex propositionibus manifesto ratione scil. materiae falsis, propter dispositionem, hoc est, ex accidenti, elici queat vera Conclusio: ita quoque ex Physicis hypothesibus in se falsis, atque neutiquam vel conciliabilibus a parte rei cum corporibus naturalibus, a ratione, subsidio maxime dispositionis, elici potest vera conclusio, quę tamen ratione suorum principiorum, si tantum propter dispositionem sit aestimanda, eque suspectari debet, atque conclusio vera vi formae Syllogisticae educta e falsis praemissis.
units.tr: 1. Metaphys. speaks thus: "The exact method of teaching of the mathematicians is not to be demanded in all things, but only in those which have no matter. Hence it follows that this is not the natural mode. For perhaps all nature has matter." Meanwhile it is remarkable how this preconceived opinion, that demonstrations are not to be admitted in physics unless they are mathematically perfect, has carried away many perverse men, who despise the rest of the natural philosophers as flitting shadows. But the same thing happened in Aristotle's own time. His words in the passage just cited are clear: "Some admit no one who teaches except in the manner of the mathematicians." When this practice had begun to be followed by Plato and his adherents in physics, Aristotle rightly argues against it as inappropriate, in the same book, chapter 2, that physics ought to pay more attention to the efficient cause and the final cause, of which the mathematicians have no account at all. On this occasion we may fittingly note that two kinds of hypotheses can occur in physics: real and notional. By real hypotheses we mean those whose demonstration in physics can be given as certain and evident, either a priori or a posteriori. And even if they cannot be proved with certainty a priori, they are nonetheless known so evidently a posteriori, that they are, as to the fact that they are, confirmed and established even by the senses themselves. It does not matter whether these principles are simple or complex, provided they are true and certain. For example, this principle: "There is no void." That this cannot be doubted at all is clear from countless experiments, which plainly show that nature abhors a vacuum with the utmost effort. But often these very principles, adopted too rashly and without analysis or a posteriori examination, with those principles of knowing neglected which will later be shown not to be lacking in physics, seem not only very plausible but are also thought certain, because by reason of arrangement and of a more convenient reasoning, rather than of physical and real grounds, they can explain, if not everything, at least most of the hidden things of nature. How many diverse opinions about the first and most universal principles constituting natural bodies did Aristotle list at the beginning of his books of Physics and Metaphysics, and could I not add three times as many, and those most absurd? But you will not give me any so absurd among them all that would not think that, through a suitable arrangement, if not a mathematical one, and with reason taking the parts as its mistress, with the aid of its own principles, very often assumed without any judgment at all, it could explain very many secrets of nature and unfold the deep recesses of nature? By a certain and indubitable argument, many of these principles, which, as first among firsts, cannot subsist together, nor even be reconciled, ought to be suspected, and consequently in physiology one must carefully distinguish between them; and it matters greatly whether we are dealing with real hypotheses, proper and peculiar to physics, or with notional hypotheses, which exist only objectively on the side of the intellect. For just as logic teaches that from propositions manifestly false in matter, by reason of arrangement, that is, by accident, a true conclusion can be drawn, so too from physical hypotheses false in themselves, and in no way reconcilable with natural bodies on the side of the thing itself, a true conclusion can be drawn by reason, chiefly with the help of arrangement. Yet if this conclusion is to be valued only for its arrangement, it must be suspected in the same way as a true conclusion drawn by the force of syllogistic form from false premises.

units.la: CAPUT

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM NONUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER NINETEEN.

units.la: De principijs Physiologiæ: speciatim de Scriptura, & quantum ei tribui debeat, quando de rebus naturalibus agit: item de sensu in Physica præ cæteris attendendo; nec non de Ratione, cui dictatoria potestas absque sensu neutiquam competere potest.
units.tr: On the principles of Physiology: in particular, concerning Scripture and how much authority it should be given when it treats of natural things; likewise concerning the sense, which must be given priority over all else in Physics; and also concerning Reason, which cannot possibly hold the power to dictate apart from the senses.

units.la: PHysicam, disciplinam præno-bilem, uti omni ævo Scepticorum natio quibuscunque machinis adhibitis evertere laboravit; sic nostrum est operam dare, ne quid eadem detrimenti patiatur: at non poterit hoc rite atque ordine à nobis fieri, nisi in antecessum ante omnia egerimus de illis cognoscendi præsidijs, quibus ipsa naturalis Philosophia indiget. Alij aliud existiment, ea tria esse statuo, ad modum principiorum cognoscendi, hic præ cæteris consideranda. Nempè: Sacram Scripturam, Sensum suo modo considerandum explicandumque, & Rationem paulo distinctius à nobis examinandam. Quod ad Scripturam, ea de rebus naturalibus duplicitèr agit, aut ex professo, aut incidenter. Ex professo de ijs agit quadrifariam: 1. Quando historice proponit earum originem, simul referendo methodum modumque, secundum quem productæ sunt. (Genef. 1. & 2. cap.) 2. Quando proponit pariter historice varios & quidem extraordinarios casus, qui ijsdem rebus acciderunt, ut, quod terra tota, usque ad montes altissimos, aquis, diluvij tempore, sit tecta, Gen. 7. & 8. cap. quod Josuae tempore, Sol steterit Iof. 10. quod Jona navigante mare commotum admodum fuerit, (Jon. 1. cap.) 3. Quando simul refert historice earundem rerum naturalium usus, ut quod Ezechias aegrotans usus fuerit ficubus, Abrahamus in cibum adornaverit vitulum, etc, 4. Quando pari ratione agit de rerum naturalium interitu, ut v. c.
units.tr: Physics, a most noble discipline, has been attacked by the Sceptical school in every age with whatever engines they could bring to bear, and so it is our task to take care that it suffers no harm. This cannot be done properly and in order, however, unless first of all we have treated of those aids to knowledge which natural philosophy itself requires. Others may judge differently, but I hold that there are three such aids, to be considered here before all others, as if they were the principles of knowing: namely, Holy Scripture; the sense, which must be considered and explained in its own way; and Reason, which we must examine a little more distinctly. As regards Scripture, it treats of natural things in two ways, either expressly or incidentally. It treats of them expressly in four respects: 1. When it sets out historically their origin, at the same time relating the method and manner by which they were produced (Genesis chapters 1 and 2). 2. When it likewise sets out historically various extraordinary events that befell these same things, such as that the whole earth, even to the highest mountains, was covered by waters at the time of the flood (Gen. 7 and 8); that the sun stood still in the time of Joshua (Josh. 10); that the sea was greatly stirred when Jonah was sailing (Jon. 1). 3. When it relates at the same time, historically, the uses of the same natural things: for example, that Hezekiah, when sick, used figs; that Abraham prepared a calf for food, and so on. 4. When in the same way it treats of the destruction of natural things, for example (2 Pet. 3) and elsewhere.

units.la: 2. Pet. 3. & alibi. Quibus omnibus in casibus atque locis, cum amanuenses Spiritus Sancti simpliciter referant, quid acciderit, saltem (si non speciali ratione, quod Spiritum Sanctum assistentem habuerint) fidem eam merentur, quae deferri solet historicis fide dignis. Neque enim aliter dici potest, quam ibi secundum veritatem historicam aliquid de rebus naturalibus referri: quam simplicem narrationem quicunque nolunt tanquam veram admittere, quid aliud faciunt, quam ut authoritatem totius Scripturae in dubium vocent, aut saltem viam muniant ad periculosam sententiam Origenis, qui omnia, quae historice in Scripturis de his illisve rebus referuntur, allegoriis implicare & pariter ad suas pręconceptas opiniones convertere solet. Incidenter de rebus naturalibus in Scriptura potissimum bifariam agituri. 1. Res naturales proponuntur tanquam argumentum divinæ majestatis, & quatenus hominem objective incitant ad Deum laudandum & celebrandum. 2. Ab iisdem petuntur similitudines & comparationes. Utro vero modo, hoc est sive ex professo, sive incidenter, de illis in ipsa Scriptura agatur, existimandum est, Spiritum Sanctum Scripturæ authorem principalem, non loqui ex mente & sententia errantis vulgi, sed ex rei veritate. quod notandum contra quosdam recentiores, eos potissimum, qui post Copernicum veterum Pythagoreorum, speciatim Philolai, Heraclidis, & Diophanti sententiam deterræ rotatione ab inferis revocarunt, qui cum viderent suæ sententiæ mirum quam officere authoritatem Scripturæ Sacræ, eo se receperunt, ut statuerent, Spiritum Sanctum de rebus naturalibus non ex rei veritate, sed ex judicio vulgi, quod sæpe hic falsum est, loqui. Quod non solum in mentem venit utrique Lansbergio, sed ex professo quoque prolixe defenditur à Paulo Antonio Foscarino in epist. subjici solita Galilæi de Galilæis Systemati Mundi, qui etiam pag. 485. non dubitat sic loqui: Sed non abs re fuerit, perpendere, cur Sacra Scriptura opinionibus vulgi tantum deferat, & cur non potius, homines de Rerum & Naturæ veritate accurate instruat. In causa est, primo, Sapientiæ divinæ benignitas, quæ suaviter omnibus rebus, secundum earum capacitatem & naturam se accommodat. &c. Secundo, quia nobis in hac vita, animum inanibus & variis curiositatibus replere non intendit, quæ nos dubios, & suspensos reddant, &c. Sed his non obstantibus, certo credendum est, Scripturam Sacram, & Sp. sanctum ejusdem authorem, quotiescunque incidenter quoque de rebus naturalibus loquitur, perpetuo ex rei veritate loqui. Nam 1. quum Apostolis Christi, & in eorum persona omnibus amanuensibus Spiritus sancti, hæc promissio facta fuerit Ioh. 16. vers. 13. Spiritus ille veritatis, dux vias vobis erit in omnem veritatem: quis est, qui existimet citra blasphemiam in Spiritum Sanctum, dici posse, quod suos amanuenses, quotiescunque aut ex professo, aut incidenter de rebus naturalibus verba facturi erant, non erudierit de ipsa veritate, sed solummodo monuerit quid ab errante vulgo statueretur? 11. Si statuendum sit, Sp. sanctum de rebus naturalibus loqui ex mente vulgi, aut non potuerit suos erudire de veritate rerum naturalium, aut si potuerit, noluit. At neutrum dici potest. Prius si statuatur, definiu
units.tr: In all these cases and places, since the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit simply report what happened, they deserve at least (if not by a special manner, because they had the Holy Spirit assisting them) that faith which is customarily given to trustworthy historians. For it cannot be said otherwise than that something about natural things is related there according to historical truth. Whoever is unwilling to admit this simple narrative as true does nothing else than call into doubt the authority of all Scripture, or at least pave the way for the dangerous opinion of Origen, who was accustomed to entangle in allegories everything that is related historically in the Scriptures about this or that thing, and to turn it to his own preconceived opinions. Scripture treats of natural things incidentally chiefly in two ways. 1. Natural things are set forth as an argument of the divine majesty, and insofar as they objectively stir a man to praise and celebrate God. 2. Similitudes and comparisons are drawn from them. But in whichever way these things are treated in Scripture, that is, whether expressly or incidentally, we must judge that the Holy Spirit, the principal author of Scripture, does not speak according to the mind and opinion of the erring crowd, but according to the truth of the matter. This must be noted against some more recent writers, especially those who, after Copernicus, recalled from the dead the opinion of the ancient Pythagoreans, specifically Philolaus, Heraclides and Diophantus, concerning the rotation of the earth. When they saw how greatly the authority of Holy Scripture stood in the way of their opinion, they took refuge in the view that the Holy Spirit speaks about natural things not according to the truth of the matter but according to the judgement of the crowd, which is often false here. This idea came not only to both Lansbergius, but is also defended at length and expressly by Paolo Antonio Foscarini, in the letter usually appended to Galileo's Systema Mundi, who on page 485 does not hesitate to speak thus: But it will not be out of place to consider why Sacred Scripture defers only to the opinions of the crowd, and why it does not rather instruct men accurately about the truth of things and of nature. The cause is, first, the kindness of divine Wisdom, which gently accommodates itself to all things according to their capacity and nature, etc. Second, because it does not intend to fill our minds in this life with empty and various curiosities, which would make us doubtful and hesitant, etc. But notwithstanding these things, we must certainly believe that Holy Scripture, and the Holy Spirit its author, whenever it speaks incidentally also about natural things, always speaks according to the truth of the matter. For, first, since this promise was made to the Apostles of Christ, and in their person to all the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit (John 16:13): That Spirit of truth will be your guide into all truth, who is there who would think, without blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, that it can be said that whenever his amanuenses were going to speak about natural things, either expressly or incidentally, he did not instruct them in the truth itself, but only warned them what was held by the erring crowd? 2. If it must be held that the Holy Spirit speaks about natural things according to the mind of the crowd, then either he could not instruct his people in the truth about natural things, or if he could, he was unwilling to. But neither can be said. If the former is maintained, it defines

units.la: definit Sp. Sanctus esse verus Deus eo ipso, quod non sit omniscius & omnipotens: Posterius autem adversatur titulo Consolatoris, quem passim in Scriptura fert: nam ut prae invidia (absit dicto blasphemia) videri posset nobis subduxisse quod ad naturalia, veritatis patefactionem; sic eo ipso definit esse consolator, quod menti ad veritatem anhelanti, videatur destinato voluisse crucem figere. III. Sententia haec e diametro pugnat cum intentione cujuscunque doctoris, abjectissimi quoque, atque e tribu Mechanicorum: quis enim ex omnibus illis, qui non quemcunque ex suis discipulis, saltem nitatur manuducere ad eam veritatem, quam in arte sua censetur exploratam habere? Secus qui faciunt, invidi, si non malefici haberi debent. Sed, si audiantur illi, quos obiter hic notamus, Spiritus Sanctus hac in parte inferior censendus fuerit viliffimo aliquo artifice? iv. Quod scriptum censeri debet purißimum, atque ab omnibus sordibus, nævisque defœcatum, in eo non debet notari quid falsi, aut quod serviat corroborando errori. Sed talis est Scriptura. Consequentia est certissima. Quis enim illud Scriptum, purum & defœcatum esse censeat, in quo, sive studio ipsius authoris, sive per imprudentiam ejusdem, sive quacunque alia ratione tione diffitendum sit, primarium Scripturæ sacræ scopum esse, ut nobis viam monstret ad vitam æternam; hic tamen principalis finis non excludit alios fines minus principales. Quum enim hæc ipsa variis in locis res naturales, earumque seriam meditationem nobis proponat, ut objective nos excitent ad Deum laudandum, quis dubitare audeat, quin de his ipsis rebus veras assertiones proponat, quarum subsidio rerum naturalium cognitionem acquirere queamus. II. Frustra sunt, quicunque existimant Spiritum Sanctum de rebus naturalibus loqui ex mente errantis vulgi potius, quam ex rei veritate; quod si hoc modo loqueretur minus fidem promereretur. Hoc enim si verum foret, pariter sequeretur, homines de rebus naturalibus philosophantes magis sufficere ad ingenerandam fidem in alijs hominibus, quam ipsum Sp. Sanctum. III. Nec audiendi sunt, qui sibi pro asserendo duro & periculoso commento, humanæ rationis pariterque sensuum infirmitatem imaginantur. Nam si omnes Scripturæ filij (Atheos & Libertinos tanquam prosanos à sacris his arcere fas est) qui invitantur ad considerationem rerum supranaturalium, sive miraculorum, ea intellectu suo apprehendere possunt; cur non magis apprehendant naturalia? Imo, cum Scriptura proponat ea, quæ acciderunt circa naturalia tanquam extraordinaria & miraculosa, cur non credendum eam de rebus naturalibus ex præscripto veritatis loqui, ad hoc ut miraculosa & supernaturalia, imo contra-naturalia ex naturalibus intelligi possint. IV. Vera explicatio rerum naturalium à Spiritu Sancto in Scriptura proposita nequaquam avertit fideles à primario Scripturæ scopo, sed illa eos ipsos convenienter ad eundem scopum dirigere potest. V. Verum quidem est, per Scripturam nos à rebus inanibus ad cælestia & perennia invitari, interim tamen propterea non debuit loqui de rebus naturalibus cum errante vulgo: sic enim ostenderet sese delectari rebus inanibus. Quid enim errore vulgi inanius censeri potest? VI. Accommodat quidem Scriptura sese nostro captui & infirmitati, sic tamen ut non desinat esse veritatis Spiritus, quo elogio sane condecorari non posset, si sic sese dimitteret ad nostram infirmitatem, ut cum mentientibus mentiretur, & cum errantibus erraret. Quod ad Scripturæ textus in contrarium adferri solitos, illi trium generum sunt, aut enim arguunt nostram ignorantiam circa illas res naturales, quas probe cognoscere videmur; aut videntur ostendere locum dandum esse locutioni tropicæ in iis, quæ de rebus quasi naturalibus è Scriptura adducuntur; aut denique videntur manifesto prodere ignorantiam Scripturæ sacræ, circa quædam, quæ de rebus naturalibus enunciat. Quantum ad primam classem, de ea nihil dicimus hoc capite, quod subsequenti fuse omnes textus ad eam pertinentes proposituri & examinaturi sumus. Ergo convertimus nos ad secundam: Cujus classis habita ratione, objici vulgo solent omnes illi textus, in quibus Deo, qui a nobis secundum infinitam & perfectissimam suam essentiam nulla ratione comprehendi potest, sive membra, sive affectus, sive quid ejus generis tribuitur: in quibus locutionibus, oppido quam frequentibus in Scriptura, cum notari debeat tropus, pariter contendunt tropum notandum esse in omnibus illis locis, ubi Sp. Sanctus de rebus naturalibus agit. Sed 1. quanta non intercedit distantia inter Deum Creatorem & res naturales ab eo creatas. Quoniam Deus utinfinitus excedit spheram intellectus nostri, Spiritus Sanctus nobiscum quasi balbutire cogitur, eumque, cujus faciem intueri non possumus, quasi a tergo nobis proponit, juxta ea ipsa, quæ Mosi acciderunt Exodi cap. 33. sed alia plane ratio est rerum naturalium; quam vis enim eas plenissime & sufficientissime cognoscendo non queamus perspicere, (ut subsequenti capite distinctius fusiusque ostendemus
units.tr: the Holy Spirit as the true God simply by the fact that he is not omniscient and omnipotent. The latter, moreover, conflicts with the title of Comforter which he bears everywhere in Scripture: for while he might seem, out of envy (let the word not be taken as blasphemy), to have withheld from us the disclosure of truth in natural matters, by that very fact he would define himself as no comforter, since he would seem to have purposely fixed a cross to a mind longing for truth. III. This opinion is diametrically opposed to the intention of any teacher, even the most abject, and even of the class of mechanics. For which of all those who do not try to lead at least one of their disciples to that truth which they consider themselves to have investigated in their art? Those who act otherwise ought to be regarded as envious, if not malicious. But if those whom we here note in passing are heard, is the Holy Spirit to be judged inferior in this respect to some most worthless craftsman? IV. A writing that ought to be judged most pure and purged of all filth and blemishes must not be found to contain anything false, or anything that serves to strengthen error. But such is Scripture. The consequence is most certain. For who would judge that writing to be pure and purged, in which, whether by the design of its author, or through his imprudence, or for whatever other reason, something must be denied, when the primary aim of Holy Scripture is to show us the way to eternal life? Yet this principal end does not exclude other, less principal ends. For since this same Scripture sets before us in various places natural things, and their orderly contemplation, so that they may objectively rouse us to praise God, who would dare to doubt that it sets forth true assertions about these very things, by whose aid we may acquire knowledge of natural things? II. Those who think that the Holy Spirit speaks about natural things according to the mind of the erring crowd rather than according to the truth of the matter are mistaken; and if he spoke in this way, he would deserve less faith. For if this were true, it would likewise follow that men philosophizing about natural things are more adequate to generate faith in other men than the Holy Spirit himself. III. Nor should those be heard who, to assert a hard and dangerous fiction, imagine the weakness of human reason and likewise of the senses. For if all the children of Scripture (it is right to keep atheists and libertines, as profane, away from these sacred things), who are invited to consider supernatural things, that is, miracles, can grasp them with their intellect, why should they not grasp natural things even more? Indeed, since Scripture sets forth those events which occurred in connection with natural things as extraordinary and miraculous, why should we not believe that it speaks about natural things according to the rule of truth, so that the miraculous and supernatural, indeed the contra-natural, may be understood from the natural? IV. A true explanation of natural things, set forth by the Holy Spirit in Scripture, by no means turns the faithful away from the primary aim of Scripture, but can rightly direct them to that same aim. V. It is indeed true that through Scripture we are invited from empty things to heavenly and enduring ones; nevertheless, for that reason it ought not to have spoken about natural things with the erring crowd, for in that way it would show itself to delight in empty things. For what can be judged emptier than the error of the crowd? VI. Scripture indeed accommodates itself to our capacity and weakness, yet in such a way that it does not cease to be the Spirit of truth, a title which it certainly could not bear if it so lowered itself to our weakness that it lied with liars and erred with those who err. As for the passages of Scripture usually adduced to the contrary, they are of three kinds: either they point out our ignorance about those natural things which we seem to know well; or they seem to show that a tropical manner of speaking must be allowed in those things which are drawn from Scripture about things that are, as it were, natural; or finally they seem clearly to betray the ignorance of Holy Scripture about certain things which it states concerning natural things. As for the first class, we say nothing about it in this chapter, since in the following one we shall set out and examine at length all the texts pertaining to it. So we turn to the second. Taking account of this class, there are objected by the crowd all those texts in which are ascribed to God, who by us cannot be comprehended in any way according to his infinite and most perfect essence, members, affections, or things of that kind; and in these expressions, very frequent in Scripture, since a trope ought to be noted in them, they likewise contend that a trope must be noted in all those places where the Holy Spirit treats of natural things. But, first, how great is the distance between God the Creator and the natural things created by him. Since God is infinite and exceeds the sphere of our intellect, the Holy Spirit is compelled to stammer, as it were, with us, and sets before us, as from behind, him whose face we cannot look upon, according to what happened to Moses (Exodus chapter 33). But the case of natural things is quite different; for although we cannot perceive them by knowing them most fully and sufficiently (as we shall show more distinctly and at greater length in the following chapter)

units.la: demus judicium: nisi quis pariter dicere voluerit Deo membra, & affectus & similia tribui secundum erroneum vulgi judicium. Pariter quippe dixeris ex vulgi judicio Deum in Scriptura ut habere proponi, quod tribuantur eidem ala atque penna, Ps. 17. v. 8. Ps. 91. v. 4. Augus. ep. iii. ad Paulinum: Quae de membris assidue Scriptura commemorat, ne quisquam secundum carnis huius formam & figuram non esse crederet similes Deo: propterea eadem & alas Deum habere dixit, quas utique nos non habemus. Deinceps accedendum ad tertiam classem, sive ad illos Scripturae textus, in quibus adversariae sententiae patroni existimant liquidum quasidocumentum sapientiae Spiritus Sancti circa res naturales proponi: atque initio quidem sollicitant, ac passim jactant decantatum illum locum Gen. i. v. 16 ubi cum luna, quam constat terra multo minorem esse, comprehendatur sub luminaribus magnis, existimant Spiritum Sanctum se accommodasse captui errantis vulgi, atque hoc de luna proposuisse, quod vulgus de eadem apprehendit. Sed, salva hic omnia sunt, si modo observetur Sp. Sanctum de luna aeque atque de sole magnitudinis verbo usum fuisse, ratione sui scopi, qui uti fuit in dicto Moisis loco delineare non minus lunae, quam ipsius solis offici-
units.tr: ...let us grant a judgment: unless someone should wish to say likewise that members, affections and the like are attributed to God according to the mistaken judgment of the crowd. For one could just as well say that, by the crowd's judgment, God is set forth in Scripture as having wings, since wing and feather are attributed to him (Ps. 17. v. 8; Ps. 91. v. 4). Augustine, Letter 3 to Paulinus: "The things Scripture constantly mentions about members are there so that no one should believe that, according to the form and figure of this flesh, they are not like God. For this reason it also says that God has wings, which of course we do not have." Next we must come to the third class, that is, to those passages of Scripture in which the patrons of the opposing view think that a clear document of the wisdom of the Holy Spirit concerning natural things is set forth. And at the start they press, and everywhere boast of, that well-worn passage in Gen. 1. v. 16, where the moon, which is plainly much smaller than the earth, is included among the great lights. They think the Holy Spirit accommodated himself to the understanding of the erring crowd and said of the moon what the crowd grasps of it. But all is safe here, provided it is observed that the Holy Spirit used the word great of the moon just as of the sun, in view of his purpose, which in that passage of Moses was to describe the office of the moon no less than that of the sun itself.

units.la: um ficium, convenienter Sp. Sanctus sic loquutus fuit: Fecit Deus duo illa luminaria magna: luminare majus ad praefecturam diei, & luminare minus ad praefecturam noctis: nam, ut hic non debet respici magnitudo molis, sed virtutis sive perfectionis, sic ratione habita muneris illuminatorij, quod de nocte ęque luna praestat, atque sol de die, concinne ea loquendi formula Sp. Sanctus, per Mosen loquens, usus fuit. Simili ratione loquitur Psaltes Ps. 136. v. 7. 8. & 9. Qui fecit lumina magna, quia in seculum est benignitas ejus. Lunam cum stellis ad dominia obtinenda noctu, quia in seculum est benignitas ejus. Atque haec interpretatio, ipsum Sp. Sanctum authorem agnoscens, jam olim arrisit ex patribus Basil. Hom. 6. in Hexaëm. Augustinus lib. 2. de Gen. ad lit. cap. 16. Ambros. lib. 4 Hexaëm. cap. 6. estque adeo accommodata, ut quamcunque sustinere queat instantiam. Dein, à Lansbergio, alijsque ejusdem cum ec sententiæ fautoribus, admodum urgentur ea, quæ occurrunt circa descriptionem maris æneî 1 Reg. 7. v. 23. & 2. Chr. 4. v. 2, sic enim arguunt: Scriptura dicit diametrum maris ænei in templo Salomonis fuisse cubitorum decem, circumferentiam vero cubitorum triginta, adeo ut proportio diametri ad peripheriam statuatur ut decem ad triginta, sive ut septem ad viginti unum.
units.tr: ...the office. So the Holy Spirit spoke fittingly: "God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night." For here one must not look to the bulk of the bodies, but to their power or perfection; and so, with regard to the illuminating function which the moon performs by night just as the sun does by day, the Holy Spirit, speaking through Moses, used this elegant form of expression. The Psalmist speaks in a similar way in Ps. 136. vv. 7, 8, 9: "To him who made great lights, for his mercy endureth for ever: the sun to rule by day, for his mercy endureth for ever; the moon and the stars to rule by night, for his mercy endureth for ever." And this interpretation, which acknowledges the Holy Spirit himself as author, has long been approved among the Fathers: Basil, Homily 6 on the Hexaemeron; Augustine, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 2, ch. 16; Ambrose, Hexaemeron, book 4, ch. 6. And it is so well suited that it can withstand any objection. Next, Lansbergius and others who favour the same opinion press hard the matters that arise concerning the description of the bronze sea (1 Kings 7. v. 23; 2 Chron. 4. v. 2). They argue thus: "Scripture says that the diameter of the bronze sea in Solomon's temple was ten cubits, but its circumference thirty cubits, so that the proportion of diameter to circumference is set as ten to thirty, or as seven to twenty-one."

units.la: Cum tamen Archimedes, cui tanquam artifici in sua arte pro cateris fides adhibenda, deprehenderit, proportionem diametri ad peripheriam sese habere ut septem ad viginti duo. Quibus decretum est, thesin suam omnibus modis tutari, nec illam missam facere, hic sibi valde plaudunt, caeterum praeter omnem causam, ut ex subsequentibus rationibus liquebit. 1. Non videtur maris aenej figura fuisse exacte sphaerica, sive rotunda, sed, ut Iosephus perhibet lib. 8. Antiq. Iud. cap. 2. femiorbis figurae. 2. Falso praesupponitur, apodictice a Geometris demonstratam esse certam ac infallibilem proportionem diametri ad peripheriam, cum post Archimedem & Euclidem, qui coacti sunt ignorantiam suam fateri, aqua etiamnum hic haereat viris in pulvere erudito exercitatissimis. 3. Familiare est Sp. Sancto duntaxat numerum majorem sive rotundum proponere, suppresso numero minori. Sic Abrahae posteri, ut liquet ex Exod. 12. verf. 48. & Galat. 3. verf. 17. afflicti fuerunt quadringentis & triginta annis; nempe ab initio peregrinationis Abrahae, ad exitum ex Aegypto: at Gen. 15. verf. 13. Abraham dicitur solummodo affligi annis 400. Pariter secundum Stephanum Actor. 7. verf. 14. dicuntur 75. animae cum Jacobo in Aegyptum descendisse, quod verum quoque est, si numeras numeres 5. filios Ephraim & Manassis: cæterum in textu Ebraeo Gen. 46. v. 27. recensentur solummodo animæ 70. Denique 2. Sam. 5. v. 5. David dicitur regnasse annos 40. & menses sex: cum tamen 1. Reg. 2. v. 2. sex illi menses prætermittantur. Tertio non minus sibi Lansbergius cum suis placet circa ea, quæ occurrunt Pl. 19. quando enim David actus à Sp. Sancto de Sole sic loquitur: Est tanquam sponsus prodiens e thalamo suo, lætatur tanquam robustus decursurus viam: existimat se confecisse, quod intendit, atque ostendisse graphice Sp. Sanctum in Scriptura de rebus naturalibus non loqui nisi ex mente erraniis vulgi. Sed cum hic occurrat locutio tropica, quæ non intelligenda est exacte secundum literam, sed secundum rationem analogiæ, omnia salva sunt. Atque uti ratione ornatus & splendoris Sol convenienter comparatur cum sponso in thalamo prodeunte, ita non minus conjunctè respectu celerrimi atq; indefessi motus & procursus componitur cum herôe velociter procurrente. Quarto addunt Ps. 58. ubi cum vers. 5. fiat mentio aspidis surda, & aurem suam obturantis, omnino existimant sibi jam triumphum deberi, & quidem duplici nomine. 1. quod vulgo persuasum sit aspides incantari posse. 2. quod idem ipsum credat, aspides obturando do aures, se munere posse adversus susurros magicos, ne ab iis laedantur. accedit hisce Valesius cap. 3. de sacra Philos. existimans a Davide Apologum aut moralem fabulam propositam esse. Sed bona verba! 1. Dicimus Davidem illuminatum a Spiritu Sancto in illa locutione figurata, per quam laborat exaggerare aulicorum Saulis pervicacem malitiam, presupponere de facto (ut loquuntur) a Magis adversus serpentes, ac speciatim aspides [quamvis interim neutiquam aut ipse, aut ullibi quoque Scriptura probet] adhiberi incantamenta; eaque ex permissione Dei, ad exarmandos quasi serpentes vim habuisse, ostendere videtur Virg. Eclog. 8. quando dicit:
units.tr: "Yet Archimedes, to whom, as an expert in his own art, credence is to be given above all others, has found that the proportion of diameter to circumference is seven to twenty-two." Those who have resolved to defend their thesis by every means, and not to abandon it, here congratulate themselves greatly; but they do so without any real ground, as will be clear from the following reasons: (1) The bronze sea was probably not exactly spherical or round in shape, but, as Josephus reports (Jewish Antiquities, book 8, ch. 2), of the form of a half-sphere. (2) It is wrongly presupposed that geometers have demonstrated with certainty and infallibility the proportion of diameter to circumference; for after Archimedes and Euclid, who were compelled to confess their ignorance, the matter still sticks even with men most practised and learned in working out problems in the dust. (3) It is customary for the Holy Spirit to state only the larger or round number, leaving out the smaller number. Thus Abraham's descendants, as is clear from Exod. 12. v. 48 and Gal. 3. v. 17, were afflicted for four hundred and thirty years, namely from the beginning of Abraham's sojourning to the going out from Egypt; yet at Gen. 15. v. 13 Abraham is said to have been afflicted only for four hundred years. Likewise, according to Stephen (Acts 7. v. 14), seventy-five souls went down into Egypt with Jacob, which is also true if you count the five sons of Ephraim and Manasseh; but in the Hebrew text of Gen. 46. v. 27 only seventy souls are listed. Finally, at 2 Sam. 5. v. 5 David is said to have reigned forty years and six months, although at 1 Kings 2. v. 2 those six months are passed over. (4) Lansbergius and his followers are no less pleased with themselves concerning the passage in Ps. 19, where, when the Holy Spirit moved David to speak of the sun thus: "It is like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, rejoicing like a strong man to run his course," he thinks he has achieved his aim and shown clearly that the Holy Spirit in Scripture speaks of natural things only in accordance with the mistaken mind of the crowd. But since this is a tropical expression, which is not to be understood exactly according to the letter but according to the rule of analogy, all is safe. And just as, by reason of its ornament and splendour, the sun is fittingly compared to a bridegroom going out of his chamber, so in respect of its very swift and tireless motion and course it is likewise fittingly compared to a hero running swiftly. (5) Fourthly, they add Ps. 58, where, since mention is made at v. 5 of "the deaf adder that stops its ear," they think a triumph is already owed to them, and on a double count: first, because it is commonly held that adders can be charmed; second, because the same people believe that by stopping their ears adders can guard themselves against magical whisperings and so not be harmed by them. Valesius also joins them in his chapter 3 on sacred philosophy, thinking that David set forth a fable or moral apologue. But let us speak fairly! First, we say that David, enlightened by the Holy Spirit in that figurative expression by which he labours to magnify the stubborn malice of Saul's courtiers, presupposes as a matter of fact (as they say) that charms were used by the Magi against serpents, and especially against asps [although neither he himself nor Scripture anywhere proves this]; and that such charms, by the permission of God, had power to disarm serpents, as Virgil seems to show in his Eclogue 8, when he says:

units.la: Frigidus in pratis cantando rumpitur anguis: quomodo & Ovidius testatur lib. 7. Metam.
units.tr: The cold snake bursts in the meadows from the singing: as Ovid also bears witness in book 7 of the Metamorphoses.

units.la: Vipereas rumpi verbis & carmine fauces. Ac, ne quis dubitet de poetarum fide, quam elevare videtur Plin. lib. 30, cap. 2. Classicus apud Vallesium testis, [quamvis alias Plinius jure merito hic suspectari posset, utpote qui lib. 2. cap. 7. negaverit inferos, & consequenter daemones] ipse Salomon hoc probat Eccl. 10. verf. 8. Si momorderit, inquit, serpens incantatione nondum adhibita, tunc nucum est emolumentum incantationis tenetiminti verba ejus. Quid, quia ipse Deus Deut. cap. 18. verf. 11. prohibet uti incantatione: quod præceptum sane, frustra à Deo præscriptum fuisset, nisi re ipsa incantationes in usu fuissent, quas ex Dei permissione aliquando vim habuisse, nullum dubium; alias diabolus ijsdem per suos clientes utens, cum ijs prostitutus ludibrioque habitus fuisset. 2. Non dixerim quidem, rationem constare Isidoro Hispalensi, quando lib. 12. Orig. cap. 4. sic loquitur: Aspis, cum coeperit pati incantatorem [qui eam quibusdam carminibus propriis evocat, ut eam de caverna educat] quum exire noluerit, unam aurem ad terram ponit, alteram cauda obturat & operit; quamvis hoc placuerit quoque Hieronymo, Augustino, Cassiodoro, aliisque: quum non sit verosimile, animal illud eo modo se componere, ad hoc ut non audiat incantantium voces; sed potius attendendam esse phrasin Scripturæ, quæ ideo obturatarum ab aspide quasi aurium meminit, quod, ex Dei singulari judicio, adversus ejusmodi aspides nihil potuerit incantatio, alias, tanquam valida à Deo permitti solita. Simili ratione legitur Iirm. 8. v. 17. Ecce ego immissurus sum in vos serpentes hæmorrhoides contra quas nulla prodest muffitatio, ut mordeant vos. Qui locus si comparetur cum loco è Psal. 58. in margine quasi scripta invenietur explicatio, juxta juxta Rabbinorum familiare dictum. Postremo, quam plurimi, praeeunte Lansbergio, Spiritum Sanctum proptorea in ordinem redigere instituerunt, quod neget Balænas per homines posse capi, quum tamen ipsis Hollandis quotannis inde uberrimus ptoventus accidat. Locus, quo potissimum nituntur, notatur Iob. cap 41. ubi verf. 1. & 2. sic legitur: An extrahas balænam hamo, aut fune, quem demerserit lingua ejus? An apponesjuncum nasoejus, aut spina perforabis maxillam ejus? Sed, & hic salva sunt omnia: nam praeterquam, quod 1. apud Iobum mentio fit Leviathanis, sive balænae molis immensę ac portentosæ; à qua tanquam humanis viribus atque artibus non subigenda, haut quaquam licet progredi ad balænas reliquas, minoresque, quae quotidie capiuntur: Amplius (2) non valet consequentia à Iobi saeculo, populisque Orientalibus armis sufficienter non instructis, ad praesens seculum, populosque eo viventes. Olim terra Canaan tam foecunda erat, ut dicatur latte atque melle fluxisse, hodie vero comparet admodum sterilis, sic ut terra Canaanæa in terra Canaanæa desiderari videatur. Tempore Saulis non erat faber in tota terra Israelitarum, nec erat gladius, aut hasta penes totum populum, 1. Sam. 13. v. 19. & 22. subsequentibus vero temporibus, atque praesenti hoc seculo, omnia ibi plenissima armorum sunt. Quibus, pro afferenda hac praeconcepta opinione, placet injuriis esse in Scripturam, amplius hoc urgent, quod non solum Augustinus, & Lactantius, verum etiam ipse Zacharias Pontifex Romanus, cum condemnaret Virgilium Salisburgensem Episcopum, praetextu Scripturae gravissime deceptus fuerit, & quidem usque adeo ut crediderit nullos Antipodes dari. Resp. Haec est illa cantilena, quae toties occinitur non solum in hac ipsa controversia, sed cujus subsidio quidam palliare quoque laborant hoc suum principium, in scientia scil. rerum naturalium nihildum tribuendum esse authoritati humanae. (eam negligi quis miretur ab iis, qui hic securi sunt authoritatis divinae.) quare operae pretium fecerimus, si, omnia huc pertinentia, quam distincte excusserimus. Ergo 1. dicimus, dato Augustinum, Lactantium, multosque alios non credidisse dari Antipodes, ob quosdam Scripturae textus haut probe intellectos, neutiquam inde sequetur Spiritum Sanctum in Scriptura de rebus naturalibus loquentem fidem non mereri; sed hoc solum, quoldam prae ignorantia phrasios Scripturae, familiares fovisse erroneam sententiam de quibusdam rebus naturalibus. 2. Neque Lactantius lib. 3. Divin. Instit. cap. 24. neque Augustinus lib. 16. de Civ. Dei cap. 9. disputantes adversus eos, qui negabant admittendos esse Antipodes, pro se Scripturam adduxerunt, sed ex falsis progredientes principiis, in illum errorem inciderunt. Nam uti Lactantio videtur absurdum, statuere terram rotundam esse; ita Augustinus eam sententiam amplexus fuit, quod existimaret vastum mare occurrere, quod trajici non posset, nec caperet, quomodo homines Adamo prognati ad Antipodum quasi sedes delati fuissent.
units.tr: Vipers' jaws are broken by words and charm. And lest anyone doubt the trustworthiness of the poets, whom Pliny seems to disparage (book 30, chapter 2), the witness Classicus, cited by Vallesius, [though Pliny might rightly be suspected here, since in book 2, chapter 7 he denied the existence of the underworld and consequently of demons], and Solomon himself proves it in Eccl. 10, verse 8: If a serpent bites before the charm has been applied, then the charmer gains nothing from his words. What is more, God himself in Deut. 18, verse 11, forbids the use of charms. This precept would surely have been laid down by God in vain, unless charms were in fact in use, and it is beyond doubt that by God's permission they sometimes had power. Otherwise the devil, using them through his clients, would have been exposed and made a laughing-stock. 2. I would not indeed say that the reasoning of Isidore of Seville holds good, when in book 12 of the Origines, chapter 4, he speaks thus: When the asp begins to suffer the charmer [who calls it out of its cave with certain special songs], and when it refuses to come out, it places one ear on the ground and stops and covers the other with its tail. Although this view was also held by Jerome, Augustine, Cassiodorus and others, it is not likely that the animal arranges itself in this way so as not to hear the voices of the charmers. Rather, the phrasing of Scripture must be attended to, which speaks of asps with stopped ears precisely because, by God's singular judgment, charming could do nothing against such asps, although it was otherwise accustomed to be permitted by God as effective. In a similar way we read in Jer. 8, verse 17: Behold, I will send among you serpents, basilisks, against which charming is of no avail, and they shall bite you. If this passage is compared with the passage in Psalm 58, the explanation will be found as if written in the margin, to use the familiar saying of the rabbis. Finally, very many, following Lansbergius, have set about calling the Holy Spirit to account for this reason: that he denies that whales can be taken by men, although the Dutch themselves every year draw a very rich harvest from them. The passage on which they chiefly rely is noted in Job 41, where in verses 1 and 2 we read: Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook, or with a cord which he lets down with his tongue? Can you put a rope in his nose, or pierce his jaw with a thorn? But here too all is safe. For, apart from the fact that, 1. in Job mention is made of Leviathan, that is, a whale of immense and monstrous size, which, as not to be subdued by human strength and skill, is in no way permitted to be extended to the other and smaller whales that are caught every day; further, (2) the inference from the age of Job, and from peoples of the East not sufficiently equipped with arms, to the present age and the peoples who live in it, does not hold. Once the land of Canaan was so fruitful that it is said to have flowed with milk and honey; today it appears very barren, so that the land of Canaan seems to be lacking in the land of Canaan. In the time of Saul there was no smith in the whole land of the Israelites, nor was there a sword or spear among all the people (1 Sam. 13, verses 19 and 22). But in later times, and in this present age, everything there is full of arms. Those who, in order to uphold this preconceived opinion, are willing to do violence to Scripture, press this further: not only Augustine and Lactantius, but even Pope Zachary himself, when he condemned Virgilius, bishop of Salzburg, was most gravely deceived under the pretext of Scripture, and indeed to such an extent that he believed there were no Antipodes. Reply. This is that old tune which is sung over and over, not only in this very controversy, but with whose support some also labour to cover up their principle, namely that in the science of natural things nothing is to be granted yet to human authority (no one need be surprised that this is neglected by those who here feel secure in divine authority). Therefore it will be worth our while to examine distinctly everything pertaining to this. First, we say that, granting that Augustine, Lactantius and many others did not believe in Antipodes on account of certain passages of Scripture not properly understood, it by no means follows that the Holy Spirit, speaking in Scripture about natural things, does not deserve belief. Rather, this only shows that, through ignorance of the idiom of Scripture, some men cherished an erroneous opinion about certain natural things. 2. Nor did Lactantius, in book 3 of the Divine Institutes, chapter 24, nor Augustine, in book 16 of the City of God, chapter 9, when disputing against those who denied that Antipodes must be admitted, bring Scripture forward in their own support. Rather, proceeding from false principles, they fell into that error. For just as it seemed absurd to Lactantius to hold that the earth is round, so Augustine embraced that view because he thought that a vast sea lay in the way which could not be crossed, and that he could not grasp how men descended from Adam could have been carried to the Antipodes as to their seats.

units.la: 3. Ex Augustini Comment. in Psal. 24. v. 1. patet eum abusum quoque fuisse eo loco, ubi dicitur terra fundata esse supra maria; sed duo ad illum locum dici possunt: primo notandum, esse phrasiologiam linguæ Hebrææ, quæ cum careat comparativis, ad eorum defectum supplendum uti solet prepositionibus, præ, super, &c. Ita ut sensus sit, terra est altior mari: quomodo dicitur Ps. 119. v. 103. eloquia tua super mel, id est, dulciora melle. Vel secundo dici potest, terram super mare esse, ratione quarundam partium, sunt enim quædam flumina, & sinus marini qui sub terra labuntur. 4. Quod ad historiam Virgilij, falso accusatus fuit, quod docuerit esse alium mundum, & alios homines sub terra, aliumque Solem, & Lunam; quod admitteret vero Antipodes (ut patet tum ex Bonifacij Germaniæ quasi Apostoli, & Zachariæ papæ literis) neutiquam vitio ei datum fuit; imo absolutus fuit, simulaë constitit, eum, nihil quasi monstri amplius alere, quam sententiam de Antipodibus; ut convenienter colligit Marcus Velserus lib. 5. rerum Boicar. nec falsus est hac in parte Baronius in Annal.Eccles. ad annum Christi 748. Vindicata hac ratione Scripturæ existimatione, amplius quæri posset, quousque se extendat, quod ad naturalia, cognitio amanuensium Spiritus Sancti? De quibusdam exillis refertur, tanquam singulare quid, quod in disciplinis exotericis quasi, atque illis, quæ alias aptæ sunt Theologiæ ancillari, mirum quam profecerint. Quomodo expresse de Mose dicitur Act. 7. v. 22. quod eruditus fuerit omni sapientia Ægyptiorum. de Daniele, illiusque sociis, quod Deus iis dederit notitiam & intelligentiam in omnibus literis & sapientia, Dan. 1. v. 17 & de Iosepho Patriarcha, quod informaverit seniores Ægyptiorum, Ps. 105. v. 22. de Salomone vero, quod sapientia ipsius major fuerit, quam omnium Orientalium, & quam omnis sapientia Ægyptiorum. 1. Reg. 4. v. 31. Præterea verissimum est, eos omnes, quoties acti fuerunt à Spiritu Sancto, sic sublevatos fuisse, ut ineffabiliter fuerint progressi in omnibus illis, quæ proloquebantur & scribebant, usque adeo, ut errare neutiquam potuerint: interim, nemo dederit, eos extra hanc ecstaticam quasi dispositionem, omnia, quod ad scientias naturales, perfectissime explorata habuisse. Nam si (constat ex infinitis documentis, speciatim ex altercatione Pauli cum Barnaba Act. 15. verf. 39.) sermones quoque eorum extra hunc statum non semper divinitus inspirati fuerunt, & sale illo sapientiæ & prudentiæ spiritualis conditi, nequaquam concedi ijs potest perfectissima omnium disciplinarum cognitio. Quare, nescio quid impulerit Aristarchum quem Theologicum, cui alias solemne est in omnes censuram stringere, ut argueret Celeberrimum Vossium eo nomine, quod scripserit lib. 3. de Idolol. cap. 99. Prophetas & Apostolos, divinitus vocatos atq; missos ad viam salutis annunciandam, non per omnia, atque plene & sufficienter exploratas habuisse naturas omnium rerum, licet (ut a nobis quoque factum) concedat, eos in veritatem deductos fuisse, quotiescunque, aut ex professo aut incidenter, de iis ex suggestione Sp. Sancti in suis scriptis aliquid perhibuerunt.
units.tr: 3. From Augustine's commentary on Psalm 24, verse 1, it appears that he too was misled at that passage where it is said that the earth is founded upon the seas. Yet two things can be said about that passage. First, it should be noted that this is a phraseology of the Hebrew language, which, lacking comparatives, customarily supplies their lack by prepositions such as præ, super, and so on. So the sense is: the earth is higher than the sea, just as Ps. 119, verse 103 says: your words are sweeter than honey (eloquia tua super mel), that is, sweeter than honey. Or secondly, it can be said that the earth is above the sea with respect to certain parts, for there are some rivers and bays of the sea which flow beneath the earth. 4. As for the case of Virgilius, he was falsely accused of teaching that there is another world, and other men under the earth, and another sun and moon. That he admitted Antipodes (as is clear both from the letters of Boniface, the so-called apostle of Germany, and from those of Pope Zachary) was by no means held against him as a fault. Indeed he was acquitted, since it was also established that he held no other monstrous opinion beyond that about the Antipodes, as Marcus Welser conveniently gathers in book 5 of the Rerum Boicarum, and Baronius too is not wrong in this respect in his Annals of the Church at the year of Christ 748. Having vindicated in this way the reputation of Scripture, one might further ask how far the knowledge of the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit extends to natural things. Of some of them it is reported, as something singular, that in the exoteric disciplines, and in those which are otherwise suited to be handmaids of theology, they made wonderful progress. Thus it is said expressly of Moses in Acts 7, verse 22, that he was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians; of Daniel and his companions, that God gave them knowledge and understanding in all letters and wisdom (Dan. 1, verse 17); and of the patriarch Joseph, that he instructed the elders of Egypt (Ps. 105, verse 22); of Solomon indeed, that his wisdom was greater than the wisdom of all the Easterners and than all the wisdom of the Egyptians (1 Kings 4, verse 31). Moreover, it is most true that all of them, whenever they were moved by the Holy Spirit, were so uplifted that they advanced ineffably in all those things which they uttered and wrote, to such an extent that they could by no means err. Meanwhile, no one would grant that they had, outside this ecstatic state, perfect knowledge of everything pertaining to the natural sciences. For if (as is established by countless proofs, especially by the dispute between Paul and Barnabas in Acts 15, verse 39) their speeches too outside this state were not always divinely inspired, and seasoned with that salt of spiritual wisdom and prudence, then the most perfect knowledge of all disciplines cannot be conceded to them. Hence I do not know what drove Aristarchus, the theologian, who is otherwise accustomed to censure everyone, to accuse the very famous Vossius on this ground: that he wrote in book 3 of On Idolatry, chapter 99, that the Prophets and Apostles, divinely called and sent to proclaim the way of salvation, did not have the natures of all things explored in every respect, fully and sufficiently, although (as we too have done) he grants that they were led into truth whenever, either expressly or incidentally, they set forth something about such things in their writings at the prompting of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Atque ut hactenus non minus Scripturæ authoritatem vindicauimus, quam evicimus eandem statui posse principium cognoscitivum naturalis Philosophiæ, sic ex re est amplius monere, Christianos quosque, sive, omnes illos, qui Scripturæ filij agnosci cupiunt, quando ipsam Scripturam (seu potius Deum in Scriptura loquentem) sollicitant velut testem veritatis Physicæ, non debere aut præconceptas suas opiniones, aut verius commeta sua ad ipsam Scripturam adferre, & quidem eum in finem, ut iisdem à tanto teste applausum impetrent; sed potius eos suas, si quas præconceperint opiniones, eum in finem adferre debere, ut post diligens examen ab ipsa Scriptura aut probentur, aut emendentur: Quod equidem si factum fuisset à Paracelso & tot illius asseclis, item à Fluddo in Philosophia Mosaica, (alios, quos in proclivi esset nominare, studio prætereo) tot nugæ Physicæ specioso titulo Scripturæ (in se alias infallibilis) palliatæ, rerum imperitis, atque ocitantibus naturæ rusparoribus propinatæ non fuissent. Ne vero hic ingrediar Labyrinthum, atque varijs difficultatibus me implicem, existimaverim quinque subsequentes regulas attendi debere, ab eo, qui legitime ex ipsa Scriptura rerum naturalium explicationem tum petere, tum etiam docere desiderat. I. Ea neutiquam potest adversari ullis fidei dogmatibus, aut secundum literam, aut secundum legitimam consequentiam notis. 2. Debet institui ex ratione phrasiologiæ à Spiritu Sancto in Scriptura observari atque frequentari solitæ. 3. Nullatenus aut sensuum judicio, aut rationi ipsi sensus moderanti adversari potest. 4. Quod Sp. Sanctus tanquam infallibilis Doctor sibi per omnia respondeat, unum dogma, quod ad naturalia è Scriptura petitum, cum altero nullatenus confligere debet.
units.tr: And so, having thus far vindicated the authority of Scripture as much as we have shown that it can be set up as the cognitive principle of natural philosophy, it is worth further warning that all Christians, that is, all those who wish to be counted sons of Scripture, when they consult Scripture itself (or rather God speaking in Scripture) as a witness to physical truth, ought not to bring to it either their preconceived opinions or, more accurately, their own inventions, and that too with the aim of winning applause from so great a witness. They ought rather, if they have any preconceived opinions, to bring them forward for this purpose: that after careful examination they may be either approved or corrected by Scripture itself. Indeed, if Paracelsus and his many followers, and likewise Fludd in his Mosaical Philosophy (I deliberately pass over others whom it would be easy to name), had done this, so many physical trifles would not have been cloaked under the specious title of Scripture (which in itself is infallible), and served up to the ignorant and to idle rummagers of nature. But lest I enter this labyrinth here and entangle myself in various difficulties, I think that five following rules ought to be observed by anyone who wishes to seek and also to teach a explanation of natural things lawfully from Scripture itself: (1) It can by no means be opposed to any dogmas of the faith, whether according to the letter or according to a legitimate consequence drawn from them. (2) It must be established from the manner of speaking that the Holy Spirit is accustomed to observe and frequently use in Scripture. (3) It can in no way be opposed to the judgement of the senses, or to reason itself, which moderates the senses. (4) Since the Holy Spirit, as an infallible Teacher, agrees with himself in all things, one doctrine drawn from Scripture concerning natural things must in no way conflict with another.

units.la: 5. Ipsa illa, quæ è Scriptura de rebus naturalibus eruta est veritas, debet magis rationabilis esse, quam quæcunque sententia eidem adversans. Accedimus ad secundum criterium sensus scil. cum quibus proxime componere convenit experientiam: at, cum de utroque quam sufficienter præcedentibus libris egerimus, nihil occurrit quod hic super addamus; modo hoc notaverimus, in Physicis sensus & experientiam, eo modo, velut principia cognoscitiva adhiberi, quem antea ex professo definivimus. Unum solum contra quosdam hic præmunien dum, nempe, sensus ideo suspectandos non esse circa res naturales, quod ratione sui exercitij non eas ipsas, sed speciem duntaxat earundem attingant, siquidem subsidio indiget. Quæ ratio si hic deberet attendi, Deus bone, quę non colligi poterunt absurda! Nam pari ratione suspectare licea ipsam intellectionem: siquidem intellectu nostet, qui intelligendo omnia fieri dicitur, indiget speciem subsidio, quibus mediantibus ipsum objectum intelligibile repræsentatur. Quoniam species est adæquata suo objecto in repræsentando, adæquate etiam illud exhibet; necà parte speciei, qua speciei, provenit ipsi sensationi fallacia, sed duntaxat à parte inadæquationis, quatenus scil. non concurrentibus, aut minus commode concurrentibus requisitis sensuum, species quoque examinem atque adæquate non possunt exhibere sua objecta. Verum quidem est, nec negari potest, ipsas quoque species sensibiles à sensu percipi, ut subjecta quæ, (in Scholis sic loqui solent) interim tamen principaliter percipiuntur, ut subjecta quibus. Sic enim percipiuntur ipsæ species à facultate sensitiva intrinseca, & per eam in homine ab intellectu, ut pariter nos ducant ad ipsum objectum: quod uti exhibent, sicab eodem veluti à parentibus soboles, progenitæ sunt. exhibent quippe per modum repræsentationis objectum, quod in iis tanquam in tabella quadam, expressum est. Quemadmodum vero proxime à sensu com-
units.tr: 5. The truth itself, which is drawn from Scripture concerning natural things, ought to be more reasonable than any opinion opposed to it. We come to the second criterion, namely the senses, with which experience must be compared closely. But since we have treated both of these sufficiently in the preceding books, there is nothing here that we need to add, except to note this: in physics the senses and experience are employed as cognitive principles in the way we defined earlier in detail. There is one point only to be guarded against here, against certain men: that the senses ought not to be suspected in matters concerning natural things on the ground that, by the nature of their exercise, they touch not the things themselves but only their species, since they need an aid. If this reasoning were to be applied here, good God, what absurdities could not be drawn from it! For by the same reasoning one might also suspect the intellection itself: since our intellect, which is said to become all things by understanding, needs species as an aid, through which the intelligible object itself is represented. Since a species is adequate to its object in representing it, it also presents the object adequately; and the fallacy does not arise on the side of the species, as species, nor for the sensation itself, but only on the side of inadequacy, namely when the requisites of the senses do not concur, or concur poorly, so that the species too cannot examine and adequately present their objects. It is true, and cannot be denied, that the sensible species themselves are perceived by the sense as the subjects which (as the Schools are accustomed to put it), yet in the meantime they are principally perceived as the subjects by which. For the species themselves are perceived by the sensitive faculty inherent in us, and through it in man by the intellect, so that they in turn lead us to the object itself; and just as they present it, so they are produced from it as offspring from parents. For they present the object by way of representation, as if it were expressed in them as on a certain tablet.

units.la: mut muni apprehenduntur ipsæ imagines ceu species,& per ipsas obiecta;sic contingit aliquando ( quando scil. somniamus) ut præsentibus solum speciebus in memoria reconditis, existimemus pariter nos res ipsas apprehendere, quatenus phantasia nescit distinguere inter species jam antea á rebus profusas & memoriæ scrinio commissas, easque, quas præsentibus ipsis obiectis recipit & dijudicat: quem tamen errorem dijudicamus, simulac fugato somno, ratio rursum functionibus suis vacare coeperit. Quod & ipse Aristoteles docet in libel. de somn. quando dicit saepe nos decipi, putantes imaginem Corisci, quem phantasia intuetur, esse ipsum Corisicum. Quem tamen errorem mox vigilantis ratio iterum corrigit, judicando non fuisse Corisicum, sed duntaxat simulacrum aliquod, per quod verus Corisicus cognoscitur. Atque in hunc sensum non inconvenienter Augustinus loquitur lib. 12. de Gen. ad lit. cap. 12. Cum in somniis ( inquit ) vel in ecstasi, corporum exprimuntur imagines, non discernuntur omnino à corporibus, nisi cum homo redditus sensibus corporis, recognoscit se in illis fuisse imaginibus, quas non per sensum corporis hauriebat. Quotquot vero ideo in sensibus fallacias suspectant, quod sensus non pertingant ad res ipsas, sed ad rerum imagines, velut earundem characteres es, quę pariter procedere debent ex hoc principio; quicquid per characterem & aliquam sui imaginem cognoscitur, vere non cognoscitur. Sed quid tum fiet Christo, quem Apostolus ad Hebr. 1. v. 3. vocat characterem personæ Patris? quique ad Philippum dicit Joh. 14. v. 9. Philippe, qui vidit me, (hoc est, cognovit) vidit Patrem? ex quo loco uti omni ævo Orthodoxi collegerunt Filium eadem essentia præditum esse cum Patre, ita valeret Arrianorum cavillatio, Filium ideo Patre debere minorem censeri, si modo id quod per imaginem exhibetur tanquam minus & inferius quid deberet censeri distinctum ab ipsa re, quam repræsentat. Vindicatis iterum sensibus [de quibus tamen in superioribus prolixius actum] convertimus nos ad rationes sive tertium Physiologiæ principium. Quæ in hac disciplina non solum admitti debet propter sensuum judicium, quo convenienter scil. hoc instituatur; verum etiam eo ipso, quod Physica sit scientia, habeatque suas demonstrationes verasac proprie sic dictas: quia demonstrationes neque instituí possunt, neque etiam examinari, nisi subsidio rationis, quę sola uti discurσiva est, ita non potest non illius in Physicis, ut etiam in omnibus alijs scientijs, maxima necessitas notari. Interim hujus rationis (iupra sensum æstimandæ) prætextu, nullus circumveniri debet, sic, ut cum cogitaverit Physicam esse scientiam, & demonstrationes habere, credat pariter eidem solam rationem sufficere, atque duntaxat secundum eam sequestratis sensibus censendam esse. Quod si admitti debeat, quæ non somnia in nobilissima disciplina poterunt admitti? Quivis enim, qui modo ingenio pollet, excogitare certas aliquas hypotheses poterit, (de illis jam antea actum fuit) atque ad easdem, velut chordas rationis suæ, ipsas res naturales examinare; quæ mentis dictata si secundum solum ratiocinium, exclusis sensibus valere atque recipi debeant, omnis generis somnia atq; ineptiæ in Physicum agrum sese exonerabunt: Nullaque tam absurda occurret sententia, quæ non possit hoc prætextu palliari, quod sic videatur rationi, quæ hoc in casu se tamen magis hypothetice, quam thetice & universalitet, omnium hominum ratione prodit. Fieri non potest, ut ratio exafciato constantique sensuum judicio, cum quo experientia conspirat, adversetur: ea semper se patitur examinari ad sensuum judicium, siquidem fieri neutiquam potest, ut eidem, quando hoc ipsum probe institutum est, ulla ratione contrarietur.
units.tr: Just as the images, as species, and through them the objects, are apprehended immediately by the common sense, so it sometimes happens (namely when we dream) that, when only the species stored in memory are present, we think that we likewise apprehend the things themselves, since the imagination does not know how to distinguish between the species already poured out from things and committed to the chest of memory, and those which it receives and judges when the objects themselves are present. Yet we judge this error as soon as sleep is dispelled and reason begins again to perform its functions. Aristotle himself teaches this in the libel. de somn., when he says that we are often deceived, thinking that the image of Coriscus which the imagination beholds is Coriscus himself. Yet reason, on waking, corrects this error again, judging that it was not Coriscus, but only some likeness through which the true Coriscus is known. In this sense Augustine speaks not inappropriately in book 12 of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapter 12: When in dreams or in ecstasy images of bodies are impressed, they are not wholly distinguished from bodies, unless when the man, restored to the bodily senses, recognises that he was in those images which he did not draw in through the bodily sense. But all those who suspect fallacies in the senses because the senses do not reach the things themselves but only their images, as if they were their characters, ought to proceed from this principle as well: whatever is known through a character and some image of it is not truly known. But what then will become of Christ, whom the Apostle in Heb. 1:3 calls the character of the person of the Father? And who says to Philip in John 14:9, Philip, he who has seen me (that is, has known me) has seen the Father? From this passage, as all orthodox writers in every age have inferred, that the Son is endowed with the same essence as the Father, so the cavil of the Arians would be of no force, that the Son must therefore be considered less than the Father, if what is exhibited through an image had to be considered as something lesser and inferior, and distinct from the thing it represents. Having again vindicated the senses (concerning which, however, we have treated at greater length above), we turn to reason, or the third principle of physiology. This principle must be admitted in this discipline not only on account of the judgement of the senses, by which this is properly instituted, but also because physics is a science and has its own true demonstrations, properly so called; for demonstrations can be neither set up nor examined except with the aid of reason, which alone is discursive. Thus the very great necessity of reason in physics, as in all other sciences, must be noted. Yet no one ought to be deceived by the pretext of this reason (which is to be esteemed above the senses), so as to think, once he has grasped that physics is a science and has demonstrations, that reason alone is sufficient for it and that, with the senses set aside, it is to be judged by reason alone. For if this were admitted, what dreams could not be admitted in this most noble discipline? Anyone who is merely gifted with wit could devise certain hypotheses (of these we have already treated) and examine natural things by them as if by the strings of his own reason; and if the dictates of the mind were to hold and be accepted on reasoning alone, with the senses excluded, every kind of dream and absurdity would unload itself into the field of physics. No opinion, however absurd, would fail to be cloaked by the pretext that it seems so to reason, which in such a case reveals itself as hypothetical rather than thetical and universal to the reason of all men. It cannot happen that reason, when the sound and constant judgement of the senses (with which experience agrees) is present, should be opposed to it: reason always allows itself to be examined by the judgement of the senses, since it can in no way happen that it should be contrary to that judgement, when this has been properly carried out.

units.la: Gnā Gnarum hoc iis, qui occupantur circa eam Physiologiæ partem, quæ consideratcorpus humanum, qui ut speciatim Anatomicorum nomen ferunt, ita pro primo principio suæ artis agnoscunt illud ipsum verbum, quod Samaritanis,suispopularibus, annunciabatJo. 4. v. 29. Venite, Videte; creduntque cum ratione se arguere, convenientia licet, Hippocratis, Aristotelis, & Galeni ratiocinia circa artus humanos, quod ex diametro adversentur constantibus, & ex lege diligentiæ atque prudentiæ institutis sectionibus. Sed quæ ratio humani corporis, habentis rationem objecti partialis in Physiologia, eadem ratio reliquorum corporum, quibus si Intellectus aliquid affingat, quod sensus non admittit, æque proscribitur, atque in triumviris jam antea nominatis, celeberrimis licet, conveniens & alias apprime consentiens ratiocinatio de membris humani corporis. Prolixius de hac re nolo hoc loco agere, quod perquam abunde in precedentibus idem egerim.
units.tr: This is well known to those who are engaged with that part of physiology which deals with the human body, and who, as anatomists by name, acknowledge as the first principle of their art that very word which was announced to the Samaritans, their fellow countrymen: Come, see (John 4:29). They believe they argue with reason against the reasonings of Hippocrates, Aristotle and Galen about the human limbs, though these are famous and otherwise in close agreement, because those reasonings directly contradict what is constant and what has been established by careful and prudent dissections. But the same principle that applies to the human body, which is an object of part of physiology, applies to the other bodies: if the intellect attributes to them something that the senses do not admit, it is rejected just as the reasoning about the members of the human body was rejected in the three men already named above, however famous they are, and however agreeable and otherwise well consistent their reasoning. I do not wish to treat this matter at greater length in this place, since I have already dealt with it very fully in what precedes.

units.la: CAPUT VIGESIMUM PRIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWENTY-FIRST.

units.la: E Scriptura Sacra ostenditur, nostram in naturalibus rebus scientiam imperfectam esse, simul Physicam scientiae nomen merari probatur & defenditur.
units.tr: From Holy Scripture it is shown that our knowledge of natural things is imperfect, and at the same time it is proved and defended that the name of Physics is deserved.

units.la: SIcut Polycleti statuam examussim solus Polycletus cognoscit, & de Appelleæ manus elegantia solus Apelles, aut, qui ei vix cessit, Parrhasius judicare potest; atque in genere quilibet artifex, in sua arte non solum præ aliis fidem meretur, verum etiam exactissime de suis operibus calculum fert: ita quoque Deus Opt. Max. qui solus est creator, & solus talia opera conficere potest, quæ ne ars quidem imitando assequi valet, sua opera solus per omnia perspecta exploratraque habet, usque adeo, ut nulla creatura, nequaquam homo, ea aut perfecte cognoscere, aut ad intimos earundem recessus penetrare queat. Quod adeo verum est, ut ipse sæpe in Scriptura cum homine, propositis suis operibus, tanquam eidem impervestigabilibus, expostulet, & parum quin arguendo ejus ignorantiam, etiam insultet. Hinc Jobi cap. 38. Deus ipse, cum Jobo quasi agens, sic introducitur loquens: An unquam praecepisti matutino tempori, notum fecisti aurorae locum suum. Vt carperet oras terrae, quum excutiuntur improbi ex ea. Vt ea notata sint argilla sigillari, sisterentur illi velut indumento obducto; Vt prohiberetur ab improbis lux eorum, & brachium elatum frangeretur; Pervenistine usque ad profunditates maris, atq; in penetrali abyssi inambulasti? An revelatae sunt tibi portae mortis, an portas umbrae lethalis vidisti? Considerastine usque ad latitudines terrae? Indica, si nosti eam totam. Quanam via itur, ubi habitat lux, & tenebrarum ubi est locus? Quum perceperis horum unumquodque usq; ad terminum suum, & quum intellexeris semitas domus ejus: noveris te jam tum natum fuisse, & numero dies tuos esse multos. Pervenistine ad thesauros nivis? aut in thesauros grandinis inspectionem habes? Quae cohibeo ad tempus angustiae, ad diem conflictus & belli. Quaenam est via, qua in partes destitit lux, dispergente Euro super terram. Quis dividit inundationi aquae ductum? & viam nimbo sonoro? Demittendo pluviam in terram vacuam vino, in desertum, in quo non est homo. Ut satiet vastatum & pervastatum locum, efferatque productio ductionem tenerae herbae? Esne pluviae pater? Aut quis genuit guttas roris? Ex cujus utero egreßa est glacies? aut pruinam caeli quis genuit? Tanquam lapide aquas abscondentes, quum superficies abyssi concrescit? An constringes delicias Plejadum? aut lora Orionis dissolves? Aut arcturum cum filiis suis duces? An cognoscis de statutis caeli? An disponere potes dominatum ejus in terra? an attollere potes ad densam nubem vocem tuam, ut effluentia aquarum tegat te? An emittere potes fulgura, ut abeant? an dicent tibi, ecce nos? quis indidisset praecordiis sapientiam? aut, quis dedisset menti intelligentiam? Quis sapphirinas efficit nubes sapientia? & uteros caeli quis profernat? Ut perfusio fit fermentandae terrae, ut conglutinentur glebae? Hactenus Deus apud Iobum, cum eodem expostulans. Cui loco, quamvis alia plura testimonia succenturiari queant, instar omnium tamen esse potest. nec hoc ita solum intelligendum, quasi in cognoscendis rebus naturalibus, extensive consideratis, deficiamus, in singulis quoque, intensive spectatis, deficimus; nec ad ullius quoque substantiae, qua substantiae, penetralia cognoscendo accedere possumus. Cognoscimus quidem aliquid substantiale, ipsam tamen men substantiam qua substantiam, prae intellectus nostri imbecillitate, per fe cognoscendo attingere haut magis possumus, atque caligans noctuae oculus lumen solis intueri.
units.tr: As only Polyclitus knows exactly the statue of Polyclitus, and only Apelles, or Parrhasius, who barely yielded to him, can judge the elegance of Apelles' hand, and as in general any craftsman deserves trust in his own art above others and bears the most exact verdict on his own works, so God, the best and greatest, who alone is the Creator and alone can produce works of this kind which not even art can equal by imitation, alone has his works perfectly seen and examined in every respect. So much so that no creature, and certainly no man, can either know them perfectly or penetrate into their innermost recesses. This is so true that in Scripture he himself often sets his works before man and challenges him as if they were beyond his investigation, and he almost mocks him by pointing out his ignorance. Hence Job 38, where God himself is introduced speaking as if to Job: "Hast thou commanded the morning since thy days, and caused the dayspring to know his place; that it might take hold of the ends of the earth, that the wicked might be shaken out of it? It is turned as clay to the seal; and they stand as a garment. And from the wicked their light is withholden, and the high arm shall be broken.
