Hast thou entered into the springs of the sea? or hast thou walked in the search of the depth? Have the gates of death been opened unto thee? or hast thou seen the doors of the shadow of death? Hast thou perceived the breadth of the earth? declare, if thou knowest it all. Where is the way where light dwelleth? and as for darkness, where is the place thereof? When thou shouldest take it to the bound thereof, and that thou shouldest know the paths to the house thereof? Knowest thou it, because thou wast then born? or because the number of thy days is great? Hast thou entered into the treasures of the snow? or hast thou seen the treasures of the hail? Which I have reserved against the time of trouble, against the day of battle and war. By what way is the light parted, which scattereth the east wind upon the earth? Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters, or a way for the lightning of thunder? To cause it to rain on the earth, where no man is; on the wilderness, wherein there is no man; to satisfy the desolate and waste ground; and to cause the bud of the tender herb to spring forth? Hath the rain a father? or who hath begotten the drops of dew? Out of whose womb came the ice? and the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it? The waters are hid as with a stone, and the face of the deep is frozen. Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion? Canst thou bring forth Mazzaroth in his season? or canst thou guide Arcturus with his sons? Knowest thou the ordinances of heaven? canst thou set the dominion thereof in the earth? Canst thou lift up thy voice to the clouds, that abundance of waters may cover thee? Canst thou send lightnings, that they may go and say unto thee, Here we are? Who hath put wisdom in the inward parts? or who hath given understanding to the heart? Who can number the clouds in wisdom? or who can stay the bottles of heaven, when the dust groweth into hardness, and the clods cleave fast together? Thus far God speaks with Job, challenging him. To this passage, although many other testimonies could be added in support, it may nevertheless serve in place of all. Nor is this to be understood merely in this sense: that we fail in knowing natural things when they are considered in their extent, while in individual things, viewed intensively, we do not fail. Nor can we approach by knowledge to the innermost parts of any substance as such. We indeed know something substantial, but by reason of the weakness of our understanding we can no more reach the substance itself as substance by knowing it through itself than the owl's dazzled eye can look upon the light of the sun.

units.la: Interim tamen Physica, secundum quam nos censemur, sive, Physica in concreto considerata, neutiquam debet coufundi cum ipsa Physica, in se, sive, ut loquuntur, in abstracto. Haec siquidem cum non habeat respectum ad certum subjectum cognoscens, sed consideret res naturales tanquam cognoscibiles, nod minus intensive, quam extensive perfecta censeri debet. Verum quidem, hanc ipsam Physicam videri similem ideae Platonicae, nec in ullo omnino homine post lapsum inveniri [Salomon, considératus à nobis antea, magnus quidem extitit Physicus, sic ut homine in statu lapsus considerato, parem forte non habuerit, quis tamen tanquam epoptem aliquem, omnia, nullis exceptis, cognovisse dixerit?) interim tamen cum ratione, tanquam regula, atque norma perfectissima, ad quam omnis cognitio Physica, per partes ab hominibus possessa, exigitur, agnosci debet. Sed missa hac Physica, ea ipsa, secundum quam nos tanquam Physici censemur, scientiae quoque nomen meretur. Non adferam ad hoc probandum multas
units.tr: Meanwhile, however, Physics, by which we are judged to be natural philosophers, or Physics considered concretely, must by no means be confused with Physics itself in its own nature, or, as they say, in the abstract. For the latter, since it has no reference to a particular knowing subject, but considers natural things as knowable, must be judged perfect no less intensively than extensively. It is true that this very Physics seems similar to the Platonic idea, and is found in no man at all after the Fall. [Solomon, whom we considered earlier, was indeed a great natural philosopher, so that, if man in a fallen state is considered, he perhaps had no equal; yet who would say that he knew all things, without exception, like some initiate of the mysteries?] Nevertheless, it must be acknowledged along with reason, as the rule and most perfect standard to which all physical knowledge possessed by men in parts is brought. But setting this aside, that very Physics by which we are regarded as natural philosophers also deserves the name of science.

units.la: [The first printed word of the first line reads "men" aster "quam" at the end of the previous page's fragment.] tas rationes, quum hæc una instar trecentatum, imo omnium, esse possit: Quæcunque scientia habet proprias, atque veras demonstrationes, illa est scientia: Atqui Physica etiam quatenus in hominem cadit, habet proprias verasque demonstrationes. Ergo. Major propositio est certissima, nec de ea aut dubitare licet, aut pro ea multa verba facere necessum. Minor confirmari posset exemplis sine numero, nisi plena manu, eadem omnia, imo singula, Systemata suppeditarent. Nec 1. quicquam ad rem facit, quod non omnia, quæ ad disciplinæ hujus objectum pertinent, demonstrari queant. Hoc quippe imputari debet nostræ imbecillitati, ex qua aut colligere licet, nondum plene ac sufficienter à nobis res naturales cognosci, sic sufficit, ex ijs, quæ cognoscimus, liquere, quantumcunq; modo illud est, quod cognoscimus, non esse titulo scientiæ frustrandum. 2. Peregrinos se esse in rebus naturalibus illi probant, qui omnes illas mutabiles atque inconstantes esse clamant. Neque enim hæc mutabilitas in motu currsuque corporum cælestium observari potest: multique lapides, maxime pretiosiores, item metalla, vix mutationis umbram præse ferentia, in hoc usque tempus perdurant. 2. Audiri quoque non meretur Heraclitus, cujus meminit Philosophus tum lib. 1. tum lib. 4. Metaph. licet magna voce proclamet Naturalem scientiam duntaxat agere de singularibus, & corruptibilibus: quum Physica non consideret res naturales secundum existentiam, quo sensu certum est eascem corruptibiles esse; sed duntaxat secundum essentiam, & quatenus essentialiter sunt indefectibiles. Sive, ut alij non incommode loquuntur: Physica res naturales considerat secundum esse specificum & completum, quod per se a natura est intentum; neutiquam vero secundum esse individuale, quod per accidens a natura intenditur, quum esse specificum non conservetur nisi in singularibus. Idem voluit Albertus Magnus, quum jam olim dicere Res naturales esse mutabiles, secundum quod sunt in determinato suppositò; neutiquam vero secundum esse universale: Considerari vero in Physiologia non illo, sed hoc modo.
units.tr: [The first printed word of the first line reads "men" after "quam" at the end of the previous page's fragment.] There are many reasons, since this one argument alone is worth three hundred, indeed all of them: Whatever science has its own true demonstrations is a science. But Physics, insofar as it falls within human reach, has its own true demonstrations. Therefore it is a science. The major premise is most certain, and there is no need either to doubt it or to say much in its defence. The minor premise could be confirmed by countless examples, indeed by all the Systems in full supply, both as a whole and in each part. (1) Nor does it matter that not everything that belongs to the object of this discipline can be demonstrated. This must be imputed to our weakness. From it one may conclude that natural things are not yet fully and sufficiently known by us; but it is enough to make clear, from what we do know, that however much we know, it must not be cheated of the title of science. (2) Those who cry that all natural things are changeable and inconstant prove that they are strangers to natural things. For this changeability cannot be observed in the motion and course of the heavenly bodies, and many stones, especially the more precious ones, and metals, which show scarcely a shadow of change, endure to this day. (3) Heraclitus, whom the Philosopher mentions both in book 1 and book 4 of the Metaphysics, deserves no hearing either, although he proclaims in a loud voice that natural science deals only with singulars and corruptibles. Physics does not consider natural things according to their existence, in which sense it is certain that they are corruptible, but only according to their essence, and insofar as they are essentially indefectible. Or, as others say not inappropriately: Physics considers natural things according to their specific and complete being, which nature intends in itself, and by no means according to their individual being, which nature intends accidentally, since specific being is preserved only in individuals. Albertus Magnus meant the same when he said long ago that natural things are changeable insofar as they exist in a determinate subject, but by no means according to universal being; and that in Physiology they are considered not in that way but in this.

units.la: 5. Neutiquam Aristoteles, naturæ licet rusticator diligens & accuratus, censeri debet regula ipsius naturalis scientiæ: quamvis enim multum eidem tribuamus (ut pluribus explicabimus alibi) non tamen eum adoramus: imo in Physicis admodum eum falsum fuisse, ostendit doctrina de æternitate mundi, motu, tempore, etc. 6. Quamvis nostro respectu &Ctu non solum individua naturalia, sed etiam ipsæ species infinitæ videantur, utraque tamen sunt finita in se; omnesque res naturales in scientia naturali considerantur, quatenus tum ad definita genera, tum etiam ad distinctas species sunt reductæ. 7. Quum antea scientiæ naturam secundum sua requisita consideraverimus, nihil hic occurrit, quod magnopere ex re sit, distinctè annotare, hoc unum modo si addiderimus: pro ratione scientiæ haut quaquam requiri, ut omne propositiones sint veræ atque evidentes, quum sufficiat aliquas duntaxat tales esse, secundum quas fieri possit denominatio. Licet enim immisceantur quam plurimæ propositiones, quæ solum probabiles sunt, à potiori tamen parte, æquum est fieri qua specificationem, qua denominationem.
units.tr: (5) Aristotle, though a diligent and accurate observer of nature, must by no means be regarded as the rule of natural science itself. For although we attribute much to him (as we shall explain at greater length elsewhere), we do not worship him. Indeed, that he was quite wrong in Physics is shown by his doctrine of the eternity of the world, of motion, of time, and so on. (6) Although, from our point of view and aspect, not only individual natural things but even the species themselves seem infinite, both are nonetheless finite in themselves; and all natural things are considered in natural science insofar as they are reduced both to definite genera and to distinct species. (7) Since we have already considered the nature of science according to its requisites, there is nothing here that is greatly to the point to note in detail. I will add only this: for the nature of science it is by no means required that all propositions be true and evident, since it is enough that some of them be of this kind, according to which the denomination can be made. For although very many propositions that are only probable may be mixed in, nonetheless, for the most part, it is fair that the characterisation be made either by the species or by the denomination.

units.la: CAPUT VIGESIMUM SECUNDUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWENTY-SECOND.

units.la: Occurritur vulgatæ illi objectioni, quæ Physica dicitur incerta esse, propterea quod nulla certa principia habeat.
units.tr: Objection to the common view that Physics is uncertain because it has no certain principles is answered.

units.la: MUltoties à viris in sacris Philosophicis subtilissimis, in controversiam Physicæ certitudinem trahi, ex eo cognovi, quod ea ipsa censeatur destitui certis principiis: quod ut probent, pro se adducere solent ipsummet Aristotelem, qui lib. 1. Phys. & iterum lib. 1. Metaphys. deposita quasi Philosophi persona, totus in eo est, ut enumeret varias illas sententias, quibus antiqui Philosophi inter se circa constitutionem principiorum corporibus naturalibus competentium, dissenserunt, quomodo antiqui quoque Ecclesiæ Doctores, Clemens Alexandrinus, Tertullianus, Origenes, Justinus Martyr, Lactantius, Eusebius Cæsariensis, aliique, conflictum hunc, & multiplex opinionum divortium considerantes; concludere solent Philosophiam ut ut inflatam, falsam erroneamque esse. Sed, ut ordine agamus, atque nihil intactum relinquamus, prænotamus, principia esse duum generum, cognitionis, & compositionis. Illa, ratione cujusque disciplinæ, iterum dupliciter sese habent, vel enim sunt principia generalia sive communia, in pluribus disciplinis usum habentia, vulgoque considerantur in disciplina universalißima, ceu Metaphysica; vel sunt principia cuique disciplinæ peculiaria, ac vocantur particularia. Utriusque ordinis principiis gaudere Physicam in confesso est, nec de eo ambigere licet, sic tamen, ut principia generalia, de quibus postea occasione Metaphysicæ aɛturi sumus, debeant censeri eatenus, quatenus in naturali scientia considerantur, modificata esse ad ipsam Physiologiam. Sed missis principiis hisce complexis, ceu cognoscitivis, de quibus lis non est, præ cæteris in confiderationem veniunt principia constitutiva, eaque non particularia, sed universalia, & quidem simplicissima, de quibus adhuc hodie tamt ambitiose contenditur, ut quisquis modo habuerit fiduciam aliquam sui ingenij; hoc seculo, quod ferax admodum est novorum Philosophorum, ausit intrepide quoq; nova principia in gratiam corporum naturalium fingere. Sed nihil est periculi. Initio hoc dico, principia generalissima & omnibus corporibus naturalibus communissima, à nullo mortalium comprehendi posse certo & definite, sic, ut norit illa principia talia esse, ut præter illa nulla alia essendi principia, tanquam universalia, dari queant. Verum hoc esse, patet ex Scripturæ loco, quem superiori capite Jobo subduximus, ex quo, infallibili ratiocinio, sic argumentari licet: Si ne quidem naturas particulares, eaque, quæ ex parte sub sensum cadunt, homo caligantibus intellectus sui oculis perrimari potest, quis dederit eundem certo definire posse communissima principia in universum omnia corpora naturalia, eorumque species, concernentia? Consequentię ratio est infallibilis. Ut enim eo loco Deus ignorantiæ Jobum arguit circa spiritualia, ex eo, quod terrena nosse non queat, argumentando à majori ad minus: sic, pari ratione ab ignorantia hominis circa ventos, fulmina, glaciem, etc. argumentari licet ad ignorantiam ejusdem circa prima & universalia corporum naturalium principia, quum enim in iis cognoscendis, quę apud Jobum enumerantur, quadantenus sensuum præsidio instructus sit, quam non magis hallucinari debet circa simplicissima & universalissima principia, neque per se sub sensum cadentia, neque etiam in corporibus naturalibus ordine, & specifice considerandis, lefe prodentibus, quum nullus homo possit per omnes species discurrere, atque quotidie adhuc novę eidem cognoscendę offerantur. Præterea si certo & liquido principia constitutentia generalissima, in Physiologia cognosci possent, ea indicaret aut Scriptura, aut sensus, aut ratio, aut ratio cum sensu. Scriptura hic tacet: quamvis enim variis in locis nobis inculcet, principium productivum ac conservativum corporum naturalium esse solum Deum um, unum essentia, sed trinum ratione personarum æqualiter ratione originis, dignitatis, atque cultus se habentium, nullibi tamen definite aut tangit, aut indicat principia constituentia, communi modo se habentia. sensus quoque hanc difficultatem non expedit, quum enim occupetur circa singularia, & duntaxat adhæreat objecto sibi definito, aut universaliter aut particulariter sese ratione sui habenti; neutiquam index esse potest principiorum universali ratione se habentium: sive enim dicas ea ex accidenti & per aliud duntaxat sentiri, sive sentiri in singularibus, sensus hac in parte submotum is. nam si duntaxat ex accidenti hæc principia qua talia sentiuntur, eo ipso sensum vaspectum reddis, idem enim facis ac si contenderes in crumena numis repleta, tibique oblata, numos necessario aureos esse debere. ad hoc, ex singularibus si faciendum sit judicium, illa omnia ut sensibus offerenda essent, aut saltem liquido deberet constare, pauca, quæ offeruntur, indubitatum indicium omnium facere. Ad hoc, ratio sibi soli relicta non potest ad communissima hæc principia pervenire: vel enim ideam eorum mens circumferet, & sic omnes (ut in axiomatibus Mathematicis contingit) qui modo terminos intelligent, suo suffragio hæc principia comprobabunt; vel per rationis discursum eadem proponentur, sed, ut jam antea oftensum, discursus hic rationis, quod ad Physiologiam, non potest ab illius objecto aberrare; semper enim cogitandum est, illud esse sensibiliter corporeum. Denique ratio sensibus copulata hic sufficere non potest, nam ut ea, quemadmodum antea patuit, sensuum moderatrix est; sic ea non tam subserviente, quam primas obtinente, tum inductiones, tum etiam demonstrationes Physicæ peraguntur: sed, ut inductio hic maximum subsidium præstare posset, ita, ubi eadem quam legitime quoque circa primorum principiorum investigationem procedere videtur, multis modis deficit atque vacillat: siquidem per inductionem, ut ut convenienter atque legitime institutam, hoc duntaxat colligit, esse quædam communia principia corporibus naturalibus in communi consideratis convenientia; sed, an ea se habeant ad modum principiorum constituentium, quomodo ediderat? Sic, v. c. colligit quidem ratio, extensionem, figuram, locum, situm, tempus, etc. omnibus in universum corporibus naturalibus convenire, sed, an eadem pariter habeant rationem principiorum constitutivorum, quomodo colligat per hoc inductivum ratiocinium? quid, quod contingit sæpe apprehendi subordinata principia operationis, quę propterea non possint pariter censeri principia constitutionis, quod necessario dependenter se habere debeant. Eoque, quotquot ex Physicis præcipiunt quid de communissimis & simplicissimis principiis corporis naturalis, necesssum est, sibi præsupponant certas quasdam hypotheses ratiocinativas, secundum quas eatenus convenienter progrediuntur, quatenus quæ ex illis educunt, sic cum iis consentiunt, ut pariter corpori naturali in communi & secundum omnes suas species considerato applicari queant. quemadmodum non solum circa Aristotelis ipsius principia ostendi posset, verum etiam eorum Philosophorum, quos ipse ad examen vocavit, quibus quadantenus injuriam à Philosophio factam suisse, alibi prolixius ostendo. Vt ut sit interim, nihilominus certa manet Physica in suis demonstrationibus, & consequenter, ipsi merretur nomen scientiæ: siquidem in demonstrationibus, non causarum remotarum (tales ad summum erunt principia generalissima) sed proximarum ratio habetur.
units.tr: I have often learned that some of the most subtle philosophers in sacred matters bring the certainty of Physics into question on the ground that it is thought to lack certain principles. To prove this, they usually cite Aristotle himself, who in Book 1 of the Physics and again in Book 1 of the Metaphysics, speaking in the person of a philosopher, devotes himself entirely to listing the various opinions by which the ancient philosophers disagreed among themselves about the principles belonging to natural bodies. Likewise the ancient Doctors of the Church, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Origen, Justin Martyr, Lactantius, Eusebius of Caesarea and others, considering this conflict and the many-sided division of opinions, usually conclude that Philosophy, however much it puffs itself up, is false and erroneous. But, to proceed in order and leave nothing untouched, I note first that principles are of two kinds, of knowing and of composition. Each of these again falls into two classes according to the nature of the discipline: either they are general or common principles, having use in many disciplines and commonly considered in the most universal discipline, such as Metaphysics; or they are principles peculiar to each discipline and are called particular. It is agreed that Physics enjoys principles of both kinds, and there is no room to doubt this. Yet the general principles, which we shall treat later on the occasion of Metaphysics, must be regarded as they are considered in natural science, that is, as modified for Physiology itself. But setting aside these complex principles, which are principles of knowing and about which there is no dispute, the principles of constitution deserve the first consideration. These are not particular but universal, and indeed the simplest of all. Concerning them, even today, there is so much ambitious contention that whoever has any confidence in his own talent dares, in this age which is so fruitful of new philosophers, to invent fearlessly new principles for the sake of natural bodies. But there is no danger. At the outset I say this: the most general principles, which are most common to all natural bodies, cannot be grasped by any mortal certainly and definitely, so that he would know that these principles are such that, besides them, no other principles of being can exist as universal ones. That this is so is clear from the passage of Scripture which in the previous chapter we drew from Job, from which the following argument can be made by an infallible reasoning: If a man whose intellect's eyes are dim cannot penetrate even the particular natures, and those which fall in part under the senses, who will grant that he can define with certainty the most common principles concerning all natural bodies in general and their kinds? The consequence is infallible. For as in that place God convicts Job of ignorance regarding spiritual things, because he cannot know earthly things, arguing from the greater to the less, so by the same reasoning one may argue from man's ignorance concerning winds, lightnings, ice and so on to his ignorance concerning the first and universal principles of natural bodies. For since in knowing those things that are listed in Job he is equipped, to some extent, with the aid of the senses, why should he not be much more mistaken about the simplest and most universal principles, which fall neither directly under the senses nor, in considering natural bodies in their order and by species, betray themselves? No man can run through all the species, and every day new ones are still offered to him for knowing. Moreover, if the constituent general principles could be known clearly and certainly in Physiology, Scripture, sense, reason, or reason joined with sense would indicate them. Scripture is silent here. For although in various places it impresses upon us that the productive and conserving principle of natural bodies is God alone, one in essence but three in person, equally in respect of origin, dignity and worship, nowhere does it define or indicate the constituent principles, which stand in a common manner. Nor does sense resolve this difficulty. For since it is occupied with singulars and clings only to its own defined object, which stands in relation to itself either universally or particularly, it can by no means be an indicator of principles which stand in a universal relation. For if you say that these principles are perceived only accidentally and through something else, or that they are perceived in singulars, the sense is set aside in this matter. For if these principles as such are perceived only accidentally, you make the sense itself suspect; you would do the same as if you contended that the coins in a purse full of coins offered to you must necessarily be gold. Besides, if judgment is to be made from singulars, all of them would have to be offered to the senses, or at least it would have to be clearly established that the few which are offered are a sure indication of them all. Again, reason left to itself cannot arrive at these most common principles. Either the mind will carry about the idea of them, and thus all who merely understand the terms (as happens with mathematical axioms) will confirm these principles by their assent; or they will be proposed through a process of reasoning. But, as shown above, such a process of reasoning, so far as Physiology is concerned, cannot stray from its object, for it must always be thought of as sensibly corporeal. Finally, reason joined with sense cannot suffice here. For as was shown before, reason is the moderator of the senses; and so it is not subordinate but holds the first place when Physical inductions and demonstrations are carried out. But although induction could provide the greatest help here, and although it seems to proceed legitimately and properly even in the investigation of the first principles, it fails and wavers in many ways. For induction, however suitably and legitimately conducted, gathers only this: that there are certain common principles agreeing with natural bodies considered in general. But whether these stand in the manner of constituent principles, as it has described them, it does not say. Thus, for example, reason indeed gathers that extension, figure, place, position, time and so on belong to all natural bodies in general; but whether these likewise hold the character of constituent principles, how does it gather this by such inductive reasoning? Moreover, it often happens that subordinate principles of operation are grasped, which therefore cannot equally be considered principles of constitution, since they must necessarily depend on something else. Hence, whatever the physicists lay down concerning the most common and simplest principles of a natural body, they must necessarily presuppose certain hypotheses of reasoning, according to which they proceed rightly only so far as what they draw from these agrees with them in such a way that it can be applied equally to natural body in general and to all its species. This could be shown not only regarding the principles of Aristotle himself, but also regarding those philosophers whom he summoned to examination, to whom, I show at greater length elsewhere, the Philosopher did some injustice. However that may be, Physics nonetheless remains certain in its demonstrations, and consequently deserves the name of science, since in demonstrations regard is had not to remote causes (these at most would be the most general principles) but to proximate ones.

units.la: CAPUT VIGESIMUM SECUNDUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWENTY-SECOND.

units.la: De Metaphysica, sive Ontologia, de qua ut ipsi Reformati Theologi diversimode existimant, sic quid de eadem statuendum sit, breviter ostenditur, simulque occurritur omnibus, qua adversus illam adferri possent.
units.tr: On Metaphysics, or Ontology: what is to be held about it, since the Reformed theologians themselves judge it in different ways, is briefly shown, and at the same time all the objections that might be brought against it are met.

units.la: Post assertam Physicam, circa quam aliquanto diutius occupari contigit, converto me ad disciplinam illam, quæ vulgo Metaphysica dicitur, quam quamvis antiqui Sceptici intactam reliquerint, nullas adversus illam dirigendo machinas, nihilominus tamen hoc loco eam considerare debemus, quod circa illam ipsi Theologi Reformati ambigere consueverint, quibusdam laudibus in cælum eam extollentibus, arctoque nexu sibi vindicantibus, aliis vero eandem prorsus rejicientibus, & nescio quibus non convitiis proscindentibus. Inter eos, qui submovere hanc disciplinam laborarunt, primo loco nominandus est Petrus Ramus, qui, cum non minus excæcatus esset odio in Aristotelem, quam amore erga Logicam, quam à se primitus perfectam esse somniabat, adeo inclementer Metaphysicæ dixit, ut non dubitarit Præf. ad Scholas Metaphys. Arist. sic proloqui: Theologiam, quam Aristoteles in Metaphysica docet, impietatem omnium impietatum maxime detestabilem & execrabilem esse confirmo; flagitiumque inexpiabile statuo, in Christianis quibusdam Scholasticis, etiam (quod magis mirere) purioris Theologiæ studiosis confirmare publicatis scriptis: Metaphysicam Aristotelis Christiana religionis calumniam quandam esse. Quumque negare non posset, saltem illorum terminorum, quos explicat Metaphysica, usum aliquem esse, eos omnes ad suam Logicam referre instituit, quasi ibi propriam sedem habeant, atque explicari debeant. qua in parte præivisse videtur Antonius Mirandulanus de sing. certamine lib. 13. sect. 6. & 7. Rami vestigia premens Rev. D. Amesius, Theologus eximius, atque de orthodoxa religione meritissimus, aliquando in Academia Franequerana peculiari Disputatione universam Metaphysicam subvertere laboravit, Disputationem ipsam obsignando P. Rami verbis, jam antea laudatis. Ab eo haut longe recedit Rev. D. Henricus Alting, ad annos aliquot in Academia Groningæ & Ommelandiæ Collega mihi plurimum observandus. Hunc enim in modum Probl. Theol. parte 1. Probl. 2. hanc ipsam disciplinam, tanquam Theologiæ inutilem, imo noxiam, incessit: Metaphysicę nullus usus est in Theologia, siquidem ea tantum speculantur quæ ejus propria sunt, non autem transfumpta ex alijs artibus aut disciplinis. Abusus vero est multiplex: 1. Quæ Theologiæ propria sunt, de Deo, Angelis, Creatione, sibi vendicat obtentu peculiaris modi considerandi. 2. Subtilitates vanas, quæstiones otiosas, opiniones ambiguas ad res Theologicas transfert. 3. In utramque partem disputat omnia, & vix quidquam certi habet. Hinc Sceptica Theologia nata quæ tandem exit in Atheismum: Qui enim de omnibus dubitat, nihil tandem credere incipit. Huc pertinet illud, Semper discentes, sed nunquam ad cognitionem veritatis pervenientes, 2. Tim. 3. v. 7. 4. Distinctionibus frivolis & ineptis omnia eludit & elidit; mater omnis Sophisticæ & deceptionis. 5. Terminos novos, monstrosos, insulsos, phrases improprias, obscuras invehit, quibus sanos sermones Theologicos in fide & charitate corrumpit. Hactenus D. Alting. Maximis hisce viris complures ex ipsis Orthodoxis quoque Theologis obsistunt, & acriter obloquuntur, ex quibus suffecerit adduxisse unum D. Alstedium, sic loquentem lib. 4. Didact. cap. 9. Reg. 1. Miseret, inquit, me supina illius inscitia, qua laborat quidam ex recentioribus Theologus, qui Academiam quandam Germaniae felicem praedicat, quod inde studium Metaphysices exulet. Quo rite atque ordine progredi nobis liceat, omniaque, ad dubia haec pertinentia, convenienter a nobis explicentur, praemissis quibusdam praeambulis observationibus, tria potissimum agemus. 1. Expendemus, num admittenda sit quaedam Metaphysica? 2. An ea distincta sit a Logica? 3. An quis usus a Metaphysica in Orthodoxam Theologiam redundare queat? Quod ad observationes praeambulas, primo ratione nominis nolumus cum quoquam hic contendere, videtur hoc quibusdam ominosum esse, atque haut aliter suspectant atque nomen Magiae, cum tamen in se sit innocuum, nec quid incommodi complectatur. Non agnoscit quidem illud Aristoteles, interim est antiquum, utpote usurpatum a Plutarcho in Alexandro, & notum Nicolao Damasceno, quibusdam haut praeter omnem rationem architectum ejusdem statuentibus Andronicum Rhodium, qui illud fabricatus fuerit ex inscriptione librorum Metaphysicorum: ipsam disciplinam quippe Philosophus modo Primam Philosophiam, ut sub finem lib. 1. Phys. modo sapientiam in limine lib. 1. Metaph. aut scientiam de ente in principio lib. 3. Metaph.
units.tr: Having asserted physics, on which I have spent rather a long time, I turn to that discipline which is commonly called Metaphysics. The ancient Sceptics left it untouched and aimed no engines against it, but we must consider it here, because the Reformed theologians themselves are accustomed to disagree about it. Some extol it to heaven with various praises and claim it for themselves by a close bond, while others reject it altogether and tear it apart with I know not what reproaches. Among those who have laboured to remove this discipline, the first to be named is Petrus Ramus. Blinded no less by hatred of Aristotle than by love of Logic, which he dreamed had been first perfected by himself, he spoke so harshly against Metaphysics that in the preface to his Scholae Metaphysicae of Aristotle he did not hesitate to put it thus: "I affirm that the theology which Aristotle teaches in the Metaphysics is the most detestable and accursed of all impieties; and I declare it an inexpiable crime that certain Christian Scholastics, and (what is more surprising) students of purer theology, have affirmed in published writings that the Metaphysics of Aristotle is a certain slander against the Christian religion." Since he could not deny that at least the terms which Metaphysics explains have some use, he undertook to refer them all to his own Logic, as if they had their proper seat there and ought to be explained there. In this respect Antonius Mirandulanus, De singulari certamine bk. 13, sects. 6 and 7, seems to have gone before him. Treading in the footsteps of Ramus, the Reverend Mr Amesius, an outstanding theologian and most deserving of the orthodox religion, once laboured in the Academy of Franeker, in a special disputation, to overturn all of Metaphysics, sealing the disputation itself with the words of Ramus already cited. Not far from him departs the Reverend Mr Henricus Alting, for some years my colleague in the Academy of Groningen and the Ommelands, whom I greatly esteem. For in this manner, in his Problemata Theologica part 1, problem 2, he assailed this very discipline as useless, even harmful, to theology: "Metaphysics has no use in theology, since it speculates only on those things which are proper to it, and not on things borrowed from other arts or disciplines. Its abuse is manifold: 1. It claims for itself what is proper to theology, concerning God, angels and creation, under the pretext of a peculiar way of considering them. 2. It transfers vain subtleties, idle questions and ambiguous opinions to theological matters. 3. It disputes everything on both sides and has scarcely anything certain. Hence a Sceptical theology was born, which at last ends in atheism: for whoever doubts about everything begins at last to believe nothing. To this belongs that saying, always learning, but never coming to the knowledge of the truth, 2 Tim. 3:7. 4. By frivolous and inept distinctions it mocks and destroys everything; it is the mother of all sophistry and deception. 5. It introduces new, monstrous, insipid terms and improper, obscure phrases, by which it corrupts sound theological speech in faith and charity. Thus far Alting." Many of the Orthodox theologians themselves also resist these greatest men and speak sharply against them. Of these it will suffice to have cited one, Alsted, who speaks thus in his Didactica bk. 4, ch. 9, rule 1: "I pity that supine ignorance, he says, from which a certain one of the more recent theologians suffers, who praises a certain happy German Academy because the study of Metaphysics is banished from it." In what right and order we may proceed, and so that all matters pertaining to these doubts may be fittingly explained by us, after certain preliminary observations have been set out, we shall chiefly treat three questions. 1. We shall weigh whether some Metaphysics is to be admitted. 2. Whether it is distinct from Logic. 3. Whether any use of Metaphysics can flow into Orthodox theology. As for the preliminary observations: first, as regards the name, I do not wish to contend with anyone here. To some this seems ominous, and they look on it with suspicion no differently than on the name of Magic, although in itself it is harmless and carries no inconvenience. Aristotle indeed does not acknowledge it, yet it is old, having been used by Plutarch in his Life of Alexander and being known to Nicolaus Damascenus. Some, not without reason, hold that Andronicus of Rhodes was its architect, who fashioned it from the title of the books of the Metaphysics. The Philosopher himself called the discipline now First Philosophy, as at the end of Physics bk. 1; now wisdom, at the beginning of Metaphysics bk. 1; or the science of being, at the beginning of Metaphysics bk. 3.

units.la: lib. 4. Metaph. cont. 4. modo denique per antonomasiam absolute Philosophiam nominavit: quo postremo nomine semper in aliis libris usus est, quotiescunque digitum intendit in illas res, quas uberius in libris Metaphysicorum consideraverat, ut videre est in fine lib. 1. Phys. lib. de motu animal. cap. 6. & alibi. Recentioribus quibusdam placuit, hisce omnibus rejectis, nomen Ontologiae amplecti. Modo de re ipsa constaret, ratione nominis nulli controversiam moverem. Agnoscatur scientia quaedam generalissima, quae agat de ente qua ente, atque eodem redibit, quocunque tandem nomine ea ipsa condecoretur: nec me fatigabo ulterius circa Etymologiam Metaphysicae, si admissa fuerit disciplina de ente in genere, distincta à consideratione cujuscunque Entis particularis. Secundo frustra est Rev. D. Amesius post Ramum, quando Metaphysicae genuinae patronis affingit, quasi Aristotelem illius regulam esse statuant. Scio multos prae nimio amore Aristotelis (circa quem lib. sexto aliquid notabimus) parum quin insaniisse, sed paucorum delirium non debet imputari omnibus in universum Philosophis, qui cum ratione distinguere sciunt inter ea, quae nituntur duntaxat authoritate, & quae praeter authoritatem pro se adducere possunt liquidas rationes. Persuasum quidem vellet Campanella, libros Metaphysicorum Aristotelis esse aliquod Lexicon Philosophicum, quod potissimum Philosophus in iis occupetur circa terminorum explicationem; sed, qui non sunt peregrini in lectione eorundem, iis exploratum est, multas res valde concinne & subtiliter in iis ipsis explicari. Interim, in illis libris, quaedam occurrunt, quae neutiquam possunt subsistere, cum iis, quae per divinam revelationem ex Dei verbo edocti sumus. Nam, ut pauca solum proponam, quam non periculosa est illa locutio, quae occurrit lib. 12. Metaph. tex. 51. Deus quadam non cognoscit, ne vilescat intellectus ejus: nam quaedam adeo vilia sunt, ut nobilius sit ea ignorare, quam nosse. Imo quam non periculosa est universa Philosophi disputatio de mundi aeternitate, quam habet eodem libro duodecimo cont. 30. quae uti nititur hoc fundamento, Deum agere ex necessitate naturae; sic multis modis Dei, qui est perfectissimus, naturae adversatur. Tertio distinguere convenit inter tractationem Metaphysicae concretivam, & abstractivam: si haec disciplina consideretur prout ab hoc illo ve Metaphysico Doctore est tractata, nullum dubium est, quin admixtos habeat varios errores; (soli Iesuitae, prae aliis Fonseca atque Suarez, testes esse possunt) sed quam iniquum errata artificum imputare ipsi arti, aut præconceptos errores Theologicos, hujus sive Pontificii, sive Sociniani, sive Lutherani Doctoris, intempestive atque fallaciter infartos aut Systematibus, aut tractatibus Metaphysicis, acceptos referre ipsi Metaphysicæ, quæ haut magis æstimari debet ex hisce mangonibus, quam Epistolæ Apostoli Pauli, ex iis, de quibus Petrus jam sua ætate testatus est, quod nonnulla in iis difficilia intellectu detorquerent, 2 Petr. 3. v. 16. Quarto non Metaphysicæ, sed petulantibus quibusdam, & in doctrina de Methodo haut satis versatis Metaphysicis imputari debet, quod vulgo in Systematibus Metaphysicis, doctrina de Deo & Angelis proponatur. Uuiversalissima disciplina, ut est Metaphysica, sic distincta manere debet ab omnibus disciplinis particularibus, atque duntaxat occupari circa ens, & communissima ejusdem attributa. Si fas ei sit descendere ad tractationem de Deo & Angelis, cur non pariter agere quoque poterit de quocunque ente particulari? Sed, ita per Metaphysicam, velut Pansophiæ compendium abolebuntur omnes aliæ disciplinæ. Quinto, doctrina de Deo, quatenus ex naturæ lumine depromi potest, peculiarem disciplinam, quam Theologiam naturalem vocare licet, sibi arrogat; quod vero de
units.tr: Metaphysics bk. 4, ch. 4; and finally, by antonomasia, he simply named it Philosophy. He always used this last name in his other books whenever he pointed to those matters which he had considered more fully in the books of the Metaphysics, as may be seen at the end of Physics bk. 1, in the book On the Motion of Animals ch. 6, and elsewhere. Some more recent writers have preferred to reject all these and embrace the name Ontology. If only the thing itself were agreed, I would raise no controversy over the name. Let some most general science be acknowledged which treats of being as being, and it will come to the same thing whatever name it is adorned with; nor shall I weary myself further over the etymology of Metaphysics, provided that the discipline of being in general, distinct from the consideration of any particular being, is admitted. Secondly, the Reverend Mr Amesius is wrong to follow Ramus when he ascribes to the defenders of genuine Metaphysics the view that Aristotle is its rule. I know that many, from excessive love of Aristotle (about whom we shall note something in book six), have been little short of mad. But the madness of a few ought not to be imputed to all philosophers in general, who know how to distinguish with reason between those things which rest merely on authority and those which can bring forward clear reasons apart from authority. Campanella would indeed have us believe that the books of Aristotle's Metaphysics are a kind of philosophical lexicon, since the Philosopher is occupied in them chiefly with explaining terms. But those who are not strangers to reading them know that many things are explained in them very neatly and subtly. Meanwhile, in those books there occur some things which by no means can stand with what we have been taught through divine revelation from the Word of God. To propose only a few: how dangerous is that statement which occurs in Metaphysics bk. 12, text 51: God does not know certain things, lest his intellect be cheapened; for certain things are so base that it is nobler to be ignorant of them than to know them. Indeed, how dangerous is the whole philosopher's disputation on the eternity of the world, which he gives in the same book 12, ch. 30. As it rests on this foundation, that God acts from the necessity of nature, so in many ways it is opposed to the nature of God, who is most perfect. Thirdly, it is proper to distinguish between the concrete and the abstract treatment of Metaphysics. If this discipline is considered as it has been treated by this or that Metaphysical teacher, there is no doubt that it contains various mixed errors (the Jesuits alone, above others Fonseca and Suárez, can bear witness to this). But how unfair it is to impute the errors of craftsmen to the craft itself, or to refer to Metaphysics itself the preconceived theological errors of this or that teacher, whether Papist, Socinian or Lutheran, inopportunely and deceptively crammed into systems or treatises of Metaphysics! Metaphysics ought not to be judged by such hacks any more than the Epistles of the Apostle Paul should be judged by those of whom Peter already in his own day testified that they twisted some things in them that are hard to understand, 2 Pet. 3:16. Fourthly, it is not Metaphysics but certain petulant Metaphysicians, not well versed in the doctrine of method, who should be blamed for the fact that the doctrine of God and of angels is commonly set out in Metaphysical systems. A most universal discipline, such as Metaphysics is, ought to remain distinct from all particular disciplines and be occupied only with being and its most common attributes. If it were permissible for it to descend to the treatment of God and angels, why could it not likewise treat of any particular being whatever? But in this way, by means of Metaphysics as a kind of compendium of Pansophy, all other disciplines would be abolished. Fifthly, the doctrine of God, insofar as it can be drawn from the light of nature, claims for itself a peculiar discipline, which may be called natural theology. But as for what concerns angels (and how little that is!), it can be drawn from the same source ...

units.la: Angelis (at quantulum hoc!) ex eodem fonte hauriri poterit, ad Pneumaticam (in ea quidam quoque de Deo agere instituerunt, quamvis infinita intercedat distantia inter infinitum, independentem, & perfectissimum Deum, qui Spiritus vocatur Ioan. 4. v. 24. & angelos, Spiritus ministratorios, Heb. 1. v. 14.) referri debet: Ad Metaphysicam vero à quibusdam utraque doctrina relata est, aut exemplo Aristotelis, qui tamen in libris Metaphysicorum Methodi negligentior est; aut, quod existimarent eadem tam pauca esse, ut non sufficerent constituendæ justæ disciplinæ; aut denique, quod crederent se convenienter explicaturos esse analogiam entis, si proposita pleniori perfectissimi Dei tractatione, ex illius comparatione cum quolibet ente finito, cognoscendum proponerent quanta distantia inter ens infinitum, & quodlibet ens finitum intercedat. Sexto, quemadmodum universa Philosophia, ratione omnium & singularum suarum partium fasces submittere debet Revelatæ Theologiæ, sacræque Scripturæ, quæ hujus principium; sic speciatim Metaphysica eidem tale obsequium debet: frustraque sunt viri eximii, quando existimant eam in explicatione doctrinæ de Deo, nihil de suo conferre: ut enim illa doctrina convenientissime per terminos Metaphysicos
units.tr: Angels (but how little this is!) can be drawn from the same source and should be referred to Pneumatics, in which some have also undertaken to treat of God, although an infinite distance lies between the infinite, independent and most perfect God, who is called Spirit (John 4:24), and the angels, who are ministering spirits (Heb. 1:14). Some have assigned both doctrines to Metaphysics: either following the example of Aristotle, who is nonetheless rather careless about method in the books of his Metaphysics; or because they thought these doctrines too few to constitute a proper discipline; or finally because they believed they would explain the analogy of being suitably, if, after a fuller treatment of the most perfect God, they set out to show by comparing him with any finite being how great the distance is between the infinite being and any finite being. Sixth, just as the whole of philosophy, in respect of all and each of its parts, must submit its fasces to revealed theology and to Holy Scripture, which is its principle, so Metaphysics in particular owes this same deference. Those eminent men are wrong who think it contributes nothing of its own to the explanation of the doctrine of God. For just as that doctrine is most fittingly explained through metaphysical terms,

units.la: explicatur, sic hactenus de suo quid confert Metaphysica ad explicationem tanti Mysterii, quando eorundem terminorum convenientem intellectum proponit. Septimo non diffitendum subtilitatibus pluribus instructam esse Metaphysicam: verum non exiistimandum omnes illas graves atque praejudiciosas esse Theologicae veritati, siquidem per quasdam subtilitates contingit nos a vero abduci; per alias vero devenimus ad liquidam cognitionem omnium eorum, quae in quaque re vera sunt. Porro, de subtilitatibus Metaphysicis non incommode exiistimavit Scaliger, quando Exerc. 307. sect. 3. sic loquitur: Subtilitates Metaphysicae quanquam sint animis otiosis otiosae atque inutiles: tamen vegetis ingeniis summam cognoscendi adferunt voluptatem. & paulo post: Harum indagatio subtilitatum, etsi non utilis est ad machinas faciendas: exuit tamen animum inscitia rubigine, acuitque ad alia. Eo denique splendore afficit, ut sibi praeluceat ad nancisccendum primi opificis similitudinem. His in antecessum praemissis, Metaphysicam admittendam esse probare pergimus. Non multis vero hic opus argumentis, cum unum atque alterum instar omnium esse possit. Ergo 1. sic argumentamur: Quicquid ut objectum in nulla alia disciplina quam in Metaphysica citra confusionem considerari potest, per illud tanquam suum objectum Metaphysica determinari debet: Sed doctrina de ente, & communibus illius attributis, in nulla alia disciplina, quam in Metaphysica considerari potest. Ergo. Major propositio est certissima, nititurque hoc indubitato principio, quod disciplinæ tum distinguantur tum determinentur per propria obiecta. Minor pariter patet, & probari potest per inductionem: quascunque enim disciplinas percurreris, eas offendes particulares esse, & non agere de Ente in communi considerato, sed de hoc illove particulari Ente. Cumque particularia entia sufficiant ad modum obiecti, pro constituendis particularibus disciplinis: æquum omnino est, ut ens in genere, sive communiter consideratum, pariter sufficiat pro generanda distinƈta scientia. Quum hæc regula sit infallibilis: Ubi datur obiectum disciplinæ distinƈtum, à nobis cognoscibile per propƩas suas affectiones, ibi dari quoque debet propria disciplina. Deinde: Si debeat dari architectonica aliqua disciplina, quæ definiat aliis inferioribus disciplinis suum obiectum, proponatque pariter generalia axiomata servientia directioni omnium inferiorum disciplinarum, dari quoque debet Metaphysica. Sed verum prius. Antecedens inde probatur, quod cum nulla inferior disciplina probet suum obiectum, sed praesupponat illud dari, omnino requiratur pariter superior aliqua disciplina, quae officio hoc fungatur: praeterea quum dentur generalissima axiomata, quae inferiores disciplinae, & in actu exercito, utiloquuntur, sibi quod ad usum arrogant: nae pariter opus est superiori disciplina, in qua eadem illa axiomata quasi abstracte, & in actu signato (utor locutione in Scholis recepta) distincte considerentur. Alias illa ipsa axiomata generalissima, nunquam qua talia cognoscerentur, quum in inferioribus disciplinis, quae particulares sunt, duntaxat considerentur particulariter, & sub ea considerandi ratione, quae cuique inferiori disciplinae propria atque peculiaris est. Consequentia aeque certa est. Percurrantur quippe per modum Inductionis, omnes reliquae disciplinae, & nulla invenietur, quae hoc agat, quod Metaphysica. Nomen Metaphysicae si quem hic offenderit, ferre possum: Iam antea quippe dixi, propter nomen solum non esse movendas controversias. Deinceps despiciendum, num ipsa Metaphysica cum Logica, Rami exemplo, convenienter confundatur. Non diffitendum, has disciplinas, ratione non solum usus verum etiam obiecti & finis universaliter se habentes, si componantur cum inferioribus, ceu particularibus disciplinis, videri magnam cognationem inter se colere: (nam omnes & singulæ particulares disciplinæ utriusque subsidio ex æquo indigent; ad hoc hæ duæ disciplinæ, tanquam inter se maxime cognatæ ob universalitatem objecti & finis, se invicem in sua tractatione cum maxime juvant) interim tamen in tribus sic differunt, ut neutiquam confundi, nedum coire queant. 1. Ratione objecti intrinseci, quod ab aliis vocatur objectum considerationis. Metaphysica quippe occupatur circa ens reale qua reale, Logica vero circa ens rationis, quatenus directivum est operationum intellectus, sive, ut alii loquuntur, circa notiones secundas, quæ, quatenus tales sunt, ad modum entis rationis censeri debent. Dicunt quidem multi, Logicam versari circa omne ens, qua scil. ens reale, & qua ens rationis; sed dum ita loquuntur, confundunt objectum extrinsecum ceu tractationis, cum ipso objecto intrinseco.
units.tr: so far Metaphysics does contribute something of its own to the explanation of so great a mystery, in that it sets out a suitable understanding of those same terms. Seventh, it must not be denied that Metaphysics is furnished with many subtleties; but we should not think that all of them are grave and harmful to theological truth. For through some subtleties we may be led away from the truth, while through others we arrive at a clear knowledge of all that truly exists in each thing. Moreover, Scaliger was not wrong to judge of metaphysical subtleties when, in Exercise 307, section 3, he speaks thus: Metaphysical subtleties, although they are idle and useless to idle minds, nevertheless bring the greatest pleasure of knowing to lively wits. And a little later: The investigation of these subtleties, although it is not useful for making machines, nevertheless strips the mind of the rust of ignorance and sharpens it for other things. Finally, it brings such brightness that it lights the way for us to attain a likeness to the first craftsman. Having premised these things by way of preface, we proceed to prove that Metaphysics is to be admitted. Here we need not many arguments, since one or two may serve as well as all. First, then, we argue thus: whatever can be considered without confusion as an object in no other discipline than Metaphysics must be determined by Metaphysics as its own object. But the doctrine of being and of its common attributes can be considered in no other discipline than Metaphysics. Therefore it must be so determined. The major premise is most certain, and rests on this indubitable principle, that disciplines are both distinguished and determined by their proper objects. The minor premise is equally clear, and can be proved by induction: for whatever disciplines you run through, you will find them to be particular and not to treat of being considered in common, but of this or that particular being. And since particular beings suffice as the kind of object for constituting particular disciplines, it is entirely fair that being in general, or considered in common, should likewise suffice for generating a distinct science. Since this rule is infallible: wherever there is a distinct object of a discipline, knowable by us through its own attributes, there a proper discipline must also be given. Again: if there must be some architectonic discipline, which defines its object for the other, inferior disciplines and likewise sets out the general axioms serving to direct all the inferior disciplines, then Metaphysics must also be given. But the first is true. The antecedent is proved thus: since no inferior discipline proves its own object, but presupposes that it is given, a superior discipline must of necessity exist to perform this office. Moreover, since there are most general axioms, which the inferior disciplines use in actual practice and claim for their own use, there is likewise need of a superior discipline in which those same axioms are considered abstractly and in the signate act (to use the term received in the Schools), distinctly. Otherwise those most general axioms would never be known as such, since in the inferior disciplines, which are particular, they are considered only particularly and under that mode of consideration which is proper and peculiar to each inferior discipline. The consequence is equally certain. Run through all the remaining disciplines by induction, and none will be found that does what Metaphysics does. If the name of Metaphysics offends anyone here, I can bear that: for I have said before that controversies should not be stirred up merely over a name. Next we must consider whether Metaphysics ought to be confused with Logic, after the example of Ramus. It must be admitted that these disciplines, being universal in their use, their object and their end, appear to have a close kinship with one another when placed alongside the inferior, particular disciplines (for all and each of the particular disciplines equally need the help of both; and these two, as most closely akin on account of the universality of object and end, greatly assist one another in their treatment). Nevertheless they differ in three respects, so that they can by no means be confused, let alone merged. (1) By reason of the intrinsic object, which others call the object of consideration. Metaphysics is occupied with real being as real, whereas Logic is occupied with being of reason, insofar as it directs the operations of the intellect, or, as others put it, with second notions, which, insofar as they are such, ought to be regarded as a kind of being of reason. Many indeed say that Logic is concerned with every being, both as real being and as being of reason; but in saying so they confuse the extrinsic object of treatment with the intrinsic object itself.

units.la: 2. Ratione ipsius exercitii, ceu modi in exercendo observari soliti; quamvis enim utraque disciplina, omnibus, atque singulis inferioribus disciplinis inserviat, non tamen pari passu per inferiores has disciplinas progrediuntur: siquidem Logica patitur sese applicari tum iis quæ universaliter, tum etiam iis, quæ particulariter in inferioribus disciplinis tractantur;
units.tr: (2) By reason of the exercise itself, the manner usually observed in practising them. For although each discipline serves all and each of the inferior disciplines, they do not advance through these inferior disciplines at the same pace: Logic allows itself to be applied both to those things treated universally and to those treated particularly in the inferior disciplines;

units.la: Metaphysica autem, utpote Universalis, haeret duntaxat circa ea, quae universaliter sese habent. 3. Ratione potestatis, nam respectu aliarum disciplinarum, Metaphysica Architectonica censeri debet, & quodam quasi imperio gaudet, quod in eo maxime prodit, dum aliis disciplinis suum objectum definit: Logica vero duntaxat ad modum ancillae sese habet, quae citra ullum imperium, omnibus, quae non solum in disciplinis tractantur, verum etiam quae cognosci a nobis possunt, citra ullam relustationem se applicari patitur. Ad rem vero non facit, quod Logica, in ea maxime parte, quae Topica, & secundum quosdam, proprie Dialectica dicitur, videatur eadem illa tractare, quae a Metaphysica considerantur; atque eidem nexu in ancipioque propria esse videntur: nam primo ipsa Logica in abstracto atque secundum suam indolem considerata, non potest; aut debet confundi cum Systemate aliquo Logico ab hoc illove scripto. Certum quippe est, multos, qui Logica Systemata evulgarunt, imprudenter admodum Metaphysicam cum ipsa Logica confudisse in plurimis capitibus. Deinde, multa, quae a Metaphysica in actu signato considerantur, Logica in actu exercito considerat, quod v. c. circa doctrinam de causis tam manifestum est, ut ipsi tyrones Logici non ignorent. Postremo, Metaphysica quatenus ordinate est tractanda, æque, atque quælibet alia disciplina, subsidio Logicæ indiget: nam circa disciplinas inter se comparatas, hoc verum, manus manum lavat, atque una alterius subsidio indiget. Omnes vero, quo Methodice tractentur, subsidio Logicæ, quę modum cognoscendi proponit, opus habent. Superest tertia quæstio, breviter hic expediunda, qua quæritur, an pro commodiori tractatione Theologiæ Orthodoxæ, subsidium Metaphysicæ requiratur? Ne nobis hic idem contingat quod aliis, ac Metaphysicam plus æquo aut dilatemus, aut circumscribamus, omnia, circa hoc quæsitum observanda, distinctis assertionibus, iisque, partim affirmativis, partim negativis, proponere laborabimus. Ex quibus hæc prima sit: Theologia non est subordinata Metaphysicæ: quamvis enim hæc sit disciplina universalissima, atque sub ente, quod est objectum Metaphysicæ, continetur quoque ens infinitum, sive Deus: neutiquam tamen ipsa Theologia subordinata eidem censeri potest, quum non solum sub alia formalitate de suo objecto agat Theologia, verum etiam occupetur circa objectum materialiter diversum, particulare scil. atque Metaphysica pro objecto interim sibi vindicet omne ens qua ens.
units.tr: but Metaphysics, as being universal, clings only to those things which stand universally. (3) By reason of power. For with respect to the other disciplines, Metaphysics must be regarded as architectonic, and enjoys a kind of rule, which is especially evident in its defining the object for the other disciplines. Logic, however, stands only in the manner of a handmaid, who, without any rule over others, allows herself to be applied without any reluctance to all things that are treated not only in the disciplines but also that can be known by us. It is no objection that Logic, especially in that part which is called Topics, and according to some, properly Dialectic, seems to treat the same things that are considered by Metaphysics, and that these appear to be connected with it and in the same ambit: for, first, Logic itself, considered abstractly and according to its own nature, cannot, or ought not, be confused with any one Logical System written by this or that author. It is certain that many who have published Logical Systems have, in very many chapters, imprudently confused Metaphysics with Logic itself. Then, much that Metaphysics considers in the signate act, Logic considers in the exercised act, as is so manifest in the doctrine of causes that even the novice logicians do not fail to see it. Lastly, Metaphysics, insofar as it must be treated in an orderly way, like any other discipline, needs the aid of Logic: for with respect to disciplines compared with one another, the truth is that one hand washes the other, and each needs the help of the other. Moreover, all of them, if they are to be treated methodically, need the aid of Logic, which sets out the method of knowing. There remains a third question, to be briefly disposed of here, namely whether the aid of Metaphysics is required for the more convenient treatment of Orthodox Theology. Lest we here suffer the same thing as others, who either extend Metaphysics beyond measure or restrict it, we shall labour to set out everything to be observed concerning this question in distinct assertions, partly affirmative and partly negative. Of these the first is this: Theology is not subordinate to Metaphysics. For although Metaphysics is the most universal discipline, and under being, which is the object of Metaphysics, the infinite being, that is God, is also contained, nevertheless Theology cannot in any way be regarded as subordinate to it, since Theology treats of its object under a different formality, and is occupied with an object materially different, namely particular being, whereas Metaphysics claims for its object every being as being.

units.la: 2. Non sunt eadem quoque principia Theologiæ & Metaphysicæ, ut enim hujus principium supremum est ratio, sic in illa ipsi rationi dominatur Scriptura, & divina revelatio, usque adeo ut ei cedere debeat ratio. Quomodo de seipso dicit Paulus Gal. 1. v. 15. & seq. Quando libuit Deo, qui separaverat me ab utero matris meæ & vocavit per gratiam suam: Revelare filium suum in me, ut Evangelizarem ipsum inter gentes, non statim propterea contuli cum carne & sanguine. 3. Pro Scriptura intelligenda ad salutem, non simpliciter quoque opus est Metaphysica: præterquam enim quod Deus genuinum sensum verbi sui per Spiritum suum revelare potest, amplius ad media ordinaria, Scripturæ explicationi servientia, neutiquam pertinet Metaphysica, qua tuto carere potest is, qui secundum admonitionem Apostoli sensus habet exercitatos ad discretionem boni & mali, Heb. 5. v. 14. quique, ut idem monet 1 Cor. 2. v. 13. novit spiritualia cum spiritualibus conferre.4. Multo minus, ut quibusdam olim in Papatu persuasum fuit, ex Metaphysicis Aristotelis libris perfecta de Deo cognitio hauriri potest. Utroque pollice amplector ea, quæ habet eximius Theologus And. Hyperius lib. 1. de rat. stud. Theol. cap. 7. De consumendis, inquit, aliquot annis in Aristotelicis Metaphysicis, quod nonnullos nostra memoria in Italia facilitasse habemus compertum, adolescenti Theologicis studiis destinato in mentem non veniat: sed, iis omissis, cogitet vera absolutaque Metaphysica in sacris literis sibi esse proposita. 5. Neutiquam vero consultum est, tyrones, & novitios Theologiæ orthodoxæ mystas, admittere ad Pontificios Metaphysicos, minime ad Suarezij controversias, Fonsecæ commentarios in libros Metaph. Aristotelis, aut Hurtadum de Mendoza, Arriagam, Oviedonem, similesve. Quamvis enim Cadmæi hi fratres sæpe inter se confligant, nihilominus tamen sæpe periculosa & Scripturæ adversantia dogmata proponunt, totique in hoc sunt, ut prætextu subtilitatum Metaphysicarum, aut incrustent, aut temerent simplicem & castam veritatem Sp. Sancti, radiantem in libris Veteris & Novi testamenti. Idem dictum fit de multis Lutheranis, speciatim Iacobo Martini, Scheiblero, Calovio, aliisque. nec tacendum, Timplerum, quondam a Conrado Vorstio Collega suo in Schola Steinfurtensi seductum, in sua Metaphysica, a pluribus aliias commendata, multa proponere, quæ periculosa admodum sunt. 6. Interim tamen Metaphysica, ratione quorumdam terminorum, & locutionum, quæ in Scriptura occurrunt, ei operam utilem navare potest. Quis enim v. c. commode intelligatea, quæ de habitibus Heb. 5. v. 14. de subsistentia Heb. 1. v. 3. de concursu causæ primæ, Act. 17. v. 25. 27. & 28. de natura & essentia Dei, Phil. 2. v. 7. Gal. 4. v. 1. Rom. 1. v. 20. proponuntur, si in sacris Metaphysicis planeperegrinq fuerit. & terminos illi9 nesciat distinguere 7. Si Theologia consideretur secundū formulas consensus, quibus continetur, & modum, quo à tot seculis in Scholis doceri solet, omnino Theologo, Orthodoxo quoque, opus est Metaphysicæ cognitione: tam crebro enim termini Metaphysici ibi occurrunt, ut v. c. nemo citra Metaphysicæ cognitionem intelligere possit vel primum articulum Symboli, quod vulgo Apostolicum dicitur. Ut enim dicimus nos credere in Deum Patrem omnipotentem: sic ipsum nomen potentiæ ad Metaphysicam respectat, atque pro intelligendo commode hoc articulo, ex re est nosse duplicem esse potentiam, activam, & passivam, atque hujus tam expertem esse Deum, quam illa sola in eum cadere potest. 8. Usus hic magis se prodit ratione controversiarum, quæ in Theologia ventilari solent, ad quas tractandas ne quidem accingere se is poterit, qui Metaphysicę plane ignarus est. V. c. an non subsidium Metaphysicæ requiritur, cum quæritur, an attributa Dei re vel ratione distinguantur? An possit dici Persona realiter differre a Dei essentia? An caro Christi habuerit propriam subsistentiam? An bona opera sint necessaria ad salutem? An peccatum sit quid positivum, an pura privatio? An peccatum originis sit substantia? An liberum arbitrium consistat in indifferentia? An possibile omne sit objectum divinae omnipotentiae? An baptismus necessitate medii sit necessarius ad salutem? An omnis creatura sit bona? An in eucharistia accidentia panis subsistant sine substantia? An Deus sit purus actus? An actus primus salva rei essentia a subjecto separari queat? etc. IX. Maxime vero, ratione adversariorum Ecclesiae, hic usus, si non Metaphysicae necessitas, se prodit. Quis enim cum Pontificiis, Socinianis, & Lutheranis congredi praesumat, qui non pariter in Metaphysicis sit exercitatissimus? Quum experientia constet eos, in Professione Theologica reliquam suam eruditionem prostituisse, qui citra Metaphysicae subsidium ausi fuerunt Cathedram conscendere.
units.tr: 2. The principles of Theology and Metaphysics are also not the same. The supreme principle of Metaphysics is reason, but in Theology Scripture and divine revelation rule over reason itself, so much so that reason must yield to them. Paul says this about himself, Gal. 1.15ff.: When it pleased God, who had set me apart from my mother's womb and called me by his grace, to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately confer with flesh and blood. 3. Nor is Metaphysics simply needed for understanding Scripture unto salvation. God can reveal the genuine sense of his Word through his Spirit, and beyond that, Metaphysics has no real bearing on the ordinary means that serve the explanation of Scripture. A person can do well without it if he has "senses exercised to discern good and evil" (Heb. 5.14), as the Apostle urges, and if, as the same Apostle notes (1 Cor. 2.13), he knows how to "compare spiritual things with spiritual." 4. Much less can a complete knowledge of God be drawn from the Metaphysics of Aristotle, as some in Popery were once persuaded. I wholeheartedly embrace what the outstanding theologian Andreas Hyperius says in book 1 of his On the Method of Studying Theology, chapter 7: "A young man destined for theological studies should not think of spending some years on the Aristotelian Metaphysics (which, as we know, some in our own time in Italy have made easier), but should set those aside and reflect that true and complete Metaphysics is set before him in the sacred letters." 5. Yet it is certainly not advisable to allow beginners and novices in orthodox Theology to become acquainted with the Papist metaphysicians: least of all with the disputations of Suárez, the commentaries of Fonseca on the Metaphysics of Aristotle, or Hurtado de Mendoza, Arriaga, Oviedo, and similar writers. For although these Cadmean brothers often fight among themselves, they nonetheless often put forward dangerous doctrines that contradict Scripture, and they are wholly intent, under the pretext of metaphysical subtleties, either to encrust or to defile the simple and pure truth of the Holy Spirit, which shines in the books of the Old and New Testaments. The same may be said of many Lutherans, especially Jacob Martini, Scheibler, Calovius, and others. Nor should we pass over in silence that Timpler, once led astray by Conrad Vorstius, his colleague at the school in Steinfurt, proposes in his Metaphysics, which many others have otherwise commended, many things that are very dangerous. 6. Nevertheless, Metaphysics can render useful service to Scripture by way of certain terms and expressions that occur in it. For who could understand properly what is said about habits (Heb. 5.14), about subsistence (Heb. 1.3), about the concurrence of the first cause (Acts 17.25, 27, 28), and about the nature and essence of God (Phil. 2.7; Gal. 4.1; Rom. 1.20), if he were a complete stranger to sacred Metaphysics and did not know how to distinguish its terms? 7. If Theology is considered according to the formulas of consensus in which it is contained, and according to the method by which it has been taught in the schools for so many centuries, then even the orthodox theologian absolutely needs knowledge of Metaphysics. Metaphysical terms occur so frequently there that no one without knowledge of Metaphysics can understand even the first article of the creed commonly called the Apostles' Creed. When we say that we believe in God the Father almighty, the very word "power" refers to Metaphysics, and to understand this article properly it is useful to know that there are two kinds of power, active and passive, and that God is as free of the passive kind as only the active kind can apply to him. 8. This use appears more clearly in the controversies that are commonly debated in Theology, which no one who is wholly ignorant of Metaphysics could even begin to handle. For example, is not the help of Metaphysics required when we ask whether the attributes of God are distinguished really or by reason? Can it be said that a Person differs really from the essence of God? Did the flesh of Christ have its own subsistence? Are good works necessary for salvation? Is sin something positive, or a pure privation? Is original sin a substance? Does free will consist in indifference? Is everything possible an object of divine omnipotence? Is baptism necessary for salvation by the necessity of means? Is every creature good? In the Eucharist, do the accidents of bread subsist without substance? Is God pure act? Can a first act be separated from its subject while the essence of the thing remains? And so on. 9. Above all, this use, if not the necessity of Metaphysics itself, appears in dealing with the adversaries of the Church: the Papists, the Socinians, and the Lutherans. For who would presume to engage them unless he were equally most practised in Metaphysics? Experience shows that those who dared to ascend the professor's chair without the support of Metaphysics have squandered the rest of their learning in their theological profession.

units.la: CAPUT VIGESIMUM SECUNDUM.
units.tr: Chapter Twenty-Two.

units.la: De communissimis sive generalissimis principiis cognoscendi, sive axiomatibus, & quodnam inter ea primum censeri debeat.
units.tr: On the most common or most general principles of knowing, or axioms, and which of them ought to be regarded as first.

units.la: QUum Metaphysica agere quoque debeat, tanquam generalissima disciplina, de generalissimis axiomatibus; (alii denegant hoc primæ Philosophiæ, quo vero jure, ipsi viderint) operæ pretium facturi videmur, si hoc capite aliquanto distinctius, quam hactenus ab aliis factum fuit, de iis, eorumque ordine egerimus. Præmonendum ergo, non hic agere nos velle aut de principiis essendi, aut de principiis cognoscendi particularibus, quæ in quacunque disciplina particulari, pro instituto proprio, tum proponi, tum applicari atque explicari solent, sed de principiis universalissimis, quæ non solum communia sunt omnibus scientiis, verum etiam respiciunt cum omne ens in communi, sive transcendentaliter consideratum, tum etiam quodcunque ens particulare, atque secundum suam speciem distinctum. Atque initio quidem, quo de talibus principiis convenienter agere queamus, ostofubsequentes assertiones distincte præcognosci debent. 1. Axiomata hæc ratione conceptus distingui debent, ab iis ipsis, consideratis ratione terminorum, quibus proponuntur: quum enim illo modo universalissime se habeant, haut pariter hoc modo. siquidem quoscunque adhibueris terminos, pro definito axiomatis conceptu, eosdem distinguere varia ratione debebis. & quidem eo magis, quo ipse terminus universalius & magis transcendentaliter se habebit: eoque conceptus magis respectu, quam axiomatice, sive secundum propositionem, qua efferuntur, consideraridebent. 2. Quamvis nullus, terminis intelle&is, hisce axiomatibus contradicendo refragari queat, non tamen eorum veritas censeri debet nobis esse insita & natura nota; sic ut ipsa axiomata, qua talia, & ut vulgo suis terminis concipiuntur, ac doctrinæ gratia proponuntur, dici possint nobis naturaliter explorata esse. Nam præterquam, quod ad hæc axiomata, ut proponuntur intelligenda, requiritur subsidium habitus, ipsa sive Metaphysica, sive generali aliquo habitu, mente nempe aut intelligentia (ut quibusdam placet) in partes veniente; amplius laboriosa eorundem explicatio & multorum circa eadem ratione explicationis fluctuatio abunde ostendunt, hæc ipsa, ut certis terminis comprehenduntur, natura neutiquam esse nota. 3. Et tamen intellectus cujusvis hominis, hæc ipsa axiomata, modo terminos, quibus concipiuntur, intellexerit, ut vera probat citra discursum, aut prolixum examen: quoniam enim aut à parte sui, aut etiam à parte connexionis axiomaticæ, qua subjectum cum prædicato conjungitur, nullam repugnantiam offendit, talibus axiomatibus mox assentitur. 4. Hæc ipsa axiomata, ut ut menti clara, præsupponunt cognitionem sensitivam; quæ ut eorundem servit explicationi, ita dupliciter potest considerari: vel enim intellectus axioma, universalissimum licet, præcognoscit implicite in experimento sensuali: vel, per experimentum simile, quod ut certum præsupponit, confirmatur in axiomate ex terminis suis cognito. Ut ut fit, eo ipso, quod axiomata hæc universalissima esse debeant, neutiquam possunt refragari ulli experimento sensitivo, legitimè atque convenienter instituto. 5. Quod quidam hujus notæ axiomata in dubium vocent, illud mihi videtur ob sex subsequentes rationes fieri. Primo, quoniam non intelligunt terminos, quibus axiomata illa concipiuntur. Secundo, quia terminorum ambigue habentium limitationem aut non vident, aut non attendunt. Tertio, exemplo Zenonis, qui negavit motum dari, quod teneantur, & argumentum objectum solvere non possint, insurgunt adversus axioma, à quo premuntur. Quarto, in quibusdam mentis imbecillitas ac summa phantasiæ confusio eousque occurrunt, ut propterea nullam habeant dispositionem vel ad ullam propositionem, ut veram comprehendendam. Quinto, ideo negantur talia axiomata à multis, quod neque ante eorum propositionem, neque post illam illa inveniant; quæ simulac offendunt, sese pariter corrigunt. Sexto, disputandi gratia, atque verbo magis tenus quam serio, multi talia axiomata & negarunt antehac, & etiamnum negant. 6. Hęc axiomata, neque per discursum, neque per causam, neque per quodcunque aliud medium cognoscuntur, sed immediate, cognitis enim legitime terminis, intellectus eadem æque clara esse judicat, atque ipsum Solis lumen.
units.tr: Since Metaphysics too, as the most general discipline, must deal with the most general axioms (others deny this to first philosophy, and they must judge for themselves on what right), it seems worthwhile to treat these axioms and their order in this chapter somewhat more distinctly than others have done hitherto. It should first be said that we do not intend to deal here either with the principles of being or with the particular principles of knowing, which in any particular discipline are usually proposed, applied and explained according to that discipline's own purpose. We mean the most universal principles, which are not only common to all sciences but also concern every being considered in general and transcendentally, and also every particular being, as distinguished by its kind. To treat such principles properly, the following assertions must first be clearly understood. 1. These axioms must be distinguished by their concept from the same axioms considered in respect of the terms in which they are proposed. For although they stand in the same way universally, they do not stand in the same way in this respect: whatever terms you adopt for the defined concept of an axiom, you must distinguish them in various ways. And the more universal and transcendental the term itself is, the more the concept must be considered in respect of its relation, rather than axiomatically, that is, according to the proposition in which it is expressed. 2. Although no one who has understood the terms can contradict these axioms without being refuted, their truth must not be regarded as implanted in us and known by nature, so that the axioms themselves, as such, and as they are commonly conceived in their terms and proposed for the sake of teaching, could be said to be naturally known to us. For apart from the fact that understanding these axioms as they are proposed requires the aid of a habit, either Metaphysics itself or some general habit of mind or intelligence (as some like to say) coming into play, their laborious explanation and the great fluctuation of many over how to explain them amply show that these things, as they are comprehended in certain terms, are by no means known by nature. 3. Yet the intellect of any man, once it has understood the terms in which these axioms are conceived, recognises them as true without discursive reasoning or lengthy examination. For since it finds no repugnance either in itself or in the axiomatic connection by which the subject is joined to the predicate, it assents to such axioms at once. 4. These same axioms, however clear to the mind, presuppose sensory knowledge, which serves to explain them. This can be considered in two ways: either the intellect foreknows the axiom, however universal, implicitly in sensory experience; or, through a similar experiment which it presupposes as certain, it is confirmed in the axiom as known from its terms. However that may be, from the very fact that these most universal axioms must be what they are, they can by no means be refuted by any sensory experiment legitimately and properly conducted. 5. That some call such axioms into doubt seems to me to happen for six following reasons. First, because they do not understand the terms in which the axioms are conceived.
