Second, because they either do not see or do not attend to the limitation of terms that are ambiguous. Third, following the example of Zeno, who denied that motion exists because they cannot solve the argument put against it, they rise up against the axiom by which they are pressed. Fourth, in some men weakness of mind and great confusion of imagination occur to such a degree that they have no disposition to grasp any proposition as true. Fifth, such axioms are denied by many because they find them neither before nor after their proposition; but as soon as they encounter them, they correct themselves likewise. Sixth, for the sake of disputing, and more in word than in earnest, many both denied such axioms before and still deny them. 6. These axioms are known neither through discursive reasoning, nor through a cause, nor through any other middle term, but immediately. For once the terms are rightly understood, the intellect judges them to be as clear as the light of the sun itself.

units.la: 7. Et tamen veritas horum ipsorum axiomatum, à posteriori quasi, trifariam evinci potest. Primo per inductionem, ut si quis neget totum sua parte majus esse, inductione probandum erit. Secundo sensu; neget enim v. c. aliquis ignem esse calidum, eique admoveatur, mox fatebitur. Tertio redargutione, atque ex proprio responso negantis: exempl. gr. aliquis neget totum esse majus quaque sui parte, & vult emere panem, pistor obtrudit truftulum panis, quod renuit accipere, postulando integrum panem.
units.tr: 7. And yet the truth of these very axioms can be proved in a threefold way, as it were a posteriori. First, by induction: if someone denies that the whole is greater than its part, he must be proved wrong by induction. Second, by the senses: if someone denies, for example, that fire is hot, and it is brought near him, he will soon confess it. Third, by refutation drawn from the denier's own response: for example, if someone denies that the whole is greater than any of its parts, and wants to buy bread, the baker thrusts a small crust of bread at him, which he refuses to accept, demanding a whole loaf.

units.la: 8. Et tamen inter hęc axiomata ordo aliquis intercedit, de quo agemus, ubi primo oftenderimus talia axiomata admittenda esse. Admittenda vero esse hujus ordinis axiomata, quivis, si modo in se descenderit, perspicere potest: quandoquidem cognitis modo horum universalissimorum axiomatum terminis, non potest non iisdem suum assensum concedere, quum tamen circa axiomata particularia, quæ ad universalia examinari debent, explicatis quoque terminis, hæreat, nec aliter eadem liquido cognoscere queat, quam quatenus ad communiora axiomata exiguntur. Quomodo v. c. nullus decempedam ingero minorem esse aut apprehendet, aut concedet, nisi antea decempedam velut partem, & iugerum tanquam totum apprehenderit; atque hoc axioma, Decempeda minor iugero est, expenderit ad axioma communissimum & universalissimum; Totum quoque sui parte majus est. Praeterea, cum abunde jam antea evicerimus, hos aliquid scire posse, consequens quoque est, ut scientia nostra sit ordinata; quod fieri neutiquam poterit, nisi deveniatur ad prima quaedam & indemonstrabilia principia: ut enim in aliquibus principiis, tanquam primis, convenit subsistere, sic nisi occurrerent talia principia, nihil in universum sciromus. Sicut enim nulla est deambulatio, si nullum sit principium deambulationis, ita nulla quoque cognitio esse potest, si nullum sit principium cognitionis, atque misere obcrrabit mens circulo inexplicabili implicita, nisi devenerit ad aliqua prima principia, à quibus non minus possit progredi, quam ad eadem omnia examinare. Si enim cognosceremus coclusionem per majorem & minorem, & iterum cognosceremus majorem per conclusionem & minorem, vel etiam probaremus majorem per conclusionem, necessario circulus, & quidem longe ineptissimus, committeretur. Quod absurdum avertitur, admissis principiis primis, ex quibus alia omnia cognoscuntur. Nam ut visus clarius colores videt per lumen, non autem videt lumen per colores, quod color non sit clarior lumine: ita intelligimus conclusionem minus claram. Ut ergo liquet admittenda esse communissima quædam principia, ita ulterius inquirere convenit in ordinem, qui inter illa intercedit: oportet quippe subsistere in aliquo principio ita primo, ut eodem alterum prius non detur. quodnam vero illud ipsum sit, controversum quam maxime est, nec hic convenit inter maximos quoque Philosophos. Ego, omnibus quam diligenter excusis, exististimem nos hic debere distinguere & notari hic differentiam inter triplicis ordinis principia: scil. inter principium apprehensionis universalis, principium apprehensionis particularis, & principium directionis. Principium apprehensionis universalis, quoniam implicatur, qualiscunque etiam sit, in omni conceptu, per se & secundum suam naturam primo cognoscitur, eltque non minus primum principium cognoscitivum, quam principium productivum primum: concipi vero potest hisce terminis, Est Deus, sive, Existit unum ens, quod est infinitam & independens. Principium hoc vocamus primum apprehensionis universalis, aut apprehensionis universaliter se habentis: nam quodcunque ens creatum, quocunque etiam modo apprehenderis, necessario in illo conceptu debet præ-suppo supponi esse Deum: quod uerum est, ratione quoque ipsorum Atheorum & Epicureorum, qui volunt omnia facta esse casu: nam cum casus fit causa per accidens, omniuo debet reduci ad causam per se, ut si v. c. musicus aedificet per accidens, in musico quid debet esse, quod per se aedificet; scil. architectus. Ita si mundus factus est casu, est factus a causa aliqua per se, quae est Deus, quemadmodum ipse Aristoteles sic philosophatur lib. 2. Phys. Sed, quoniam principium hoc, in se primum licet, combinatur cum conceptu quocunque objectivo, cui quasi inaratum est, nec nisi per ratiocinium abstractive (etiam ratione cognitionis de Deo insitae, quae ideo insita dicitur, quod progrediatur ab insitis menti principiis, hoc ipsum principium includentibus, ad illud ipsum abstractive considerandum) ut per se cognoscitur, ideo a multis, quod abstractionem ratiocinando facere non instituant, aut non agnoscitur, aut perperam agnoscitur, dum scil. cum ipsa re objecta, in qua concipitur, & a qua abstrahi deberet, coalescit & combinatur. hoc ipsum autem omnis idololatriae verum est initium. Atque huc spectat illud Apostoli ad Rom. 1. v. 22. &c.
units.tr: 8. And yet among these axioms there is a certain order, which we shall discuss once we have first shown that such axioms must be admitted. That axioms of this order must be admitted anyone can perceive, if only he looks into himself. For once the terms of these most universal axioms are merely understood, he cannot but give them his assent. Whereas with regard to particular axioms, which must be examined by means of universal ones, he hesitates even when the terms have been explained, nor can he know them clearly except insofar as they are traced back to more common axioms. Thus, for example, no one will either apprehend or concede that a ten-foot rod is less than an acre, unless first he has apprehended the rod as a part and the acre as a whole, and has weighed this axiom, A ten-foot rod is less than an acre, against the most common and universal axiom, The whole is also greater than its part. Besides, since we have already shown abundantly that we can know something, it follows that our knowledge is ordered. This cannot be done unless we arrive at certain first and indemonstrable principles. For just as it is fitting to rest on some principles as first, so unless such principles existed, we would know nothing at all. Just as there is no walking if there is no principle of walking, so there can be no knowledge if there is no principle of knowledge, and the mind would wretchedly wander, entangled in an inexplicable circle, unless it came to some first principles from which it could progress no less than it could examine all things. For if we knew the conclusion through the major and minor premises, and again knew the major through the conclusion and the minor, or even proved the major through the conclusion, a circle would necessarily be committed, and a very absurd one at that. This absurdity is averted once first principles are admitted, from which all other things are known. For just as sight sees colours more clearly through light, and does not see light through colours, because colour is not clearer than light, so we understand the less clear conclusion through the more clear principles. Therefore, as it is clear that certain most common principles must be admitted, it is fitting to inquire further into the order that exists among them. For one must rest on some principle so first that no other is prior to it. What that principle is, is most disputed, and it is not agreed even among the greatest philosophers. I, having examined all things as carefully as I could, think that here we ought to distinguish and note the difference among a threefold order of principles: namely, the principle of universal apprehension, the principle of particular apprehension, and the principle of direction. The principle of universal apprehension, since it is implied, whatever it may be, in every concept, is known first through itself and according to its own nature, and is no less the first cognitive principle than the first productive principle is. It can indeed be conceived in these terms: There is God, or, There exists one being which is infinite and independent. We call this principle the first of universal apprehension, or of what is universally apprehended. For whatever created being you apprehend, in whatever way, must necessarily presuppose God in that concept. This is true even with respect to the Atheists and Epicureans themselves, who want all things to have been made by chance. For since chance is a cause per accidens, it must altogether be reduced to a cause per se. As, for example, if a musician builds per accidens, there must be something in the musician that builds per se, namely the architect. So if the world was made by chance, it was made by some cause per se, which is God, just as Aristotle himself philosophises in lib. 2 Phys. But since this principle, though first in itself, is combined with whatever objective concept it is, to which it is as it were ingrafted, and is known per se only by abstractive reasoning (even with respect to the knowledge of God that is implanted, which is called implanted because it proceeds from the principles implanted in the mind, which include this very principle, to consider that very principle abstractively), it is therefore either not recognised or wrongly recognised by many, because they do not undertake the abstraction by reasoning, and it coalesces and is combined with the very thing in which it is conceived, from which it ought to be abstracted. And this very thing is the beginning of all idolatry. To this refers the Apostle's word in Rom. 1, v. 22, etc.

units.la: 23. Quum se dicitentes sapientes, stulti facti sunt. Mutarunt enim gloriam incorruptibilis Dei in efformatam imaginem corruptibilis hominis, & volucrum, & quadrupedum, & reptilium. Interim hoc principium manet id quod est, & ut Deus est absolute primus, sic in omni conceptu implicatur Est Deus. Nam omnis conceptus aut est de Deo, & sic veritati stat sua ratio, aut de ente à Deo diverso, quod cum iterum sit aut corporeum, aut incorporeum, utrumque tamen sic dependenter se habet, ut eo ipso, quo cogitatur existere, pariter concipiatur Deus esse, nam nisi Deus esset, & hoc ipsum quod concipitur, esse suum à Deo haberet, neque esset, neque posset concipi secundum essendi atque existendi rationem. Verum hoc quoque est ratione ipsius mentis, quæ quando in se reflectitur, dum semetipsam concipit: in semetipsa tanquam in aliquod inferiori Deum concipit: non quod divertat ad Dei ideam in se existentem (hoc enim ante refutavimus) sed quod se, utpote dependentem, non posset concipere, nisi illi conceptui includatur Dei existentia, non consi-deranda ad modum idex, in mente ipsa, verum in ipso Deo: quemadmodum Thomas p. 1. qu. 16. art 7. & p. 1. q. 84. art. 5. post Augustinum lib. 14. de Trin. cap. 15. l. 3. cap. 5. de lib. arb. recte philosophatur de æternis veritatibus, quas sic statuit in solo Deo inveniri, ut earum veritatum finita apprehensio, sive intellectualis in homine apprehensio, aeterna dicatur esse, quatenus ideae in mente divina respondent. Nec desiderium, quo tendit homo intelligens ad ulteriorem perfectionem, arguit existentiam realem ideae de Deo in mente humana; sic enim homo animalis, a tali idea sibi inexistente, ad desiderandum excitatus, ob motionem ejusdem ideae & interiorem ejus apprehensionem, tenderet ad fruitionem ejusdem. Sed hoc Scripturae adversarium, quae hominem ante conversionem ad Christum, censet esse expertem Dei, Eph. 2. v. 12. atque ex exemplo Adami recenter lapsi, & a Dei facie fugientis, Gen. 3. v. 10. abunde liquet, neutiquam ob inexistentiam ideae de Deo in homine, in hoc ipso esse desiderium, quo feratur ad Dei ut perfectioris fruitionem. nam seclusa hac idea, apprehensio rationis & functionum ejusdem, nihil amplius hic valet, quam apprehensio cujusque alterius rei: nam mens ut apprehendit se dependentem, sic quaecunque res finita non potest aliter apprehendi quam dependens. Nihil vero ad rem facit, quod mens se deprehendat incorpoream & quantitatis expertem, ut enim eo ipso manet finita, sic, non valet hoc ratiocinium: Mens est incorporea, ergo in ea agnoscenda idea Dei: siquidem, sic adæquatur quod finitum est, enti infinita, quod absurdissimum esse, antea patuit. Principium primum apprehensionis particularis æstimari debet ratione cujusque apprehendentis personæ, quatenus id, quod aliquis apprehendit primo, ut inde progrediatur ulterius, convenienter ratione illius, tale principium censeri poterit. Nec hic ratione omnium hominum, uti nos antea fusissime expendimus, valere poterit illud, Cogito, ergo sum. Siquidem ut non omnes illud possunt intelligere, sic apprehensio alicujus quod cogitatur, sive vere intelligendo illud, sive de eo dubitando, præsupponit aliquid ut prius existens, & quatenus apprehenditur mente, sic non apprehenditur nisi quatale, puta aut dubitatio de hac re, aut apprehensio intellectiva hujus illiusve entis. Audio quidem hanc cogitationem, à quibusdam transformari in ipsam mentem cogitantem, aliosque credere, mentem se ipsam sine subsidio phantasmatis posse directe cognoscere; sed hoc gratis dicitur, nam quamvis Dei, angeli, &animæ nostræ non dentur propriæ species phantasticæ, intellectus tamen non potest, quamdiu corporis vinculis est astrictus, ea ipsa entia, non potest cognoscere nisi per comparationem ad corpora sensibilia, quorum sunt aliqua phantasmata. ut recte loquitur Thomas 1. qu. 84. a. 7. Nam (verba sunt illius, qui nomen fert Dionysij lib. 1. de Divin. nomin.) incorporeas substantias, in statu praesenti vita cognoscere non possumus, nisi per ienotionem, vel aliquam comparationem ad corporalia. Et ideo cum de ejusmodi aliquid intelligimus, necesse habemus converti ad phantasmata corporum; licet ipsorum non sint phantasmata. Sed de hoc antea egimus. Porro hujus ordinis principia pro ratione intelligentium ut variant, ita cum eorum ipsorum ratione debeant æstimari, hic distincte nec considerari nec enumerari possunt. Superest principium primum directionis, quod & singulari ratione, velut Κεφαλαιον supremum omnis veritatis aliorumque principiorum, nomen meretur principij primo-primi. Estque hoc: Omne aut est, aut non est. quod ipsum axioma, ut valet ratione omnium inferiorum entium, quocunque etiam modo eadem apprehendantur, sic universaliter acceptum ratione τὸ εἶναι aut entis [quod pro diverso significatu, si, cum nihilo, aut non ente comparetur, medium habere recte statuitur] pariter non procedit. Interim est axioma non minus certum quam universalissimum: ut enim non contingit aliquem
units.tr: 23. When they professed themselves wise, they became fools. For they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of creeping things. Meanwhile this principle remains what it is: just as God is absolutely first, so God is is implied in every concept. For every concept is either of God, and so its reason stands on truth, or it is of a being other than God. Since such a being is either corporeal or incorporeal, both kinds depend on God in such a way that, by the very fact that it is thought to exist, God is conceived to exist along with it. For unless God existed, and unless that which is conceived had its being from God, it would neither exist nor be capable of being conceived in terms of its essence and existence. This is also true by the nature of the mind itself, which, when it reflects on itself and conceives itself, conceives God in itself as in something lower. It does not do so by turning to an idea of God existing within itself (we have already refuted this), but because it could not conceive itself as dependent unless the existence of God were included in that concept. This existence is not to be considered as residing in the mind as an idea, but in God himself. Thus Thomas rightly reasons about eternal truths, I. q. 16, art. 7, and I. q. 84, art. 5, following Augustine, De Trinitate, book 14, ch. 15, and De libero arbitrio, book 3, ch. 5. He holds that these truths are found only in God, so that the finite apprehension of those truths, or the intellectual apprehension of them in a human being, is called eternal insofar as the ideas correspond to the ideas in the divine mind. Nor does the desire by which the thinking human being strives for further perfection prove the real existence of the idea of God in the human mind. For a natural man, roused to desire by such an idea inhering in him, would, through the motion of that idea and his inner apprehension of it, strive toward its enjoyment. But this is contrary to Scripture, which holds that a man before his conversion to Christ is a stranger to God (Eph. 2.12). It is abundantly clear from the example of Adam, newly fallen and fleeing the face of God (Gen. 3.10), that the desire by which he is carried toward the enjoyment of God as more perfect does not arise from the presence of an idea of God in man. For with this idea set aside, the apprehension of reason and its functions has no more value here than the apprehension of any other thing. For as the mind apprehends itself as dependent, so any finite thing can be apprehended only as dependent. Nor does it matter that the mind perceives itself as incorporeal and free of quantity, for the reasoning The mind is incorporeal, therefore the idea of God is to be recognised in it does not hold. Even if the mind remains finite by that very fact, what is finite is thereby equated with the infinite Being, which was shown earlier to be utterly absurd. The first principle of particular apprehension must be judged by reference to the person who apprehends, insofar as what someone apprehends first, from which he proceeds further, may fittingly be regarded as a principle in relation to that person. Nor can the saying I think, therefore I am hold here with respect to all human beings, as we set out at length earlier. For just as not everyone can understand it, so the apprehension of anything thought, whether by truly understanding it or by doubting it, presupposes something existing beforehand, and insofar as it is grasped by the mind, it is grasped only as being of such and such a kind, namely either doubt about this matter or the intellective apprehension of this or that being. I indeed hear that this thought is by some transformed into the thinking mind itself, and that others believe the mind can know itself directly without the help of an image; but this is asserted without grounds. For although there are no proper phantastic species of God, of angels, or of our souls, the intellect, as long as it is bound by the chains of the body, cannot know those very beings except through comparison with sensible bodies, of which there are certain images. So Thomas rightly says, I. q. 84, a. 7. For (these are the words of the one who bears the name of Dionysius, On the Divine Names, book 1) we cannot know incorporeal substances in the present state of life except through negation or some comparison with corporeal things. And therefore, when we understand anything of this kind, we are necessarily led to turn to the images of bodies, although these are not images of them. But we have treated this before. Moreover, the principles of this order vary according to the capacity of those who understand, and so they must be judged together with the capacity of those very persons; they can be neither distinctly considered nor enumerated here. There remains the first principle of direction, which deserves the name of first-of-the-first principle, both by its unique character, as the supreme Κεφαλαιον [summit] of all truth and of other principles. It is this: Everything either is or is not. This axiom, which holds good with respect to all inferior beings, however those same beings are apprehended, does not hold in the same way when taken universally with respect to τὸ εἶναι [being] or to a being [it is rightly held that, in its different sense, when compared with nothing or with non-being, it has a middle].
